Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Since the transforming influence from Dàxià spread eastward.
Trust was established and the Way was opened; generations have varied between purity and corruption.
This is due to the confusion of the three firm resolves of emotion and the obscuration of the four illuminations of wisdom.
Hence, it has caused those of corrupt and shallow parties
to heedlessly promote evil trends,
while the pure and upright followers
have often encountered glib sophistry.
This is why the teachings shifted to Zhèndàn for over six hundred years,
and the despots' oppression in Zhèndàn led to three instances of severe suppression, with disaster quickly following.
Reflecting on past good deeds, the calamities have fallen upon them.
They became a laughingstock to all under heaven.
Moreover, faith is the mother of virtue, and wisdom is indeed the cause of sagehood, initiating the origin of the Way and culminating in the true fruit.
Based on this reasoning,
internally, the delusions of the eight haughtinesses are overcome;
examining this to seek the truth,
externally, the hindrances of the six dusts are swept away.
Serenely, beyond external appearances,
it is not the ascent of a minor path;
expansively, soaring high,
it is the gathering place of the highest benevolence.
However, as time has passed through three eras,
the evils of the five impurities have sunk deep.
Knowledge is obscured by right and wrong,
and the heavenly net of discerning people and Dharma is in disarray.
Therefore, the inner teachings are woven into a framework,
establishing laws and principles to guide beings.
The virtuous and enlightened among the outer populace
have laid down texts and treatises to widely promote models.
In the past, during the Liáng dynasty, on Zhōngshān, there was the monk Yòu (僧祐) Lǜshī of Dìnglín Sì.
His learning encompassed the nine schools of thought, and his understanding embraced the ten truths.
His feelings were deeply compassionate and salvific, and his aspiration was to uphold the Dharma.
He extensively summarized the prominent heroes of the various courts of Liáng and Jìn,
devoting his mind to Buddhist principles, composing and arranging essays.
He compiled one collection, the Hóngmíng Jí, in fourteen volumes.
He explored the styles of Yán (顏) and Xiè (謝),
and encompassed the school rules of Zhōu (周) and Zhāng (張).
His debates and general discussions
exhaustively sought the profound principles of reason,
and his thorough examination of nature and spirit
was truly the lofty attainment of a wise person.
Preserved in the imperial library, it widely revealed the minds of mortals.
However, the wise are not deluded; the deluded are not wise.
Therefore, the wise scholar speaks
by presenting the main idea and clarifying the gist,
while the deluded, seeking enlightenment,
are moved by elaborate words to open their divine minds.
As for the arrival of faith and understanding, it truly relies on divine function.
Harmony must be pure and refreshing, and affairs must follow a mysterious pattern.
Therefore, there are three types of faith:
one is 'knowing',
two is 'seeing',
and three is 'ignorance'.
Knowing refers to innate knowledge,
possessing the three firm resolves and entering the correct assembly.
Ignorance refers to the ignorant old man,
stuck in the four delusions and immersed in the dust of desire.
Transformation cannot shift the utterly ignorant and the supremely wise.
But the mediocre, who see and believe, follow goodness
as if it were a flowing stream.
This is why the Dharma has been submerged for three eras,
all due to the entanglement of limited learning.

Hence, those who follow their own minds and make arbitrary judgments have accumulated misfortune according to their plans. If they were to consult the eight treasuries of texts and summarize the clarity of their meanings, or to delve into the nine consciousnesses to reach the giải (解) of the confusion of emotion and wisdom, then true faith would be like the bright sun.
Even if obscured by the five defilements, it would still shine brighter.
I have extensively consulted previous accounts and broadly summarized Hóngmíng,
considering that in the five generations south of the Jiāng River, the Three Jewels flourished again.
The feelings of rulers, ministers, scholars, and common people were not different;
they upheld and praised the texts of the nation.
Wisdom opened through texts.
In the Central Plains, during the Zhōu and Wèi dynasties, governance alternated between darkness and light,
honoring the old and slighting the Buddha.
Faith and destruction alternated in trade.
This caused eloquent words to be spoken, and flatterers to be present.
The times were not lacking in worthy individuals,
who sincerely and exceptionally distinguished themselves, standing out from the crowd.
There were also such people.
Thus, light and darkness were mutually manifest, and good and evil taught each other.
Judging by appearances, they were as far apart as clouds and mud;
discussing their essence, they nurtured each other through reliance and concealment.
Therefore, the six arts flourished during the Buddha's era,
and Sān Zhāng (三張) encroached upon the Dharma stream.
These were all expedient means of great Bodhisattvas,
and the appropriate transformations of enlightened beings.
This is like Mǎnyuàn (滿願) practicing the evil views of the three poisons,
or Jìngmíng (淨名) subduing the demon kings of the six desires.
All opened different paths of encouragement and guidance,
each establishing grand strategies for turning towards or away.
Now, let's take their actions to resolve the stagnation of their followers,
likening it to guiding a clear spring to flow through the sea of nature.
As for the alliances formed by Kòu Qiānzhī (寇謙之) and Cuī Hào (崔浩),
their fortunes and misfortunes were evident.
Zhèng Ài (鄭藹) resisted Zhōu Jūn (周君),
and success and failure were instantaneous.
Yáo Ān (姚安) composed treatises,
depressing the Dao in the Confucian stream.
Chén Lín (陳琳) wrote essays,
elevating the釋 (Shì) above the court canons.
These criticisms and discussions are like being immersed in black ink without being stained.
Falling under various categories, they are somewhat difficult to integrate.
Moreover, the two Wǔ (武) of Liáng (梁) and Zhōu (周)
each exhibited ceremonies of manifestation and concealment.
The two Míng (明) of Sòng (宋) and Wèi (魏) both adopted strategies of grand inducement.
Shěn Xiūwén's (沈休文) compassionate salvation
and Yán Zhītuī's (顏之推) devotion
were distinguished in their literary style, soaring high above the ordinary.

I have tried to raise awareness of their shortcomings in my ordinary old age, gathering the scattered fragments. There was a monk, Jì Zàn (繼贊) of Hànyīn (漢陰), who had extensive knowledge; I, Gu (顧) only recorded what was written down.
I named this collection, presented in chapters and arranged like a mirror.
If one seeks out the threads and ponders their meaning, one will gain enlightenment.
Isolated passages and fragmentary notes are gathered and attached.
It is named Guǎng Hóngmíng Jí (廣弘明集).
One collection, thirty volumes.
That which was compiled during the Liáng dynasty,
or not yet thoroughly examined,
is briefly listed according to its categories and titles.
This is to allow those who have not yet seen it to gain understanding, widely spreading faith and resolving doubts, and to classify people accordingly.
It is certainly not a false attribution.
If there are any omissions,
the reader should examine them in detail.
Preface:
Indeed, the tangled controversies of truth and falsehood, and the vast differences between the wise and the ignorant, are profound.
Unless one is a supreme sage, how can one embrace both?
That is why even the lord of the *Mārā* (demon king), desirous of dominating, can transform into the appearance of a Buddha.
How much more can one speak of other physical forms?
Thus, it is understood that in one continent there are ten thousand nations, and in one transformation there are a thousand kings.
Their rise and fall, establishment and overthrow, are not worth discussing.
Therefore, the ninety-six heterodox schools
trace their origins to the celestial roots of the upper realm.
The twenty-five *tattvas* (principles)
investigate the profound essence of ultimate reckoning.
All of them set forth an orthodox calendar,
proclaiming the Three Jewels among men.
All claim great salvation,
spreading the four *samas* (equalities) throughout the world.
Furthermore, there is Kǒng Shì of Lǔ Bāng,
who guided ritual and music throughout the Nine Provinces.
There is Lǐ Gōng of Chǔ Guó,
who opened up the mysteries of the Five Sacred Mountains.
They did not claim to be religious founders;
they merely composed works based on the ancient kings.
They praised the current era and served the state,
each serving as officials in governmental affairs.
These all represent divergent paths and limited domains, their administration of discord is varied, and their principles are fundamentally different from heaven.
They are distinctly separate.
How can this be demonstrated?
Indeed, in the great western regions of *Xī Yǔ Dà Xià*,
the multitudes' reckoning is founded upon our deities.
In the eastern lands of *Dōng Huá*, Confucianism and Daoism
largely preserve the body and the state.
Who can untangle the deluded thoughts and clinging loves that entangle beings in the nine abodes?
Who can dispel the inverted emotions and persistent attachments
from the seven consciousnesses?
This leaves the mind covered by the net of delusion, unable to know where to turn.
The confused waves stir the eyes, making it impossible to discern where to return.
One must not imitate;
one must return to the root.
Originally, "minor path" and "great path" have been common topics since ancient times.
And "great sage" and "minor sage" have always been discussed together.
As for those who have personally received instruction face-to-face,
they have never truly awakened to knowledge.
They blindly follow the crowd, attaching themselves to others, competing with them.
Thus, some claim to become sages by controlling their thoughts, while others are called mad geniuses.
Yet, these discussions do not reach the ultimate point.
In the past, when the Awakened One (*Huáng Jué*) resided in *Shè Wèi*,
for twenty-five years,
the nine hundred million households were more than half rebellious or compliant.
When the Uncrowned King (*Sù Wáng*) was in *Chì Xiàn*,
his disciples numbered three thousand.
Zǐ Xià disparaged him and raised doubts,
while Yán Huí alone said he was unfathomable.
To discuss the Dao based on this
is also perplexing.
Indeed, by gathering the upright, one becomes a sage,
with nothing left unknown.
Roots and dust are unhindered in existence and emptiness;
temperament and cultivation are not constrained by nature and desire.
Form cannot be attained through external appearance;
he manifested the golden body with thirty-two marks.
The mind cannot be sought through intellect;
he revealed the eighteen unique characteristics.
This person alone is called a Buddha-sage.
Therefore, he can bring salvation to all beings,
the hidden and the manifest alike taking refuge in him.
All others are like mere wild geese,
who have not yet ascended the celestial path.
And indeed, their respective domains and positions are distinct, their righteousness not presumptuous.
If there are not two suns in the sky, nor two kings in a country,
then only the Buddha can be called the Great Sage,
whose light illuminates myriad worlds.
Therefore, today his monastic order flourishes daily,
and no country does not admire his teachings.
His doctrines and righteousness are continually refined,
and all sentient beings participate in his assembly.
Those Kǒng and Lǎo, their status is common, not different from ordinary people.
They merely transmitted the words of ancient kings and had no teachings of their own.
How can they be compared to the Buddha in contention?
Moreover, considering the brief principles of *yīn-yáng* and the eight destructive forces,
and the altars for venerating mountains and rivers,
the seven assemblies discard them as if they were nothing,
and the five precepts are abandoned without a second thought.
Looking at this path,
its lofty nature is sufficient to evoke sincere devotion.
What's more, there are holy lineage and worthy traces,
serving as teachers and models for humans and gods.
Thus, it is known that above and below the heavens, only the Buddha is honored.
The six realms and four modes of birth are nothing but suffering.
The body and mind are constantly in suffering, meaning they are driven and tormented.
Do not dwell on this thought and falsely maintain a lofty and grand view.
If it is truly great and capable of greatness, it will not fall into conditioned existence.
Since it treads the extraordinary, it can surely return to perfect enlightenment.
Such matters exist,
hence I venture to write this preface.
Tài Zǎi Pǐ asked Kǒng Zǐ,
"Is the Master a sage?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied,
"Qiu is learned and has a strong memory, but is not a sage."
He then asked,
"Are the Three Kings sages?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied,
"The Three Kings were good at using wisdom and courage.
Whether they were sages is not what Qiu knows."
He then asked, "Are the Five Emperors sages?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied,
"The Five Emperors were good at using benevolence and righteousness.
Whether they were sages is not what Qiu knows."
He then asked,
"Are the Three Sovereigns sages?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied,
"The Three Sovereigns were good at adapting to the times.
Whether they were sages is not what Qiu knows."
Tài Zǎi was greatly astonished and said,
"If so, who then is a sage?"
Kǒng Zǐ's expression changed for a moment and he said,
"Qiu has heard that in the West there is a sage
who governs without chaos,
speaks without needing to be believed,
and transforms without needing to act.
Vast and boundless, no one can name him."
Based on this, it can be said
that Kǒng Zǐ deeply knew the Buddha to be a Great Sage.
Because the time was not yet ripe, he kept silent and recognized it.
When the opportunity arose, he mentioned it,
but was not yet able to speak of its full implications.
Lǎo Zǐ's *Xī Shēng Jīng* says:
"My teacher traveled to *Tiān Zhú* (India) and skillfully entered *Ní Huán* (Nirvana)."
Fú Zǐ says:
"Lǎo Shì's teacher's name was Shì Jiā Wén (Śākyamuni)."
I have found that throughout antiquity, the Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, and imperial rulers rarely traveled east, but often went west.
Therefore, Xuān Yuán traveled to the land of *Huá Xū*.
Wáng Shào says,
"This is *Tiān Zhú*."
He also ascended to the ruins of *Kūn Lún*,
which is *Xiāng Shān*.
Lǎo Zǐ's traces disappeared in *Fú Fēng*,
and history records him in *Liú Shā*.
And all the Daoist records
say he ascended *Kūn Qiū* in the West and then went to heaven.
Examining these events,
they all relate to the Buddha's land.
Thus, Bó Yì described the country of *Shēn Dú* in *Shān Hǎi* (mountains and seas),
where people are intimate with and love one another.
Guō Pú, a scholar of ancient matters, said,
"*Shēn Dú* is *Tiān Dú* (India)."
Regarding the rise of *fú tú* (Buddhism),
I now hear it said that
the land of *Yīn Tǔ* has abundant and beautiful treasures.
The people are broadly benevolent and wise, and their customs highly value philosophy.
In establishing virtue and enriching life, how are they inferior to *Zhū Xià* (China)?
It has been called a country that loves people since ancient times,
and has produced worthy sages for generations.
How could this be a false construction?
The tradition says:
In the third year of Yǒng Píng of Emperor Míng,
the Emperor dreamt of a divine being,
with a golden body sixteen feet tall and a halo of light around his head.
Upon waking, he questioned his officials.
Fù Yì responded to the imperial decree,
saying, "There is a Buddha who appeared in *Tiān Zhú*."
So, he dispatched envoys to seek him,
and they successfully brought back scriptures, images, and two monks.
The Emperor then established a Buddhist temple for them and painted murals,
with thousands of carriages and ten thousand riders circling the pagoda three times.
He also depicted the standing Buddha images and the *Sì Shí Èr Zhāng Jīng* (Sutra of Forty-two Sections)
at the Qīng Liáng Tái in the Nán Gōng, and above the Gāo Yáng Mén and in Xiǎn Jié Líng.
These were sealed in the stone chamber of the Lán Tái,
as extensively shown in Mú Zǐ's previous collection.
The tradition says:
At that time, there were two *shāmén*, Jiā Shè Mó Téng and Zhú Fǎ Lán,
whose conduct and cultivation were unfathomable.
Their aspiration was to enlighten and transform.
Cài Yīn, the envoy, reached them and invited Téng to travel east.
He did not adhere to regional boundaries and followed him to Luò Yáng.
He enlightened people's minds and glorified the true source of faith.
The Emperor asked Téng,
"Buddhist teachings have appeared in the world; why have they not reached here for transformation?"
He replied,
"The country of *Jiā Pí Luó Wèi*
is the center of the three-thousand great-thousand worlds, with hundreds of millions of suns and moons.
All Buddhas of the three times are born there.
Even *devas*, dragons, ghosts, and spirits who have vows and practices are born there.
They receive the Buddha's righteous transformation and all attain enlightenment.
Beings in other places have no connection to evoke the Buddha,
so the Buddha does not go there.
Although the Buddha does not go,
his light reaches those places.
Sometimes after five hundred years,
sometimes after a thousand years,
and sometimes beyond a thousand years,
there are always sages who transmit the Buddha's teachings and guide them."
The detailed explanation of the teachings is extensive, hence it is abbreviated here.
The biography states:
On the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
Daoist priests from the Five Sacred Mountains and other mountains,
during their New Year's audience,
said to each other,
"The Son of Heaven has abandoned our Daoist teachings
and is seeking foreign teachings from the Hu people.
Now, taking advantage of this assembly, we can present a memorial to protest this."
The memorial roughly stated:
“Your humble servants, Chǔ Shànxìn and others, disciples of the Tàishàng Sāndòng from the Five Sacred Mountains and eighteen other mountains,
a total of six hundred and ninety people, facing death, respectfully submit:
We have heard that the Tàishàng is without form or name,
without limit, without superior, empty, and natural.
The Great Dao emerged before creation,
was revered in antiquity, and remains unchanged through a hundred kings.
Now, Your Majesty’s Dao surpasses Yìhuáng, and your virtue is higher than Yáo and Shùn.
We secretly hear that Your Majesty has abandoned the root to pursue the branches, seeking teachings from the Western Regions.
What is worshipped is merely a Hu deity,
and what is taught does not align with Huáxià.
We humbly request Your Majesty to pardon our sins
and allow us to conduct a trial.
We, the Daoist priests from various mountains,
many of us possess clairvoyance, clairaudience, and extensive knowledge of the classics.
From Yuánhuáng onwards,
the Tàishàng’s various records and the Tàixū’s talismans and incantations
have all been thoroughly practiced and mastered to their utmost limits.
Some command ghosts and spirits,
some swallow clouds and drink qi,
some enter fire without being burned,
some walk on water without drowning,
some ascend to heaven in broad daylight,
some become invisible and unpredictable.
As for magical arts, there is nothing we cannot do.
We wish to compete and compare our abilities.
Firstly, this would ease the Holy Emperor’s mind;
secondly, it would allow for the discernment of truth from falsehood;
thirdly, the Great Dao would find its proper place;
fourthly, it would prevent confusion among the Huá customs.
If we are inferior in this comparison, we will willingly accept your severe judgment.
If we are superior, we beg you to eliminate what is false.”
An imperial edict ordered Shàngshūlìng Sòng Xiáng to usher them into the Chánglè Palace.
It was declared that they should gather at Báimǎ Temple on the fifteenth day of this month.
The Daoist priests then set up three altars.
Each altar had twenty-four gates.
Chǔ Shànxìn, a Daoist priest from Nányuè;
Liú Zhèngniàn, a Daoist priest from Huàyuè;
Huán Wéndù, a Daoist priest from Héngyuè;
Jiāo Déxīn, a Daoist priest from Dàiyuè;
Lǚ Huìtōng, a Daoist priest from Sōngyuè;
Qí Wénxìn and others, Daoist priests from Huòshān, Tiānmù, Wǔtái, Báilù, and eighteen other mountains,
each brought 509 scrolls of Lǐngbǎo Zhēnwén, Tàishàng Yùjué, Sānyuán Fúlù, etc.
These were placed on the western altar. 235 scrolls of philosophical texts by twenty-seven masters, including Máochéngzǐ, Xǔchéngzǐ, Huángzǐ, Lǎozǐ, etc.,
were placed on the central altar.
Food offerings and sacrifices to a hundred deities were placed on the eastern altar.
The Emperor’s temporary palace was at the south gate of the temple.
Buddhist relics, scriptures, and images were placed to the west of the Daoist altars.
On the fifteenth day, after the vegetarian meal,
the Daoist priests, with torches made of kindling, sandalwood, and agarwood,
circled the scriptures and wept, saying,
"We respectfully appeal to the Tàijí Dàdào, Yuánshǐ Tiānzūn, and all the immortal beings and a hundred spirits.
Now, a Hu deity is disturbing Huáxià, and the ruler believes in evil.
The true teaching has vanished, and the profound tradition is broken.
We dare to place the scriptures on the altar and test them with fire,
wishing to enlighten the deluded and discern truth from falsehood."
Then, they set fire to the scriptures.
The scriptures were consumed by the flames and turned into ashes.
The Daoist priests looked at each other, their faces drained of color, greatly frightened.
Those who intended to ascend to heaven or become invisible
were powerless to do so.
Those who commanded and summoned ghosts and spirits
received no response, and each felt deep shame.
Fèi Shūcái, a Daoist priest from Nányuè, died of remorse.
Tàifù Zhāng Yǎn said to Chǔ Xìn,
"Your tests have shown no results; therefore, they are false.
You should convert to the true Dharma from the West."
Chǔ Xìn said,
"Máochéngzǐ said,
'The Tàishàng is Lǐngbǎo Tiānzūn.'
The act of creation is called Tàisù.
How can this be false?"
Zhāng Yǎn replied,
"Tàisù has the name of 'noble virtue,'
but not the attribute of 'spoken teaching.'
Now you say it has spoken teaching,
which makes it false."
Chǔ Xìn fell silent.
At that time, the Buddhist relics emitted five-colored light,
which soared into the sky, swirling like a canopy,
covering the multitude and overshadowing the sunlight.
Fǎshī Mó téng leaped high and flew,
sitting and lying in the air, manifesting great divine transformations.
At that moment, heavenly flowers rained down upon the Buddha and the monks.
Heavenly music was also heard, moving people's hearts.
The multitude was all delighted and exclaimed that they had never witnessed such a thing.
They all gathered around Fǎlán to listen to his exposition of the Dharma essentials,
and also chanted Sanskrit sounds praising the Buddha's merits.
He also led the multitude to praise the Three Jewels,
explaining that good and evil karma all have their retributions,
and that the six realms and three vehicles manifest in various forms.
He also spoke of the highest merit of renouncing the world.
Establishing the first Buddhist temple is equivalent to the boundless blessings of Brahmā.
Sīkōng, Yángchénghóu Liú Jùn,
along with over a thousand officials, scholars, and common people, renounced the world.
Lǚ Huìtōng and others, Daoist priests from the Four Sacred Mountains and various other mountains,
a total of six hundred and twenty people, renounced the world.
Yīn Fūrén, Wáng Jiéyú, etc.,
along with two hundred and thirty palace women and other women, renounced the world.
Then, ten monasteries were established:
seven outside the city to accommodate monks
and three inside the city to accommodate nuns.
From this time onwards, Buddhism flourished widely.
The biography has five scrolls,
but this is a brief account and not a complete record.
Some people suspect this biography is recent
and that there was no such contest.
However, the Wú Shū
clearly records Fèi Shūcái's death from remorse,
thus confirming the biography as a true record.
The treatise states:
"Buddha," in Hàn, means "awakening."
It is intended to awaken all sentient beings.
Its teachings primarily emphasize cultivating good and compassionate hearts.
Not killing living beings, solely pursuing purity, and diligently progressing are what define a Shāmén.
In Hàn, this means quieting the mind, shaving the head, leaving home, severing passions, and cleansing desires,
thereby returning to non-action.
It also holds that when a person dies, their spirit is not extinguished
but reincarnates again.
The good and evil deeds performed
will all result in retribution in future lives.
The most important thing is to do good to refine one's spirit.
If this refinement is continuous,
it will lead to non-birth
and enable one to become a Buddha.
A Buddha is sixteen feet tall,
golden in color, with the light of the sun and moon around their neck.
They transform constantly
and can enter anywhere.
Therefore, they can transform and pervade all things, greatly saving all sentient beings.
There are thousands of scrolls of scriptures,
which take emptiness as their core principle.
They encompass the subtle and the coarse, leaving nothing unturned.
They excel at grand and profound discourse.
What they seek is within the body;
what they illuminate is beyond sight and hearing.
They return to the mysterious and subtle, profound and distant, difficult to fathom.
Therefore, when kings, dukes, and great men
contemplate the cycle of birth, death, and retribution,
they cannot but feel awestruck and lost.
The Wèi Shū states:
“The Buddhist scriptures generally say that all forms of life
arise from karma.
There are past, present, and future three existences.
The stages and levels of cultivating the Dao are not singular,
but all proceed from the shallow to the deep,
relying on the subtle to manifest the obvious.
This primarily involves accumulating benevolence and compliance, eliminating desires,
and practicing emptiness and tranquility to achieve comprehensive enlightenment.”
And so on.
In the fourth year of Chìwū of Sūn Quán.
There was a chief minister's eldest son from Kāngjū kingdom.
He abandoned worldly life and became a śramaṇa.
His name was Sēnghuì.
His surname was Kāng.
He had a dignified and upright bearing, taking the propagation of the Dharma as his duty.
At that time, the Three Kingdoms stood in a tripartite division,
each wielding their power.
Buddhist Dharma had long been spread in the Central Plains,
but had not yet reached the lands south of the Jiāng.
Sēnghuì desired to spread the Way to the unheard,
and to make the teachings flourish in the southern country.
He first arrived in Jiànyè, established a thatched hut,
set up images, and practiced the Way.
The people of Wú, seeing him for the first time, considered him strange and marvelous.
An official reported this to the emperor.
The Lord of Wú said,
"What spiritual efficacy does Buddhism have?"
Sēnghuì replied,
"Buddha concealed his spiritual traces over a thousand years ago,
but his relics, the śarīra, manifest themselves in countless ways."
The Lord of Wú said,
"If we obtain śarīra, I will erect a pagoda for them."
After twenty-one days, śarīra were indeed obtained.
They shone with five colors, illuminating the sky.
When cut, they became even harder.
When burned, they did not combust.
Light emerged from the fire,
forming a great lotus flower.
It illuminated the palace and amazed the ministers and the lord, who exclaimed at this rare auspicious sign.
Their faith greatly blossomed.
A pagoda was built for them.
People were converted and temples were established.
The place where Sēnghuì resided was named Fótuólǐ.
Furthermore, as the teaching and Dharma first flourished there,
it was named Jiànchū Sì.
An imperial edict was issued, asking Shàngshū Lìng Kān Zé,
"How many years have passed since the time of Emperor Míng of Hàn?
Buddhism entered Hàn long ago,
but why has it only now reached Jiāngdōng?"
Kān Zé replied,
"From the tenth year of Yǒngpíng of Emperor Míng of Hàn, when Buddhist Dharma first arrived, until now, the fourth year of Chìwū,
is one hundred and seventy years.
Initially, in the fourteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
at the time when the Daoists of the Five Sacred Mountains competed with Móténg,
the Daoists were defeated.
The Nányuè Daoists, Chǔ Shànxìn, Fèi Shúcái, and others,
died of self-reproach at the assembly.
Their disciples buried them at Nányuè.
They did not engage in monastic life, so there was no one to propagate it.
Later, due to the decline of Hàn politics and continuous warfare,
many years passed, and only now has it begun to flourish."
The Lord of Wú also asked,
"Can Kǒng Qiū and Lǐ Lǎo be compared with Buddha?"
Kān Zé replied,
"Your servant has heard that Kǒng Jūn of Lǔ was a brilliant and outstanding talent, whose sagely virtue was unparalleled.
He was known as the 'uncrowned king' in his time.
He compiled classics,
promoted and rewarded the Way of Zhōu,
and educated future generations.
The influence of his scholarly teachings has enriched the past and present.
There were also reclusive scholars like Xǔ Chéngzǐ, Yuányángzǐ, Zhuāngzǐ, Lǎozǐ, and the hundred schools of masters' writings.
They all cultivated themselves and indulged in their own pleasures,
roaming freely in mountains and valleys, letting their hearts run wild.
Their learning inclined towards tranquility and detachment, diverging from human relationships.
The etiquette between elders and juniors was also not conducive to pacifying the populace and transforming the people.
It was not until Emperor Jǐng of Hàn, considering the principles of Huángzǐ and Lǎozǐ to be particularly profound,
changed 'masters' to 'classics' and first established Daoist studies.
He decreed that the court and commoners alike should recite them.
If one were to compare the two teachings of Kǒng and Lǎo with Buddhist Dharma,
they are far, far apart.
The reason for this is,
the two teachings of Kǒng and Lǎo
emulate Heaven and regulate human conduct,
not daring to transgress Heaven.
All Buddhas establish their teachings,
and Heaven's laws are observed and carried out, not daring to transgress the Buddhas.
Judging by this,
they are truly not comparable." The Lord of Wú was greatly pleased.
He appointed Kān Zé as Tàizǐ Tàifù.
Etc., etc.
Emperor Wén,
was the third son of Sòng Gāozǔ.
He was intelligent, learned, and widely acclaimed as enlightened and accomplished.
He reigned for thirty years.
One leisure day, he casually consulted Shìzhōng Hé Shàngzhī and Lìbù Yáng Xuánbǎo, saying,
"I have not read many Buddhist scriptures since my youth.
Recently, I have been even busier.
I have not yet fully comprehended the concept of cause and effect across three existences, nor have I settled my mind on it.
However, I dare not take a differing stance,
precisely because you, my worthy and distinguished officials, collectively respect and believe in it.
Máng Tài and Xiè Língyùn often said,
'The texts of the Six Classics are fundamentally for managing society and governing the state.
If one seeks the true profundity of the spirit and nature,
how can one not take Buddhist principles as a guide?'
Recently, I saw Yán Yánzhī's refutation of the 'Dáxìng Lùn' [Treatise on the Comprehension of Nature]
and Zōng Bǐng's rebuttal of the 'Báihēi Lùn' [Treatise on White and Black].
They illuminate Buddhist Dharma, which is vast and profound.
They are particularly renowned for their logical reasoning.
Both are sufficient to enlighten people's minds.
If all within the realm [of the empire] could earnestly uphold these teachings,
then I would achieve great peace effortlessly.
What more would there be to do?"
Hé Shàngzhī replied,
"Many of the common folk do not believe in the Dharma.
For your servant, despite his mediocrity, to receive such praise and encouragement,
is not something he dares to accept.
As for the illustrious figures of previous generations,
they would not fail to uphold your clear pronouncements.
The central court is long past,
and it is difficult to know all of them.
Since crossing the Jiāng,

there have been Wáng Dǎo, Zhōu Yǐ, Yǔ Liàng, Wáng Méng, Xiè Shàng, Xī Chāo, Wáng Tǎn, Wáng Gōng, Wáng Mì, Guō Wénjǔ, Xiè Fū, Dài Kuí, Xǔ Xún, as well as your deceased ancestor's brothers, and Wáng Yuánlín's brothers, Fàn Wāng, Sūn Chuò, Zhāng Xuán, Yīn Jì, and others.
Some were leading officials and dignitaries,
others were exemplary figures among humanity.
Some dedicated their feelings to the realm between heaven and humanity,
others elevated their conduct beyond the mists and clouds.
All were committed to seeking refuge and devoted their hearts to reverence and belief.
Among them, when compared,
Lán Hù, Kāi, and Qián were deeply reclusive and highly esteemed.
All of them followed the path of the 'Yellow Middle' (Daoist principles),

Master Huìyuǎn once said,
'The transformation of Śākya [Buddha] is applicable everywhere. It is naturally the source of teaching for the Way,
and also an essential task for benefiting society.'
I secretly find this saying to be in accord with crucial principles.
If every family upholds the precepts,

What Your Majesty called 'achieving great peace effortlessly'

Yáng Xuánbǎo stepped forward and said,
"This discussion pertains to the realm between heaven and humanity;

Perhaps there is nothing to be gained from this."
The Emperor said,
"This is not a tool for the Warring States period.
It is indeed as you say."
Hé Shàngzhī replied,
"If recluses are honored, warriors become lax.
If benevolence and virtue are valued, military spirit declines.
If one's ambition is like Sūn and Wú,

The Emperor said,

As the saying goes, 'bad words do not enter one's ears'."
From then on, Emperor Wén paid attention to Buddhist scriptures.

At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Zhú Dàoshēng,

He once described Zhú Dàoshēng's theory of sudden enlightenment.
The monks all raised great objections.

At that time, Yán Yánzhī wrote the 'Líshì Lùn' [Treatise on Departing from Consciousness].

In the first year of Zhèngguāng.

On the fourteenth day of the ninth month, at the hour of Zǐ (midnight).

at the age of eighty-five, seeing the decline of Zhōu's virtue,
he went west with Yǐn Xǐ, the magistrate of Sànguān, to convert the Hu.
This is sufficiently clear."
Zùi replied,
"The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhāo of Zhōu.
He entered Nirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mù.
Calculating from his entry into Nirvāṇa, three hundred forty-five years passed
before the third year of King Dìng arrived.
Lǎozǐ was only then born.
After his birth, eighty-five years passed,
reaching the first year of King Jìng.
A total of four hundred twenty-five years elapsed
before he first absconded west with Yǐn Xǐ.
Based on these dates, there is a vast discrepancy in years.
Is this not erroneous?"
Bīn replied,
"If the Buddha was born during the time of King Zhāo of Zhōu,
what historical records confirm this?"
Zùi replied,
"The Zhōushū Yìjì and the Hàn Fǎběn Nèichuán

Bīn replied,
"Since Kǒngzǐ was a sage who established laws,

Zùi replied,
"Your view is like looking through a pipe; you do not have a broad and far-reaching perspective.
According to Kǒngzǐ's Sānbèi Bǔjīng,
which deals with Heaven, Earth, and Man,
the Buddha's teachings appear in the section on Man.
If you had studied it earlier, you would not be so confused."
Bīn replied,
"Kǒngzǐ was a sage;
he knew without speaking.
Why would he need divination?"
Zùi replied,
"Only the Buddha is the King of all Sages,
the foremost of the four types of beings.
He comprehends the auspicious and inauspicious outcomes, and the beginnings and endings, of all sentient beings in the past and future,
without needing divination.
Other lesser sages,
though they may understand the principles of what has not yet happened,
must rely on milfoil and tortoise shells to connect with spiritual hexagrams."
Shìzhōng Shàngshūlìng Yuán Yì then proclaimed an imperial edict, saying,
"Daoist Jiāng Bīn's arguments lack basis.
He should be removed from his seat."
He also asked,
"Where did the Kāitiānjīng come from?
Who wrote it?"
