and believed in barbarian demons and ghosts to disrupt the constant norms of Heaven.
Since ancient times, the Jiǔzhōu [Nine Provinces] have never seen such a thing.
Exaggerated and grand words that are not based on human nature;
in the declining ages,
ignorant rulers and chaotic lords were all deluded by them.
As a result, government and education ceased to function,
rites and righteousness were greatly corrupted,
and the Way of ghosts flourished,
treating the laws of the king as nothing.
Since then, successive generations have suffered calamities and chaos, with extreme divine retribution causing the death of the populace.
Within the five服 [zones of royal domain], all turned into ruins.
For a thousand *lǐ*, it was desolate, with no human traces.
All this is due to it.
I, who have inherited the heavenly lineage,
am faced with the ills of this failing age.
I wish to eliminate falsehood and establish truth,
restoring the governance of Xī and Nóng, and completely eradicating barbarian gods and destroying their traces.
May I thus not be ashamed before the Fēng [i.e., Fúxī] clan.
From now on, anyone who dares to serve barbarian gods
or create their images, whether clay figures or bronze figures, will have their household exterminated.

Even if one speaks of barbarian gods and asks current barbarians if they exist or not, these are all fabrications by unscrupulous Han descendants from previous generations, such as Liú Yuánzhēn and Lǚ Bóqiáng, who adopted the fantastic tales of barbarian beggars
and employed the emptiness and falsity of Lǎo-Zhuāng,
adding to them.
None of it is true.
This has led to the royal law being discarded and not practiced.
They are truly the ringleaders of great treachery.
There are extraordinary people in the world
who can perform extraordinary deeds.
Who but I can remove these false objects of past generations?"
The officials were ordered to proclaim:
"In all places, all Buddhist temples, images, and barbarian sūtras are to be shattered and burned.
All śramaṇa, regardless of age, are to be buried alive."
This was in the third month of the seventh year of Zhēnjūn.
Although Gōngzōng's words were not heeded,
he still delayed the promulgation of the edict,
allowing people far and near to know in advance and make their arrangements.
Many śramaṇa in the capital and the four directions fled and escaped.
Their gold, silver, precious images, sūtras, and treatises
were largely hidden and preserved.
However, the wooden and earthen monasteries and stūpas, wherever the teachings had spread,
were all completely destroyed.
The compilers of this record state:
The emperor was originally from a land of warhorses,
and had always been unacquainted with literary pursuits.
Having joined military affairs, wherever he went, he brought extermination.
He focused solely on governance, without engaging in other discussions.
Therefore, he killed the historiographers, being ashamed to have his faults recorded.
Under the secret instigation of Cuī Hào's treacherous eloquence,
he proceeded with the extermination.
At the time, this was considered a great pleasure for that generation.
Soon, however, calamity struck,
and there was no way to repent.
He regarded Cuī Hào as an enemy,
and his cruel and severe punishments became a laughingstock throughout the realm.
Initially, Cuī Hào and Kòu Qiānzhī were fellow adherents.
Kòu Qiānzhī bitterly argued with Cuī Hào, but Cuī Hào would not listen.
Kòu Qiānzhī said:
"You will now shorten your lifespan and destroy your household."
By the eleventh year of Zhēnjūn,
Cuī Hào was executed, suffering the five punishments.
He was seventy years old at the time.
The emperor somewhat regretted it,
but the deed had already been done, making restoration difficult.
Gōngzōng secretly wished to revive it,
but dared not speak of it.
At that time, the laws became lax.
Believing families secretly served śramaṇa,
and those who secretly wore monastic robes and lectured were numerous.
In the second month of the thirteenth year, he died of an illness.
His son Huǎng died due to slander,
and his grandson was enthroned.
A separate biography records:
Cuī Hào slandered and disparaged the Buddha-dharma,
revering the Celestial Master Kòu Qiānzhī,
and learning the Way of Immortals.
His wife, Lady Guō, devoutly believed in Buddhist scriptures
and recited the *Jīngāng Bōrè* [Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra].
Cuī Hào took it and burned it,
tossing the ashes into the latrine.
When he was imprisoned in a caged cart and sent to the south of the city,
ten guards were ordered to urinate on him from above.
His cries of agony were heard by passersby.
Cuī Hào said:
"This is the immediate retribution for my throwing away the sūtras."
Initially, Cuī Hào was able to indulge his treachery,
exterminating the Buddhist community.
He added grave accusations and slander, and an imperial edict was issued,
declaring it the chief of demons and ghosts.
The emperor had not entrusted it (to others).
It could be said that he was an extraordinary person
who could perform extraordinary deeds.
This is indeed true.
After Cuī Hào's household was executed,
the Cuī clan of Qīnghé, near and far,
as well as the Lú clan of Fànyáng,
the Guō clan of Tàiyuán, and the Liǔ clan of Hédōng,
all being Cuī Hào's relatives,
had their clans completely exterminated.
The *Shī* [Odes] says:
"Slanderers are boundless,
creating chaos in the four states."
This is proven true.
The compilers of this record state:
Among the executions of the three dukes since ancient times,
this was the most cruel.

Was it not that he hated their deception, treachery, and the abusive poisoning of benevolent temples, which brought calamity upon himself, leaving him no escape from public execution for his slanderous conspiracy, secretly regretting his former path?
To restrain oneself and return to ritual propriety is indeed difficult to emulate.
He did not blame himself for his ignorance and delusion,
but instead inflicted cruelty and blamed others.
In the end, he did not pass away peacefully,
and ultimately met the fate of one who bites his own navel (i.e., too late for regret).
In ancient times, Lóng Fēng encountered Xià Jié,
Bǐ Gàn was disemboweled by Yīn Xīn.
The *páoluò* [bronze pillar punishment] was established as a severe penalty,
and the wine pool was made to please concubines.
How could the people of that time consider this righteous governance?
They indulged in and embellished errors, praised and promoted good deeds.
But later, (Jié) was exiled to Náncháo, and (Xīn's) head was hung on a white banner.
There was no one to take their place; they themselves bore the consequences.
Their states were abolished, their lives lost, with nothing to retrieve.
Calamity followed close behind, bringing sorrow upon themselves.
Following this,
generation after generation, such was the case with the Way of abdication.
Wèi Wén opened its true record,
scrutinizing it against all antiquity.
Even Yáo and Shùn might have found it wanting.
Therefore, the Buddhist sūtras say:
"Even the two instruments (Heaven and Earth) perish,
what permanence can a state have?"
These are profound words.
If Shìzǔ had been able to reflect and ask himself why his original subservience to the dark capital, where rites and righteousness were not practiced, and benevolence and relief
had always been unknown—
how did he, by what karma, suddenly possess the Central Plains?
How could he indulge in such confusion and cruelty,
and practice such arrogance and tyranny?
These actions were unacceptable.
By this standard, if he had exerted himself and repented, would it have been impossible?
At that time, there was a Śramaṇa named Xuángāo.
He was an outstanding figure among the Buddhists.
He possessed spiritual powers and influenced the masses.
When the Way flourished in Héxī and Liángpíng,
he returned east, and Emperor Tàiwǔ respected him.
He became the teacher of Crown Prince Huǎng.
Huǎng was naturally filial and revered the Buddha Dharma.
Cuī Hào and Kòu Qiān, having gained favor with the emperor,
feared that if Huǎng assumed regency, they might be endangered or exiled.
They secretly slandered him to the emperor, saying that he harbored disloyal intentions, and asked if this should not be considered in advance.
The emperor believed them.
So he imprisoned the Crown Prince in a deep palace.
The emperor dreamed that his ancestors, holding swords, angrily said,
"The Crown Prince is benevolent, filial, loyal, and truly outstanding.
How can you believe slander?"
The emperor awoke and gathered his court officials to relate the dream.
The powerful nobles said,
"The Crown Prince has done nothing wrong.
He is unjustly imprisoned and humiliated."
The emperor again believed them.
In the first month of the fifth year of Zhēnjūn,
he issued an edict saying:
"I have inherited the glorious legacy of my ancestors,
desiring to expand their great enterprise and make it flourish for ten thousand generations.
Although military achievements are manifest, literary education has not yet spread.
This is not how to uphold the rule of great peace.
Now, the realm is peaceful and prosperous, and the common people are rich and flourishing.
It is fitting to establish a system to serve as the law for ten thousand generations.
For Yin and Yang have cycles of return,
and the four seasons have their succession.
Entrusting the son with responsibility and appointing the worthy ensures safety and mutual support.
This is how to rest the weary and secure lasting stability.
This is an enduring decree from ancient times to the present.
Let the Crown Prince succeed in managing all affairs of state and overseeing all policies.
Let worthy and capable individuals be further promoted to fill various offices.
Select and appoint people, and then dismiss or promote them accordingly.
All court officials and common people
shall profess allegiance to the Crown Prince."
And so on.
Cuī Hào again slandered, saying,
"The Crown Prince truly harbored rebellious intentions before.
But he associated with Grand Master Gāo's Way,
which is why the former emperor descended in a dream.
Such matters involving public opinion and events are difficult to discern.
If he is not removed soon, he will surely become a great menace."
The emperor again accepted this.
He then imprisoned the Crown Prince, who died.
He also arrested Xuángāo in Píngchéng and hanged him in the south.
This was in the twenty-first year of Yuánjiā of the Sòng dynasty.
That night, his disciples did not know of his death.
Suddenly, a bright light encircled the pagoda and entered the room.
A voice said,
"I have already passed away."
The disciples rushed to the place of the corpse.
They asked for his final instructions.
Xuángāo sat up with a start and said,
"The Great Dharma adapts to change, flourishing and declining with circumstances.
Flourishing and declining are but appearances; the principle itself remains eternally pure.
But remember, you too will soon be like me.
After your deaths, the Dharma will flourish again.
Cultivate your minds well, lest you have regrets."
After speaking, he lay down and expired.
Cuī Hào's slanderous words were so profound
that they could make a father suspect his son,
even to the point of death in confinement.
How much more so for Śramaṇas?
Emperor Tàiwǔ died on the fifth day of the second month of the thirteenth year of Zhēnjūn.
The Crown Prince had already died in confinement.
The King of Wú ascended the throne on the ninth day.
He changed the era name to Yǒngpíng.
On the first day of the tenth month, the King of Wú also died.
The emperor's grandson, Jùn, ascended the throne.
He changed the era name to Xīng'ān.
This was Emperor Wénchéng.
His temple name was Gāozōng.
Yet, the Buddhist teachings are vast and bright, spreading across the four seas.
In all the myriad nations of this continent, there is no king who does not revere them.
Although they were suppressed in northern Wèi, they flourished even more in Southern Sòng.
To call Emperor Tàiwǔ a "Zhēnjūn" (True Ruler) or "Míngzhǔ" (Enlightened Lord)
is it not a delusion?
To suspect one's son and trust villainous ministers,
who would not lament this?
To incur a plague and bring disaster upon oneself,
is this not exceedingly cruel?
The people longed for a return to righteous governance.
There were many who survived.
In the first year of Xīng'ān, Gāozōng ascended the throne.
He issued an edict saying:
"Indeed, an emperor must devoutly serve the enlightened spirits and conspicuously manifest benevolence.
Those who have bestowed kindness upon the people and benefited the multitude,
even if they lived in ancient times, their noble deeds are still recounted.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals praise the rites of honoring the enlightened,
and the sacrificial canons record the clans who rendered meritorious service.
How much more so for the teachings of the Buddha (Rúlái), whose merits benefit the great cosmos and whose kindness flows through the dusty realms!
Those who contemplate life and death sigh at its profound insight.
Those who examine its texts and meanings value its subtle gate.
It aids the kingly governance with its prohibitions,
and enhances the good nature of benevolence and wisdom.
It dispels all evil,
and expounds perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, since ancient times, none have failed to revere it.
It is also what our nation has always respected.
Emperor Shìzǔ Tàiwǔ expanded the frontiers, and his virtuous benevolence spread far and wide.
Śramaṇas and Daoist priests of pure and sincere conduct,
such as Huìshǐ and his ilk, reached everywhere.
Inspired by their virtues, they gathered like a forest.
Indeed, in the depths of mountains and seas, there are many strange creatures.
Likewise, among those given to promiscuity and deceit, there are some who gain acceptance by false pretenses.
Among the various monasteries, there have been vicious factions.
Therefore, the former court, taking advantage of their flaws and transgressions, executed the guilty ones.
However, the officials missed the point and banned everything indiscriminately.
Emperor Jǐngmù always regretted this profoundly.
But due to numerous military and state affairs,
he did not have time to restore it.
I have inherited the great legacy and rule over myriad nations.
I wish to fulfill the former emperor's aspiration to promote this Way.
Now, I decree that in all prefectures, cities, and counties,
in places where people gather,
each may construct one Buddha shrine.
Their financial resources are not limited by any fixed amount.
As for those who are fond of the Dharma and wish to become Śramaṇas,
regardless of age,
if they come from good families, are naturally sincere in conduct,
and are well-regarded by their communities, they may become monks.
The quota shall be fifty people for large prefectures
and thirty for small prefectures.
This is sufficient to transform evil into good and spread the teachings of the Way."
Thereupon, the whole empire was influenced, and within a short time, the pagodas and monasteries that had been destroyed
were all restored.
Buddha statues and scriptures were all brought forth.
At that time, there was a Śramaṇa from the royal family of Jìbīn, named Shī Xián,
who traveled east to Liángchéng.
He also traveled to the capital.
He happened to be there when Buddhism was suppressed.
He temporarily assumed the guise of a physician but maintained his spiritual practice unchanged.
On the day of restoration, he immediately became a Śramaṇa.
There were five others like him.
The emperor personally shaved their heads.
Xián was appointed the Sēngtǒng (Chief Monk).
And so on.
In the first year of Xīngguāng, an imperial edict instructed the officials
to cast five statues of Śākyamuni for the five emperors from Tàizǔ downwards,
at the Wǔjí Great Monastery.
Each statue was sixteen feet tall,
using 250,000 catties of red copper.
The Śramaṇa Tányào was honored by the emperor as his teacher.
He requested the emperor to open five caves in the stone cliffs of the Xīshān mountains in Wǔzhōu, west of the capital,
and engrave one Buddha statue in each.
The tallest was seventy feet,
the next sixty feet.
Their carvings were wonderfully grand, excelling all generations.
Those who see them today recount that
the valley is thirty *lǐ* deep.
To the east is a Buddhist monastery
named Língyán.
To the west end is a nunnery.
Each has stone grottoes carved,
capable of holding a thousand people.
The returning ones follow one after another, as close as the teeth of a comb.
The central seven *lǐ* of the stone cliff are extremely high and steep.
Buddha grottoes are connected in other places.
At times, there are interruptions and continuations.
Who can estimate the number of Buddha statues?
There was a Daoist,
eighty years old,
whose work was to prostrate before the statues.
He would bow once for each statue, until he reached the central grotto and died.
His body lay stiff on the ground.
It was sealed with stone.
It is still there today.
No one knows the era.
It is located three hundred *lǐ* east of Shuòzhōu, and twenty *lǐ* west of Hèng'ān Zhèn.
Those who come and go often speak of it.
It is truly a blessing beyond imagination.
In the first year of Huángxīng, Emperor Gāozǔ Xiàowén was born.
At the North Terrace of Hèng'ān, he erected the Yǒngníng Temple, a seven-story pagoda.
It was over three hundred feet tall.
Its foundation and framework were vast and sprawling,
making it the foremost in the world.
Also, at the Tiāngōng Temple,
he commissioned a statue of Śākyamuni,
forty-three feet tall,
using 100,000 catties of red copper and 600 catties of gold.
He also constructed a three-story stone Buddha pagoda, ten *zhàng* high.
Its rafters, ridges, beams, and pillars were compactly joined, top and bottom.
All parts, large and small, were of stone.
Its solidity, ingenuity, and precision made it a magnificent sight in the capital.
In the first year of Yánxīng, Xiǎnzǔ Xiànwén abdicated in favor of Crown Prince Sēnggài, also named Hóng,
who was Xiàowén.
He was five years old, intelligent and sagacious, with profound insights.
After first ascending the throne,
Xiǎnzǔ moved to the Chóngguāng Palace in the northern imperial garden to study profound texts.
He built the Lùyě Buddha Pagoda on the western mountain within the garden,
ten *lǐ* to the right of Chóngguāng, with rock chambers and meditation cells.
Buddhist monks resided there.
In the first year of Chéngmíng, Xiǎnzǔ Dà Shànghuáng passed away.
The Jiànmíng Temple was built.
Thereafter, numerous temples were erected, and monks were ordained for the sake of fortune.
In the sixteenth year of Tàihé, an edict was issued,
stating that annually on the eighth day of the fourth month and the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
one hundred people from large prefectures were permitted to become monks or nuns,
fifty from medium prefectures, and twenty from small prefectures.
This was established by decree as a permanent regulation.
In the nineteenth year of Tàihé, the emperor frequently visited the Báitǎ Temple in Xúzhōu.
He addressed the princes and attendant ministers, saying:
"This temple recently had a famous monk, Fǎshī Sōng,
who received the Chéngshílùn from Luóshí.
Later, he taught Fǎshī Yuān.
Yuān, in turn, taught Fǎshī Dēng and Fǎshī Jì.
I always enjoy studying the Chéngshílùn;
it can clarify profound human emotions.
That is why I have come to this temple."
Dào Dēng was truly learned in the Dharma.
Gāozǔ admired and favored him, always inviting him to expound on doctrines within the palace.
When he passed away, the emperor grieved deeply.
He bestowed a thousand bolts of silk.
He ordered all monks in the capital to observe a vegetarian fast for seven days and perform circumambulation.
An edict stated:
"My teacher, Fǎshī Dēng, suddenly passed away.
The pain in my heart is unbearable, and my grief is ceaseless.
Although I have been taking medicine,
the mourning period prevents me from attending immediately.
Therefore, in accordance with the teacher's principles, I will weep outside the palace gates."
Both monastics and laypeople honored this.
A śramaṇa from the Western Regions named Bátuó,
who possessed profound spiritual attainment,
was highly respected by the emperor.
An edict was issued to build the Shàolín Temple on the northern side of Shàoshìshān
for him to reside in.
The government provided for his clothing and sustenance.
In the fifth month of the twenty-first year, an edict stated:
"Fǎshī Luóshí can be said to have had a divine spirit excelling in the five talents and a will dedicated to the four practices.
Even now, there are still traces of him at the Chángzhù Temple.
My admiration and desire to follow his path are profound, reaching far and wide.
A three-tiered Buddhist pagoda should be built at the site of his old hall.
Furthermore, he was forced into secular life and sacrificed his precious body for the Dharma.
Since he temporarily adopted worldly customs,
he should have had descendants.
Inquiries should be made to find them, and they should be given proper recognition and assistance."
Previously, the Jiānfúcáo had been established.
It was later renamed Zhāoxuán,
complete with officials to manage monastic affairs.
This is equivalent to the modern Chóngxuánshǔ at the Tóngwén Temple.
During Gāozǔ's time, famous śramaṇas included Dàoshùn, Huìjué, Sēngyì, Huìjì, Sēngfàn, Dàobiàn, Huìdù, Zhìdàn, Sēngxiǎn, Sēngyì, and Sēnglì.
All were highly regarded for their righteous conduct.
Wèi Xiàowén was a sagely Son of Heaven.
He ascended the throne at five years old and began wearing the imperial crown at ten.
In the eighteenth year of Tàihé, he moved the capital to Luò.
In the twentieth year, he changed his surname to Yuán.
His hundred essays were unsurpassed throughout history.
Initially, when issuing edicts, he used officials to draft them.
After Tàihé, he composed them himself.
No subsequent emperors could match him.
This is evident in the edicts he issued on monastic conduct.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict stating:
"Since monastics and laypeople are distinct, their laws are also different.
Therefore, the teachings of the Dharma are manifest in their mutual distinction,
and injunctions and encouragements are appropriate for each.
If a monk commits a crime such as murder or worse,
they shall be judged according to secular law.
For other offenses, all cases shall be submitted to Zhāoxuán
to be judged according to monastic rules and regulations."
In the first year of Xīpíng, an edict sent the śramaṇa Huìshēng
on a mission to the Western Regions to collect sutras and Vinaya texts; he traveled for seven years.
In the winter of the third year of Zhèngguāng, he returned.
He had acquired 170 Buddhist sutras and treatises.
In the early Jiǐngmíng period, Shìzōng ordered the Dàchángqiū Qīng
to construct two grottoes for Gāozǔ and Wénzhāo Huángtàihòu at Yīquèshān south of Luò,
modeled after the stone grottoes of Língyán Temple in the former capital.
They were to be 310 feet from the ground.
Later, because cutting into the mountain at such a height was too difficult and costly,
a memorial was submitted to move them to a lower, flatter location,
100 feet from the ground,
and 140 feet north to south.
During the Yǒngpíng period, three grottoes were built for Shìzōng.
From the first year of Jǐngmíng to the fourth year of Zhèngguāng, it took twenty-four years to complete them.
The work used 802,366 laborers.
During Sùzōng's Xīpíng period, the Yǒngníng Temple was built within the city.
The Língtàihòu personally led all officials
to lay the foundation and erect the stupa.
The pagoda had nine stories,
over forty *zhang* high.
The cost was immeasurable.
The pagoda of Jǐngmíng Temple was also comparable.
Thereafter, the number of official and private temples and pagodas was immense.
In the first year of Shénguī, the Sīkōng Shàngshūlìng, Rènchéngwáng Chéng,
memorialized that the increasing number of temples and pagodas was obstructing the people's dwellings.
He briefly stated:
"The Tathāgata propagated his teachings mostly in mountains and forests.
However, these monks now cling to cities.
How can crowded and narrow places be suitable for walking meditation?
How can bustling noise be a place for sitting meditation?
It must be that desire draws their hearts, and they cannot stop themselves.
Moreover, those who reside there have lost their true essence,
and those who build often diminish their blessings.
They are the dregs of Buddhism,
the 'rats in the ancestral shrine' of the Dharma.
They are not tolerated by the internal precepts
and should be cast out by royal law."
The memorial was approved.
Not long after, the empire fell into chaos,
further compounded by the disaster of Héyīn.
Many court officials who died had their homes converted into temples,
and the prohibitions were no longer enforced.
In the second year of Xīnghé, an edict designated the old palace in Yèchéng as the Tiānpíng Temple.
From Shìzōng's time until the end of Wǔdìng,
the famous śramaṇas included Huìměng, Huìbiàn, Huìshēn, Sēngxiān, Dàoyín, Sēngxiàn, Dàoxī, Sēngshēn, Huìguāng, Huìyóng, Fǎróng, and Dàocháng.
All were highly esteemed by both monastics and laypeople.
From the Wèi dynasty's founding until its abdication,
Buddhist scriptures circulated widely and gathered in China.
There were 415 categories in total,
comprising 1,919 scrolls.
After Zhèngguāng, the empire faced many troubles,
and corvée labor was particularly severe.
Consequently, common households everywhere joined together to enter monastic life,
falsely professing admiration for śramaṇas but in reality avoiding conscription and labor.
This was an extreme abuse.
Since Buddhism came to China,
nothing like this had ever happened.
Roughly estimating the monks and nuns,
there were over two million,
and more than thirty thousand temples.
The widespread corruption reached such a point that it could not be controlled.
Therefore, those who knew sighed deeply.
The origin of Daoism lies with Lǎozi.
He claimed
to have been born before heaven and earth, sustaining all myriad beings.
He resided in the Yùjīng above, as the patriarch of divine kings,
and dwelt in the Zǐwēi below, as the lord of flying immortals.
He underwent a thousand transformations, sometimes possessing virtue, sometimes not.
Responding to perception and interacting with things, his traces were impermanent.
He instructed Xuānyuán at Éméi.
He taught Dìkù at Mùdé.
Dàyǔ heard the secret of eternal life.
Yǐnxǐ received the teachings of the Dàodé Jīng.
As for the *danshu zizi* (cinnabar books and purple characters),
the scriptures on ascending to Xuan and flying steps, and the *yushi jinguang* (jade stone golden light),
and the marvelous doctrines of numinous caverns,
they are innumerable.
Its teachings
all remove evil burdens, cleanse the mind and spirit,
accumulate good deeds and establish merits, and increase virtue and goodness,
even to the point of ascending to heaven in broad daylight and living eternally in the world.
That is why Qín Huáng and Hàn Wǔ were wholeheartedly devoted and tireless,
exhausting their minds and efforts in their relentless pursuit.
Ultimately, they could not achieve it,
and regretted it afterward.
Hence, there were the executions of Luán Dà and Xú Shì.
However, its doctrines captivated people, and many followed them.
Língdì placed canopies at Zhuólóng,
establishing altars for rituals.
And Zhāng Líng received the Dao at Húmíng,
then transmitted 1,200 chapters of heavenly palace texts.
His disciples passed them down, and the practice became widespread.
Fasts, sacrifices, kneeling, and bowing each had established forms.
Thus, the Sānyuán and Jiǔfǔ, the 120 officials,
and all gods were brought under their dominion.
They also spoke of *jiéshù* (kalpas), somewhat borrowing from Buddhist scriptures.
And when a kalpa ended,
they claimed heaven and earth would both be destroyed.
Their books contained many secret prohibitions;
those who were not their followers were forbidden to read them.
As for methods of transmuting gold, dissolving jade, performing talismans, and commanding water, along with myriad strange formulas and miraculous techniques,
the highest claimed feathered ascent to heaven,
and the next claimed elimination of calamities and misfortunes.
Therefore, those who loved the unusual often respected and served them.
Initially, Wéndì entered Jìn as a guest.
His attendants said,
"He ascended to immortality at Yīquè."
Tàizǔ loved the words of Lǎozi
and recited them tirelessly.
During the Tiānxīng period, the Yícáoláng Dǒng Mì
presented several dozen chapters of immortal elixirs.
Consequently, a 'Doctor of Immortals' was appointed,
and immortal workshops were established to refine various elixirs.
Xīshān was designated to supply firewood.
Criminals sentenced to death were made to consume the elixirs.
Many died without any verifiable results.
Tàizǔ, however, still specifically continued the practice.
The Imperial Physician Zhōu Dàn was troubled by the arduous task of concocting and gathering ingredients
and wished to abolish the practice.
Secretly, he instructed his wife to bribe the concubine of Zhāng Yào, the Doctor of Immortals, and thereby uncovered Yào's hidden transgressions.
Fearing death, Yào
requested to practice *bìgǔ* (abstention from grains).
Tàizǔ permitted it.
Yào was provided with resources
and a quiet chamber was built for him in the imperial garden.
Two families of commoners were assigned to clean it.
However, the officials responsible for refining elixirs continued their work without cessation.
After a long time, Tàizǔ's interest waned somewhat, and he finally stopped.
During the reign of Shìzǔ, there was a Daoist named Kòu Qiānzhī, whose courtesy name was Fǔzhēn.
He was the younger brother of Zànzhī, the Governor of Nányōngzhōu.
Early on, he was fond of the immortal arts and practiced the methods of Zhāng Lǔ.
He consumed elixirs and medicines for years without effect.
There was an immortal, Chéng Gōngxīng,
who worked as a servant in the Kòu family.
Later, Kòu Qiānzhī was calculating the seven luminaries,
but was bewildered and could not comprehend it.
Chéng Gōngxīng said,
“Why are you unable to resolve it?”
Kòu Qiānzhī replied,
“I have studied calculation for many years,
but my extended calculations are inconsistent with the entire system.”
Chéng Gōngxīng told him to arrange them according to his words.
Soon after, it was resolved.
Kòu Qiānzhī admired and submitted to him, wanting to take him as his master.
Chéng Gōngxīng firmly declined and requested to be Kòu Qiānzhī’s disciple.
Not long after, Chéng Gōngxīng entered Huàshān and resided in a stone chamber.
Chéng Gōngxīng gathered herbs and gave them to Kòu Qiānzhī to consume.
He no longer felt hungry.
They also entered a stone chamber in Sōnggāoshān together, and Chéng Gōngxīng said, “Someone will bring medicine.
Just eat it; do not doubt.”
Soon, someone arrived with medicine.
It was all poisonous, foul-smelling stuff.
Kòu Qiānzhī was frightened and fled.
Chéng Gōngxīng returned and asked him in detail.
Then he sighed and said,
“Sir, you are not yet an immortal.
You can only be a teacher for emperors.”
Chéng Gōngxīng served Kòu Qiānzhī for seven years.
Then he said,
“I cannot stay long.
I should leave at dawn.”
When the appointed time came, he indeed passed away.
Two young attendants were seen, one holding ceremonial robes and one holding a tin staff and an alms bowl, arriving at Chéng Gōngxīng’s corpse.
Chéng Gōngxīng suddenly rose,
put on his robes, held his alms bowl, grasped his staff, and departed.
Kòu Qiānzhī steadfastly cultivated his will on Sōngyuè.
In the tenth month of the second year of Shénruì,
he encountered a great god riding clouds and driving dragons, followed by a hundred spirits gathered on the mountain peak.
He called himself Tàishàng Lǎojūn.
He said to Kòu Qiānzhī,
“Since the passing of Tianshī Zhāng Líng,
the position on earth has been vacant.
Kòu Qiānzhī of Shànggǔ has a righteous character and principles.
Therefore, I bestow upon you the position of Tianshī.
I grant you twenty scrolls of the New Code from the Clouds.

Since the creation of the world, these have not been transmitted. You shall propagate my New Code, purify and rectify Daoism, eliminate the false methods of the Three Zhāngs, the rent-rice and money taxes, and the 'joining of qi' techniques for men and women.
The Great Dao is pure and void; how can such things exist?
You must prioritize rituals and regulations,
and supplement them with the consumption of elixirs and inner cultivation.”
He ordered twelve Jade Maidens of Jiǔyí to transmit guiding incantations to Kòu Qiānzhī.
Thus, he achieved辟穀 (bìgǔ, abstention from grains) and a vigorous spirit,
and his complexion became fresh and beautiful.
More than ten of his disciples
all mastered his techniques.
In the tenth month of the eighth year of Tàicháng, there was Mùtǔ Shàngshī Lǐ Pǔwén,
who came to Sōngyuè and said,
“I am the great-great-grandson of Lǎojūn.
Formerly, I resided in Sānggān, Dàijùn.
During the Hàn Wǔ period, I attained the Dao and became the Lord of Mùtǔ Palace,
governing the affairs of thirty-six earthly humans and ghosts.
My territory was 180,000 *lǐ* square.
Among these, there were 360 squares,
each 10,000 *lǐ* square.”
He sent his disciple saying,
“I grant Kòu Qiānzhī the 10,000 *lǐ* square of Guǎnghàn, which Sōngyuè oversees.”
He made a proclamation, and so on.
“I recorded sixty scrolls of diagrams
and true scriptures for you.
Assist the Lord of Tàipíng Zhēnjūn of the North in promulgating the method of the Jinglún Heavenly Palace.
If you can successfully establish and achieve this, you will transcend and ascend to become a true immortal.”
He also said,
“The final kalpa is approaching for the living beings on earth.
It is very difficult to propagate the teachings.
Men and women should establish altars and worship morning and evening, and so on.”
He also said,
“Between Heaven and Earth, there are thirty-six heavens.
Each heaven has thirty-six palaces.
Each palace has a lord.
Chìsōng, Wángqiáo, Hánzhōng, Zhāng Ānshì, Liúgēn, and Zhāng Líng,
recent immortals,
all serve as attendants.
I command Kòu Qiānzhī to befriend the assembly of immortals.”
He also said,
“The Buddha formerly attained the Dao in Xīhú.
He is the Lord of Yánzhēn Palace in the thirty-two heavens.
His teachings are brave and ascetic.
Therefore, his disciples all shave their heads, dye their robes,
and sever human relationships.
The celestial robes are all like this.”
In the Shǐguāng years, Kòu Qiānzhī first presented his writings.
He presented them to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ then ordered Kòu Qiānzhī to reside in the place where Zhāng Yào practiced bìgǔ, and provided him with food.
The court and common people heard of it, feeling both its existence and non-existence,
not fully believing it.
Cuī Hào alone found his words extraordinary.
Consequently, he became Kòu Qiānzhī’s disciple
and received his methods.
He submitted a memorial to commend and clarify the matter, saying,
“Your servant has heard that when a sagely king receives the mandate, there are heavenly responses.
However, the River Chart and Luò Book
convey their messages through patterns of insects and beasts.
This cannot compare to today's direct communication between humans and gods, with written records
that are clear, profound in meaning, and exquisite in their wording.
There has been nothing like this since ancient times.
In the past, Hàn Gāo was an heroic sage,
yet the Four Hoary Ones still felt ashamed of him
and would not compromise their integrity.
Now, pure-virtued hidden immortals
arrive without being summoned.
This is truly a sign that Your Majesty emulates Xuānhuáng and corresponds to Heaven's mandate.
How can one disregard the command of the divine spirit with worldly common talk?
Your servant secretly fears this.”
Shìzǔ was pleased and ordered an usher to offer jade, silk, and sacrificial animals to Sōngyuè.
He summoned the remaining disciples who were in the mountains.
Thereupon, he revered the Tianshī,
established Daoist altars, and promoted the new methods.
The teachings were proclaimed throughout the realm, and Daoism greatly flourished.
Cuī Hào served the Tianshī very diligently and performed prostrations.
Some people mocked him for this.
At that time, over thirty Daoists from Zhōngyuè
came and established the Tianshī's Daoist temple southeast of the capital.
It had five layers of altars,
built according to the regulations of the new scriptures.
One hundred and twenty Daoists were provided with clothing and food.
They prayed solemnly six times a day.
Monthly feasts were held for several thousand people.
Kòu Qiānzhī memorialized, saying,
“Your Majesty, as a true lord ruling the world,
has established the Jinglún Heavenly Palace.
This is unprecedented since ancient times.
You should ascend and receive the talismans and scriptures to manifest your sagely virtue.”
Shìzǔ followed his advice.
He went to the Daoist altar and received the talismans and registers.
His imperial retinue and banners were all blue,
in accordance with the color of the Daoist school.
Thereafter, subsequent emperors followed this practice upon their accession.
Gōngzōng saw that Kòu Qiānzhī proposed building the Jinglún Heavenly Palace to such a height that no chicken or dog could be heard, to communicate with the heavenly spirits.
The project involved tens of thousands of laborers and remained unfinished after a year.
He then spoke to Shìzǔ, saying,
“The paths of humans and heaven are different, and their high and low stations are fixed.
Now Kòu Qiānzhī wishes to tie us to an unachievable timeline and speaks of impossible things.
Wealth and resources are wasted, and the common people are exhausted.
Is this not unacceptable?
If it must be as he says,
it would be easier to use the ten thousand *rèn* cliff of Dōngshān as the foundation for the work.”
The Emperor deeply agreed with this.
But because Cuī Hào supported it, he found it difficult to go against his wishes.
He deliberated for a long time and said,
“I also know that this undertaking will not succeed.
Since it is so, why regret a mere five or three hundred laborers?”
In the ninth year of Zhēnjūn, Kòu Qiānzhī died.
He was buried according to Daoist rites.
His disciples believed that he had shed his corpse and departed through transformation.
The Jinglún Heavenly Palace was never completed and was stopped.
At that time, Wéi Wénxiù of Jīngzhào was living in seclusion on Zhōngyuè.
Shìzǔ summoned him to inquire about the alchemical golden elixir.
He replied,
“Divine powers are obscure and changes are unfathomable.
They can be encountered unexpectedly,
but are difficult to predict.
Your servant received this from his former master,
but has not yet achieved it.”
Shìzǔ valued his prominent family and refined demeanor.
He dispatched him with Shàngshū Cuī Zé to Wángwūshān
to synthesize the elixir, but it was ultimately unsuccessful.
At that time, several dozens of *fāngshì* (occult practitioners) arrived,
one after another.
Many notable individuals emerged.
Qí Xiān of Hédōng was skilled at physiognomy.
Shìzǔ esteemed him
and appointed him Shàng Dàfū.
Jiàng Lüè of Yǐngyáng and Wú Shào of Wénxǐ practiced Daoist breathing exercises and nourished their essence.
They were over a hundred years old, yet their spirit and vitality did not decline.
Yán Píngxiān of Hángnóng extensively read the hundred schools but could not fully express his meaning.
Nevertheless, his responses were worth recording.
The Emperor offered him an official position, but he firmly declined.
Lǔ Qí of Fúfēng suffered during the atrocities of Hèlián.
He took refuge in Hánshān and taught hundreds of people.
He was fond of occult arts and had few desires.
Luó Chóngzhī of Hédōng consumed pine resin and abstained from grains.
He claimed to have received the Dao on Zhōngtiáoshān.
There was a cave that led to Kūnlún and Pénglái,
where he could see immortals coming and going.
The Emperor ordered him to return to his hometown, establish an altar, and pray.
He issued an edict for Hédōng to provide for his needs.
Luó Chóngzhī entered the cave for a hundred paces
but reached its end and was summoned back.
The officials accused him of deceit and impropriety,
and memorialized to punish him.
Shìzǔ pardoned him
to show his openness towards attracting worthy individuals.
Wáng Dàoyì (王道翼) of Dōnglái (東萊) lived as a recluse on Hánxìn (韓信) Mountain for over forty years.
He abstained from grains, eating only wheat, thoroughly studied scriptures, and practiced incantations and talismans, having no contact with the worldly.
Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) ordered the Prefect of Qīngzhōu (青州) to summon him to the capital.
He nevertheless maintained his principles.
So, he ordered the monastic authorities to provide him with food and clothing for life.
In the fifteenth year of Tàihé (太和) [491 CE],
an imperial edict stated:
"The ultimate Way is formless, with emptiness and stillness as its essence.
Since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, altars and shrines have been established.
The previous dynasty, considering its utmost compliance admirable,
established temples for it.
Formerly, within the capital, dwellings were scarce.
Now, houses and residences are dense like teeth of a comb, and humans and spirits gather profusely.
This is not conducive to revering the supreme Dharma and purifying the divine path.
It can be moved to the south of the capital, to the northern bank of the Sānggān (桑乾) River, and the southern slope of Yuè (岳) Mountain.
Forever establish its location there and grant fifty households [to it],
to provide for its fasting and sacrifices.
It shall henceforth be named Chóngxū (崇虛) Temple.
Recluses from all prefectures can be summoned,
numbering ninety people.
When moving from Luòyáng (洛陽) to Yè (鄴),
this practice should be followed as before.
Its Daoist altar is in the southern suburb,
two hundred paces square.
On the seventh day of the first month, the seventh day of the seventh month, and the fifth day of the tenth month,
the Daoist masters of the altar and one hundred and sixty singers shall perform the bowing and sacrificial rituals.
Few Daoists were capable of achieving mastery,
nor did they possess any noteworthy talent or skill.
In the sixth year of Wǔdìng (武定) [548 CE], the authorities abolished it.
Zhāng Yuǎnyóu (張遠遊) of Hédōng (河東) and Zhào Jìngtōng (趙靜通) of Héjiān (河間), among others, were received by Qí Wénxiāng Wáng (齊文襄王).
A separate residence was established for them in the capital,
valuing their Daoist arts and receiving them with禮.
I examined Tiānshī (天師) Kòu Qiānzhī's (寇謙之) account, stating what Tàishàng Lǎojūn (太上老君) said.
It is like the dwelling of Pénglái (蓬萊) being beneath the sea,
and Kūnlún (崑崙) flying above the sky.
It also says:
"Thirty-six lands, ten thousand *lǐ* (里),
divided into three hundred and sixty squares."
How is this different from Zhāng Jiǎo's (張角) thirty-six *fāng* (方)?
According to the *Biography of Huángfǔ Sōng (皇甫嵩)* in the *Hòuhànshū (後漢書)*, it states:
"Zhāng Jiǎo (張角) of Jùlù (鉅鹿) called himself the 'Great Worthy Master' (Dàxiánláng).
He served Huáng-Lǎo (黃老) teachings,
practiced the arts of Zhāng Líng (張陵),
used talismanic water and incantation methods
to cure all illnesses.
He dispatched eight disciples to spread his Daoist teachings in all directions,
deceiving and misleading one another.
In over ten years, his followers numbered hundreds of thousands.
From the people of the eight prefectures of Qīng (青), Xú (徐), Yōu (幽), Jì (冀), Jīng (荊), Yáng (揚), Yǎn (兗), and Yù (豫), none failed to respond.
Consequently, he established thirty-six *fāng* (方).
A *fāng* (方) was like the title of a general.
A great *fāng* (方) had over ten thousand people,
a small *fāng* (方) six thousand.
They spread the rumor: 'The Azure Heaven is dead, the Yellow Heaven shall rise.
The year is *Jiǎzǐ* (甲子),
the world will be greatly auspicious.'
They wrote *Jiǎzǐ* (甲子) characters with white earth on the temple gates of the capital and prefectures.
In the third month of the first year of Zhōngpíng (中平) [184 CE], on the fifth day, they all rose up, both inside and outside.
All wore yellow Daoist robes and yellow turbans.
Some killed people as sacrifices to Heaven.
At that time, the bandit hordes numbered hundreds of thousands.
They first rose in Yǐngchuān (穎川), causing chaos throughout the world.
All were suppressed and annihilated by Huángfǔ Sōng (皇甫嵩).
The remnants smoldered but were not extinguished.
Even now, they still wear them."
Shào (劭) said:
"Buddhism is beyond what a narrow view can grasp.
I merely spoke rashly.
I also cited the *Lièzǐ* (列子) and *Yùkòu Shū* (御寇書),
which describe Shāng Tàizǎi (商太宰) asking Kǒngzǐ (孔子) about the affairs of a sage,
and Huángdì (黃帝) dreaming of traveling to the land of Huáxūshì (華胥氏).
The land of Huáxūshì (華胥氏)
is merely where the Buddha's spirit roams.
What is said here vaguely resembles Buddhism.
During the eras of Shí Hǔ (石虎) and Yáo (姚), scriptures and translations became widespread.
Perhaps it was to soften and subdue people's hearts;
therefore, there are many parables used as expedient means.
I do not know what kind of miraculous and boundless marvel this is!
Its discourse on the good and evil of human beings, and the causes and conditions of worldly affairs,
with 'compassion, joy, renunciation, constant bliss, self, and purity,'
is explained in writings with such precision and clarity, like the sun and moon.
Who but an enlightened one could verify it?
All who are compliant and submissive give their lives to it.
Enlightened people are careful with their speech and actions, cultivating wisdom and concentration,
achieving equality, liberation, and ultimate Bodhi.
But the perverse, being unable to comprehend its principles,
merely pursue wasteful expenditures of wealth and effort, seeking merit and becoming muddled.
Even the Six Classics all have their shortcomings,
and they have not delved deeply enough, alas.
I once wrote 'The Chapter on Creation'
to learn from the ancients and govern the present,
extending it by analogy.
Now there is this text again,
combined with 'Questions to Heaven,'
as a wandering thought, that's all.
I heard that in primeval times, a great fire burned!
And the waters were vast and boundless!
Nǚwā (女媧) refined stones to mend the azure sky!
Gònggōng (共工) struck Bùzhōushān (不周山)!
Hé (河) and Luò (洛) fought in the deep abyss!
Huángdì (黃帝) and Yán (炎) fought at Zhuōlù (涿鹿)!
Nǚjì (女妓) and Jiǔzǐ (九子) led the people!
Chīyóu (蚩尤) cast weapons for thousands of years! Ten suns appeared during Yáo's (堯) time!
Yì (羿) then shot down the suns, was this truly so?
Who transmitted the tale of Cháng'é (常娥) fleeing to the moon?
Fēnglóng (豐隆) rode clouds as an immortal!
What caused Xià Qǐ (夏開) to ride a dragon?
How could Fù Yuè (傅說) be entrusted to a star and proclaimed?
Kuāfù (夸父) and Dènglín (鄧林), their meaning is also difficult!
The Xúnmù (尋木) tree a thousand *lǐ* (里) high, how easy to discuss!
Mù Wáng (穆王) traveled extensively, going back and forth!
Hézōng (河宗) and Wángmǔ (王母) could converse!
The green bird revealed sincere truth!
Five-colored jade and stones came from the western side!
The ruins of Kūnlún (崑崙) between the northern seas!
Twelve thousand *lǐ* (里) from Zōngzhōu (宗周)!
The *Shānjīng* (山經) and ancient books are chaotically compiled!
Guō (郭) and Shì (釋) both lacked precision and firmness!
Above, there is vital energy, say the Daoists!
The sun, moon, and five planets all hang in emptiness!
Inverted reflections depart from the earth, rising as clouds and smoke!
Below the nine earths, there seems to be a heaven!
Tǔbó (土伯) and Jiǔyuē (九約), who was first?
In the West, Rùshōu (蓐收) guards the metal gate!
At the North Pole, Yúqiáng (禺強) exists eternally!
The Emperor's two daughters wander the Xiāng (湘) and Yuán (沅) rivers!
Xiāomíng (霄明) and Zhúguāng (燭光) still shine brightly!
Tàiyī (太一) and Sīmìng (司命) are the origin of ghosts!
Mountain sprites and national heroes are wandering souls!
Jiāwéiluówèi (迦維羅衛)'s Way is most revered!
Who can trace the origin of the golden body?
The unseen fixed stars can be discussed!
Its words are brilliant, many are the sayings of sages!
Within the Six Directions, principles are often muddled!
The mysterious and strange make the wise confused!
The Hétú (河圖) and Luòshū (洛書) are truly reliable!
Kǒng Jiǎ (孔甲) raised dragons, an ancient shared tale!
During Yǔ's (禹) time, Fángfēng (防風) dwelt at Yú (隅) Mountain!
In the Spring and Autumn period, where did the long-haired Di (狄) originate?
What was the reason for what was seen in Líntáo (臨洮)?
The waters of Pénglái (蓬萊) are shallower than before!
The waves of the Eastern Sea have become mulberry fields!
How many thousands of years since mountains collapsed and cities sank!
Stones grow and earth expands, surely over many years!
The Hàn (漢) dynasty dug Kūnmíng (昆明), charcoal remained intact!
The Wèi (魏) dynasty opened Jǐqú (濟渠), shells and mussels were firm!
Who caused the sun to appear twice in midday?
Where are the unseen Big Dipper stars hidden?
The Jiànzhāng (建章) Palace and Fèngquè (鳳闕) glowed divinely!
The Wèiyāng (未央) Palace's bells and ornaments bore fresh flowers!
Bronze was used for weapons before Qín (秦)!
Men wore colored silks before the Six States!
Women of Zhōu (周) appeared in the world!
Bān Jūn (班君) wore silk slippers and roamed Tài (太) Mountain!
Between humans and ghosts, there are recluses!
Beyond the Four Seas, what is square and what is round?
Wòjū (沃沮) and Sùshèn (肅慎) are in the northeast!
Long-armed and two-faced people also travel by boat!
The Wō (倭) country to the southeast, all tattooed!
Beyond them are the Black-Teeth and then the Naked People!
Dwarfs three feet tall are also neighbors!
In the northwest, Dīnglíng (丁零) and Wūsūn (烏孫)!
Chēshī (車師) and Yuèzhī (月支), various tribes!
The country of horse-hoofed people,
as if galloping!
In the southwest, Wūyì (烏弋) and Jìbīn (罽賓)!
Tiānzhú (天竺) and Yútián (于闐),
all Hu (胡) people!
Tiáozhī (條支) and Ānxī (安息) on the shores of the Western Sea!
Human tracks reach as far as Dàqín (大秦)!
Coral, bright pearls, copper, gold, and silver!
Líulí (琉璃) and mǎnǎo (馬腦) come mixed and displayed!
Chēqú (車渠) and Shuǐjīng (水精), none are fake!
Realgar and orpiment come from mountain ridges!
Blue and white lotus flowers cover the watersides!
Palaces and pavilions are all seven treasures!
Beyond the vast land and boundless sea, there are also people!
Long-legged and deep-eyed, are they rulers and subjects?
Husband and wife, and the three-bodied people!
Chest-knotted, backward-tongued, one-armed people!
Tip-toeing, cross-legged, and winged people!
The land of the deathless, what is their reason?
Vast and boundless creation, its principles are hard to follow!
Sages cannot fathom it, much less ordinary people!
In my leisure from writing, I made this text!
At dusk, thunder and lightning, enough to forget sorrow!
And to show you!
Shì
Sì says:
The inner teachings have many paths. Becoming a monastic is merely one method among them.
If one can maintain sincerity and filial piety in their heart,
and take benevolence and compassion as their foundation,
then a Sudatta (須達) or a stream of water (流水) need not shave their hair.
How can it be that all fields must be exhausted to erect stupas and temples,
and all households impoverished to become monks and nuns?
These excesses all stem from the government's inability to restrain them.
This has allowed unlawful temples to impede the people's farming,
and unproductive monks to deplete the nation's taxes and revenues.
This is not the original intent of the Great Enlightened One.
Furthermore,
seeking the Dao is a personal concern,
and conserving resources is a national strategy.
Personal concerns and national strategies cannot both be fully realized.
A loyal minister dedicates himself to his lord and abandons his kin;
a filial son secures his family and forgets the state.
Each has their own course of action.
There are Confucians who refuse to bow to kings and nobles, upholding their principles highly.
There are hermits who renounce kingship and decline ministerships, withdrawing to mountains and forests to avoid the world.
How can one fault them for their tax and labor exemptions?
If all common people could be transformed and enter the Dao,
as in the time of Miàoyuè (妙樂) or the land of Shàngqié (儴佉),
then there would be natural rice and endless treasures.
Why then seek the benefits of agriculture and sericulture?
Shì
Wǔ says:
Though the physical body dies, the spirit endures.
When a person lives in this world,
their expectations for a future life
seem unconnected. But after their death, it is like the old and young, or morning and evening, of their former self.
In the world, there are countless instances of souls and spirits manifesting in dreams,
or descending upon servants and concubines,
or affecting wives and children,
seeking food and drink, or requesting blessings and protection.
Indeed, there are not a few such cases.
Today, people who are poor, lowly, sick, and suffering
invariably complain and blame
not having cultivated merits in a previous life.
Considering this, how can one not make preparations for it?
To have descendants is merely to be one common person between heaven and earth.
How is it related to one's personal affairs that one should lovingly protect and establish a foundation for them?
How much more then should one not suddenly abandon one's own spirit?
Therefore, Liǎngshū (兩疎) gained a single corner [of wisdom],
and it has been chanted through generations, shining ever brighter.
Ordinary people are deluded and cannot see the future,
hence they say that the next life and this life are not a single entity.
If one possessed the heavenly eye to perceive how each thought vanishes, and how life after life is continuous,
how could one not be terrified?
Moreover, a jūnzi (君子) living in the world
values the ability to conquer oneself, restore propriety, benefit the times, and help others.
One who governs a family desires the prosperity of that family.
One who governs a state desires the well-being of that state.
What kinship do servants, ministers, and common people ultimately have with one's own body?
Yet one toils and cultivates virtue for their sake.
In the same way, Yáo (堯), Shùn (舜), Zhōu (周), and Kǒng (孔) seemingly forfeited their personal joy.
How many common people can one person practicing the Dao save and deliver?
How many bodies can they free from the burdens of sin?
Please consider this carefully.
When a person lives in the world,
they must attend to worldly affairs and establish a household.
They cannot abandon their wives and children and all become monastics.
Instead, they should simultaneously cultivate practices, devote themselves to reading and reciting,
to serve as provisions for the next life.
A human body is difficult to obtain.
Do not let it pass in vain.
The sun and moon are constant and bright.
Without their light and radiance, they could not cast their illumination.
Sōnghuá mountains nurture life.
Without wind and clouds, how could they evoke such feelings?
Great sages are born, responding to the times and coming into the world.
This is how they rectify customs and correct human relations.
Without the Qíu-Suǒ, Fén-Diǎn, Shī, Shū, Lǐ, and Yuè,
how could such majestic achievements be made and such pervasive transformations be brought about?
Thus, when the Great Wilds saw the decline of the Way,
Dì Hào initiated the hexagrams and their lines.
When the meaning of knotted cords became obscure,
Huáng Jié created written characters.
From then on, successive generations adopted different customs.
Achievements were made, and order was established, each with its own records.
When the orthodox lineage was extinguished, music collapsed, and rites were destroyed,
the laws of the former sages were like scattered banners.
Thus, Zhòngní sighed, saying,
"When the Great Way was practiced,
and during the flourishing of the Three Dynasties,
Qíu did not live to see it,
yet he had aspirations for it."
What he aspired to was that
ancient texts were still cherished.
Therefore, after returning from Wèi to Lǔ,
he first established the practice of a "plain king."
Thereupon, he abridged the Shī and Shū, and settled the Lǐ and Yuè.
He listed the "Five Beginnings" in the Chūnqiū,
and created the "Ten Wings" for the Yìdào.
After the Master's demise, his subtle teachings were almost lost.
When the seventy disciples also perished, the great principles diverged.
By the time of the Warring States period, customs were different, and governance varied.
A hundred schools arose in competition, and the nine currents emerged simultaneously.
Yíng Zhèng detested this,
hence the disaster of burning books and burying scholars.
It was not until the fourth year of Hàn Huì's reign
that the law against possessing books was abolished.
Thereafter, externally there were the collections of the Tàicháng, Tàishǐ, and Bóshì;
internally there were the archives of Yángé, Guǎngnèi, and Mìshì.
The path for presenting books was opened,
and officials for transcribing books were appointed.
By the time of Xiàochéng's reign,
many had been lost or scattered.
So, he sent the messenger Chén Nóng to seek lost books throughout the land.
Guānglù Dàfū Liú Xiàng and his sons Jí and Xīn, and others,
collated the texts.
Each time a volume was completed, they would record and present it.
When Xiàng died, during Āi [Dì]'s reign,
the Emperor ordered Xīn to continue his father's work.
He then moved the books from the Wēnshì to the Tiānlù Gé.
Xīn subsequently compiled all the texts
and presented his Qīlüè.
Even in the Later Hàn dynasty, the Lántái
still managed the book department.
Also, at the Dōngguān and Rénshòu Tà,
new records were compiled.
Xiàoshū Láng Bān Gù and Fù Yì both managed the secret archives.
Gù then, based on the words of the Qīlüè,
composed the Hàn Shū Yìwén Zhì.
Thereafter, among authors,
Yuán Shānsōng also recorded them in his work.
During the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, literary works became even more extensive.
All were stored in the Mìshū and the three outer pavilions.
Wèi Mìshū Láng Zhèng Mò abridged and corrected old texts.
Commentators of the time said he distinguished "purple" from "crimson."
Jìn Lǐng Mìshū Jiān Xún Xù,
building upon the Wèi Zhōngjīng, compiled a new register.
Although it was divided into more than ten scrolls,
it was generally categorized into four divisions.
During the chaos of Huì and Huái,
most of its books were lost, and in the Jiāngzuǒ, barely one in ten remained from the initial compilation.
Although later gathered,
they were extremely disordered.
Then, Zuòzhù Zuǒ Láng Lǐ Chōng began to abridge and correct them.
Following Xún Xù's old register and the four-division method,
he changed the books in categories Bǐng and Yǐ,
omitting the names of many chapters,
and generally ordered them by Jiǎ and Yǐ.
From that time onward, generations followed this tradition.
Sòng Mìshū Jiān Xiè Língyùn, Chéng Wáng Jiǎn, Qí Mìshū Chéng Wáng Liàng, Jiān Xiè Fěi, and others,
all made new advancements.
They revised and compiled catalogs into Qīzhì.
Among them, the remaining books from the Central Dynasties were collected somewhat widely,
yet those lost still constituted more than half.
At the end of Qí, the fires of war spread to the Mìgé.
At the beginning of Liáng, many were missing.
Thereupon, Mìshū Jiān Rèn Fǎng was ordered to personally lead the collection.
Additionally, a separate collection of books was housed in the Wéndé Diàn.
Scholars like Liú Xiàobiāo and others were made to review and present them again.
They then divided the texts on mathematics and techniques
into a new category.
Fèngcháoqǐng Zǔ Huàn was tasked with compiling its catalog.
Within the Shàngshū Gé, classics, histories, and miscellaneous books were separately stored.
In Huálín Yuán, Buddhist sūtras and treatises were also collected.
Since the flourishing of writings in Jiāngzuǒ,
none has surpassed the present era.
Xiàoxù loved books since childhood,
and never tired of them in adulthood.
While ill and living in seclusion, with no worldly distractions nearby,
as soon as the morning light appeared, his silken satchel was already open.
When the night watches were divided, the scroll case was just being closed.
Yet, he still could not exhaustively study the general outlines or fully explore the profound mysteries.
Every time he reviewed the records, he often found many deficiencies upon self-reflection.
He was quite fond of collecting obscure and hidden records.
Whenever there were collections of books from the Sòng and Qí dynasties, belonging to kings, dukes, or high officials,
if they indeed accumulated texts,
he would certainly seek to obtain their catalogs.
Whatever he encountered, whether seen or heard,
when compared with official catalogs, many omissions were found.
So, he compiled all the family collections
and created a new catalog.
As for the records within the mundane world, from classics to technical arts,
they were combined into five categories,
called the "Inner Chapters."
Buddhist and Daoist works, each forming one category, were called the "Outer Chapters."
In total, there were seven categories,
hence the name Qīlù.
In the past, Sīmǎ Zǐcháng recorded events spanning thousands of years.
Former sages pitied his diligence.
Although he was called a good historian,
he still bore the responsibility of "gathering crumbs."
How much more so when compiling over forty thousand volumes of books,
discussing and investigating each, and marking their main points?
My talent is lacking in comprehensive understanding, and my learning is far from extensive.
I do not have the gift of Bān Sì's bestowed books,
nor the privilege of Huáng Xiāng's access to the Dōngguān.
Should I wish to consult, internally I lack scrolls and books.
If there are doubts or ambiguities, there is no one nearby to enlighten me.
The errors and mistakes,
are they not numerous?
I fear that those who later fault this humble person
will certainly point to this record.
If there are corrections to be made,
I await the gentlemen.
In the past, Liú Xiàng, when collating books,
would create a record for each,
discussing its main points and debating its errors.
Upon completion, he would present it,
all of which were included in the main book.
At that time, separate collections of records were also made,
called Biélù.
That is the Biélù of today.
His son, Xīn, extracted its essentials
and wrote the Qīlüè.
Its first chapter was the summary of the other six.
Thus, it was named "Summary."
Next was the Liùyì Lüè.
Next, the Zhūzǐ Lüè.
Next, the Shīfù Lüè.
Next, the Bīngshū Lüè.
Next, the Shùshù Lüè.
Next, the Fāngjì Lüè.
Wáng Jiǎn's Qīzhì changed Liùyì to Jīngdiǎn,
Zhūzǐ remained,
Shīfù became Wénhàn,
Bīng became Jūnshū,
Shùshù became Yīnyáng,
and Fāngjì became Shùyì.
Although Xiàng and Xīn called it Qīlüè,
it actually had six categories.
Therefore, he established a Túpǔ Zhì
to complete the seven divisions.
Outside of this, he listed books missing from the Qīlüè and the Hàn Yìwén Zhì's catalog,
as well as non-Confucian scriptures.
Buddhist scriptures and Daoist scriptures each formed a separate record; although they followed the Qīzhì,
they were not counted among its seven.
The Qīlù compiled today refers to and weighs the works of Wáng [Jiǎn] and Liú [Xiàng/Xīn].
Wáng considered the term Liùyì insufficient
to label the classic titles and changed it to Jīngdiǎn.
Now, we follow this.
Therefore, the preface for the Jīngdiǎn Lù is "Inner Chapters, First."
Liú and Wáng both combined all histories with the Chūnqiū.
In Liú's time, historical books were very few.
Including them with the Chūnqiū was indeed appropriate.
Today, family records and biographies are more numerous than classics.
Still following this tradition
would indeed be cumbersome.
Moreover, the Qīlüè's Shīfù was not included in the Liùyì and other sections.
This was probably because the books were numerous,
hence a separate category was made for them.
Now, following this precedent, all histories are separated out.
The preface for the Jìzhuàn Lù is "Inner Chapters, Second."
The term Zhūzǐ is consistent between Liú and Wáng.
Liú also had a Bīngshū Lüè.
Wáng considered the character bīng to be shallow, while jūnyán was profound and broad.
Therefore, he changed bīng to jūn.
I humbly believe that in ancient times, there were terms like bīnggé, bīngróng, zhìbīng, and yòngbīng.
These are all general names for military affairs.
Therefore, I revert jūn to bīng.
Since military books are few,
they do not warrant a separate record.
Now they are appended to Zǐ, and the combined term is Zǐbīng.
Thus, the preface for the Zǐbīng Lù is "Inner Chapters, Third."
Wáng believed that the name Shīfù did not encompass other forms of composition.
Therefore, he changed it to Wénhàn.
I humbly believe that the literary works of an era
are collectively called jí.
Changing hàn to jí
is even more fitting for the name.
Therefore, the preface records the collected works as the fourth inner section, Nèi Piān (內篇) sì.
Wáng (王) considered the term "numerology and techniques" to have the fault of being too broad and complex.
He changed it to Yīnyáng (陰陽).
The discussions of Fāngjì (方技) had no basis in classical texts.
So he changed it again to Yìshù (藝術).
I secretly felt that Yīnyáng (陰陽) was too narrowly focused.
It was not as comprehensive as "numerology and techniques."
And Yìshù (藝術) was too broad, encompassing the Six Arts and numerology.
It did not capture the essence of Fāngjì (方技).
Therefore, I reverted to following Liú Shì (劉氏) and retained the original names for each.
However, as Fángzhōng (房中) and Shénxiān (神仙) already fall under the immortal path,
and Yījīng (醫經) and Jīngfāng (經方) do not warrant a separate category,
I combined them under the designation "techniques and skills" (shù jì) to name a single record as the fifth inner section, Nèi Piān (內篇) wǔ.
Wáng Shì (王氏)'s maps and charts (túpǔ) were a category not found in Liú Lüè (劉略).
Although Liú (劉)'s "numerology and techniques" (shùshù) contained
calendrical charts (lìpǔ), these differed from the present charts.
I secretly felt that a section on illustrations
should be categorized according to what is illustrated.
Therefore, I appended each to its relevant record according to its title.
As for annotations and similar types of records,
they should align with historical narratives.
Therefore, they are placed at the end of the records and biographies (jìzhuàn).
All the above constitute the inner sections (Nèi Piān).
Buddhism (Shì Shì zhī jiào) truly spread throughout China.
Its lectures, explanations, recitations, and reflections parallel the Confucian classics (Kǒng jí).
Although Wáng Shì (王氏) included them in a section,
they were not within the scope of his treatise.
To seek principles from matters in such a way was not what was comfortable.
Therefore, I have prefaced the Buddhist teachings (Fó Fǎ),
recording them as the first outer section, Wài Piān (外篇) yī.
Books on the immortal path (xiāndào)
have a long history.
Liú Shì (劉氏) placed "Immortals" (Shénxiān) at the end of Fāngjì (方技).
Wáng Shì (王氏) placed "Daoist Scriptures" (Dàojīng) outside the Seven Treatises.
Now, I combine and preface the immortal path,
recording it as the second outer section, Wài Piān (外篇) èr.
Wáng (王) placed Daoism before Buddhism;
now I place Buddhism before Daoism.
This is because their tenets differ,
and also because their teachings have varying depths.
In total, the two inner and outer sections comprise seven records.
It is hoped that all lost books and secret records in the world
are exhausted herein.
In the fourth year of Pǔtōng (普通) of Liáng (梁),
the year of Dān'è (單閼), on the seventeenth day of the middle spring month,
within the forbidden inner residence in Jiànkāng (建康),
I began to compose this book.
Liú Yǎo (劉杳) of Píngyuán (平原), a learned man,
was traveling with me.
He spoke about this matter.
Yǎo (杳) had a similar ambition,
but had long been unable to take up the brush.
Hearing that I had already begun,
he was delighted and understood.
All the materials he had collected
he gave to me to broaden my knowledge and experience.
He indeed rendered great assistance.
This is like Kāngchéng (康成) with his commentaries,
all of which were eventually attributed to Zǐshùn (子順)'s writings.
