Xiàoxù (孝緒) was from Chénliú (陳留).
He was the great-grandson of Xīn (歆), the Zhonglǐngjūn (中領軍) of the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
His grandfather, Huìzhēn (慧真), was the Grand Administrator of Línhè (臨賀).
His father, Yàn (彥), was the Síxíng Cóngshì Zhōngláng (太尉從事中郎).
At thirteen, Xiàoxù (孝緒)
had a general understanding of the main principles of the Five Classics.
He accompanied his father as the Xíngshì (行事) of Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
He did not record the southern documents to maintain his father's integrity.
At sixteen, he observed mourning for his parents' deaths.
He did not wear padded silk.
Even if vegetarian food tasted good, he would spit it out.
Once, while listening to a lecture on Zhōngshān (鍾山),
his mother, Wáng Shì (王氏), suddenly fell ill.
Xiàoxù (孝緒) was startled during the lecture and returned home.
A medicine required fresh ginseng.
He personally gathered it from the high ridges of Zhōngshān (鍾山).
For days, he found nothing.
Suddenly, a deer walked in front of him.
He found it strange and followed it to where it rested.
Indeed, there was ginseng.
His mother's illness immediately healed.
Wáng Yàn (王晏), the Shàngshūlìng (尚書令) of Qí (齊), held great power and influence.
He came to visit Xiàoxù (孝緒).
His attendants announced his arrival with great fanfare.
Xiàoxù (孝緒) disliked this
and escaped by crawling through a fence.
Yàn (晏) left a gift, which Xiàoxù (孝緒) refused to accept.
He once ate some delicious soy sauce.
When asked, he learned it was sent by the Wáng (王) family.
So he ordered the sauce to be discarded.
When Yàn (晏) was later executed,
Xiàoxù (孝緒) was spared because he was not implicated.
He often used Lùlín (鹿林) as his hermitage.
He surrounded it with woods and ponds, severing social ties.
Few people ever saw him.
Rèn Fǎng (任昉), the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), wanted to visit him but dared not.
He gazed at Lùlín (鹿林)
and said to his brother Lǚ (履),
"His dwelling is near,
but the man is very distant."
Yīn Yún (殷芸), a Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫), sent him a poem.
Rèn Fǎng (任昉) stopped him, saying,
"If our inclinations differ, why bother each other?"
From then on, the court nobility ceased their visits and invitations.
He only associated with Péi Zhēnzǐ (裴貞子). In the twelfth year of Tiānjiān (天監),
Fù Zhāo (傅昭), the Mìshūjiān (秘書監), recommended him, but he still did not attend.
The Son of Heaven thought he was merely creating a false reputation to gain fame.
From then on, he was no longer summoned.
Thus, Hé Yìn (何胤) and Xiàoxù (孝緒) were both able to fulfill their lofty ambitions.
Nánpíng Yuánxiāng (南平元襄) said to Lǚ (履),
"In the past, your grandfather refused to seek trouble by socializing.
Why does your virtuous younger brother alone cling to this ambition?"
Xiàoxù (孝緒) replied,
"If all deer and pheasant could be harnessed,
how would they be different from Lùjì (騄驥)?"
Wáng (王) composed 'Èr'àn' (二闇) and 'Xìngqíng Yì' (性情義).
He showed them both to Xiàoxù (孝緒)
and asked him to polish them.
Shìzǔ (世祖) wrote 'Zhōngchén Zhuàn' (忠臣傳)
and compiled Buddhist stele inscriptions.
Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹) recorded 'Yánshén Jì' (妍神記).
They all first consulted the hermit
before putting them into practice.
Póyáng Zhōngliè Wáng (鄱陽忠烈王) was Xiàoxù (孝緒)'s brother-in-law.
The prince and his sons sent gifts annually,
but he accepted none.
He once divined his own death date, saying,
"I will die in the same year as Compiler Liú."
That autumn, Liú Yǎo (劉杳) passed away.
Xiàoxù (孝緒) peered out and said,
"How much longer do I have?"
Several tens of days later, he indeed died.
He was fifty-eight years old.
The Crown Prince sent an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices.
The funeral gifts were very generous.
His son, Nù (恕), upholding his father's will, firmly declined them.
His disciples posthumously honored him as Wénzhēn Chǔshì (文貞處士).
Xiàoxù (孝緒) had extensively studied all kinds of books,
and there was nothing he was not proficient in.
His strong energy and powerful memory were revered by scholars.
He authored 'Qīlù' (七錄), 'Xiāofán' (削繁), and other works, totaling 181 volumes.
All circulated in the world.
The compilation of Buddhist and Daoist texts
into "sections beyond the secular" (Fāngwài zhī piān)
began with him.
Liáng Gāozǔ Wǔdì.
At thirty-four years old, he ascended the throne.
He governed for forty-nine years.
Though managing myriad urgent affairs, he never let go of his scrolls.
He embraced both inner Sūtras and outer classics.
He composed thousands of volumes of commentaries and explanations.
Yet, he was frugal and self-controlled.
He did not wear silks or brocades.
His sleeping quarters were simple and unadorned.
He was diligent day and night.
Thus, he used a cloth quilt, a rush mat, straw sandals, and a ge-towel.
From the moment he first assumed the great treasure (throne), he maintained these practices.
He ate only one meal a day, permanently abstaining from pungent foods and meat.
Among emperors, few could match this.
In earlier times, Lǎozǐ's followers valued talismans and diagrams.
Upon thoroughly investigating their origins, they were found to be as baseless as false creations.
The Emperor then personally wielded his divine brush, issuing an edict to abandon Daoism.
The text stated:
On the eighth day of the fourth month of Tiānjìan three years,
Xiāo Yǎn, the Emperor of the Liáng kingdom from Lánlíng, prostrates and bows in reverence [to the Buddha].
To the Buddhas of the ten directions, the esteemed Dharma of the ten directions, and the holy Saṅgha of the ten directions.
I humbly observe that the Sūtras say:
“One who awakens bodhicitta is immediately a Buddha mind.”
No other good deeds can compare to this.
It enables sentient beings to exit the gates of suffering in the three realms
and enter the supreme path of wu-wei.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, with defilements exhausted and wisdom solidified, attained awakening.
His ultimate Dao connected with all beings, and his virtues perfected, he achieved sainthood.
He kindled the torch of wisdom to illuminate the deluded,
and mirrored the stream of Dharma to purify defilements.
He revealed auspicious signs in the heavens,
and shone with spiritual majesty beyond phenomena.
He rescued the deluded multitude from the ocean of desire,
and guided sentient beings to Nirvāṇa.
He ascended the high mountain of permanent joy,
and emerged from the deep abyss of the river of love.
His words transcend the four propositions, and his speech is free from the hundred errors.
Manifesting in the sahā world, he was born into a royal palace.
He walked through the three realms as the honored one,
and illuminated the entire great chiliocosm.
But because minds are shallow and prone to weariness,
he then profoundly expounded the perfect and eternal [Dharma],
and also subtly concealed his splendor under the twin Sāla trees.
King Ajātaśatru eradicated his sins, and Vaśusobhū removed his calamities.
If one does not encounter the great holy Dharma King,
who can rescue and receive them?
Though his physical manifestation may be hidden, his Dao remains undiminished.
For a long time, this disciple was lost in delusion, indulging in the teachings of Lǎozǐ.
Through generations, this was inherited,
and I was tainted by this heterodox Dharma.
Due to karmic causes and the arising of good [thoughts],
I abandon delusion and know how to return.
Today, I abandon the old physician and take refuge in the Right Awakening.
I pray that in future lives, I may be born as a pure youth, leave home,
widely propagate the Sūtras and teachings, convert and save sentient beings, and together attain Buddhahood.
Rather would I long sink in evil paths within the Right Dharma
than enjoy temporary rebirth in heaven by following Lǎozǐ's teachings.
I embark on the Mahāyāna mind, free from the thoughts of the two vehicles.
May all Buddhas bear witness to this true vow,
and may Bodhisattvas receive me.
Your disciple, Xiāo Yǎn, bows in reverence.
At that time, the Emperor, along with twenty thousand people, both monastics and laity,
in the upper chamber of the Chóngyún Diàn,
personally wrote this text, awakening bodhicitta.
By the eleventh day of the fourth month,
he again issued an imperial edict to the Secretariat:
The great Sūtras state:
There are ninety-six kinds of Dao,
but only the Dao of the Buddha is the Right Path.
The other ninety-five kinds are called heterodox paths.
I abandon the heterodox outer paths to serve the Right inner [Dharma]
of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. If any high officials can enter this vow,
each should awaken bodhicitta.
Lǎozǐ, Zhōu Gōng, Kǒngzǐ, and others,
though they are disciples of the Tathāgata in a sense, their transforming traces are ultimately heterodox.
They represent only worldly good [teachings],
unable to transform ordinary people into saints.
Therefore, officials, civil and military, marquises, kings, and imperial relatives
should turn from falsehood to truth, abandoning heterodoxy and entering the right.
Thus, the Sūtras and the Chengshi Lun state:
If one strongly adheres to outer paths and lightly to the Buddhadharma,
this is called heterodox view.
If the mind is neutral,
it is of an indeterminate nature, neither good nor evil.
If one's mind strongly adheres to the Buddha and weakly to Lǎozǐ,
this is true pure faith.
Regarding "pure faith":
Pure means clean both inside and out.
All defilements, vexations, and karmic burdens are exhausted.
Faith means believing in the right, not in heterodoxy.
Therefore, it is called a "pure-believing Buddhist disciple."
All other kinds of faith are heterodox views
and cannot be called pure faith.
The Secretariat is to implement this quickly.
By the seventeenth day of the fourth month,
the Grand Councilor, General who Pacifies the Front, and Dānyáng Governor, Shàolíng Wáng, submitted a memorial, stating:
Your servant, Lún, has heard that
the Tathāgata's majestic form is sublime, towering above the highest realm,
and his subtle and wondrous body is vast, manifest without bounds.
He relies on the golden wheel to enlighten beings,
and takes the silver grain to respond to the mundane.
He sharpens the keen knife of Prajñā,
and gathers the wondrous fruit of Nirvāṇa.
He crosses the bitter sea of transmigration,
and delivers constant joy to the other shore.
Therefore, he can bring down clouds of compassion and sprinkle rain of sweet dew.
In seven places and eight assemblies,
the meaning of his teachings is inexhaustible.
With the Four Noble Truths and five periods,
the methods of benefit are endless.
Together, the pure sun shines brighter, the mist disperses, and the clouds clear.
The flickering flame obscures the light, and the dust and heat naturally subside.
It can be said that he enters the mundane to transform the ignorant,
and transcends the world to subtly align with suchness.
He makes those in thickets of delusion and heterodox paths yearn for the Dharma gate without weariness,
and those parched by craving, deaf and blind, eager to explore the profound and know how to turn back.
The Bodhi tree began in Kāpilavastu,
and its virtuous sounds flourished in Jīngluò.
The fixed stars were unseen when Zhōu Jiàn conceived,
and the full moon's perfect form was experienced by Hàn Gǎn in a night dream.
The five Dharmas were transmitted, and myriad virtues began to manifest.
The glorious customs were subtly initiated, competing to spread the noble spirit.
Relying on these three insights, he illuminates the errors of the迷途,
and with these seven factors of awakening, he extracts beings from the suffering of long nights.
It happens that His Majesty the Emperor, a Bodhisattva, responds to heaven, governs the world, and faces the screen to rule the people.
He holds light within the universe, illuminating the pure lands beyond the seas.
He delivers unobstructed eloquence to receive the common people,
and with his original vows, he embraces sentient beings.
Thus, he can adapt to circumstances, administer medicine, reveal expediency, and manifest causes.
He champions the doctrine of the one vehicle,
and expands the foundation of the ten stages.
Therefore, all nations turn back, all receiving right understanding.
Both the visible and invisible spiritual beings all receive guidance and salvation.
People awaken the vow of equal enlightenment,
and all beings give rise to bodhicitta.
None fail to diligently aspire to the ultimate goal,
joyfully returning to the source.
They mutually uphold compassion and cultivate patience.
This is what is called covering and protecting, enriching and benefiting, providing bridges and ferries for salvation.
As the Dao shines widely, the people are also transformed.
Thus, Arhats fly their staves, ascend into the void, take form, and refute heterodoxy.
Outer paths uphold the right nation's monasteries and vihāras.
Precious stūpas stand in sight of each other.
Lecture assemblies transmit Sūtras, and virtuous sounds fill the ears.
Your servant, in the past, did not comprehend the source of truth,
and adhered to heterodox paths.
It was like wishing for sweet fruit but planting bitter trees,
or wanting to quench thirst but going to saltwater.
Now, I awaken from delusion and roughly know how to return.
I receive the great Bodhisattva precepts,
disciplining my body and mind.
I abandon the heterodox ways of Lǎozǐ
and enter the true teachings of the Dharma stream.
I humbly pray for Your Heavenly Compassion to graciously grant this.
Respectfully submitted.
On the eighteenth day of the fourth month, Rèn Xiàogōng, a Grand Secretariat Drafter, proclaimed an imperial edict, saying:
To be able to change from delusion to the right [path]
can be called having deeply planted excellent causes.
You should further exert courageous effort.
Formerly, Lù Xiūjìng, a Daoist priest from Jīnlíng,
was a prominent figure in Daoism.
During the Sòng and Qí dynasties, he perpetuated the teachings of the three Zhāngs and expanded those of the two Gěs.
Scholars of Xī and Zhāng guarded their gates and received talismans.
He then presumptuously added and invented, widely instituting uniform rituals,
which were exceedingly cumbersome and expensive, intending for the ruler to revere and follow them.
When Liáng Zǔ began his reign, he issued an edict to abandon Daoism.
Lù Xiūjìng could not bear his indignation.
Consequently, he, along with his disciples and fugitives from the border regions,
rebelled and defected to Northern Qí.
He also disbursed gold and jade, gifting them to various nobles,
entrusting them with his aspirations, hoping to revive Daoism.
The Emperor was thus misled.
In the ninth month of Tiānbǎo six years,
he issued an edict to summon ten learned Bhikkhus and Daoists
to personally contend before him.
At that time, the Daoists magically blessed the Bhikkhus' robes and alms bowls,
which either flew or spun.
They blessed the beams and pillars,
which either lay horizontally or stood vertically.
The Bhikkhus, having never studied magic,
remained silent and offered no rebuttal.
Men and women crowded around noisily, and people of noble and humble birth changed their minds,
all believing Lù Xiūjìng's followers to be superior.
The Daoists leaped and climbed with joy,
gazing proudly at the sky, boasting and exalting themselves,
showing off their Daoist magic.
Then they also proclaimed:
“Divine powers are temporarily manifested to subdue the arrogant and powerful.
If the Bhikkhus show one, I shall show two.
Now, we have briefly shown a small skill,
and they have all retreated in defeat.
The matter is thus clear.”
The Emperor ordered the Grand Overseer, Fǎshī, to compete with Jìng.
The Grand Overseer said,
"Occult arts and petty tricks
are disdained by common scholars,
let alone by renunciants.
Nevertheless, a divine command compels me to refuse,
how can I remain silent?
Let the monk in the lowest seat contend with him."
He immediately went to search for him.
There was a monk, Fójùn, also known as Tánxiǎn,
whose origin was unknown.
He wandered about without fixed abode,
eating and drinking like a layman.
Sometimes he would speak freely,
with profound and far-reaching insights.
The Grand Overseer knew his deep capacity
and privately befriended him.
At that time, many famous monks were gathered,
and Xiǎn sat in the lowest seat.
He was heavily drunk, sitting upright but swayingly.
The officials dared not summon him.
They reported the matter to the Grand Overseer.
He said,
"The Dàoshì offering master, Cháng Dào, acts as he pleases.
This drinking monk can speak with him."
"Help him here."
Thereupon, all the assembled monks were awed and fearful.
Fǎshī's authority prevented anyone from offering remonstrance.
So, two men helped Xiǎn onto the high seat.
Once seated, he stood up and smiled, saying,
"I am heavily drunk.
I heard something in my ear saying,
'If the Shāmén manifests one, I will manifest two.'
Is this statement true or false?"
The Dàoshì said,
"It is true."
Xiǎn immediately stood on one foot and said,
"I have manifested one.
You may manifest two."
None of them could respond.
Xiǎn said,
"The earlier incantation that made various clothes and objects fly
was merely me opening the door to test your magic."
He ordered them to take the robes and bowl of Chóu Chánshī and incantate over them.
All the Dàoshìs simultaneously exerted themselves and chanted spells together.
Nothing moved at all.
The Emperor commanded to retrieve the robes.
Even ten men pulling could not move them.
Xiǎn then ordered the robes to be placed on beams of wood,
and again ordered them to incantate.
There was no effect whatsoever.
The Dàoshìs looked at each other, helpless.
Still, they prided themselves on their verbal debate.
Then they said,
"Buddhists call themselves 'inner,'
so 'inner' is small.
We call our Dàojia 'outer,'
so 'outer' is great."
Xiǎn immediately retorted,
"If so, then the Son of Heaven dwelling 'inner' is certainly small,
and the hundreds of officials dwelling 'outer' are certainly great!"
Jìng and his followers sealed their mouths and had nothing to say.
The Emperor observed their true capabilities with his own eyes,
then issued an edict saying,
"The Dharma gate is not two; the true lineage is one.
To seek it on the right path, tranquility is fundamental.
The Dàoshìs, the offering masters, are false delusions in the world.
Ignorant common people still revere them.
Where is purity when fermented grains are consumed?
With sweet meat, compassion is forever separated.
They are deviant from humanitarian temples above and contrary to sacrificial rites below.
All should be forbidden and no longer followed.
Proclaim and enforce this far and wide, making it known to all.
Those Dàoshìs who submit
shall all be handed over to Zhāoxuán Grand Overseer, Grand Fǎshī, to be ordained and allowed to leave home.
Those who have not yet resolved their minds
shall be ordered to shave their heads and be dyed."
On that day, many were beheaded.
Those who claimed to be immortals
were ordered to ascend the Sānjuétái and throw themselves down to fly away.
They all shattered their bodies and splattered the ground.
Such falsehoods were thus eradicated.
This caused the territory of Qí to have no two faiths.
Up until the time of Zhōu and early Suí,
their arts gradually reopened, continuing to Dōngchuān today.
This lineage is minor and unworthy of contention.
The Emperor's personal name was Yáng.
He was the second son of Gāo Huān, the Chancellor of the former Wèi.
His elder legitimate brother, Chéng, was hasty and arrogant,
and was killed by his servant.
Yáng succeeded to his position and became the Chancellor.
When the Wèi dynasty was nearing its end,
Yáng built an altar in the southern suburbs.
Divination yielded the hexagram of Dàhéng, which was auspicious, like that of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
So he cast a golden statue,
which was formed in a single pouring.
Wèi Shōu drafted the abdication text, and the Wèi Emperor signed it.
He then received the abdication and established Dà Qí.
His conduct and actions were unfathomable in terms of wisdom or folly.
He entrusted governance to Púshè Yáng Zūnyàn.
The Emperor greatly built Buddhist temples.
Monks and nuns filled all the prefectures.
Offerings were made and the Dao was practiced ceaselessly throughout winter and summer.
At that time, Chóu Chánshī admonished the Emperor, saying,
"Benefactor, a Ràchà rules the country.
Look at yourself in the water."
The Emperor followed his advice.
He saw a group of Ràchàs behind him.
Thereupon, he stopped eating meat.
He banned hawks and falcons, dismissed officials,
and all fishing, butchering, pungent foods, and strong-smelling herbs were removed and not allowed into the market.
The Emperor often sat in meditation all day long.
He bowed to the Buddha and circumambulated,
moving as fast as wind. He received precepts from Zhāoxuán Grand Overseer
Fǎshī, who covered the ground with his robe
and ordered the Emperor to step on his hair to receive them.
Earlier, when the Emperor was in Jìnyáng,
he sent a man on a camel,
ordering,
"Go to the temple and fetch the sutra box."
The messenger asked for its location.
The Emperor said,
"Let the camel go out of the city at will."
Upon exiting, he suddenly arrived at a mountain as if in a dream.
Halfway up the mountain was a Buddhist temple.
A group of Shāmís remotely called out,
"Gāo Yáng's camel has arrived!"
They then led him to see an old monk, who bowed and said,
"How is Gāo Yáng as the Son of Heaven?"
He replied, "Sagely and enlightened."
He asked, "Why have you come?"
He replied, "To fetch the sutra box."
The monk said,
"Yáng was lazy in the temple and didn't read sutras. Go to the north side, east end, and give it to him."
The messenger returned and reported.
At first, the Emperor arrived at the Mùjǐng Fósì temple in Gǔkǒu.
There was an "idiot who sacrificed his body" (shěshēn chīrén) who could not speak.
Suddenly, he said to the Emperor,
"I go, you come later."
That night, the shěshēn chīrén died.
Soon after, the Emperor collapsed and died in Jìnyáng.
Originally, the two paths of concealment and prominence
cannot definitively determine honor or disgrace.
The two ends of truth and worldliness—
who can unify their differences?
Therefore, the truly reclusive find the marketplace no more boisterous than the wilderness,
and the highly self-reliant find no sorrow in mountains and rivers.
Emptiness is not outside form;
heaven and earth are spontaneously identified as one.
Fame is not within righteousness;
liver and gall can be as distinct as Chǔ and Yuè.
Whether speaking or silent,
it surpasses the methods of speech and silence.
Whether existing or not,
it truly transcends the boundaries of existence and non-existence.
It is like the cloud-borne swan flapping its wings, causing the peacock to lament its distant flight;
Vimalakīrti (Jìngmíng) manifesting illness, making the bhikṣus (bǐqiū) dread his profound辯.
The resolve to cultivate (fāxīn) is itself becoming a monastic;
what concern is the cutting of hair?
Abandoning worldly customs is truly entering the Dharma;
why must one pull out one's hairpin?
These are the gates of defilement and purity,
the expedient and the real, which remain uncomprehended.
These are the principles of reliance and reversal,
of good and ill fortune, which remain undiscerned.
Thus, Zhuāng Shēng (莊生) championed the doctrine of the leveling of all things,
and the Buddha's disciples (shìzǐ) expounded the meaning of the three vehicles uniting into one.
How profound!
Truly, it is deep and far-reaching, exceedingly difficult to fully grasp.
I have heard that when yin and yang (yīnyáng) combine, all things are formed;
when salty and bland are harmonized, the eight delicacies become delicious.
Why then do the four seasons perpetually maintain their order, and the five flavors still remain distinct?
Judging from this,
how can truth and worldliness be confused, or concealment and prominence be different?
Some, with limited hearing and shallow understanding,
wish to surpass Zhōu Gōng (周公) and Kǒngzǐ (孔子) in wisdom.
Some, being minor, undistinguished officials,
then compare their position to that of emperors.
They forcefully exalt themselves to establish their person,
believing that they alone are preeminent.
They do not believe in cause and effect (yīnguǒ),
and thus assert there is no Buddhist Dharma (fófǎ).
They lightly slander ascetics (níyuè) and trample upon śramaṇas (shāmén),
foolishly following corrupt Confucians, thereby inviting dark calamities.
Others, upon first shedding their lay attire, appear like virtue-crowned celestial beings.
As soon as they assume a monastic name, their ambition seems to soar above the seas.
Arrogantly, they occupy honored positions, believing themselves to be ultimate saints.
How do they know that the ten fetters (shíchán) still obstruct them, and the three studies (sānxué) remain unheard of?
They do not adapt to circumstances in dealing with others,
and ultimately cling to their ignorance, self-contained.
Alas, these two types of people, though their paths diverge, are both utterly contradictory.
How can a noble-minded, enlightened person possibly endorse such conduct?
Hoping to resolve these disputes and blunt sharp edges,
I will metaphorically set up flags and drums.
Although there will be both praise and criticism,
the ultimate goal is to champion the Way (dào).
It is like multi-colored brocades interwoven,
converging near Mount Suméru (Xūmí).
The myriad forms are arrayed,
all gathering according to empty space.
Returning to the root, the myriad things, though numerous,
are like rivers emptying into the vast ocean.
This truly is to illuminate and praise the Buddhist Way (Fódào),
and to elaborate upon and commend the profound path (xuánmén).
May it cause us to be without self and without evil, truly humble and truly reverent,
thus passing on this discourse to future generations.
There was a gentleman named Fànháng Xiānshēng (梵行先生) who kept himself aloof from worldly dust, dwelling alone in the hills and mounds.
His brilliant wisdom surpassed the nine heavens,
and his spirit encompassed the eight directions.
He used grass as a mat, a stone as a pillow, cut his hair, and purified his mind (huīxīn).
His rag robe was unlike Yáng Xù's (羊續) gown;
his rope bed was different from Guǎn Níng's (管寧) couch.
He had lived in seclusion in the Western Mountains for several decades.
He was firm and unyielding, tranquil and inactive.
He often sighed and said,
"When poor, one cultivates oneself alone;
when prominent, one benefits the world."
But the common people are restless, bound by the net of desire,
unable to achieve pure ascension themselves.
To sit by and watch them suffer in misery,
one must again leave the forests and glades to seek alms among humanity.
Thereupon, he temporarily curtailed his reclusive life and journeyed,
reaching the capital city (Jīngyì), staying at Bàshàng (灞上).
There was a young nobleman named Xínglè Gōngzǐ (行樂公子).
He reined in his dragon-like steeds by the stream (Lìushuǐ),
and his crane-feather canopy flew through the floating clouds.
His embroidered robes and aristocratic attire were fragrant with the warm breeze.
His jade reins and golden saddle competed in brilliance with the sun.
It was evident that the love from thrown fruits belonged to Pān Shēng (潘生),
and the favor of the cut sleeve had captivated the Hàn Emperor (Hàndì).
He joined carriages at the city corner, accompanying the feast of Cáo Wáng (曹王),
and linked stirrups by the pond, pursuing the enjoyment of Shān Gōng (山公).
He met the gentleman on the road, and surprised, asked,
"Sir, your appearance is like a scholar from Yān and Zhào (Yān Zhào),
your hair like a guest from Wú and Yuè (Wú Yuè).
Your complexion seems distressed like those in Chén and Cài (Chén Cài),
and your clothing style does not belong to Chǔ or Lǔ (Chǔ Lǔ).
You walk slowly, look down, speak softly, and furrow your brow.
You constantly hold a clay bowl,
different from Yán Huí's (Yán Huí) gourd utensil.
Your tin staff occasionally rings,
distinct from Yuán Xiàn's (Yuán Xiàn) thorny stick.
This place has never seen such a person;
I have never heard of such a person.
May I ask, Sir, from where have you come?"
The Master remained silent for a long while, then slowly replied:
"I see you are galloping after fame and profit, and are confused by sensual pleasures.
Though you live under heaven, you do not fathom its height;
though you tread upon the earth, you do not know its thickness.
I have heard that
within a shallow well, there are no fish that can swallow a boat.
Between the elm and the thorny zanthoxylum,
how can there be wings that touch the clouds?
I am not of your kind.
How can you understand?
Allow me to explain it to you.
I hope you will lend your noble ears for a moment.
My Teacher's (Shī) virtue is deeply rooted,
established from the beginning of the three kalpas.
His wondrous fruit alone rose high and was accomplished at the end of a hundred kalpas.
He comprehends the entire Dharma-realm with his wisdom,
and extends throughout empty space as his body.
How can it be merely that his vital energy permeates the two primal forces and his Way encompasses all things?
Thus, his body is nowhere not present,
its measure extends beyond all rules and standards.
His wisdom is all-accomplishing,
its function transcends all thought and deliberation.
He cannot be measured by human affairs,
nor can he be discussed in terms of specific locations.
To enlighten the sight and hearing of ignorant folk,
he must manifest the traces of a true person.
Just as valley winds follow the roaring tiger,
and auspicious clouds pursue the soaring dragon,
mutual responsiveness is but a constant principle.
Therefore, he descended as a spirit in the Tuṣita (Dōulǜ) Heaven,
and manifested his form in the land of Kapilavastu (Jiāpí).
His clan name was Gautama (Qútán),
his lineage was called Kṣatriya (Chàlì).
His secular name was Siddhartha (Xīdá),
and his spiritual name was Nengrén.
He was the Crown Prince of King Śuddhodana (Báijìng Wáng).
His family line had been succeeded by Cakravartin (Lúnwáng) kings;
his family tradition was based on the continuous succession of the Sacred Path.
The three thousand [kingdoms] on earth
were distinct from Luòyì;
the eighty thousand [kingdoms] of his dynasty
surpassed Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (Jīulǐng).
His royal relatives were numerous and illustrious;
who could fully recount them?
When my Teacher (Shī) was born,
the earth quaked six times and he took seven steps.
Flowers rained down throughout the five pure realms and filled the kingdom;
two dragons sprinkled water everywhere in the sky.
Divine omens and auspicious signs all converged.
Looking back over a hundred generations, none had ever seen such things.
Moreover, his conception was more extraordinary than that of Yáo and Xuān, and his birth more exceptional than that of Yǔ and Xiè.
As for the omen of the Black Emperor entering a dream,
and the auspicious sign of white light filling the room,
they are merely called auspicious;
how can they be compared or discussed?
Around his body was a golden aura of one zhàng;
between his brows was a white urna hair of five chi.
The svastika symbol unfolded on his chest;
a thousand-spoked wheel appeared on the soles of his feet.
In total, there were thirty-two major marks.
It is not possible to compare my Teacher's wondrous form, or judge its superiority or inferiority, by using the dragon-face, tiger-nose, or the eight-colored double pupils [of others].
Although Lǚ Gōng recognized Emperor Gāo's physiognomy and was considered a judge of character in his time,
if compared to Śivadatta's (Sītuó) view of my Teacher, it is not comparable in the same day.
Thereupon, he cultivated great karma and occupied the position of a young prince.
His palace gates stood wide open, and his lofty imperial towers were majestically erected.
As for his manifold talents and skills, truly accomplished in both literary and martial arts,
these were not due to teachers and guardians, but from his innate heavenly nature.
Whether during his leisure strolls by the Crown Prince's (Tàizǐ) pond,
or during his chariot races in the Bówàng (Bówàng) Garden,
his strength could wrestle a fragrant elephant, and his spirit surpassed divine prowess.
Trying to compare Jī Fā or Cáo Pī to him is impossible;
Hàn Yíng and Xià Qǐ are not even worth mentioning.
His royal father's (Fùwáng) guards were extremely strict, and his surveillance was meticulous.
Within the nine-layered forbidden palace,
his fame reached forty lǐ;
in the secret palaces for the three seasons,
there were twenty thousand beautiful attendants.
Yet, with his serene and steadfast spiritual nature and firm aspirations,
although dwelling in the realm of the three delusions,
he did not change his single-minded resolve.
He passed through the four gates of the royal city (Wángchéng),
and grieved over the three sufferings of old age, sickness, and death.
He then sighed to himself,
"If human life is like this, how can one endure in the world?
To cast off one's shoes and seek the truth, this is the time!"
At that time, peach blossoms were raining down new flowers;
early spring was just in its middle.
The moon was a half-disk hanging low in the pavilion;
the long night was just beginning to deepen.
He observed the sleeping courtesans as if they were corpses;
he realized the inner palace was like a decaying tomb.
Heavenly kings carried his white horse over the city wall;
attendants held his precious crown and proceeded to the palace gate.
Although Xiāo Shǐ in the Qín (Qín) era and Zǐ Jìn in the Zhōu (Zhōu) era,
Xǔ Yóu washed his ears at Mount Jīshān (Jīshān),
and Zhuāng Zhōu dragged his tail in the Púshǔi,
compared to his renunciation of the world, how insignificant they are!
Thus, the immortal grove became the place where he first pulled out his hairpin;
the river of meditation began the traces of his ascetic practices.
He bathed in the pure water of the golden stream,
and wandered among the auspicious trees of the Bodhi (Dàocháng) site.
He ate the gruel offered by Jīa Xiàn and sat on the grass provided by Shī Cǎo.
Thereupon, his ten powers and wisdom became complete, and his six supernormal powers were perfected.
The demonic armies were swept away, and the great task was accomplished.
He alone was called "Buddha" (Fó).
This is my Teacher (Shī).
The Dharma wheel was first turned in the Deer Park (Nà Guó);
the first monk to be converted was Kaundinya (Jiàochén).
As for Kāśyapa (Jiāyè) and his brothers,
Maudgalyāyana (Mùlián) and his friends,
Mahāsthāmaprāpta (Dàshì) in the west,
Samantabhadra (Biànjí) in the east,
the lords of the twenty-eight heavens,
and the kings of the sixteen countries,
none did not submit to his Way and incline their hearts,
eating the wind and pressing their palms together.
Thereupon, in the Tāpālavāsanavartin (Tāhuà) Palace, he expounded the ten bhūmis;
and on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (Qíshéshān), he gathered the three vehicles.
Subhūti (Shànjí) spoke of the doctrine of non-attainment;
Vimalakīrti (Jìngmíng) manifested the essence of non-verbalization.
He subdued the ten heterodox immortals,
and restrained the six groups of bhikṣus.
From his chest, he could emit rivers;
within his palm, he could shake mountains and valleys.
When speaking of kalpas, even stone slabs repeatedly wear away;
when debating numbers, even specks of dust can be exhausted.
This is the great Teacher (Dàshī) of the three realms,
the unique wanderer of all ages.
I am but a common talent; how can I fully describe him?
Even if Dī (Zhōu Gōng) formulated rites and created music,
Kǒngzǐ (Kǒngzǐ) edited the Yì (Yì) and compiled the Shī (Shī),
Zǐ Cì's (Zǐ Cì) eloquence,
and Zǐ Xià's (Shāng Yǎn) literary accomplishments, as well as Zuǒ Yuánfàng (Zuǒ Yuánfàng), Gě Xiàoxiān (Gě Xiàoxiān), Héshàng Gōng (Héshàng Gōng), and Zhùxià Shǐ (Zhùxià Shǐ),
if they all competed within this world,
what are they worth mentioning?
Since my spiritual awareness, my blessings have ended, and the Dharma King has passed away.
Thus, facing north by the Nairañjanā (Tíhé) River, his spring and autumn were eighty.
His manifested body was shattered into particles; what can recall the flowing blood?
They contended to resolve their last doubts,
and vied to offer their final tributes.
Alas! The lamp of wisdom extinguished, the cloud of compassion vanished.
How truly pitiable are all beings in this long night!
Thereupon, they gazed upon his auspicious marks on sandalwood,
and recorded the verbal teachings on palm leaves.
The Tripiṭaka (Sānzàng) was upheld and received, and the Four Reliances took their place.
Thus, my Teacher's (Shī) Dharma wind has not diminished.
However, the ways of the world are bustling and extravagant, and human sentiments are fickle. Generations come and go.
As the Dharma-image (xiàngyùn) era was coming to an end in the north, it gradually moved eastward.
Thus, the golden man appeared in Emperor Míng's (Liú Zhuāng) dream,
and Mātaṅga (Móténg) responded to Cài Yīn's (Cài Yīn) invitation.
The transmission of his teachings to the Hàn (Hàn) land
first began here.
To this day, it has been over five hundred years.
Afterwards, Kāng Sēnghuì (Kāng Sēnghuì), Zhú Fǎwéi (Zhú Fǎwéi), Fótúchéng (Fótúchéng), and Jiūmóshí (Jiūmóshí)
followed in succession, propagating the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) teachings.
This led to companions like Dàoshēng (Dàoshēng) and Dào'ān (Dào'ān),
and disciples like Huìyán (Huìyán) and Huìguān (Huìguān),
all quieting their voices, hanging up their official hats, and earnestly returning to the Way.
The Buddhist (Zīmén) community flourished beyond words.
I grew up in Shāndōng (Shāndōng),
admiring the elegant karma of the Uncrowned King (Sùwáng).
Later, I traveled in Guān Yòu (Guān Yòu),
admiring the profound words of Huáng Lǎo (Huáng Lǎo).
Both are still unable to cross the river of suffering,
still submerged in the burning house.
That which can endure and be great, is it not Buddhism (Fójiào)?
So, I aspired to the pure dust of previous generations,
and looked up to the distant traces of the noble ones.
I returned to this Right Path, extricating myself from the mire.
My original name was "Hermit of Leaving Desire" and "Great General who Crushes Evil."
Do my comrades refer to this?
The young master (Gōngzǐ) frowned and said,
"Watching your arguments,
one could talk about heaven.
But what you say is too fantastic.
I secretly observe that when the Buddha (Fó) first began his teachings,
it was during the era of our Zōng Zhōu (Zōng Zhōu).
He himself said,
'The Sahā (Suōpó) world is entirely encompassed, there is nowhere that does not return.'
Or that 'his light shone without bounds, his voice shook the highest heavens.'
Or that 'the eight classes of beings gathered like clouds, and the ten directions converged like spokes.'
Given that Tiānzhú (Tiānzhú) is over a hundred thousand lǐ away from us,
both being south of Mount Sumeru (Xūmí),
and both within Jambudvīpa (Yánfú),
why is it that suddenly none of the common people here reached the Buddha's (Fó) presence?
And why did the Tathāgata (Rúlái) alone choose not to bestow his light on others?
He was not born in our Qín (Qín) and Hàn (Hàn) dynasties,
nor recorded in our books.
Detailed examination of these two or three points makes my doubts even greater.
I have heard that the chaste do not abandon society, and hermits do not forsake their families.
Therefore, one should blend one's light in the dust,
and blossom like a lotus in fire.
As for wearing belts and dangling caps, it does not hinder cultivating virtue.
Keeping a beard and long sideburns is sufficient for a leisurely life.
Moreover, the Way is fundamentally pervasive, and there is nowhere it is not present.
Why abandon caps and hairpins, and focus solely on robes and begging bowls?
I secretly believe that not harming one's body is the beginning of filial piety.
Are we not all subjects of the king, ultimately following the court's commands?
Now you are clad in ochre robes and have shaven heads.
I am unclear as to your crime."
Not serving the Son of Heaven.
Are you not being arrogant, daring to consult this humble sir?
Please allow me to elaborate.
The Master said:
I have heard that great music does not penetrate rustic ears.
Is this the proof?
You still wish to view the sky with a small tube and measure the ocean with a tiny conch.
Yet my Dharma gate is far-reaching,
not something my son can fully comprehend.
I shall now
rely on divine power to speak of it further. My teacher's transformative Dao is vast and profound, its spiritual harmony reaching far and wide.
However, sentient beings have shallow karma,
thus limiting themselves.
How can it be that the Buddha's majesty is not great
or that his sacred grace is not universal?
It is like the sun and moon hanging bright in the sky,
and thunder resounding through the earth,
yet they are overlooked by the deaf and blind.
How can it be that their light is dim or their sound small?
Furthermore, when the Buddha traveled in Shèwèi, for more than two decades, three hundred million households
still did not hear or see him.
How can one wonder about a borderland a hundred thousand *lǐ* away?
I secretly believe that when Zhōu Kǒng lived,
it was solely within the cities of Huáxià.
Why did the barbarians not believe his principles?
As for Dōngfāng Shuò ascending to heaven,
and the King of Huáinán entering the register of immortals,
there were indeed people who rode phoenixes and parted mists in the world.
If they were not superior in immortal arts, these things would have been kept secret and not recorded.
How could they understand the Daoist arts of my teacher
and record them in the official histories?
Moreover, during Qín Huáng's burning of books, the classics were incomplete.
How can one cling to such limited texts
and thus lack great insight? However, there may be some who, being truly righteous, are content with following worldly customs.
They have not yet realized that their bodies are not pure.
How can they comprehend their destiny?
If one constantly enjoys and takes pleasure, the cycles of transmigration will not cease.
If one is stingy and greedy, not a single hair will fall.
Such petty and stubborn people are truly pitiful.
I no longer have concern for my physical form.
Who would bother with physical beauty?
My hair and beard are shorn, and my mind is naturally subdued.
My robes are of muted color; how can love arise?
Therefore, I make five types of repairs to uphold right thought,
and six times a day I fix my mind.
Thus detached from worldly things, this is called swimming against the current.
I have secretly heard that when Xià Yǔ channeled rivers, he toiled with his hands and feet.
When Mò Dí benefited the people, he did not spare his head or heels.
To sacrifice one's life to achieve benevolence,
or starve to death to preserve righteousness—
these all go against great filial piety,
yet they are highly praised in many books.
How much more so for me, cultivating my nature, dwelling in the profound, establishing my character, and practicing the Dao!
I seek to widely save the six realms and aspire to myriad virtues.
How can a scholar restrict me to minor details
and concern for skin and hair?
To pursue fleeting fame is a trivial matter,
like serving at court as a subject.
If the achievements are shallow and the salary meager,
it is only tiresome to run errands.
If the merit is high, there is no leisure; if the position is extreme, one constantly fears danger, excess, and instability.
To abandon a pearl worth a thousand *rèn*—how cheap one holds such a treasure!
But the lotus within the fire is not something I have produced.
How can you know "being stained yet not stained"?
The young master said:
You, Master, are boastfully decorating wrong with flowery words,
and protecting overgrown fences without sweeping them clean.
Please listen to my blunt but sincere criticism.
I will briefly list four of its faults.
I have heard that a jade tree does not grow in a reed marsh,
and a majestic phoenix does not flock with sparrows and swallows.
Though your Dao, Master, is subtle and profound,
why are your disciples so common and lowly?
Some are of unsightly form and humble lineage,
or of low status and dim spirit.
They lack the three virtues to join the multitude of scholars,
and lack ten *mǔ* to be considered ordinary men.
They are not skilled in royal affairs,
and are ashamed of not establishing their own private households.
They find refuge from labor in Buddhist temples,
barely fitting themselves beneath the Dharma robes.
They cannot exchange greetings with people,
and when reading scriptures, do not understand the correct pronunciation or meaning.
They only know how to hold a high opinion of themselves before common people,
and disregard rites towards their parents.
This is not how to bring honor to oneself.
This is the first fault.
I have heard of the frugality of thatched roofs and earthen steps,
by which Táng Yáo nurtured the people.
And the extravagance of jade palaces and platforms,
by which Shāng Xīn ruined customs.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, whose conduct is only of little desire and whose virtue is fundamentally great compassion!
He should only sit peacefully in graveyards
and walk beneath trees.
How is it proper to adorn nine-story stūpas
and build seven-jeweled platforms?
Not pitying the laborers' toil,
nor feeling shame for the residents' ease.
This is not how to restrain oneself.
This is the second fault.
I have heard that not boasting of one's achievements is Lǎo Dān's ultimate teaching,
and not praising one's own virtue is the Buddha's maxim.
To be diligent and humble leads to ultimate good fortune for a gentleman.
To be self-restrained and yielding is the highest virtue for a sage.
If inner virtue is truly abundant, it will naturally resonate outwardly,
evoking praise from guests and companions without effort.
How much more so for the Buddha's mind, which is clear and calm, free from the faults of gain and loss!
How then can you uniquely grant the title of "Shìzūn" (World-Honored One)
and not wish to defer to others?
Yet, among those scriptures, which are the unparalleled root,
each claims the title of "first."
This creates internal contradictions.
How can this be resolved?
This is not how to be modest. This is the third fault.
I have heard that holding two treasures in mind and being cautious of the four knowings
is called the refined broad-mindedness of an enlightened person
and the lofty integrity of an honest scholar.
Sometimes they share with their relatives,
or discard their wealth in mountains and rivers.
How much more so for the profound Dao, which is pure and clean!
Yet, monastics who renounce worldly life still indulge in insatiable desires
and covet worldly gains.
When exhorting laypeople, they tell them not to withhold even marrow or brain.
When discussing donations, they instantly allow no yielding of a single fraction.
When nobles pass by,
or honored guests arrive,
they do not receive them with an open mind,
but first declare the multiple amount expected for a handout.
This is a common ailment among the discerning,
known by all within the four seas.
This is not how to be incorruptible.
This is the fourth fault.
My direct words, though bitter, can serve as medicine and stone.
I only hope, Master, that your lofty insight will consider them thoroughly.
Xiānshēng 曰:
“Wúzi, if you don't laugh, what is the Dào?
You merely like what is similar,
how can you know what is different?
You merely wish to ruin and destroy, but the adamantine is not yet harmed.
Our Dào is vast and profound, how can it be taken lightly?
I have heard that when all affairs are brought together,
the Sagely Emperor is therefore called great.
When a hundred rivers are taken in,
the giant ocean is therefore deep.
A king does not reject the common people,
and the sea does not cast aside small streams.
How much more so our master's Great Dào, which is vast and omits none in its salvation!
All who have a mind are embraced without distinguishing between grudges and affections.
Naturally, it categorizes the small and great of precepts and virtues,
and blends the high and low of clans and types.
Hence, there are ordinary people who clear dung,
who unexpectedly attain the position of non-birth;
and noble scholars who respond to the call of books,
who fall headlong into the Avīci Hell.
What is secretly hidden and hard to know, who can comprehend its outer form?
How can you presume to act as the standard of judgment?
I do not yet allow you to be a clear mirror.
If one merely judges people by their appearance,
one will be far mistaken.
Thus, Shūxiàng uttered words of contempt
and the elder awakened to the words of the śrāmaṇera.
Moreover, prosperity and adversity have their turns, good and ill fortune are not constant.
Some begin in glory and end in disgrace,
some are initially humble and later rise to prominence.
Different paths spin in confusion,
it can be briefly stated.
As for those without a place to stand even an awl,
they did not necessarily admire the virtue of Yáo and Shùn.
Those whose remaining plans were not inherited,
did they necessarily transmit the sagacity of Tāng and Wǔ?
How could one know that the one who swallowed the Six States
was previously a horse herdsman?
And the one who 'simplified the laws to three chapters'
was merely a fugitive village chief?
Fán Kàn and Guàn originated from vendors and butchers.
Yī Yǐ and Lǚ came from the kitchen and fishing.
Through successive generations, high families followed each other,
thus becoming the powerful clans of the four seas and the Wǔlíng.
Noble families, their caps and coronets reaching the clouds, their refined elegance
covering the age, are like the morning sun drying dew, envying the difficulty of retaining a dark-skinned slave.
Old grass bearing frost mixes with ants, indistinguishable.
From this, one knows that in terms of being employed or not, how can tigers and mice be constant?
Seeking the end and tracing the root, human affairs are all the same.
How can one suddenly lightly ride in a carriage and despise these 'jar-windows'?
Even if one's talent equals Zhōu Dàn,
what is there to see?
Let me try to explain.
The court and market are vain anxieties, body and mind are fruitlessly exhausted.
The wise universally discard them, the worthy commonly scorn them.
One merely feels that this embrace is accessible,
and so retreats from the world and returns.
I am tired of the coming suffering and realize the wrongs of yesterday.
You, however, indulge in past desires and are deluded by present rights.
Rather, be content in poverty and delight in the Dào, be humble when young but capable when old.
Why use the sacrificial oxen of the Tàimiào
or the geese cooked by the servants?
I now live in my natural state, my silent thoughts are pure.
I do not rely on guidance from benevolence and righteousness,
how can I disturb my thoughts with luxury and splendor?
Indeed, I abandon the male and female, forgetting food and sleep.
How can I cling to the petty talents of 'warmth and cold'
or the meager skills of 'sound and meaning'?
Cultivating the mind can repay kindness,
why be confined by the rituals of morning and evening greetings?
Broadening transformation can attract and guide,
why be limited to bowing and looking up?
This is what I call the first superiority.
Our master's abode of emptiness and tranquility is not limited to settlements.
He values and accepts the humble and insignificant, not exclusively pearls and ornaments.
Therefore, he dwells in the five mountains, his spirit roams the three abodes.
Sometimes he accepts earth given by children,
sometimes he eats horse fodder.
He praises the small offerings made with a pure mind,
and criticizes the abundant donations made with mixed intentions.
He hopes that through this, good roots may be established,
and through this, sincerity and trust may be demonstrated.
This is merely an initial offering, a general principle of constant giving.
It is not that the Buddha's body desires it,
but rather it is the aspiration of sentient beings.
However, because ordinary people are difficult to enlighten and arrogance and jealousy are not yet removed,
they compete to offer famous treasures, believing wealth brings much good fortune.
Thus, jade platforms and lofty pagodas
soar to the mid-sky, eclipsing the sun.
Embroidered rafters and flying eaves
connect with the clouds, covering the whole land.
Competing for fame and preferring such things,
where then is goodness?
Clinging to forms with meager understanding,
it has come to this.
Although it deviates from the principle of ultimate truth,
it is sufficient to inspire the joy of glory and splendor.
For sentient beings, this is an accomplishment.
How can the Tathāgata suppress such a teaching?
This is what I call the second superiority.
I have heard that speaking of priceless rare treasures
is hoped to save the poor.
Praising the deathless divine incense
is only to cure illnesses.
But sentient beings believe in the wild drugs of evil shamans,
abandoning the sweet dew of the Rightly Awakened.
Their affliction is already deep, their delusion self-inflicted for a long time.
When our master appeared in the world,
he originally took salvation as his accomplishment.
Those who know me are few, there is no room for silence.
To make beings know the truth and turn towards it,
how can one distinguish right and wrong and take it for oneself?
If two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously in the world,
and two suns do not share the sky,
then his title is unparalleled, intending to spread the ultimate teaching.
It is not like a gentleman's petty saintliness, who cultivates a spirit of humility and deference.
It is already known that ultimate principles converge, but differing explanations arise from varying sentiments.
Therefore, this Sūtra is called supreme, each should hear it appropriately.
This is what I call the third superiority.
I have heard that without pursuing the profits of the four classes of people,
one cannot obtain a hundred ounces of gold.
But great suffering is not yet gone, there is still something to sustain.
I am called a beggar,
so I receive it with contentment.
You are called a donor,
so you pour out your wealth, even a state or city.
How can you blame me for greed,
without yourself measuring your own stinginess and concealment?
This proves
that sharing wealth appropriately, why should it only be Guǎn Bào?
I have heard that when the Heavenly King's armory issues provisions,
it still does not go through his subordinates.
How much more so our master's blessings and provisions,
how can they be solely managed by ordinary monks?
Although they originally come from the four groups,
they are now used for the Three Jewels.
For the Dào to establish offerings means the principle of acting for blessings.
Since it is for the constant residence of the ten directions,
it is not said to be privately owned by oneself.
If one acts on one's own, the Vinaya does not permit it.
If one asks the assembly, then harmony cannot be achieved.
What virtue do you have to consume it?
What feelings do I have to dare to appropriate it?
I only fear sharing the same fault,
how could I desire greed?
I privately believe that a grain of rice weighs seven catties,
if thrown into water, smoke and fire will boil.
One bowl of leftover rice,
if given to others, multitudes will be filled.
The Buddha shows no miserliness towards hungry dogs,
how could he be sparing towards people?
Therefore, one knows that random use truly invites blame,
while giving back in return allows for gain.
This is truly the meager fortune of sentient beings,
definitely not the narrow-mindedness of our master.
As for hungry ghosts not seeing flowing rivers,
and sick people not tasting delicious food,
the sin lies with the hungry and sick,
how can it be that the river or the taste is absent?
I secretly heard that when meritorious ministers serve their lord,
grain and silk are bestowed without distinction to reward their achievements.
When an enlightened king reproaches himself,
the blue sky silently manifests its virtue.
You cannot lament your own lack of spiritual connection,
but instead solely slander our master for his lack of beneficence.
With such gluttony, what kind of person are you?
As for the Duke of Zhèng who squandered his wealth on friends,
and Lord Tián who spread his heart to guests,
they merely sought the reputation of extravagance and influence,
how could they compare to sowing in the field of merit and spreading it widely?
This is what I call the fourth superiority.
Although my words are insufficient, the principle has an abundance.
You are merely surprised by what you have not heard and confused by what you have not seen.
What I have said, you can now understand.”
Gōngzǐ 曰:
“Though you, Xiānshēng, speak eloquently to clear yourself, you ultimately resemble one who ‘waits by the stump’.
The retribution you speak of, how profoundly subtle it is!
I have heard that when chaos was first divided, the pure and the turbid separated.
The thin and thick received different endowments, and the foolish and sagely diverged.
As for the roundness of heads and squareness of feet,
the scales and feathers of those who fly and those who dive,
the length or shortness of one's fate, the honor or disgrace of one's body and name,
none are not the creations of nature,
how can they be the doing of past karma?
I have secretly observed that those who practice admirable conduct
die young and suffer calamities.
Those who are arrogant and rude
live out their full years and enjoy blessings.
If occurrences are like this, how can cause and effect be proven?
Moreover, when breath gathers, one is born; when it scatters, one dies.
Form and spirit, the former ascends, the latter sinks.
All things are vast and empty; a hundred years is over.
Where is the Heavenly Palace? Who is in hell?
This is what common people believe,
but enlightened scholars have not spoken of it.
Xiānshēng, you are still bound by confusion,
please reconsider.”
The Master said:
Young Master is indeed an eloquent speaker!
Yet your understanding is so superficial.
What you discuss does not exceed a hundred generations,
and what you have experienced does not go beyond the eight wildernesses.
How can you understand the ultimate end of retribution,
or discern the fundamental reality of cause and condition?
One must not limit oneself to the ordinary six consciousnesses and ignore the saintly three insights.
I have heard that sowing and planting all grains
is not solely due to the merit of water and soil.
The creation of the four modes of birth,
how can it be merely the power of yin and yang?
Since there are roots in species,
it is also inseparable from aggregation and arising.
I observe that some couples, though united, cannot conceive children and grandchildren;
others are neither widowers nor widows, yet the numbers of men and women are not balanced.
As for fireflies flying, cicadas transforming, beehives, and ant eggs,
their production is not formed from two essences.
How could it be due to the function of two stores?
If it were merely received from Heaven and Earth,
then why would people rely on parents?
If all merely relied on fate, what would become of parental kindness and filial piety?
Thus we know that causes are inherently varied, and only then do results interlink.
These branch into three retributions, scattered like stars among myriad kinds.
Some are received quickly in this life;
others are achieved later in the next life.
This principle is inevitable, so how could it perish?
I humbly believe that rewards and punishments are not arbitrary,
which is the enlightened law of a ruler.
Sins and blessings are without discrepancy,
which is the great achievement of the path of karma.
In human governance, there are the five punishments and rewards of emolument and position.
In the unseen realm, there are the punishments of the three evil paths and the blessings of human and heavenly realms.
What is before our eyes can serve as a warning and admonition.
How could this be an empty theory I have invented?
If you haven't yet been imprisoned, who would believe there's a Tíngwèi?
If one does not travel to Dàizōng, one then assumes there is no ghost realm.
But when good and evil accumulate, disaster and blessings abound.
This is recorded in excellent classics, but you do not yet know it.
As for the cases of Shūlè,
and the gushing spring,
the great river and the horizontal stone's inspiration,
Yáng Gōng and his white jade, Guō Jù and his gold,
the piebald horse marking Bào Xuān,
and the pearl descending for Kuài Cān's crane.
As well as King Xuān's demise caused by Dù Bó,
and Duke Xiāng's fright caused by Péng Shēng.
The omen of Bái Qǐ's willing death,
the verification of Lǐ Guǎng not being ennobled as a marquis.
Lù Kàng's calamity was inherited by his descendants.
Guō Ēn's misfortune stopped with his own person.
These are all very clear.
Who can say they are obscure?
Although the Liùjīng do not speak of them,
yet sacrificing to gods and ghosts has been passed down since the Sāndài.
If death leads to nothingness,
why seek to exist through benevolent conduct?
It is not proper to abandon the minor teachings of Rú Mò,
and lose the great principle of the unseen and the seen.
It is regrettable that your good talent is so extremely foolish and stubborn.
You should quickly return, repent, and embody my true words.
The Young Master said:
"Though you, Master, possess a torrential and unrestrained eloquence,
there are still things that obscure your view.
I have heard that Heaven gives birth to the myriad people, pairing the firm with the yielding,
thereby transforming forms and vessels, and nourishing the vital spirit.
Marriage has been a grand rule since ancient times;
taking a wife or marrying off a daughter has been a constant rite through successive generations.
Sin should not pertain to offspring,
nor should the Way be hindered by wives and concubines.
Thus, Shàn Huì (善惠) permitted the flower-selling agreement,
and Miào Guāng (妙光) accepted the offering of pearls.
The sixty thousand fragrances are still called 'Dharma Masters,'
and the two thousand of Vimalakīrti (毘耶) are still called 'Great Beings.'
Why then alone abandon this marital pairing and suppress such sentiments?
A 'proud dragon will have cause to repent' (亢龍有悔) –
if its desires are such,
how then can living things be born?
Through whom will the Buddha-seed be continued?
This is the first obscurity of your view, Master.
I have heard that fierce beasts are the karma of violent people,
and venomous insects contain the nature of harming creatures.
Therefore, in accordance with the qi, we hunt in autumn,
and to eliminate harm, we till in summer.
What crime is there in the constant Way of Heaven that we should fear?
As for cattle and pigs filling the sacrificial offerings, and lambs and geese preparing the rites,
their destiny is to fall into the hands of the cook,
their bodies interred in the stomachs of honored guests.
Originally born by Heaven, for what else could they be used?
And yet, if a bird dies a natural death, Bān Tīng (班聽) applies internal regulations.
How then can one neglect to nourish form and life, and merely become dust and dirt?
This is the second obscurity of your view, Master.
I have heard that Heaven arrays the Dipper constellation (Jī Xīng 箕星) and Earth settles Quán Jùn (泉郡).
As for wine, its origin is quite ancient.
Is it uniquely suited to dispel sorrow and harmonize nature?
Thus, the Seven Sages, Jī Ruǎn (嵇阮),
stirred their emotions with measures of dou and shi.
The two sages, Xūn Huá (勛華),
showed their great virtue in their consumption of zhong and hu.
Guǎn (管) relied on it to discuss the profound,
and Yú (于) used it to judge cases.
I have heard of the ancient wise ones;
they never failed to hold banquets.
As long as one adheres to propriety,
why obstruct the many and remain uniquely
pure? This is the third obscurity of your view, Master.
I have heard that the Eight Policies (Bā Zhèng 八政) emphasize food as the people's Heaven,
and the five flavors provide for the body, the vessel of the Way.
From this, we breathe the wind and mists, and consume the dew of immortality-herbs.
Dare we say that all living beings do not rely on these?
If one can eat one's fill,
and one's mind is not neglectful of the path of cultivation,
what need is there to hold a fast,
wearying the strength and diminishing diligence in practice?
This is the fourth obscurity of your view, Master.
If you, Master, would change these obscurities,
I too would admire you."
The Master said:
"I have heard that the rigid and strong are difficult to transform; it is indeed as you say.
As for your obscurities,
you do not know them to be obscurities.
As for my pervasiveness (通),
how can you recognize its pervasiveness?
From this perspective,
one cannot yet speak of the Way with you.
I secretly believe that rude words are uncivil, yet still avoid close relatives.
Evil conduct is unkind, yet still shames those who came before.
However, if a male has barely left his swaddling clothes,
he longs for a flying pair and seeks a wife.
If a female has just ceased suckling,
she laments an empty room and harbors feelings.
If one greedily seeks small pleasures and publicly practices worldly rites,
and long-standing habits become the norm, who would find it strange?
To be shameless in this regard is even worse than quails and magpies.
Do not take the marriage customs of common folk as daring to defy the refined elegance of the noble.
Moreover, 'hūn' (婚, marriage) is 'hūn' (昏, dusk).
The affair relies on the completion of the dusk (昏成).
It is clearly not a bright and splendid standard,
but indeed a dangerous practice of the vulgar and base.
Only the integrity of Zhǎn Qín (展禽) at Liǔ Xià (柳下)
can reprimand licentious men.
The art of Péng Zǔ (彭祖) sleeping alone
can nourish a harmonious nature.
These are indeed propagated in good books,
and lauded in historical records.
How much more so are these the perfected teachings of our Master,
the fundamental scriptures that promote pure conduct!
How can one then follow those evil trends,
and become entangled in the net of desire?
To transcend the realm of the Six Heavens (liù tiān 六天),
one still does not take concubines.
Having surpassed the Four Empty Realms (sì kōng 四空),
how can one cling to wives and children?
Only the white-clad practitioners of the second fruit
are permitted by karmic ties.
The recluse who shares a single bed (yī chuáng jū shì 一床居士) is pure and difficult to defile.
However, the birth of living things
has its own karmic causes.
Why must they await our pairing to propagate?
Have you not heard, regarding our Master, that all beings are born through transformation, men have no female karma, all are free from the four great elements, and are nourished by the joy of Dharma?
This is what I call the first pervasiveness (tōng 通).
I have heard that birth and death, coming and going, fundamentally move like an inchworm (bù huò 步蠖).
Manifestation and obscurity, rising and falling, are no different from cycles.
As karma operates, how can humans and animals be constant?
Thus, followers like Wèi Jī (衛姬) and Shǔ Dì (蜀帝),
and those like Niú Āi (牛哀) and Bó Qí (伯奇)—
foxes becoming beautiful women, badgers becoming scholars—
these matters are indeed hard to conceive,
how can they be easily understood?
I secretly believe that observing precepts fears no ghosts or dragons;
embodying virtue fears no bees or scorpions.
A frightened pigeon casts a shadow, a fierce tiger crosses a river.
If I am good, it repays me with bright pearls;
if a person is evil, it responds with poisonous qi.
This is indeed due to the qi of life and death.
How can animals be solely harmful?
Though flying and walking creatures differ in form,
they are no different in cherishing their bodies.
In endless cycles of rebirth, who is not one's relative?
If one takes oneself as an analogy, what can one not bear to do?
How can one butcher the flesh and blood of living beings
to fill useless flesh and skin?
As for returning to the earth upon death, all things and I share the same fate.
Thus, Huáng (黃) did not eat soft-shelled turtles,
and Kǒng (孔) still covered the jar of vinegar.
How much more so my compassionate pity:
who could find fresh fat delicious?
But the five precepts are gradually revealed, and the Twin Groves (shuāng lín 雙林) establish eternal rules.
This is what I call the second pervasiveness (tōng 通).
I have heard that drinking like an ox from a wine pond was recorded in the past.
Though the numbers of the hundred and six were exhausted,
chaotic states still arose from it.
The thirty-five failings
indeed had their origins there.
But if one is intoxicated in this life,
this can be verified.
What will become of the gloom of the next life?
As for Wén Jǔ (文舉)'s goblet never being empty,
and Xuán Shí (玄石)'s difficult-to-awaken slumber,
these were merely the crazed guests addicted to wine.
How can they discuss the ultimate Way?
Excessive indulgence in deep drinking is too much;
a slight banquet is a minor transgression.
To say that drinking is without calamity
has never been the case.
The solemn warnings of past sages
must be for this reason.
