how is this not exalting the worthy?
Once valuing and loving exist, then beauty and ugliness must be manifest.
This is not what "what is the difference" means.
Another later chapter says,
"What people teach, I also teach others.
My words are very easy to know,
yet no one in the world can know them."
Moreover, it is said:
"I shall take this as a teaching." Yuán Sī (原斯) discussed this.
It is not a complete learning.
What is meant by "complete" (絕)?
Is it the learning of Yáo (堯) and Kǒng (孔)?
The learning of Yáo (堯) and Kǒng (孔) established teachings according to the times.
The words of Lǎo Shì (老氏) unify what he values. Establishing teachings according to the times
allows the Dào (道) to be communicated through a hundred generations.
Unifying what one values
inevitably leads to stagnation in adapting to change.
This is another obscurity
that cannot be understood.
"The Dào (道) is empty, yet its use is inexhaustible."
"It harmonizes its light and identifies with its dust."
Shèng (盛) believes that Lǎo Dān (老聃) can be said to "know the Dào (道),"
but not to be one who "embodies the Dào (道)."
In ancient times, when Táo Táng (陶唐) governed the world,
was there ever a day of respite?
Thus, Wéi Zhāo (維昭) appointed many teachers and bestowed upon commoners.
Then, he grandly abdicated the throne.
Was this not "empty yet using it," and "light and dust identifying with him"?
Bó Yáng (伯陽) was not like that.
Already in a defiled position, he further guided the Xī Róng (西戎) afar.
In his actions, Chāng Kuáng (昌狂) confused his traces.
In writing his book, he twisted and deceived with his words.
Is "harmonizing light and identifying with dust" truly like this?
I firmly believe that he "knew the Dào (道)" but did not "embody the Dào (道)."
The Dào Jīng (道經) says:
"These three cannot be fully investigated;
they blend into one."
"Continuous, indistinct, it cannot be named;
it returns to the state of no-thing."
"The image of no-thing is called the vague and indistinct (hū huǎng 忽怳)."
The next chapter says:
"The Dào (道) as a thing, is vague and indistinct (huǎng yǔ hū 怳與忽)."
"Oh, indistinct (hū)! Oh, vague (huǎng)! Within it there is an image."
"Oh, vague (huǎng)! Oh, indistinct (hū)! Within it there is a thing."
These two chapters either speak of "no-thing"
or speak of "having things."
There is something inappropriate from the start.
"Hold to the Dào (道) of antiquity to manage the existence of today."
The preceding chapter says, "He who grasps loses, he who acts fails."
Yet it then says, "Hold to the Dào (道) of antiquity to manage the existence of today."
Sometimes it advocates grasping, sometimes not.
Is it not falling into contradictory arguments?
"Abandon sageliness, discard wisdom, and the people will benefit a hundredfold."
Sūn Shèng (孫盛) said:
"Indeed, where there are benevolent sages, there must be virtues of benevolent sages.
If one does not revere these traces,
then the teachings of Táo (陶) will dissolve.
If benevolence and righteousness are not valued,
then the Dào (道) of filial piety and compassion will be lost."
Lǎo Shì (老氏) already said "abandon sageliness,"
yet in every chapter he frequently refers to "the sage."
If he refers to "the sage," how can these traces be abandoned?
If what he wishes to abandon
are the traces of Yáo (堯), Shùn (舜), Zhōu (周), and Kǒng (孔),
then "the sage" he refers to
whose traces are they?
Even if it is as he says,
that there are sages whose traces should be extinguished,
and those whose traces should be extolled,
if extolling and extinguishing differ, whom should we follow?
"Abandon benevolence, discard righteousness, and the people will return to filial piety and compassion."
If this is the argument,
then if benevolence and righteousness are not abandoned, people will be unfilial and uncompassionate.
He further says:
"Dwelling in a good place, associating with good benevolence."
I am unsure whether the "benevolence" in "associating with good benevolence"
is the same as the "benevolence" he previously said he wished to abandon or not.
If it is the same,
then it should not be mentioned again.
If it is not the same,
then the meaning of these two types of benevolence is not clear:
one benevolence should be abandoned,
one benevolence should be elucidated.
This is another point he has not clarified.
If he means the "sageliness of not being a sage" and the "benevolence of not being benevolent,"
then the teaching he condemns would not need such high-sounding pronouncements.
Going further, to Zhuāng Zhōu (莊周) it is said, "If sages do not die, great bandits will not cease."
And it is also said:
"Tián Cháng (田常) usurped benevolence and righteousness to seize the state of Qí (齊)."
Heaven and Earth cast and mold, nurturing both good and evil.
Each receives its natural principle, and they are not related to each other.
Owls and shrikes unleash their venom
without needing to learn from phoenixes.
Jackals and tigers commit harm
without borrowing techniques from麒麟 Qí Lín (麒麟).
These are all natural qualities;
they do not require external things.
Why should only vicious and stubborn people need to feign benevolence and righteousness to carry out their villainy?
As for Mò Dú (冒頓) who killed his father, and Zhèng Bó (鄭伯) who stole Kuài (鄶),
did they first feign filial piety to achieve their ultimate harm?
Yet Zhuāng (莊) and Lǐ (李) attack and destroy the root, refuting and rejecting correct teachings.
How is this different from hating thieves and bandits but melting down spears and shields,
or seeing someone choke on food and then discarding all good grains?
Later commentators, though they twistedly tried to argue and explain its meaning,
all struggled with "killing sages" and stumbled over "forgetting parents."
"Few know me, then I am esteemed."
The preceding chapter says:
"When the sage is in the world,
the common people all direct their ears and eyes to him."
Teacher-student esteem and love will surely manifest throughout all things.
If this is the case, how can those who know him be few?
Why should those who know him be few necessarily be esteemed?
Even if one is personally esteemed,
how can the nine regions attain it?
To disregard facts and speak defiantly that one is esteemed
because few know him,
this is probably to try and curb the common customs,
hence these exaggerated words were uttered.
The teachings of the sages are not like this.
They temper their words with reason to instruct and guide.
Therefore, it is said:
"At home, one must hear [of him];
in the state, one must hear [of him]."
To hear means to comprehend.
"Not seeing goodness, yet without discontent"
is the virtue of the "hidden dragon."
"Not being known by others, yet without resentment"
is the Dào (道) of the gentleman.
"When the multitude likes him, he must examine them."
"When the multitude dislikes him, he must examine them."
He is neither glorified by being known by many,
nor is he esteemed by being known by few.
The instruction and guidance are ample, naturally conforming to reason.
How can they be compared with the words of Lǎo Dān (老聃) on the same day to judge their superiority or inferiority?
"Ritual is the thinness of loyalty and trustworthiness,
and the beginning of disorder."
"Foreknowledge is the flower of the Dào (道),
and the beginning of foolishness."
"Therefore, the great person dwells in its depth, not in its thinness;
dwells in its reality, not in its flower."
Sūn Shèng (孫盛) said:
"Lǎo Dān (老聃) knew well that the rites and music of the sages
are not tools of profound excellence,
but were created only out of necessity.
Yet why did he intentionally disparage them?
It was to set aside ritual studies to complete his
'natural principle' (zì rán zhī lùn 自然之論).
Did he not know that in later ages,
one could no longer return to the Dào (道) of nature?
He simply wished to express his personal preference.
Thus, he could not avoid being swayed by what pleased him;
he was not one who concentrated on saving the world.
Not only did he not save,
but he encouraged its defects."
Someone asked:
"The reason Zhuāng (莊) and Lǎo (老) put forth these pronouncements
is probably that they are the inner and outer aspects of the sage's teachings.
In their molding of things and clear instructions,
their ultimate goal is one."
Shèng (盛) believes this is not so.
"Indeed, the Dào (道) of the sages is vast and complete.
It is like the sun and moon hanging in the sky;
what is there that it does not illuminate?
The words of Lǎo Shì (老氏) are all derived from the Six Classics.
How could there be any deficiencies that await
assistance from Dān (聃) and Zhōu (周)?
Even as Zhuāng Zhōu (莊周) said, 'The sun and moon are out, yet the torch fires do not cease.'
As for those illusory, deceitful, strange, and bizarre words,
they are still confined to one perspective,
yet are falsely proclaimed as uncanonical marvels."
"Kings and lords obtain the One, and thereby become the '贞' (zhēn) of the world."
Zhēn (貞) means "upright."
The next chapter says:
"Who knows its ultimate? Its being without uprightness."
"Uprightness reverts to strangeness,
goodness reverts to evil."
Examining these two chapters,
one speaks of "the world being upright,"
the other speaks of "being without uprightness."
It already says, "Good people are the teachers of bad people,"
yet then says, "reverts to evil."
The goodness of all under Heaven is one.
Yet some are masters and some are monsters.
The right path of all under Heaven is one.
Yet what is called uprightness often becomes eccentricity, and this is contrary.
My humble understanding has not been able to grasp this.
Shèng Zì Ānguó (盛字安國)
served in the Jìn (晉) dynasty as a Gěishìzhōng (給事中) and Mìshūjiān (祕書監).
From a young age, he delved into the Fén (墳) and Sù (素) records, but kept historical works in mind.
Thus, he said:
"The sages are profound and distant, understood beyond words,
but benevolence and love are cultivated within us, permeating all beings.
The功 (gōng) of gradual impregnation is surpassed by none other than the classics and histories."
He authored over thirty volumes of Jìnyáng Chūnqiū (晉陽春秋).
He rated Lǎozi (老子) among the class of middle worthies.
Therefore, he knew that it was Yǐn Shù (尹述) who wrote the book.
His ancestor Chéng (承) had a basis, as Jīzi (嵇子) said,
that Lǎozi (老子) learned the art of the Nine Immortals from Juānzi (涓子).
Upon examining the practice of nurturing and guiding,
this statement has evidence.
As for a sage,
it is not said that they learn.
Therefore, the saying goes:
"Those who know from birth are superior,
those who learn to know are next."
Wáng Hé (王何) placed his position in managing the grand principles.
Thus, Bān Gù (班固) classified people into nine ranks.
Kǒngqiū (孔丘) and his like were the highest,
all belonging to the category of sages.
Lǐ Ěr (李耳) and his like were the middle-highest,
all belonging to the category of worthies.
Among sages, there are ultimate sages and quasi-sages.
Among worthies, there are great worthies and middle worthies.
Both are due to the sharpness or dullness of their divine mechanisms,
hence their wisdom and application are gradual or sudden.
Shèng (盛) stated that Lǎo (老) was not a great worthy,
taking into account his leisurely and self-restrained nature, unable to benefit all under Heaven,
passively observing the decline of Zhōu (周) and retreating to the western frontier.
His journey reached the lands of Qín (秦),
he died in Fúfēng (扶風),
and was buried in Huáilǐ (槐里).
He was truly not an immortal who transcended the world.
From the beginning of Heaven and Earth, when human life began,
it was distant and obscure, beyond words.
How can it be beyond words?
Because there are images that can be spoken of.
As for the vast emptiness of the Great Void,
the boundless obscurity without beginning,
how can words and images not merely fail to perceive it?
It is truly that the mind's thoughts cease concerning such matters.
And when Heaven and Earth came to dwell within it, a mere speck,
like the tip of a hair floating in a vast sea,
even this comparison falls short.
Nevertheless, the time since the existence of this Heaven and Earth
is but a single thought.
What we consider long-lasting is none other than Xuān Xī (軒犧).
But the existence of Heaven and Earth in that Great Void
is like Xuān Xī (軒羲) in this Heaven and Earth.
Petty individuals only consider Hèxū (赫胥) to be ancient.
How confined are their thoughts!
The existence of Buddhas in the world has no known beginning.
Former Buddhas and later Buddhas, their Way does not differ.
The Dharma-body is calm and clear, each manifesting according to responsiveness.
Summoned by responsiveness,
it spans a great chiliocosm yet is as close as a foot.
If the karmic affinity is not yet due,
even treading in its footsteps will not reveal it.
The southern boundary of Sahā (娑婆) is called Jambudvīpa (閻浮).
West of the Onion Mountains (葱嶺), the path is close.
But before the karmic affinity opened, it was naturally separated by principle.
How can this be explained?
Before the Xià (夏) and Yīn (殷) dynasties, written records were scarce.
When the Zhōu (周) house received its mandate, the classics were fully preserved.
Even foreign envoys from various regions received appointments,
and interpreters brought tribute, encompassing distant wild lands.
Yet the Eight Barbarians and Five Di (狄) were all ignorant and crude.
They could not recognize characters nor understand meanings.
They all presented offerings to the royal court and ascended to the Pure Temple of Music.
The Western Regions, though their path was not distant,
even if their leaf-script and horizontal writing differed from Huá (華) (Chinese),
deep meanings and subtle principles naturally emerged from them.
During the Táng (唐), Yú (虞), and Three Dynasties, it is impossible that they did not exist.
It is only that the matter was limited to the West, and the Way had not yet flowed East.
Is it not that the karmic affinity for the small Central States had not yet been activated?
To seek its convergence and its essential principles, how can it be spoken of on the same day as the pleasures of the Four Barbarians?
It was not neglected by Jī Gōng (姬公);
rather, it is because this Dharma was meant to be concealed.
During the era of Yán (炎) and Hào (昊),
without fire or grains, people ate meat and wore skins.
Feelings of compassion had not yet arisen in their hearts.
Without meat and skins, death would instantly arrive.
Even if great sages diligently pondered how to save and exempt them,
since their lives depended on these, it was difficult to suddenly remove them by principle.
It was indeed appropriate to guide them gradually and slowly open the source.
Thus, Suìrén (燧人) introduced fire, transforming raw into cooked.
Once raw and cooked were transformed,
this was perhaps the budding sign of Buddhism.
Why?
Transforming raw into cooked was a gradually difficult task.
Accumulating such gradual difficulties can lead to great achievements.
Later, Shénnóng (神農) further provided guidance.
Excellent grains were first sown, and people began to eat grains.
With full stomachs and replenished emptiness, one could be satisfied without meat.
Then, the preservation of life and reduction of killing became increasingly common.
From this point onward, care and protection grew daily.
Spring hunts exempted pregnant animals.
Summer culling targeted those that harmed grains.
Autumn and winter hunts certainly caused much harm.
The difficulty of sudden abolition has been previously explained.
The two sages, Zhōu (周) and Kǒng (孔), expanded their principles slightly.
They saw life and could not bear its death.
They heard its sound and could not eat its flesh.
The cutting of plants and trees had its seasons.
Fawns and eggs were not to be wantonly harmed.
Fishing did not drain the lakes.
Hunting did not burn the plains.
They fished with hooks, but not with nets.
They shot with arrows, but not at roosting birds.
Meat-eating and silk-wearing were only for the elderly.
Cattle, sheep, dogs, and pigs were not killed without reason.
These are the five branches of precepts.
This also opened up one of them.
As for indulging in alcohol,
being infatuated with lust,
deceiving others,
and plundering for oneself,
what is forbidden by external scriptures needs no Buddhist teachings.
Four of these transgressions harm humans.
Humans are the foremost of sentient beings.
One transgression harms animals.
Animals are the lowest of living beings.
The ultimate sages establishing principles should have a sequence.
This is also why the Buddhist precept against killing humans is the most serious.
Inner sages and outer sages share the same righteousness and principle.
Yet those who are blinded by principle cling to external teachings,
believing that boiling sheep and raising pigs is inherently proper.
Some also say,
"If, according to Buddhist scriptures,
all actions have karmic retribution,
then Yǔ (禹), Tāng (湯), Wén (文), and Wǔ (武) would all suffer dismemberment,
and Zhōugōng (周公) and Kǒngzi (孔子) would all enter the cauldron."
How deeply deluded they are in their understanding of the Way!
Try to examine this evidence,
and you may gain enlightenment.
The treatise says:
The way of former Buddhas and latter Buddhas is not different.
When the Zhōu House received its mandate, auspicious signs were sent to the Dídī, who received their posts according to their region.
The secret path to the western lands was not far.
It cannot be that during the Táng-Yú and Sān Dài periods it did not yet exist.
It is only that the matter was limited to the west, and the Dharma had not yet flowed eastward.
This was not because Jī Gōng overlooked it,
but rather because this Dharma was meant to be concealed.
Suìrén making fire for grain, changing raw into cooked,
was perhaps a harbinger of Buddhism.
The doctrines of the two sages, Zhōu and Kǒng, gradually expanded.
Seeing life, they could not bear its death;
hearing its sound, they would not eat its flesh.
The felling of plants and trees had its seasons;
fawns and eggs were not to be wantonly harmed.
Moreover, there are five precepts.
Four of these are offenses against humans,
humans being the foremost of sentient beings.
One is harming animals,
animals being the lowest of living things.
Inner saints and outer saints, their principles are similar, their reasoning is one.
A question is posed:
Carefully examining the Buddhist scriptures,
the rise of a single Buddha spans many eons.
I am unsure how long the interval between former Buddhas and latter Buddhas should be.
Shìjiā’s appearance was recent, during the reign of Zhūang Wáng.
Why must it have already existed during Táng-Yú, Xià, and Yīn?
Zhōu Gōng did not speak of it,
perhaps because it had not yet emerged,
not because it was meant to be concealed.
Ashoka’s building of stupas began in the era of Jìng Wáng.
Since there are four continents in Jambudvīpa,
then it is impossible that the Eastern Kingdom was entirely without it.
The Master (Kǒngzǐ) himself promoted his teachings with Chinese rites.
Why would he then speak of barbarian laws?
Therefore, he lamented that China had lost its rites
and sought them among the Four Yi.
This also had another meaning.
Moreover, the music of the Four Yi
scarcely originated from the remote wildernesses,
cast among the four frontiers,
also close to the lands of peril and avian creatures.
Yǔ’s footprints did not reach the source of the Yellow River.
Even Yuèsháng’s white pheasants were called "repeated translations."
Thus, Tiānzhú and Jìbīn had long been completely separated from the Upper Kingdom.
Only occasionally after the decline of Zhōu were there mentions.
Therefore, Zōu Zǐ believed that Chìxiàn within the universe
was merely one of the nine continents.
In early Hàn, there were indeed Fútú (Buddhists) in Cháng’ān, but the scriptures and images were obscure.
Although Zhāng Qiān was sent on a mission to Dàxià,
and Gān Yīng reached Ānxī afar,
they still could not proclaim and translate the teachings and expound this Dharma.
It was only when it appeared in a dream to the emperor
that it gradually began to flourish and become prominent.
This seems to indicate that at times there are obstacles to communication,
not that there are fluctuations in fate.
If it must be that circumstances lead to encounters,
then what sin did the pure and honest people of old commit?
What fortune do the shallow and corrupt people of today have?
Suppose this Dharma was originally meant to save the corrupt.
Indeed, no sin is greater than killing.
When eating meat, what is more egregious than killing?
Yet, we waited until the advent of fire and grain to have the seeds of this teaching.
Does this not represent a setback for the divine power of great compassion?
If rice and other grains were not yet sown,
the act of killing would be difficult to cease.
I wonder by what Dharma the past Buddhas taught in earlier times?
And at which Buddha’s time did this teaching emerge?
Furthermore, among the four precepts, those violating humans
receive a lighter retribution for a momentary offense,
while the single act of harming animals receives a heavier retribution.
Starting light and ending heavy also seems illogical.
The way of establishing humanity
is called benevolence and righteousness,
as spoken of by Zhōu and Kǒng.
Not eating meat upon hearing the sound,
and cutting down trees only at certain times,
these were meant to greatly illuminate the way of benevolence and righteousness.
If this applies even to birds, beasts, plants, and trees,
how much more so to humans, who should not be treated with cruelty?
This is not to say that their inner introspection was insufficient,
but rather that their intention was based on causal retribution.
The traces might seem similar,
but the underlying sentiment is entirely different.
I am unsure whether the matters of the inner and outer saints
can be considered equal in this regard.
There are discrepancies here that are difficult to grasp immediately.
I humbly present this for your clarification.
I wish you would fully enlighten me regarding all obscurities.
The retort says:
“Shìjiā’s appearance
was recent, during the reign of Zhūang Wáng.
Why must it have already existed during Táng-Yú, Xià, and Yīn?
Zhōu Gōng did not speak of it,
perhaps because it had not yet emerged,
not because it was meant to be concealed.
Ashoka’s building of stupas
began in the era of Jìng Wáng.
Since there are four continents in Jambudvīpa,
then it is impossible that this Dharma was entirely absent from the Eastern Kingdom.”
The reply says:
The year and month of Shìjiā’s birth are unknowable.
Since Buddhist scriptures have no records of years and dates,
and this Dharma had not yet flowed eastward,
how can one know that it was during the time of Zhōu Zhuāng?
It is nothing more than taking as evidence the *Chūnqiū* record that in the seventh year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ, in the fourth month, on the *xīnmǎo* day, the fixed stars were not seen.
The calendars of the Three Dynasties differed.
We do not know what calendar foreign countries used.
How can one know that the fourth month of Lǔ Zhuāng
was the fourth month of foreign countries?
If foreign countries used the Zhōu calendar,
then the *xīnmǎo* day in the fourth month in the long calendar would only be the fifth day, certainly not the eighth.
If they used the Yīn calendar, Zhōu’s fourth month would be Yīn’s third month.
If they used the Xià calendar, Zhōu’s fourth month would be Xià’s second month.
None of them align with the Buddhist date of the eighth day of the fourth month.
If one takes Lǔ’s fourth month as proof,
then the discrepancy in months and days makes it impossible to determine.
If this is not taken as proof,
then there is no evidence to find the year and month of the Buddha’s birth.
Moreover, when Shìjiā was first born,
only the sky itself brightened;
it does not say that the stars were not seen.
Furthermore, among the auspicious signs, there was the sun, moon, and stars stopping and not moving.
It also says,
“When the morning star appeared, he fell to the ground and walked seven steps.”
There is absolutely no mention of stars not appearing.
This is fundamentally at odds
with the *Chūnqiū* record of fixed stars not appearing.
If Ashoka’s building of stupas was in the era of Jìng Wáng,
and since there are four continents in Jambudvīpa, this Dharma had already spread to the Eastern Kingdom,
then from Jìng Wáng until the Six States period,
records and annotations are numerous and detailed, yet there is never a single mention.
Ashoka’s erection of stupas was not in the time of Jìng Wáng,
which is also clear.
Based on this,
the rise of Shìjiā could not have been in the recent Zhōu era.
How could the sentiments of Gōng Dàn be such that it did not yet exist?
The retort says:
“The Master (Kǒngzǐ) himself promoted his teachings with Chinese rites.
Why would he then speak of barbarian laws?
Therefore, he lamented that China had lost its rites
and sought them among the Four Yi.
This also had another meaning.”
The reply says:
The sequence of spreading the teachings has already been detailed in the previous discussion.
I will not debate it again.
The retort says:
“The music of the Four Yi
scarcely originated from the remote wildernesses,
cast among the four frontiers,
also close to the lands of peril and avian creatures.
Yǔ’s footprints did not reach the source of the Yellow River.
Even Yuèsháng’s white pheasants were called ‘repeated translations.’
Thus, Tiānzhú and Jìbīn had long been completely separated from the Upper Kingdom.
Only occasionally after the decline of Zhōu were there mentions.
Therefore, Zōu Zǐ believed that Chìxiàn within the universe
was merely one of the nine continents.
In early Hàn, there were indeed Fútú in Cháng’ān, but the scriptures and images were obscure.
Although Zhāng Qiān was sent on a mission to Dàxià,
and Gān Yīng reached Ānxī afar,
they still could not proclaim and translate the teachings.
It was only when it appeared in a dream to the emperor
that it gradually began to flourish and become prominent.
This seems to indicate that at times there are obstacles to communication,
not that there are fluctuations in fate.”
The reply says:
Originally, the western regions were close, yet the great Dharma was not received.
This was probably because the conditions for its spread had not yet arisen,
not because the path was far.
Since the path was close, yet this Dharma never flowed eastward,
if not for the conditions not yet being ripe,
what could have caused this?
Later, its eastward spread was all due to ripe conditions.
The obstacles to communication
each have their time,
as already exhausted in the previous discussion.
The question is raised:
If it must be that circumstances lead to a gathering [of karmic retribution],
then what sin did the pure and honest people of the past commit?
What good fortune do the corrupt and shallow people of today possess?
Suppose this doctrine was originally intended to save the corrupt.
Indeed, of sins, none is greater than killing.
When eating meat, what is more extreme than killing?
Yet, [Buddhism] only awaited the propagation of cooked grains before its teachings could sprout.
Does this not present an obstacle to the great compassion and divine power [of the Buddha]?
If grains were not yet sown,
it would be difficult to stop the act of killing.
I wonder, what doctrine did the past Buddhas of former times
use to teach?
In which Buddha's time did this teaching sprout?
Moreover, for those who violate the four precepts, their retribution is initially light,
while killing an animal and receiving its karmic consequence is heavier.
The beginning being light and the end heavy is also not well-understood.
Indeed, the way of establishing humanity
is said to be benevolence (rén) and righteousness (yì).
As Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ said,
"hearing its cry, one cannot bear to eat its flesh,"
and "felling trees in due season."
This was to greatly illuminate the way of benevolence and righteousness.

He killed the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng 齊王) and ten of his sons.
On the first day of the first month, he changed the era name to Dàchéng (大成).
He abdicated to his son, Yǎn (衍).
He changed the era name to Dàxiàng (大象).
He styled himself Tiānyuán Huángdì (天元皇帝).
Then he reopened the Buddhist Dharma.
However, the misfortune was deep and the blessings shallow; his faults overshadowed his achievements.
He died in the fifth month of the following year.
His posthumous title was Wénxuān (文宣).
In the first month of the year after, the era name was changed to Dàdìng (大定).
In the second month, he abdicated to the Suí (隋) dynasty.
Therefore, Fù Yì (傅奕) remarked,
"Observing Emperor Wǔ's (Wǔdì 武帝) governance,
he was decisive and capable.
This was his aspiration.
Having eliminated the perverse and evil teachings,
he focused solely on strengthening the military.
Within five years, great achievements were assembled; it was a flourishing period.
He had indeed achieved success."
The compiler says:
Fù Yì (傅奕) said:
"Without Buddhism, the state would be secure and its reign long."
How could the founder of Zhōu (Zhōu Zǔ 周祖) have scarcely finished his purges before a violent death suddenly befell him?
Then Fù Yì (傅奕) must be mad.
Indeed, Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì 武帝) was only martial, never hesitating.
He readily acted on his impulses, carrying out executions.
Harming his uncle, destroying Buddhism, and deceiving were already deeply ingrained.
A short reign and a shifted destiny were indeed fitting.
Moreover, the epidemic affected his own person; what use were his lamentations?
Calamity befell him, and disaster gathered, which is truly regrettable.
He even called the correct Buddhism "perverse and evil,"
and revered false Daoism (dào) as his master.
Ignorant rulers and dissolute lords—need we mention those of Xià (夏) and Yīn (殷)? The Bureau of Posthumous Titles (shì fǎ zhī sī 諡法之司)
assigned "Wǔ" (武) to the emperors of Wèi (魏) and Zhōu (Zhōu) who suppressed the Dharma—is this not fitting?
Is this not appropriate?
Other details of destruction and the suffering it incurred
are described separately.
Regarding the purging of monks and the reverence due them:
The emperor's surname was Liú (劉).
His personal name was Jùn (駿).
He was the third son of Emperor Wén (Wéndì 文帝).
He avenged his father by suppressing rebels.
He executed his elder brother Shào (邵) in the southern suburbs,
along with his thirty-one sons.
He enthroned himself and changed the era name to Xiàojiàn (孝建).
In the second year, he executed his uncle Yìxuān (義宣).
In the second year of Dàmíng (大明), he executed Wáng Sēngdá (王僧達) and his son.
There was a Qiāng (羌) person, Gāo Jú (高闍), who rebelled.
The matter involved the monk (shāmén 沙門) Tánbiāo (曇標).
An imperial edict stated:
"The Buddhist Dharma is corrupted, and monks are mixed.
They are not sufficient to aid the great teaching, but instead form a refuge for criminals.
Moreover, their treacherous intentions frequently arise, and their violent acts are repeatedly heard of.
They damage the Way and corrupt customs, angering both humans and spirits.
They shall be handed over to their respective regions for thorough purging and investigation.
Henceforth, those who violate this shall be severely punished." Thus, various prohibitions were set forth.
Those who were not strict in their precepts and diligent in their practice
were all compelled to return to lay life.
Though the edict was severe, it was not ultimately enforced.
Previously, during the reign of Emperor Chéng (Chéngdì 成帝) of the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty,
Yǔ Bīng (庾氷) monopolized power.
He wanted to compel monks to pay reverence to the ruler.
Hé Chōng (何充), Wáng Mì (王謐), and others debated against this, disagreeing.
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) usurped the throne,
he again proposed the former idea, but it was also not carried out.
The details are described separately.
In the sixth year of Dàmíng (大明), Shìzǔ (世祖)
ordered officials to submit a proposal to make monks pay reverence.
Having already carried out cruel dismemberments,
he whipped Yán Jùn (顏竣) in the face and then executed him.
People could not bear his cruelty.
Moreover, monks bowing was not a national tradition,
nor was it enforced.
In the eighth year of Dàmíng (Dàmíng), he died.
His son, Yè (業), ascended the throne.
He was soon deposed by Emperor Míng (Míngdì 明帝).
Yet Fù Yì (傅奕) described him as an emperor of high discernment.
With such indiscriminate punishments, how could his discernment be considered high?
His lineage was abruptly cut off, and his name and person perished together.
This serves as a grave warning.
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's (蕭子顯) account,
"The Sòng (Sòng) clan claimed the virtue of water (shuǐdé 水德),
and received the mandate, deviating and twisting.
Eight rulers held the correct position, and their reign lasted five *jǐ* (紀).
Four times their direct lineage ended, and three times they saw a 'restoration.'
The internal strife and disasters, the mutual oppression within the family—
how can one even speak of it?"
Regarding the edict to purge the two sects of Buddhism and Daoism (Shì Lǐ èr zōng 釋李二宗):
Towards the end of the Wǔdé (武德) era, the emperor found many monks deviant.
He issued an edict to clarify, simplify, and purify the remaining Dharma.
This was not meant as annihilation,
and calling it so was a great misinterpretation of the decree.
Thus the edict stated:
"I have received the mandate to govern the universe,
to promote and flourish the teachings, deeply considering their benefits.
My heart is in protecting and upholding them.
To distinguish jade from stone, and to differentiate between fragrant and foul.
To preserve the wondrous Way for a long time and secure the field of blessings eternally.
To rectify the root and purify the source, a purge is appropriate."
This was a righteous edict.
Yet Fù Yì (傅奕) described it as suppressing the Dharma, thus slandering the ruler and confounding justice.
He encountered a lenient policy and a net with holes large enough for boats to pass.
Therefore, only the leaders were kept.
The rest is described later.

Fù Yì (傅奕) also cited Yuán Wèi (元魏) Grand Secretary (shàngshū lìng 尚書令), Prince Chéng (Chéngwáng 澄王) of Rènchéng (任城), who argued against building more monasteries (jiālán 伽藍) in towns, as it interfered with people's residences.
He also cited Grand Secretary (shàngshū lìng 尚書令) Gāo Zhào (高肇) who proposed distributing the communal grain (sēngqí hù sù 僧祇戶粟) to the poor. Reviewing his memorial, there were no
accounts of destruction or damage, but only of rectifying governance and managing the teachings, eliminating their deviations and dangers.
This detailed scrutiny and these regulations for protection and admonition
are indeed clear.
Zòu Yì Xù.
Shí Hǔ (石虎) issued a decree asking,
“The Buddha is called the World-Honored One, and he is revered by the state.
Should commoners and those without official titles
be allowed to worship the Buddha?
Moreover, all śramaṇas should be noble, pure, and upright.
Only those whose conduct is refined and pure should be allowed to be Taoist priests.
Currently, there are many śramaṇas.
Some are cunning and rebellious,
and many avoid service and are not worthy of their position. This should be investigated and rectified.
Deliberate carefully and then present your memorial.”
Because the king offers sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and worships a hundred spirits,
there are established rituals for regular offerings.
The Buddha was born in the Western Regions,
not a deity revered by the Central Plains.
When the Hàn (漢) dynasty first acquired his doctrine,
it only permitted Hú (胡) people from the Western Regions to establish temples in the capital.
The Wèi (魏) dynasty followed the Hàn (漢) system.
Zhào (趙) requested that, according to old regulations, Zhào (趙) people not be allowed to visit temples.
Those who had already become śramaṇas should be returned to their former attire.
Many court officials agreed with this proposal.
Hǔ (虎) then issued an edict saying,
“It has been deliberated that the Buddha is an foreign deity, not one revered by the various Huá (華) peoples.
I emerged from the border regions,
and it is fitting to follow my native customs.
Indeed, systems established by the superior become eternal norms.
If the matter is handled appropriately without flaw,
why be bound by previous generations?
Let the Yí (夷) and Zhào (趙) become Taoist priests.
Those who delight in serving the Buddha are all permitted to continue as before.”
Yì (奕) embellished much of this with deceptive fabrications.
Taoist texts have been fraudulent from ancient times.
The ‘Yellow Books’ (‘Huáng Shū’ 黄書) combine vital energies, leading to licentious behavior between men and women.
The ‘Red Chapters’ (‘Chì Zhāng’ 赤章) use incantations for exorcism, causing chaos between the visible and invisible worlds.
This shows that those who fabricate recklessly will meet misfortune,
and those who disrupt customs will be executed.
Their crimes are more than sufficient.
Why?
Yì (奕) said,
“Fó Túdēng (佛圖澄) ordered his disciples to travel and preach in various commanderies and states.
Zhī Dùn’s (支遁) followers served as his trusted aides,
misinterpreting the profound principles of the Three Metaphysical Treatises to adorn heterodox teachings.”
Such words are slanderous and intolerable by Heaven and Earth. Why?
Fó Túdēng (佛圖澄) was a sage.
Light flowed from his nipple,
needing no lamp or torch for illumination.
He could see a bell reflected in his palm,
observing the patterns of success and failure while sitting.
Two rulers revered him as a god,
and all officials respected him as a Buddha.
He predicted the succession of the Eastern Heir Apparent
and foretold the disaster of Shí Cōng (石葱).
When the crisis arose and omens appeared,
he admonished Hǔ (虎) that his excessive punishments and harsh laws meant his lifespan would not be long.
These words were extremely apt.
Yet Yì (奕) claimed,
“He instructed Hǔ (虎) to kill his nephew and seize the imperial throne.”
How utterly mistaken are these words!
He also said,
“Zhī Dùn’s (支遁) followers served as his wings.”
The Jìn (晉) dynasty moved south, and Zhī Dùn (支遁) lived only in the Taoist forest. Though they were contemporaries,
rivers and mountains separated them (like Hú (胡) and Yuè (越)).
How could he have scattered his body to rush north and serve as an aide in the Zhào (趙) court?
He also said,
“They misinterpreted the profound principles of the Three Metaphysical Treatises to adorn heterodox teachings.”
This is also a baseless statement; how can one make such groundless accusations?
Furthermore, the Taoist texts are limited to five thousand characters;
all other thousands of volumes are fraudulent.
Have you thoroughly investigated the matter of Jiāng Bīn (姜斌) in the Wèi (魏) period?
However, those who judge themselves carefully
believe that monks are also like this.
Moreover, the Buddha’s teachings are comprehensive and coherent,
with logical consistency throughout, without contradiction.
Upon examining Taoist scriptures, how much blatant plagiarism there is!
They cannot establish a single original doctrine,
but merely borrow from Buddhist traditions.
Sometimes the ‘Four Fruits’ and ‘Ten Stages’ are copied directly into their inner scriptures,
or ‘Hell’ and ‘Heaven’ are entirely derived from Buddhist tenets.
These are all about the rise and fall of karmic actions,
and the principles of retribution.
If asked about the ranks and stages of conduct,
the matter is more vast than the Milky Way.
How can such narratives be collected and circulated to mislead the ignorant and confuse the true?
They offer not the slightest aid to transformation,
but accumulate offenses as vast as mountains.
They unjustly perish at the end of their years.
This is also lamentable!
Cài Mú (蔡謨), courtesy name Dàomíng (道明),
was from Chénliú (陳留).
Péngchéng Wáng Hóng (彭城王紘), a Grand Minister from the Jìn (晉) dynasty, submitted a memorial
stating that Sùzǔ (肅祖) was fond of Buddhism and Taoism.
He personally painted images in the Lèxián Táng (樂賢堂).
After enduring banditry and troubles, the hall still stood.
He suggested that the Imperial Archives be ordered
to all compose eulogies
to make known Sùzǔ’s (肅祖) virtues. Hóng (紘) presented this memorial and elicited broad discussion.
Mú (謨) said,
“The Buddha is a barbarian.
I have only heard of barbarians adopting Chinese ways,
never of Chinese adopting barbarian ways.
The late emperor was divinely talented,
and merely painted this image casually.
It is not a portrayal of the splendid virtues of the great Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Now, to issue a royal command ordering imperial historians to laud the late emperor’s love for the Buddha above, and to compose a eulogy for a barbarian image below,
is ethically questionable.”
When Emperor Kāng (康) ascended the throne, Mú (謨) was appointed Sītú (司徒).
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Yǒnghé (永和) (348 CE), an imperial edict was issued.
He stubbornly refused the appointment.
He submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
When Emperor Xiàozōng (孝宗) presided over the court,
Mú (謨) was summoned but did not appear.
The Empress Dowager ordered the court dismissed.
The high officials proposed sending Mú (謨) to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) to be punished according to the law.
Mú (謨) led his sons and younger brothers, dressed in plain clothes, to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) to await punishment.
An edict pardoned him as a commoner.
He then shut his gate and did not go out.
These are all stubborn and narrow-minded individuals,
confined to a small perspective like a frog in a well.
Yet Yì (奕) praises them as loyal officials.
This is not a sound judgment.
Why? Mú’s (謨) admonition
was confined to the single region of Shénzhōu (神州),
which he considered the Central Kingdom.
The Buddha, however, universally encompasses the entire Jambudvīpa continent,
which Mú (謨) considered a borderland.
Looking at it directly,
this country (China) is bordered by the sea to the east.
The other three sides are not.
If there are no borders on three sides, it cannot be said to have visible borders.
This continent, however, is surrounded by the sea on all four sides.
Tiānzhú (天竺) (India) is the center of the Earth; during the summer solstice, when the sun travels north,
there is no shadow at noon. Thus, it is the true central country of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, the Buddha was born there.
Moreover, the scope of his influence
extends to the center of three thousand suns and moons, and countless worlds.
Only the Buddha’s realm is beyond Mú’s (謨) comprehension.
Furthermore, common people naturally cling to narrow views and are bound by ice.
They insist on equating themselves with the ancients,
believing their own land is the best place to live,
and their own people are the finest.
This is not surprising.
In the Central Plains, at Sōng (嵩) and Luò (洛), a gnomon
measures the shadow to determine the center.
However, this is merely a specific center within Shénzhōu (神州).
At certain times, the remaining divisions cannot be fixed.
The island barbarians south of the Yangtze River live in low-lying land with harsh climate, and their spirits are soaring and unrestrained.
Therefore, it is called Yángzhōu (揚州).
When the Jìn (晉) dynasty fled there, they renamed it the ‘Cultured State’.
“Barbarians adopt Chinese ways”—this saying has its origins.
Therefore, Confucius residing among the Jiǔ Yí (九夷) was not a sign of barbarity.
Moreover, those with virtue rule,
while those without virtue cause chaos.
Thus, Xià Yǔ (夏禹) was born in the Western Qiāng (羌),
and King Wén (文) grew up among the Eastern Yí (夷).
The Tuòbá (拓跋) clan of Yuán Wèi (元魏) were Northern Dí (狄),
yet they ruled over sacred mountains and rivers,
facing south towards enlightenment.
How could their origins outside the various Huá (華) peoples
negate their civilizing influence?
For instance, Yóu Yú (由余) was a loyal minister from the Western Róng (戎),
and Duke Mù of Qín (秦穆) used him to establish his hegemony.
Rì Dī (日磾) was of the humble Xiǎnyǔn (玁狁) tribe,
yet Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武) accepted him and his position was preserved.
Thus, we know that where the Tao exists, there is honor,
regardless of whether one is Yí (夷) or Xià (夏).
Cài Mú (蔡謨) was rigid and self-righteous,
and cannot be called an enlightened person.
He defied imperial edicts and commands, incurring guilt and being demoted.
Punishment was appropriate.
Moreover, to examine this in detail:
Pearls and jade, an inch in length or diameter, originally came only from remote regions.
But sagely individuals who exhaust the divine and reach principle are not limited by direction or dimension.
Therefore, Kōngtóng (崆峒) is not restricted to the nine provinces,
and Kūnlún (崑崙) is the land of the Five Indias.
Both the Yellow Emperor Xuānyuán (黃帝軒轅) fled west to reach it,
and Lǐ Lǎo (李老) and Yǐn Xǐ (尹喜) followed in their footsteps to ascend it.
Why is this so?
It shows where one should return.
Furthermore, one acts upon observing the opportune moment,
without awaiting a fixed standard.
Consider Xià Jié’s (夏桀) governance:
he burned the Yellow River maps and executed Lóng Fèng (龍逢).
Qín Zhèng’s (秦正) cruelty and tyranny:
he burned classics and buried scholars alive.
The common saying of the time
was that these were tyrannical rulers.
However, making pottery bricks and tiles is not attributed to Jié’s (桀) achievements.
Founding an emperor is not to exalt Lǚ Dé (呂德).
However, continuous generations of flourishing actions still require praise and censure.
The ancients said,
“Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) were not necessarily completely sage,
and Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂) were not necessarily utterly foolish.”
Yet, blame is consistently placed on Xià (夏) and Yīn (殷),
and reverence is accorded to Táng (唐) and Yú (虞).
This is a strange classic of biased and illogical judgment.
Cài Shì’s (蔡氏) narrow-mindedness is hardly commendable.
Zhèng Gōng Wèi Zhēng (鄭公魏徵), the Special Advanced Official of Táng (唐), had a hundred policies.
One of them stated,
“Ask about the early or late rise and fall of Buddhist practices.”
答 zhū xīng yè yǔn.

benevolent nurturing was primary.
The emperor renounced desires and ate vegetarian food.
Monastics lived in dharma halls and righteous caves.
Their bold conduct, like tiny fly-specks, was enough to intimidate jackals and tigers.
For an enlightened person to make an argument,
they would generally remove flaws and cover up faults.
This is the constant duty of a scholar.
Therefore, among the Confucian practices in Lǔ, only Kǒngzǐ was truly one.
Those who falsely flattered and usurped positions merely brought ruin to the state.
The true and false, expedient and real among monastics are difficult to distinguish;
only the Buddha knows.
Others merely observe and listen.
Therefore, Jìyún's lack of understanding makes further discussion unnecessary.
I regret that he was already scorched by fire and presented his arguments.
How could he not know to reform?
Jìyún said:
"The Buddha's遗教 (last instructions) state
not to till fields,
not to store wealth or grain,
and to make begging for food and wearing rags the practice of a dhūta.
Now it is not so.
Hundreds of thousands of people have no intention for the wilderness retreat (araṇya).
Many follow the teaching of not tilling,
causing the world to have the worry of famine.
If the Dharma is established in violation of the teaching,
and it doesn't work, why need this Dharma?"
Neither his advance nor his retreat is entirely reasonable.
This is the fifth point not according to the sūtras.
However, Jìyún knows of the遗教 (last instructions),
and thus knows of the followers of the wilderness retreat.
He does not know that the teaching has flexibility (zhāngchí).
How can he understand the foundation of the Three Jewels' enterprise?
The Buddha's virtue is vast and great;
even celestial offerings naturally descend upon monastic fields.
His blessings are so extensive that divine soil should rightfully spring forth.
The teaching has open and closed aspects, adapting to the roots (capacities) and suiting the occasion.
One cannot be constrained to using mere grains for the Way,
but rather to benefit all beings.
Therefore, the sūtra says:
"If my disciples practice according to the Dharma,
from the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata's white curl, one hundred thousand millionth part is taken,
and supplied to my disciples for inexhaustible enjoyment."
Thus, we know that one leaves home for the Way,
performs offerings for the Way,
receives for the Way,
and propagates blessings for the Way.
The Way is fundamentally empty and pervasive, not to be deliberated by worldly calculations.
Therefore, receiving the four requisites returns to the Buddha's virtue.
The sūtra says:
"If one receives alms according to the Dharma, one thousand gold coins may be accepted.
If one violates the Buddha's teaching, not even a cup of water is permitted."
How can one idly say that they only covet wealth and food?
Again, the sūtra says:
"Those who dwell in my giving and receiving, enter darkness and see nothing.
Those who act contrary to this are like the inexhaustible emptiness."
This shows that outside the mind there is no realm; seeing a realm is the mind.
Therefore, offerings and giving follow
the mind; accumulation and dispersion are not external.
The sūtra says:
"The six perfections are in the mind, not in actions."
This is a true statement.
Citing evidence makes this clear.
Jìyún said:
"The Nirvāṇa Sūtra asks:
'After the World-Honored One's parinirvāṇa,
how can the sūtras be distinguished from Māra's sūtras?'
Observing this question, even in Gautama's lifetime,
his disciples could not distinguish true from false.
How much more so the deceitful companions in Zhōnghuá who evade corvée, how could they not be confused?"
Examining Jìyún's words,
he is entirely ignorant of the enlightened understanding of parinirvāṇa.
Māra and Buddha are difficult to distinguish.
How could he speak of the Buddha's time?
His disciples do not know the three kinds of four foundations (catvāri pratisaṃśraya) in the sūtras,
which determine Māra and Buddha,邪 (heterodox) and 正 (orthodox).
This is not what Jìyún knows,
nor does he mention it.
He also said:
"How could the deceitful companions in Zhōnghuá who evade corvée not be confused?"
This is an honest statement,
but truly what he does not comprehend.
Only those who do not evade corvée can distinguish this.
Why then does he not discuss covering up good and promoting evil as his sole task?
The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"If those who leave home to evade corvée have no aspiration for the Way,
I shall dismiss them and make them return to lay life to be employed by the king's policies."
This is a true statement.
Why did he not record the above?
Qí again cited the Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
recounting the story of Ajātaśatru harming his father and Jīvaka's account.
The Buddha used principle to resolve it, leading him to understand.
Worldly people, bound by affairs, have their net of delusion deepen.
Therefore, by seeking his father within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and entrances (āyatanas), he could not find his true origin.
It was merely a delusion that he called his father.
In reality, a person brazenly planned to harm him to seize his important position.
If he had understood beforehand that his father was fundamentally empty,
why would he have committed such a rebellious act?
The kingdom also does not truly exist.
Through the Buddha's teachings, he realized his deluded mind,
repented with shame, and gained unshakeable faith.
Jìyún, failing to grasp this, used affairs to argue against principles.
He criticized the emperor for commenting on sūtras,
ridiculed his ministers for rebellion,
claimed the Buddha taught "no father,"
and that "no father" requires removal.
Clinging to external forms and slandering the teaching,
it is not surprising that he is ignorant and deluded.
There are other trivial matters similar to these,
and the comparisons and extensive arguments are all of the same ilk.
He also cited Zhāng Róng's and Fàn Zhěn's "Three Refutations" arguments,
which were detailed in the previous collection.
Arguments refuting Róng and Zhěn
are seen in the later accounts.
Yet he said:
"Róng and Zhěn established arguments that no one could refute."
This is a false statement.
Jǐ (濟) said:
Since ancient times, imperial teachers and feudal lords' guests and friends
are met once in a thousand years, as if morning and evening.
The wise and sagely are rare in the world, standing alone in the universe.
Now, to shave one's head
and have thousands of groups not act as subjects, and ten thousand people call one an imperial teacher,
is unacceptable.
Yáo Shí (姚石) ate three thousand vegetarian meals in Buddhist temples,
and eight hundred Qióng (瓊) palaces offered generous reverence.
In the end, he obtained Miáo Yìn (苗胤) and was slaughtered.
Since Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊), no one has learned from past failures.
Furthermore, there are ugly words slandering monks,
enough to cover one's ears.
All of them are words cursing the emperor,
like Zhuāng Měng's (莊蒙) allegories.
He also said:
Monks come from humble origins, planning to avoid taxes and labor service.
They have no intention of reaching the Way, their minds are set on greed and lust.
They steal splendid classics and usurp court power.
There are ten such categories:
First,
they construct grand mansions,
usurping the imperial residence.
Second,
they build large halls and adorn barbarian images,
usurping the Míng Táng (明堂) and Zōng Yòu (宗祐).
Third,
they extensively translate heretical words and encourage their circulation,
crushing the emperor's edicts.
Fourth,
they collect money and sell the illusory rewards of heavenly five blessings,
usurping the sovereign's virtuous rewards.
Fifth,
they pre-collect ransoms to avoid the false calamities of hell's six extremes,
usurping the ruler's punishments.
Sixth,
they call themselves the Three Jewels and falsely claim the Four Dependencies, sitting arrogantly before kings.
This is a tactic to seize power.
Seventh,
they build many temples and images, extensively ordaining monks and nuns.
This is the foundation for establishing their order.
Eighth,
the Three Longs, Six Periods, and Four Great Dharma Assemblies,
these are separate calendars and secret conscriptions.
Ninth,
they set up music to entice the ignorant and young,
and performers to attract distant gatherings.
They expound on the peace and joy of the Buddhist land,
and denounce the dangers and suffering of royal rule.
This is to change customs, shift traditions, and collect taxes.
Tenth,
at Dharma assemblies, they gather for evil schemes and innovations.
They offer gold as they please and suffer slander for destruction.
This is Lǚ Shàng's (呂尚) Six Strategies and secret plans.
None of these ten matters should be tolerated.
If even a slight hint emerges, they should be executed.
Now, they indulge in their propagation, undermining my royal governance.
They also strike great bells on high platforms,
aiming for the palace's water clock.
They hang banners and canopies at large temples,
imitating the full court's honor guard.
They summon imperial meals for vegetarian gatherings,
mixing with the feasts of kings and dukes.
They chant praises and hymns of great transcendence,
likening them to the ascending songs of state banquets.
When praising merits, they compare them to the written prayers of scribes.
When receiving donations, they are like the different grades of silk bundles.
When establishing solemn ceremonies, they emulate the flags and regalia of cultural artifacts.
All their actions secretly imitate court rituals.
Your Majesty, you further deplete your stores to supply temples.
The sovereign of ten thousand chariots acts like a vassal.
You bow respectfully to monks and nuns.
The three highest officials perform the rites of subordinate ministers.
Since favor is so great,
insult is also severe.
There are four things this minister disapproves of.
Observing the ten items listed by Jǐ,
they all lead to one falsehood.
They are fabricated and combined to stir the emperor's heart.
He clearly understands the emperor's temperament,
and deeply resents the emperor's disrespect.
How else could he communicate?
He harbors resentment and uses slander to openly mock.
His words may seem like a subject's, but his intent is truly contemptuous.
Why? The above listed monastic falsehoods,
sparing no evil in their exposition.
To say the emperor values them clearly indicates the emperor's ignorance.
This makes him a solitary ruler, a benighted lord.
It reveals itself without words.
His embellished words and hidden deceit
are clearly exposed.
Therefore, it is said:
To know people is truly difficult.
People are indeed hard to know.
One who knows its difficulty is found only once in a thousand years.
Liáng Zǔ (梁祖) deeply knew Jǐ's disposition, that he was unfit to govern.
Hence, he said:
He has talent but is prone to rebellion.
How can this be mere talk?
However, later generations' memorials to the throne
all depend on Jǐ's talent and eloquence.
The difference is vast.
Hence, he showed his clumsiness.
Jǐ said:
Your Majesty believes that cause and effect have a definite term,
and retribution is an unshifting karma.
Therefore, you greatly revere the Dharma image, and offerings are increasingly generous.
You labor the people, fell trees,
burn and dig up ants, harming natural harmony.
How can this be concerned with the compassion of the Great Awakened One?
If barbarian ghosts can bring blessings,
then Confucianism and Daoism can be abolished.
If bald Shāk (釋) can remove calamities,
then shields and spears can be discarded.
Now, you double the barriers to guard against unforeseen events,
and beat the watchman's clapper to contest empty land.
You kill ants to accumulate merits,
which deviates from Buddhist scriptures. You worship evil spirits and perform obsequious sacrifices,
which also harms the renowned teachings.
Even a five-foot herdsman knows not to doubt this.
How can the most revered in the four seas be inconsistent in their virtues?
For Your Majesty, this minister disapproves of five things.
Jǐ thoroughly uses events to prove principles.
Now, I use principles to explain events.
Indeed, cause and effect and retribution are like shadows following a form.
If one does not believe in prior causes and subsequent effects,
then one would not say that a moving form is followed by a shadow.
The principles of things are evident.
How can one be confused?
Felling trees and digging ground
are ancient practices of heaven's permanence.
Building temples and offering sacrifices
are profound respects of human relations.
Laboring the people and harming ants – what emperor has not done so?
Therefore, blessings are not self-generated,
and the four classes do not shirk labor.
Sins do not reach others,
and hundreds of insects die without blame.
To call the true Dharma evil writings,
and pure vegetarianism obsequious sacrifices,
this is something both the seen and unseen grit their teeth at,
and the wise and holy lament and pity.
However, Jǐ does not know that the great gods of mountains and rivers worship Buddha and pray for blessings,
and the spiritual beings of heaven and earth bow their heads and ask for profound scriptures.
Therefore, they can stand firm in the universe and attain the four fearlessnesses,
and dwell alone in the realm of emptiness and existence, possessing the four analytical skills.
This is unknown to Jǐ,
or he knows it but deliberately slanders to provoke the emperor's emotions.
Jǐ said:
Qín Zhèng (秦正) was deceived by the Three Mountains,
and Hàn Chè (漢徹) was deceived by Wǔ Lì (五利).
Believing and following demonic falsehoods
led to this extent.
Not discerning truth from falsehood, how can one learn from past mistakes?
He further cited five matters to show:
During the Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊) dynasties, Buddhism and monks were highly revered.
The reason the state changed and temples were altered
was precisely because of Buddhist demons and monastic falsehoods.
With cunning and deceit as their heart,
they induced abortions, killed children,
and engaged in promiscuity, corrupting the Way.
Thus, Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊) were wiped out.
Now, Sòng (宋) and Qí...
The temple images are still present.
If Your Majesty serves them,
then the changes of the Sòng and Qí dynasties will be self-evident without further words.
Now, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who observe the summer retreat do not kill even ants,
because they love the lives of sentient beings.
Yet, they disrespect their rulers and fathers, forgetting benevolence towards insects.
They abort fetuses and kill children, yet raise mosquitoes and gnats.
Indeed, the *Yì* [Jīng] speaks of the three cardinal guides and six disciplines: ruler and minister, husband and wife, father and son.
Now, in Buddhism, the ruler is not treated as a ruler,
and even the son is not treated as a son.
The cardinal guides and disciplines are in disarray.
Jièyǐn and the Sòng and Qí believed in the Buddha and perished early.
This is deceiving the emperor; why only slander the Buddha?
It also slanders the spirits and deities.
The rise and fall of destiny and karma are the constant numbers of Heaven.
Abdication and banishment, these are the transformations of nations.
Former kings enjoyed their positions for myriad years,
but later emperors, without good reason, took their thrones.
This is the constant principle of interaction and change,
the great cycle of birth and death.
How can one cling to the eternal existence of one generation
and be deluded by the changed destiny of a hundred kings?
This is utterly unacceptable.
The emperors of the Qí and Sòng dynasties revered the Buddha and honored bhikṣus
because they knew the imperial throne had its origins.
Thus, they harbored gratitude and repaid great virtues.
They also knew the imperial throne could not be preserved,
so they performed good deeds and looked up to long-term rewards.
Since the former causes were short,
they could not be extended for myriad years;
thus, there was the Liáng's acceptance of abdication.
Now, the causes are not yet complete,
so one cannot immediately achieve results from them;
thus, one receives retribution in the future.
This is how karmic cycles follow one another, like the four seasons without fail.
How can slighting the Buddha lead to no retribution?
If slighting brings no retribution,
then all the gods of the suburban altars and temples, the Hào Tiān (Heavenly) Round Mound, the Dì Qí (Earthly) Square Mound, mountains, rivers, and all those who receive sacrifices must be abolished.
Why should only Buddhist bhikṣus be unjustly slandered and misled?
It is said,
"Aborting fetuses and killing children
allows for good enemies to survive."
You are also a "good enemy";
why meddle in politics and not see yourself?
After the memorial was presented,
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was furious.
He gathered his court officials, intending to publicly execute him.
Xún Jì secretly fled to Wèi, hoping to assist Emperor Jìng.
His plot was exposed, and he was burned and killed by Wénxiāng of Qí.
He was over eighty years old.
What Xún Jì did was unreasonable.
He presumptuously displayed his talent and skill,
meddled in politics, and sought glory.
His intelligence ultimately destroyed him.
An ancient saying goes:
"One who is not in that position does not plan its governance."
Xún Jì, a commoner,
meddled in the affairs of the imperial court, which was excessive.
Buddhism promotes benevolent transformation and harms neither kings nor ministers.
It upholds precepts, purifies the mind, eliminates evil, and eradicates delusion.
This is the teaching of the Buddha.
Thus, the Three Learnings and Eightfold Noble Path guide those who renounce home.
The Six Pāramitās and Four Great Vows are used to enlighten the laity.
Its universality and specificity adapt to circumstances, leading to enlightenment as its core principle.
Other things are not the Buddha's intention.
Yet, Xún Jì did not discuss bhikṣus who practice proper conduct,
but focused on those who engaged in disruptive activities.
He used falsehood to discredit truth, evil to overcome righteousness,
the few to attack the many, and perversity to disrupt integrity.
He did not consider his own misfortune,
secretly presenting his supreme canon.
His remaining karma was not exhausted,
and ultimately he suffered the retribution of being burned alive.
How deeply lamentable!
Zǐ Tuó, a native of Wèi Jùn,
was a Confucian scholar during the Wǔpíng reign of Qí.
At that time, Buddhism was highly revered, and its construction was extravagant.
All fertile lands were given to bhikṣus.
The imperial treasury was emptied to fill the Buddha's field of merit,
surpassing what laypeople could do.
Zǐ Tuó, a minor official, was certainly not fortunate in this regard.
So, he presented a memorial, stating:
"Emperors serve Hào Tiān above and govern the common people below.
The cardinal guides of ruler and minister, husband and wife, have their roots.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, barbarian demons have disrupted Huáxià.
They turn against rulers and rebel against fathers, neither marrying wives nor husbands.
Yet, they are promiscuous and extravagant, controlling power and authority,
receiving respect while lightly deceiving scholars and commoners.
Consorts and empresses enter bhikṣus' rooms by day;
sons and younger brothers stay overnight in bhikṣuṇīs' chambers.
He also said:
'Your servant, without fear or trepidation, and not avoiding the cauldron of death,
has bathed and prepared his coffin, respectfully presenting this memorial.'
It contained more than ten pages.
When the memorial was presented,
the emperor was furious and wished to kill him.
Gāo Nàgōng said:
'This Hàn man seeks fame and desires death.
If Your Majesty chops off his head,
it will fall into his trap.'
'It is better to imprison him and let him die naturally.'
This was followed.
After two years, Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu released him from imprisonment during the Píng Zhāi period.
He was still alive during the early Suí dynasty.
His ultimate fate is unknown.
Now, reading Zǐ Tuó's memorial,
it only describes the bhikṣus' debauchery and accumulation of wealth.
There is no other specific point.
His words are verbose and heavy, greatly expanding on each matter.
The ignorant might think there are many important points,
but the discerning realize there are only two themes:
wealth and lust.
It is largely similar to Xún Jì's words.
In terms of talent and reason, he is miles apart from Xún Jì.
During the Wèi and Qí dynasties, famous bhikṣus were like a forest.
Ten heads managed them,
and the Zhāo Xuán administration oversaw them.
The pure community was bright and could not be corrupted.
Zǐ Tuó's family was always poor and distressed.
He had no one to turn to for shelter.
What sustained his body were only clothes and food.
He suffered from poverty and long-term cold and hunger.
Jealous of the bhikṣus' generous donations, he presented his opposing memorial.
Ultimately, he was suppressed and retired, failing to achieve his goal.
One might say it was the verbose and unconstrained rhetoric of a Hàn academic.
Fù Yì further embellished it,
making his words even more superficial and fragmented,
laughed at by the utterly ignorant,
let alone by those of higher understanding.
He was a native of Hédōng.
His distant ancestors followed an official post and settled in Shǔ.
At the end of the Liáng dynasty, he became a monk, appearing mad and unrestrained.
When the Zhōu dynasty pacified Shǔ,
he consequently entered Guān.
In the second year of Tiānhé (567 CE), he submitted a memorial.
It roughly stated:
During the transformation of Táng and Yú,
there were no Buddhist stupas to govern the state,
yet the state attained peace.
During the Qí and Liáng periods,
there were temples to convert the people,
yet the people could not establish themselves—this was not in accord with the Way.
If it is said that the ruin of the people was not due to temples,
how could the governance of the state be dependent on Buddhist stupas?
One should simply teach the people's hearts to accord with the Way.
If the people accord with the Way, then there is peace.
If the Way nourishes the people, then governance is established.
Thus, Qí and Liáng competed to build Buddha images, erecting nine-story pagodas that reached the clouds,
while Táng and Yú worried about the common people, piling up earthen steps that touched the ground.
However, Qí and Liáng were not without merit concerning temples, yet their deceit did not last.
How could Táng and Yú have engaged in Buddhist affairs,
yet their rule lasted long? It is simply by benefiting the people and aiding the state that one aligns with the Buddha's heart.
Now, the Buddha's heart takes great compassion as its root,
bringing peace and joy to all sentient beings, never toiling the common people.
Revering clay and wood causes harm to sentient beings and benefits insentient objects.
Yet, the Great Zhōu inaugurated its reign, succeeding the previous era and receiving the mandate, unifying all under heaven
with a single mind, like the twin illumination of the sun and moon.
It nourishes all living beings like the thick earth, covering myriad surnames,
similar to the profound heaven, truly a revival of the Sān Huáng.
Alas, the common people are just encountering this,
establishing a new rule like the Wǔ Dì.
Rejoice that the common folk have met such a time!
How could one not admire the excellent customs of Táng and Yú,
and abandon the degenerate practices of Qí and Liáng?
Sōng requests the construction of a Grand Temple of Píngyán,
capable of accommodating all the people within the four seas,
and not to encourage the establishment of narrow-minded monasteries,
which only provide comfort for the Two Vehicles and Five Sections.
Now, the Temple of Píngyán
does not discriminate between monastics and laypeople, nor distinguish between close and distant.
It loves and nourishes the common people equally, without holding or destroying.
It takes city walls as its temple pagodas,
and the Zhōu ruler as the Tathāgata.
It uses towns and villages as monastic quarters,
and harmonizes husbands and wives as the holy assembly.
It diligently uses sericulture to fulfill household taxes,
and supplies government taxes to repay national grace.
It promotes virtuous elders to be the Sān Gāng,
and respects the aged as the Upāsanās (senior monks).
It selects the benevolent and wise to be stewards,
and seeks the brave and strategic to be Dharma masters.
It practices the Ten Virtues to subdue the restless,
and demonstrates non-greed to stop theft and robbery.
Thus, it clothes the cold, shelters the exposed, nurtures orphans, pairs widowers with widows,
shows compassion to the old and sick, and relieves the poor.
It rewards loyal and filial households,
and strikes down rebellious factions.
It promotes pure and upright officials,
and dismisses sycophantic ministers.
It ensures that within the six directions there are no voices of complaint against Zhòu,
and throughout the eight wildernesses there are songs praising Zhōu.
Birds and fish rest in their nests and burrows,
and creatures of land and water are allowed to live out their natural lives.
Sōng's memorial here
has its reasons.
He once read the Zhìlùn
and saw the policies of the Tiānwáng Fó.
Therefore, he proposed Píngyán.
However, his description of the Buddha's great compassion, bringing peace and joy to sentient beings,
is indeed reasonable.
But the proposed actions are not so.
Husbands and wives, even if harmonious, cannot cut off desires.
City walls serving as temples are not sacred foundations.
Therefore, it is impermissible.
To see form as emptiness,
only true wisdom can comprehend.
To see the mundane as sacred,
how can ordinary people understand?
Therefore, it requires both truths to operate in tandem, both wheels turning together,
to connect the Way with the secular.
Then, liberation can be expected.
Sōng said not to encourage the establishment of narrow-minded monasteries
because they harm humans and animals.
If built, they would contradict the great compassion of all Buddhas.
In the past, King Yù constructed stupas,
and myriad spirits were employed in one day.
Now, building Buddhist stupas
causes damage to wealth and life over many years.
Moreover, when earth is mixed to make mud bricks and tiles,
it creates a fire calamity for grass insects
and helps ants to cause floods.
Presumably, a benevolent and compassionate ruler should not permit this.
This is indeed a warning.
Therefore, when Bhikkhus build dwellings, they first remove obstacles.
If there is harm to life, it must not be done.
To cherish objects and evoke compassion is to build a benevolent pagoda.
The principle is perfectly sound,
but the practice is rare.
He further said:
Please exempt virtuous poor people from corvée tax,
and wealthy monks without conduct from corvée tax.
If wealthy monks pay taxes and are exempt from corvée,
then all monks will surely hope for tax suspension and strive to overcome stinginess and greed.
If poor people are exempt from corvée, then all people will surely hope for corvée exemption and compete to cultivate loyalty and filial piety.
This would promote the Buddha Dharma and stabilize the country,
and truly not destroy the Three Jewels or endanger the common people.
There are fifteen articles,
all expressing this sentiment.

Encouraging equality is not destroying the Buddha Dharma; encouraging inequality is destroying the Buddha Dharma. Encourage practicing the Mahāyāna. Encourage compassion for the poor. Encourage abandoning stinginess and greed. Encourage people to confess. Encourage benefiting the citizens. Encourage public service for the people. Encourage harmony among people. Encourage affectionate gatherings. Encourage establishing market benefits. Encourage practicing reverence and care. Encourage temples to be free of soldiers. Encourage establishing Sānzàng masters without greed. Encourage fewer Sānzàng masters. Encourage establishing monastic training for monks. Encourage respecting Mahāyāna precepts.
The matters listed above,
if reversed, destroy the Dharma;
if followed, propagate the teaching.
He also presented memorials and two treatises on Buddhism and Daoism.
He wrote a dialogue distinguishing between major and minor.
Sōng believed that according to reason, he did not serve the two schools;
he only served the Zhōu founder.
Because the two schools merely stated their words,
while Emperor Zhōu personally carried out the deeds.
Therefore, "I serve the Emperor, not Buddhism or Daoism."
His arguments were extensive and verbose,
over thirty pages.
The general idea was to prioritize compassionate salvation,
criticizing monks for extravagance and not upholding the Dharma.
He did not speak ill of the Buddha,
but instead aligned with the true Way.
Thus, Táng official Lǐbù Táng Lín's Míngbàojì says:
He was a native of Qínjùn.
He became a monk and resided at Zhìchéng Temple in Yángdū.
He possessed talent and learning.
He was recognized by Sòng Lúlín Wáng.
He authored the Jūnshàn Lùn, whose arguments were difficult to fully grasp.
Later, the Fǎyì Piān elaborated on it.
It roughly states:
One should know that the Six Pāramitās and the Five Teachings operate in parallel,
and faith and compassion stand together.
Different paths lead to the same destination,
so one should not cling to the starting point of one's journey.
He was a native of Nánjùn, orphaned and poor in his youth.
He studied under Liú Huán of Pèiguó and was outstanding and unique.
He stayed with his teacher for many years,
wearing straw sandals and coarse clothes, traveling on foot.
His words were bold and his arguments lofty.
He vigorously asserted that there was no Buddha, only nature.
His words
are also fully contained in the later Fǎyì Piān.
Shěn Xiūwén refuted him,
so there is no need to record it here.
He was a native of Wújùn.
Seeing that the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism mutually slandered each other,
Huān authored the Yíxià Lùn to unify them.
It roughly states:
In Buddhism, it is called the "true form";

It is unrighteous to listen to such indiscriminate and privately fabricated accounts.
This is also laughable.
It can only deceive those with limited knowledge on the borders,
but is not sufficient to be shown to the heartland of China.
What a pity that a pure awareness, once tainted, immediately sinks into stagnation!
When can it return to its origin?
The people listed above
are also, as previously judged, mostly responsible for rise and fall,
detailed according to their categories.
Checking Táng Lín's Míngbàojì, it says:
Grand Astrologer Fù Yì,
from the beginning of Wǔdé to the fourteenth year of Zhēngguān,
constantly slandered Buddha and monks.
In the autumn of that year, he died of a sudden illness.
Initially, Yì was on good terms with the Daoist priests Fù Rénjūn and Xuē Zé.
Later, Fù and Xuē both received official appointments.
Rénjūn died first.
Zé dreamed of Jūn, who said:
"The money you previously owed can be given to the 'mud man'."
Zé asked, "Who is that?"
He replied, "It is Fù Yì."
That night, Fēng Chángmìng of the Less Fǔ, also dreamed they were in the same place.
They saw many who had died previously.
Chángmìng asked,
"Are the karmic consequences mentioned in Buddhist scriptures real?"
They replied, "They are all certainly real."
He further asked,
"Since Fù Yì did not believe in Buddha during his lifetime,
what retribution will he receive after death?"
The answer was,
"Fù Yì has already been assigned to Yuèzhōu to become a 'mud man'."
The next morning, Chángmìng entered the palace courtyard
and saw Xuē Zé recounting his dream.
Zé also recounted his dream.
The two dreams matched perfectly.
Lín was by their side and sighed with them.
Zé then sent the money to Yì
and recounted his dream.
A few days later, Yì died.
The "mud man" refers to a person in Nílí.
Nílí is another name for Dìyù.
The Eight Great Dìyù are underground.
The other various minor Dìyù are scattered in mountains and oceans, where sufferers endure torment.
How deeply sorrowful!
Emperor Tàozhì,
ascended the throne in the eighth year of Míngyuán Dì's Tàicháng era,
at the age of eight.
Still in his tender youth,
his administration relied solely on his prime ministers.
At that time, the Sītú Cuī Hào especially disbelieved in Buddhism.
When the Emperor consulted him on state affairs,
he always expressed the opinion
that Buddhism was illusory and fantastical, a waste and a harm to society,
while Huáng-Lǎo Daoist immortal practices could nurture the mind.
Since Hào deeply believed in immortal practices,
he taught the Emperor Daoist scriptures.
The Emperor accepted his words without any deliberation.
He immediately set up an altar for Daoism and summoned Daoist alchemists from all directions.
At that time, Buddhism was flourishing.
Hào harbored internal jealousy
and constantly sought flaws and pretexts.
It happened that Gài Wú rebelled in Xìngchéng,
causing unrest in Guānzhōng.
The Emperor then campaigned westward.
Hào accompanied him.
Upon arriving in Cháng'ān,
there were Buddhist monks
growing wheat in a monastery.
The imperial attendants pastured horses.
When the Emperor entered to inspect the horses, his retinue followed.
In their private chambers, bows and arrows were found.
These were brought out and reported to the Emperor.
The Emperor angrily said,
"These are not for monks to use.
They must be conspiring with Gài Wú to harm people!"
He ordered the authorities to execute everyone in that monastery.
Their property, as well as goods deposited by provincial governors and wealthy individuals, were inspected.
These amounted to tens of thousands.
An edict was then issued to burn and destroy Buddhist statues.
An imperial order was sent down to the Retained Terrace,
stating that all four directions should follow the example of Cháng'ān.
In the fifth year of Tàipíng Zhēnjūn,
the Emperor was twenty-nine years old,
in the prime of his life and military power.
Cuī Hào's wicked schemes were constantly intertwined with and fanned by Daoist alchemists.
Daoist temples were visited daily.
