The pure community of Buddhism was about to be annihilated.
Another edict was issued, stating:
"Ignorant commoners, devoid of understanding, believe in falsehoods and are deluded by evil.
They privately keep masters and shamans, and hide prophetic texts.
Monks,
falsely using the distant lands of the Western Regions,
induce evil and calamity.
This is not how to unify governance and spread pure virtue throughout the world.
From princes and nobles
down to commoners,
anyone privately harboring monks
must turn them out by the fifteenth day of the second month of this year.
If the deadline is passed and monks are not turned out, the monks themselves shall die, and those who harbor them shall have their entire household executed."
At that time, Gōngzōng, as太子 (tàizǐ, crown prince) and regent,
had always respected Buddhism.
He repeatedly submitted memorials arguing against the excessive execution of monks
and the innocence of images.
"If their way is abolished and the gates of all monasteries are closed,
and they are not maintained by the world,
then wooden, earthen, and painted items will naturally decay and be destroyed."
He repeated this plea several times, but it was not granted.
At that time, there was a monk named Xuán Gāo,
a prominent figure of the Buddhist community.
Crown Prince Huǎng took him as his master.
Huǎng revered him as if he were the Buddha.
Cuī Hào, having gained favor with the Emperor,
feared that if Huǎng assumed regency,
he might be endangered or expelled.
He secretly slandered Huǎng to the Emperor, saying Huǎng had ulterior motives.
"If you do not plan ahead, you will regret it later."
He also said, "Huǎng is colluding with Xuán Gāo,
and Gāo communicates with spirits and ghosts, and is good at winning people's hearts.
How can you not be suspicious?"
Initially, the Emperor did not comply.
Later, he imprisoned him.
He also dreamed that his ancestors said,
"The Crown Prince is innocent."
He then asked his officials,
all of whom said,
"The Crown Prince is benevolent and filial.
He has been unjustly imprisoned and humiliated."
The Emperor then released Huǎng and returned governance to him.
Hào slandered him again.
The Emperor believed him and had Huǎng secretly imprisoned to death within the palace.
He also had Gāo hanged in the southern suburbs.
Hào was triumphant in the court.
None of the other officials dared to speak out.
Then, in the third month of the seventh year of Tàipíng Zhēnjūn, an edict was issued,
to completely purge everything.
All images and "Hu" scriptures were to be smashed and burned.
All monks, regardless of age, were to be buried alive.
These were all due to Cuī Hào's intentions.
Later, when the Emperor was afflicted with pestilence,
Hào was executed along with his family.
Sighs and long laments were of no avail.
The events are extensively detailed in the biography of monks and Daoists as previously mentioned.
Zhōu Gāozǔ (周高祖) was suspicious and jealous at heart.
He harbored resentment and suspicion.
Dà Zhǒngzǎi (大冢宰) Jìn Guógōng (晉國公) Hù (護)
managed all government affairs and decided on general policies.
The Emperor secretly envied him,
fearing he would usurp power.
He summoned Hù (護) into the inner palace
and personally executed him.
Six other prominent ministerial families were also exterminated, along with their clans.
The Emperor, having achieved his ambition in the realm,
had no more worries.
However, he trusted prophecies and omens, and took them to heart.
It had been passed down since ancient times that "the black one shall obtain it."
This meant that one with the corresponding black (sign) would obtain the realm.
Just like at the end of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, a rumor spread that "the yellow-clothed shall be king,"
symbolizing yellow replacing red to inherit the mandate.
The saying about black was similar.
Therefore, Zhōu Tàizǔ (周太祖), when he fled west with Wèi (魏),
changed all his clothes, objects, and banners to black,
in order to fulfill the prophecy.
This was also a remnant of Hàn Guāngwǔ's (漢光武) fate.
In the past, when Gāo Yáng (高洋) initiated the Qí (齊) dynasty,
a similar popular rumor existed.
Yáng (洋) said, "The 'black one' is Chan Master Chóu (稠), the black-robed Son of Heaven!"
He intended to execute him.
Fortunately, Chóu (稠) had foresight
and understood, thereby escaping harm, as explained elsewhere.
Therefore, Zhōu Zǔ (周祖) initially valued Buddhist dharma and respectfully greeted monks,
and made them wear yellow robes to forbid black.
There was a Daoist priest, Zhāng Bīn (張賓),
who used deception to mislead the Emperor
and secretly advanced his faction.
He designated black Buddhism as a national taboo
and Huáng-Lǎo (黃老) Daoism as a national auspicious sign.
The Emperor accepted his words,
believing in Daoism and disparaging Buddhism.
He personally received talismans and registers, and wore Daoist robes and hats.
There was a former monk, Wèi Yuánsōng (衛元嵩),
who, in close collaboration with Bīn (賓), incited the Emperor, saying:
"Monks are mostly lazy and greedy for food and wealth;
they are not worthy of respect."
The Emperor summoned a hundred monks
to practice the Way for seven nights in the palace.
As they were already secretly aware, each applied himself diligently.
The Emperor also stayed and slept with the monks, observing their conduct.
Sometimes he would read aloud for the monks,
or chant praises and repent.
The monks were all awe-struck, none failed to be surprised by the Emperor's discreet actions.
When the seven-day period was complete, it ended without incident.
Then, in the fourth year of Tiānhé (天和), the year of Jǐchǒu (己丑), on the fifteenth day of the third month,
an imperial edict summoned virtuous monks, famous Confucian scholars, Daoist priests, and civil and military officials, over two thousand people in total.
The Emperor presided over the main hall and discussed the Three Teachings,
placing Confucianism first,
Buddhism last,
and Daoism highest.
This was because it originated before the nameless
and transcended the bounds of heaven and earth.
At that time, the debaters were in disarray, with conflicting opinions and faults,
and dispersed without resolution.
On the twentieth day of that month,
they assembled again for discussion as before.
The debate between right and wrong became even more extensive, but the Emperor's mind remained firm.
The Emperor said,
"Confucianism and Daoism have always been honored in this country.
Buddhism came later, and I do not intend to establish it.
What do you all think?"
At that time, the debaters presented their arguments, but there was no way to eliminate them.
The Emperor said,
"The three teachings influence the populace,
but their principles cannot coexist."
In early April,
they assembled again as before.
"You must speak your arguments thoroughly,"
he said, "do not merely agree."
He also issued an edict to Sīlì Dàfū (司隷大夫) Zhēn Luán (甄鸞)
to thoroughly examine the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism,
determine their profundity and shallowness, and discern their truth and falsehood.
In the fifth year of Tiānhé (天和), Luán (鸞) then submitted three scrolls of the Xiào Dào Lùn (笑道論) (Treatise on Laughing at the Dao).
He used it to ridicule the names of the Three Caverns.
On the tenth day of the fifth month,
the Emperor gathered all his ministers to examine Luán's (鸞) memorial.
He considered it damaging to the Daoist dharma.
The Emperor personally received it,
but it did not satisfy his original intention.
He immediately burned it in the palace courtyard.
At that time, Dharma Master Dào Ān (道安)
also submitted the Èr Jiào Lùn (二教論) (Treatise on Two Teachings),
saying that there were inner teachings and outer teachings.
The art of training the mind is called the Three Vehicles,
the inner teaching.
The art of saving the physical form is called the Nine Schools,
the outer teaching.
Daoism has no separate teaching; it is within the Confucian stream.
This is like the "modest and unassuming" of the Yì (易).
The Emperor read the treatise and questioned his court officials.
No one could refute it.
Thus, it was set aside.
After five years, in the third year of Jiàndé (建德),
the year of Jiǎwǔ (甲午), on the seventeenth day of the fifth month,
he initially abolished both Buddhist and Daoist teachings, ordering all monks and Daoist priests to return to lay life.
The wealth and assets of the Three Jewels were distributed to his officials.
Temples, monasteries, pagodas, and shrines were bestowed upon princes and dukes.
Other details are as described elsewhere.
At that time, Wèi Wáng (衛王) could not bear this matter.
He directly entered the palace and burned the Gānhuà Mén (乾化門).
He attacked the Emperor but failed to take him down.
He retreated to Hǔláo (虎牢),
where he was captured and brought to the capital.
Twelve people, father and sons,
along with all their co-conspirators, were executed.
There was a remarkable young scholar from Dōngdū (東都),
who asked the knowledgeable Master Tōngfāng (通方) in Xījīng (西京), saying:
"I have heard that when trends decline,
the Six Classics are compiled and revised.
When boasting and show increase,
the Two Chapters are composed.
Therefore, that which is gentle and enriching, and surely benefits things, is called Confucianism.
That which is used without exhaustion, and surely pervades things, is called Daoism.
These are the divine achievements of Kǒng (孔) and Lǎo (老),
which can be understood in detail.
Recently, I have observed that Buddhist scriptures are extensive in text and rich in meaning.
Looking at their guidance, they are earnest and skillfully persuasive.
Examining their essential direction, they are diligent and profoundly good.
However, though the Three Teachings differ, their exhortation to goodness is one.
Their paths and traces are indeed different, but their underlying principles are the same.
As for Lǎo's (老) sigh over bodily ailments and Kǒng's (孔) lament over the flowing river,
they certainly desired to disregard external things to preserve life,
and to understand the transformation of things by reflecting on the past.
How is this different from the Buddhist scriptures' teaching of aversion to the impermanent body?
However, those who are constrained by convention have not yet broadened their high perspectives.
They cannot equalize heaven and earth with a single finger, nor unify right and wrong in a single breath.
This causes discussions to always be different.
This is what is called 'hiding the maṇi-pearl in its shell,'
'obscuring the great light in deep night,'
'harming the pure wind of the non-duality,'
and 'blocking the profound guidance of pervasive unity.'
Even if one seeks for kalpas,
how can one encounter it?
I respectfully ask you, Master, to explain this."
Master Tōngfāng (通方) said,
"Your question is indeed profound!
It can be said that you have exhausted your arguments but not fully grasped the principle.
Although I am not clever, I have investigated doubts in this advanced country,
cherished the divine chapters, and absorbed wisdom from humble seats.
Now I shall briefly explain the essentials for you.
All transformations fundamentally arise from non-birth and are born;
what is born is non-born.
The three powers manifest from non-beginning and begin;
what begins is non-beginning.
Therefore, non-birth and non-beginning are the nature of things.
Transformation and birth are the aggregation of people.
Although the aggregation is one body, form and spirit are distinct.
Although dispersion is a separation of substance, mind and consciousness do not perish.
Therefore, the teaching that saves the physical form
is called 'outer teaching.'
The scripture that aids the spirit
is called 'inner scripture.'
Thus, the Zhìdù (智度) has inner and outer scriptures.
The Rénwáng (仁王) distinguishes between inner and outer treatises.
The Fāngděng (方等) clarifies inner and outer precepts.
The Bǎilùn (百論) speaks of inner and outer paths.
If one discusses inner and outer broadly,
it encompasses both China and foreign lands.
If one restricts it to this region,
then it can be called Confucianism and Buddhism.
Buddhism is the inner teaching, and Confucianism is the outer teaching.
This is fully elucidated in the sacred scriptures;
it is not a falsehood.
Upon detailed examination of records and tracing their origins,
there are only two teachings, how can there be three?
Why? In ancient times, when things were simple and rustic,
the pronouncements of the Fén (墳) and Diǎn (典) were not widespread.
As the pure customs gradually departed, the writings of the Qiū (丘) and Suǒ (索) appeared.
Therefore, the seven scriptures and the nine schools are broadly discussed.
All are strategies for governing the state,
and all are methods for cultivating oneself.
Thus, the Yìwén Zhì (藝文志) says:
'The Confucian school
originated from the Sītú (司徒) official.
They assist the ruler in harmonizing yin and yang and enlightening through education.
They wander through the Six Classics
and focus on the Five Virtues.
They transmit the doctrines of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜),
emulate Wén (文) and Wǔ (武),
and take Zhòngní (仲尼) as their grand master.
Their Way is the highest.'
'The Daoist school
originated from the Sǐguān (史官) (historians).
They maintain purity and emptiness,
and hold themselves with humility and weakness.
This is the art of a ruler facing south.
It aligns with Yáo's (堯) yielding and the Yì's (易) modesty.
This is their strength.'
'The Yīnyáng Jiā (陰陽家) (Yin-Yang school)
originated from the Xīhé (羲和) official.
They respectfully follow the vast heavens,
chart the movements of the sun, moon, and stars,
and respectfully instruct the people on the seasons.
This is their strength."
The school of the Fǎjiā
originated from officials of justice.
They believed in certain rewards and strict punishments to assist the system of ritual.
The Yì [Jīng] says:
"The former kings used clear punishments to enforce laws."
This is their strength.
The school of the Míngjiā
originated from officials of ritual.
In ancient times, when names and positions differed, rituals also varied.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is imperative to rectify names!"
If names are not rectified, speech will not be smooth.
If speech is not smooth, affairs will not be accomplished.
This is their strength.
The school of the Mòjiā
originated from officials of the Pure Temple.
With thatched roofs and rafters made of firewood,
they valued frugality.
By supporting the three elders and five dependents,
they practiced universal love.
By selecting scholars and holding grand archery contests,
they honored the worthy.
By revering ancestral sacrifices,
they believed in spirits.
This is their strength.
The school of the Zònghéngjiā
originated from officials who handled foreign relations (xíngrén).
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Though one recites three hundred poems, if sent to the four quarters, one cannot respond independently.
Even if many, what good are they?"
He also said:
"An envoy! An envoy!"
This means they should act according to circumstances, adapt to situations, accept mandates but not mere words.
This is their strength.
The school of the Zájiā
originated from officials of deliberation.
They embraced both Rú and Mò, and included Míng and Fǎ.
They understood that the state structure contained these [elements].
They saw that the king's rule permeated everything.
This is their strength.
The school of the Nóngjiā
originated from officials of agriculture (nóngjì).
They sowed the five grains and encouraged farming and sericulture
to ensure sufficient clothing and food.
Thus, in the Eight Policies,
the first is food,
the second is goods.
This is their strength.
If one categorizes and differentiates them,
there should be nine teachings.
If one synthesizes and combines them,
they all belong to the Rú Zōng.
Discussing their offices,
each was a function of one of the imperial courts.
Speaking of their writings,
they were all part of the royal family's books.
To desire that within one era, the Nine Streams contend on the Great Way, and in an age, minor achievements compete in debate,
would it not harm the principle of the imperial ultimate being singular above,
and below open the evils of constraint, abandon, and coarseness?
Truly, it is what is called a giant pestilence and a great scheme that dazzles the court and wilderness.
Buddhism (Fójiào) comprises maxims that exhaust principles and fully understand nature,
a path for transcending the world and entering truth.
If one discusses its texts, they are divided into twelve sections.
If one speaks of its gist, there are four kinds of Siddhāntas.
Its subtle principles are within the realm [of existence],
hence not something that names can reach.
Its transformative power extends beyond the bonds [of phenomena],
and is not something that emotions or intellect can seek.
As for abandoning burdens and shedding snares,
cultivating the spirit and exhausting illumination,
drawing near to transcend birth and death, and distantly realizing Nirvāṇa,
it propagates and elucidates the five vehicles,
connecting with the deep and shallow capacities of beings.
It comprehensively illuminates the six realms,
distinguishing the ascent and descent of good and evil.
Its ultimate aim is to transcend the world, yet its principles are all-encompassing.
Compared closely with royal transformation, its affairs are all complete.
It can be broad and concise, neither crude nor refined.
If not for the utmost wisdom in the world,
who could attain this teaching?
Although Rú and Dào have a thousand schools, and Mò and Nóng have a hundred clans, selecting and rejecting, driving and rushing,
they have not reached its measure.
Only the teaching of Shìshì [Buddhism] is rich in both expedient means (quán) and ultimate truth (shí).
What is incomplete or not understood is called quán.
What is complete and fully understood is called shí.
Generally called skillful guidance,
how does it become a wondrous appreciation?
You say that although the Three Teachings (Sān Jiào) differ, their meaning of encouraging good is one.
I say that good has its subtle and coarse, superior and inferior, and should differ.
The subtle transcends a hundred transformations and ascends high.
The coarse follows the nine abodes and does not cease.
How can they be compared in the same year to discuss their superiority or inferiority?
You also say:
"Although the manifestations of teachings (jiàojì) are indeed different, their ultimate principles (lǐhuì) are the same."
You then cite worldly instructions to align with the profound teaching.
This is what the unenlightened (yōuyōu) obscure,
not reaching its root.
What is teaching?
It is the explanation of principles.
What are principles?
That which teaching explains.
If teachings are truly different, how can principles be the same?
If principles must be the same, how can teachings be different?
A fish trap is not for fish, a snare is not for rabbits.
If it is for names, where is the sameness of principle?
The earnest affection for life and the cautions against bodily suffering thus arose.
The lament for flowing streams and swift changes arose from not understanding.
Both are the utmost discourses within the mundane realm,
truly not the great pronouncements transcending the mundane.
Why? Pushing form to its ultimate minuteness
is what Lǎoshì did not debate.
Investigating the mind to its exhaustion in birth and destruction is what Xuānnī (Kǒngzǐ) also did not speak of.
It can be said that looking at them, they seem complete;
upon closer examination, they are not ultimate.
Therefore, the Nirvāṇa Jīng says:
"Distinguishing form and mind involves immeasurable aspects
unknowable to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
Furthermore, Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas,
both transcend the realm of delusive thoughts.
Bodhisattvas, however, benefit all nine paths,
while Śrāvakas are good only for themselves.
This is like a dewdrop moistening a giant ravine,
a speck of dust compared to Mount Sūmí.
How much more so for the consciousness and thoughts of ordinary beings?
How can they be equated?
Therefore, the Jìngmíng [Jīng] says:
"Do not equate sunlight with a firefly's glow."
Now, if by equalizing, one equalizes the unequal, then the unequal remains unequal.
If by equalizing, one equalizes the already equal, then the equal is not truly equalized.
I have heard that those who truly equalize the world do so by treating the unequal as unequal.
Why must one level mountains and fill oceans to achieve flatness?
Or extend a wild duck's legs and shorten a crane's neck to make them equal?
This is the crude opinion of an impetuous person,
how can it be the correct view of an enlightened scholar?
Therefore, the proverb says:
"Purple obscures crimson;
madness abuses wisdom."
Please let me expand on this category to further enlighten your thoughts.
From the Son of Heaven above to the common people below,
none do not rely on form and mind to constitute their bodies,
and are endowed with yin and yang to transform their beings.
One cannot, because form and mind are equal, then confuse the wise with the foolish.
How can one, because the meaning of yin and yang is equal, then equate the noble and the humble?
The impossibility of this is evident in ultimate principle.
Even if forced to equalize, where is the meaning in that?
Question:
"Sir, you clearly distinguish Kǒng and Shì (Buddhism) as distinct as the Jīng and Wèi rivers, pure and turbid, greatly divergent.
You are overly arbitrary in your acceptance and rejection of Rú and Dào.
Sǐmǎ Qiān (Shǐqiān) placed the Dàojiā first among the six schools.
Bān Gù placed Rú Zōng highest among the nine streams.
Examining their ancestral traditions, all can be named as schools.
Discussing their institutions, none depart from classic norms.
To say they are all wrong, my feelings say it's not possible.
If they are all correct, what then should be chosen or discarded?"
Answer:
"Conflicting paths and principles must be resolved.
The distinction between purple and crimson should long have existed.
The Ten Treatises of the Hàn Shū are all ancient standards.
How could the Five Phases of arts and literature only begin now?
Sǐmǎ Qiān did not mention agriculture as the root of governance.
How could the official records entirely omit the Zònghéng?
Therefore, Bān Jiān's (Bān Gù's) compilation
has been praised for its correctness by ancient and modern scholars.
Zǐcháng's (Sǐmǎ Qiān's) discourse
has been criticized for its errors in the past.
Therefore, the Qián Hàn Shū says:
'Sǐmǎ Qiān, in his preface to ancient books,
first placed Huáng-Lǎo, then the Six Classics.
In discussing wandering knights, he deprecated recluses and advanced treacherous heroes.
In narrating wealth accumulation, he honored power and profit, and shamed poverty and low status.
These are his defects.'
The Hòu Hàn Shū says:
'Grand Astrologer Sǐmǎ Qiān compiled from Zuǒshì [Chūnqiū] and Guóyǔ, abridged Shìběn,
and based on Zhànguócè and Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū, listed contemporary events.
From the Yellow Emperor down to the capture of the Qílín,
he wrote Basic Annals, Hereditary Houses, and Biographies,
as well as Treatises and Tables, a total of one hundred and thirty chapters,
though ten chapters are missing.
As for collecting classics and gathering traditions, dispersing the affairs of the hundred schools,
there are many omissions and superficialities, not as good as the originals.
He aimed to make extensive knowledge and broad recording his achievement,
but his discussions were shallow and not profound.
In his discussions of learning and arts,
he honored Huáng-Lǎo and disdained the Five Classics,
slighted benevolence and righteousness, and despised upholding integrity.
These are his grave defects, transgressions that harm the Way, faults worthy of extreme punishment.'
The Jìn Shū Lǐyuè Zhì also says:
'The world says that Zǐcháng's Shǐjì is extraordinary but incomplete.
Extraordinary refers to its broad ancient knowledge and far-reaching insight.
Incomplete means it harmed Rú and Dào.
Since Rú and Dào were harmed, the sagely teaching did not flourish.
How could a king emulate it?
Honoring Dào and discarding Rú confused and disordered the world,
corrupting customs and destroying traditions.
This led to the decline of Wèi and Jìn,
with the Four Barbarians invading and China weakened.'
These are all texts from official national histories.
Why should I alone differentiate and compare their merits and demerits?
These are extensively listed in the classics and records.
My choosing and rejecting, exalting and demoting, has nothing to do with my humble thoughts."
Question:
Lǎozi’s (老子) teachings
are broadly about cultivating oneself, governing the state, rejecting extravagance, and abandoning eminence.
When discussing the Great Dào (大道), it is the origin of the three powers (Sāncái, 三才).
When distinguishing the supreme virtue, it is the basis of the five affairs.
It is like the potter’s wheel forming and creating;
it is like the bellows that are inexhaustible.
Why, then, does the Master place him below Rú (儒)?
Answer:
I have heard that those with tranquil minds and great harmony do not strive to alter what is constant.
Those who are content with their times and abide by what is顺 (shùn) do not seek to revert to antiquity.
Therefore, the Shī (詩) says: “Without
offense, without forgetfulness,
they follow the old regulations.”
Among the flourishing arts and literature,
the Yì (易) is the most excellent.
What do you think of Lǎo (老) and Yì (易)?
In ancient times, Fúxīshì (宓羲氏)
looked up to observe the images in heaven
and looked down to examine the patterns on earth.
He drew near for examples from his own person and far for examples from external things.
It was then that he first created the Bāguà (八卦),
to connect with the virtue of the numinous and intelligent
and to classify the dispositions of the myriad things.
Wénwáng (文王) added the six lines,
and Kǒngzǐ (孔子) expanded upon the ten wings.
Therefore, it is said:
“The Dào (道) of Yì (易) is profound!”
Humans have passed through three sages, and the world has experienced three antiquities.
Therefore, the Xìcí (繫詞) says:
“The Yì (易) has the Tàijí (太極),
which gives rise to the Liǎngyí (兩儀).”
The Yìshuō (易說) says:
“That which has form is born from that which is formless.”
Therefore, it is said:
“There is Tàiyì (太易), Tàichū (太初), Tàishǐ (太始), and Tàisù (太素).”
Tàiyì (太易) is when the Qì (氣) has not yet been seen.
Tàichū (太初) is the beginning of Qì (氣).
Tàishǐ (太始) is the beginning of form.
Tàisù (太素) is the beginning of substance.
The fundamental Qì (氣), form, and substance are not yet separated,
hence it is called Hùndùn (混沌).
“Looked at, it cannot be seen; listened to, it cannot be heard; pursued, it cannot be grasped.”
Therefore, it is called Yì (易).
The Xiàojīngshuō (孝經說) says:
“Odd numbers are the joints of Yáng (陽);
even numbers are the foundations of Yīn (陰).
From Yáng (陽) it is completed;
with Yīn (陰) it resides.
Numbers pairing together is Dào (道).”
Therefore, it is said:
“One Yīn (陰) and one Yáng (陽) is called Dào (道).”
“The inscrutability of Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) is called Shén (神).”
From this perspective, it is far more worthy than Lǎo (老).
You say that benevolence arises from the loss of virtue,
and ritual gives birth to thin loyalty and trustworthiness.
Being content with what one is accustomed to, and destroying what one does not see.
Furthermore, great music is in harmony with heaven and earth;
great ritual corresponds to the rhythms of heaven and earth.
How can it be in a time of superficial reverence or an age of demanding reciprocity?
However, the essence of the Lǎo (老) school fundamentally seeks to remedy superficiality and extravagance.
Emptiness, softness, and putting oneself below are suitable for self-cultivation.
But if one does not value the worthy and capable, how can governance be continued?
Since it upholds the humility of Yì (易),
it is already a branch of Rú (儒).
Fortunately, do not abandon the five virtues completely.
Question:
I reverently examine the excellent treatise, which analyzes and combines, saying:
“Divided, there should be nine teachings.
Unified, they belong to the same Rú (儒) lineage.”
Seeking a rational example, I still deem this inappropriate.
Why are the names of Dèng (鄧) and Yǐn (尹) mixed with the laws of Kuī (悝) and Shāng (商)?
Mò (墨) came from Hú (胡), and the farmers arose from the common folk.
These were all created by sagacious and enlightened individuals.
They cannot be considered as the heads of teachings.
Are Kǒng (孔) and Lǎo (老) sages?
They can be designated as teachings.
Therefore, among the nine streams, only two are discussed:
the Rújiào (儒教) and the Dàojiào (道教)—is this not fitting?
Answer:
Your question,
it seems, has not reached far enough.
When emperors achieve accomplishments, they create music;
when they establish order, they institute rituals.
These are grand affairs of imperial undertakings.
The Zǔoshǐ (左史) records words,
and the Yòushǐ (右史) records events.
Events become the Chūnqiū (春秋);
words become the Shàngshū (尚書).
A hundred kings share their customs,
and ten thousand generations follow their tracks.
If one has position but no talent,
it still falls short of grand exposition.
If one has talent but no position,
it is clearly entirely lacking.
In ancient times, Zhōugōng (周公) acted as regent for seven years
and then instituted the six offices.
What kind of people were Kǒng (孔) and Lǎo (老) to become founders of teachings?
Kǒng (孔), though a sage and accomplished, had no position.
It was only when he returned from Wèi (衛) that he began to propagate the cultural standards.
He can indeed be said to have revised and compiled, but not to be the source of a teaching.
Moreover, the Zhùshǐ (柱史) was in court, not originally for harmony and praise.
He left Zhōu (周) and entered Qín (秦) to act as Yǐn (尹) and speak of the Dào (道).
He was unheard of by the feudal lords,
let alone the Son of Heaven.
Since he was an immortal sage,
it is appropriate that both (position and fame) were lacking.
That Dào (道) belongs to the Rú (儒) school has already been clearly stated in the previous document.
Question:
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) sought knowledge of rites from Lǎodān (老聃),
thus the meaning of master and disciple existed.
Furthermore, the Lúnyǔ (論語) states
that Kǒngzǐ (孔子) himself said:
“I transmit but do not innovate.
I believe in and love antiquity.
I humbly compare myself to our Lǎo Péng (老彭).”
You say Kǒng (孔) is a sage and Lǎo (老) is worthy—where is the meaning of comparison here?
Praising and criticizing against one’s true feelings is surely insulting to the sage.
Answer:
Since I am dull and ignorant, how dare I be inventive?
Setting aside my own intellect and relying on sincerity, I only follow the authoritative texts.
Jīzǐ (嵇子) said:
“Lǎozi (老子) learned the art of the nine immortals from Juānzǐ (涓子) and sought elixirs.”
This may be true.
As for being a sage, it is not said that he learned.
The Lúnyǔ (論語) says:
“Those who are born with knowledge are superior.
Those who acquire knowledge through study are next.”
According to the former Hànshū (漢書),
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) is classified as the highest among the highest category,
all of whom are sages.
Lǎoshì (老氏) is classified as the middle-highest stream,
all of whom are worthy.
Furthermore, Hé Yàn (何晏) and Wáng Bì (王弼) both said:
“Lǎo (老) has not yet reached sagehood.”
These are all positions established by authoritative scholars.
How can I differ from them?
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
“I have no constant teacher.”
To ask about rites from Lǎodān (老聃)
is in this spirit.
When asked about farming, he said:
“I am not as good as an old farmer.”
And when asked about gardening, he said:
“I am not as good as an old gardener.”
Upon entering the Grand Temple, he asked about everything.
Are the farmers, gardeners, or temple custodians
more worthy than Kǒngqiū (孔丘)?
“Humbly comparing myself” is a modest expression of this kind.
Therefore, we know that others’ evaluations are close to the truth, while self-deprecating remarks are merely humble.
The talk of insulting the sage, I fear, will only burden yourself.
Question:
Lǔ Yǐngōng (魯隱公) was a worthy ruler who yielded his state,
yet the Rénbiǎo (人表) rated him as the lowest of the low.
Lǎozi (老子) was a great sage of non-action,
yet the Hànshū (漢書) rated him as middle-highest.
Thus, it is known that Bān Biāo (班彪) and his son evaluated things precariously.
Why does the Master cite them as evidence?
Answer:
My son, you closely follow Dù Yù’s (杜預) remarks,
but overlook the intention of the Chūnqiū (春秋) from afar.
Yǐngōng (隱公) was the illegitimate elder brother of Huángōng (桓公).
When Huángōng (桓公) was young, he acted as regent.
When Huángōng (桓公) grew up, he returned the governance to Huángōng (桓公).
Although he could return the governance, he could not eliminate suspicion.
Malicious advice thus ran rampant,
and he was subsequently assassinated by Huángōng (桓公).
He neither protected himself nor saved his younger brother from injustice.
Where, then, was the beauty of yielding the state?
If this is not low, what is low?
The evaluation in the Hànshū (漢書)
is thus justified.
Furthermore, Kǒngzǐ (孔子) received the mandate
and was thus called Sùwáng (素王).
I have never heard in any records
of Lǎo (老) being called a sage.
Words not based on classics
are a source of shame for a gentleman.
Question: The Shàngshū (尚書) says:
“Only the mad can reflect and become a sage;
only the sage, if unmindful, becomes mad.”
You say:
“A sage does not need to learn.”
What kind of statement is this?
Answer:
Kǒng's words are about innate knowledge;
learning is about accumulated habits.
The former refers to discussions on Confucianism;
it has not yet been explained.
The highest wisdom and the lowest ignorance are fundamentally not transformed by change.
Those of middling capacity, however, yield to and shift with transformation.
If a sage can become mad, then he is not of the highest wisdom.
If a madman can become a sage, then he is not of the lowest ignorance.
The texts distinguish between madmen and sages;
both are of middling capacity.
Lǎozi said:
“Abolish sageliness, discard wisdom, and the people will benefit a hundredfold.”
This refers to the sage of middling talent,
not of the highest wisdom.
Question:
The Master says,
“The teaching that saves the physical form
is called external teaching.”
Upon careful review of your elegant discourse, this truly seems unconvincing.
The Yì Jīng says:
“To know the subtle beginnings—is this not divine?”
How can we then assert, in blanket agreement, that all seven canons are teachings for the physical form?
How then can the explanation and distinction of "saving the spirit" have any meaning?
Answer:
The Shū Jīng speaks of knowing the distant past;
the distant past reaches back to Táng and Yú.
The Chūn Qiū attributes words;
its words exhaust the imperial enterprise.
As for the reverence and goodness of rites and music,
and the warmth and purity of poetry and the Yì Jīng,
all illuminate the self, without discussing the three existences.
Thus, it is known that the teaching that resides in the physical form
is not fully endowed with great blessings,
and that which is shown to be beyond life
is merely existent and not yet discussed.
The Yì Jīng says:
“The subtle beginning is the most minute impulse of movement.”
To be able to illuminate its minuteness, how can it not be divine?
This speaks of divinity,
but it does not distinguish the cultivation of the spirit.
One who cultivates the spirit closes off emotions and opens up illumination,
expecting the spirit to endure through vast kalpas, the subtle soul never perishing.
Through accumulated habits, one achieves sageliness,
ascending the ten bhūmis to ever greater clarity,
and traversing the nine dwellings with lofty steps.
This is what the Buddhist teaching promotes.
The sūtra says:
“To save the spirit and alleviate suffering, nothing is better than cultivating goodness.”
The six perfections gather sentient beings and purify the mind; this is not a trivial matter.
Question:
Buddhism speaks of Nirvāṇa;
Daoism speaks of immortal transformation.
Buddhism speaks of non-arising;
Daoism speaks of immortality.
Their principles are one;
how can they be different?
Answer:
Those who ascend spiritually and transform into feathered immortals
all attribute it to the power of the divine elixir.
Those who are free from illness, light, and strong
also speak of the efficacy of ingesting medicine.
Alas, they do not know that good deeds are accumulated in previous lives,
that distinctive vital forces are produced,
that longevity or short life depend on causes,
and that duration depends on karma.
Buddhist dharma considers existence as empty illusion;
thus, it forgets the self to benefit others.
Daoist dharma considers our self as real;
thus, it ingests elixirs to nourish life.
If life after life is not valued, what achievement is there in preserving existence?
Even if life is prolonged, one cannot avoid death.
Therefore, Zhuāng Zhōu referred to Lǎozi, saying:
“In ancient times, this was called hiding the celestial form.
At first, we considered him human;
now, he is no longer human.”
Even this is not the immortal who hides the celestial form;
thus, there was the lament of Qín Yì.
He died in Fúfēng and was buried in Huáilǐ.
Nirvāṇa is permanence, constant coolness, and no more birth and death.
The mind cannot be known by intellect;
the form cannot be measured by images.
When one does not know how to name it, it is forcibly called tranquility.
Its attainment
is also ultimate.
Even if the dual sāla trees cease their light, the spiritual wisdom remains eternal.
Though the body is shown in cremation, the relics are always present.
Even if the great chūn tree lives a long life, it considers Péngnián a premature death;
even if the non-conceptual realm endures many kalpas, it is but a contrast to the infinite.
The principles of ordinary beings and sages are vastly different; motion and tranquility are as distant as heaven.
How can their rise and fall be judged simultaneously?
My friend, why do you raise a small flame beneath the sun and moon,
and wish to contend for brightness with Xīhé?
As for being obstinate,
why go to such an extreme?
Question:
Master, your lofty discourse on longevity, short life, and accumulated deeds from previous lives and karma is detailed, but it remains brief on spiritual elixirs.
Furthermore, the ultimate goal of Daoism
is ultimate longevity.
Breathing the Great One, expelling the old and taking in the new—
do you wish to belittle this? How can that be possible?
Answer: The essence of Lǎoshì's thought
is primarily based on emptiness and non-being,
and uses softness and weakness.
He profoundly considers the celestial origin and holds human affairs as lofty yet tranquil.
He nourishes harmony with vast qi, unmoved by gain or loss.
In poverty, he does not seek advancement; in success, he does not seek self-interest.
This is why scholars inquire and admire the lingering traces, and his Dao seems to exist.
However, cultivating and ingesting golden elixirs, consuming dawn clouds, and eating jade,
with the spirit ascending, wings shedding, and the corpse transforming into a new form—
these are all fundamentally contrary to the original principles stated by Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi.
Their eventual degeneration
is not of the same kind as the Dao. Although there are records of such strange things,
those who speak of the Dao do not adopt them.
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was fond of esoteric arts,
which led to the sorcery of Luán Dà.
Emperor Guāngwǔ believed in prophetic texts,
which led to Huán Tán's criticism.
Books on esoteric arts are not included in the canon;
people who are alchemists have nothing to do with proper refinement.
My friend, why do you abandon the great and pursue the small,
turning away from reason and rushing towards absurdity?
Question:
In the Western Regions, it is called Buddha;
in this land, it is called觉 (jué, enlightenment).
In the West, it is called Bodhi;
in this land, it is called 道 (dào, the Way).
In the West, it is called Nirvāṇa;
in this land, it is called 无为 (wúwéi, non-action).
In the West, it is called Prajñā;
in this land, it is translated as 智慧 (zhìhuì, wisdom).
According to this analogy, Kǒng and Lǎo are Buddhas,
and 无为 and the Great Dao already existed before.
Answer:
The vulgar cannot be spoken to about the Great Dao
because they are stuck in form.
The narrow-minded cannot debate ultimate principles
because they are constrained by names.
According to Mèngzǐ, a sage is a "prior enlightened one."
Among sages, what could be more ultimate
than the Buddha?
Therefore, translators of sūtras translate Buddha as 觉 (jué).
There are three kinds of enlightenment:
self-enlightenment, enlightening others, and perfect enlightenment.
Could Mèng Kē's single argument encompass these three Bodhis?
According to the Dà Zhìdù Lùn (Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra), it says:
“Supreme wisdom is a shining wisdom that penetrates spiritually.”
Its meaning is translated as Dao.
Although the name Dao is the same, its meaning is profoundly different.
Why? If we discuss the Confucian school,
the name Dao applies to both the great and the small.
The Lúnyǔ says:
“Even small ways
certainly have something to observe, but pursuing them far may lead to entanglement.”
If we discuss Buddhist scriptures,
the name Dao applies to both the heterodox and the orthodox.
The sūtra says:
“Ninety-six are all called Dao.”
Listening to their names, true and false cannot be distinguished.
Examining their principles, heterodoxy and orthodoxy become clear.
The Bodhi Great Dao takes wisdom and perfection as its essence.
Lǎoshì's Dao takes emptiness as its form.
Since essence and function are vastly different, it is indeed difficult for them to resemble each other.
The external texts' concept of wúwéi means ceasing affairs.
The internal sūtras' wúwéi means no activity of the three marks.
The names are the same, but the realities are different; they are fundamentally dissimilar.
Therefore, know that borrowing the terms of this land
to translate the doctrines of that region,
using names to discuss reality, what doubt can there be?
According to this example, Kǒng and Lǎo are not Buddhas.
How can this be demonstrated?
In the past, the Grand Tutor of Shāng asked Kǒng Qiū:
“Is the Master a sage?”
He replied:
“Qiū is widely learned and has a strong memory;
he is not a sage.”
He then asked:
“Are the Three Kings sages?”
He replied:
“The Three Kings were good at using wisdom and courage;
sageliness is not what Qiū knows.”
He then asked:
“Are the Five Emperors sages?”
He replied:
“The Five Emperors were good at using benevolence and trustworthiness;
sageliness is not what Qiū knows.”
“Who then is a sage?”
Kǒngzi, with a changed expression and a pause, said:
“In the Western regions, there is a sage
who governs without chaos,
speaks not yet is trusted,
transforms not yet acts by himself.
Vast and boundless, the people cannot name him.”
If Lǎoshì were necessarily a sage, why would Kǒng not have said so?
Comparing them in this way, it is reasonable to laud the Buddha.
Question.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
“The miraculous transformations of Buddhist doctrine arose from 身毒 (Shēndú). Examining its teachings on purifying the mind and releasing burdens,
and its principle of simultaneously discarding both emptiness and existence,
it is of the same stream as Daoist texts.”
Based on this,
then Daoism encompasses Buddhism.
Moreover, Buddhist sūtras say:
“All written texts
are entirely spoken by the Buddha,
not books of external paths.”
Yet, you, sir, hold a high position in expounding Buddhism,
superior to both Confucianism and Daoism.
Will you not limit yourself and thus come close to slandering the sage?
Answer:
My friend, you quote the *Hàn Shū* to ask,
and I too shall answer by quoting the *Hàn Shū*.
The “Western Regions” chapter of the *Hòu Hàn* states:
“When Zhāng Qiān (Zhāng Qiān) went to 天竺 (Tiānzhú),
he only said that the land was mostly damp and hot.
When Bān Yǒng (Bān Yǒng) listed the details of 身毒 (Shēndú),
he explicitly stated that they revered the Buddha and refrained from killing, and that their texts were refined,
and their virtuous laws spread widely.”
Nothing about their achievements was recorded.
What I heard later was a different account.
That country was tranquil like the central plain, with harmonious khí (qì) like a jade candle.
It was where spiritual wisdom descended and gathered,
and where virtuous saints emerged.
Its divine signs and strange wonders were beyond human reason;
its clear and manifest verifications were otherworldly.
Yet, Zhāng Qiān (Zhāng Qiān) heard nothing of this.
Could it be that its path was closed in earlier ages, and its numbers only opened in later generations?
Otherwise, why would its classics be so abundant?
From the time of Chǔ Yīng (Chǔ Yīng) of Hàn, the observance of斋戒 (zhāijiè) began to flourish.
Emperor Huán (Huán Dì) also adopted the decorations of a canopy.
Perhaps the subtle meaning had not yet been translated,
but only the divine powers were recognized.
Moreover, loving benevolence, hating killing, removing evils, and promoting goodness –
these are the reasons why many virtuous and enlightened gentlemen accepted its teachings.
However, it also tended to be grand and uncanonical, with endless strange and deceptive elements.
Even Zōu Yǎn’s (Zōu Yǎn) eloquent discourses on heaven
and Zhuāng Zhōu’s (Zhuāng Zhōu) arguments on a snail’s horn
are insufficient to encompass one ten-thousandth of it.
Examining the records of the *Hàn Shū*,
both aspects are corroborated.
If one takes its subtle meanings as yet untranslated,
then it is called a stream of Daoist texts.
If one speaks of its wondrous divine verifications,
then it is said that its principles are beyond the heavens.
Only the four extensive collections and the two truths presented together,
when discussing all nine paths, are nothing but Buddhist teachings.
When clarifying the three vehicles, Confucianism and Daoism are not of the same stream.
This is a clear proof from my perspective,
is it not a clear judgment from yours, my friend?
Question:
The sūtras say:
“Shìjiā (Shìjiā) became a Buddha countless æons ago.
Sometimes he was the patriarch of Confucian scholars,
sometimes a national teacher or a Daoist priest.”
Thus, it is known that Buddhism and Daoism align like tallies.
Moreover, the *Qīngjìng Fǎxíng Jīng* says:
“The Buddha sent three disciples to civilize 振旦 (Zhèndàn).
Rútóng Púsà (Rútóng Púsà) was there called Kǒng Qiū (Kǒng Qiū).
Guāngjìng Púsà (Guāngjìng Púsà) was there called Yán Yuān (Yán Yuān).
Móhē Jiāyè (Móhē Jiāyè) was there called Lǎozi (Lǎozi).”
Your arguments for difference seem rather self-serving.
Answer:
The holy path is empty and tranquil, its responses perfectly pervasive and without fixed direction.
Its unfixed responses resonate with all beings.
Capacities have shallow and deep,
and resonances have thick and thin.
Thus, the formless form
pervades the ten directions,
the wordless word
fills the eight extremities.
There are broadly two types of actual responses in the dust-like sands:
The eight phases of realization culminating in the appearance and extinction at the Twin Sālas –
this is the great.
The expedient entry into the six paths, concealing traces in the dust and light –
this is the small.
The small may involve drawing hexagrams to govern the times,
or planting crops to benefit the world,
or undertaking campaigns to quell chaos,
or performing rites to admonish people,
or speaking of non-being and disdaining glory,
or speaking of being and valuing titles.
Why would Lǎozi (Lǎozi) alone not be one such trace?
Therefore, the *Xūmí Sìyù Jīng* says:
“Bǎo Yìngshēng Púsà (Bǎo Yìngshēng Púsà) is named Fú Xī (Fú Xī).
Bǎo Jíxiáng Púsà (Bǎo Jíxiáng Púsà) is named Nǚwā (Nǚwā).”
However, the Daoist priests of today originated with Zhāng Líng (Zhāng Líng).
They are of the ghost path,
unrelated to Lǎozi (Lǎozi).
How do we know this?
Lǐ Yīng’s (Lǐ Yīng) *Shǔ Jì* says:
“Zhāng Líng (Zhāng Líng) avoided malaria in a shrine of hills
and obtained a book of ghost-commanding spells.
From this, he mastered the art of commanding ghosts.
Later, he was swallowed by a great snake.
His disciples falsely claimed he ascended to heaven.”
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
“Zhāng Lǔ (Zhāng Lǔ) of Pèi (Pèi),
whose mother was attractive
and also practiced ghost-manipulation,
often visited the home of Liú Yān (Liú Yān).
The Inspector of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu), Liú Yān (Liú Yān), then appointed Lǔ (Lǔ)
as the Commandant of Righteous Militia.
Lǔ (Lǔ) then, with a separate commandant, Zhāng Xiū (Zhāng Xiū),
led troops to ambush and kill Sū Gù (Sū Gù), the Administrator of Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng).
They cut off the Xié Gǔ (Xié Gǔ) and killed the Hàn envoys.
Once Lǔ (Lǔ) obtained Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng),
he killed Zhāng Xiū (Zhāng Xiū) and absorbed his followers.”
He was a rebel against Hàn.
He wore yellow turbans and yellow coarse cloth robes.
Lǔ’s (Lǔ) courtesy name was Gōngqí (Gōngqí).
His grandfather Líng (Líng), in the reign of Emperor Shùn (Shùn Dì),
was a sojourner in Shǔ (Shǔ), studying Daoism in Hè míngshān (Hè míngshān).
He created talismans and scriptures to delude the common people.
Those who received his teachings always had to offer five dòu (dòu) of rice.
Hence, he was called the “Rice Thief” by the world.
Líng (Líng) passed his teachings to his son Héng (Héng).
Héng (Héng) passed them to Lǔ (Lǔ).
Lǔ (Lǔ) then styled himself Tiānshī Jūn (Tiānshī Jūn).
His early followers
were called “ghost soldiers.”
Later, they were called Jìjiǔ (Jìjiǔ).
Each Jìjiǔ (Jìjiǔ) commanded a group of followers.
The larger ones were called Zhìtóu (Zhìtóu).
All were taught sincerity and trustworthiness,
and not allowed to deceive or lie.
If ill, they only needed to confess their faults.
Various Jìjiǔ (Jìjiǔ) established communal shelters along the roads.
Roadside pavilions provided rice and meat for travelers.
Eaters took only enough to fill their stomachs;
taking too much meant ghosts would sicken them.
Offenders were first given three warnings
before punishment was carried out.
No regular officials were appointed;
Jìjiǔ (Jìjiǔ) served as administrators.
The Yi (Yí) people believed in and followed him.
The imperial court could not suppress him,
so they appointed Lǔ (Lǔ) as Zhènyí Zhōngláng Jiàng (Zhènyí Zhōngláng Jiàng)
and allowed his tribute.
Lǔ (Lǔ) was in Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng) for almost thirty years.
In the 20th year of Jiàn’ān (Jiàn’ān) of Emperor Xiàn (Xiàn Dì)
(215 CE), Cáo Cāo (Cáo Cāo) campaigned against him, reaching Yángpíng (Yángpíng).
Lǔ (Lǔ) wanted to surrender Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng), but his younger brother Wèi (Wèi) disagreed.
Wèi (Wèi) led tens of thousands of troops to resist at the pass and hold it firmly.
Cáo Cāo (Cáo Cāo) defeated Wèi (Wèi) and beheaded him.
Lǔ (Lǔ) heard that Yángpíng (Yángpíng) had fallen
and intended to prostrate himself in surrender.
Yán Pǔ (Yán Pǔ) advised,
“If you go now in haste, your merit will be light.
It is better to rely on Bāzhōng (Bāzhōng) for a while and then submit.
Your merit will surely be greater.”
Thereupon, he fled to the vicinity of Nánshān (Nánshān).
He wanted to burn all his treasures and granaries.
Lǔ (Lǔ) said,
“My original intention was to submit to the state;
that intention has not changed.
My flight today
is to avoid the sharp edge of battle,
not out of malice.”
So he sealed and left them.
Cáo Cāo (Cáo Cāo) entered Nánzhèng (Nánzhèng) and greatly praised this.
Also, seeing Lǔ (Lǔ) originally had good intentions,
he sent someone to comfort him.
Lǔ (Lǔ) immediately came out with his family to meet him.
He was appointed Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn) and enfeoffed as Marquis of Lángzhōng (Lángzhōng Hóu).
As for Zhāng Jiǎo (Zhāng Jiǎo), Zhāng Lǔ (Zhāng Lǔ), and others,
they originally based their actions on ghost prophecies that at the end of Hàn, a yellow-clothed king would emerge.
Thus, they began to wear such clothing.
When Cáo Cāo (Cáo Cāo) received the mandate, yellow replaced red.
The Yellow Turban bandits were finally pacified at this time.
From then on, this evil practice continued.
Until Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) of Sòng (Sòng),
all were completely suppressed.
During Kòu Qiānzhī’s (Kòu Qiānzhī) time,
they gradually reappeared.
Now that it is an age of the Great Dao, customs should be unified.
The small sorcerers’ turbans and colors should indeed be changed back.
Moreover, Lǎozi (Lǎozi) was a great sage, who renounced wealth and status,
and was also a court official.
How could his attire and colors be different?
In ancient times, there were specialized studies of classics,
but no distinctions in attire.
The yellow turbans and coarse cloth robes originated from Zhāng Lǔ (Zhāng Lǔ).
The clear imperial decrees, how could they be false?
The teachings of sages and worthies are broad, generous, gentle, and mild.
Those of ghosts and spirits are stern and harsh, causing chills and fevers.
Lǎozi (Lǎozi) admonished against indulgence, yet all Jìjiǔ (Jìjiǔ) drank.
Zhāng (Zhāng) created ghost attire, uniformly yellow cloth.
The genuine and the false are clear, the urgent and the slow are discernible.
Below, a few of Zhāng (Zhāng)’s erroneous claims are briefly cited,
to correct what has not been heard: some prohibited sūtras and stopped charging fees,
some falsely claimed to be true Dao,
some absolved sins by holding qi (qì),
some stirred up rebellion by manipulating Dao,
some wrote memorials to attack virtue,
and some wore talismans out of fear of ghosts.
Some devised levies for the people.
Some removed tomb gates.
Some suffered from mistaken belief in escaping calamity.
Some committed sins in dreams.
Some lightly practiced ominous flattery.
These are all the demonic methods of Sān Zhāng.
How could they be the teachings of Lǎozi?
From ancient times down to Fú Yáo’s era,
everyone referred to Buddhist monks as Dàoshì.
It was not until Kòu Qiānzhī
that he began to usurp the title of Dàoshì
and privately change the name of Jìjiǔ.
His affairs are simple, and the records of Yáo can be thoroughly investigated.
However, as for the Fǎxíng Jīng (法行經),
no one has translated it.
Although it falls into a category of doubt, it does not harm the grand principle.
Mahākāśyapa (Móhē Jiāyè), a disciple of Śākyamuni (Shìjiā),
received the doctrine and expounded the teachings.
How could he hope to equate himself with the talismanic records of Sān Zhāng,
falsely attributing them to Lǎozi’s words, collecting deceptive phrases
to assist each other?
Furthermore, they cited actual discussions to prove their empty assertions.
Alas, it is lamentable!
I hope you will deeply examine this.
Question:
Upon a respectful inquiry into Dàojiā,
its categories are threefold:
First, Lǎozi’s principle of wúwéi (non-action).
Second, the elixirs and ingestibles of the immortals.
Third, talismans, records, prohibitions, and suppressions.
Among their forms and styles, there is a great deal of refinement and crudeness.
The crude ones suppress people and kill demons.
The refined ones refine corpses and prolong life.
Furthermore, there are Qīnglù (青錄),
which require gold and silk.
If princes and marquises receive them, their years are extended and their blessings increased.
If common people receive them, they become light, healthy, and less prone to illness.
Why do you not discuss these, but only disparage the contemptible ones?
Answer:
What you have said,
how narrow-minded it is!
The rise of a monarch is not achieved by fraud or force.
It must be due to a spiritual mandate that corresponds to heaven and humanity.
As for auspicious omens and portents, there are indeed different grades.
The highest are the Hétú (河圖) and Luòshū (洛書).
Next are the tortoise, dragon, qílín (麟), and phoenix.
These are the talismans and records of emperors.
Now, Dà Zhōu rules the universe, receiving the mandate and the charts.
Emanating from Zhèn (震), like a divine bolt of lightning, it illuminates all scenes.
Above, it illuminates the Qúshì (衢室); below, it opens the Língtái (靈臺).
It aligns the three luminaries and sways the two powers.
Its virtue rivals that of ancient times, and all living things show their efficacy.
Its benevolence parallels the two cosmic forces, and both the visible and invisible worlds offer sacrifices.
Therefore, the true form is manifested,
no need to seek it at Jùcí (具茨).
Its clear illumination and profound teachings
have no need to be sought from Xiàngwǎng (象罔).
It encompasses both speech and silence, condemning name and word.
It transcends being and non-being, far surpassing this and that.
It treats the myriad mechanisms as straw dogs,
so it cannot be called “being.”
It shows filial piety and compassion to the multitudes,
so it cannot be called “non-being.”
The four seas are one family,
so it cannot be called “that.”
The nine provinces are vast,
so it cannot be called “this.”
Therefore, those who wander in it cannot fathom its depth.
Those who tread upon it cannot exhaust its thickness.
Moreover, the three-legged crow, nine-tailed fox, red sparrow, and green turtle—
auspicious omens follow one another, arriving without being summoned.
This is the great Dào whose vast benevolence fills the four quarters,
whose auspicious spirits gather, and whose abundant blessings are boundless.
How could the pure tranquility of a sagely virtue,
or the numerous scholars of the celestial court,
still believe in tales of ghost records
or continue to spread the sayings of shamans?
In the past, when the deity bestowed Guó Tián (虢田),
it was as if the meaning of seeking fields began.
When the people supplied Zhào Què (趙雀),
it was a sign of initially receiving titles.
These are all vulgar sayings from alleyways,
which you would not approve of.
However, the尊極 of the emperor embodies the righteousness of heaven and humanity.
The names of kings exhaust the achievements of霸功.
When receiving the mandate from the divine ancestors,
they expand the transforming influence throughout the universe.
When performing the fēngshàn (封禪) sacrifices on mountains,
they report their accomplishments to heaven and earth.
One does not see ghost stories at the beginning of their discussions.
There are never deceptive theories that reach the essence of distant goals.
They only delude the common people and damage the royal teachings.
The true and the vulgar are disturbed, and there is no way to return to righteousness.
Only Kǒngzǐ valued knowing fate,
and Bóyáng (伯陽) abandoned eccentric preferences.
Why adopt ghost talismans hoping to attain longevity?
If it is said that receiving them is certainly beneficial,
then all Dàoshì who wear talismans should be able to live long lives.
And common people without records should all be short-lived.
Since the facts do not support this,
what Dào is there in it?
Question:
Lǎo Jīng (老經) of five thousand words is the most superficial and simple.
The Sān Dòng (三洞) of Shàngqīng (上清) are profound and abstruse.
Moreover, the Língbǎo Jìngjīng (靈寶禁經) with its celestial writing and jade characters
surpasses the Nine Schools and the Hundred Schools.
How could Rú Tǒng Dàojiā (儒統道家) ever reach this level?
Answer:
Lǎozi’s Dào Jīng (道經) is simple and worthy of reverence.
Zhuāngshēng’s (莊生) Nèipiān (內篇) are masterworks that can be understood.
Beyond these, all others are created by ordinary human sentiments.
Huángtíng Yuányáng (黃庭元陽) extracts from Fǎhuá (法華) to replace Buddhist teachings with Dào,
a change that is particularly clumsy.
Língbǎo (靈寶) originated with Zhāng Líng (張陵),
first appearing in the Chìwū (赤烏) era of Wú.
Shàngqīng (上清) originated with Gé Xuán (葛玄),
circulating between the Sòng and Qí dynasties.
Examining the sages’ establishment of teachings, their fundamental purpose was to encourage and guide.
What do the great celestial characters interpret or explain?
Starting from ancient script, both large and small seal scripts,
if one uses these as examples, they are entirely dissimilar.
The ghost writing of Yángpíng (陽平) is where this is evident.
During the Yuánkāng (元康) era of the Jìn dynasty,
Bào Jìng (鮑靖) created the Sān Huáng Jīng (三皇經) and was executed.
The event is recorded in Jìn Shǐ (晉史).
Later generations, avoiding taboo,
changed its name to Sān Dòng (三洞).
Although the name changed, its essence remains.
It still clarifies the Sān Huáng as its ultimate principle.
These all originate from ordinary minds; they are truly not teachings.
They do not come from a sage’s mouth; how can they be classic scriptures?
And followers of Zhāng and Gé
all mix talismans and prohibitions to transform the populace.
Their fantastic and contradictory claims deviate from wúwéi.
Alas, how lamentable! How can one point to insect traces and compare them to Cāng Wén (倉文),
or liken poisonous milk to sweet dew?
Question:
Dào Jīng (道經) is profound and concise, fundamentally connecting with sharp-witted people.
Fó Jīng (佛經) is explicit and extensive, originally designed to uplift dull-witted individuals.
By examining principles and citing facts, this is clearly discernible.
Answer:
Buddhist scriptures are vast and radiant, encompassing both the profound and the explicit.
Their profound chapters are immense, allowing for both extensive and concise understanding.
The Dà Zhìdù Lùn (大智度論) says:
“For sharp-witted people, it is briefly expounded
for the sake of understanding the meaning.
For sharp-witted people, it is extensively expounded
for the sake of recitation and upholding.
For dull-witted people, it is briefly expounded
for the sake of recitation and upholding.
For dull-witted people, it is extensively expounded
for the sake of understanding the meaning.”
This is repeated dozens of times.
If the Zhì Diǎn (智典) is like this, all other scriptures are the same.
To say that it is extensive for the dull-witted,
how greatly you misrepresent it!
Fragrant cities and golden tablets, dragon palaces and jade slips—in heaven and on earth, Buddhist scriptures are immeasurable.
The eighty categories of texts are boundless in number.
The twelve divisions encompass everything without exception.
It can be said that of the three hundred poems,
the covering meaning is but one word.
Applying this analogy,
the extensive and concise nature can be seen.
Examining the thirty-six sections of Dào Jīng, if extensive, they are definitively extensive with no concise parts to collect.
This means they are purely for the dull-witted; what benefit is there in that?
If extensive yet capable of being concise, then it is not definitively extensive.
If concise yet capable of being extensive, then it is not definitively concise.
The profundity of Buddhist scriptures
lies precisely in this.
Question:
The teachings established by Jī Kǒng [Confucius]
can pacify the ruler, govern the people, and transform customs.
The profound discussions of Lǎo Zhuāng [Laozi and Zhuangzi]
can lead to a return to simplicity and purity, and an cessation of striving and doing.
These are sufficient for transformation.
Why bother with foreign scriptures?
Moreover, shaving one's hair, disfiguring one's appearance, and changing one's surname
might transform those wild barbarians,
but cannot be applied in Zhōngxià [China].
It is like a cart that can transport goods by land but not by water;
a boat that can travel by water but is unsuitable for land transport.
Buddhist scriptures are bizarre and incredible, grand yet without evidence.
They terrify with hell,
making the timid tremble with fear;
they entice with heaven,
making the foolish harbor vain hopes.
They speak of eons as if they were not distant,
and discuss myriad worlds as if they were not far off.
Some say poverty comes from stinginess, and wealth from giving;
nobility from reverence, and lowliness from insult and arrogance.
Compassion and non-killing prolong life;
much cruelty, plunder, and hunting shorten one's lifespan.
Seeking and examining such claims,
it is difficult to find them consistent.
I have secretly observed that those who are generous and non-harming are poor and die young,
while the stingy, greedy, and murderous are rich and long-lived.
Those who practice Chan [Zen] and austere precepts suffer from illness;
those who mercilessly slaughter are greatly rewarded and achieve high status.
It is truly said that distress arises from delusion,
and爵祿 jiáolù [titles and emoluments] are obtained through killing.
It is like planting a horn and expecting reeds to grow,
mother and son at odds;
or growing reeds from ox hair,
cause and effect not matching.
Though they speak of karmic retribution, it does not satisfy the mind.
To merely speak of the future is no different from tying a shadow.
It is better to let creation arise from nature,
and all things be equalized by singular transformation.
Suddenly there is existence, then suddenly it vanishes.
Good and ill are subject to fate; union and separation are not of my doing.
When a person dies, the spirit perishes, like a lamp when oil and light are both exhausted – how can one know where it goes?
Why bother with steps in empty talk,
or gallop in the realm of the unproven?
Answer:
How strange are your assertions,
and how shallow!
Indeed, you are bound and confined, like a frog in a well, guarding but one corner.
Mèngzǐ [Mencius] said:
"What people know
is not as much as what they do not know." This is true!
I shall inform you.
In ancient times, those who understood the Great Dao,
after five transformations, could speak of names and forms;
after nine transformations, could speak of rewards and punishments.
Therefore, within this world, gradual progress is necessary, and sudden realization is not possible for all.
As for forbidding fishing and hunting at certain seasons to curb the violence of the four classes,
and the three rituals demonstrating the benevolence of the king's rule—
these can be called beautiful, but not perfectly good.
One finds that the works of the masters limit their scope to the universe [寰宇 huányǔ],
Heaven is divided into twelve regions, and the land extends to the quicksands.
Earth is arranged into nine provinces, reaching west to the Black Water.
They discuss the past and briefly mention the future,
but confine matters to one life, never discussing the three worlds.
Is it that the enlightened sages did not know,
or simply that the opportune connection had not yet formed?
Shìjiā [Shakya, Buddha] uttered the true chant from the ultimate source,
and expounded boundless compassion.
It reached from the highest sages down to ants.
Equally practicing non-killing
is the ultimate benevolence.
As for the Dao encompassing both truth and convention, and its meaning surpassing spirits and essences,
it transfers benevolence and longevity to Bodhi [enlightenment],
and shifts the meaning of teachings to expediency and reality.
It enables those who uphold emptiness to realize the meaning of emptiness;
and those who uphold existence to advance through precepts and concentration.
Thus, the light of wisdom shone far and wide.
King Zhuāng [Zhuāng Wáng] then saw the night-shining [pearl].
The divine elixir flowed,
and Emperor Míng [Míng Dì] had a wondrous dream, truly signifying understanding through karmic connection and awakening through conditions.
A single century is equal to ten thousand kalpas.
Thus, Qín Jǐng [Qín Jǐng] was sent westward, and Mó Téng [Kāśyapa Mātaṅga] came eastward.
The Dao flourished in the court of the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty,
and its teachings spread during the Yǒngpíng [Yǒngpíng] era.
Things were no longer like glow-worms, and people bowed like grass.
Only then was it known that the blossoming of Huá [China] was still dim,
and Wén Xuān [Confucius] had not yet risen like the sun.
You initially claimed they were the same,
but you failed to perceive their differences.
Therefore, what you initially thought was the same is not truly the same;
and what you later thought was different is not truly different.
Why? Those who cultivate the pure Dao strive to reverse worldly customs.
If customs can be reversed, then the Dao can be purified.
No plan for reversing customs is more fundamental than tonsure.
Shaving hair and disfiguring one's appearance are acts of profound purity,
renouncing family and severing love are paths to holiness.
They remove desires from the initial mind,
and forget the physical form in the ultimate outcome.
Why cling to the three realms?
Why linger in the six paths?
Tàibó [Tàibó] tattooed his body and cut his hair;
he was not a Western barbarian.
Fàn Lǐ [Fàn Lǐ] changed his surname and altered his name;
was he not from Dōngxià [Eastern China]?
In recent times, one yielded a thousand chariots—
the Analects praised his supreme virtue.
In ancient times, one relinquished nine dwellings—
how could one be constrained by clan?
Therefore, the Āhán Jīng [Āgama Sūtras] says:
"The four castes, having left home, become of one Shìzhǒng [Shākya clan]."
Zhuāngzǐ's [Zhuāngzǐ] analogy of chariots and boats
compares how ancient and modern times, like rituals, have gains and losses, and music has changes and developments.
Why do you arbitrarily speak of different lands?
The teachings of the sages have no fixed direction;
they are not separated by differences between humans and devas.
Their marvelous transformation is boundless;
how could it be hindered by differences between Huá [China] and Róng [barbarians]?
Therefore, with one voice, the Dharma is expounded, and all beings attain awakening.
How could it be separated by Yi [barbarians] and Xià [Chinese]?
The Wéimó Jīng [Vimalakīrti Sūtra] says:
"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with one voice,
and sentient beings, according to their kind, each understand."
Indeed, the evil of even a tiny speck will not perish through kalpas;
the good of a hair's breadth will forever serve one's being.
However, misfortunes and blessings follow each other, with hidden dependencies.
Gains and losses succeed each other, their weight subtly transmitted.
When blessings are fulfilled, heaven naturally arrives;
when sins accumulate, hell appears.
This is an inevitable principle,
allowing no room for doubt.
If one performs good deeds in secret and receives rewards openly,
the world calls it "secret virtue,"
and everyone believes it.
If one commits evil openly and receives retribution in secret,
this principle is equally true.
How can one not believe it?
The Yì [Yìjīng] says:
"Families that accumulate good deeds are sure to have overflowing felicity;
families that accumulate evil deeds are sure to have overflowing calamity."
Yet Shāngchén [Shāngchén] committed great evil and attained a long life.
Yánzǐ [Yánzǐ] was almost perfect but died young.
Bó Niú [Bó Niú] embodied harmony but suffered illness.
Dào Zhí [Dào Zhí] embraced brutality and despised strength.
These are all instances where good and evil seem to have no evidence, giving rise to confusion.
If there were no Buddhist teachings, this path would forever be impeded.
The sūtra says:
There are three retributions for karma.
The first is immediate retribution.
The second is birth retribution.
The third is later retribution.
Immediate retribution means that
good and evil originate in this very body,
and suffering and joy are experienced in this very body.
Birth retribution means that
it is received in the next body.
Later retribution means that
it is received after two, three, a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand births,
only then to be experienced.
The experience of this has no master but must come from the mind.
The mind has no fixed office but must be influenced by events.
Because karmic conditions have strengths and weaknesses,
retribution therefore has its speed and slowness.
Therefore, the sūtra says:
“Just as when repaying a debt, the strongest claim is satisfied first.”
This refers to the rewards and punishments of cause and effect,
and the profound meaning of the three retributions.
Without versatile talent and penetrating insight,
one rarely grasps its entrance.
Sometimes in the world, one accumulates good deeds yet encounters misfortune,
or one is malicious and perverse yet achieves prosperity.
These are all cases where current karma has not yet ripened, but previous retribution has already manifested.
Therefore, it is said:
“The upright and auspicious meet calamity, while the monstrous and evil enjoy blessings.”
The suspicion of such seeming contradictions lies precisely here.
Thus, the short life of Yán Zǐ
was due to retribution accumulated in the past.
The accumulation of virtue today will benefit one in the future.
The long life of Dào Zhí
was a reward for past good deeds.
The current indulgence in evil will lead to decline in the future.
The commentary says:
Chǔ Mù Wáng, personal name Shāng Chén,
was the crown prince of Chǔ Chéng Wáng.
Since he committed the transgression of killing his father,
he was posthumously given the epithet Mù.
The discrepancy between name and reality arises from this.
These are all cases of birth and
later retribution, not immediate retribution.
Therefore, the sūtra says:
“Mixed karma leads to mixed experiences.”
For example, when Ká Lí Wáng amputated Xìan Tí’s limbs,
he was immediately struck by lightning.
When Mò Lì Fū Rén offered alms to Xū Pú Tí,
she immediately became a queen.
Such instances
are all immediate retribution.
Zǐ Yún said:
“Much cruelty is the cause of wealth and nobility;
upholding precepts is the root of illness.”
The sūtras contain clear explanations,
which allows us to speak on this.
Sometimes evil conditions trigger good karma,
leading to titles through much killing.
Sometimes good conditions trigger evil karma,
leading to illness despite much meditation and adherence to precepts.
Illness is invited by evil karma;
how could it be obtained by cultivating good?
Nobility arises from good karma;
it is not brought about by mass slaughter and cruelty.
Therefore, the treatise says:
“It is the condition that is unfixed, not the experience that is unfixed.”
When it is said that experience is fixed, it means
the cause cannot be changed.
It is like planting rice and getting rice;
it will certainly not produce wheat.
Although wheat is not produced,
it cannot be planted on dry land.
The land is the condition,
and rice is the cause.
However, cause and effect are vast and profound;
it is truly difficult to investigate them in detail.
Relying on the sūtras, we briefly mention two types:
The first is birth karma.
The second is experience karma.
All performing the ten good deeds together obtain a human body—
this is birth karma.
Poverty, wealth, nobility, lowliness, intelligence, dullness, short life, long life—
this is experience karma.
Thus, giving leads to great wealth, while stinginess leads to poverty.
Patience leads to a proper appearance, while anger invites ugliness.
These are corresponding causes and effects.
However, the principle of karmic retribution is subtle, and even enlightened people are still confused by it.
Thought cannot grasp it,
and thus wrong views arise.

Some say that when a person dies, the spirit perishes, and there is no future rebirth. Or they say that aggregation and dispersion are unknowable, and the mind and spirit are not separate. Or they say that good fortune, misfortune, suffering, and joy are all brought about by Heaven. Or they believe that all phenomena occur naturally and are not determined by causes to yield effects.
They assert that the numbers of disaster and blessing alternate in the six palaces,
and the retributions of suffering and joy take turns and operate in parallel.
This leads to those who encounter them not corresponding to what they deserve,
thus they say that the books of orthodox teaching have no ultimate purpose,
and that the retribution of good and evil has no verification below.
If one can examine the three retributions to observe the distinctions between prosperity and adversity,
then the non-answer of Ní Fù
and the verdict of Zhòng Yóu can be understood.
Therefore, Wén Zǐ quotes the words of Huáng Dì, saying:
“The form may decay, but the spirit does not transform.”
By using that which does not transform to ride on transformation, its changes are inexhaustible.
Moreover, the burial inscription of Yíng Bó says:
“The bones and flesh return to the earth,
but the spirit and vital energy go everywhere.”
Buddhist scriptures say:
“Consciousness is formless, it temporarily rides on the four snakes.”
Form has no constant master, and the spirit has no constant home.
These are all clear proofs that the spirit roams the six paths,
and a clear explanation that the form perishes in a single life.
If one cannot believe the sūtras, one should carefully examine Xuān Gào.
From this perspective,
the reason Buddhist sūtras surpass the six classics and stand apart from the nine schools
is surely because they penetrate the divine essence, reach the crucial points, mold the spiritual abode, exhaust the origins, complete transformation, and are boundless as a water mirror.
Thereupon,
the young lad, looking sullen, indignantly said:
“I have heard that the Buddhist canon is profound and abstruse,
not to be deliberated upon by the Confucian teachings.
The mysterious wind [of Daoism] is distant and remote,
how can it be encompassed by [worldly] forms and phenomena?
Therefore, those who are stained and steeped in its customs
cast off the shackles of form at the outset of their minds,
and those who diligently pursue its principles
cleanse the dust of their minds at the end of their considerations.
They elevate their aspirations to match those of Yí Hào,
and purify themselves to emulate Yán Zhèng.
They disregard fame and honor, and abandon desires.
However, Buddhist practices have gradually become excessive and luxurious.
Above, they reduce the parents' resources;
below, they diminish the share of wives and children.
Assembly feasts exhaust the delicacies of food;
pagodas and monasteries are adorned with extreme beauty.
They deplete the annual savings of private households
and squander the military and national resources.
Yet, among the śramaṇas, few are outstanding or exceptional.
Receiving such great benefits, they fail to reciprocate the kindness.
Some cultivate fields and gardens, no different from farmers;
some deal in goods to seek wealth, competing for profit with merchants.
Some ally with the powerful and noble to boast their status;
some practice divination to determine good and ill fortune, pursuing fame.
Thus, the clear source gradually becomes turbid, and the flowing stream grows increasingly muddy.
The reason for my astonishment
lies precisely in this.
I had hoped to purify my mind through the Buddhist Dharma and admire its remaining influence,
but seeing this, I am disheartened and have no place to entrust my aspirations.”
The master, looking surprised, smiled and said:
“I have heard that creatures with scales [fishes, reptiles]
do not understand matters of the high land;
and feathered tribes [birds]
how can they comprehend the forms of the flowing streams?
It is natural for different categories to be distinct.
Only the Ten Natures are profound and extensive, encompassing all sentient beings equally.
The Two Truths are comprehensive and deep, penetrating both self and phenomena.
When existence is debated, the Nine Paths are distinct;
when emptiness is discussed, all phenomena are tranquil.
Therefore, the Prajñā Sūtra says:
‘Form is Sarvajñā,
Sarvajñā is form.’
Yet, form is an unfeeling, inert substance,
while Sarvajñā is the enlightened wisdom of all Buddhas.
When discussing existence, they are truly indistinguishable;
when speaking of non-existence, they are in no way different.
How ultimate, how ultimate!
Lǎo Zǐ’s emptiness sets forth its meaning by being external,
while the Buddha’s Dharma-nature enters the profound by being inherent in form.
Entering the profound does not obstruct forms and phenomena;
how then can it be necessary to eliminate them?
Being inherent in form and subtly aligned with Dharma-nature,
then both realm and wisdom are equally tranquil. The Prajñā Sūtra says:
‘Without destroying conventional names, one speaks of the ultimate reality of all dharmas.’
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
‘One only eliminates the disease, but not the Dharma.’
Truly, this path,
who can attain it?
