Liú Yuān’s usurpation of the Jìn did not originate from Zhōngxià.
Because he was not of the righteous tradition, he was called one of the Wǔ Hú.
During the Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn eras, Buddhist influence was already extensive.
The Sòng, Zhào, Fú, and Yàn dynasties long practiced and revered it.
Your Majesty feels shame to be equated with the Wǔ Hú in extensively cultivating the Buddha-dharma.
I request that, like the Hàn and Wèi, you do not let its lineage be cut off.”
The Emperor decreed,
“Although Buddhist doctrines are extensive, I have also occasionally perused them.
Their words are often empty and grand, their language prone to extravagance.
For sins, they are fond of attributing them to the past.
Without blessings, they point to the future.
Actions lack evidence, and their practice leads to much delusion.
In terms of encouraging good, they do not differ from ancient rites.
In scrutinizing the cessation of evil, how are they different from secular laws?
I once studied them briefly for the purpose of abolishing them.
I definitively know them to be without benefit, which is why I have eliminated them.”
Rèn Dàolín memorialized,
“The principles are profound and the language grand,
not to be measured by shallow sentiments.
The times are distant and the matters profound,
how can a small capacity wish to debate them?
To reject the universal consensus of long ages
with the limited views of one lifetime—
is this not a great mistake to be stubbornly deluded and suddenly awakened?
Therefore, Buddhist principles extend to the Dharma-realm itself,
and the body of its teachings penetrates both internal and external.
When discussing practice, both self and others benefit; when debating results,
constant joy and non-action establish profound virtue and grace.
Heaven and Earth impart the Way, broadly benefiting without bounds.
When displaying wonders, supernatural powers are at liberty.
When spreading transformation, all nations return to it.
When offering salvation, enemies and loved ones are equally rescued.
When showing compassion, all sentient beings are unharmed.
It prohibits external evils and stabilizes the mind’s wrongs.
Its wisdom illuminates past and present, its knowledge encompasses all things.
If every household practiced this, there would be no unruly people.
If every nation cultivated it, then weapons would be useless.
Now, without practicing it, where can one find benefit?”
Then he presented another memorial, saying,
“Your servant has heard that filial piety is the ultimate principle of Heaven,
and obedience is the supreme nourishment of Earth.
Thus, it communicates with the divine and illuminates the four seas.
Of the hundred practices, what is more important than filial piety?
In former times, when the world was on the verge of collapse and the Wèi dynasty was crumbling,
Tàizǔ displayed his might, mending Heaven and pacifying difficulties.
He founded the royal enterprise.
Your Majesty, building on this grand foundation, ascended to the imperial throne,
ruling over the four seas and extending your virtue to all under Heaven.
Reflecting on this immense debt, it cannot be repaid in a lifetime.
How can one trust one’s own mind and intellect, stubbornly holding to one’s own interpretations?
Relying on one’s own claws and teeth, and indulging in royal power,
one destroys the temples Tàizǔ established,
smashes the sacred images Tàizǔ revered,
abolishes the Dharma teachings Tàizǔ worshipped,
and degrades the esteemed masters Tàizǔ respected.
Moreover, one would not dare to damage the beds and tables of one’s parents,
much less lightly destroy the matters personally attended to by one’s father.
The longevity or brevity of the state’s fortune does not depend on the Buddha.
The rise or fall of governance has nothing to do with the Dharma.
How can one rely on a temporary thought to incur the ridicule of ten thousand generations?
This foolish servant, defying death, specifically argues that this is impermissible.”
The Emperor decreed,
“The meaning of filial piety is indeed ultimate.
However, if one exclusively adheres to it, it only benefits oneself.
This is why great wisdom employs expedient means, acting contrary to the norm to accord with the Way.
Tāng and Wǔ attacked their lords, yet their benevolence and wisdom were not deemed wrong.
Wěishēng kept his word, but disaster struck and he perished.
If a matter is beneficial, even if it ostensibly violates principles, it must be carried out.
If it is not reasonable, even if it seems compliant, it must be cut off.
One cannot protect one’s own reputation and cause the four seas to be deluded.
Outwardly going against Tàizǔ but inwardly benefiting the common people,
ordering the Śramaṇa to return to secular life and serve their parents
completes the filial piety of all under Heaven.
Each lives independently and does not bother others,
enabling all within the realm to be protected and benefited.
Abandoning the barbarian and following the Xià, the six unifications become one.
This is to glorify Tàizǔ for ten thousand generations.
This is the ultimate of filial piety.
How can it be said to be wrong?”
Rèn Dàolín memorialized,
“If it is said that destroying the Buddha is beneficial and harming monks benefits the people,
then Tàizǔ, in his time, surely observed ten thousand principles and comprehended a thousand paths.
If Buddhist Dharma truly harmed transformation, he would have eliminated it immediately.
How could he have revered it for years and caused it to flourish throughout the land?
Furthermore, when Buddhist Dharma existed, what were its harms?
Since its destruction, what benefits have been achieved?
If there are truly no benefits, is this not unfilial?”
The Emperor decreed,
“The Dharma arises at certain times, and the Way is also difficult to ascertain.
Regulation comes from above, and rulers set the example.
Even if there are small benefits, it must still be abolished.
Moreover, since the Buddha is without benefit, it is not logically permissible.
Why? Reverence for it has no evidence, and its call has no effect.
Since it cannot even save itself from distress, how can it benefit the nation?
Since its abolition, the people’s labor services have decreased,
taxes and levies have increased annually, and military strength has grown daily.
We pacified the Qí in the east and subdued the demonic barbarians in the west.
The nation is secure and the people are happy; is this not beneficial?
If it were truly beneficial,
Tàizǔ often campaigned against Qí during his lifetime.
How come he did not achieve victory?
I destroyed the Buddha-dharma.
If this were a transgression or harm, I should have perished.
Since I have pacified Eastern Xià,
it is clear that it is beneficial.
Its abolition is reasonable, and there is no reason for its revival.”
He memorialized:
“From the founding of a state and the establishment of government, the most valued is the Dào.
To regulate transformation and nurture the people, nothing is higher than Dé.
I have only seen the Dào diminish and states perish;
never have I seen a strong military ensure a long reign.
This is why the cruel Zhòu, relying on his multitude, brought disaster upon his imperial enterprise.
King Wǔ of Zhōu, cultivating Dé, gathered blessings for his royal foundation.
Fūchā, proud in battle, ultimately met his demise.
Gōujiàn, through the Dào, though in peril, found peace again.
Judging by this,
how can the destruction of Buddhism and the expulsion of monks be related to pacifying Dōngxià?
It is merely the destruction of Buddhism.
At this time of established peace,
this meeting happened by chance.
It is mistakenly said that destroying the law is beneficial.
If that were so, then Tāng's campaign against the Xià,
King Wén's destruction of Chóng,
King Wǔ's execution of Zhòu,
Qín's unification of All-under-Heaven,
and the Chì Hàn's overthrow of Xiàng –
none of these lords were able to achieve this through destroying Buddhism.
Subsequently, there were discussions criticizing and slandering the people's law,
some for disrespecting the sovereign and parents,
some for presumptuously claiming a ‘Buddha-nature’,
some for criticizing the analysis of form and mind,
some for emphasizing repeated non-virtuous acts,
or some for pointing out that the body is fundamentally Yīn and Yáng.
I, Lín, have resolved all these difficulties as they arose.
Though Your Majesty repeatedly raised difficulties, three or five times, exhausting reason and nature,
I, Lín, left no doubt unresolved,
and overcame every difficulty.
The Emperor said:
“Your words state that karma does not deviate from principle,
and that whenever there is an opportunity to enter sainthood,
nature is not outside of karma.
The Dào has a path for reaching the ordinary.
Thus, the Dào is omnipresent, encompassing both the ordinary and the sacred.
Therefore, there is no need for Kǒng or Shì to be vainly revered.
Such words
penetrate both the secular and the religious.
Adding the mere ornamentation of shaving and cutting [the hair] [is unnecessary].
It is known that emperors are none other than Tathāgatas;
there is no need to set up a zhàngliù (sixteen-foot Buddha statue).
Kings and dukes are none other than Bodhisattvas;
there is no need to trouble Wénshū.
Elderly people can serve as upāsaka (senior monks);
there is no need for Bīntóu.
Benevolence and kindness are truly dāna (charity);
why abandon one's country?
Peace and harmony are the foremost pure monks;
why bother with pūṣada (recitation of precepts)?
Chastity and conscientiousness are already prātimokṣa (precepts);
why receive vows?
Frugality and simplicity are truly having few desires;
there is no need for dhūta (ascetic practices).
Vegetarian food is the best long-term fasting;
why abstain from grains?
Releasing attachments is wonderfully like having no self;
what need for the understanding of emptiness?
Forgetting merits fully approximates Mahāyāna;
why hope for Prajñā?
Civil and martial arts are precisely the two kinds of wisdom;
they do not observe emptiness or existence.
Strategic schemes directly lead to skillful means;
why await transformations?
Granting official titles is truly a prediction of Buddhahood;
there is no need to seek certification of the fruit.
Obtaining titles and emoluments simultaneously achieves heaven;
why await the upper realms?
Punishments and executions already evoke hell;
there is no need to point to niraya.
Treating the people as one's children
can be called great compassion.
Regarding the four seas as one's home
is identical to the Dharma-realm.
Governing with reason
is no different from saving beings.
Bringing peace and joy to the common people
is not distinct from relieving suffering.
Punishing and eliminating the corrupt and harmful
is logically subduing demons.
Ruling over All-under-Heaven
truly constitutes attaining the Dào.
How is its vastness different from the Pure Land?
How is its multitude inferior to Kāpī (Kapilavastu)?
You harbor divergent views and cling to misguided biases.
Looking at the facts, where is there not the Dào?”
He memorialized:
“I respectfully accept Your Majesty's decree.
Its profound meaning and deep words merge the Dào with the mundane, dispelling specific attachments.
It enables everyone to embrace the truth everywhere, all sentient beings to be in the Dào, and all things, self and others, to be in harmony, making thousands of paths into one.
It is beautiful, indeed it is beautiful.
However, this foolish minister still has doubts.
If the ultimate Dào were truly one,
then there would be no two to merge.
If principles are always internal and external,
then they can naturally remain distinct.
If one is not one,
then it is half right and half wrong.
If two are not two,
then it is sometimes Dào, sometimes mundane.
This would lead to confusion between the monastic and the lay, and disorder between Confucianism and Buddhism.
Internal and external would be mixed, and upper and lower ranks would be confused.
This would not only deeply obscure pure transformation,
but also mislead the common people nearby.
Thus, while Yīn and Yáng share the same energy, their functions of creation and destruction are always distinct.
While Heaven and Earth share the same form, their heights and lows are always different.
One cannot, because they share the same form, make the earth move and the sky still.
Or, seeing that they share the same energy,
make Yīn create and Yáng destroy.
In reality, such principles never exist.
Empty words are difficult to put into practice.
Therefore, though forms are alike and energy is one,
it can be said they are similar.
However, in terms of creation, destruction, height, and lowliness, there is no meaning without distinction.
Thus, they are alike yet not alike,
one yet not one.
The principles of the Dào and the mundane have similarities but no sameness;
they naturally differ without deliberate action.
Furthermore, even if a king's name is singular, the ordinary and the sacred are as different as heaven.
The forms of affairs are slightly similar, but their scope is entirely different.
Therefore, Confucianism and Buddhism arose together from timelessness,
and the Dào and the mundane transform together with Heaven and Earth.
If one wishes to obliterate them into one,
one can only abolish the mundane by means of the Dào.
If both benefit the world,
then both principles, hidden and manifest, shine equally.
Now, to promote one and abolish the other,
is truly impermissible.”
An edict said:
“Your words state that the Dào and the mundane are as different as heaven, completely distinct in internal and external.
It could also be said that the Dào should be just the Dào, without involvement with the mundane.
Buddhism should be just Buddhism, without reliance on Confucianism.
If the Dào were only the Dào,
what benefit would the Dào bring?
If the Buddha were solely the Buddha,
what merit would his transformation have?
Therefore, the Dào and the mundane rely on each other, and Confucianism and Buddhism mutually enhance each other.
If you do not follow My words,
what do you wish to discuss?
Therefore, internal and external rise and fall, one suppressing the other,
and now the national law is not followed, being prohibited by royal law.
Rise and fall are within the natural order, and constant principles are not violated.
If there is no constant rise, what fault is there in decline?”
He memorialized:
“I respectfully receive Your Majesty's decree,
as if parting the clouds to see the sun.
I respectfully listen to Your Majesty's instruction;
it is truly as Your Majesty says.
The Dào does not exist independently; it is not manifest without the mundane.
The Buddha does not exist independently; only the sovereign can promote him.
Therefore, since Buddhist teachings spread eastward, five hundred years have passed.
To extensively propagate the Dharma-transformation relies essentially on royal power.
Thus, the Dào is advanced by people, and spiritual power is evoked by things.
The flourishing and decline of the Buddha's teachings are due to Your Majesty's will.
The Dào has its rise and fall; its meaning is not eternal.
The Dharma has its hidden and manifest phases; its principle cannot always endure.
Since it has been abolished, its meaning cannot be immediately enforced.
Since its suspension has been long, the time for its revival is next.
Alternating with abolition, it naturally responds to the times.
Following the trends of the world,
is it not fitting?”
An edict said:
“The method of emperors is to wisely decide what to accept or reject, clearly determining what to go with or abandon.
They carefully discern similarities and differences and subtly observe the extraordinary.
Regarding Buddhist teachings,
I have pondered deeply within My inner thoughts,
compared them with ancient and modern times,
verified them through deeds,
and calculated their gains and losses.
Their principles are extraordinary but not essential,
their writings profound and wondrous but useless.
It is not without reason that they are abandoned and abolished.
Why should there be love or hatred for Confucianism or Buddhism?”
He memorialized,
“The foundation of propagating the Dharma
must begin by focusing on those who are insightful and adept at transforming others.
One must maintain an aspiration for the righteous path.
Do not, upon encountering those who oppose you with malice,
harbor feelings of alienation.
Nor, upon encountering those who accommodate you with kindness,
happily draw near to them.
To do so is to be deluded by what you see,
and disturbed by what you hear.
You should not, upon frequently hearing slanders against the righteous,
immediately believe, accept, and echo them, thereby creating disputes.
Nor should you constantly seek out faults and shortcomings, daily harboring contempt.
This is to replace truth with falsehood,
and let popular opinion confuse your will.
Therefore, those who should be kept at a distance are instead drawn closer,
and those who should be close are instead pushed away.
This leads to biased discussions and errors in judgment regarding acceptance and rejection.
This is indeed a calamity that harms truth,
and an evil accumulation that undermines virtue.
Thereupon, the emperor did not reply,
but instead opened a different avenue to initiate discussion.
He asked,
“I have heard that a *jūn zǐ* (君子) in all their actions must accord with propriety.
The wise and sagacious in their movements must respond to the opportune moment.
Recently, I have repeatedly bestowed food upon you,
but you say you do not drink alcohol or eat meat.
Moreover, alcohol is a medicine that harmonizes the spirit,
and meat is a sustenance that nourishes the body.
Both have been enjoyed from ancient times to the present.
Why do you alone disdain them?
If your body were in mourning clothes,
the rites would forbid eating them.
But now, being gifted, you may certainly eat them.
To be able to eat but not eat, is this not a fault?”
He memorialized,
“Coveting wealth and delighting in beauty are disdained by a virtuous man.
Fondness for fine dishes and exquisite flavors are abhorred by an honest scholar.
Sacrificing personal feelings to follow the Dao is praised by past worthies,
and suppressing desires to uphold virtue is lamented by ancient sages.
Furthermore, meat comes from taking life, and alcohol can disturb the spirit.
Not eating them is in accordance with reason.
How can it be considered a fault?”
The emperor’s edict said,
“Meat comes from harming life,
so abstaining from it is indeed justified.
But alcohol does not harm life,
so why abolish it entirely?
If it causes no harm,
then in terms of culpability, there is no fault to be called wrong.
Drinking water and eating rice should also incur blame.
But in reality, it is not so.
Why is alcohol uniquely forbidden?”
He memorialized,
“The establishment of precepts follows the circumstances, and culpability is judged by the mind.
The substance of meat involves harm, so eating it immediately constitutes a transgression.
The nature of alcohol is not inherently harmful, but its fault arises from impairing the spirit,
leading to transgressions elsewhere.
These transgressions arise from alcohol.
Abolishing alcohol eliminates them.
Therefore, the prohibition differs,
not because the substance of alcohol itself is a transgression.”
The emperor’s edict said,
“A transgression has a prohibitive nature,
and the substance of alcohol causes transgression.
Now there are people who can tolerate alcohol,
who can drink without becoming intoxicated,
and whose spirit is not impaired,
nor do they commit transgressions.
These people should not be considered to transgress by drinking alcohol.
In this case, those who can drink commit no fault,
while those who cannot incur blame.
How does this relate to abolishing alcohol to achieve the goodness of the precepts?
It could be said that those who can drink and tolerate alcohol are constantly upholding the precepts,
while those who become drunk from a little are great sinners.”
He memorialized,
“Establishing prohibitions against faults and preventing wrongdoings is fundamentally for the sake of generating goodness.
*Jiè* (戒) is a quiescent goodness, where body and mouth are without transgression.
When the karmic condition ceases, both prohibitive natures are cut off.
This is then called the goodness of the *jiè*.
Now, for a person who tolerates alcohol,
since their spirit is not disturbed,
they have not violated the precept of drinking.
In truth, it is not a transgression.
However, transgressions arise from drinking.
Drinking constitutes a violation of the prohibition.
And through the condition of teaching, offenses arise.
Therefore, it is still considered a transgression.
To contravene the ‘no drinking’ rule is still not upholding the *jiè*.”
The emperor’s edict said,
“A great *shì* (士) who embraces the Dao must do so through marvelous comprehension.
An ultimate person, high-minded and insightful, values non-attachment.
Their mind merges with the vastness of the Dharma-nature;
their intention extends to the boundlessness of empty space.
There is nothing among myriad things that is not good.
How can beauty and ugliness be anything but the Dao?
Therefore, dwelling amidst alcohol and lying among meat,
how can there be sin?
To wander with a wife and children,
how can it be said to produce fault?
Thus, the Crown Prince attained the Dao by taking a wife,
while Jí Tuó (周陀) fell into depravity by abandoning his wife.
Wéi Mó Jié (淨名) achieved high insight by living in the secular world,
while Shēn Zǐ (身子) became stubbornly foolish by leaving home.
Therefore, what is good cannot necessarily be perfected as good,
and what is evil, how can it be called evil?
The marvel of forbidding alcohol and cutting off meat
is greatly at odds with the Great Dao.”
He memorialized,
“Dragons and tigers excel with their scales and fangs.
Apes and birds possess talent through leaping and soaring.
A *jūn zǐ* takes comprehension and action as their Dao.
Sages and worthies achieve virtue through truth and reality.
Thus, they are praised both internally and externally, and both monastics and laity hold them in high esteem.
If there is only comprehension without action,
it is like a well in the sand, without fertility.
If one is solely empty and unreal,
it is like empty clouds without rain.
Therefore, the creator of myriad things takes the ruler and compass as uprightness.
The ruler of the world takes law and principle as the foundation.
Thus, they can effectively prevent evil sprouts and detect treacherous individuals.
Therefore, one lapse in conduct is as painful as cutting flesh.
One good word is more valuable than a thousand pieces of gold.
If the root of the mind has marvelous comprehension,
then dwelling in evil becomes good.
If divine wisdom is clear and empty, then being in sin becomes a blessing.
One could also move a humble subject to a heavy responsibility in heaven,
or shift a most honored sage to a lowly position among subjects.
This would lead to a chaotic mix of ruler and minister, and an upside-down order.
Such a thing is impractical;
it has never happened in ancient or modern times.
How is this different from discoursing on loyalty and filial piety while constantly engaging in rebellion,
or discussing compassion and giving while regularly committing murder and theft?
One may be skilled in a hundred techniques verbally but incapable in practice,
or speak of traveling ten thousand *lǐ* (里) but never leave the house.
These are all cases where feelings are passionate but actions extravagant,
lofty but useless.
Therefore, there are talents that are great but useless,
and principles that are small but universally applicable.
To cling to this as the Dao
is truly difficult to trust.”
The emperor’s edict said,
“Those who cling to feelings cannot discuss the Dao.
Those with shallow wisdom are difficult to talk to about truth.
Thus, a fish in a small well
can hardly know the vastness and depth of the East Sea.
A swallow or sparrow soaring by the fence
how could it envy the flight of the *péng* (鵬) or phoenix?
These all cling to the small, thereby contradicting the great aspiration,
and adhere to convention, thereby harming the general path.
If I consider myself as the world,
then there is nothing that is not me.
If I consider the world as myself,
then there is nothing that is not the world.
Since I am not different from the world,
how can the world be different from me?
When both self and world are forgotten, and self and other are equalized,
those with an empty mind find nothing dissimilar.
Those who abandon merit find nothing impossible.”
He memorialized,
“Upon reverently receiving your sacred decree,
its meaning is profound and vast, its origin boundless.
It is impossible to thoroughly investigate it.
The matter is like peeking at the sky;
who can measure its breadth?
It is also like measuring the sea;
who can know its depth?
If one takes the small as small within the great,
then there is nothing great that is not small.
If one takes the great as great within the small,
then there is nothing small that is not great.
If the great is universally great, then an autumn hair is not small.
If the small is universally small, then Mount Tài (泰) is not great.
Thus, the great is not great-small,
and the small is not small-great.
Therefore, smallness and greatness are different from sameness,
and smallness and greatness are the same in difference.
Without the difference or sameness of smallness and greatness,
how can there be the sameness or difference of smallness and greatness?
Only then can one know that non-difference can be made different and same.
How can sameness be made same and different?
Without sameness that can be made same and different, there is no difference and sameness.
Without difference that can be made different and same, there is no sameness and difference.
Therefore, to be the same without sameness is not sameness.
To be different without difference is not difference.
How can sameness and difference be made different and same?
And how can non-difference and sameness be made same and different?”
The emperor then did not reply.
Thereupon, the ruler and minister were silent and spoke not for a long time.
The emperor then asked,
“Why are you so silent?
You are about to disperse existence and return to non-existence.
Do not, because the discussion is not to your liking, cease your clear debate.”
He memorialized,
“Ancient people were fearful when they ought to speak,
and worried when they spoke.
Therefore, there were ancient rulers who did not speak,
and there are historically famed scholars who forgot their merits.
Thus, silence expresses knowledge.
It is not because the discussion is unsuitable.”
The imperial edict stated:
The perfect person acts without acting, yet has never not acted.
The wise person speaks without speaking, yet has never not spoken.
There are also parrots that speak but are useless.
The Fènghuáng does not speak, yet establishes a standard.
Wood without purpose survives.
Geese that do not cry meet their death.
How do you, our minister, choose and reject to suit yourself now?
It also said:
A scholar may be known by a single word.
Truth may exist by merely meeting one's gaze.
There are also those who discern feelings by observing facial expressions.
And those who distinguish virtue by listening to words.
Our conversations with you, our minister, have been ongoing for a long time.
How could the essence of them not be generally understood?
You, our minister, should record these for us in the proper place and present them.
Let all people of the world know Our intentions.
This would be assisting Us.
How could it be considered a lack of loyalty?
Lín Yǐ, fearing death, requested permission to appeal against the subversion of Buddhist law.
The emperor's sentiment was comparatively stubborn, and Lín Yǐ's arguments were not accepted.
Although the debate was clear, it ultimately did not reflect the emperor's original intent.
After the abolition of Buddhism in Cháng'ān,
a separate Tōngdào Guān was established later.
Those who studied there focused solely on Lǎozhuāng thought.
They enjoyed setting up empty discussions and extended them to the Three Teachings.
Hoping to use this momentum to clarify the Buddhist section,
Lín Yǐ then submitted a memorial.
He requested that ten of the most intelligent and eminent Shāmén from the Yèchéng Academy
be allowed to join the Tōngdào Guān.
Upon reading the memorial, the emperor immediately said:
It is excellent for you, our minister, to enter the Tōngdào Guān to study diligently.
There is no discourse that is not profound there.
It will greatly benefit you personally.
After a meal was served, he further said:
You, our minister, should pack your bags and enter the pass; the others will return.
On the first day of the fifth month,
Lín Yǐ arrived at Cháng'ān and was granted an audience at the Yánshòu Diàn.
On the twenty-fourth day, the emperor went to Yúnyáng Gōng.
On the first day of the sixth month, the emperor passed away.
Tiānyuán Dēng Zhà was in Tóngzhōu.
On the thirteenth day of the ninth month,
Cháng Zōngbó Qí Gōng completed his memorial.
The emperor granted permission, saying:
Buddhist principles are vast, and the Great Way is profoundly subtle.
There are rules for its propagation; the Dharma must be studied.
Such repeated memorials may cause delay or transgression.
The memorial replied:
My original appeal was solely for the propagation of the Dharma.
I have repeatedly pleaded with earnestness, wishing only for it to be implemented soon.
Now, the Sacred Emperor has granted approval, and the deliberative officials have made their decision.
With harmony above and below, there will certainly be no differing views.
Once promulgated, the whole world will rejoice.
How dare I speak further?
On the fifteenth day of the first month of Dàchéng first year,
an edict stated:
The profound teachings are to be widely established, and the Three Jewels are to be respected.
Special reverence is appropriate.
The Dharma's transformative power is vast, and it is right to revere and uphold it.
Seven of the former Shāmén who possessed high virtue and purity
are to reside and practice the Way in the west of Zhèngwǔ Diàn.
On the twenty-sixth day of the second month, the reign title was changed to Dàxiàng.
Another imperial edict stated:
The Buddha-Dharma is vast and has been revered throughout the ages.
How could it be obscured, abandoned, and not practiced?
From now on,
from princes and dukes down to the common people,
all should cultivate and understand Our intention.
On that very day,
the majestic statues in the palace were adorned, and devout reverence was fully performed.
At that time, from both the Buddhist and Daoist communities,
one great virtuous master was selected to ascend the Dharma seat
and propagate the subtle scriptures.
This caused people to harbor no fear,
and to express subtle words to each other. Buddhist principles are vast, profound, and immeasurable.
The Daoist lineage is superficial and easily understood.
Their sharpness was dulled in the assembly, and the princes and dukes sighed in admiration.
On the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month,
an edict was issued, stating:
Buddhist teachings are profound and wonderfully vast.
It is essential to widely open up the teaching methods
and facilitate their practice.
Devotees should examine themselves according to the scriptures.
Followers of the Way need not cut their hair
or disfigure themselves, thereby deviating from the Great Way.
It is appropriate to retain hair and beard and wear solemn attire to pursue higher aspirations.
Let one hundred and twenty of the former Shāmén, those of eminent virtue, purity, profound learning, clear reputation, and admirable prestige, be selected
to practice the Way for the nation at Zhìkù Sì.
It is intended that their four needs of sustenance will be amply provided.
As for meditation and chanting among the populace,
there shall be no hindrance whatsoever.
Only in the capital city and Luòyáng
shall one temple each be established.
Permission for other prefectures and commanderies has not yet been granted.
On the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month of Zhōu Dàxiàng first year,
Fǎshī Rèn Dàolín
was instructed to reside at Wèidào Hǔ Zhái in Tóngzhōu,
to compile and present these matters.
Nèishǐ Pèi Gōng Yǔwén Zé personally reviewed them.
Xiǎo Nèishǐ Línjīng Gōng Yǔwén Hóng read them aloud.
Zhǎnglǐ Shàngshì Tuòbá Xínggōng was entrusted with the initial review, and Dū Shàngshì Chìkòu Chén with the final verification.
Former Monk King Míngguǎng.
On the twenty-seventh day of the second month of Dàxiàng first year, Wáng Míngguǎng responded to Wèi Yuánsōng's memorial concerning the destruction of Buddhist law.
Wáng Míngguǎng, a grandson of Fótúchéng from the Bái Mǎ Sì in Yèchéng (the former capital of Zhào Wǔdì),
humbly and fearfully submits this memorial, deserving of death.
Míngguǎng states:
Wèi Yuánsōng, the false Daoist from Yìzhōu Yě'ān Sì,
with his sharp eloquence and extraordinary talent, disguised wrong as right.
He requested the abolition of Buddhist images and the destruction of monastic laws.
This is a biased statement that misled the emperor, difficult to clarify at first.
The great nation believed him, and counsel was not accepted.
The common people privately discussed it, and the populace gazed in bewilderment.
Indeed, nothing is more inconvenient than this.
My learning is not youthful, and my talent falls short of innate wisdom.
I have perused a single record,
and read various treatises.
I have sought out a hundred schools and further examined the Six Classics.
I have verified and tested Wèi Yuánsōng's words and found them completely unsubstantiated.
Alas, the Buddha-Dharma has existed for a long time!
What is regrettable is to see it unjustly decline today.
Indeed, those who flatter to save themselves are thieves of the state.
Those who speak plainly and do not fear severe punishment are blessings to the state.
Relying on this principle, I dare to die to express my sincerity.
My refutation of Wèi Yuánsōng's six points is presented below.
I humbly beseech Tiānyuán Huángdì,
to open his four eyes and clear his four ears,
to briefly lower his divine authority and slightly turn his sacred thoughts,
to listen but once.
I await the penalties of grace and punishment, submitting to the law.
Respectfully submitted.
I, your servant Míngguǎng, respectfully respond:
The Shī Jīng says:
"No virtue goes unrewarded,
no word goes unanswered."
Although I am humble and ignorant, I have heard from my predecessors:
The ultimate Way transcends mental contemplation.
Great virtue emerges from reputation.
A gentleman does not engage in empty talk.
All Buddhas certainly engage in earnest discourse.
They remove delusion, break attachment, and open the Way for the ignorant masses.
Deference from humans and devas has been for a long time.
Good words teach beings, and both ordinary and holy beings return to benevolence.
Who has seen the virtue of sweet dew and orchid ganoderma?
Even if Yáo was called "ultimate in the Way,"
no golden dream was seen in Píngyáng.
Shùn was known for "non-action,"
yet the auspicious light in Púbǎn was still distant.
Alas!
It is easy to live in vain and die, but difficult to hear the True Dharma.
The pure and victorious customs have largely faded,
and flattering words are difficult to use.
If it were true that the states of Qí and Liáng declined because they promoted Buddhism, and their national fortunes were not prosperous,
how could Táng and Yú have dedicated themselves to monastic life?
If the imperial lineage had no heirs and the people were starving and sickly,
how could one hear from the history of Liáng that the flooding was a natural disaster that began in Yáo's time?
A complete Way is not exclusive to the lands of Táng and Yú.
The ruin of the people is not limited to the regions of Qí and Liáng.
As for righteous conduct enriching the nation,
erecting splendid halls is not considered burdensome.
When rituals are abandoned for years,
living in an earthen dwelling is considered leisurely.
Therefore, Fù Yì said:
"The world praises
Shénnóng's personal plowing and Yáo and Shùn's thatched huts.
This is rhetoric from a decadent age,
not the Way of the former kings."
The pagodas and temples of Qí and Liáng
themselves created causes for blessings and virtues.
How could they demand immediate reciprocation?
Therefore, Zéngzǐ said:
"When a person delights in goodness,
although blessings have not yet arrived,
misfortune is far away.
When a person commits evil,
although calamity has not yet arrived,
blessings are far away."
Bǎopǔzǐ said:
"The wise are not necessarily long-lived, nor are the foolish necessarily afflicted.
Goodness does not guarantee immediate blessings, nor does evil guarantee immediate calamities."
Why then seek immediate verification and abandon great, distant evidence?
The past and present shift, and quality and refinement change with the times.
In governing the state and aiding the populace, appropriateness to the times is paramount.
I fear that the victorious customs of Táng and Yú,
though said to be right, are not exclusively right.
And the latter Dharma of Qí and Liáng,
though said to be wrong, is not exclusively wrong.
Your servant, Guǎng, replied again.
The *Shī Jīng* says:
"One with outstanding virtuous conduct,
the four states will obey him."
Creation is natural, how can it involve human affairs?
The six *tiān* implore, the myriad nations take refuge.
The halls of the seven places and eight assemblies are immeasurable.
How can they be merely a monastery for a thousand monks?
If there is no great worthy, who will pay reverence?
If there is no great sage, who will come to stay?
The *Nièpán Jīng* says:
"Do not seize others' wealth and possessions,
but constantly bestow kindness on all.
Build *zhāotí* monastic dwellings,
and you will be reborn in the Immovable Land (*Bùdòng Guó*)."
Since the various *jīng* clearly show that there are reasons for all matters,
how can it be slandered as not conforming to the Buddha's heart?
The monastery is called Píngyán, yet Sōng makes a baseless argument.
The Buddha established *gālán*, how can it be called a narrow view?
This is a comparison exceeding proper limits, giving and taking contrary to propriety.
What is the difference between this execution and beating a drum while laughing at Léimén,
or boasting about an anthill in front of the Heavenly Court?
To persuade that husband and wife are the holy assembly,
indulging in licentious marriage;
to say that the national ruler is the *rúlái*,
hoping to foster flattery.
Are the upright remonstrating officials truly like this?
How is this different from Wèi Líng seeking favoritism and persuading the King of Chǔ to take his son's wife?
Or Zǎi Pǐ seeking immediate gain and explaining the 'dark dream' for the King of Wú?
They knew it was not right in their hearts, but spoke beautiful words with their mouths.
Those who believed their evil words were thus led to destroy their states.
Yuán Sōng will certainly incur great sin.
The monastic official was expelled.
Out of anger, shame, and humiliation, he slandered the decree.
Fearing that the logic of overturning nests and destroying monasteries would not be accepted,
he incited the emperor's heart by calling him 'Buddha' as a title of respect.
This is bending to the will of one person,
burying the fields of the Three Jewels.
Among the common people who hear of this, who does not sigh with regret?
Since the arrival of the Buddhadharma, it has been eternal and boundless.
Dwelling in Heaven and residing on Earth, it is revered wherever it is.
Which former emperor or later king did not deeply respect it?
Why is it despised only in this country?
In the past, Biàn Hé was distressed in Chǔ, and Kǒngzǐ was in peril in Chén.
Comparing the present to ancient times, I fear it will invite ridicule.
Your servant, Guǎng, replied again.
The Buddha is a compassionate father, a charioteer of gods and humans.
He is good in the beginning, middle, and end, bringing benefit and peace to all.
From the time he concealed his divine power under the twin trees, the earth shook in the ten directions.
His hair was given to the four *tiān*, and his relics were distributed among the eight nations.
The *Nièpán Jīng* says:
"If one builds a Buddha image or a stupa,
even as small as a thumb,
and constantly has a joyful heart,
one will be reborn in the Immovable Land (*Bùdòng Guó*)."
It is clear that supporting one's father and serving one's teacher are related to classical teachings.
The initiation of *shùxiū* launched the Confucian teachings.
Such arguments are truly hard to come by.
Wèi Sōng's baseless criticisms
entered the hall and did not perish.
How can one not speak?
In ancient times, Táng Yáo's governance emulated Heaven,
but Heaven suffered the disaster of overflowing waters.
The Zhōu established the rites of ancestral temples,
yet the temples had no power to bring rain.
If one says that stupas bring no blessings,
and if there is fault, one should return;
then ancestral temples could also be sought in vain,
and should likewise be abandoned.
If we deduce the hidden workings by reason,
recognizing the grace of the Heavenly Temple can also be attributed to fate reaching its end.
How can halls and stupas save?
Even if Fèi Gōng could shrink the earth and Lǔ Zǐ could turn back the sky,
they could not save those destined to die;
how could they extend lives already ended?
If fate is not fixed,
then blessings can alter it.
The meaning differs from the previous argument;
compassion and protection are necessary.
For instance, before the image of Pǔxián, lepers who took refuge were cured.
In the Zhīhuán monastery, those with chronic illnesses were appeased, and suffering was relieved and disasters averted—there are many such instances, not just one.
I will address other difficulties and not elaborate further.
Moreover, the Way does not solely pervade; virtue is not absent anywhere.
A thousand paths lead to one goal; why limit it to the inner mind?
As for the construction of treasure stupas by Shūjiā,
a hundred *guǐ* assisted with daily effort.
The erection of *fútú* by Quèlí,
the four *tiān* supported its night power.
How great it is, moving Heaven and Earth and stirring *guǐshén*!
To say that external cultivation brings no blessings—what kind of talk is that?
If this were to compel the poor to work,
the people might complain of toil.
But the meaning is in tolerance, being able to give without weariness.
If it is truly because stupas and monasteries ruined the country and impoverished the people,
then now that monks have been abolished,
the poor should suddenly become rich.
Yet the cities are more impoverished and withered than in former years.
Can this be attributed to the Buddha?
If *guǐ* are not respected and thus called flattery,
then why worship and seek at ancestral trees, leading to so much delusion?
If one says that ancestral trees are relied upon by *guǐ*, and their veneration is not a fault,
then it can also be said that temple halls and stupas are where the Buddha resides, and their construction and maintenance should certainly be according to the Dharma.
If one says the Buddha is in the void and does not reside in mud or wood,
then *guǐshén* should also be obscure and formless;
how could they be within trees?
Indeed, conforming to reason and benefiting beings is what the sacred teachings originally unveiled.
Unrighteous gain is not permitted by the *jīng*.
There are quite a few heavenly palaces and Buddha stupas
that have been dismantled to make walls for bridges and screens.
Embroidered images and Dharma *jīng*
are used to make clothes stained with pus and blood.
The world is hungry and poor day by day,
the common people wither year after year.
Even minor *guǐshén* should not be deceived;
how can the great spiritual beings, the Buddhas, be abandoned?
The *Shī Jīng* says:
"Heaven does not fulfill its virtue,
sending down destruction and famine."
This is what is meant.
Let's speak of the meritorious officials of past dynasties and the mighty generals of today.
They pacified distant lands with weapons.
In life, they enjoyed exceptional honors,
with red gates and purple chambers.
Upon death, many commoners are made to build temples and erect tombs, offer sacrifices to the dead, and kill living beings.
They venerate the void and damage the real, toiling without benefit.
This was not mentioned at all before.
How much more so the *Shìjiāmóuní Rúlái*, whose Way covers three thousand worlds and whose transformation thrives in a hundred million!
Looking forward, none obstruct; looking backward, who can surpass him?
He was able to subdue masters of external paths,
and skillfully pacify the party of *tiānmó*.
He used not an inch of weapon, nor expended a foot of blade.
His five lights shone everywhere, and no suffering was not dispelled.
His four brilliant arguments flowed widely, bringing peace and joy to the deluded.
As a general and commander, his name is high and his position great.
What harm is there in the existence of monasteries and temples?
A clay dragon cannot bring rain,
yet people still follow it to seek blessings.
Even if a clay Buddha does not speak,
how can those who revere it be without evidence (of efficacy)?
In the past, Mǎ Qīng admired Lìn and Kǒng Fù dreamed of Zhōu.
Therefore, they respected ancient people and revered old virtues.
How much more so the Buddhas of the three ages, whose transforming influence and principles are the same!
Even if Mílè were to first emerge,
one should not suddenly abandon the Dharma teachings of Shìjiā.
Your servant, Guǎng, replied again.
It is reasonable to tax rich monks who lack virtue.
It is unjust to seize monasteries from virtuous poor monks.
For example, Guǎn and Cài were disloyal,
but one cannot slaughter all of the Jī clan.
Bǔ Shāng was stingy,
but how can all of Kǒng's disciples be instantly demoted?
A herdboy,
first removes the horses that stray from the herd.
A cowherd boy
specially protects the cows in the herd.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The Way is everywhere.
Those who accord with it comprehend it.
To merely encounter strangeness
does not align with the ultimate Way."
This is all there is to it.
As for Shìjiā, Zhōu, Kǒng, Yáo, Shùn, Lǎo, and Zhuāng,
though their teachings and traces differ, their ultimate goal is one.
How can the era of knot-tying be uniquely called righteous governance,
and tonsured monks be solely called expedient means?
The narrow-mindedness is extreme!
Where can the understanding of the equality of things (*qíwù*) be found?
Lǎozǐ said:
"The superior person, hearing of the Way, diligently practices it.
The mediocre person, hearing of the Way, seems to keep it, seems to lose it.
The inferior person, hearing of the Way, laughs loudly and scorns it."
Yuán Sōng is already an inferior person of the Buddhadharma.
He assumes the form of Dharma robes but does not recognize the preciousness of Jīng.
He wrongly measures the Hé treasure.
Ugly words come from his false mouth,
disrespect is valued at the tip of his brush.
If there were few people of substance in the land west of the pass,
who would believe such incorrect writings?
Guǎng has often seen travelers who fled mountains and crossed seas,
and people from the Eastern *Yí* and Northern *Dí*.
In the past, they came out of admiration for goodness;
now, due to the destruction of the Dharma, they are scattered.
It can be said that one loves profit but not the gentry and common people,
and thus incurs the fault of dispersal and loss.
Yet, foreign goods and wealth are not heard to be unused,
but foreign teachers' instructions are uniquely seen as unrespected.
The world's strange expectations arise from this.
Since Guǎng sincerely holds loyalty in his mind,
it is reasonable for him to speak and he has long hoped to submit this petition.
However, the former emperor had a different understanding and adopted Sōng's words.
What is past cannot be undone; what is done cannot be gainsaid.
Three years is a long time.
I have thought thrice before speaking.
If there is one point that can be followed,
I beg for an immediate change in the rules.
Your servant, Guǎng, further replied.
I humbly submit that mountains contain both fragrant orchids and bitter mugwort, and seas hold both dragons and snakes.
The beautiful and the ugly flow together; the wise and the foolish are mixed.
If dragons and snakes are both favored, there will be no distinction between right and wrong.
If orchids and mugwort are both cut down, who will discern gain and loss?
If those with virtue are necessarily preserved and the unworthy are removed,
firstly, it will enrich the family tradition;
secondly, it will not confuse the masses;
thirdly, Heaven will not be reproached for hindering good;
fourthly, the people's virtue will return to its厚.
Our great Zhōu
corresponds to a thousand-year period
and holds the position of myriad foundations.
It expounds rites and clarifies music, aligning earth and leveling heaven.
Its military achievements are arrayed, its literary brilliance shines, assisting the true and clarifying customs.
Worthy monks are instruments of the state;
they do not cause the people of Yáo to suffer from war.
The holy multitude flocks to us;
how can this be merely the ranks of Qīcí?
Some are outwardly compassionate and receptive, inwardly intelligent and discerning,
developing the Mahāyāna, ferrying the common people.
Others hide their wings in the Chan groves, or are fish swimming in tranquil waters,
steadfastly holding to their floating rafts and firmly maintaining their armor of endurance.
Yet others change their form and shed their robes, appearing to be different from ordinary people,
but their indulgence is boundless, still akin to the ignorant populace.
Yuán Sōng's request to select and remove them is indeed reasonable.
The utmost achievements of Heaven and Earth have their times of activity and stillness.
Even the lengthening and shortening of the sun and moon can be variable.
Nowadays, the teachings of Zhuāng Lǎo are rarely encountered among people.
If the whole country were made to practice them,
surely those who violate the rules would be punished.
How do we know this?
We see that people of our time who embrace Confucian teachings
and conquer themselves to observe the rites often deviate in their actions.
The Lǐ Yún says:
"Dried meat is not eaten."
Have we not seen people given meat but asking for vegetables?
"A full goblet is not drunk."
Have we not seen people not urging others to drink when their cups are full?
"At the height of a feast, one does not drink more than three cups."
Have we not seen people get drunk when indulging in wine?
"The Son of Heaven does not surround game."
"Feudal lords do not make collective hunts."
"Common people do not take fawns or eggs."
Since Guǎng was young, he has been slightly influenced by the Xuan Gate [Daoism],
and is not skilled in matters of "surrounding game" or "collective hunts."
But looking around, he sees everywhere people who are "taking fawns and eggs."
How then can it be said that those who do not conform to rites should not abandon their Confucian robes?
Indeed, transformation is achieved by the prevalence of the Way, and governance is perfected by rites.
Honor and disgrace are shown to the noble person;
punishment is used to control the petty person.
Like the method of cultivating fields,
grain and weeds must be separated.
When tending mulberry trees,
how can all of them be cut down?
Your subject Guǎng again replied,
"Loyal ministers, filial sons, and righteous people have many paths.
Why must personally tilling the land and paying rent be considered the highest?
The *Lǐ* says,
'Minor filial piety uses strength.
Medium filial piety uses toil.
Great filial piety is inexhaustible.'
The filial piety of a Shāmén
is, at its highest, to follow the wishes of all Buddhas;
in the middle, to repay the four great kindnesses;
at its lowest, to benefit all sentient beings.
These three are inexhaustible, and this is the same as great filial piety.
Therefore, the *Shī* says,
'A gentle and benevolent ruler,
seeks blessings without straying.'
If one necessarily dismisses the Six Classics and instead trusts empty words,
the righteous path will be abandoned and diminished; this is what I do not wish for.
If one serves parents only with physical strength,
it can only be called minor filial piety.
To pay rent and taxes to the sovereign makes one a commoner.
To give alms to monks and revere images are both reasonable.
To stand against Sōng like a spear and shield is to obstruct oneself.
He speaks contemptuously of others,
calling reverence for stone figures 'foolish monks,'
and reverence for images 'ignorant customs.'
Even beasts understand lust for wives and love for children.
To sing and cherish thoughts of this, how lowly!
The *Xiàojīng* says,
'Our body, hair, and skin,
we received from our parents;
we dare not injure them:
this is the beginning of filial piety.
To establish oneself in the world, practice the Way,
and leave a good name to posterity,
thereby making one's parents illustrious:
this is the culmination of filial piety.'
If one says that Shāmén who leave home are subject to the criticism of abandoning their parents,
then Zēngshēn serving Kǒngqiū could also be considered an unfilial son.
That they are enlightened in the Way and heard in the sacred texts,
observe rituals and are in harmony with propriety, what offense do monks have?
Lǎozǐ said,
'If the four phenomena do not operate,
the great phenomenon has no way to flourish.
If the five notes do not sound,
the great sound has no way to reach.'
If you wish to forever extinguish the Two Vehicles,
then the Mahāyāna also has no way to flourish.
As for Sōng, if his will is clear in leaving home, he will not regret it.
If his will is not clear, why must he regret?
In the past, Dīng Gōng entered the Hàn,
but first suffered the disgrace of Zhìdiǎn.
Mǎ Mǔ rebelled against Jiāng,
thereby bringing upon herself the fate of 'spilled water cannot be gathered.'
This proves that a defeated army
cannot be used by a loyal minister.
A wife who flees her husband
ultimately loses her name for chastity and virtue.
Sōng originally took refuge in Shìjiā;
this can be called a good beginning.
But to tire of the Way and return to lay life
is not a good end.
How is this different from those promiscuous women and treacherous ministers?
Heaven does not tolerate evil for long; how can one preserve oneself for long?
To turn from the truth and return to common ways,
what is the difference?
Regarding the request to reduce the number of monks and temples:
I have heard that precious gold and jade are treasured by all people,
and the distinct meanings of玄 (Xuán, i.e. Daoism/Buddhism) and 儒 (Rú, i.e. Confucianism) are followed by all, far and near.
Why must one only follow Kǒng Shēng because he is from one's own country,
and abandon the Buddha because he is from a distant land?
Overcome by the urgency of the matter, I presume to present my foolish opinions.
I dare not claim exclusive authority on matters of right and wrong.
In the past, Kǒngqiū departed, and his temples became a model for a thousand years.
Shìjiā departed, and his temples became sacred pagodas for ten thousand generations.
This is to make people remember him upon seeing his form, and turn their hearts to him upon seeing his image.
Revering teachers and being loyal to the sovereign are one and the same in principle.
As for Dīng Lán, who wore a belt
to dutifully serve a wooden mother figure,
and Wújìn, who removed her necklace
to offer to the Pagoda of Duōbǎo Buddha –
gazing back through vast antiquity, envisioning pure dust,
once sown, a forest grows; this principle does not change.
Moreover, according to the *Lǐjīng*,
the Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples,
feudal lords five temples,
and high officials and ministers have their respective grades.
Therefore, Heaven is called 'Shén' (God),
and sacrifices to Heaven are made at the Round Mound.
Earth is called 'Qí' (Spirit),
and sacrifices to Earth are made at the Square Marsh.
Humans are called 'Guǐ' (Ghosts),
and sacrifices are made to them in ancestral temples.
For the dragons and spirits who bring rain,
and the oxen who toil at the plow,
shapes are sometimes erected in villages and images placed at city gates.
How much more so for the Great Master of the Three Realms, above and below Heaven,
the compassionate father of the four kinds of birth, here and in other lands?
His majestic virtue is revered by hundreds of millions,
and his transformative influence is a model for myriad spirits.
Thus, good people turn to him,
like all streams returning to the ocean.
His great light embraces and receives all,
like the two luminaries accompanied by all the stars.
From the time his shadow was left in Yuèzhī and his body turned to ash in Nàjié,
his relics spread widely, and the Qíhuán was built.
Both the virtuous and the holy rely on this auspicious fortune.
Both the noble and the exalted hope to find peace here.
Should the seven-tiered, nine-storied shrines collapse and their structures fall,
and the four gates and eight windows become disordered?
If order is achieved without command,
and ritual teachings adapt to the times,
then ultimate truth is obtained without words.
Scriptures and images can naturally be allowed to spread.
Enlightened people and distinguished scholars apply them appropriately,
assisting the true Way and illuminating customs, with sagely inspiration responding to the times.
If one waits for Tàigōng to be a minister,
there will be no Tàigōng for a thousand years.
If one insists on Luóshí as a teacher,
there will be no Luóshí for ten thousand generations.
The Dharma does not manifest itself; its propagation must rely on people.
How can one allow the wheel of Dharma of the Great Zhōu to be extinguished forever?
Your Majesty, with six principles, governs things; your nine virtues are self-evident.
Crooked reasoning finds no application; direct words are certainly used.
In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng excavated Kǒngqiū's tomb,
and disaster struck for three days.
Wèi Tàiwǔ destroyed Buddhist monasteries,
and calamity arose for seven years.
Cuī Hào's words are understandable;
Wèi Sōng's words are difficult to use.
The benevolent do not harm others to benefit themselves.
The wise do not delight in misfortune to gain fame.
Yuán Sōng, whom Heaven has abandoned, has no helper;
once his human life is over, where will he be reborn?
I, Guǎng, acknowledge the guidance and am ashamed of my lack of faith.
If I do not reply, I fear it will harm the many good people.
To forgive the shortcomings of others is an act of generosity.
To remember the virtues of things is the wisdom of benevolence.
Even if the good and bad among monks are equally balanced,
how can one expel all of them without leaving any?
The whole world would be disappointed, and all within the realm would lament.
I foolishly believe that if this path is not illuminated, how can the virtues of Zhōu prevail?
To revere Confucian scholars to show respect,
and to despise Buddhist monks to satisfy one's own desires,
is this any different from despising gold and valuing stones?
Considering the boundless kingly Way, how can this be reasonable?
Earth is flat because it bears water.
Wood is straight because it yields to the line.
An enlightened ruler accepts honest criticism without hesitation.
A perceptive scholar likes to hear his faults.
The wise are not easily angered,
allowing the views of the humble and ignorant to be expressed.
The benevolent do not easily cut off,
allowing the field of the Three Jewels to stand firm.
Heaven covers all without exception.
Earth carries with great breadth, mountains embrace, and oceans contain.
What cannot be accommodated?
Within ten households, there must be loyal and trustworthy people.
Within a country, can there be no virtuous monks?
I humbly pray, Heavenly Yuán Emperor,
to promote virtue, accept the worthy, recruit heroes, and select the excellent.
Reduce the numerous and keep the essential, preserving one temple per prefecture.
Allow residence freely in mountain forests and rock caves.
For those with relics, permit the construction of pagodas.
The temple should be named 'Zhōu Zhōngxīng' (Zhōu Restoration), allowing the monks to cease their debates and seek understanding.
This will benefit both internal and external affairs, without harm to public or private interests.
This would bring great fortune to both the secular and the religious, and joy to both Xuan (Daoist/Buddhist) and Ru (Confucian).
The imperial enterprise of the prosperous Zhōu would surpass a hundred kings.
The ruler of Dàxiàng would shine throughout the four seas.
Heaven is high, and hearing is far.
I make bold to speak common words,
with trembling heart and floating soul,
risking death while alive.
I beg for the descent of the majesty of thunder and lightning,
and the spreading of the virtue of wind and rain.
Respectfully submitted.
On the twenty-seventh day of the second month."
The minister Nàyán,
Hán Chángluán, received the memorial. The Grand Master of the Inner Scribe, Guīchānggōng Yǔwén Zé, and the Grand Master of the Inner Scribe, Tuòbá Xínggōng, etc., asked Guǎng,
"Fótúchéng was a man of three hundred years ago.
You are not even thirty; is it not a mistake to call yourself a disciple of a former sage?"
Guǎng replied,
"As for those who succeed the Zhōu,
even after a hundred generations, one can still know them.
Although my former teacher lived some three hundred years ago,
in terms of generations, it's merely ten.
What is there to be confused about?"
Zé said,
"Yuán Sōng's memorial presented the biased view that *jiālán* harm the people and damage the state.
What is your opinion in now advocating for their establishment?"
Guǎng replied,
"Jié and Zhòu lost their states; the people of Yīn turned to Zhōu.
The loss of states and ruin of homes did not come from Buddhist Dharma.
Both the internal and external scriptures, the secular and the sacred, have clear writings.
From antiquity until now, they cannot be abolished.
Therefore, I request their establishment."
Zé again asked,
"The ruler of Qí, Gāo Wěi,
did he not establish Buddhist Dharma, yet his state was broken and his family ruined, suffering such destruction?"
Guǎng replied,
"The Lord of Qí lost his state for two reasons,
unrelated to Buddhist Dharma.
First, the cosmic cycles have an end;
since the creation of heaven and earth,
no state has been seen that does not perish.
Second, rewards and punishments were imbalanced.
A noble man dislikes dwelling in a low position,
and so they returned to Zhōu.
This is unrelated to Buddhist Dharma."
Zé then asked,
"How can the sūtras, which are illusory and fallacious writings,
be cited as factual evidence?"
Guǎng again replied,
"You call Buddhist sūtras false;
I also say that the teachings of Kǒng [Fūzǐ] are not true."
Zé again asked,
"On what grounds do you base your claim that the teachings of Kǒng [Fūzǐ] are not true?"
Guǎng replied,
"Zhuāng Zhōu had the conduct of Kǒngzǐ.
Past events are similar.
Though [Kǒngzǐ] has become like a discarded straw dog, he still causes a hundred generations to sing of his lingering influence,
and for a thousand years, it is chanted without end.
Having thoroughly searched all the masters, I have not seen a single person call Fó illusory and fallacious!"
Zé then asked,
"Your analogy of Dīng Lán's wooden mother is inappropriate.
Why?
In ancient times, someone stumbled over the wooden mother,
and the wooden mother bled for him.
Since Gāozǔ destroyed temples,
which clay Fó or stone statue has bled?"
Guǎng replied,
"In ancient times, Xià established the Nine Dǐng to pacify the Nine Provinces.
If one province was restless, one dǐng would boil.
If the Nine Provinces were restless, all nine dǐng would boil.
Recently, we have seen two states engaged in battle and the four directions disturbed,
yet not a single dǐng has boiled.
Today, dǐng are still set up in front of the palace according to ancient practice.
Why single out clay, wood, and stone statues for not bleeding,
and immediately abandon them?"
On the first day of the third month,
an imperial edict granted food and drink.
They were seated in the Northern Palace in advance.
After eating, the imperial carriage departed and returned to the capital.
The emperor exited the south gate of the Northern Palace,
and personally bid farewell to and received obeisance from the petitioners.
After the obeisance, the Imperial Secretary Tuòbá Xínggōng announced
the imperial decree:
"Though the sun and moon are bright, they are still aided by the shining of many stars.
Even a sagely enlightened king still needs the assistance and rescue of his ministers.
I, with my shallow virtue,
appreciate each of you presenting loyal counsel.
This is deeply commendable.
The documents are extensive,
and I have not yet thoroughly examined them.
I shall immediately review and study them.
There will be a separate inspection.
You should all reside well."
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
the Grand Master of the Imperial Secretariat, Yǔwén Zé, announced the imperial decree:
"Buddhism has flourished for many years.
To discuss its ultimate principles is indeed difficult to clarify.
However, because the world has gradually become frivolous and does not follow Buddhist teachings,
the pure Dharma has become defiled and turbid.
This is why Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì
abolished it and did not establish it.
It was precisely for this reason.
Now, I am devoted to the ultimate Way [dào]
and wish to promote good Dharma.
I am preparing to select and practice diligently to cultivate this principle.
Now that the monastic robes are not changed and virtuous conduct still exists,
extensive places of practice [dàocháng] are set up, and good Dharma is to be practiced.
All below the princes and dukes should be informed."
Minister Yì said,
"Your servant has heard that Xī [Fú], Nóng [Shì], Xuān [Yuán], and Xù [Gāo Yáng Shì]
governed in harmony with the ways of Lǐ [Ěr] and Lǎo [Dān]; Yú [Shùn], Xià [Yǔ], Tāng [Zhōu], and Jī [Fā]
had policies that accorded with the teachings of Zhōu [Gōng] and Kǒng [Fūzǐ]. Although there may be a succession of sages, their virtues do not differ.
Although there are changes in rulers, their methods of governance are still the same.
I secretly heard of eighty-year-old elders striking the ground and singing,
and fifteen-year-old youths patting their bellies for joy.
Farmers could yield their fields,
and passers-by did not pick up lost items.
Filial sons inherited the family,
and loyal ministers filled the state.
When the ruler of the state faced difficulty, they would sacrifice their lives to avenge him; when parents were ill, they would attend to them throughout their lives.
Was this not a time when friends like Zēng Cān and Mǐn Zǐ made academies [xiángxù] like a forest?

Was it not a time when those like Mò Dí and Gěng Gōng came to assist one another, when there were those who upheld the Way [dào] and embodied virtue, without desires or demands, who were startled by favor or disgrace, yet participated in court positions, and ascended dragons on the Dǐng of Jīngshān,
or followed cranes by the altar of Gōushì?
Messengers from the Queen Mother of Yáochí arrived with禮 [lǐ] to pay homage to the court.
The gods of Bìhǎi Wúyí traveled all around to visit the emperor.
The reason for this
was that at that time,
everyone adhered to the teachings of Lǐ [Ěr] and Kǒng [Fūzǐ], and there was no foreign Fó. Since Hàn Míng [Dì]'s night dream of a golden man,

and Fù Yì's response to the imperial edict, explaining him to be a foreign god, there was no belief [in Fó] in the Central Plains during the Later Hàn. During Wèi and Jìn, among the barbarians, one part believed. Fú Róng relied on Buddhist fasting to plot rebellion and fled to Jiāngdōng.

Lǚ Guāng feigned a campaign against the Hu [barbarians] but rebelled against his ruler, establishing himself in the western lands. Since then, the demonic Hu [barbarians] have proliferated greatly, half-mixing with the Chinese. Within the gentry families, they instead receive the wicked precepts of bald monks.

Among Confucian scholars, they perversely preach the wild words and twisted tunes of the demonic Hu [barbarians], which sound like plaintive songs. Listening to them, one loses one's original nature, like entering a fish market, where one loses the sense of fragrance. Moreover, they widely establish numerous magnificent monasteries, toiling artisans and sitting alone with foreign Fó, striking the grand bells of China, gathering false monks, disturbing the ears and eyes of the simple people,
extorting private wealth and goods. Women's fine silks are cut to make banners for licentious worship.
Skillful artisans' gold and silver are scattered to carve stūpas for relics. Rice and flour
are indiscriminately set up for monastic gatherings.
Incense, oil, and candles
are wrongly used to illuminate foreign gods' halls, stripping the people's wealth and depleting the state's reserves.
The noble ministers of the court have not once awakened.
This is truly regrettable. Humbly,
Your Majesty regulates the opening and closing of the heavenly gates, renewing your precious throne.
You connect the flourishing and decline of all things, regenerating the black-haired people.
Spread the non-action [wúwéi] style of Lǐ Lǎo, and the people will transform themselves.
Uphold the rites of love and respect of Kǒng Qiū, and the world will be filial and compassionate.
Furthermore, the Buddhist sūtras falsely speak of blessings and retribution. Soldiers and commoners evade service, shave their heads, and hide among them,
not serving their parents, exclusively practicing the ten evils. As years pass, the wickedness is not removed, and deceit grows even greater.
Your servant has read through historical records,
from Páoxī to Hàn Gāo [Dì],
twenty-nine dynasties and over four hundred rulers.
I have only heard of sacrificing to the Supreme Emperor in the suburbs and officials governing and observing the people.
I have never seen temples, bronze statues, or establishing altars to pacify the state.
I request that the wicked foreign Fó teachings be returned to Tiānzhú [India], and all Shāmén be sent back to their hometowns.

Let the party of tax-evaders gladly pay their taxes, and the class avoiding service always joyfully exert their efforts. Do not allow bald youths to become officials; the state will naturally have loyal ministers guarding the ancestral temples.
Then the Great Táng will be pacified and become the master of creation.

The common people will be without trouble, becoming the people of Xī Huáng. Your servant, Yì, with utmost trepidation, respectfully submits eleven articles for the benefit of the state and the people, as listed below.
Respectfully stated."
The Shāmén Fǎ Lín and others addressed the throne,
"Lín has heard that those who feel deeply will have sorrowful voices;
those whose reasons are just will have direct words.
Therefore, the destitute child wishes to convey his words,
and the toiling person wishes to sing of his affairs.
Why? Your servant secretly observed that at the end of the Dàyè era, the world was in chaos.
Heaven and earth were defiled, and the four seas boiled.
Waves surged, dust flew, hills burned, and plains blazed.
The five steeds cut off the road of floating on the Jiāng [River].
The seven youths had songs of flattening strongholds.
Beacon fires constantly warned, and urgent dispatches raced.
The passes were full of dangers, and watch drums never ceased.
The Way [dào] declined, virtue was corrupted, fate was exhausted, and numbers ran out. Transport was truly burdensome.
Taxes were collected extensively, and piles of corpses were like a wilderness.
Blood flowed as rivers.
People could not live in peace, and living beings also suffered.
There was nowhere to appeal, and nowhere to lay one's bones.
The hundred clans suffered from being in dire straits, and myriad states were distressed without a ruler.
Who would have expected the Dharma wheel to be silent and the true teaching to decline?
Your Sacred Majesty, with a heart to succor the world, followed the mandate of August Heaven.
You raised the banner of righteousness and unified the land.
At that time, both monastics and laity were blessed, and both Chinese and barbarians rejoiced.
Thus, you harmonized with heaven and earth, making the eight winds [bāfēng] unobstructed.
You discerned yin and yang and regulated the four seasons.
You harmonized states and ordered human relations.
Your accomplishments covered the mending of heaven, and your divine power equaled establishing the cosmic axis.
You sent down clouds and rain for growth and life.
You opened the sun and moon to shine down.
You initiated with clear decrees.
You recorded with cultural artifacts.
Your grace reached the humble plants, and your transformation extended to insects and fish.
You are about to reiterate the Nine Categories and again expound the Five Teachings.
You are promoting the scholarship of Shíqú and spreading the customs of xiángxù.
You distantly inherit from Xuān [Yuán] and Xī [Fú], and are closely akin to Wén [Dì] and Jǐng [Dì].
Your achievements will forever be glorious; people do not know whether to dance with their hands or stomp with their feet for joy.
Your servant secretly observed the matters submitted by Fù Yì.
Before I finished reading them, my five organs were torn apart.
After I finished reading them, my six emotions were shattered.
Alas!
Evil words delude the righteous; demonic arguments compel truth.
They are not even worthy of being heard by the utterly foolish,
much less intended to reach the heavenly ears [of the emperor].
However, Yì holds an important position at this time, and is known by public opinion.
How can he disregard human feelings and cause evil without reason?
Yet his prose is shallow and crude, and his arguments are unclear.
He disgraces the venerable principles of the former kings and harms the moral conduct of human relations.
Why?
When a person speaks, their words must be accurate.
The Master said,
'If one word is reasonable, the world will turn to it.'
'If one act goes against common sense, even one's wife and children will abandon one.'
Looking at the matters Yì submitted,
encompassing their general outline and tracing them from beginning to end,
they contain numerous fabrications against the imperial court [quētíng].
They severely insult the sages.
Yì's intention here
was originally to use this to promote himself and seek advancement.
He truly could not benefit the state or the people.
Ultimately, he is merely deluding and confusing the court and the populace.
However,"
Your Majesty accords with Heaven and follows the times.
You grasp the omens and receive the mandates.
You fulfill the aspirations of myriad nations,
and embody the felicitations of the one man.
With the power to rescue the imperiled and save the world,
and the merit to subdue the violent and quell disturbances,
you have indeed overshadowed former kings in might and surpassed past emperors in renown.
Moreover, you have set your heart on the Three Jewels and turned your thoughts to the field of blessings.
Therefore, all who have left home are filled with gratitude for the Heavenly grace.
However, it is because we monks cannot uphold the precepts and practices to repay the nation's kindness,
and ignorant individuals commit transgressions and create sins,
that this has led Fù Yì to utter these evil words.
We are so grieved our hearts are broken, with nowhere to cast our bodies.
Nevertheless, if monks and nuns have committed sins, they are willing to suffer the severest punishment.
We resent Fù Yì's slighting and insulting of the sages,
and his words being so cutting and harmful.
We deeply fear that those with erroneous views will act wrongly because of this.
According to the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the seventh year of Lord Zhuāng of Lǔ, in the fourth month of summer,
the fixed stars were not visible, and the night was as bright as day.
This was an auspicious omen at the time of the Buddha's birth.
Indeed, the Buddha possesses two bodies—the true and the manifested—two wisdoms—expedient and real—three insights, eight liberations, five eyes, and six supernatural powers.
His spirit is said to be inconceivable;
his Dharma is called the cessation of mind and action.
As for his Way,
it transports all saints to Nirvāṇa.
As for his power,
it receives common mortals from the sea of suffering.
Since the third year of Yǒngpíng of Emperor Míng of the Later Hàn dynasty,
when he dreamt of a golden man,
the teaching of images has flowed eastward, and the spiritual omens have been numerous.
These are fully recorded in the histories of Hàn and Wèi, and in the books of Yáo and Shí, among others.
As for people like Dào'ān and Dàolì,
and the likes of Túchéng and Luóshí,
they all possessed lofty conduct and profound understanding.
They were renowned monks of their time,
all recognized by kings and esteemed by the nobility.
For more than five hundred years since then,
monasteries and pagodas have spread throughout the nine provinces,
and monks and nuns have overflowed the Three Fǔ regions.
This is all due to the reverence and faith of the rulers of the time and the devotion of both court and commoners.
That the teaching of images has flourished and continued to this day
is truly thanks to the power of the human kings.
In the secular world, subjects and children still say that kindness and benevolence are difficult to repay, and that the vast heavens do not requite.
How much more so the Buddha, who is the world-transcending compassionate father of all sentient beings,
and also the good physician for both ordinary and holy beings?
To suppress and thwart him, to condemn and insult him,
is simply impossible.
Looking up to the Tathāgata, his wisdom transcends both existence and non-existence.
How could the Three Sovereigns measure it?
His power encompasses creation and transformation.
It is not something the two cosmic forces (Heaven and Earth) can match.
In ancient times, the Grand Tutor Pǐ of Wú asked Kǒngqiū,
"Is Master a sage?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"Qiū is broadly knowledgeable and has a strong memory,
but he is not a sage."
He asked again,
"Are the Three Kings sages?"
He replied,
"The Three Kings were skilled in using wisdom and courage;
whether they were sages is not what Qiū knows."
He asked again,
"Are the Five Emperors sages?"
He replied,
"The Five Emperors were skilled in using benevolence and trustworthiness;
whether they were sages is also not what Qiū knows."
He asked again,
"Are the Three Sovereigns sages?"
He replied,
"The Three Sovereigns were skilled in using timely action;
whether they were sages is also not what Qiū knows."
The Grand Tutor was greatly astonished and said,
"Then who is a sage?"
The Master, his expression changing slightly, said,
"There is a sage in the West.
He governs without disorder,
speaks not yet is trusted,
transforms not yet acts spontaneously.
Vast and boundless, the people cannot name him."
If the Three Kings and Five Emperors were necessarily great sages,
how could Kǒngqiū have concealed them and not spoken?
He would then have the fault of hiding a sage.
By this measure,
the Buddha is revered as the Great Sage.
Lǎozi's Xīshēng Jīng (Scripture of Lǎozi's Western Ascent) says,
"My teacher journeyed to Tiānzhú and skillfully entered Nirvāṇa."
Fú Zǐ says,
"Lǎo Shì's teacher's name was Shìjiāwén (Śākyamuni)."
Directly from the scriptures of Kǒngzǐ and Lǎozi,
there are not a few textual evidences of their respect for the Buddha.
How can Fù Yì alone slander him?
In ancient times, Gōngsūn Lóng authored the Jiānbái Lùn (Treatise on Hardness and Whiteness),
condemning the Three Sovereigns and faulting the Five Emperors.
Even today, when one reads it,
