people still gnash their teeth,
taking it as a prior warning.
Truly lamentable!
The Emperor, being supremely sagely and sagacious,
is now about to release the horses and rest the oxen, remove the door screens and seal the graves (i.e., establish peace).
He wishes to revive the spirit of the ancient kings
and usher in the transformation of Buddhism and Daoism.
Such wild and simplistic remarks are especially fit to be burned.
If it is said that without the Buddha, emperors enjoy great peace and long reigns,
and with the Buddha, there is tyrannical rule and short reigns,
then consider that Yáo and Shùn ruled alone but their line did not extend to their descendants.
The reigns of Xià, Yīn, Zhōu, and Qín often changed.
Internal rebellions arose, and disorder followed disorder.
At that time, there was no Buddha; what caused their short durations?
But Lín dwells in the world of Yáo,
though his daily conduct is unknown.
Seeing inconvenient matters outside,
he fears that foreign nations, hearing far away,
will consider Huáxià to be ignorant.
The Master said,
"Words filling the world yet no fault of mouth,
deeds filling the world yet no resentment or hatred."
Those who speak wish for no blame,
those who hear are sufficient to admonish themselves.
Fù Yì's words are disrespectful;
all who hear are startled.
It defiles the national customs and particularly harms the Huá culture.
I humbly record this earnest plea, daring to present it for Your attention.
I respectfully reflect,
Your Royal Highness,
endowed by Heaven with exceptional spiritual acuity, naturally intelligent and discerning.
Your demeanor is brilliant, your character profound and magnanimous.
You delight in goodness, surpassing that Dōngpíng.
You rejoice in warm discourse, even surpassing Xīchǔ.
Furthermore, you serve as the chief minister for all affairs, bringing order to the six sections of government.
Your virtue covers all, your benevolence breaks through all nets.
You open the grand mansion,
and entertain guests like Xún Qīng.
You build a garden of slender bamboos,
and feast guests of refined culture.
All are able to compose poems that perfectly express feelings and odes that exhaust the description of things.
Truly, your praises can fill the court and commoners, and your excellence can match previous heroes.
However, we, Lín and others, look within and find ourselves lacking, of little practical use.
We recall Fù Yì's extreme foolishness,
and are ashamed of the criticism leveled at ordinary monks, the "bald fellows."
This is the height of evil!
There is no greater sin!
Since Zūnlú and Hèxū,
after the separation of heaven and earth,
there has never been such a mad and perverse person as Yì.
Unable to bear the breaking of bones and the pain in our hearts,
we have respectfully recorded Yì's harmful statements,
and herewith present our humble words in response.
The detailed reply is appended as follows.
We defile your majesty and are filled with dread.
Respectfully submitted.
Yì said:
"Among those within the seas who diligently serve the king, there are few;
among those who delight in self-interest, there are many.
They externally serve the foreign Buddha, and internally harbor perverse views.
They shave their hair and skin, change their clothes,
leave the doors of subjects and sons,
and enter the households of monks and nuns.
They stand to greet the royal court, and sit to watch at the knees.
Disloyal and unfilial, they gather and form communities.
Moreover, the Buddha is in the Western Regions;
his monstrous words are from afar.
They abandon their kin to pursue wealth, fear the strong and disrespect the old,
value the rich and powerful while disdaining the poor and weak,
love the young and beautiful while despising the elderly.
They use illusion to perform arts and skills,
and deception as their principle.
Indeed, the Buddha is a ghost of a single family name.
As a ghost, he does not include other clans.
How can one drive the living Hàn people to provide for the dead Hú (foreigners)?
To demean this bright pearl and value that fish eye?
To violate and abandon one's strict father yet respect others?
How can one kneel before ten clay Hú and become a minister?
Or place a basin of leftover food and become an emperor?
Based on the Buddha's perverse teachings, it is contrary to human nature.
Furthermore, the Buddha is cunning and deceitful.
His grand words do not compare to Zhān Méng.
His extravagance and creations are deeper sins than those of Jié and Zhòu.
He is one who enters a family and breaks it, enters a nation and breaks it."
Reply: One who leaves home internally renounces dear relatives and externally abandons official glory.
Their aspiration is to seek unsurpassed Bodhi,
and their vow is to escape the bitter sea of birth and death.
Therefore, they abandon the clothes of court attendance
and don the robes of the field of blessings.
They practice the Way to repay the four kindnesses,
and establish virtue to benefit the three existences.
This is their main intention.
If it is said that the Buddha is a Hú ghost
and monks are "bald fellows,"
then consider the scriptures of Kǒngzǐ and Lǎozi, and the internal and external historical records from the Hàn and Wèi dynasties onward.
We briefly cite instances where Kǒngzǐ and Lǎozi respectfully treated the Buddha.
The textual evidence is given below
to answer the evil person
and hope that he will admit his guilt.
The Daoist Fǎlún Jīng (Dharma Wheel Scripture) says:
"If one sees a Śramaṇa, one should contemplate the immeasurable,
wishing to soon emerge (from the world) and practice the true Buddha."
It also says:
"If one sees a Buddhist temple, one should contemplate the immeasurable,
wishing that all beings universally enter the Dharma gate."

The Tàishàng Qīngjìng Xiāomó Bǎozhēn Ānzhì Zhìhuì Běnyuàn Dàjiè Shàngpǐn Jīng (Superior Scripture of the Great Precepts of the Supreme Purity and Tranquility, Subduing Demons, Preserving Truth, Calming the Will, Wisdom and Original Vows) with forty-nine vows states:
If one sees Bhikkhus or Bhikkhunīs,
one should wish that all may clearly understand the Dharma, attain the Dao like the Buddha.
The Lǎozǐ Shēngxuán Jīng states:
Tiānzūn informed Dàolíng,
“Go east to the Buddha to receive the Dharma.”
The Dàoshì Zhāng Líng Biézhuàn states:
Líng was in Húmíng Shān,
offering sacrifices to golden images and reciting Buddhist scriptures.
The Shēngxuán Jīng also states:
The Tathāgata from the East sent the Mahāsattva Shànshèng
to Tàishàng, saying:
“The Tathāgata heard that you preached the Dharma to Zhāng Líng,
so I sent him to see you.”
He said to Zhāng Líng:
“Follow me to the Buddha’s abode.
I will enable you to see what you have not yet seen and hear what you have not yet heard.”
Líng immediately bowed to the Mahāsattva
and followed him to the Buddha’s abode.
The Lǎozǐ Xīshēng Jīng states:
“My teacher transformed and traveled to Tiānzhú, skillfully entering Nirvāṇa.”
The Zhìhuì Guānshēn Dàjiè Jīng states:
“Those who study the Dao should remember to travel to the Dàfàn Liúyǐng Gōng to worship the Buddha.”
The Shēngxuán Jīng states:
“If there are Bhikkhus who wish to come to listen to the scriptures and observe the vegetarian feast,
the host must not calculate the food and drink expenses and prevent them from attending.
They should be respectfully seated in the uppermost seat, with the Dàoshì and scripture masters below them.”
The Shēngxuán Jīng also states:
“If Dàoshì offer a vegetarian feast,
and Bhikkhus come, they should be respectfully seated in the uppermost seat.
Offer them good provisions, with the Dàoshì and scripture masters below them.”
“If Bhikkhunīs come to listen to the Dharma,
they should be comfortably seated in the uppermost seat.
The host should provide offerings according to the Dharma.
They must not be obstructed.”
The Huàhú Jīng states:
“I wish to gather Udumbara flowers,
I wish to burn sandalwood incense,
to make offerings to the bodies of a thousand Buddhas,
I bow my head in reverence to Dìngguāng.”
It also states:
“Why was the Buddha born so late?
Why did he enter Nirvāṇa so early?
I cannot see Shìjiāmóuní,
my heart is constantly vexed.”
The Língbǎo Xiāomó Ānzhì Jīng states:
“The Dao takes vegetarian fasting as primary.
Diligently practice to become a Buddha, thus a great Dharma bridge is built,
to universally save all beings.”
The Lǎozǐ Dàquán Púsà Jīng states:
“Lǎozǐ is Jiāyè Púsà,
who transformed and traveled to Zhèndàn.”
The Língbǎo Fǎlún Jīng states:
“When Gé Xiāngōng was only a few days old,
a foreign Bhikkhu
saw Xiāngōng and bowed.
He held him and said to Xiāngōng’s parents:
‘This child is Shàn sī Púsà from the West.
He has come to Hàndì to teach and transform sentient beings.
He will travel the immortal path and ascend to heaven in broad daylight.’”
Xiāngōng himself said to his disciples:
“My teacher’s surname is Bōyuèzōng,
his courtesy name is Wéinàhē.
He is a native of the Western Regions.”
The Xiān Rén Qǐngwèn Zhòngshèng Nán Jīng states:
“Gé Xiāngōng told his disciples:
‘In the past, I, along with Shì Dàozhēng, Zhú Fǎkāi, Zhāng Tài, Zhèng Sīyuǎn, and four others,
made vows at the same time.
Dàozhēng and Fǎkāi
vowed to become Bhikkhus.
Zhāng Tài and Zhèng Sīyuǎn vowed to become Dàoshì.’”
The Xiāngōng Qǐjūzhù states:
“At that time, he was born into the family of Gé Shàngshū.
Shàngshū was over eighty years old,
and only then had this one son.
At that time, there was a Bhikkhu
who claimed to be a monk from Tiānzhú.
He bought a large quantity of incense in the market.
The market people were puzzled and asked the monk:
‘Last night, I dreamt that Shàn sī Púsà was born into Gé Shàngshū’s family.
I will use this incense to bathe him.’
When the time of birth came, the monk arrived, burned incense,
circumambulated seven times to the right, bowed respectfully,
bathed him, and then stopped.”
The Xiāngōng Qǐngwèn Shàng Jīng states:
“When speaking with Bhikkhus and Dàoshì, one should aspire to the Dao.”
The Shàngpǐn Dàjiè Jīng Jiàoliáng Gōngdé Pǐn states:
“Giving to Buddha pagodas and temples yields a thousandfold reward.
Giving to Bhikkhus yields a hundredfold reward.”
The Shēngxuán Nèi Jiào Jīng states:
“Or there are some people
who usually do not accumulate blessings.
When they see Bhikkhus or Dàoshì preaching and encouraging good deeds,
they are completely unpersuaded, etc.”
The Dàoshì Táo Yǐnjū
wrote a one-volume text on bowing to the Buddha.
The Zhìhuì Běnyuàn Běnjiè Shàngpǐn Jīng states:
“Distributing food to the Buddha, monks, stupas, and monasteries,
even one coin or more, yields twenty-four thousandfold
reward. The merit is small, but the reward is great.
In every generation, one will be wise and illustrious, with endless joys.
All seven generations of ancestors will enter the boundless Buddha lands.”
The Xiāngōng
Qǐngwèn Jīng states:
“Furthermore, there are ordinary people who perform such merits,
wishing to become Bhikkhus, Dàoshì, or great scholars.
In their next life, they will become Bhikkhus,
study the great Buddhist Dharma, and become Dharma masters for the multitude.”
“There is also a person
who, seeing Bhikkhus or Dàoshì fasting, meditating, and reciting scriptures,
laughs and says:
‘They are merely chanting scriptures to the empty air.
What do they hope for?
Emptying their stomachs and eating only once at midday,
these are truly sinners.’
Though the Dàoshì kindly explains to them,
they stubbornly refuse to yield.
After death, they enter hell and suffer the five torments.”
The Xiāngōng Qǐngwèn Jīng states:
“The five Confucian classics and secular professions;
Daoism and Buddhism each praise their teachings as leading to great goodness.”
The Tàishàng Língbǎo Zhēnyī Quànjiè Fǎlún Miàojīng states:
“I have observed all the heavens
from countless eons ago,
and seen Dàoshì, common men and women,
who have already attained the supreme, true, and real Dao,
high immortals and true people, naturally.
The Buddhas of the ten directions all endured past lives of diligent suffering in seeking the Dao,
which cannot be fully enumerated.”
The Fǎlún Miàojīng states:
“The Dao says:
‘The wheel of transmigration does not cease;
one can be reborn among humans.
Those with great wisdom and insight
have, from countless eons ago,
studied and become true people, high immortals, naturally.
The Buddhas of the ten directions are all attained through their practices.’”
The above records the reverent Buddhist texts of Dàojīng masters as presented.
According to the Zhōu Shū Yìjì:
“In the twenty-fourth year of King Zhāo of Zhōu’s reign, the Jiǎyín year, on the eighth day of the fourth month,
the rivers, springs, and pools suddenly swelled,
and all well water overflowed.
Palaces, human dwellings, mountains, rivers, and the great earth
all vibrated.
That night, five-colored auspicious qi penetrated the Grand Tàiwēi constellation,
spreading throughout the west, entirely becoming reddish-blue.
King Zhāo of Zhōu asked the Grand Astrologer Sū Yóu,
‘What omen is this?’
Yóu replied:
‘A great sage
is born in the West,
thus this auspicious sign appears.’
King Zhāo asked:
‘How will it be for the world?’
Yóu said:
‘There will be no immediate change.
After a thousand years, his teachings will reach this land.’
King Zhāo immediately ordered the engraving of this on stone
and buried it in front of the Tianci temple in the southern suburbs.
At this time,
the Buddha was first born in the royal palace.”
“In the thirty-second year of King Mù’s reign,
he saw auspicious qi appearing repeatedly in the West.
Having previously heard Sū Yóu’s record,
he knew that a sage was living in the West.
King Mù did not understand its principle,
and feared it was not suitable for the Zhōu Dao.
So he, with Prime Minister Lǚ Hóu,
traveled west to meet the feudal lords at Túshān
to ward off the anomalous light.
At this time,
the Buddha had long been in the world.”
“In the fifty-second year of King Mù’s reign, the Rénshēn year, on the fifteenth day of the second month, at dawn,
a sudden violent storm arose,
damaging human dwellings
and breaking trees.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth
all vibrated.
In the afternoon, the sky was overcast and cloudy.
In the West, twelve white rainbows appeared,
passing through north and south, remaining visible all night.
King Mù asked the Grand Astrologer Hù Duō,
‘What omen is this?’
He replied:
‘A great sage in the West has passed into Nirvāṇa;
these are merely signs of decline.’
King Mù was greatly pleased and said:
‘I always feared him,
but now that he has passed into Nirvāṇa, what do I have to worry about?’
At this time,
the Buddha entered Nirvāṇa.”
The historical records state:
“Wú Tàizǎi Pǐ asked Kǒngzǐ:
‘Who is a sage?’
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘There is a sage among the people of the West.
He governs without disorder,
believes without speaking,
and acts without being transformed.
Boundless, the people cannot name him.’”
The above records praise of Buddhist texts in Confucian writings as previously stated.
Yìyún:
Monastics aged sixty and below
should be drafted as commoners.
Then the army would be strong and the population numerous.
Yìyún:
Many temples and numerous monastics
cause significant waste.
All such temples
should be given to the lonely, elderly, poor, and homeless righteous scholars.
For a prefecture of thirty thousand households, only one temple should be established.
A grass hut and earthen pagoda should be used to house scriptures and images.
Two Hu monks should be dispatched to transmit the Hu dharma.
Yìyún:
The Western Region Hu people
are born from filthy mud
and thus serve mud and tiles.
They are still hairy and rude today,
with human faces but beastly hearts.
They are barn owls and Daoists,
donkeys and mules of four colors,
a wicked breed of greed and rebellion.
The Buddha was born in the West,
not of the orthodox customs of Zhōngguó.
He is but an evil spirit of demons.
Yìyún:
From Páoxī downwards for fifteen generations,
fathers and sons, rulers and ministers
established loyalty and filial piety,
upheld the Dao and practiced virtue.
Born and raised in Shénzhōu,
they obtained the righteous energy of Huáxià.
All people were pure and simple,
because there was no Buddha in the world.
Yìyún:
Qín began with Qín Zhòng,
thirty-five generations,
six hundred and thirty-eight years.
Yìyún:
When emperors had no Buddha,
their reigns were greatly ordered and long.
With a Buddha, their tyrannical rule and lifespan were short.
From Páoxī downwards,
for twenty-nine generations,
there was no Buddhist dharma.
Rulers were enlightened, ministers loyal,
and the national lifespan long.
Yìyún:
Before the Buddha,
the people were pure and harmonious,
and there was no usurpation or rebellion in the world.
Yìyún:
When the Buddha came to Hàn land,
there was harm but no benefit.
Yìyún:
During the Jiànwǔ era of Zhào,
there was a Daoist, Zhāng Guāng, who rebelled.
During the Liángwǔ era, the monk Guāng rebelled.
Given that there are now two hundred thousand monastics,
they must be abolished and reduced early.
One reply concerning the abolition and reduction of monastics:
The response is:
Outward appearances are easy to observe, but true and false are difficult to discern.
Unless one has lived there for a long time,
it cannot be known.
Formerly, Fǎshī Yuǎn, in his reply to Huán Xuán, said:
The scriptures describe three categories in total:
one is meditative contemplation to enter the subtle;
two is reciting and savoring ancient texts;
three is establishing meritorious works.
However, there are people who establish merit
but do not uphold the precepts,
and whose conduct is not that of an āraṇyaka.
Or there are those who recite many scriptures ceaselessly
but cannot eloquently explain their meaning.
Or there are those who are advanced in years,
who, although not classifiable by the three categories,
are of upright character and integrity,
and do not commit major transgressions.
By these comparisons,
selection and rejection are difficult to distinguish.
According to the Chūjiā Gōngdé Jīng, it says:
To ordain one person to leave home
is superior to erecting a treasure pagoda reaching the Brahmā heaven.
Why? Because such a person can propagate the Dao, benefit themselves and others,
purify themselves, establish themselves, and be a bridge for seven generations.
Please punish the guilty according to the law,
and let the innocent practice the Dao for the country.
One reply concerning destroying temples
and giving grass huts to the people to house images:
The response is:
The Dharma has flowed to Hàn land for over five hundred years.
Temples and monastics have existed for generations.
Shrines, pagodas, halls, and palaces were all built by previous generations.
Rooms, houses, gates, and corridors were all constructed out of faith.
Some were for the living and deceased parents,
and for the rebirth of seven generations,
seeking superior future rewards,
and planting present fields of blessings.
All these came from their good hearts,
not from the Buddha or monastics demanding their establishment.
The Shūyún says:
Accomplishments should not be destroyed.
Thus, Zǐchǎn did not destroy Bóyí's temple.
Kǒngfūzǐ called him a benevolent person.
How much more so the Buddha, who is the good field of the three realms and the parent of the four kinds of births!
He should only be revered and nourished, not destroyed.
Although the Buddha has passed away, the Dharma is entrusted to human kings.
We respectfully implore
Your Majesty
to recreate the common people and revive the Buddhist Dao.
You would then be the great Dàn yuē zhǔ of the Tathāgata.
Please follow the transformation of Hàn Míng in the Yǒngpíng era,
and be similar to Emperor Wén during the Kāihuáng era.
One reply concerning the Western Region Hu people
having human faces and beastly hearts,
being a greedy, rebellious, evil breed,
and the Buddha being born in the West,
being a demon or evil spirit:
The response is:
According to the Shǐjì, Lìdì Wáng Jiǎnmùlù, and Táo Yǐnjū Niánjì, etc., it says:
Páoxī Shì had a snake body and human head.
Dàtíng Shì had a human body and ox head.
Nǚwā Shì also had a snake body and human head. Qín Zhòng Yǎn had a bird body and human face.
Xià Yǔ was born in Xīqiāng.
Wén Wáng was also born in Xīqiāng.
Jiǎndí swallowed a swallow's egg and gave birth to Xiè. Bó Yǔ emerged by piercing his mother's chest and back.
Yī Yǐn was entrusted from an empty mulberry tree.
The Yuán Shì Wèi ruler was also born among the Yídí.
Yet, all responded to heaven's clear mandate,
some ruling as monarchs,
others reigning over myriad nations.
Although their birthplaces may have been remote and their appearances crude,
each wielded heavenly might, and people cherished their sagely virtue.
Lǎozi was also fostered by a herdsman's mother,
born from humble origins.
How can one dismiss a sage based on their lowly origin?
Kǒngfūzǐ said:
"If a jūnzi dwells there,
what squalor can there be?"
How true these words are!
All said:
"Where there is the Dao, there is respect;
why distinguish between high and low?"
Thus, it is known that the manifestation of sages is without fixed place,
appearing according to circumstances.
Tracing the ancestors of Shìjiā,
they were descendants of a thousand generations of cakravartin kings,
and princes of the Kshatriya kings.
The omens and predictions were announced, and when things responded, he appeared in the center of the three thousand worlds,
in a great kingdom of Nán Yánfútí.
He preached and set forth methods,
solely taking the benefit of sentient beings as his fundamental principle.
If one says that being born in Qiāng Hu or originating from Róng Lǔ makes one evil,
then Tài Hào and Wén Mìng are not sages.
Lǎozi and Wén Wáng are not worthy of being revered as teachers.
According to the Dìlǐ Zhì, Xīyù Zhuàn, it is said:
"The Xī Hú are merely the thirty-six kingdoms
east of the Cōnglǐng mountains.
They have nothing to do with Tiānzhú, the birthplace of the Buddha."
If one knows this is a false statement,
how deep is the sin?
If one speaks carelessly without knowing,
there will be ample blame even after death.
First answer.
From Fúxī downwards, twenty-nine generations.
Fathers and sons, rulers and ministers established loyalty and filial piety.
They upheld the Way and practiced virtue.
Those who inherited the righteous *qì* of Huáxià.
In response, it is said:
The *Shǐjì*, *Huáinánzǐ*, and other texts say:
During the time of Huángdì,
Chīyóu, with a copper head and iron brow,
caused chaos in the world.
He battled Huángdì at Bǎnquán,
leading to Huángdì's ascension to the imperial throne.
Chīyóu defied the mandate
and fought again in the wilds of Zhuōlù.
In total, there were fifty-two battles.
During the time of Zhuānxù,
the Sānmiáo were further punished at the left Dòngtíng and right Pénglǐ.
The *Jízhǒng Zhúshū* says:
Shùn imprisoned Yáo in Píngyáng
and took the imperial throne from him.
There is still a "Prison-Yáo City" to be seen today.
Shùn also fought the Yǒumiáo at the banks of the Dānshuǐ.
Yáo shot down nine suns, caused their raven feathers to fall, tied up Dàfēng at Qīngqiū,
beheaded Xiūshé at Dòngtíng,
slew Fēngshì at Dàzé,
and killed Jiǔyīng at the Xiōngshuǐ.
The *Shàngshū* says:
The floodwaters surged to the heavens, engulfing mountains and submerging hills.
The common people were trapped and starving, the populace was in misery. During Yǔ's time, the people each followed their own inclinations,
and Báigǔzǐ retired to farm in the wilderness.
The Sānmiáo did not cultivate virtuous governance,
so Yǔ personally destroyed them.
Jié of Xià resided
with the Hé and Jǐ rivers to his left, and Tài huá to his right.
Yīquè was to his south,
and Yángcháng behind his north.
He burned the imperial records and killed Lóngféng,
imprisoned Chéngtāng and indulged Mòxī.
Tāng undertook nine campaigns to reform the government,
fighting twenty-seven battles.
There was a great drought for seven years,
the Hé and Luò rivers dried up,
melting metal and shattering stones.
Gāozōng attacked the Guǐfāng.
For three years, Zhòu Xīn of Yīn was bewildered by Dájǐ.
He indulged in the harm of the ten evils,
and inflicted the punishment of the five cruelties.
He cut open the hearts of worthy men
and sliced open the bellies of pregnant women.
He imprisoned Wénwáng and forbade Jīzǐ.
King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked Zhòu at Mùyě,
where blood flowed so much it could float pestles.
He executed him at Lùtái.
The King personally shot Zhòu
and personally hung his head on the banner of Tàibái.
Yet Bóyí and Shúqí condemned this,
refusing to eat his grain.
Confucius said:
Wǔ was perfectly beautiful,
but not perfectly good.
During King Wǔ's reign, the Sānnjiàn rebelled.
In King Chéng's day, the two uncles spread rumors.
The *Shījīng* says of King Xuān's expedition in the sixth month:
"We lightly attacked the Xiǎnyǔn, reaching Tàiyuán."
The *Cǎiwēi* ode speaks of conscripted soldiers, saying:
"In the north, there is the calamity of the Xiǎnyǔn;
in the west, there is the trouble of the Kūnyí."
The *Cǎijià* also says:
"King Xuān campaigned south."
In response, it is said:
What has been stated above
all pertains to the Three Sovereigns and Three Kings.

śramaṇa Fǎ Cháng of Later Yàn,
Dào Mì of Southern Liáng,
Fǎ Xiù during Emperor Xiàowén of Wèi,
and Huì Yǎng during the Tàihé era, etc.,
all rebelled.
Reply:
Upon checking Cuī Hóng's Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms),
there are no such individuals.
From what historical records do these come?
You wantonly fabricate slanders to deceive the emperor.
Please check the national histories to confirm the falsity of your memorial.
According to the Former and Later Hàn Shū,
there were indeed dozens of bandit groups such as Kūnyáng, Chángshān, Qīngní, Yuánlín, Hēishān, Báimǎ, Huángjīn, and Chìméi.
All were lay people,
not related to Buddhist monks.
Why do you not mention them?
The Hòuhànshū states:
Zhāng Lǔ's mother, a Daoist from Pèi, was beautiful
and skilled in gui dào (the way of ghosts).
She frequented the home of Liú Yān.
Later, when Liú Yān became the Inspector of Yìzhōu,
he appointed Lǔ as the Dūyìsīmǎ.
Lǔ, together with the other department's sīmǎ, Zhāng Xiū,
led troops to ambush and kill Sū Gù, the Administrator of Hànzhōng.
They cut off Xié Gǔ and killed Han envoys.
Once Lǔ had seized Hànzhōng,
he also killed Zhāng Xiū and absorbed his followers.
At that time, feigning divine pronouncements,
it was said, "The yellow-clad will be kings."
Lǔ then corresponded with Zhāng Jiǎo and others,
gathered his followers,
and all wore yellow turbans.
Dressed in Daoist robes,
hundreds of thousands of people brought calamity upon the world.
He held Hànzhōng for nearly thirty years.
Later, he was defeated by Cáo Gōng,
and the yellow-clad movement finally perished.
At that time, there was not a single shāmen,
but a great abundance of Daoists.
Why is this not discussed silently?
Yet, during the Han and Wei dynasties, there were many famous monks of virtuous conduct,
and many who benefited the state.
Why are they not mentioned?
To only discuss evil and exclusively point out people's shortcomings,
how can this be the act of a jūnzi?
The Wèizhì states:
Zhāng Lǔ's courtesy name was Gōngqí.
His grandfather, Líng, went to Shǔ to study the Dao,
residing in Gǔmíngshān.
He authored Daoist scriptures to delude the common people.
Those who received the Dao from him paid five dǒu of rice.
The world called them the Rice Thieves.
When Líng died, his son Héng inherited the teaching.
When Héng died, Lǔ, in turn, inherited it.
Líng was called Tiānshī,
Héng was called Sìshī,
and Lǔ was called Xìshī, collectively known as the Three Masters.
He had always been on good terms with Liú Wū.
When Yān died, his son Zhāng was established.
Because Lǔ was disobedient, Zhāng killed Lǔ's mother and household.
Lǔ then occupied Hànzhōng.
He converted the people using gui dào,
based on talismans, written petitions, and prohibitions.
Those who came to learn were initially called guǐzú.
Those who received the Dao offered gold and silk.
They were called jìjiǔ.
Each led their own group.
Those with large followings were called zhìtóu.
The sick were ordered to confess their sins.
Generally, this was similar to Zhāng Jiǎo.
The Hòuhàn Huángfǔ Sōng Zhuàn states:
Zhāng Jiǎo of Jùlù called himself the Great Worthy Mentor.
He revered Huánglǎo and practiced the arts of Zhāng Líng.
He used talismanic water and incantations to treat illnesses.
He sent eight disciples
to various regions to spread his teachings.
They successively deluded and misled people.
Within ten-odd years, his followers numbered hundreds of thousands.
From the people of Qīng, Xú, Yōu, Jì, Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù — the eight provinces —
none failed to respond. They then established thirty-six "fāng."
A fāng was like a general's title.
Large fāng had over ten thousand people,
and small fāng had six thousand people.
They spread the rumor, "The Azure Heaven is dead; the Yellow Heaven is to be established.
The year is Jiǎzǐ; great fortune under heaven."
They wrote the character Jiǎzǐ with white earth on the gates of temples in the capital.
All did so.
On the fifth day of the third month of the first year of Zhōngpíng,
they rose up both inside and outside.
All wore Daoist yellow robes and yellow turbans.
Some killed people to sacrifice to heaven.
At that time, the bandit hordes numbered hundreds of thousands.
They first rose in Yǐngchuān, causing chaos throughout the realm.
They were all suppressed and annihilated by Huángfǔ Sōng.
Nánzhèng rebelled against Han and destroyed Shǔ.
Sūn Ēn practiced immortality and ruined Jìn.
Dào Yù's jiaoji (Daoist rituals) brought disaster to Sòng.
Yú Jí's practice of prohibitions almost endangered Wú.
Gōngqí (Zhāng Lǔ) studied immortality and brought about the execution of his family.
Chén Ruì practiced the Dao and brought about the extermination of his clan.
Wèi Huá betrayed her husband.
Zhāng Líng abandoned his wife.
Zǐ Dēng turned against his father, and Wèi Shū left his elder brother.
The above are Daoists from ancient times
who destroyed families and states, acting as rebels and traitors,
briefly cited as before.
The reply states:
From Líng's three generations, they exclusively practiced gui dào.
Talismans, written petitions, and jiaoji originated from the Daoist school.
Prohibitions, averting evil, and wildly discussing good and bad omens—
villainy arose from these.
However, after Wú and Wèi,
and since Jìn and Sòng,
the number of Daoists and lay practitioners who committed villainy was also not small.
Why single out the monks alone
and not discuss the two teachings of Ru and Dao?
Furthermore, at the end of the Dàyè era, Shì Chōng, Lǐ Mì, Jiàndé, Wǔ Zhōu, Liáng Shīdū, Lú Míngyuè, Lǐ Guǐ, Zhū Càn, Táng Bì, Xuē Jǔ, and others
were all commoners.
There was never a single Buddhist.
Why is this not mentioned?
This partiality in affairs and narrowness of reason, supporting evil and envying the virtuous,
clearly shows disloyalty as a minister.
Yì said:
"Please send the heterodox teaching of the Hu Buddha back to the Western Regions.
All monks and nuns should be made to return to lay life."
He replied:
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
Within the Six Harmonies,
the Sages discuss but do not argue.
Outside the Six Harmonies,
the Sages preserve but do not discuss.
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"Within the realm there are four great things, and the Dào is one of them."
Examining the essence of the Shī, Shū, Lǐ, and Yuè,
they merely aim to order the eternal human relations, clarify loyalty and filiality as paramount.
Their intention lies in revering and serving one's sovereign and father.
Even when speaking of the highest virtue,
it is only to bring peace to superiors and order to the people.
Supposing essential principles were sought,
they would not go beyond changing customs and transforming habits.
From Wèi back to Lǔ,
how could discourses on liberation be expounded?
The Six Fǔ and Nine Chóu
did not declare the ultimate goal.
As for discourses on nurturing life and equalizing all things,
and theories of dragon diagrams and phoenix records,
they too can be embraced with benevolence and faith, following the aspirations of the Lì Xiāng school,
editing classics, praising images, and completing the writings of Qù Lǐ.
First, there were the Nine Streams,
later called the Seven Summaries.
According to the catalogue of the Yìwén Zhì of the Former Hàn dynasty, it recorded 13,269 volumes of various books.
None of them failed to be beneficial in the near term,
but all failed to express distant paths.
All confined themselves to the span of a single life,
not those that transcend the three realms.
This causes the principle of present-life causes and effects
to remain obscure even in broad daylight,
and the meaning of karmic retribution, good and bad fortune,
to remain unclear even after long periods.
Thus, we know that the entire Xiāoyáo book
still clings to the emotions of "being,"
and the two chapters of Dàodé
have not entered the state of "emptiness of emptiness."
These are merely the mundane thoughts within the realm of the Six Harmonies
and the common discussions of the Five Constants.
How can they escape the vastness of the Four Streams,
which are the field of afflictions,
and the clamor of the Six Realms,
which create the karma of defilement?
Originally, the true nature (dharmakāya) is distant and profound,
surpassing the essence of essential principles.
The Dharma-body is still and silent,
transcending the profound of the profound.
Only our Great Master embodies this wondrous enlightenment.
The two extremes are instantly eliminated, and all virtues are harmonized.
Neither noisy nor silent,
how can it be sought with perception and wisdom?
Neither confused nor obscure,
how can it be grasped by form and name?
When small, it is small, yet without interiority;
when great, it is great, yet without bounds.
Therefore, he measures the Dharma realm and arises with compassion,
estimates the void and makes vows.
Hence, he manifested in the defiled land, born in a royal palace.
He displayed a golden body,
and emitted a jade-white hair light.
He spread the cloud of compassion on Grdhrakūṭa (Jí Lǐng),
and the flames of the burning house were extinguished.
He fanned the wind of wisdom on Kukkuṭapāda (Jī Fēng),
and the mist of the dark path dispersed.
When he walked, golden lotuses supported his feet;
when he sat, a jeweled throne bore his body.
When he went out, Shì Tī Huán Yīn (Indra) was in front;
when he entered, Fàn Wáng (Brahma) followed behind.
Mì Jì Lì Shì (Vajrapāṇi) assisted on the left,
taking the eradication of evil as his achievement.
Jīngāng (Vajra) assisted on the right,
taking the promotion of good as his duty.
Shēngwén (Śrāvakas) and Púsà (Bodhisattvas) stood solemnly like attendants,
and the Eight Divisions and myriad spirits guarded him reverently.
When he expounded Nirvāṇa, the earth trembled in six ways;
when he preached Prajñā, the heavens rained four kinds of flowers.
Adorned with a hundred blessings,
he resembled the full moon over the azure sea.
Shining with a thousand lights,
he was like many suns reflecting on a jeweled mountain.
With one roar of the lion, external doctrines were shattered;
with one beat of the Dharma drum, celestial Māras bowed their heads.
Therefore, the Buddha is called the Dharma King.
How can he be compared in virtue or stature to the Jiāyè of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
or associated with the Rútóng of later ages?
Therefore, in heaven and on earth,
only the Honored One, the Tamer, is supreme.
In the Three-thousand Great-thousandfold world,
all look up to his compassionate grace.
However, the principles are profound and the aim distant;
one must rely on traps and snares to realize the skillful means of the teaching gate.
One must depend on teachers and friends to fully comprehend its doctrines.
The eighty-four thousand canonical collections,
the texts of the two truths and ten stages,
the discourses of Jīyuán and Lùyuàn,
the meanings of the Ocean Palace and Dragon Palace,
the characters of jade tablets and golden books,
the words of the seven places and eight assemblies –
none of them failed to transmit the supreme Dào through a hundred kings,
and spread the profound wind through ten thousand ages.
His words are true words, words of inconceivable power.
In the near term, they bring peace to the country and benefit the people;
in the long term, they transcend the ordinary and attain sainthood.
Therefore, his form pervades the six realms, and his teachings fill the ten directions.
Truly, he is the field of blessings for the world,
and indeed, the refuge for all beings.
At that time, the multitude of reverent believers
were like the seven luminaries encircling the North Star.
Those who were transformed by his teachings
were like myriad rivers flowing into the great sea.
Examining his divine transformations, achievements, and benefits to humans and devas,
he cannot be fully described.
Having completed the causes as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
he attained the fruit of eternal joy.
Excellent indeed!
Unfathomable!
However, due to the times being not yet fully harmonized,
it led to different responses in India and China.
Therefore, the West first honored him with form and sound,
while the East only temporarily gained the benefit of hearing and seeing.
When the cloud of compassion rolled up its moisture and the sun of wisdom withdrew its light,
a golden man was dreamt of in the Yǒngpíng years,
and relics were seen in the Chìwū years.
Thereupon, during the reigns of Hàn, Wèi, Qí, and Liáng,
the iconic teaching vigorously arose.
Since Yān, Qín, Jìn, and Sòng,
famous monks appeared one after another.
Some painted full moons beside Qīng Tái,
others erected stūpas outside the Yōng Mén.
Later, translations were made north of the Hé River, and records were written south of the Hàn River.
The Dào flourished in the Three Fǔ, and faith spread throughout the Nine Provinces.
It became even more abundant across the left bank of the River,
and grew increasingly prosperous through the Jīn dynasty.
The Wèi River was replete with gardens for leisure,
and Mount Lú gathered altars for Prajñā.
Profound texts and subtle meanings were brought forth by those who came,
and eminent scholars and high monks arrived in a continuous stream.
By the time of the reign of Liáng Wǔ,
the three teachings formed a coalition, and the three vehicles raced alongside each other.
Though residing in the Zǐ Jí palace, his sentiments aligned with Fén Yáng.
He dismissed the wine officer and scattered the kitchen staff,
perfumed himself with the fragrance of precepts and tasted the joy of Dharma.
Fearing that the Four Streams would be difficult to extricate,
he personally led with his sevenfold eloquence.
He then lightened his ornate robes and wore monastic garments,
abandoned his carved carriage and sat on a grass mat.
At that time, he broadly initiated the work of the Platform of Wisdom,
and greatly opened the foundation for erecting stūpas. Consequently, the prominent families of the Five Capitals abandoned their official caps and robes to take refuge,
and renowned clans from the Four Seas forsook their glory and prosperity to enter the Dào.
From the lands where emperors resided
to the regions reached by his teachings,
none failed to bow in reverence and turn towards him, prostrating with five limbs.
The depth of his benefit to beings
has been long-standing.
How can Kǒng and Lǎo, who transmitted their teachings, be compared?
According to the biographies of famous monks in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Thirty-Six Kingdoms, Mù Zǐ, and others,
starting from the tenth year of Yǒngpíng of the Later Hàn dynasty,
Buddhism flowed eastward.
Having passed through ten dynasties, nearly six hundred years,
the famous monks and great virtuous ones respected by the world
totaled 257 people.
Those mentioned incidentally or briefly,
and kings and dukes of Yān and Zhào, high officials of Qí and Liáng, etc.,
totaled 251 people.
Their deeds and practices are broadly categorized into ten examples:
First, translating scriptures.
Second, explaining meanings.
Third, divine powers.
Fourth, practicing meditation.
Fifth, understanding precepts.
Sixth, sacrificing one's body.
Seventh, chanting scriptures.
Eighth, promoting welfare.
Ninth, masters of scriptures.
Tenth, preaching and guiding.
These eminent monks
all demonstrated virtue in accordance with the Four Reliances and completed the three karmas.
The Dharma transmitted to Zhèndàn (China) truly relied upon them.
The monk Mínggài 言 (Yán) said:
"I, Gài, have heard that the Sānhuáng (Three Sovereigns) governed the heavens and the Wǔdì (Five Emperors) ruled the earth.
Their Dào (Dao) was inclusive and far-reaching,
their Dé (virtue) covered universally and was impartial.
They spread good teachings to instruct the people,
and extended compassionate hearts to nurture all beings.
Even into the middle ages, their Dào did not diminish.
Therefore, Hàn Wǔdì (Emperor Wu of Han) admired their sagacity, saw their goodness, but could not fully achieve it.
Xiǎnzōng (Emperor Ming of Han) was wise and sagacious, embodying the Dào but not clinging to it.
Thus, he was able to humble his noble presence,
at Gānquán (Sweet Spring), he venerated the auspicious golden man,
and longed in dreams for Déyáng (the sun of virtue),
where the omen of the bronze statue descended.
Consequently, Qín Jǐng (Qin Jing) traveled west,
crossing the Liúshā (Moving Sands) to seek the Dào.
Móténg (Kāśyapa Mātaṅga) entered from the east,
crossing the Cōnglǐng (Pamir Mountains) to transmit the true Dharma.
This led to the gradual transformation of the Hàn (Han) dynasty,
and the establishment of the temple known as Báimǎ (White Horse).
The Dào flowed into the Jìn (Jin) era,
and the monastery was established with the name Qīnglóng (Green Dragon).
During this time, numerous venerated images were extensively copied, and temples and pagodas were eagerly erected.
The clouds of wisdom ascended from the falling blade,
and the Dharma waters surged from the deepest source.
It led the sentient to the forest of blessings,
and brought all beings to the land of goodness.
It opened and illuminated the Fó Fǎ (Buddhist Dharma), enlightening the ignorant.
Thus, in the final years of Yǒngpíng (Yongping era), auspicious omens arrived.
Propitious clouds flowed with moisture, and sweet dew condensed.
Auspicious horses galloped, and divine sparrows soared and gathered.
Scarlet blossoms bore buds of excellence,
and purple petals grew into intertwined branches.
This can be called an unprecedented auspicious sign,
a truly extraordinary good omen.
As a result, the Xīyù (Western Regions) sent envoys to serve, and Nányuè (Southern Yue) returned to benevolence.
Weapons were put away, soldiers rested, metal was melted down, and blades were discarded.

How could this not be due to the inspiring of sages and the descent of spirits, observing the precepts and performing good deeds, with sincerity so manifest it penetrated both the hidden and the manifest realms?
Therefore, the scriptures say:
'Heaven gives birth to divine things to bless the sagely ruler.'
Without virtue, it is concealed; with Dào, it is revealed.
Recorded in Dūn Shǐ (Dun Shi), it can be examined in detail.
As for our Great Táng (Tang) dynasty, it received the mandate of heaven, initiated its rule, seized the opportunity, governed the calendar, and established its family.
When it first rose in righteousness, its Dào harmonized with a hundred spirits.
When it first ascended the throne, its might extended to all nations.
Therefore, Shìchōng (Wang Shichong) was assimilated,
surrendering at Dōngdū (the Eastern Capital).
Jiàndé (Dou Jiande) and Wǔzhōu (Wang Wuzhou)
were contained in Běishuò (the Northern Desert).
Jīng (Jingzhou) and Wú (Wuzhou) were pacified, Qín (Qin) and Lǒng (Long) were cleared.
It is as if riding the Seven Jewels to fly,
guiding a thousand wheels to ascend lightly.
So majestic, none can compare;
so vast, who can name?
The achievements are complete,
and the tasks are finished.
Moreover, the emperor has paid attention to Fó Fǎ and devoted himself to its protection and support.
Thus, the solemnity of total retention (Dhāraṇī) was revived, and the nine-tiered structure was rebuilt.
Over a thousand Shāmén (Śramaṇa) and Buddhist disciples were ordained anew.
The transformation by images became more prevalent than in previous dynasties,
and temples and pagodas were further established in this sagely era.
We shall uphold the Sānbǎo (Three Jewels) and widely protect the Sì Yī (Four Dependents).
With palms joined and heads bowed,
we forget the nobility of emperors and kings.
With minds collected and knees bent,
we express the utmost sincerity of respect.
I, Gài, rejoice in encountering this auspicious fortune.
I wish to purify my mind in the pure land and devote my will to the profound gate.
I will diligently strive throughout the six periods (of the day and night)
to repay the virtue of this sagely era,
and exert myself with my five limbs
to requite this boundless grace.
Yet, Fù Yì (Fu Yi) suddenly uttered wild words that reached the court's ears.
With frivolous words, he disparaged the sages, and with a glib tongue, slandered the wise.
His speech was uglier than the cry of an owl,
and his voice more venomous than the sound of a zhèn bird.
He exclusively desired to destroy Fó Fǎ and abolish the Saṅgha,
cutting off their robes and provisions, and reducing temples and pagodas.
What is the reason for this?
Yì (Yi) was once a Dàoshì (Daoist priest).
Malice and jealousy reside in his heart.
Thus, he defames the sacred and diminishes the ordinary, praises the foolish and exalts the ignorant over the wise.
He slanders superiors by disparaging them, and uses shortcomings to counter strengths.
He violates reason and defies sentiment to such an extent.
But slander harms virtue, and biased listening injures the wise.
Thus, Sòng (Song) heeded Zǐhǎn's (Zihan's) words
and imprisoned Mò Dí (Mo Di).
Lǔ (Lu) believed Jìsūn's (Jisun's) assertions
and expelled Níqiū (Niqiu, i.e., Confucius).
The virtue of these two masters
could not save themselves from harm.
The slander of the eight articles
can indeed implicate others.
However,
the Sovereign is sagacious and discerning, not tolerating slander and treachery.
Even if there are three mistakes, how can there be one doubt?
But floating clouds in the sky
sometimes diminish the light of the bright sun.
Obscuring shadows passing before the eyes
make the radiant sun dim.
Fù Yì's (Fu Yi's) frivolous words confuse sight and hearing,
emotions and reason are bewildered, and speech is muddled.
One cannot exclusively listen to him;
how can one unilaterally believe him?
I request a public debate to decide between preservation and destruction, to divide the sweet and the bitter.
I, Gài, am unworthy to be among the black-robed monks, participating in the company of the Dharma.
Suddenly hearing such slander, how can I not be deeply wounded?
Even if a blade were turned to pierce my heart,
I would not consider it painful.
Even if a knife were drawn to hack my marrow,
how could I consider it cruel?
The depth of this slander and defamation wounds more severely than these.
The Sūtra says:
'Sacrifice one's body to protect the Dharma, give one's life to propagate the Dào.'
This is that time!
I shall now extract my intestines and drain my gall to avenge this perverse enemy,
and present my memorial with sincerity
to clear the slander and humiliation against my teachers and fathers.
I risk offending the august ears,
feeling extremely fearful.
Respectfully, I speak.
Respectfully, I submit this petition to refute Fù Yì's (Fu Yi's) slander against Buddha and defamation of the Saṅgha, with eight articles listed as follows.
First refutation:
'Monks and nuns under sixty years of age should be conscripted as soldiers or encouraged to farm.'
I, Gài, have heard that ultimate truth transcends words,
inherently beyond praise and blame.
The profound essence is separate from speech,
truly surpassing the beginning of verbalization and silence.
However, human sentiments do not awaken to it, so words are used to denote depth and shallowness.
The ways of the world are often confused, so forms are used to denote refinement and coarseness.
Therefore, there are distinctions between inner and outer paths, and different explanations for right and wrong.
There are separate positions for ordinary and sagely, and divisions between greater and lesser teachings.
If one were to unite them into a single vehicle,
how could one cling to it to slander the Buddha?
Ultimately leading to the supreme fruit,
it should not be sealed off by mistaken truths.
It is like a thousand rivers flowing into the vast ocean,
and ten thousand streams returning to the great sea.
The internal and external clearly prove this;
how can it be empty words?
Therefore, the Fǎhuá (Lotus) Sūtra says:
'Among all past Buddhas,
and those present or already entered Nirvāṇa,
if there are those who hear the Dharma,
none will fail to attain Buddhahood.'
Moreover, the Nièpán (Nirvana) Sūtra says:
'All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature,
and ultimately, all will attain Buddhahood.'
Furthermore, the Dàojiā (Daoist) Fǎlún (Dharma Wheel) says:
'If you see a Shāmén, reflect boundlessly,
wishing to quickly leave the world to practice the true Buddha-nature.'
'If you see a Fótú (Buddha image), reflect boundlessly,
wishing that all beings may widely enter the Dharma gate.'
Moreover, the Língbǎo Dòngxuán Zhēnyī (Lingbao Dongxuan Zhenyi) Sūtra says:
'All true immortals and high celestial beings have already attained Buddhahood.'
And the Língbǎo Tàishàng Mìyào (Lingbao Taishang Miyao) Sūtra says:
'Each in the present will attain Buddhahood together.'
Thus, we know that the non-dual wondrous gate must ultimately be entered by all equally.
The one ultimate fruit must be ascended by all alike.
To stubbornly cling to heterodoxy is to invite delusion and downfall upon oneself.
Recent scholars, swayed by their own foolishness,
have stolen true words and placed them in false canons.
Thus, the Five Paths of Rebirth are attributed to immortal scriptures,
the Three Thousand Auspicious Practices are falsely called Daoist precepts.
Receiving the Dharma from Buddha is changed to venerating the Heavenly Worthy.
Diligent practice to attain Buddhahood is transformed into reaching the Golden Palace.
Original practices are inverted into original appearances,
and Buddha's words are titled Daoist words.
They imitate the solemnity of Fó Fǎ,
and emulate the monastic rules of the Saṅgha.
Sometimes, holding the true for the false, how can they distinguish right from wrong?
Turning right into wrong, how can they know reversal?
Their actions are like a foolish thief who steals a fox fur and wears it inside out.
They are akin to a simpleton who pilfers a pearl necklace and wears it upside down.
Such categories and instances are numerous.
I will briefly mention two or three, as I cannot enumerate them all.
But Fù Yì (Fu Yi) was once a Dàoshì (Daoist priest),
dressed in yellow robes.
He did not follow the non-action style of Lǐ Lǎo (Laozi),
but exclusively practiced the military official methods of Zhāng Líng (Zhang Ling).
Sometimes he was a 'rice thief,' accumulating without end.
Known as a 'ghost soldier,' he cast curses without restraint.
His bathing and grooming were the same as common people's,
his indulgence in desires and affections, how different from the worldly?
Moreover, he harbored jealousy within and uttered wild words externally.
Slander was rampant, and curses were heaped upon curses.
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot be endured?
Now, according to the articles,
I will refute them in sequence.
May Your Sagely Discernment
kindly review them."
Yì yán.
All monks shave their heads and dye their robes.
They do not visit emperors and abandon their parents.
They are not loyal or filial.
Today's Daoists wear headcloths and kerchiefs.
They should bow to the reigning monarch.
Do they serve and support their parents at home, thus being loyal and filial?
If this is not the case, why should only monks be selectively blamed?
As for discussing loyalty:
One serves the monarch to the point of sacrificing one's life,
and gives up one's body for righteousness.
As for filial piety: one serves one's parents with utmost sincerity, providing for them in life and death.
Therefore, Dào'ān gave direct remonstrance to assist Qín,
and Fótú's loyal words rectified Zhào.
Mùlián held a bowl to feed his mother,
and Shìjiā carried a coffin to bury his parents.
How can saving the nation and benefiting the family not be loyal and filial?
Unlike Daoists like Zhāng Lǔ, who caused chaos in the Hàn dynasty,
and Sūn Ēn, who rebelled against the Jìn state.
Chén Ruì practiced Daoism and annihilated his clan,
and Gōng Qí learned immortality and brought about the destruction of his family.
How can bringing chaos to the nation and destroying families be loyal or filial?
It is also said:
All monks harbor enmity, communicate intimately within (their robes), but are externally separated (from family).

Today's Daoists, having joined their *qì* and performed purification rituals, engage in intercourse and receive the Dao.

Yet, though these couples have long been formed,

It is advisable to select them to become common people,

It is also said that there are 100,000 monks.

As for discussing the strengthening of the army:
Consider the type of people monks are.
They follow the teachings of the Tathāgata.
Their food is only plain rice and noodles,
and their provisions are only taro and konjac.
Their bodies are thin, their strength weak, their hearts empty, and their *qì* feeble.
They do not break living grass, nor do they tread on insects.
They practice endurance and cultivate compassion, love life and abhor killing.
They are often timid against enemies, and hesitant to strike.
They would only be a futile presence in battle arrays, offering no benefit to military strength.
If we consider Daoists, numbering tens of thousands,
they offer sacrifices to the Three Officials and Five Emperors, receive prohibitions, and perform talismans.
Their memorials invariably involve sacrificing chickens,
and their rituals require wine and dried meat.
They indulge in sliced meat and fermented wine to their drunken fill.
Their bodies are fat, their strength robust, their hearts brave, and their *qì* strong.
They are ruthless and indifferent, abhorring life and loving killing.
They are certainly brave in battle and strike without hesitation.
Arranged in military formations, they would definitely strengthen the army.
If their strength is compared, Daoists are stronger.
If their virtue is discussed, monks are superior.
The propriety of selection
can therefore be known.
If it is said that cultivating the land and laboring diligently is for the encouragement of agriculture,
this is a narrow view,
not a comprehensive approach.
For society cannot be regulated by a single ritual,
governance cannot be managed by a single method,
scholars cannot be judged by a single conduct,
and the people cannot be sustained by a single occupation.
Hence, the "Records of Money-Making Biographies" in the *Hàn Shū* states:
"In ancient times, the four classes of people were not allowed to mix.
Scholars discussed benevolence and righteousness at court banquets.
Artisans discussed skills and crafts in government offices.
Merchants discussed wealth and profit in the marketplaces.
Farmers discussed sowing and reaping in the fields."
These four groups each lived peacefully in their place and enjoyed their work.
Thus, they achieved what was appropriate for heaven and earth,
and contributed to the benefit of the nation.
Today, all monks also have their own occupations.
Internally, their hearts are filled with compassion and forbearance;
this is the benevolence and righteousness of scholars.
Externally, they transform beings with skillful means;
this is the ingenuity and skill of artisans.
Their conduct involves giving and receiving in return;
this is the marketplace of merchants.
Their path involves benefiting both self and others;
this is the diligent farming of farmers.
Thus, sincere devotion can move spirits and gods.
Only virtue can move heaven and earth.
They dispense compassionate hearts to bestow blessings,
and spread benevolence to nourish the times.
Therefore, with good governance,
sudden rains follow chariots, and flying locusts avoid the territory.
Wheat in the fields produces double ears, and rice plants yield nine stalks.
This is due to the achievements of good governance,
not solely the effort of diligent farmers.
It is also said:
To demand that all monks bow to emperors and be included in the court protocols,
this view is profoundly deluded.
Having fallen into the pit oneself, one tries to drag others into the well.
How can one succeed in making others fall into the same trap?
In the past, Huán Xuán, a usurper, was mad, perverse, and immoral.
He also held this view.
The court deliberated and did not comply, saying:
"Śramaṇas and disciples of Śākyamuni, having shaved their heads and dyed their robes,

Hence, the *kāṣāya*, worn with one shoulder bared,
is not a court garment.
The alms-bowl and tin staff,
how can they be instruments of the imperial hall?
Yet Xuán, being perverse and rebellious, stubbornly persisted without reform.
He humiliated the Three Jewels and caused the ancestral temples to be disrupted.
The people resented him, the gods were angered, the populace rebelled, and his relatives deserted him.
His army was defeated at Dōnglíng,
and he himself perished at Xīpǔ.
The overturned chariot is a clear mirror.
Who would not take warning?
Our great Dà Táng Emperor,
born as a sage,
responded to an era of brilliant peace,
and presided over a period of flourishing prosperity.
He stopped warfare and relieved suffering, rescued the drowning and saved the sinking.
He propagated the sagely teachings to instruct the people,
and extended utmost benevolence to nurture all beings.
The years are harmonious, the harvests abundant, the *qì* prosperous, and the times flourishing.
Who can fully record his profound virtue and merit?
Furthermore, he harbors the Four Faiths internally and reveres the Three Jewels externally.
He lowered his imperial carriage to take refuge,
and descended his imperial crown to turn towards the Dharma.
Thus, people from the eight directions bow down, and myriad nations come to court.
How could he demand that those who have left the secular world
observe the rituals of those who remain at home?
Today's Daoists wear coarse clothes, carry tablets, wear headcloths and kerchiefs.
Since they wear the clothes of ministers and officials,
they must perform the rituals of court audience.
In the past, even celestial masters, who were noble scholars, still bowed to emperors.
Today's "ghost soldiers," who are lowly men, must kneel before ministers and high officials.
It is proper to make Daoists follow their master's methods:
attend court and bow to the emperor, pay respects to officials and superiors.
Let this be entered into the court protocols.
Would this not be appropriate?
It is said:
Examining from the Hàn and Wèi dynasties onwards,
through nine generations,
among those Daoists,
those who used heterodox teachings to disrupt the court and spoke seditious words to violate the nation:
When perusing historical records, in which era were they absent?
During the Latter Hàn Emperor Xiàn's reign,
Zhāng Líng and Zhāng Lǔ fraudulently claimed to speak for ghosts,

"After the Hàn dynasty's mandate ends,

Thus, they conspired with Zhāng Jiǎo of Jùlù as an external support,
made yellow headcloths and wore yellow robes,
gathered followers and deluded foolish people,
plotting to endanger the state.
They were soon executed.
Hence, the *Lǐ* states:
"Those who disturb the populace with heterodox ways shall be killed."
Today's Daoists do not wear the court robes of Lǐ Lǎo when he attended court,
but instead wear the disruptive robes of Zhāng Lǔ.
Masters and disciples pass down their brigandage unchanged.
Since their numbers are large,
they form bandit gangs.
They might harbor ambitions; should we not be prepared?
Counting them, there are 50,000.
Select them to become able-bodied men, paying annual taxes and rent, and producing male and female offspring.
This would benefit the nation and the people, strengthen the army, and encourage agriculture.
According to my humble opinion,
those who conform to the law should be honored and followed.
Those who violate prohibitions should be removed and put to labor.
Thus, once weeds are cleared, the field seedlings will flourish.
Once villains are expelled, the populace will be pure and orderly.
Would this not be good?
Second Refutation.
If temples were made into thatched huts and earthen dwellings,
then Emperor Qín Shǐ Huáng and Emperor Hàn Wǔdì would be considered virtuous rulers.
Generally, I have heard that the Dharmakāya is formless, yet responds to beings in various ways.
Therefore, it temporarily manifested its complete body
and was placed within the Piling Pagoda (多寶之塔).
By expediency, its shattered remains were distributed,
flowing into the stūpas of Āyù (阿育).
Thus, it can gather and disperse according to circumstances, and its existence and absence are subject to phenomena.
The miraculous power and expedient transformations of the sagely are inconceivable.
However, the Buddha was born in Tiānzhú (天竺).
According to the customs of that land,
burial must involve cremation (闍維),
and the collection of relics must involve the erection of a pagoda.
A pagoda is a temple (廟).
A temple (廟) means a semblance (貌).
Sacrifices and service are performed as if the semblance of the person were still present.
The ancestral temples and altars of the state today
are mostly similar.
However, one hundred years after the Tathāgata's parinirvāṇa,
there was King Āshūjiā (阿輸伽王),
who ruled the world with an iron wheel (鐵輪御世).
With his awe-inspiring virtue, he commanded spirits and deities.
By the power of his merit, he raised spiritual temples.
Thus, eighty-four thousand pagodas
were completed in less than a day.
Halls with a thousand pillars and a hundred beams
were finished in less than a morning.
How could human effort be needed?
This was divine accomplishment.
How can the affairs of sages and worthies be doubted with the sentiments of ordinary mortals?
How is it different from measuring the ocean with a small dipper (斗筲)
or surveying the sky with an inch?
How can it be achieved?
When the Shèli (舍利) flowed eastward, King Wú (吳王) first felt the inspiration.
Sēng Huì (僧會) requested it,
and his sincere devotion led to its sudden manifestation.
Sūn Quán (孫權) tested it;
when struck by a pestle and anvil (砧磓), it became even firmer.
Then, a radiant light ascended, penetrating upwards,
shining brightly between the axe and the screen (斧扆).
Its vibrant colors spread sideways,
glowing and reflecting beneath the rock corridors (巖廊).
At that time, Huì (會) rejoiced and extensively praised its awesome spiritual power.
Quán (權) and his court officials, upon hearing this, all believed and submitted.
Immediately, a pagoda was built for it, and a Saṅghārāma (伽藍) was established.
Because of this, Buddhist affairs greatly flourished south of the Yangtze.
How is this like Tàishàng (太上), whose bones decayed in Guānzhōng (關中)
and definitively had no Shèli?
Or Tiānshī (天師), whose body was buried in the belly of a snake?
How could there be a remaining body?
Without anything to rely upon, they consequently created deceptions.
Hearing that the Buddha had eight measures (斛) of Shèli to represent his remains,
they then kept two small stones
to substitute for "immortal eggs."
However, the "immortal eggs" were originally the testicles of a wild boar,
and the "mysterious altar" was merely the temple of an old ghost.
If it is said that Shèli are "Hú (胡) bones,"
this is more reasonable than the testicles of a wild boar.
And a Fútú (佛圖) (Buddha image/stūpa) being a "Hú (胡) tomb,"
how can it be compared to the temple of an old ghost?
How can one compare them in terms of high and low, or speak of their ranks?
Thus, when present-day Daoists see Shèli, it is like a thorn in their eye;
how can they be willing to take refuge?
When they see Fútú, it is like a stab in their heart;
they specifically plot to destroy them.
Vainly harboring evil,
how can they succeed?
Throughout history, those who became emperors
all had good roots planted in previous lives and mostly held right faith.
They lavished treasures to build pagodas and offered precious items to venerate the true.
They all wished to express their sincerity in honoring the distant past
and manifest their reverence as if the presence were real.
Therefore, when pagodas of nine stories (九級) were renovated and built, all possible adornments were included.
When halls of a hundred beams were constructed, their grandeur and splendor were exhausted.
This caused a poor person's offering to instantly complete a Brahma palace (梵宮),
and an elder's stretched rope to immediately manifest a heavenly paradise.
The principle of cause and effect is thus clear and evident.
Those with dark understanding cannot comprehend it.
The treatise states:
According to the Rénwáng Jīng (仁王經),
there are five types of kings in the world:
First, the Scattered Millet King (粟散王), whose virtue and power are the weakest.
Second, the Iron Wheel King (鐵輪王), who rules Jambudvīpa (閻浮提).
Third, the Copper Wheel King (銅輪王), who governs two continents.
Fourth, the Silver Wheel King (銀輪王), who transforms three continents.
Fifth, the Gold Wheel King (金輪王), who rules four continents.
Among these five kings,
their positions differ in superiority and inferiority.
Their virtues vary in strength and weakness.
Considering Qín Huáng (秦皇) and Hàn Wǔ (漢武),
within Jambudvīpa, they only reigned over Zhèndàn (震旦).
Among the five types of kings, they were Scattered Millet Kings.
They were of weak virtue but occupied a superior palace,
of low status but resided on a high platform.
They did not move people with benevolence and grace,
but exclusively used whips and floggings to control beings.
This angered deities and spirits, and caused the common people to sigh and lament.
Thus, historians condemned them as rulers without the Dao.
Moreover, after their deaths, magnificent tombs were built,
wasting immense wealth and toiling the populace.
Consequently, their bones and flesh dissolved, and their spiritual images vanished.
With the passage of time, where are their power and blessings?
Our Shìjiā (釋迦), in his manifestation in the world, had uniquely high virtue and status.
His Dao surpassed a hundred spirits, and his divinity transcended millions.
He was the utmost holy among the holy,
his virtue surpassing that of a thousand sages before him.
He was the Dharma King (法王) among kings,
his position above a hundred kings.
How could he be compared in superiority and inferiority to Qín Huáng (秦皇) and Hàn Wǔ (漢武)?
The Buddha's virtue was high, and he resided in a superior palace.
His position was supreme, and he stood on a high platform.
He moved people solely by moral transformation,
and did not use whips to control beings.
Emperors and kings themselves joyfully donated, and spiritual deities secretly assisted,
raising pagodas and temples after his parinirvāṇa.
The Shèli did not perish, and his spiritual power remains.
Destroying them instantly incurs evil omens.
Breaking them leads to visible misfortune.
Therefore, Sūn Hào (孫皓), Lord of Wú (吳),
was extravagant, licentious, cruel, and did not fear karma (罪福), saying there was no retribution.
He dug up a bronze statue and ordered it placed in front of the latrine.
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
he urinated on the statue's head, saying,
"Today is the eighth day, and I am anointing your crown."
In a short while, he suffered from painful swelling in his groin (陰 󱦰).
The agony was unbearable.
The Grand Astrologer divined, saying,
"You have offended a great deity."
Praying to all spiritual deities brought no unusual response.
Later, hearing about the Buddha,
he then became alarmed, regretting his past transgressions.
He immediately sent for the statue, bathed it with perfumed water,
and kowtowed, apologizing for his fault.
He was cured instantly, and from this, he developed faith and was cautious and fearful for the rest of his life.
Furthermore, Xiè Huì (謝晦), a minister of Sòng (宋),
was stationed in Jīngzhōu (荊州) city.
Inside the city was a five-story temple.
The temple had a Shèli pagoda.
Huì's (晦) nature was fierce and perverse.
Previously, he had no sincere faith, saying,
"It is unsuitable for temples and pagodas to be within the city."
He ordered them to be demolished and moved out.
Thereupon, he personally led soldiers directly to the pagoda.
Everyone trembled, not daring to lift a hand.
Huì (晦) then harshly beat drums, forcing his soldiers
to strike the reliquary door and hack at the venerated statue.
Suddenly, clouds and mist darkened the ground, and wind and dust filled the sky.
Huì (晦) and his soldiers were covered in ash and dirt.
When they wiped it with their hands, their skin and flesh fell off.
They consequently developed a severe illness, with leprosy-like sores all over their bodies.
Soon after, he rebelled and was executed.
All these events are recorded in Sòng Xuān Yàn Jì (宋宣驗記).
I have briefly summarized these incidents based on records and biographies
to enlighten those who are not yet awakened and clarify their minds.
As for my humble opinion:
When Shìjiā (釋迦) appeared in the world, all beings revered him.
In ancient times, there were already temples and pagodas.
Those built today should be maintained by request.
Lǐ Lǎo (李老) abandoned the world, his mind still on emptiness.
During his lifetime, there were no residential halls whatsoever.
The current lavish competition should be reduced by request.
Third, a decisive break.
Reduce temples and pagodas in all prefectures and counties,
then the people will be at peace, and the state will be well-governed.
I have heard that in ancient times, enlightened kings, with respectful self-composure, faced south.
Their wisdom encompassed heaven and earth, yet they did not ponder by themselves.
Their eloquence embellished all things, yet they did not speak by themselves.
Why? Because they toiled in seeking suitable people,
and rested in commanding their officials.
As long as they found the right people, the world would govern itself.
Thus, they sought the Dao in the Xuānshì (宣室) and discussed governance in the Míngtáng (明堂).
They assessed duties, divided responsibilities, and assigned offices throughout the regions.
The Eight Capable Ones (八凱) stood in array, and the Ten Worthies (十亂) served at court.
They were thus able to protect and secure the state,
and bring peace to the altars of earth and grain.
Consequently, they spread the transformation of great compassion,
lightening taxes and caring for the poor.
They practiced the teaching of utmost benevolence,
reducing punishments and exercising caution in legal cases.
They diffused virtuous beneficence, reaching far and bringing peace to near.
They established great accomplishments, creating rites and composing music.
This was the utmost governance,
worthy of praise.
Therefore, the Shū (書) says,
"Governing a state is based on bringing peace to the people."
"Bringing peace to the people is rooted in good officials."
If the right people are obtained, the state will be peaceful.
If not the right people, the populace will be in chaos.
Thus, it is known that loyal ministers and good officials
can govern the state and bring peace to the people.
However, one must revere good deeds, accumulate blessings, plant roots (of merit), and cultivate causes.
Respectfully serve spiritual deities and attend to spiritual temples.
How can one destroy pagodas, abolish temples, merge monasteries, and expel monks?
Spiritual deities bring forth omens of disaster and fortune, which must be treated with caution.
Yet Yì (奕) is fiercely perverse and recklessly utters wild words.
The sagely court, with its clear discernment, will surely not be misled by such reasoning.
Discussion of words.
I surreptitiously observe that trees are designated as shè,
and bricks and stones are erected to be called jūn.
Earth is piled up to form an altar,
and bundles of straw are arranged as decoration.
As for seeking and praying in times of urgency and distress, there is a slight spiritual power.
When praying sincerely during drought or flood, blessings are quickly bestowed.
How much more so for the Buddha's divine forms, majestically present and awe-inspiring.
To wish to lightly destroy them,
how can this be achieved?
Since Emperor Míng of Hàn was moved by a dream,
temples arose with the name Báimǎ Sì.
Sūn Quán verified an auspicious omen,
and a pagoda was first built under the name Jiànchū Tǎ.
From then on, they continuously arose.
If the divine way were to vanish, how could emperors and kings revere and serve it?
If its spiritual power were to cease and diminish, how could national rulers continue to follow it?
It is because they personally witnessed and experienced it
that they returned and converted.
This is unlike the Dàojiā, which has no foundation or basis. On the day Lǐ Lǎo served Zhōu,
there was no xuántán.
On the morning Zhāng Líng conspired against Hàn,
guānshè were just beginning to be established.
Thus, during the reign of Emperor Shùn of the Later Hàn dynasty,
there was a man from Pèi, Zhāng Líng,
who traveled as a guest in Shǔ.
He heard an ancient legend that said,
"Formerly, Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
in response to the twenty-four solar terms,
sacrificed at twenty-four mountains,
and consequently became the sovereign of All Under Heaven."
Líng, without assessing his own virtue, then concocted this scheme.
He sacrificed cattle at twenty-four locations,
set up earthen altars, covered them with grass huts, and called them the "Twenty-Four Zhì."
The establishment of zhìguǎn began here.
Twenty-three locations were in Shǔdì,
and Yǐn Xǐ's one location was in Xiányáng.
Thereupon, he tricked and enticed foolish people and gathered wicked followers.
He collected rent and tax grain, planning to create a rebellion.
At that time, he was swallowed by a snake, and his perverse scheme did not come to fruition.
It was not until his grandson Zhāng Lǔ
that disaster and rebellion arose in Hànzhōng.
He was exterminated by Cáo Cāo.
From then until now, groups of evil followers have continued to emerge.
Relying on zhìguǎn, they constantly engage in demonic practices.
Thus, in the first year of Zhōngpíng during Emperor Shùn of Hàn's reign,
Zhāng Jiǎo from Jùlù

He had thirty-six generals,

His followers numbered a hundred thousand.

Until the tenth year of Kāihuáng during Suí,
the Dàoshì Pú Tóng from Chānglóng Xiàn, Miánzhōu,

Now, with the Dàtáng revolution, demonic delusions still thrive.
In the third year of Wǔdé,
Lǐ Wàng, a commoner from Chānglóng Xiàn, Miánzhōu,

In the last years of Dàyè,
there was a Dàoshì, Pú Zǐzhēn,

He was sent to Dōngjīng.
He died in Liánghàn
and was buried there.
But Lǐ Wàng falsely claimed,
"Zǐzhēn has recently returned."
Also, near a mountain in that county, there was a stone chamber,

Wàng then relied on it to perpetrate his fraud.
In the light, he would speak loudly, transmitting and receiving messages.

When officials first investigated,

Later, Cìshǐ Lǐ Dàlǐ said,
"This matter is not trivial;

Only Yuè Shìzhì, the Xiànlìng of Bāxī, deeply understood the situation's inner workings.

He saw Wàng speaking in a muffled voice, and Shìzhì then reprimanded him.
Wàng immediately confessed.
He was arrested and imprisoned in the prefectural jail.
Just as they were about to sentence him,
a few days later,
