how can they spread the teachings of the Ten Goods (shí shàn)?
Evil spirits necessarily rely on wickedness;
how can they initiate the path of the Eightfold Noble Path (bā zhèng)?
Demons fear dogs,
and evil spirits fear cats.
How then could they humble the lofty hearts of Śakra (Dìshì),
and crush the immense power of Māras (Tiānmó)?
Furthermore, companions like Tú Chéng (Fótúchéng) and Luó Shí (Jiūmóluóshí),
and peers like Dào Ān and Huì Yuǎn—
they possessed high virtue and renown, neither mad nor drunk.
How could they renounce love and decline honors,
to seek the evil path of mountain spirits and goblins (chīmèi)?
How could they toil their bodies and endure hardships,
to serve the demonic gods of ghosts and phantoms (wǎngliǎng)?
Moreover, from the Eastern Hàn (Dōng Hàn) until my time...
Great Táng.
Generation after generation, it has forbidden heterodox speech.
Everywhere, it has suppressed immoral cults.
How can it permit squandering its resources and abandoning its people
to build temples and stupas for demons and specters,
and to join the multitude of ghosts and goblins?
Moreover, there are prime ministers, high officials, paragons of humanity, and models for the world,
followers of Wáng Dǎo and Yǔ Liàng,
and those like Dài Kuí and Xǔ Xún.
They have set their hearts on the realm between heaven and man,
and conducted themselves beyond the confines of the mundane world.
All have received the teaching and taken refuge,
all have committed their hearts to belief and reverence.
How could they possibly honor demons and venerate specters to abase themselves?
It is truly because they have beheld the wondrous and known the truth that they are so!
Furthermore, Fù Yì, whose courtesy name was Wǔzhòng, was an ancestor of the Fù clan.
He possessed great talent and profound learning, and was known to his generation as a man of wide knowledge.
He elucidated Emperor Míng of Hàn's auspicious dream,
and confirmed the mystical response of the golden man.
When Buddhism spread eastward,
Fù Yì had a hand in it.
I secretly estimate Fù Lì's talent and insight
cannot compare to Wǔzhòng's.
Why then does he slander Buddha and revile the Dharma,
acting contrary to his ancestor?
Kàn Zé, the Director of the Department of State Affairs of Wú, once said to Sūn Quán, the ruler of Wú:
“The two schools of Kǒng and Lǎo are vastly inferior to the Buddha Dharma when compared.”
Why do I say this?
“Kǒng and Lǎo established teachings based on heaven to govern;
they dared not violate heaven.
The Buddhas expound teachings that heaven reveres and practices;
it dares not violate the Buddha.
From this, it is truly not a comparison.”
I think Kàn Zǐ’s argument
grasps one aspect of their superiority and inferiority.
Shouldn't all gentlemen of the hundred schools ponder his words?
Indeed, great bodhisattvas and eminent monks comprehend principles deeply.
Enlightened rulers and virtuous ministers plan for the state loyally.
And yet, why have successive generations treasured it as a great teaching?
Because they know that in exhausting principles and fulfilling nature, no doctrine surpasses it.
Fù Lì's understanding is not as profound as that of eminent monks,
nor is his thought as refined as that of former sages.
He relies solely on his own mind and turns his back on the Dharma,
lightly abandoning blessings and inviting misfortune.
How can this be loyal planning for the state?
How can this be far-sighted consideration for himself?
The Great Awakened One thoroughly comprehends the divine and knows transformation.
He profoundly urges reflection on adversity and proactive prevention.
Alas, a hundred years are easily exhausted,
and the five blessings are alas difficult to make permanent.
Life flows like a river and passes like lightning,
while karma endures like earth and extends like heaven.
The three lower realms are extremely perilous and remote,
the four currents are boundless and vast.
Rely on the Dharma-boat for beneficial crossing,
and borrow the wings of faith to soar high.
It is fitting to transform misfortune into blessing;
why be heedless and act madly?
Fù Lì said:
“During the Zhào and Liáng dynasties, there were rebellious monks.
Moreover, today there are 200,000 monks and nuns in the realm.”
This, again, is thoughtless speech.
If one were to abolish today's monastic community because there were rebellious monks in the past,
how could one abandon today's many scholars because there were rebellious ministers in antiquity?
How could one kill one's own dutiful child because a neighbor has a rebellious one?
Or not nurture today's common people because there were rebellious subjects in the past?
Indeed, among the populace under heaven,
the community of those who have left home,
does not gather in a single city,
but is truly scattered like stars across the nine regions.
They are managed by prefectures and counties,
and confined by passes and rivers.
They have no power to levy or command,
but are subject to the constraints of laws and regulations.
Even if there are five or three vicious and dangerous individuals, or one or two icchantikas,
they have no cause to gather like crows,
so what is there to worry about in their swarming like ants?
Furthermore, when shāmén enter the path,
do they harbor plans of rebellion?
When women leave home,
do they seek the use of armor?
How can he conflate the number of monks and nuns,
and indiscriminately equate them with a faction of violent rebels?
He invents falsehoods to disrupt the truth,
and obscures good to label it evil.
A gentleman has three fears;
how can one act like this?
If scholars in blue robes commit crimes,
it is not the fault of Master Kǒng.
If those in black robes do evil,
how is it the fault of the Venerable Shìjiā?
When monks violate state laws or nuns infringe upon common regulations,
it is like reciting the Vinaya while tunneling through walls,
or reading the Rites while being arrogant and rude.
It is merely that people are endowed with obstinate natures and do not turn towards good,
not that the scriptures initiate sources of rebellion and cause them to be tainted by evil.
Not all people are virtuous, but the Dharma is truly perfect in goodness.
How can one condemn goodness because of anger at evil,
or discard the Dharma because of the faults of people?
Indeed, speaking of Bó Yí and Liǔ Xiàhuì with one's mouth, but acting like Jié and Zhí with one's body,
listening to the Odes and Rites with one's ears, but harboring perverse thoughts in one's heart—
since the Xià and Yīn dynasties, which era has been without such?
How can one condemn Bó Yí and Liǔ Xiàhuì out of anger at Zhí, or discard the Odes and Rites due to hatred of evil?
Thus, people may have crimes deserving of punishment,
but the Dharma has no fault deserving of abolition.
One should only suppress wrongdoings to promote the Dharma,
not debase the Way because of people.
I secretly hold firm belief in the wondrous Dharma,
and do not indiscriminately side with shāmén.
As for weeding out weeds to plant good seedlings,
and purifying the great teaching by eliminating villains and deceitful individuals,
that is what I deeply desire!
That is what I deeply desire!
Fù Lì said:
“Dàorén, barn owls, donkeys, and mules are four types
all of which are evil breeds of greed and rebellion.”
This, again, is thoughtless speech.
Indeed, one is called a dàorén because one abandons worldly life to cultivate the Way.
Learning the Way means departing from greed; how can one be called greedy and rebellious?
If he means greedy for the Bodhi path and rebellious against the flow of birth and death,
then Master Fù's words have not grasped this meaning.
Looking at the monastic rules and conduct of shāmén,
they practice what others cannot practice,
and stop what others cannot stop.
This can be thoroughly investigated in all Buddhist scriptures.
They do not even harm crawling creatures,
how much less would they commit the deeds of owls and jackals?
They even abandon the rites of marriage,
how much less would they engage in the acts of beasts?
How can he link eminent individuals who have transcended desire
with lowly beings that gather in herds of deer?
He compares virtuous and talented people of the Way
to ignorant donkeys and mules,
and slanders the good multitude of great compassion
as ill-omened evil birds.
He calls dàorén rebellious breeds,
and equates pure conduct with bestial hearts.
How utterly severe is this harm to good, and how completely is the white slandered!
In the past, I often cited the Xìaojīng's principle of not harming or injuring
to criticize shāmén for cutting their hair and beards,
saying they defied the way of the former kings
and lost the meaning of loyalty and filial piety.
Now, however, I realize it is not so.
If one serves one's ruler and parents and exhausts one's integrity,
even if one sacrifices one's life, it is called benevolence.
If one damages loyalty and filial piety and furtively preserves one's life,
merely preserving one's body is not righteousness.
Mencius spoke of seeing danger and sacrificing one's life, while the rites guard against preserving one's life by any means when facing difficulty.
How can one indiscriminately condemn injury and harm,
or thoughtlessly care for one's skin and hair?
Cutting off a limb or offering one's liver is indeed a severe injury,
while trimming one's beard or shaving one's head is but a minor disfigurement.
To establish loyalty without regard for one's life—
commentators do not blame this.
To seek the Way without cherishing one's hair—
why alone is this considered a fault?
Tāng, out of compassion for the suffering people,
still burned his body to pray for rain.
Mò Dì, in advocating universal love,
was willing to wear down his feet to his head.
How much more, then, for the sake of one's ruler and parents above, to deeply seek blessings and benefits,
what is the harm to hair and beard worth caring about?
Moreover, the teachings of the sages have different paths but lead to the same destination,
and the way of the gentleman sometimes goes against convention but accords with righteousness.
Tài Bó was such a person.
He abandoned residing at home to care for his parents,
claiming to gather herbs and not returning.
He discarded the attire of the Central Plains,
and adopted cut hair as his adornment.
Nothing could be more contrary to convention and rebellious against the rites
than this.
Yet, Kǒng Ní praised him, saying:
“Tài Bó may be said to have possessed the highest virtue.”
Why was this?
Although his actions outwardly went against his ruler and parents, his heart was loyal to his family and state.
His form was diminished like the people of Bǎiyuè, but his virtue was complete in the Three Yieldings.
Therefore, Tài Bó discarded the customs of attire and crowns, yet it did not diminish his supreme virtue.
Then, for shāmén to abandon the appearance of officials,
how can it harm the wondrous Way?
Although changing attire and altering appearance goes against the usual conduct of subjects and children,
yet they believe in the Way and return their hearts to it, wishing abundant blessings for their ruler and parents.
They afflict their bodies and minds,
cultivating all the good deeds of leaving home,
and leave their rulers and parents
with profound blessings for eons.
Is their loyalty and filial piety
not abundant?
To call good shāmén disloyal—
I do not believe it.
Fù 傅 also said:
“The Hú 胡 people of the Western Regions are born from mud.”
Thus, it is convenient to serve [with] mud and tiles.
This, again, is an ill-considered statement.
When one reverently erects spiritual images and depicts venerable forms,
many materials are used,
not just mud and tiles.
Sometimes carved, sometimes cast,
then iron, wood, gold, and bronze are used.
To draw them or embroider them,
also uses paints, silk, and plain cloth.
Can it then be said that the men and women of the Western Regions are all born from these things?
Furthermore, the temples of Zhōngguó 中國 primarily use wood.
Can it then be said that the gentlemen who established the rites are all nurtured from wood?
Parents must not be forgotten,
hence ancestral temples are built for them.
The Buddhas must not be forgotten,
hence their images are erected
to express boundless devotion
and to convey reverence as if they were present.
To admire the sagely and respect virtue,
what fault is there in that?
Indeed, those who take good for evil
also take evil for good.
Fù 傅 also said:
“When emperors have no Buddhism, the country is well-governed and the years are long.
When they have Buddhism, the government is cruel and the reign is short.”
This, again, is an ill-considered statement.
It would imply that the teachings established by the Benevolent One [Shìjiāmóuní 釋迦牟尼]
all propagate a style of depravity and cruelty,
and that the words spoken by the Bodhisattvas [Púsà 菩薩]
exclusively promote the deeds of Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂.
To discuss it factually,
it is completely untrue.
When the Yīn 殷 dynasty lost its great treasure,
calamity arose from the words of Dájǐ 妲己.
When the Zhōu 周 dynasty lost its feudal lords,
disaster originated from the smile of Bāosì 褒姒.
The downfall of the Sāndài 三代 [three dynasties]
was all due to such things.
How could the teachings of the Sānchéng 三乘 [Three Vehicles]
be comparable to these?
The Way of the Buddha embodies compassion, joy, and protection.
It equalizes self and others, and treats enemies and kin alike.
It bestows peace and joy, and rescues from danger and suffering.
The means by which the ancients gained the people's allegiance,
the Buddha has indeed widely propagated.
The reasons why people deserted their rulers,
the scriptures have strictly warned against.
The virtues of Xīxuān 羲軒 [Fúxī 伏羲 and Xuānyuán 軒轅], Shùnyǔ 舜禹 [Shùn 舜 and Yǔ 禹],
are encompassed within the Liùdù 六度 [Six Pāramitās].
The faults of Yìzhú 羿浞 [Yì 羿 and Hánzhuó 寒浞], Guǐxīn 癸辛 [Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂],
are all forbidden by the Shí'è 十惡 [Ten Evils].
If Jié 桀 had promoted the teaching of few desires,
and Zhòu 紂 had followed the Way of great compassion,
Yī Ī [Yī Yǐn 伊尹] and Lǚ 呂 [Lǚ Shàng 呂尚] would have had no use for their strategies,
and Tāng Wǔ 湯武 [King Tāng 湯 and King Wǔ 武] would have had no means to carry out their punitive expeditions.
This could have saved Míngtiáo 鳴條 from the calamity of losing its state,
and stopped the chaos of reversed spears at Mùyě 牧野.
The Xiahòu 夏后 [rulers of Xià 夏] would have followed the songs of Luòruì 洛汭,
and the Chǔzǐ 楚子 [rulers of Chǔ 楚] would have avoided the disaster at Qiánxī 乾溪.
Thus, the civilizing influence of Shìshì 釋氏 [Buddha] is of no small benefit.
It extends good fortune and longevity endlessly,
and arrests peril and demise before they show signs.
Fù 傅 says that having it is harmful and lacking it is beneficial.
What kind of talk is this?
What kind of talk is this?
What enmity does he have with the Buddha that he slanders him to such an extent?
What has the Buddha done to him that he hates him like an enemy?
Fù 傅 also said:
“Before there was Buddhist dharma,
people were all simple and harmonious, and there were no usurpations or rebellions in the world.”
This, again, is an ill-considered statement.
When the Jiǔlí 九黎 [Nine Lí] corrupted virtue,
was that not in years without the Buddha?
When the Sānmiáo 三苗 defied command,
was that not after the dharma existed?
During the later years of Xià 夏 and Yīn 殷, how could there have been simplicity and harmony?
During the Spring and Autumn period, how could there have been no usurpations or rebellions?
Robbers, bandits, traitors, and rebels,
led Gāoyáo 皋繇 to establish the duties of officers.
When the Xiǎnyǔn 玁狁 were exceedingly rampant,
Jífǔ 吉甫 labored to conquer them.
Yet Fù 傅 says that the rise of Buddhism caused usurpation and rebellion, and the decline of dharma ruined simplicity and harmony.
He exclusively fabricates empty words, all contrary to factual records.
The Buddha even warns against stealing a single thread;
how could he promote the chaos of usurpation and rebellion?
The Buddha also guards against a single false word;
how could he destroy the Way of simplicity and harmony?
As for the Buddha's teachings,
they encourage ministers to be loyal,
sons to be filial,
states to be well-governed,
and families to be harmonious.
They promote good and display the joys of heaven,
and punish wrong by showing the sufferings of hell.
They do not merely praise with a single word,
nor do they only warn with the five punishments.
To say that they harm harmony and prolong chaos,
is this not the height of slander?
And how does it harm the Buddha-sun?
It only causes oneself to sink into the sea of suffering.
To take it lightly and not avoid it,
is truly lamentable!
Thereupon, the scholar's heart was subdued and his face showed shame. He rose from his mat and apologized, saying:
“I, due to force of habit, have lived normally, acting contrary to the Way and indulging myself.
I neglected what I had not fully investigated and delighted in what I had previously stated.
I turned my back on the true dharma and held different views,
and accepted evil words, sharing in the error.
Now that I have heard of the profound and distant wisdom of the Buddha,
I now know the loyalty and truthfulness of the Buddhist teachings.
My spirit is suddenly enlightened, and the principles are expounded;
it is sufficient to dispel delusion and remove affliction.
Although I followed evil in past years,
I request to return to righteousness this very day.
I shall diligently recite the incoming precepts as my verbal commitment.”
Someone said:
“Sages set forth blessings to encourage goodness
and display calamities to warn against evil.
Common people, believing that good deeds are useless, do not perform them;
and believing that evil deeds are harmless, do not desist from them.
However, talk of calamities and blessings
is ornate but without substance.
On the other hand, the argument that there is no benefit and no harm
is reliable and has evidence.
Why do I say this?
Bó Yí (伯夷) starved;
Qǐ Qī (啟期) was poor;
Yán Huí (顏回) died young;
Rǎn Gēng (冉耕) was ill.
Some are lavishly rich,
but their words rarely touch upon righteousness.
Some are old and long-lived,
but their names are not remembered after their death.
The benevolent are not long-lived, and the rich are not benevolent—
from the time of written records, these examples are too numerous to count.
Therefore, we know that Zhòngní’s (仲尼) words about calamities and good fortune
are merely deceiving people.
Wénmìng’s (文命) analogy of shadow and echo
is probably hard to believe.
There are those who diligently practice goodness without slackening,”
he sighed, “and are greatly misled by these words.”
Then he debated and explained, saying:
“Indeed, calamities and blessings each have their roots;
they cannot arise groundlessly.
Good and evil must receive their retribution;
it is certainly not that they lose their due and simply cease.
However, the roots are deep and the retribution is distant,
beyond the reach of our ears and eyes.
To trace the origin and investigate the end
is beyond what Confucian and Mohist scholars can achieve.
Thus, the fate encountered is measured by Heaven and difficult to comprehend,
while the years of short or long life are examined by humans and easily misunderstood.
When humans administer rewards and punishments,
they can still be clear-sighted and fair.
How then could Heaven, in sending down calamities and blessings,
instead be confused and without order?
Therefore, we know there is a principle that exists,
which cannot be misrepresented.
Unless one is a great enlightened being with complete knowledge,
who can exhaust the principle and eliminate delusion?
The words of Bǔ Shāng (卜商) and Jiǎ Yì (賈誼),
and the treatises written by Bān Biāo (班彪) and Jì Kāng (季康),
only know to vaguely call it 'fate,'
without discerning why fate is as it is.
How is this different from seeing millet in a granary
but not knowing it was obtained through cultivation?
Or seeing fine silk in a chest
but not recognizing it was made on a loom?
Mǎ Qiān (馬遷) lamented the discrepancy in retribution,
accumulating doubts without resolution.
Fàn Pāng (范滂) was perplexed by the appropriateness of good and evil,
harboring indignation without relief.
All of them saw the stream but did not trace the source,
saw one aspect but not the other.
Only by observing the scriptures and treatises of the Buddhist school
can one fully comprehend their beginning and end.
The retribution for good and evil
extends its branches and offshoots across a thousand leaves.
The destiny of differing fortunes
illuminates its roots through ten thousand ages.
It clarifies the comings and goings of the six realms
and reveals the calamities and blessings of the three existences.
Thus, we know that though the body perishes, karma does not decay,
and though a person dies, the spirit is reborn.
Some are virtuous and sagely yet suffer past calamities,
like the Sixfold Penetrations lacking food suitable for their palate.
Some are animals yet bear residual blessings,
like a quadruped carrying a wish-fulfilling jewel.
Since actions are not uniformly the same,
the resulting retribution is truly manifold.
Karma differs according to the mind,
and retribution varies like faces.
Examining their minds,
some were deluded first and recovered later;
some had a beginning but no end;
some were habitually evil and never repented;
some were purely good and always exalted;
some performed meritorious deeds while also incurring faults;
some had meager blessings but profound wisdom;
some had similar crimes but different circumstances;
some had distinct merits but common aspirations.
Therefore, their retribution
includes those who weep first and then laugh;
those who gain something and then fear its loss;
those who are humble in youth and meet a bad end;
those who start glorious and end auspiciously;
those who maintain integrity but die young;
those who behave ignobly but are rich;
those who commit the same crime but receive different punishments;
those who possess equal virtues but different ranks.
Karma is manifold and intertwined,
and its fruits are fully repaid and meticulously detailed.
It is like a painter applying colors to a canvas,
or a mirror reflecting the beauty or ugliness of a person.
Destiny summons six seals,
like Jì Zǐ’s (季子) eloquent persuasion.
Karma attracts ten thousand gold,
like Zhū Gōng’s (朱公) financial strategy.
To obtain high office as easily as picking something up
is due to the assistance of past causes.
To be accomplished in ritual and music yet suffer poverty
is due to the lack of past blessings.
Many followed to read and study treatises, but only Zhāng Wén (張文) enjoyed the glory.
Many lectured on poetry side by side, but Kuāng Dǐng (匡鼎) alone attained a high position.
Some worked diligently and meritoriously, yet their salaries did not reach Jiè Tuī (介推).
Some deserved punishment for their faults and grievances, yet Yǒng Chǐ (雍齒) was awarded a peerage first.
Wéi Xián’s (韋賢) classical scholarship was far superior to a legacy of gold.
Zhào Yī’s (趙壹) literary works
were not as good as a purse full of money.
Is this a difference in功業 (gōngyè, achievements/karma)?
It is due to the distinction in past karma.
Some have small talent yet hold great responsibility;
the prime minister may have no outstanding achievements.
Some have profound principles yet humble status;
Kǒng (孔) and Mò (墨) suffered the humiliation of being unsettled.
There are also those whose virtue and position are both eminent,
like Yuán Kǎi (元凱) in the courts of Táng Yú (唐虞).
Talent and destiny are equally prosperous,
like Fù (傅) and Lǚ (呂) entrusted with important matters.
If both causes are cultivated,
then both are achieved.
Conversely,
if only one karma is cultivated,
then its partiality is like that.
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) released prisoners and became prime minister.
Lǐ Sī (李斯) became prime minister and was executed.
Fàn Suī (范睢) was first humiliated and then honored.
Dèng Tōng (鄧通) began rich and ended starving.
It is not that they were initially inarticulate and later eloquent,
nor were they foolish in the past and wise now.
It is because the fruit matured and prosperity arrived;
because blessings ended and adversity ensued.
If one says that Zǎi Pǐ (宰嚭) ruined Wǔ Xú (伍胥),
and it was not due to past calamity;
or that Wáng Líng (王陵) saved Zhāng Cāng (張倉),
and it had nothing to do with past blessings—
this is seeing the immediate condition but not knowing the underlying cause,
and thus has the fault of limited insight.
If one says that karma bound one to a good office without remembering the grace of joint ascent,
or that fate aligned with a benevolent wind,
without being ashamed of the benefit of ‘coming to life’—
this is knowing the cause but not recognizing the condition,
and thus has the sin of ingratitude.
If one comprehends both principles and abandons both burdens,
how could advancing virtue and cultivating karma be hindered?
When good seeds are sown in spring,
they rely on summer rain to thrive and grow.
When good causes are cultivated in the past,
they are sparked and activated by present conditions.
A barren and uncultivated land receives rich moisture.
A poor and causeless scholar meets a bright era.
The principles of cause and condition are detailed in various scriptures and treatises.
They are encountered everywhere and expand,
all belonging to this category.
If one only sees one aspect and not the other,
the arising of faults and burdens will harm one’s virtue.
According to what the Buddhist scriptures clarify,
karma, both good and bad,
can be definite or indefinite.
The retribution of calamity and blessing
can be transferable or non-transferable.
In terms of virtue or fault,
only transferable karma can be averted.
Whether wise or foolish,
definite destiny cannot be changed.
When great good accumulates, disaster dissipates.
When many evils are full, blessings vanish.
This is an inevitable principle, trustworthy and unwavering.
It is like medicine overcoming illness,
or water extinguishing a fire.
A huge dike dams a trickling stream;
a sharp axe fells a morning mushroom.
However, if the illness has reached the vital organs,
good medicine sometimes cannot save.
If fire rages across plains,
a drop of water certainly cannot quench it.
The trees of Dènglín (鄧林) cannot be exhausted by a single blade.
The currents of the Cháng Jiāng (長江) cannot be blocked by one clod of earth.
Great virtue can cover minor flaws;
minor merit is insufficient to compensate for great faults.
Engraving stone is difficult;
destroying decay is easy.
When karma is weak, its retribution is not firm.
When conduct is firm, its fruit is definite.
Not firm, thus it can be changed.
Definite, thus it is difficult to alter.
The difficulty of changing [karma] is why
three chants quieted the waves of the vast sea.
The peril of immovability
is why the four fruits encountered harm from evil persons.
Liú Kūn (劉琨), a minor worthy,
caused a counter-wind to extinguish fire.
Táng Yáo (唐堯), a great sage,
suffered floods inundating the hills.
Judging by this,…”
not enough to confuse.
Jìn Wén (晉文) increased his virtue,
exterminated the giant snake at the roadside.
Sòng Jǐng (宋景) spoke out,
repelled the ominous star from the sky.
These are matters of uncertain outcome.
Zhū Wén (邾文) thought little of himself but benefited the people,
had virtue but received no response.
Chǔ Zhāo (楚昭) invited disaster but relinquished blessings,
spoke well but met a tragic end.
These are matters of predetermined fate.
Some share the same evil but experience different consequences;
some have equal goodness but receive different rewards.
All these are results of past causes.
Why be surprised at them in a single lifetime?
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"A small-minded person does not know the Mandate of Heaven and is not in awe of it."
He also said,
"Without knowing fate, one cannot be a Jūnzǐ (君子)."
What the Buddha calls "karma"
is what the Ru (儒) call "fate."
Though the words differ, the underlying principle converges;
they can be discussed together.
Fate is tied to karma,
karma arises from humans.
Humans are endowed with fate for their success and failure;
fate varies in its richness or meagerness according to karma.
The richness or meagerness of fate is none other than what one brings upon oneself.
Is it not misguided to blame Heaven and complain about superiors?
The Shī (詩) says,
"The calamities of the common people
do not descend from Heaven."
The Zhuàn (傳) says,
"Calamity and blessing have no gate,
it is only humans who invite them."
This means
Heaven cannot be pushed aside and blamed; the responsibility lies with humans.
Mèng Kē (孟軻) sought to serve Lǔ (魯),
but did not resent Zāng Cāng's (臧倉) obstruction.
Zhòng Yóu (仲由) served Jì (季),
but felt no anger at Bó Liáo's (伯寮) slander.
This is to say that humans cannot be blamed, and the responsibility is shifted to Heaven.
Although their words differ, their ultimate meaning is not dissimilar.
To summarize,
they both lead to advancing virtue,
disciplining oneself, and admonishing others,
to encourage a spirit of diligent effort.
To delight in Heaven and know fate,
and to dispel the sorrowful accusations.
Therefore, internally, one diligently performs the work of overcoming fate;
externally, one widely promotes the virtue of non-contention.
Above, there are no faults of blaming Heaven;
below, there are no burdens of blaming others.
To act in moderation and harmony,
this is where it lies.
Those of old who were skilled in the Way,
did they not engage in this?
Previously, when I first heard Buddhist scriptures, my belief was not firm.
Restricted by what I saw and heard,
I doubted what was beyond sight and hearing.
I considered the talk of past causes and future effects
to be like Zhuāng Zhōu's (莊周) fables.
The discussions of heaven above and earth below
were similar to Xiāng Rú's (相如) "nothingness."
Seeing evil doers escape the net of justice,
they committed wrongs without being punished.
Hearing of loyal and upright people meeting misfortune,
I regarded goodness lightly and felt no encouragement.
How profound this confusion was!
But knowing karma, it is not so.
Indeed, the Jūnzǐ (君子) who understands karma is selfless and entrusts himself to fate.
They admire the pure virtue of saints and sages,
and uphold the noble conduct of gold and jade.
They are not distressed by dwelling in a humble lane,
and forget about the competition for fame and profit.
Thus, they complete the remaining karma of the past,
and initiate future long-lasting blessings.
They do not care for the scorn and slander of the common crowd,
how could they seek praise and commendation from their village?
When planting, one does not see its growth,
but in time it becomes a great tree.
When grinding, one does not see its loss,
yet eventually its thickness wears away.
The immediate retribution for good and evil
is close in time but not yet ripe.
The fruit of good and ill fortune from past lives
requires the full span of years before it manifests.
It is like sowing grain to produce sweetness,
one does not sow in the morning and harvest in the evening.
Caltrops produce thorns,
they also sprout in spring and bear fruit in autumn.
Those who eat their fill without tilling
do so because of surplus grain from previous years.
Those who are rich and long-lived without being virtuous
do so because of old blessings from a past life.
The Way of Heaven has no favorites or strangers;
human karma has its ebb and flow.
From this, by inferring the Mandate of Heaven,
one can dispel doubts and confusion.
If, regarding the classics of Yú (虞), Xià (夏), Shāng (商), and Zhōu (周),
and the words of Huáng (黃), Lǎo (老), Kǒng (孔), and Mò (墨),
the Way is applied only to one lifetime,
and the words do not extend to three lives,
then there are six points of confusion.
There would be no way to explain them.
If one shows the benefits of doing good,
referring to titles, rewards, and fame,
and enumerates the harms of doing evil,
clarifying shame, disgrace, and punishment.
However, for those who shun rewards and hide their fame,
what benefit is there for them?
As for shameless scoundrels,
they would not suffer its harm.
How can this suffice as a deterrent or encouragement?
This is the first point of confusion.
If it is said that Heaven grants a hundred blessings to the good,
and that the spirits visit six extremes upon the immoral.
However, Bó Niú (伯牛), virtuous in conduct, suffered illness.
Did Heaven hate his goodness?
Dào Zhí (盜蹠), violent and brutal, suffered no calamity.
Did the spirits favor his evil?
Why are blessings and misfortunes so indiscriminately distributed?
This is the second point of confusion.
If it is said that sins perish with the body,
and merits decay along with it,
what good fortune can be discussed for goodness?
What calamity for evil should be warned against?
If retribution for good and evil
is truly real and not nonexistent.
Yǐ (夷) ate mountain ferns and died of hunger,
where was the blessing bestowed upon him?
Shí (石) ate human livers and died of old age,
when did he receive his calamity?
Why is there no retribution for good and evil?
This is the third point of confusion.
If it is said that calamities and blessings come from one's ancestors,
and misfortunes and good fortune extend to one's descendants.
Examining past records,
it is not necessarily always so.
The descendants of Bó Zōng (伯宗) and Yáng Xī (羊肸)
were exterminated in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
The descendants of Qìng Fù (慶父) and Shū Yá (叔牙)
flourished in the Lǔ (魯) state.
How could this be due to ancestors?
This is the fourth point of confusion.
If it is said that in observing good and evil,
Heaven sometimes errs,
and thus bestows blessings and inflicts disasters without equality upon the earth below.
However, how could the clear Mandate of Heaven be dark in matters of reward and punishment?
Would one actually say the Way of Heaven is inferior to the system of kings?
This is the fifth point of confusion.
If it is said that calamities and blessings are not invited by humans,
and good and evil have no retribution in the future.
Yet the hundred kings rewarded good and punished wickedness,
and the Six Classics praised virtue and condemned transgression.
Then these would be empty encouragements with no benefit, and arbitrary warnings with no harm.
Why value Kǒng Qiū's (孔丘) vast teachings?
Why blame Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) for burning books?
This is the sixth point of confusion.
Therefore, if the results of good and evil deeds,
and the hidden and manifest aspects of calamity and blessing,
are confined to a single lifetime,
and not extended through three lives,
then its principles are narrow and not expansive.
How can one clarify human confusion?
The prevention of evil is incomplete,
the guidance towards good is largely deficient.
Its meaning is still shallow,
its benefit to the people is still slight.
Compared to the ten strengths' profound words and the three vehicles' wondrous dharma,
saving all sentient beings from the burning house,
and navigating the six conveyances across the sea of suffering,
the disparity in height is
like a small mound compared to Kūnlún (崑崙),
the difference in depth is
like a puddle compared to the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) rivers.
How can they be spoken of in the same breath?
Of old, Vimalakīrti's (維摩詰) clear understanding
and Śāriputra's (舍利弗) keen eloquence
are detailed in the sūtras and commentaries;
they can be compared.
They are sufficient to surpass Xiàng Tuō (項託) and transcend Kǒng Qiū (孔丘),
outstrip Lǐ Lǎo (李老) and exceed Xǔ Yóu (許由),
subdue Mò Dí (墨翟) and crush Zhuāng Zhōu (莊周),
engulf the hundred schools and encompass the nine streams.
Nothing recorded in books can compare to them.
Nevertheless, they received from various doctrines without destroying the correct faith.
Although they understood worldly classics, they always delighted in the Buddhadharma.
They revered Śākyamuni (釋迦) as their teacher and wholeheartedly embraced his excellent guidance.
Did they not recognize the superiority of the Way and look up to it with admiration?
Hézūn.
The cautious stray from the Dao.
Why abandon evil and pursue good, thereby giving rise to discriminative thought?
Furthermore, they complain that the Buddha's teachings have too many beginnings and ends.
Discussing emptiness and speaking of existence are self-contradictory.
This is the Buddha challenging sentient beings.
Why not simply explain one kind of Dharma?
This is what the teaching of perverse emptiness says.
True emptiness is not so.
If one understands the principle of emptiness and existence,
how could one utter such words?
These are already wrong analogies and fallacious arguments.
Fearing that they will mislead future generations and increase heterodox views,
I will briefly express what I have heard and try to discuss it, saying:
As for things like dreams, illusions, echoes, and bubbles,
there is no single phenomenon that is not like this.
They encompass all phenomena and embrace everything.
Superior individuals observe them to attain sageliness.
The most sagely embody them and uniquely transcend.
Great floods reach the sky yet do not drown them.
Great winds flatten mountains yet do not scatter them.
They possess the six supernormal powers and are self-sovereign.
They transcend the three realms and roam freely.
However, principle does not enlighten itself; right perception illuminates it.
The mind does not quiet itself; disciplined cultivation calms it.
Obstacles do not vanish on their own; antidotes eradicate them.
Virtues do not complete themselves; diligent practice makes them abundant.
Once the six defilements are removed, true suchness can manifest.
If the three obstacles are not extinguished, Bodhí is extremely distant.
Therefore, ultimate truth is free from the characteristics of defilement and purity.
Conventional truth establishes the rules of right and wrong.
Pointing to things necessarily relies on differentiation.
Discussing Dharma, how can it be suitable for confusion?
The six Pāramitās cannot be acts that lead to suffering.
The three poisons cannot be bridges to transcend the world.
Falling into a valley is difficult without plummeting.
Rushing into fire, how can one not burn?
Yáo and Shùn cannot be compared to the ignorant and tyrannical.
Yōu and Lì cannot be equated with the sagely Yáo.
The loyal and virtuous cannot be banished to the wilderness.
The treacherous and sycophantic cannot be promoted in a bright court.
One cannot turn white into black.
One cannot make day into night.
One cannot allow evil to harm righteousness.
One cannot compare a Fèng to an Xiāo.
How can one equate cause and effect with a rabbit's horn?
Or liken merit and demerit to a turtle's hair?
Although they cite the wonderful words of Mahāyāna,
they do not grasp the true essence of the wonder.
Speaking it aloud may sound similar,
but applying it in the mind is different.
What is the difference?
The correct Dharma uses emptiness to eliminate greed.
Perverse teachings use emptiness to indulge one's desires.
The wise observe emptiness to remove anger.
The deluded discuss emptiness to wreak havoc.
Those who have attained realize emptiness and gain wisdom and liberation.
Those who are deluded grasp emptiness and act crazed and rebellious.
Great beings embody emptiness and advance in virtue.
Petty individuals speak of emptiness and regress in goodness.
The differences are like this.
How can they be the same in essence?
This is truly due to misusing correct words to generate perverse attachments.
A fine horse treading water labors in vain.
A boat ascending a mountain toils without progress.
Is it that the fine horse or the boat are not good?
It is simply that treading water and ascending a mountain are contrary uses.
Reading the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra (淨名) on the absence of characteristics while neglecting cultivation.
Reciting Zhuāngzhōu's words on the equality of things while indulging passions and desires.
This is no different from spurring a four-horse chariot upstream,
or rowing a square boat up a slope.
Hoping to catch up to Zàofǔ's long drive,
or wishing to rival the people of Yuè in navigating waters.
Is this not difficult?
Vimalakīrti (淨名) possessed lofty virtue.
Zhuāngzhōu was free from the burdens of craving and desire.
Hence, one knows that the discourse on emptiness that breaks all views
is contrary to the path of non-action.
The profound essence of the wondrous Dao
is to clarify emptiness based on all existing phenomena.
Upon encountering the real, one knows it is provisional.
Likewise, from the diverse, one illuminates the identical.
What is it like?
For example, observing a wide mirror from the side,
or gazing down at a clear pond.
All phenomena brilliantly appear to the eye, visible but without substantial nature.
Born from conditions, they come into being and form.
Separated from conditions, they lose their substance.
Water meets cold and ice solidifies.
Ice meets warmth and its hardness is lost.
All that arises from conditions exists.
Even if greatly existing, what reality does it have?
Therefore, heaven and earth and I are all empty.
I and all myriad things are one.
Bodhí cannot be said to exist.
How much less so sentient beings and all techniques?
Thus, observing objects, they are not objects.
Taking from the body, it is not the body.
Adorning the sky, all is illusory.
Firmly on the ground, lofty but not true.
Discussions exhaust reason yet there is nothing to say.
Guests fill the hall yet there is no one.
Beautiful colors surpass the world yet there is no beauty.
Precious treasures fill the eyes yet there is no value.
Good and evil are different paths yet not two.
Sages and ordinary beings are different ranks yet always equal.
To trace the main purport of the Sūtras and Śāstras:
From conditions, it clarifies non-existence.
From conditioned arising, it argues non-nothingness.
Things exist but have no wondrous reality.
Meaning is empty but not a great void.
No person is like the silence of a closed door.
No view is like the foolishness of facing a wall.
No speech is like the mouth of a golden statue.
No body is like the body of a thorny monkey.
No movement is like the appearance of mountains and peaks.
No distinction is like the flattery of echoing others.
No truth is like a fish-eye jewel.
No reality is like a letter tied to a goose's foot.
Wealth compared to dream-wealth is no different.
Form compared to illusory form, how does it differ?
Yī Dùn's wealth equals Yuán Xiàn's possessions.
The beauties of Sònglǐ are comparable to those of Píngchéng.
Those who know the Dao realize emptiness and are free from bondage.
Those with worldly sentiments are attached to existence and constantly constrained.
People and karmic retribution are not existent.
Karmic retribution follows people and is not non-existent.
Heaven is like heaven yet not illusory.
Hell is like hell yet empty.
This is not like Yáng Xióng falsely calling a jade tree,
or Màn Dū wrongly seeing a divine abode.
How can one take empty words and go against the meaning?
And cite plants and trees to compare them?
The treasures of night pearls and emeralds,
The beauty of Nánwēi and Máoqiáng,
Everyone sees their existence and gives rise to love.
Who can embody their emptiness and remain untainted?
The smallest grievance, like a scorpion's sting,
Or the enmity of a green fly and brocade pattern,
No one fails to cling to their appearance and give rise to indignation.
Few can compare them to emptiness and feel no resentment.
They solely believe that despicable conduct is empty and needs no戒 (precepts).
Good Dharma is empty and needs no observance.
The three afflictions should be abandoned but are not repented.
The five virtues should be cultivated but are instead abandoned.
They do not observe emptiness to dispel burdens.
They merely grasp emptiness to abandon goodness.
Is this the profound meaning of Vimalakīrti (淨名)'s non-duality?
Or the mysterious purport of Zhuāngzhōu's equality of things?
Great indeed is the sage's embodiment of emptiness!
Attesting to the fundamental stillness of all things,
Knowing the four great elements are provisional,
Viewing Xīshī as a public latrine,
Comparing southern gold to broken tiles.
The five desires cannot disturb their mind.
The four Māras cannot change their elegance.
The sun of wisdom shines brightly and virtue is abundant.
Afflictions are removed daily and faults are few.
Even with hands and feet severed, they have no regret.
Begging for head and eyes, they can abandon them.
The eight worldly dharmas do not give rise to dualistic characteristics.
All things are viewed as a single horse.
Thus, they can attain unsurpassed wisdom and become Sarvajña. If one understands its principle, liberation is like this.
Those who misunderstand its purport suffer such faults.
How can one commit wrong without fear and uphold evil as right?
Indeed, seeing a boat and seeing water are neither ultimate truth.
Yet to cross a great river, one cannot do without a boat.
The diseased body and the nature of medicine are equally empty.
Yet people die from illness and illness is removed by medicine.
Rhinoceros horn and zhèn bird feathers are like bubbles.
Yet those who drink zhèn die, and those who take rhino horn live.
Plain water and strong liquor are both not truly existent.
Yet juice does not confuse people, while alcohol can cause trouble.
Loyalty and rebellion are all like echoes.
Yet rebels are punished, and the loyal are rewarded.
The nature of sin and merit is equal and non-dual.
Yet merit is achieved through goodness, and calamity is caused by evil.
Good and evil dharmas are equally empty and without characteristics.
Yet good dharmas assist the path, and evil dharmas create obstacles.
Thus, one knows that the true nature of all phenomena is of a single suchness.
Yet it does not prevent there being myriad differences within the Dharma of causality.
The two gates of emptiness and existence do not contradict each other.
The two truths, ultimate and conventional, converge to the same destination.
If one says that Hīnayāna (小乘) speaks of sin and merit,
and Mahāyāna (大乘) has no words for right and wrong,
it is like the distinct paths of Hú and Yuè,
or like spears and shields resisting each other.
Even a child would be ashamed of such contradiction.
How could a sage behave indecisively?
This is truly due to hearing on the road and speaking on the way.
Thus leading to erroneous judgment and poor understanding.
If one broadly investigates and deeply reflects,
doubts will surely be resolved and confusion cured.
Reverently, I consider the Ten Powers, the Hero of the World, the Supreme Compassionate Father.
His words are never untrue, His compassion is never not universal.
No characteristic is not detached, no sight is not seen.
No virtue is not complete, no fault is not removed.
No good is not encouraged, no evil is not deterred.
Anointed with perfume, He is not pleased; cut by a knife, He is not angry.
He does not love obedience, nor hate defiance.
His blessings and wisdom are perfect, with nothing left over.
Afflictions are completely exhausted, with no remaining trace.
He rescues the drowned from the three realms and enlightens the deaf and blind of the four births.
Emptiness and existence are both illuminated to mutually assist each other.
Truth and convention are both fully understood and upheld.
The aim is to prescribe medicine according to the illness.
One should not deviate from the middle path and cling to a partial view.
As for the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) teachings, the One Vehicle (Yīchéng), and the Eight Sections (Bābù) of Prajñā (Bōrě), which are the pinnacle of sacred wisdom
and the head of Mahāyāna (Dàchéng),
none fail to extensively describe the benefits of upholding them
and deeply enumerate the faults of slandering them.
The sūtra also says:
"Deeply believe in cause and effect, and do not slander Mahāyāna."
How can it be said that the principle of Mahāyāna is entirely without cause and effect?
If one takes form as the basis for doing good,
then that goodness is not yet refined.
If one sees form and then ceases evil,
then that cessation will be followed by recurrence.
If one awakens to the nature of goodness as quiescent and unconditioned,
if one understands the essence of evil as empty, then what is there to cease?
This enables the three obstacles (sānzhàng) to melt away like ice and become quiescent,
and all myriad virtues (wàndé) to gather like clouds and fill all space.
Wisdom is like the ocean,
not to be measured by a single oyster shell.
The Way surpasses humans and devas,
how can it be fathomed by a small tube?
To liken it to a Táowù (Táowù),
and measure it with foolish shortcomings,
is it not erroneous?
As for those who speak of emptiness and indulge their desires,
they cannot be without suffering.
If pain and illness afflict them, they cannot sleep peacefully.
If knives and saws injure them, their bodies are not complete.
If they do not eat all day, they suffer hunger.
If they have no fur coat to ward off winter, they suffer cold.
If so, then the karma (yè) that brings suffering,
how can it be lightly regarded and not avoided?
As for the five blessings (wǔfú) and the six extremes (liùjí),
human emotions cannot reconcile them.
Thus, one in poverty thinks of prosperity,
one in danger seeks peace.
One afflicted by illness wishes for recovery,
one in sorrow envies joy.
One loves longevity and dreads early death,
one glorifies worldly prosperity and is ashamed of bodily disfigurement.
When joy comes, one smiles happily,
when suffering strikes, one sighs in worry.
How can one be indiscriminate about good and evil and not cultivate the causes of blessings?
Observing the diverse endowments of the myriad people,
they are indeed of a thousand types and differing ranks.
Some enjoy a long life and more,
some die young and do not reach it.
Some wear simple cloth and are unharmed,
some wear thick padded clothes and still feel the cold.
Some rely on grass and earth and are peaceful,
some dwell on beds and mattresses and suffer from wind-damp.
Some recover without treatment,
some do not recover even with treatment.
Some are without skill but their bodies are healthy,
some are good at self-care but still fall ill.
On the surface, their forms all have hair and skin.
Inside the skin, how do their organs differ?
All contain blood and flesh, connected by sinews and supported by bones.
Why is one long-lived and one short-lived?
Why is one plump and one gaunt?
What spirit do they receive that makes one substantial?
What energy do they receive that makes one deficient?
The deficient one does not solely make its body from dust and dirt,
nor does the substantial one exclusively make its body from metal and stone.
It is not necessarily true that those who live long have medical skills,
or that those with short lives have no knowledge of the Dao (Dào).
How can it be said that it solely depends on self-care and not on karma (yè)?
There are also those who die young in the womb,
or infants who fall ill.
Their joy and anger have not yet fully developed, their desires have not yet opened.
They have not yet experienced the cold and heat,
nor have they been withered by sorrow.
How do they die young?
Where does illness come from?
Then, the reason for this,
is it not due to past karma (yè)?
As for the two rulers, Hàn Zhāodì (Hàn Zhāo Āi) and Āidì (Āi),
and the two emperors, Wèi Wénmíng (Wèi Wénmíng) and Míngdì (Míng),
some ascended to the heavens before thirty (sānjiǔ),
others departed the world barely past forty (wǔbā).
Prognosticators gathered like clouds,
but only to praise Lǐ Bùwèi's (Lǐ shì) spirit.
Magicians were like a forest,
but could not save Cāngshū (Cāngshū) from dying.
Kings did not lack medicine,
and shamans and doctors did not conceal their arts.
Why did they not recover from illness?
Why could their short lives not be prolonged?
Is it not that the retribution was received according to karma (yè), which medical arts could not remedy?
However, sūtras praise the merit of giving medicine,
and the Buddha (Fó) extols the virtue of the King of Physicians (Yīwáng).
Kǒng Gōngmíng (Kǒng Gōngmíng) had rules for prudent care in illness,
and Lǎozǐ (Lǎozǐ) had principles for preserving life.
Those who do not believe in karma (yè) are deluded,
and those who do not follow doctors are also confused.
One who can discern the depth of cause and effect (yīnguǒ),
will then understand the efficacy or inefficacy of medicine.
It can be investigated with wisdom,
but is difficult to fully express in writing.
As for Gōngmíng (Gōngmíng) who discerned diseases and Biǎnquè (Biǎnquè) who removed illnesses,
Guō Pú (Guō Pú) from Hédōng (Hédōng) and Huà Tuó (Huà Tuó) from Qiáojùn (Qiáojùn),
Wú Pǔ (Wú Pǔ) from Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng) and Fán Ā (Fán Ā) from Péngchéng (Péngchéng):
some averted misfortune and brought good fortune,
some stopped illness and brought harmony.
How can one not believe in the benefits of medical skills?
However, Jǐngchún (Jǐngchún) knew the day of his execution,
but could not prevent the execution from happening.
Gōngmíng (Gōngmíng) knew the year his life would end,
but could not prevent the year from ending.
Biǎnquè (Biǎnquè) and Huà Tuó (Huà Tuó) could not prevent their parents from dying.
Wú Pǔ (Wú Pǔ) and Fán Ā (Fán Ā) could not prevent their own demise.
How can one not believe that length of life has its karma (yè)?
Doctors gather due to karma (yè), medicine comes together due to conditions (yuán).
Doctors indeed have merit, medicine is not without value.
For a fatal illness, even a sage cannot cure it.
A curable illness awaits a doctor before it heals.
The soul returns due to karma (yè),
thus a corpse may encounter medicine for rebirth.
Life ends due to karma (yè),
thus a divine doctor becomes a handful of earth for a coffin.
The length or brevity of life, the comfort or suffering of the body,
the success or failure of encounters, beauty or ugliness, swiftness or slowness,
a thousand varieties and ten thousand forms, all are presided over by karma (yè).
The three realms (sānjiè) and six paths (liùqù) are where one dwells according to karma (yè).
Myriad plants are insentient,
thus their beauty or ugliness is not related to karmic retribution (yèbào).
The four births (sìshēng) have life,
thus their causes and conditions (yīnyuán) differ from grass and trees.
Axes chop wood without alarm,
but knives and staffs inflicted on people cause fear.
Gourds and claws are tied and not eaten,
but feathers and fur are eaten and run wild.
To compare sentient beings to the ignorant,
why draw inappropriate analogies?
Briefly speaking of emptiness and existence, it is all guided by the karma (yè) of the mind.
Earlier, it sang of constant life,
now it displays the true Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).
Hīnayāna (Xiǎochéng) takes dependent retribution (yībào) as karmic existence,
Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) takes all phenomena as created by consciousness.
According to illusory karma (yè), heaven and earth are manifested.
Following deluded mind, the grass of consciousness appears.
It is like seeing sky-flowers with clouded eyes,
or like a dream manifesting birth and aging.
If one awakens to the karma (yè) of the mind,
then one only hears the Buddha-Dharma (Fódào).
Originally, Hīnayāna (Xiǎochéng) and Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) are like elementary school and university.
In youth, one is only taught reading and arithmetic;
in adulthood, one is broadly educated in rites and music.
One begins ignorant and numerous like ox hair,
but ends up outstanding and rare like a unicorn's horn.
This is the sequence of instruction;
how can there be differences to be stripped away?
Indeed, because the roots of sentient beings (zhòngshēng) are sharp or dull,
therefore the teachings of the sages are sometimes gradual, sometimes sudden.
Some lead to the profound and distant,
some advance by inches.
Though a hundred considerations lead to one goal,
different paths can also lead to conflicting theories.
Then there are those who cling to the empty gate (kōngmén) and oppose the teaching,
who discuss Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) and slander Hīnayāna (Xiǎo).
The Buddha (Fó) does not contend with sentient beings (zhòngshēng), sentient beings (zhòngshēng) themselves do not understand.
It is like a dark room without a candle,
or like traveling at night without understanding the dawn.
Thus, they contend and wrangle,
competing over right and wrong and causing disturbance.
How is this different from plucking lotus flowers from treetops,
or searching for Wú (Wú) and Chǔ (Chǔ) in Yān (Yān) and Zhào (Zhào)?
Is it not erroneous?
One water cannot flavor a soup.
One piece of wood cannot build a house.
One garment cannot fit all bodies.
One medicine cannot cure all diverse illnesses.
One color cannot make an embroidery.
One sound cannot harmonize a zither.
One word cannot encourage all good deeds.
One precept cannot prevent many faults.
How can one wonder at the difference between gradual and sudden,
and insist on a single Dharma (Fǎ) gate?
The many types of Dharma (Fǎ) gates
are like the different efficacies of medicines.
To relieve cold, warming things are used.
To remove heat, cold medicines should be abundant.
Some are particularly suitable for dispelling dampness,
some are especially needed for stopping wind.
One cannot use different medicines for the same illness,
nor the same medicine for different illnesses.
If one guards the stump (shǒu zhū) and is bound,
one can only reach understanding by adapting to change.
How can one cling to a single path and criticize others, starting conflict within it?
The three times (sānshì) cause and effect (yīnguǒ) are not deceived by the Buddha (Fó).
The Ten Powers (Shílì) advise and warn, one should not doubt upon hearing.
What is advised should be cultivated,
what is warned against should be avoided.
Repressing ordinary human emotions that one indulges in.
to act according to the wishes of the holy and wise.
How can one contravene what the sūtras and treatises clearly state,
make judgments based on one's own subjective opinions,
and then claim that good and evil are utterly empty, without benefit or harm?
Truly, with a clear Dharma-eye, there is no Dharma that is not thoroughly understood.
With a broad and long tongue, there is no word that is not true.
When it analyzes existence,
a single hair becomes myriad.
When it equates with emptiness,
all phenomena are one.
It guards against the arising of errors of nihilism and eternalism,
combining emptiness and existence to remove afflictions.
That subtle principle of Bodhi
is indeed profound and subtle.
If you are weary of worldly defilements and seek the wisdom of liberation,
you must be cautious and not indulge in negligence.
Those who are not sages will surely meet with misfortune;
those who follow the Dao will ultimately be auspicious.
Do not say you disbelieve;
it is as clear as the brilliant sun.
Preface says:
Indeed,
when ignorant customs create obstacles,
the wondrous scriptures are a boat master.
The greatest among masters
is what is called a Wáng.
Therefore, a Wáng is one who goes forth,
like the hundred rivers flowing into the sea.
The title of Wáng is likened to this.
However, when speaking generally of Wángs,
due to various conditions, there are many types.
Dividing them into two according to principle and phenomena, there are primarily two.
The first refers to those who detail phenomena;
the second refers to those who elucidate principles.
Thus, a Wáng who details phenomena
is an earthly king or a heavenly king.
Their transforming influence lies in phenomena,
and phenomena are limited to the body.
When the body exists, the influence acts;
when the body perishes, the influence ceases.
This is to consider their body externally,
without contemplating their inner consciousness.
Therefore, their transforming influence
is called the outer teaching.
The second refers to those who elucidate principles;
this is a Fǎwáng or a Buddha-enlightened one.
Their transforming influence lies in principles,
and principles reside in the mind.
When the mind exists, the influence acts;
when thoughts cease, the realm is extinguished.
This is to examine one's mind internally,
and not to be conditioned by external objects.
Therefore, their transforming influence
is called the inner teaching.
Thus, to strengthen the body and preserve life
leads to an endless cycle of births;
to renounce life and cast off emotions
leads to the cessation of emotions and quiescent illumination.
This causes the teaching of preserving the form to be uniformly observed across myriad nations,
and the method of refining the mind to be consistent among a thousand sages.
This is how the two teachings, worldly and spiritual, ascend and descend, enter and exit.
The worldly enters into existence and sinks into form,
and the six realms thus continue endlessly.
The spiritual emerges from emptiness and ascends to position,
and the three sages thus prosper and illuminate.
Since the true Dao flowed eastward,
over six hundred years have passed.
To enlighten the ignorant and lead them to faith,
its followers have not been uniform.
There have been two or three instances of despots
who oppressed and massacred monks and destroyed images.
Yet, there have also been many enlightened monarchs who revered the Dao
and erected temples and pagodas.
Such as Wú Wáng, who extensively studied Buddhist sages
and understood where heavenly and human beings returned;
and Sòng Jūn, who recounted Buddhist virtues
and clarified the reverence of wise officials at court.
As for other obscure matters,
they are not worth elaborating upon.
Therefore, this preface describes auspicious signs of manifest traces,
and also elaborates on the splendid virtues in the eulogies composed.
By surveying these according to their categories, how can one not illuminate the mind-nature?
Now, the Dao by which humans are established
is called Rén (仁) and Yì (義).
However, Rén and Yì have a foundation,
which is called Dào (道) and Dé (德).
In ancient times, at the end of the Jī Zhōu (姬周) dynasty, there was a great sage called Fó (佛).
He was the crown prince of Bái Jìng (白淨), the Shì (釋) King of Tiānzhú (天竺).
His maternal clan name
was Qiú Tán (裘曇).
He upheld the spiritual lineage with great inheritance,
relying on the lingering fragrance of his sagely predecessors.
He absorbed the profound transformations of centrality and harmony,
and was endowed with the vastness of Bái Jìng.
Born from his mother's right flank,
he could speak when young.
He truly esteemed the heavenly rank for not being added,
and indeed found sufficiency in having no need for worldly emoluments.
Therefore, he was always vigilant in the evenings in the upper echelons, like a sojourner in the purple court.
He felt a deep yearning in the儲 Gōng (儲宮), desiring to soar beyond the mortal realm.
Soon after, he ascended high and surveyed the countryside,
opening the imperial gates on all four sides,
and observing the sufferings three times.
The poets' inspiring words spurred him on,
and he accepted them willingly, without opposition.
He sought the great Dào from those who possessed it,
lamenting that the current situation caused such delay.
Thus, at dawn, he embarked on a distant journey, dwelling in quiet seclusion.
He shed the heavy treasures of the imperial heir,
hoping to rise lightly without dependence.
He cast off the splendid ornaments of the dragon robes,
and exchanged them for the coarse garments of the impoverished cliffs.
His accompanying retinue turned back from the precipice.
Thereupon, he set his will firm as a rock,
and rested in Rén as steadfast as a mountain.
He made his dwelling among variegated flora,
and forged his resolve, making a vow.
He regulated the breath of Ān Bō (安般),
and applied the "ten calculations" to purify his mind.
He discarded the "eight records" of the "four movements,"
and followed the "two conformities" to scrutinize his mind.
He severed the two extremes of "sending" and "receiving,"
and linked the wondrous "one" to the tip of his nose.
He manifested the subtle beginnings of the "three quietudes,"
penetrated the "four contemplations," and merged with emptiness.
The Wǔ Yīn (五陰) moved to the returning abode,
and the Liù Qíng (六情) became empty in the tranquil forest.
He cooled the fires of desire within his Wǔ Nèi (五內),
and expanded the vast mind of the great essence.
He purified his Dé (德) with Bōrě (般若),
and immersed himself in the seven stages, drawing forth the profound.
He sought the hidden fish in the "six extinctions,"
and once the teeth were established, discarded the fish trap.
He abolished the accumulated habits of myriad kalpas,
and achieved innate knowledge in that very year.
He overshadowed the Wǔ Zhuó (五濁) with his brilliance,
and succeeded the Liù Fó (六佛) with a subtle transmission.
Grand was his stature of one Zhàng (丈) and six Chǐ (尺),
his body adorned with a circular aura.
He opened the path of salvation, centered and balanced,
his complexion resplendent like purple gold.
His movements soared through the void,
swift as a fleeting glimpse.
His eight tones emitted fragrant sounds,
his ease and joy spread forth.
He subtly perceived the unmanifested,
thus transcending the six realms.
When his perfect formation was manifested,
his transformations flourished among the Three and Five.
His immeasurable breadth was vast as the great void,
his spirit enveloped the two primary forces.
Simplicity and ease awaited him to take form,
great harmony likened him and called him excellent.
The round stalks symbolized his spiritual tranquility,
the square hexagrams modeled his comprehensive wisdom.
He illuminated the lingering auspiciousness of accumulated blessings,
and, in accordance with the primordial destiny, created.
Sometimes he wove with Dé and Yì,
sometimes he dispersed with a fierce wind.
He knew that forms changed daily,
and hoped that the wondrous master would be inexhaustible.
He was more beautiful than indigo from blue,
and achieved purity through a hundred refinements.
He guided all beings to return to the source,
and uprooted the external barriers of Yáo (堯) and Kǒng (孔).
He spoke of the ultimate with billions,
and covered the ancient texts to establish his doctrine.
He plucked the "three non-existences" of the Dao-practice,
and connected Lǎo (老) and Zhōu (周) as his remote ancestors.
His spiritual transformation manifested in the Xīyù (西域),
like the morning sun rising in the Yáng Gǔ (暘谷).
People looked to his light and followed his path,
just as melodies harmonize with the Gōng (宮) and Shāng (商) notes.
At that time,
Xī Yí (希夷) was distant and remote from the Fú Xī (伏羲) era,
and the divine and wondrous surpassed the Huáng Xuān (皇軒) era.
His profound radiance flourished vaguely through the Zhōu and Táng (唐) dynasties,
and his praises held lingering flavor in Zōu (鄒) and Lǔ (魯).
He can truly be called the chief leader of divine transformations,
the foundational counsel of emperors and kings.
He exceeded the age of "following his heart" and vanished into Níhuán (泥洹).
Indeed, the ultimate person acts at the opportune time and ceases at the opportune time.
Sometimes he hides here and appears there.
His traces vanished in the Sahā world,
and he secretly returned to Wéiwèi (維衛).
The common people, accustomed to the ordinary, were startled by the extraordinary,
and thus filled with notions of existence and extinction.
As for the nature of spiritual awakening,
the "three fruits" withered and perished.
It was like a river overturning,
or a heaven collapsing.
The common people were plunged into the same gloom as eternal night,
the dark currents left behind like a dried-up ford.
The Liù Dù (六度) were stripped away along with the collapsing peaks,
and the Sān Chéng (三乘) unharnessed their reins from the broken axle.
His disciples wept tears of blood and mourned in their hearts,
a hundred spirits held grief and trembled with emotion.
Indeed, when the Dào is lofty, its response is humble;
those who travel widely earn praise from their kin.
Therefore, weeping occurred without being sought;
how could this not be "forgetting the world entirely makes the world forget entirely"?
Although his spiritual throne traversed and spread throughout the six directions,
his chronological influence ended in Chì Xiàn (赤縣).
Therefore, later generations heard of him,
and looked up to his divine form,
but his deeds ceased a thousand years ago.
The Jīhuán (祇洹) has already drifted away and fallen,
the jade trees have also ultimately become overgrown.
The Dào is lost, the man is gone; it is truly too late.
I, Dùn (遁), though untalented, respectfully follow the great Dào,
pursuing the morning sun but failing to reach it,
leaning on the mulberry and elm, but not yet ascending.
My spirit flies to the past, wishing to pay homage again.
So, I took up my brush to evoke antiquity and express my distant thoughts.
Its words are:
The Primordial Supreme is distant indeed!
The Táng (唐) ruled heaven.
Kǒng (孔) also followed Zhōu.
His humble dwelling passed through three transmissions.
Bright, bright is Shìjiā (釋迦),
truly the emperor's precursor.
He responded to the destined time with sagely works,
his transformations melting throughout India.
He nurtured harmony with serenity,
purified by the profound source.
He surpassed worldly kings in his conduct,
leading the central mystery as his lineage.
Grand, grand is his vast model,
displaying the finest qualities of the rounded spirit.
His noble birth was like Kūnlún (崑崙) mountains,
his measure encompassed the great azure.
The great image is rarely glimpsed,
yet he rounded out its brilliance.
The profound sound is rarely struck,
but he articulated it with eight voices.
Resplendent, resplendent is the torch of wisdom,
illuminating my night journey.
People admire his wisdom,
but who knows his mystery?
Looking at him, he soars like clouds,
approaching him, he is also a cloudy ford.
His majesty spreads like summer's heat,
his tenderness like the awakening of spring.
He compares instruments by their form,
but excels at stratagem by his spirit.
When he contracts, he vanishes like smoke;
when he expands, he stretches like a dragon.
He inspires the boats and valleys,
his spiritual energy ever new.
Who works with him in this creation?
He alone operates the potter's wheel.
The "three non-existences" are central to the profound,
billions lead to the distant.
When the two parts are expansive,
the twin wings are canonical.
Filled with precious wonders,
calm with ease and simplicity.
Stored in treasure chests,
truly they are excellent and good.
The excellent and good follow their causes,
thus they are praised and expounded.
Devoting attention to past words,
how could it merely be an amplification?
The sun and moon are truly bright,
their revealing and hiding all-pervasive.
Life is like scattered mist,
dimly arriving, already withered.
The ultimate person fully transforms,
his traces fading with the world.
If we speak of Níhuán,
it is like saying farewell and returning.
His lingering influence covers the six directions,
his fragrance awaits in the central capital.
If the formless image does not exist,
who will awaken the mystery?
With a clear mind, I set down my brush,
hoping to glimpse his profound radiance.
Beyond the six directions of the universe
is not what books and records can explore.
The divine path, in its mysterious way,
how can it be fathomed by those with conventional thoughts?
Therefore, it is said:
What a person knows
is less than what they do not know.
Every time, in ordinary situations,
one wishes to use what cannot be seen
to conclude what cannot yet be understood.
Thus, the well frog boasts of its small dwelling,
and Féngyí boasts of the autumn waters.
This is indeed appropriate.
I have wandered far and wide,
my heart weary of the boundless.
Taking advantage of this quiet leisure,
I again recount various wonders.
Buddhist scriptures record that in the West there is a country,
named Ānyǎng.
It is exceedingly distant and remote,
the path traversing more than the sands of the Gaṅgā.
Only one who is unattached
cannot travel its borders.
Only one who is not swift
how can one reach it quickly?
Its Buddha is called Āmítuó,
which in Jìn language means "Immeasurable Life."
The country has no king's system, no order of titles;
the Buddha is its sovereign,
and the Three Vehicles are its teaching.
Men and women are all born and nurtured within lotus flowers,
without the defilement of gestation.
Residences and palaces
are all made of the seven treasures.
All are naturally suspended constructions,
their design not by human artisans.
Parks, gardens, and ponds
flourish with wondrous splendor.
Birds and beasts soar and sink freely in the depths and groves;
the myriad creatures that dwell there live in their true nature.
The gates of heaven have no panels in the jeweled forests;
jade-like sounds spontaneously harmonize with flutes and pipes.
From the dark sky fall flowers,
and throughout the realm, a divine wind
brushes away the old and brings in the new.
Sweet dew miraculously descends,
sweetening the fragrant breeze,
guiding virtue and spreading fragrance.
Sacred sounds respond with thunderous echoes;
wisdom's grace descends like clouds, pouring forth purity.
The Awakened Father draws them in with precious words;
true people follow the mysterious and abandon frivolous play.
The Five Pāramitās transcend the void and enter non-existence;
Prajñā moves beyond knowledge and emerges from the profound.
All wonders are greatly revealed here,
and divine transformation is thus eternally transmitted.
There are other scriptures and records
that record its beauty.
During the late Five Dynasties period of the Jìn state,
there were those who observed the proper Buddhist precepts,
recited the Āmítuó Sūtra,
vowed to be born in that land,
and did not falter in their sincerity.
When their lives ended, their spirits departed and transformed to that place,
saw the Buddha, gained divine enlightenment, and immediately attained the Way.
I, living in these later times,
am ashamed to be among the remaining traces.
My heart races toward the divine land,
yet it is not something I dare to hope for.
Therefore, I commissioned an artisan
to illustrate and erect a divine stele,
looking up at its lofty design
to examine that which is heavenly.
Verbal praise is insufficient,
so I appended a short eulogy.
Its words are:
The kingly virtue extends outwardly,
the divine path soothes inwardly.
How majestic is the Right Enlightenment,
truly encompassing both founder and teacher.
Peace and stability shine forth,
the central yellow displays its magnificent form.
Tranquility and wisdom intermingle and dissolve,
the three attainments mystically tranquil.
Opening the golden realm,
the distant path is long and winding.
Transforming by divine influence,
awakening to responsive mechanisms.
The Five Pāramitās sharpen conduct,
the six wisdoms refine the subtle.
Emptiness and existence are alike in form,
the profound gate penetrates deeply.
Songs and praises are abundant,
profound meanings accord with the divine.
The mysterious market is vast,
the Three Vehicles thronging.
Concealing the past, modeling the old,
knowing the future, only renewing.
Who lowers the two talents?
Enlightening the ignorant depends on people.
The creator establishes the realm,
clouds form, soaring high.
Purple halls stand like stars,
resplendent palaces are arrayed like constellations.
Jade gates connect the directions,
golden walls open at the corners.
Light tilts toward the morning sun,
beauty flourishes with the dawn's glow.
Divine dikes crisscross,
the nine springs are profoundly deep.
Waves are without traps or forgetfulness,
fish rarely enticed by bait.
The marsh does not supervise,
startled wings shelter in the woods.
Guests drive their retinue,
both burying their scheming hearts.
Sweet dew is profoundly moist,
orchids and irises lend their sound.
Transformation follows the dense clouds,
customs become pure with the wind.
Flowering buds scatter in the sky,
spiritual breezes sweep away the petals.
Jeweled forests resonate,
the eight musical tones perfectly formed.
Precious stones gleam brightly,
lotus flowers bask in the sun.
The flowing water is clear in its purity,
the stamens spread their fragrance.
Hidden splendor subtly shines,
carried and soaring, they come.
Nurturing beauty within the flowers,
forming spiritual, secluded fragrance.
All kinds of transformations,
excellently combining in growth.
Ten thousand ways transform into one,
following the same rule of sitting in oblivion.
Childhood innocence leads to profound attainment,
spiritual transformation is truly long-lasting.
Formerly, I was the Dragon King's awakened seed,
now I wander in dreams.
Suddenly, I ride the divine waves,
taking lofty steps in Vimalakīrti's realm.
Extracting this ethereal essence,
reflecting that serene, empty hall.
Touching all categories, encountering pure convergence,
seeing with the eye, transcending all dualities.
Brahmā and Śakra admire the auspicious assembly,
warding off evil, embracing flowing fragrance.
Great people follow the mysterious path,
the young and lost ascend to the void.
The master, in his comprehensive wisdom, abandons himself,
Śākyamuni enters serene seclusion.
Mílè inherits the divine succession,
holy records preserve his spiritual chapters.
Riding the qian trigram due to the nine-five position,
the dragon flies to Tuṣita Heaven.
The Dharma drum vibrates in the mysterious palace,
its extraordinary sound resonates throughout the three thousand worlds.
Shining, radiant, with a pure form,
sitting in meditation, brilliant on the fragrant lotus.
Vast and bright, lofty aspirations arise,
the eight musical tones flow naturally.
Tranquil wisdom profoundly reaches the subtle,
singing ethereally of the double mystery.
Going through seven times seven eons,
responding to destiny, arriving at the central jewel.
Manifesting this form of four and eight excellences,
shining brilliantly in the flower garden.
Diligently, the mysterious wheel turns,
three times revealing past conditions.
Vimalakīrti embodies divine nature,
surpassing transformation, illuminating the gate of opportunity.
Neither possible nor impossible,
wandering into form and name.
If people stir, I become agitated;
if people are calm, my energy is peaceful.
How can tranquility and agitation be merely form and shadow?
Form and shadow respond to the mind's intentions.
Mysterious rhymes follow the ten sages,
soaring and contending with the four heroes.
Forgetting expectation, encountering Nǚshǒu, diligently praising life and death.
Profound harmony breathes forth pure energy,
giving rise to this child destined for the world.
Ascending the platform, uttering spring hymns,
lofty aspirations following distant traces.
Riding the void, sensing spiritual awakening,
unfurling the net, inspiring the ignorant.
Outward appearances rely on the vastness,
existence and non-existence spontaneously merge in the profound.
Forgetting loftiness, thus not descending,
lonely in a few feet of space.
Through flowers, requesting non-attachment,
soaring in the void, scattering lotuses.
The benevolent one articulates profound verses,
form itself is naturally empty.
Traces of emptiness and existence intermingle,
profound knowledge works without conscious effort.
Divine timing issues forth enlightenment from the trap,
suddenly and spontaneously attaining spiritual understanding.
Then in the past, there was an auspicious gathering.
On this day, many spirits gathered.
Wéimó, with profound resonance,
