Water by nature has no bubbles,
but a strong current creates foam.
Immediately differentiating, it forms shapes,
then dissipates and returns to the void.
A noble person recognizes the root,
why bother with labor and struggle?
Ignorant commoners are alarmed by change,
and suddenly feel joy and sorrow.
Innately, they manifest forms,
without flame, how would one know fire?
Continuously, they push and shift each other,
glowing faintly, not toward me.
How can those who are attached
remain confused about cause and effect all year?
Life's distinctions are originally diverse,
the banana tree knows not singularity.
If the sepals close without forming a core,
how can blooming flowers bear fruit?
The sage is good at using metaphors,
who can govern without a ruler?
Do not cling to the time of coming together,
but consider the day of dispersion.
The phantom works, the same and different.
Who again would say they are not real?
Once perishing things have passed,
what can be presented about the past?
The deluded doubt proximity and distance,
the enlightened all treat them as guests.
Do not give rise to feelings of separation and union,
for there will be no one lasting a hundred generations.
Awakened, one says sleep is without knowing,
yet in slumber, it is not without seeing.
Mental images fill the bright fore,
likes and dislikes alternately change ten thousand times.
Once awakened, one realizes the past is minuscule,
yet regrets being entangled by fleeting things.
Who beholds the end of the Sahā world,
would it truly not be the Red County?
Echoes and shadows follow form and sound,
drawing on things for natural principles.
Once they are swiftly gone,
by what cause can they be similar?
All beings are like this,
in obscure darkness calling it "self."
Even the four colors have no root,
on what can the eight subtle elements rely?
Overflowing is the dark side of the bright moon,
dense is the rain on Nánshān.
Able to be used for change and movement,
yet in myself, there is nothing to grasp.
Suddenly, they scatter and disperse,
how can they again be gathered and accumulated?
Since all dharmas are without self,
how can there be "mine"?
Like a dazzling lightning flash, it passes,
visible but not to be chased.
After constant things arise and cease,
who again would scrutinize their speed or slowness?
Be very careful not to retain empty thoughts,
lest they shame the divine principle.
forget feelings, and blessings endure.
An edict says:
Last year, I commanded Yú Chǎn and others to compile a record of the Buddha,
and to write a preface.
The style of the preface was not fitting,
and frequent revisions still have not achieved the desired effect.
It seems Buddhism uses the three provisionalities to entrust the Dharma,
and relies on the two truths to clarify the principle.
To attain the essence by seeking the phenomena, without adhering to the assembly of the Dào,
the discourse on its ultimate purpose seems not to have reached the extreme.
Therefore, you should not be troubled by this.
This is also a good deed in one aspect.
It can be put to paper.
Thus, I issue this specific edict.
The concluding style of the preface by Chǎn and others also seems slightly different.
Your servant Yūe Yán says:
The preface to the Fó Jì is now respectfully submitted.
Its words and meaning are not commendable;
I harbor self-reproach.
Respectfully reported.
An edict says: The record and preface have now been seen; I now command them to be copied and circulated.
The preface reads:
The myriad types of sentient beings
are not exhausted by records and tallies.
Every single thing that receives life,
how could it be measured by accumulated dust?
None fail to arise from unreason and reach non-birth.
Although there is an ultimate end, the original beginning is unheard of.
If not for the brilliantly illuminating, uniquely perceptive, whose ultimate source is present,
then reason would be closed, initial mechanisms would be beyond penetration and inquiry,
not only would the Four Fruits not be discussed,
but also the Ten Bhūmis would be beyond glimpse.
Vast and distant,
it exists, yet no one knows its origin.
When the Tathāgata overturned the basket, and first spoke of ascending the eternal path, arising and ceasing, circling and swirling, rushing without pause,
coming and going through the Five Paths,
the Great Chiliocosm is likened to a hair's tip.
Returning through the Three Realms,
a single kalpa is not enough to describe the distance.
Accumulating brightness and continuous illumination, thought after thought ceaselessly,
departing from this arising and ceasing, one actualizes the subtle fruit.
Indeed, both emptiness and existence are dismissed,
how could it merely be like the shift from Qí to Lǔ?
Vast and profound,
yet clinging to what words can describe.
The perfect person is without self,
how could he value words and meanings?
This is because myriad delusions fan each other, and obscurity and clarity arise alternately.
Provisional karma and conditions open, so matters need to be clearly understood.
From a single utterance, no thought is unsubmitted.
Meaning lies in accommodating beings, movement is never for oneself.
The Dharma roar shakes and spreads to the limitless,
sweet dew brilliantly shines in the Dragon Palace.
Establishing the teaching and expounding the doctrine is achieved gradually.
He points out the Four Noble Truths in the Deer Park,
distinguishes the hundred non-existent states under the twin Sāla trees.
He expands the non-dual Dharma gate,
and broadens the long road of the One Vehicle.
Those lost on the path find their way back, the weak and bereaved know where to return.
Yet, they respond differently, their paths divergent and not uniform.
The light from the white hair between his brows shines,
pervading worlds as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā.
Taking seven steps upon his descent,
he suppresses the dragon mounds and is universally covered.
He pushes to the extreme the divine way, fundamentally originating from the mind.
Summoned by response, he crosses boundless distances as if they were咫尺 (a cubit).
When conditions are discordant, one faces the Dharma city yet cannot perceive it.
And when the image-teaching reached its end, the scriptures recorded its eastward flow.
Hot slopes were difficult and long, cold mountains steep and obstructed.
Horizontal writings and left-hand scripts were understood only after tens of thousands of changes.
Shredded leaves formed texts, but repeated translations remained unclear.
From then until now, more than half of a thousand years have passed.
Spiritual traces gradually emerged, famous monks appeared intermittently.
The Vinaya and Vaipulya canons gradually arrived.
Many hidden in the Western Lands have not yet arrived.
Although the profundity of the eternal Dharma-body is distant,
and the vastness of the two truths and three provisionalities is immense,
to realize the Dào and seek its essence is sufficient here.
And the benevolent one revered this great sage as the fundamental teacher.
The innumerable multitude of beings, to whom spiritual essences are tied,

However, divine transformations and responses appear divergently.
Moreover, the lineage, names, and customs of their native lands are scattered and fragmented.
The various sections are difficult to fully investigate.
Divine merits and wondrous powers, though one in origin, have different names.
Descending into a womb to seek the Dào is not limited to one form.
Taking birth in Kapilavastu was originally a provisional manifestation.
Emanating from the northern gate was not the beginning of his realization of the Dharma.
Illuminating the entire East was not the extreme of his universal transformation.
Since embarking on the Dào,
for forty-nine years, there were many wondrous responsive events.
It is fitting to collect them comprehensively and form a distinct area.
As for old records of sutras and images, and remaining accounts of realms and monasteries,
the merit of their propagation is far-reaching.
The great powerful ones are expansive, sacrificing themselves to save beings.
The Arhats are upright and unwavering, their hearts not for themselves.
Their paths may differ, their destinations not necessarily the same.
The divine paths are varied and difficult to argue by conjecture.
Spiritual wonders are unrestrained, beyond words.
Tú Chéng's dragons appeared in Zhào and Wèi.
Róu Shén's phoenixes gathered in Guān and Fǔ.
Jiàn Tuó recently traveled to Jīng and Luò.
Shàn Kāi journeyed far to Luófú.
Although their traces are the same as worldly ones, their intentions are imperceptible.
The path out of the Jade Gate, the Dharma seat is not far.
The seven places and eight assemblies stand majestically before one's eyes.
Spiritual responses and manifestations abound, especially westward of Yánzé.
Brilliant light and visions are frequently seen beyond Tiānshān.
Monks with aspirations often travel and experience them.
Divine traces are clearly manifest, all with written records.
Their complexity and inconsistencies truly require compilation.
He divides the five paths in the human and celestial realms,
and sets up heavy prisons in the thick earth.
Each follows the power of their karma, without any deviation.
These are all the expansion and contraction of truth and convention, the beginning and end of names and forms.
If the sacred path is profound, vast, and great,
then it leads directly to the Bodhimaṇḍa.
If its proofs are precise, proximate, and minor,
then it serves to encourage later learners.
This is truly the comprehensive ferryboat,
the broad road of great compassion.
Although wisdom may be dim, vision limited, and form constrained to a cubit's measure,
when conditions move, it will certainly respond.
How much more so for those who progress beyond this!
Therefore, the ultimate sages diligently always strive to guide,
leaving writings to reveal their meaning and bestow them upon future generations.
The Emperor's conduct has reached completion since beginningless time, his Dào inherited through countless kalpas.
The ten titles are upon his person, the three insights unhindered.
He condescends to this subtle existence, sharing this turning wheel.
He grieves for the deluded and pities the confused who have long strayed from the right path.
Those who are eager to learn vainly aspire to penetrate and look up.
The scattered streams are vast and distant, difficult to bring together.
Those with shallow aspirations and laborious karma achieve nothing.
This is not how to open up the four crossroads and lead them out of the burning house.
Therefore, an edict was issued to the Zhongshū Shìláng, Yú Chǎn, the Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ, Dào Gài, and the Hòujūn Jìshì, Zhōu Shě,
to extensively search the sutra treasury and collect annotations and explanations,
to categorize and branch them out, attaching each to its proper class.
With little time and much work,
this can be accomplished.
It is named Fó Jì (Record of the Buddha),
totaling thirty chapters.
Among those streams of responsive events whose types are similar,
only one is chosen, and all others are not recorded.
Or if someone died and was reborn, relating what they saw in the scriptures,
but the matter is obscure and there is no evidence to verify it,
these are also not included, treating them as doubtful.
Or relying on others' words, or forming dreams from imagination,
these are particularly difficult to believe and understand, and none are recorded.
Now, if one wishes to travel far,
one must remember well where one came from.
If one wishes to awaken to the Dào,
one must subtly recognize what one reveres.
Only then can one truly find the gate and personally receive the teaching.
No one who does not know the path or cannot distinguish the person can, with eyes closed and blindly treading, spontaneously align with principle.
Therefore, we lead those many streams to return to the one source,
so that the countless sentient beings may look at the path and know where to go,
and by sharpening their arrows, return to the right path,
not wandering aimlessly at crossroads,
so that the pure believers may also benefit from this.

A brief list of the ancient King Āyù pagodas of the Dà Táng dynasty follows.
The pagoda in Màoxiàn, three hundred seventy lǐ east of Yuèzhōu:
In the second year of Tàikāng of the Western Jìn, the śramaṇa Huì Dá felt it rise from the earth.
It was one chi four cùn high,
and seven cùn wide.
Its露盤 had five layers.
Its color was green, like stone but not.
Its four sides were carved with hundreds of thousands of wondrous images.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng built a wooden pagoda to enclose it.
The Bāwáng, Yú, toured the surrounding areas.
Now, divine auspicious light, sounds, and holy monks are seen,
as detailed in a separate biography.
The pagoda of Chāohuàsì in Zhèngzhōu:
It is located over a hundred lǐ south of the prefecture.
Its foundation exists to this day.
The monastery courtyard walls are all ancient stone, tightly fitted.
Iron was used for the delicate joints.
The stones are eight chi long,
and the delicate joints on all four sides are one chi five cùn long,
and five cùn deep.
Beneath the stones is all mud.
South of the pagoda's foundation, over ten springs emerged,
each three chi in diameter.
They gush silently.
In the Yǒnghuī era, a Kūnlún
entered the spring and descended to its depths.
Only stone pillars were arranged there.
Its limits could not be fathomed.
Within it was a stone pagoda in the void.
The water solidified and did not reach it.
Thirty lǐ northwest of Línhuángxiàn in Jìzhōu is Āyùwáng Shèlìsì.
Recently, nuns resided in the temple.
There is an ancient pagoda,
with a stone-laced foundation.
The pagoda emerges from the bottom of the water.
On three sides, the water is extremely deep.
Only the western side is passable.
On the path there are lotus roots.
People fear them and dare not gather or catch them.
The Fǎménsì pagoda, twenty lǐ north of Qíshānxiàn, south of Qíshān in Qízhōu, is on a plain. Since ancient times, it has been opened once every thirty years.

In the fifth year of Xiǎnqìng, an imperial edict commanded the monk Zhìcóng

A brilliant light illuminated the area, visible to both monastics and laity.

The śarīra resembled the knuckle bone of an adult's finger,

Its color was white and luminous,

The Fúgǎnsì pagoda in Chéngdū, outside the city walls of Yìzhōu.

He broke off a piece of stone from the side,

It is now preserved in the Bǎoxìngsì pagoda, outside the north gate of Luòxiàn, a hundred lǐ north of Yìzhōu.

Over a hundred lǐ southwest of Yìzhōu,

The King Āyùsì of the Zhōu dynasty.

The golden auspicious image of King Āyù in Yángzhōu

Two stone images floating in the Sōngjiāng River in Wújùn.

The statue of King Udayana made of sandalwood at Dàmíngsì in Jīngzhōu.

When Emperor Tàizōng was still in the palace, he went to pay homage, and it was grandly adorned and embellished.

In Xiāngzhōu, on Xiàn Shān, at Huáyán Temple, there is a miraculous statue of Lúshènà.

The entire region was afraid.
By the seventh month, the Hàn Shuǐ overflowed and entered the city walls,

In the Chén dynasty, the Chóngyún Diàn flew into the sea.
This palace hall was built by Liáng Wǔ.
Inside, statues and all precious treasures were placed.
After the Liáng fell and the Chén rose, Emperor Wǔ of Chén died.

With ample manpower, people approached from all sides.
Suddenly, clouds and mist surrounded it,
and heavy rain poured down with thunder and lightning striking.
The workers scattered.
Then, flames appeared in the sky, interconnected by fire.
The great hall of Chóngyún, along with the Buddha statues within it,
all ascended upwards, reflecting smoke and fire, and swiftly moved eastward.
The entire nation looked up,
until it disappeared from sight.
When the rain cleared that day, only the foundations remained.
A month later, someone came from an eastern prefecture,
who on that day had seen the hall traveling through the air and entering the sea.
Those who gaze at the sea today sometimes see it.
In the Northern Wèi, the pagoda of Yǒngníng Temple in Luòjīng was struck by lightning and went to the Eastern Sea.
The events are largely similar.
In Jiāngzhōu, on Lú Shān, there is a miraculous statue of Wénshūshīlì.
In antiquity, the famous Jìn official Táo Kǎn built it.
South of the sea, a fisherman saw light on the seashore.
He reported it to Kǎn, who ordered him to investigate.
Soon, a golden statue was seen floating on the waves towards the boat.
The inscription showed it was a Wénshū (Mañjuśrī) made by King Ashoka.
It was sent to Hánxī Temple in Wǔchāng.
Later, when Táo Kǎn moved to Jīngzhōu, he tried to welcome the statue onto his boat.
The boat immediately sank.
Master Yuǎn welcomed it into Lú Shān.
There was no impediment whatsoever.
It is now in the multi-story pavilion in the eastern forest of the mountain.
In Yúzhōu, a hundred *lǐ* to the west, north of Xiāngsī Temple,
on a stone mountain, there are twelve Buddha footprints.
All are three feet long, one foot one inch wide, and nine inches deep.
Inside are fish patterns.
They are fifteen steps north of the Buddha hall.
It is said that monks reside there.
In Xùnzhōu, northeast of Xīngníng County, north of Língkān Temple, on a stone, there are over thirty Buddha footprints.
The largest are five feet long and below.
In Jīngshī, Dàxīngshàn Temple
has many miraculous Buddha statues, Buddha bones, Buddha teeth, and so on.
In Fǔzhōu, in the Xiǎnqìng reign, there was a walking statue from Tánzhōu.
It moved by itself to a place twenty *lǐ* east of Fǔzhōu.
On the mountain path, two footprints appeared,
three feet long, separated by over five hundred *lǐ*.
Initially, its origin was unknown.
Someone exploring the mountain saw the strange sight.
He informed people far and near, who tried to move it to a temple, but it would not budge.
The prefect and other officials, facing a severe drought,
walked to the statue and requested it be returned to the prefecture temple.
Three people lifted it and brought it to the prefecture.
As they walked, clouds gathered, and that night there was a heavy downpour,
resulting in a good harvest that year.
It is now in Fǔzhōu.
During the Suí dynasty, the Buddha hall of Xīnghuáng Temple in Jiǎngzhōu was burned.
A copper statue, one *zhàng* and six feet tall, was directly beneath the ridge beam.
When the fire broke out and the beam fell,
the statue moved itself five or six feet to the south,
and its form remained safe.
On all four sides, tiles, earth, ash, and charcoal
were five or six feet away from the statue.
Not a speck of dust or blemish touched it.
It is now in Báimǎ Temple, where birds and sparrows do not intrude.
In Jiǎnzhōu, at Sānxué Shān Temple, there is a Buddha footprint.
Every night, a divine lamp appears in the sky.
It is visible from afar but disappears up close.
On the nights of the six fasts, there are many such lamps.
In Fángzhōu, northeast of Yùhuá Temple, in Cíwū Chuān,
in the Wǔdé reign, a resident named Hǎo Biàn,
who had always been a believer,
noticed deer frequently dwelling on the mountainside, which was unusual.
So he dug at that spot and unearthed a stone statue.
It was fourteen or fifteen feet tall.
He then moved it out and placed it in his home in the ravine.
Its appearance was very similar to the one east of Yùhuá Temple.
Ancient tales say
that during the time of Kāyè Fó,
over forty such statues were hidden in this mountain.
Now two are visible.
The rest have not yet emerged.
In Xíngzhōu's Shāhé County, there is a four-faced bronze Buddha.
It is about four chi tall.
At the beginning of the Suí dynasty, someone entered the mountains
and saw a monk guarding this statue.
He then requested to offer worship.
The monk disappeared.
That person wanted to carry it out, but it would not move.
People from various places heard of it and came to help pull it, but it was still the same.
The monks of Shāhé Temple heard of it
and tried to pull it, whereupon it immediately moved to the temple.
Later, someone found a塊 of gold beside the temple,
on which were two crow shapes.
The inscription said:
“Intended to plate the four-faced Buddha,” so it was used to plate it.
The Buddha's form was covered everywhere with crow shadows.
After the Suí 后主 (Hòuzhǔ) heard of this auspicious sign,
he sent artisans to cast a replica.
The casting was never completed,
always having imperfections.
After two hundred days, they stopped.
It is now in the temple.
The divine stupas and auspicious statues before this opened the common and guided the ordinary.
Those who did not deeply understand were inspired to believe by this.
Once they believed in the extraordinary form, they could concentrate their minds,
peruse scriptures, discuss, and facilitate divine understanding.
Only then would they know that the four Māras constantly disturb and the six thieves perpetually oppress.
Aware and fearful, transcending the ordinary would have its day.
Otherwise, sinking and drowning would be no different from beginningless time.
How could the path of enlightenment be like that?
As for scriptures not burning,
this accords with asbestos cloth.
Writing in the air without getting wet is like the spirituality of the celestial canopy.
Sacred temples have been built many times,
and their bell sounds flow far and wide.
Divine monks have appeared numerous times,
receiving offerings from both the clergy and the laity.
Such instances are many,
recorded in the Gǎntōng Jì (感通記).
In the eighth month of Dàtóng (大同) four years
(538 CE), the moon trespassed on Wǔchē (五車)
and the old man's star (Canopus) appeared.
The Āyùwáng (阿育王) stupa at Chánggān (長干) Temple was rebuilt.
From it were unearthed śarīras, the Buddha's hair, and nails.
Āyùwáng was an iron-wheel king.
The king ruled over all of Jambudvīpa (閻浮).
In one day and night, he commanded ghosts and spirits to build eighty-four thousand stupas.
This was one of them.
The emperor's carriage visited Chánggān Temple,
where an unimpeded dharma feast was held.
An imperial edict stated:
“Heaven and Earth wax and wane, correlating with the times.
All things cannot perpetually maintain their foolish existence.
The two energies (yin and yang) cannot perpetually sustain their covering and bearing.
Therefore, ease and toil differ year by year, and joy and sorrow vary day by day.
Last year's crop failure caused the price of grain to soar.
The people suffered from destitution, leading to this excess.
Examining the circumstances and faults, some may be worthy of pity.
‘Dismounting to inquire about crimes’
is heard in ancient pronouncements.
The blame rests with the monarch, truly upon Our person.
If all were to be strictly disciplined by law, there would be no path to self-renewal.
Does the Shū (書) not say:
‘Rather than kill the innocent, it is better to err on the side of not punishing according to the classic.’
The Yì (易) says:
‘The meaning of adapting to the times is truly great!’
Now, the true form śarīras have reappeared in the world.
Encountering such a rare event,
arouses the thought of a difficult meeting.
Now, from the Āyùwáng Temple, an unimpeded assembly is declared.
Old and young alike are filled with joy,
like the long-hungry finding food,
like those long-separated seeing relatives.
The unseen and seen turn their hearts, near and far look up with admiration.
Scholars and women spread out like clouds, carriages and hats gather like a canopy.
Taking advantage of the times to spread virtue truly aligns with human spirit.
Therefore, all crimes under heaven, regardless of severity, are pardoned.”
In the seventh month of Dàtóng four years
(538 CE), an imperial edict stated:
“Heaven's benevolence broadly covers, and its righteousness encompasses all.
How can convenient means to benefit beings be limited to specific places?
Lǐ Yìnzhī (李胤之), a commoner from Shàngyú County, dug up an ivory statue.
It was less than two inches square.
Its two sides, when joined, formed a beast shape.
Inside, on one side, were twelve Buddha figures;
on the other side, fifteen figures.
The carvings are clear and pure, the craftsmanship exquisitely marvelous.
It must have been created by divine spirits, not by human effort.
Within it are six true form śarīras.
The eastern province previously reported this,
but We did not take it seriously.
However, Yìnzhī (胤之) was bound and imprisoned.
The true form śarīras descended to the central office,
emitting brilliant light, displaying a rare sign.
Great compassion saves from suffering; truly there is a reason for this.
It is fitting to rely on the Buddha's power to extend this great clemency.
Therefore, all crimes under heaven, regardless of severity,
committed before dawn on the sixteenth day of this month,
are all pardoned.
Immediately, [Yìnzhī] shall be released.
Reverently escort the Dharma body back to the capital for offerings.”
Your minister, Gāng (綱), states:
“Your minister has heard that humble roadside songs aspire to elegance,
and the simple tunes of Bārén (巴人) truly look up to the melodies of Yángchūn (陽春).
Thus, the small leaves of turnip and mallow still yearn for the morning sun,
and the faint light of a torch cannot extinguish itself.
I humbly consider Your Majesty,
whose ultimate virtue is admirable and brilliant, whose profound principles are widely applied.
You are both divine and sagely, Your Dao (道) surpasses Xuān (軒) and Guī (媯).
Your perfect enlightenment and true reality match the ultimate completeness.
You find joy in permanence and sweetness in the Dharma.
Your compassionate rain covers the boundless,
and Your sagely transformation reaches the hidden and manifest.
Therefore, the eight winds are harmonious, the four qi are correct,
the world is stable, and lands beyond the seas are peaceful.
You expand the might of the Dragon's Den
and inherit the Dharma of Vulture Peak.
Without action, yet nothing is left undone; truly, you pity all beings.
Without form, yet you proclaim and guide to the true realm.
You establish this Bodhi (菩提) tree and manifest this golden image,
so that those who make vows may create good causes,
and those who prostrate may increase their blessings.
The path to assembly is one; who in ancient and modern times can be two?
I humbly recall the dew-receiving vessel by Bǐǎo (表) and the commemorative inscription from Dōng'ē (東阿).
The auspicious appearance of the yellow dragon in Zhōngshān (中山) inspired eulogies.
Though Your minister is not clever, he truly has a foolish heart.
I respectfully present a hymn to the Bodhi tree.
My learning falls short of ancient research, and my thoughts are not profound.
It is insufficient to illuminate Your Majesty's splendid virtue, even a corner of it.
I am ashamed of my humble words, and trembling as I put them to paper.
Respectfully submitted.”
An imperial rescript noted the memorial:
“I have read the hymn to the Bodhi tree you presented.
It selects and gathers excellent phrases, and its meaning is pure.
It praises the Dharma King and extols the Bodhi tree.
Your thoughts, words, and even handwriting
achieve the goodness of the three karmas.
However, the praise for the state is all irrelevant to facts.
Indeed, it is not without the fault of flowery language.”
By imperial decree.
I humbly submit that:
Conditioned existences are temporary,
a result of the dull roots of sentient beings.
The Dharma is fundamentally not so,
it is the subtle principle of the perfected ones.
Therefore, the Three Realms (Sānjiè) and Six Paths (Liùqù) revolve around karmic obstructions and are lost in self-delusion.
The Eight Emancipations (Bājiě) and Ten Knowledges (Shízhì) guide one back to the fundamental principle, leading to emptiness and vastness.
Thus, the Great Master Néngrén (Shākyamuni Buddha) propagated the Dharma according to circumstances,
pitying the burning house of suffering,
and grieved over the perpetual rushing of the stream of desires.
He took refuge in the palace of Purity (báijìng zhī gōng),
illuminating with the color of gold.
Dwelling amidst the three delusions (sān huò), he showed that the painted casket (huà qiè) is not real.
Stepping out of the four gates (sì mén), he awakened to the fleeting nature of floating clouds.
Thereupon, the Buddha-sun rose,
the Dharma-thunder rumbled.
He set forth the gradual teaching (jiàn jiào),
and manifested expedient traces (quán jì).
The Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) appeared in the world, and the single path (yī dào) became known.
Greatly embraced by the common people, those yet to be delivered were saved.
The nourishment of the Dharma-clouds (fǎ yún) and Dharma-waters (fǎ shuǐ)
made the world boundless.
The light of the wisdom-lamp (zhì dēng) and wisdom-torch (zhì jù)
made the void without limit.
As things became immeasurable due to transformation, the karmic causes for cessation were about to begin.
Forests opened to the white sun, trees reflected green branches.
Alas, the Six Consciousnesses (liù shí) sink into the Eight Sufferings (bā kǔ).
If there were no great saint, who would bridge the path of wisdom?
The Emperor embodies the sagely virtue of Qiányuán,
embracing the pure sincerity of Heaven and Earth.
He illuminates with the spirit of a jade mirror,
and wields the fortune of great peace.
He swallows Yú (虞) and conceives Xià (夏), overshadowing Hàn (漢) and embracing Zhōu (周).
He governs the six qi (liù qì) and shepherds the common people,
waving the two yí (èr yí) to spread prosperity and nurture.
He weaves music (yuè) and arranges rites (lǐ), lays down arms and cultivates culture.
No autumn punishment (qiū tú) is imposed, abolishing the severe laws of the nine codes (jiǔ lǜ).
Spring rains cherish life, undoing the dense nets of the three chases (sān qū).
Truly, the spirits of Xiánchí (Xiánchí) themselves felt ashamed,
and the virtues of Fénshuǐ (Fénshuǐ) knew remorse.
Shàoyáng (Shàoyáng) promoted goodness in yuánzhēn,
and vassal officials changed their tastes in huái gǔn.
The scholars of the Eight Prodigies (Bākǎi), Three Seats (Sānzuò), Nine Thorns (Jiǔjí), and Four Categories (Sìkē)
inwardly proclaimed royal affairs, devising strategies and moving freely.
Generals who administered cities and promoted merit
outwardly guarded the borders, unifying script and carriage-gauge.
The myriad regions were united.
Chiefs with pierced chests and carved torsos,
rulers with short bodies and long arms—
from the South Vietnamese (Nányuè) who burn stones to the Northern Pole (Běijí) with its heavenly sands,
east to the sun's branches and west beyond the moon's circuits—
none failed to climb peaks,
hanging over distant, unsurpassable mountains;
none failed to sail the seas and cross the deep,
floating on the waves of light down.
They offered tribute from all directions,
presenting loyalty and requesting office.
They offered birds with shared hearts,
and beasts with joined shoulders.
Thereupon, auspicious signs competed to appear, precious treasures gathered.
Auspicious ganoderma (língzhī) oozed dew, moon-like, in suburban gardens.
Righteous phoenixes (yìfèng) and benevolent tigers (rénhǔ) were reported daily in commanderies and states.
Like pearls and jade,
they illuminated the central imperial domain;
like clouds, yet not clouds,
they also hovered over the palace battlements.
Thus, he led the common people to benevolence and longevity,
and saved both sentient and insentient beings from the netherworld.
The years were bountiful, the people prosperous, households well-provided.
The aged did not need support,
children sang praises.
Following goodness like flowing water, responding to influence like grass in the wind.
They opened farms and rooted in agriculture, melting blades and blunting spearheads.
Red grains filled basins, green ducks were piled high.
Above, it illuminated the heavens; below, it flowed from springs.
Heaven was thus perfected, Earth was thus pacified.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) then treated all his children equally, pitying all living beings.
He demonstrated the cause of right conduct,
and marked the path to liberation.
He widely established bodhimaṇḍas (dàocháng) and greatly propagated the wonderful Dharma.
The precious raft of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán bǎo zhào)
received confused multitudes flowing against the stream.
Compassionate radiance (cí bēi guāng míng)
illuminated the bewildered masses who were yet unenlightened.
The Dharma wheel (fǎ lún) spread throughout the great chiliocosm (dà qiān),
and coolness covered the small leaves.
Therefore, celestial beings danced phoenixes, leaving the shining garden to praise goodness.
Bodhisattvas flew on elephants, crossing fragrant lands to come and pay homage.
Five hundred precious canopies (bǎo gài) soared and converged with light.
Ten thousand jeweled necklaces (yīng luò) hung down from the sky.
The grottoes were adorned, the land was exceptionally unique.
He built halls for the three periods (sān shí zhī diàn),
and erected platforms with four pillars (sì zhù zhī tái).
Even the palace of Empress Hàn (Hàn hòu) that awaited spirits, and the observatory of Xuānyuán (Xuānyuán) that awaited immortals,
were not enough to even vaguely resemble the precious clouds (bǎo yún) and the form of enlightened ones (děng jué).
Thereupon, contemplating the beginning of enlightenment (chéng dào),
he erected the Bodhi tree (Pútí zhī shù).
The four seas presented treasures, and a hundred artisans offered their skill.
Gold was carved, jade was engraved, mirrors were set, pearls were hung.
It was crafted to resemble a snow mountain (xuě shān), shaped like a flying canopy.
Its shade spread in four directions, covering all things on five sides.
Its fame surpassed the full moon, its grace exceeded universal coverage.
It rivaled the splendor of trees with a thousand lights,
connecting blossoms of five colors.
The jade-like sun emitted luster, and jade belts gave rise to smoke.
As a gentle breeze slowly stirred, the precious branches became music.
Majestically, its wondrous colors shaded these curving branches,
appearing like a golden mountain, revered like a gathering moon.
It represented the first taste of belief for faithful women,
and the form of the four bowls of the devas.
Auspicious grasses scattered profusely, green sparrows flew in succession.
It subdued demons that吐電 (tǔ diàn),
and repelled ghosts that carried mountains.
Its wondrous forms and exquisite qualities are beyond words.
This is truly a wonderful condition for generating goodness, and a profound blessing for progressing on the path.
The present splendor was unheard of in past generations.
It should perpetually illuminate virtue without end,
suspending it with the sun and moon.
Lofty and eternally joyful, for ten thousand times ten thousand years— I humbly offer this eulogy:
Throughout history, it has been observed,
spiritual texts are like subtle mirrors.
Precious scrolls flourish,
imperial maps are brilliant.
Bird-omens proclaim auspiciousness,
dragon-writings signify celebration.
Kindness is spread across the nine provinces (Jiǔzhōu),
five-stringed lutes play songs.
How magnificent and ultimate!
The Great Liáng (Dàliáng) established a sage.
His merit covers all ancient times,
his achievements surpass those ordained.
The golden wheel (jīnlún) descended with the Dao,
the jade steelyard (yùhéng) aligned governance.
None thought not to submit,
those with aspirations flourished.
The One Vehicle (Yīchéng) emerged,
the Five Eyes (Wǔyǎn) became clear.
Sentient beings received wisdom and sang,
insects attained their nature.
Shùn’s (Shùn) kitchen, the spiritual fan;
Yáo’s (Yáo) courtyard, the divine capsules.
How could they compare to the Bodhi tree,
whose covering grace spreads widely?
Dense and minute, it sheds light,
fragrant and layered.
At times, a hundred flowers stir,
sometimes, a thousand leaves open.
It manifests the Dharma-body (fǎ shēn),
illustrating this auspicious record.
The sea crosses with six boats,
the city is pacified with four embrace-principles (sì shè).
Benevolence and grace are widely sown,
pure customs universally adopted.
A bright and clear wisdom realm,
a pure and vast Dharma spring.
A hundred spirits sigh in admiration,
a thousand Buddhas praise and transmit.
Glorious light moves and shines,
the jade candle (yù zhú) adjusts the year.
Bodhi (Pútí) stands eternally,
Prajñā (Bōrě) is perpetually proclaimed.
Majestic and enlightened sovereign,
may your lifespan be as eternal as Heaven.
Indeed, the ten evils are a great cause of confusion for the mind's path.
The myriad good deeds are weak in power, making it difficult to move spiritual nature.
Thus, Mahā-Karaṇā, going into fire, established the resolve for the Bodhimaṇḍa.
Sattvas, sacrificing their bodies, are certain to attain wonderful awakening.
Living beings, accumulating defilements, drift about and do not return.
The sea of suffering is easy to sink in, while the waves of compassion are empty and vast.
Thirst and love share the same gate with life and death.
Ignorance shares the same path with the tangled net.
Each heads towards a hundred wrongs, entangled by these four sufferings.
People should exert themselves to illuminate those three illuminations.
Therefore, the Tathāgata responds to circumstances to transform.
Like a great physician king, dispensing medicine according to the illness.
Currently, the foundation of imperial transformation
reaches to heaven and covers the earth.
It spreads the benevolent wind for ten thousand ages,
and changes the seasonal trends of the world for a hundred kings.
It covers and sustains all living beings, compassionately nurturing the common people.
To the ends of the earth and overseas, they honor righteousness and partake of its influence.
They hold their crops and blow their lips, embracing benevolence and drinking virtue.
The people, whether worthy or unworthy, are loved equally as one's own child.
You all should each restrain yourselves with sincere devotion, calming your minds to arrive at full satisfaction.
Reverently pay homage to the most revered Śākyamuni Buddha of the Suōpó Shìjiè.
Zhāntán Dézūn of the Huānxǐ Shìjiè.
Yuèdiàn Rúlái of the Shuǐjīng Chàtǔ.
Shānhǎi Huìfó of the Bǎomíng Shìjiè.
We respectfully pray that the sacred reign be as glorious as heaven and earth.
May its compassionate illumination be as bright as the sun and moon.
May the nine realms be blessed with prosperity.
May the eight directions enjoy the grace of benevolence and longevity.
May the beauty of the jade candle shine brightly in distant lands daily.
May the songs of striking the earth be heard throughout the world.
Reverence arises from the heart,
which is why the five limbs show outward respect.
Feelings emerge from within,
which is why the six consciousnesses reach everywhere.
Thus, one good deed that dyes the mind will not decay for myriad kalpas.
A hundred lamps shining broadly illuminate a thousand *li*.
Rely on the Dharma to achieve peace, accumulate good deeds to extend blessings.
Today, we are fortunate to encounter this guidance.
How can we not exhaust our hearts' path to respectfully pay homage on behalf of the Crown Prince to the Bǎohǎi of the East,
Dēngmíng of the South, Wúliàng of the West, and Xiāngdé of the North?
We respectfully pray that his enlightened wisdom shines within, perfectly harmonious without.
His virtue vibrates like jade, floating like clouds; his fame echoes like gold, reflecting like the sea.
His countenance is radiant daily, and the four virtues flow like a breeze.
Having already mastered the virtue of gentleness and refinement,
he truly bears the heavy responsibility of supervising the nation.
All living beings drink of his virtue, and the intelligent partake of his benevolence.
His internal transformation harmonizes and assists; his deeds are manifest throughout history.
His virtues are praised for their splendor; his teachings are esteemed above those of the grand historians.
Thus, he aligns with rectitude, serving heaven,
manifesting the seven teachings through benevolence and virtue.
He propagates influence and collects wisdom, spreading the six commands with warmth and compassion.

Each should collect your minds and respectfully pay homage on behalf of the noble consorts to the fifty-three Buddhas, thirty-five Honored Ones, the thousand Buddhas of the future Bhadrakalpa, and the present hundred and seventy.
We respectfully pray that her moon-like visage shares in all good fortunes.
May her golden voice be blessed in all four seasons.
May she inspire the seven factors of awakening to shine brightly.
May she rely on the ten wisdoms for constant joy.
May the household guard benevolence, and the palace store honor.
May her splendor be like stacked jade, radiant as Qúnqióng.
Indeed, we have heard that Sōnggāo, being a mighty peak, serves as a shield for the imperial house.
The imperial relatives are like a fortress, firmly established as a bedrock.
Thus, their kinship is equal to the states of Lǔ and Wèi, and their responsibilities are comparable to Xiāo Hé and Cáo Cān.
The three dukes occupy their proper seats, discussing the Dao while sitting.
The nine ministers diligently serve the king, respectfully handling connected affairs.

Each should direct your minds and respectfully pay homage on behalf of the Princes of Línchuān, Ānchéng, Jiàn'ān, Póyáng, Shǐxīng, Yùzhāng, and also Nánkāng, Lúlíng, Xiāngdōng, Wǔlíng, and all other imperial relatives of the royal households, the six ministries' esteemed dignitaries, to the Śarīra images, the wonderful Bodhi pagodas, the many treasures appearing, and the broken body of Śākyamuni.
We respectfully pray that their minds be as clear as a mirror, and their blessings as vast as a mountain.
May they successfully elevate the imperial altars and forever flourish the imperial branches.
May all of you, with one mind, take refuge in the Three Jewels.
The three realms have different practices, and the five paths diverge.
Humans and devas plant karma, each returning to a single fruit.
Ghosts and spirits are bound by retribution, their affairs manifest in the dark paths.
The flower and fruit of the ten good deeds have deviated from the righteous power.
The five defilements and vexations of the mind are increasingly burdensome.
Even if one is intelligent and upright,
the sacrifices of three animals are not diminished.
Though Yin and Yang are unpredictable,
the hindrances of the six sense organs are still stained.

You all should each sincerely and devotedly pay homage on behalf of the devas, nāgas, eight classes of beings, guardian kings of pagodas, and even the Asuras with eight arms and Mahêśvara with three eyes.
All for respectfully paying homage to the revered scriptures, the righteous canons, the pure Prajñā, the ultimate Nirvāṇa, the texts of the Lotus Sūtra assembly,
and the non-dual teachings of Vimalakīrti.
May all good deities
forever sever ignorance and always follow the true root.
May they rest in a treasure palace and sit among fragrant offerings.
May Indras be profound and vast,
sailing the boat of Prajñā.
May the Pure Abodes be deep and tranquil,
driving the beautiful ox-cart.
May their grace reach the three realms, brightly illuminating the four heavens.
The great compassion that alleviates suffering is manifest in previous scriptures.
The boundless kindness that bestows joy is extolled in famous teachings.
Thus, spiritual powers descend,
appearing and disappearing in various ways.
Bodhisattvas harbor their positions,
manifesting and concealing through many skillful means.
Boundless intense afflictions
fan the eight sufferings along the long path.
With ties that bind emotions,
they circle the six destinies on perilous paths.
Even with golden chains and jade beds, one still yearns for liberation.
Carved pearls and adorned silks are not as good as the path.
Such as being tossed by hot winds, or the vast, chilling ice water.
A thousand layers of dark rooms, a hundred *ren* of black cities.
Iron wheels crush bones, copper pillars scorch intestines.
Knife-like peaks emerge from the sides, sword-edges draw out horizontally.
Such numerous sufferings are especially dangerous and fragile.
If one breath is not pursued, then there is eternal separation for myriad kalpas.
If one moment is temporarily severed, then there is long departure for a thousand generations.
We mutually rely on this ephemeral existence in Jambudvīpa, a place of illusion.
This fragile body is more perilous than a mayfly.
The speed of wind and lightning is truly hard to hold back.
Moreover, the three characteristics hasten together, and two rats gnaw at danger.
Poison arrows and venomous snakes are especially to be feared.
May we rely on the True Dharma to eradicate these accumulated defilements.
May we long enjoy a hundred blessings and forever sever the six dusts.
In the face of the peerless, only the Buddha can be relied upon.
Now, for the six paths, four births, three evil realms, and eight difficulties, with compassion and earnestness, we arrive.

With one mind, we universally bow to the ten-stage Bodhisattvas, the three-practice Śrāvakas, respectfully bow to Guānyīn, the savior of the world, offer canopies to Bǎojī, Dàshì of the West, Miàoyīn of the Eastern land, the four-eloquence Vimalakīrti, the two realms' Luójì, Zhūjǐng, Shànxiù, Mílè, Wénshū, Jīngāng Zàng, Jiětuōyuè, Qìyìngài, Chángjǔshǒu, the ten great disciples, and the five hundred Arhats.
May prisons be empty, and sickness and distress cease.
Within the realm, a hundred counties; beyond the realm, a thousand cities.
May all those in confinement universally be released.
May people cooperate like removing a snake, and customs transform like correcting ants.
May they be like those who consume Zhèn bird's poison yet do not die.
May they be like those who draw a sword yet are unharmed.
May sentient beings not be enslaved, but turn from death to warmth.
May the Wèiqiáo daily be satiated, and there be no hunger under the mulberry trees.
May the three evil realms be blocked, and hells be shattered.
May the demonic armies be broken, and the armies of life and death be destroyed.
May Yánluó initiate the mind of the ten good deeds.
May Niúbàng begin the karma of the five precepts.
Like fish with little water, or birds in a sparse forest.
Upon hearing the Dharma sound, they immediately abandon their defiled bodies.
May people use their five limbs to take refuge in the three revered ones.
Indeed, ultimate awakening is profoundly clear, fundamentally beyond verbal expression.
Wonderful contemplation is empty and pervasive, naturally transcending snares and images.
Though it is free from all hundred wrongs, it responds when there is cause.
Its principle transcends the four propositions, so there is no sensation it does not illuminate.
His Majesty's Dao illuminates before the occasion, his thoughts transcend the bound.
When he calms his spirit by the Fén River, his mind is free from the world.
When he condescends to the Xuānqiū, his body toils within the universe.
This is the descent of the Dharma-patience,
manifesting in the realm of Jambudvīpa.
The great power abides on earth, condescending to respond to the domain of Suōpó.
Therefore, he wishes to cleanse and liberate all beings, saving the multitude.
Cleansing with pure water in the treasure pond.
Shading under high branches of the Bodhi tree.
His benevolence of subjugating and embracing reaches its ultimate when encountering conditions.
His virtue of harsh words and soft speech, when there is sensation, then it is uttered.
Daily, unconsciously, benefits are boundless.
All of you, together, increase your devotion.
Reverently pay homage to the most revered, with the five limbs taking refuge.
So it is.
We humbly pray that His Imperial Majesty's supreme Dao operates in unison with the four wanderings.
May his profound influence spread as widely as the eight directions.
May he return to the pure source of the three ancient eras.
May he abandon the corrupt waves of the nine generations.
The ultimate reign has already been witnessed today.
The great Dao has returned at this time.
Tigers and leopards wag their tails without alarm.
Vipers and snakes are trampled upon and do not bite.
Gold is buried, jade is discarded; contracts are destroyed, and texts are burned.
Auspicious grains grow, and sweet springs emerge.
Golden carriages and jade horses shine together.
Black cranes and vermilion phoenixes fly and sing, coming and going.
Wherever light shines,
wherever boats and chariots travel,
none fail to bend their knees, bow their heads, turn their faces, and change their voices.
Entering to serve in the imperial street, welcoming and bowing at the Wèishuǐ.
May he be as enduring as heaven and earth.
May he be as firm as metal and stone, even more so.
The Central Peak may shift, the long river may clear.
Yet our sacred emperor becomes ever more gentle and serene.
He transforms without speaking.
He governs without action, and his teachings are revered.
Indeed, his Dao is fully prepared for governance, his foresight surpasses the prime minister's.
He discerns the distant and knows the subtle,貫宗包極.
He needs no embellishment, awaits no elaborate persuasion.
Moreover, he empties the void in tranquility, viewing the true and the conventional alike.
He is capable of acting and speaking, believing and upholding.
All of you, with sincere hearts, respectfully pay homage to His Royal Highness the Crown Prince.
Take refuge and pay homage.
So it is.
We humbly pray that His Royal Highness the Crown Prince's profound virtue embodies the vast heavens.
May his broad capacity be comparable to the great rocks.
May the Morning Star shine brightly, and the Eastern Gate be resplendent.
May his gracious inquiries reach far, and his harmonious aura permeate the sky.
Exceptional talents contend to enter, upright people arrive in multitudes.
May his jade body be serene and pure, his golden voice wonderfully transcendent.
Indeed, his abundant accomplishments and distinguished reputation mean his Dao is comprehensive and his virtue vast.
The nobility of holding the scepter and wearing the ceremonial robe,
the honor of sitting under the槐 tree and resting under the棠 tree.
Yet, he should still cherish the eastern dawn and regret the western sunset.
Awaken to the unreality of the banana and reed.
Know the emptiness and pretense of the moon in the mirror.
Believe that lightning does not linger.
Verify that water drawn upon immediately rejoins.
He should only be illuminated by the lamp of wisdom and cleansed by the precious waves.
May this sagacious root be strengthened, and this wonderful foundation be established.
Furthermore, each of you, with increased devotion, respectfully pay homage to His Royal Highness the Grand Commandant and all other princes.
So it is.
仰願諸王 (Yǎngyuàn Zhūwáng),
既明且哲 (jìmíng qiězhé).
聲跨於河楚 (Shēng kuàyú Héchǔ),
令問令望 (lìngwèn lìngwàng),
道均於旦奭 (dàojūn yú Dànshì).
德貫右戚義藹周親 (Dé guàn yòuqī yì'ǎi Zhōuqīn),
作鉉則與二曜相終 (zuòxuàn zé yǔ èryào xiāngzhōng),
臨岳則與四維等固 (línyuè zé yǔ sìwéi děnggù).
若彭涓 (Ruò Péngjuān)之遐永 (zhī xiáyǒng), 譬松筠之貞悅 (pì sōngyún zhī zhēnyuè).
觀夫天枝峻密常葉英芬 (Guānfū tiānzhī jùnmì chángyè yīngfēn),
莫不玉振蘭搖金鏘桂縟 (mòbù yùzhèn lányáo jīnqiāng guìrù).
覩寸文而驗錦 (Dǔ cùnwén ér yànjǐn),
觀一毛而測鳳 (guānyìmáo ér cèfèng).
並能才高銅殿 (Bìngnéng cáigāo Tóngdiàn), 辭富雲臺 (cífù Yúntái).
彬彬亹亹超超灼灼 (Bīnbīn wěiwěi chāochāo zhuózhuó).
以斯勝善奉逮諸王殿下 (Yǐ sī shèngshàn fèngdài Zhūwáng Diànxià).
敬禮 (Jìnglǐ).
云云 (Yúnyún).
仰願諸王殿下穆穆與清風並扇 (Yǎngyuàn Zhūwáng Diànxià mùmù yǔ qīngfēng bìngshàn),
英英將白雲共朗 (yīngyīng jiāng báiyún gònglǎng).
永鍾清祉長享元吉 (Yǒngzhōng qīngzhǐ chángxiǎng yuánjí).
出牧則聲高民上 (Chūmù zé shēnggāo mínshàng),
入朝則譽先物右 (rùcháo zé yùxiān wùyòu).
德重山王 (Dézhòng Shānwáng), 智超海藏 (zhìchāo Hǎicáng).
鏗鏘麗於珠樹 (Kēngqiāng lìyú zhūshù),
皎鏡光於玉田 (jiǎojìng guāngyú yùtián).
夫道流雲屋 (Fūdào liú Yúnwū), 德感椒闈 (dégǎn Jiāowéi).
必以前籍勝因宿稟嘉數 (Bì yǐ qiánjí shèngyīn sùbǐng jiāshù).
況重霑法雨更披慧日 (Kuàng zhòngzhān fǎyǔ gēngpī huìrì).
雖異姜后解珥請罪於周王 (Suīyì Jiānghòu jiě'ěr qǐngzuì yú Zhōuwáng),
不待樊姬捨肉有激於荊后 (bùdài Fánjī shèròu yǒujī yú Jīnghòu),
而遵恭儉去嗜欲 (ér zūngōngjiǎn qùshìyù),
棄彫璣徹靡麗 (qìdiāojī chè mílì).
了心不滯正見無疑 (Liǎoxīn bùzhì zhèngjiàn wúyí).
眾等齊誠奉為六宮眷屬 (Zhòngděng qíchéng fèngwéi Liùgōng juànshǔ).
歸命敬禮 (Guīmìng jìnglǐ).
云云 (Yúnyún).
願六宮眷屬 (Yuàn Liùgōng juànshǔ),
業華姬日 (yèhuá Jīrì), 聲麗媯辰 (shēnglì Guīchén).
振采鐫圖 (Zhèncǎi juāntú), 傳芳詩史 (chuánfāng shīshǐ).
位齊寶印 (Wèiqí bǎoyìn), 行等月光 (xíngděng yuèguāng).
具六神通 (Jù liùshéntōng), 得四無礙 (dé sìwú'ài).
夫稟閑明之德懷深妙之心 (Fū bǐngxiánmíng zhīdé huáishēnmìao zhīxīn).
豈非修習有木 (Qǐfēi xiūxí yǒumù),
故能依止無倦 (gùnéng yīzhǐ wújuàn).
義興 (Yìxīng)等諸公主 (děng Zhūgōngzhǔ).
忘斯華重甘此翹到 (Wàngsī huázhòng gāncǐ qiáodào), 並宿世之所記莂 (bìng sùshì zhī suǒjìbié).
故現前所以信了 (Gù xiànqián suǒyǐ xìnliǎo).
影響至真 (Yǐngxiǎng zhìzhēn), 寤寐玄極 (wùmèi xuánjí).
人各增到 (Rén gè zēngdào).
仰為諸公主歸命敬禮 (Yǎngwéi Zhūgōngzhǔ guīmìng jìnglǐ).
云云 (Yúnyún).
願諸公主 (Yuàn Zhūgōngzhǔ),
日增智性彌長慧根 (rìzēng zhìxìng mízhǎng huìgēn).
四攝四依已尊已蹈 (Sìshè sìyī yǐzūn yǐdǎo),
七善七定靡退靡輟 (qīshàn qīdìng mǐtuì mǐchuò).
盛此王姬 (Shèngcǐ Wángjī), 光茲帝女 (guāngzī Dìnǚ).
長享湯沐與河山而同固 (Chángxiǎng tāngmù yǔ héshān ér tónggù),
永服緹綺貫寒暑而無窮 (yǒngfú tíqǐ guànhánshǔ ér wúqióng).
夫三相雷奔八苦電激 (Fūsānxiàng léibēn bākǔ diànjī).
或方火宅 (Huòfāng huǒzhái), 乍擬駛河 (zhànǐ shǐhé).
故以尺波寸景大力所不能駐 (Gùyǐ chǐbō cùnjǐng dàlì suǒbùnéngzhù),
月御日車雄才莫之能遏 (yuèyù rìchē xióngcái mòzhīnéng'è).
其間飲苦飡毒抱痛銜悲 (Qíjiān yǐnkǔ cāndú bàotòng xiánbēi).
身口為十使所由 (Shēnkǒu wéi shíshǐ suǒyóu),
意思乃八疵之主 (yìsī nǎi bācī zhīzhǔ).
眾等相與彼我齊到 (Zhòngděng xiāngyǔ bǐwǒ qídào),
懺悔業纏 (chànhuǐ yèchán).
無始以來至于今日 (Wúshǐ yǐlái zhìyú jīnrì),
所為十惡自作教他 (suǒwéi shí'è zìzuò jiàotā),
見善不贊聞惡隨喜 (jiànshàn bùzàn wén'è suíxǐ).
焚林涸澤 (Fénlín hézé), 走犬揚鷹 (zǒuqǔan yángyīng).
窮鄭衛之響 (Qióng Zhèngwèi zhīxiǎng),
極甘旨之味 (jí gānzhǐ zhīwèi).
戲笑為惡 (Xìxiào wéi'è), 倏忽成非 (shūhū chéngfēi).
侮慢形像 (Wǔmàn xíngxiàng), 凌踐塔寺 (língjiàn tǎsì).
不敬方等 (Bùjìng fāngděng), 毀離和合 (huǐlí héhé).
自定權衡 (Zìdìng quánhéng), 棄他計用 (qìtā jìyòng).
愧心負理 (Kuìxīn fùlǐ), 昧主欺親 (mèizhǔ qīqīn).
雖七尺非他方寸 (Suī qīchǐ fēitā fāngcùn),
在我而能任其情 (zàiwǒ ér néngrèn qíqíng).
在人未易恣此心口 (Zàirén wèiyì zìcǐ xīnkǒu).
眾罪所集各運丹懇 (Zhòngzuì suǒjí gèyùn dānkěn).
五體自投歸命敬禮 (Wǔtǐ zìtóu guīmìng jìnglǐ).
云云 (Yúnyún).
願現前眾等 (Yuàn xiànqián zhòngděng),
身口清淨行願具足 (shēnkǒu qīngjìng xíngyuàn jùzú).
消三障業朗三達智 (Xiāosānzhàngyè lǎngsāndázhì).
五眼六通得意自在 (Wǔyǎn liùtōng déyì zìzài).
夫有非自有 (Fūyǒu fēizìyǒu),
有取所以有 (yǒuqǔ suǒyǐ yǒu).
無非自無 (Wúfēi zìwú),
無著所以無 (wúzhuó suǒyǐ wú).
故有取之惑興倏成萬累 (Gù yǒuqǔ zhīhuò xīng shūchéng wànlèi),
無著之念起一超九劫 (wúzhuó zhīniàn qǐ yīchāo jiǔjié).
是知道之所貴 (Shìzhīdào zhī suǒguì),
空有兼忘 (kōngyǒu jiānwàng).
行之所重 (Xíngzhī suǒzhòng),
真假雙照 (zhēnjiǎ shuāngzhào).
稟氣含靈莫聞斯本 (Bǐngqì hánlíng mòwén sīběn).
宵形賦影靡測由來 (Xiāoxíng fùyǐng mǐcè yóulái).
故發茲識窟猶綿蒙 (Gù fāzī shìkū yóumiánméng),
其莫辯導此愚根 (qímò biàndǎo cǐ yúgēn).
尚窈冥而未悟 (Shàng yǎomíng ér wèiwù),
茫茫有同暗海 (mángmáng yǒutóng ànhǎi).
幽幽實在危城 (Yōuyōu shízài wēichéng).
業風縈薄三有長騖 (Yèfēng yíngbó sānyǒu chángwù),
惑水邅迴二死相屬 (huòshuǐ zhānhuí èrsǐ xiāngshǔ).
以苦捨苦從暗入暗 (Yǐkǔ shěkǔ cóng'àn rù'àn).
尋本不離色心 (Xúnběn bùlí sèxīn),
即事莫非生滅 (jíshì mòfēi shēngmiè).
是用抱此纏蓋淪迴生死 (Shìyòng bàocǐ chángài lúnhuí shēngsǐ),
恣其六愛興其八邪 (zìqí liù'ài xīngqí bāxié).
或狙詐而克昌 (Huò jūzhà ér kèchāng),
乍仁義而溘死 (zhà rényì ér kèsǐ).
或才均智等 (Huò cáijūn zhìděng),
此賤彼豪 (cǐjiàn bǐháo).
或共日並時 (Huò gòngrì bìngshí),
人升我墜 (rénshēng wǒzhuì).
唯言報施寂寥 (Wéiyán bàoshī jíliáo),
不知因對皎徹 (bùzhī yīnduì jiǎojié).
曩緣今果過現殖成 (Nǎngyuán jīnguǒ guòxiàn zhíchéng).
有如符契不謬毫髮 (Yǒurú fúqì bùmiù háofà).
而欲以促生運其長術浮命迴其冥數 (Éryù yǐ cùshēng yùnqí chángshù fúmìng huíqí míngshù).
當知剎那交謝瞬息不留 (Dāngzhī chànà jiāoxiè shùnxī bùliú).
東扶裁吐西崦已仄 (Dōngfú cáitǔ xīyān yǐzè).
譬閱川之駛流 (Pì yuèchuān zhī shǐliú),
若栖葉之輕露 (ruòqīyè zhī qīnglù).
偽城易弛毒樹自攻 (Wèichéng yìchí dúshù zìgōng).
若非假實兩明真俗俱辯 (Ruòfēi jiǎshí liǎngmíng zhēnsú jùbiàn),
豈能寫誠迴向刻意修習不退不沒愈堅愈固 (qǐnéng xiěchéng huíxiàng kèyì xiūxí bùtuì bùmò yùjiān yùgù).
南平大王殿下 (Nánpíng Dàwáng Diànxià),
含辰象之正氣 (hán chénxiàng zhī zhèngqì),
畜海岳之淳靈 (xù hǎi'yuè zhī chúnlíng).
宿侍八恒 (Sùshì bāhéng), 早遊七覺 (zǎoyóu qījué).
藉妙因於永劫 (Jièmiàoyīn yú yǒngjié), 招勝果於茲地 (zhāoshèngguǒ yú zīdì).
若真金之愈鎣 (Ruò zhēnjīn zhī yùyíng),
美玉之載琢 (měiyù zhī zàizhuó).
是用未積已散 (Shìyòng wèijī yǐsàn),
不藏而捨 (bùzáng érshě).
故今式招靈指仰屈神儀 (Gù jīnshì zhāolíngzhǐ yǎngqū shényí),
建此齋肅譬茲關揵 (jiàncǐ zhāisù pìzī guānjiàn).
盛來緇素濟濟洋洋 (Shènglásuī zīsu jìjì yángyáng).
名香遍室 (Míngxiāng biànshì), 寶花覆地 (bǎohuā fùdì), 高梵宛轉 (gāofàn wǎnzhuǎn).
寧止震木遏雲 (Níngzhǐ zhènmù èyún),
清桴遙奕非直騰魚仰馬 (qīngfú yáoyì fēizhí téngyú yǎngmǎ).
仰願四部至誠五體歸命東方 (Yǎngyuàn sìbù zhìchéng wǔtǐ guīmìng dōngfāng).
云云 (Yúnyún).
願大王殿下 (Yuàn Dàwáng Diànxià),
五畏內遣十力外扶 (wǔwèi nèiqiǎn shílì wàifú).
百福莊嚴 (Bǎifú zhuāngyán), 萬祉周集 (wànzhǐ zhōují).
愕夢無干其慮 (Èmèng wúgān qílǜ),
甘寢有恬其神 (gānnǐng yǒutián qīshén).
更闢寶衢 (Gēngpì bǎoqú), 愈興慧業 (yùxīng huìyè).
夫玄極凝淡非學者所窺 (Fū xuánjí níngdàn fēixuézhě suǒkuī),
妙本難思豈行人能測 (miàoběn nánsī qǐxíngrén néngcè).
是以十地云睹有羅縠之疑 (Shìyǐ shíshì yúndǔ yǒu luóhú zhīyí),
三乘稱見懷兕羊之惑 (sānshèng chēngjiàn huáihǔyáng zhīhuò).
自非鑒窮機覺照極冥虛窮理盡性體元含一 (Zìfēi jiànqióng jījué zhàojí míngxū qiónglǐ jìnxìng tǐyuánhányī),
安能濟世仁壽拯物阽危 (ānnēng jìshì rénshòu zhěngwù diānwēi).
道包碧海 (Dàobāo bìhǎi), 聲高赤縣 (shēnggāo chìxiàn).
昔堯曜唯在即世 (Xī Yáo yào wéizài jíshì),
舜黑不兼來果 (Shùn hēi bùjiān láiguǒ).
四巡疲於禹迹 (Sìxún píyú Yǔjì),
六事倦於湯身 (liùshì juànyú Tāngshēn).
並域中之勤勞 (Bìngyù zhōngzhī qínláo),
方內之成益 (fāngnèi zhī chéngyì).
豈有度元元於苦海 (Qǐyǒu dù yuányuán yú kǔhǎi),
拔冗冗於畏塗 (bárǒngrǒng yú wèitú).
運神力震法吼 (Yùnshénlì zhènfǎhǒu),
究香城之妙理 (jiùxiāngchéng zhī miàolǐ),
窮金河之奧說 (qióngjīnhé zhī àoshuō).
慧高龍樹 (Huìgāo Lóngshù), 智出馬鳴 (zhìchū Mǎmíng).
必欲洗濯臣民獎導緇白 (Bìyù xǐzhuó chénmín jiǎngdǎo zībāi).
天覆地養 (Tiānfù dìyǎng), 水產陸生 (shuǐchǎn lùshēng),
咸降慈悲悉蒙平等 (xiánjiàng cíbēi xīméng píngděng).

聲出 Jī Sòng dàoyuè Hàn Zhuāng.
永沐 zhìshuǐ chángzhào huìrì.

弘chǎn zhìjiào shàolóng jìxiàng.

夫 xiǎochéng zhìliè shì wéi yī jǐ.

今日 tánzhǔ.

眾děng gè guīchéng.

敬禮 zūnyí língxiàng Pútí bǎotǎ.
云云.
大乘 Àozàng Miàofǎ Shēnjīng.
大身 wúbiānshēn.
大力 wúliànglì.
四向 sìguǒ bāxián bāshèng.
願 liùqì fēnyūn sìxù xīmù.
至治 guāng wàn yǔ xuánhuà dòng jiǔyōu.
襲jiǎ pīlín shīshēng luǎnhuà.
八苦 liùqióng sāntú wǔdào.
俱méng huìlì bìngshí zūnyī.
刀林 chuòrèn jiànshù cuīfēng.
迷城 kāidào zhízhǐ sìqú.
闇室 shēngmíng dàqǐ sānyào.
俱xiàng dàocháng tóngdēng zhǒngjué.
夫 yuǎnzì wúshǐ zhì yú yǒu shēn.
生死 lúnwù.
塵lì mò zhī bǐ.
明暗 dìlái.
薪火 bùnéng pì.

千月 nánbǎo.
蓼chóng xíkǔ.
桂dù xǐgān.
大睡 jù yú jùwú.
長昏 shènyú zhěnqū.
義 fēi tāzhào shìshí jǐzhāo.
曾 bùzhī bǐng cǐ xínghái suóyóu ér zhì.
將 sī xīnshí jìngyù héguī.
唯 yǐ shìwèi xiānggāo.
爭 jiāohuá yú yīdàn.
車徒 zìshèng.
競chíwù yú dāngnián.
莫 bùshì qí xióngxīn zhuàngchǐ hóngyán zīfà.
口zì féinóng shēnān qīngmí.
繁xián cùzhù.
極 tāopiāo ér bùyàn.
玉chuáng xiàngxí.
窮mǐmàn ér wúyǐ.
謂 Méng Quán Ruò Mù chūmò.
曾 bùguānrén.
蹲wū gùtù shēngluò.
常 zìzài bǐ.
殊 bùzhī mìngjūn cuìcǎo shēnwéi kǔqì.
何yì quǎnyáng zhī qù túshì.
麋鹿 zhī rù zhànchú.
秋é fúyàn ér bùyí.
春cán yíngsī ér míwù.
未biàn xiānduì bùshí yīnxí.
及其 yīchù wèitú.
Mèngmén fēixiǎn.
轘liè zhījiě fāngsī bùzhēnjí tòng.
斷zhǐ záojiān bǐzī wèijíqí kǔ.
輪huí qǐfú yǎoyǎo yōuyōu.
是以 Tiānzhōngzhītiān jiàngbēi tíyǐn.
壅 Xiàhé zhī chángxiè.
撲 qiūyuán zhī měngliáo.
或tóng Shāngzhǔ zhàděng Yīwáng.
形biàn sānqiān jiàochuán bǎiyì.
或zì qí shénlì.
或jí zhūfànjìng.
言zé sāntú líkǔ.
笑zé sìshēng shòulè.
乃yìngbìng tóujī jiěfēn shuōlǐ.
制 zhī rìyè chēngwéi Bāguān.
以 Bāzhèng Yuè wéi fǎguān jiānhán.
斯shí chūshì zhī miàojīn.
在家 zhī xióngxíng.
眾děng xiāngyǔ yùnchéng.
奉dài Nánpíng Wáng Diànxià Lǐ.
云云.
願 Dàwáng Diànxià,
叡業 qīnghuī yǔ Nányuè ér xiānggù.
貞心 jùnjǐe děng Dōngmíng ér gòngguǎng.
萬lèi yānxiāo bǎizāi wùmiè.
巧huàn suǒ bùhuò.
強mó mò néngráo.
逐cǎnshū ér shìtǐ.
隨xuānliáng ér déxìng.
自bǐng yítiān zhī qì.
永gù shànwèi zhī dào.
得 liùshéntōnglì.
具 sìwú'àizhì.
夫 rìzài Kūnwú zé lǜfán shìrǎo.
景luò Méngfàn zé shénjìng zhìtián.
璧yuè zhūxīng héhuá xiāngzhào.
輕雲 bóvù lángrán zìjí.
鳴zhōng fúxiǎng guāngdēng tǔhuī.
法zhuàng juǎnshū.
拂gāoxuān ér xúbó.
名xiāng yùfù.
出zhòngdān ér qīngzhuǎn.
金biǎo hányìng zhūzhù dòngsè.
況fù Tiānzūn duānyì wēiguāng sìzhào.
煥fā qīnglián róngyǔ kēxuě.
覺 Qíwèi zhī zhǐchǐ.
若 línyuán zhī sī zài.
大zhāo lígòu zhī bīn.
廣jí yìngzhēn zhī lǚ.
清fàn hántǔ yīchàng sāntàn.
密yì yìyáng liánhuán bùchuò.
Nánpíng Wáng,
體dé jī zhīmǐn.
資rù shén zhīwēi.
抱dé hánhé jīngrén wěiyì.
善wú xì ér bùqióng.
累yǒu qīng ér bìshě.
受tóng xūyuè zhàorú xuánjìng.
忘 Lǔ Wèi zhī zūngāo.
略 Dì'è zhī huázhòng.
建 xīyǒu zhī shèngxí.
臨 nányù zhī fǎcháng.
相yǔ wǔtǐ guīmìng jìnglǐ.
云云.
願 Dàwáng Diànxià,
入 bù'èimén dēng yīxiàngdào.
德jiē bùdòng zhìchāo yuǎnxíng.
洋yì huìshēng yǔ bāfēng ér gòngyuǎn.
優yóu yùtǐ děng liùlǜ ér xiāngdiào.
餐xuěshān zhī liángyào.
挹lùchéng zhī gānwèi.
袞fú huán'guī yǔ sìshí ér yǒngjiǔ.
朱lún tízhì guànqiānsì ér chángrán.
Your minister, [given name omitted].
Your minister has heard that when eight nations pray together,
the matter is loftier than the fundamental Dharma.
When seven regions all contain it,
the principle is as complete as a gushing spring.
Therefore, there is no reason not to see the ivory bed and white parasol.
The golden vase and jeweled casket emerge for those who have the缘 (yuán).
I humbly reflect, Your Majesty,
that you suspend the celestial mirror over the world,
wielding great authority throughout the universe.
When the three realms are all dreaming,
you illuminate them with the sun of wisdom.
When all plants wither,
you moisten them with the rain of compassion.
Your movement and stillness are not self-determined; your action and inaction depend on things.
No one can describe it,
how then can your minister praise it?
Therefore, with 昭光赤書 (Zhāoguāng Chìshū),
I deem the auspicious omens of former historians as lowly.
Wearing 芝景玉 (Zhījǐng Yù),
I scoff at the treasures of past eras.
What is truly rare to encounter is the Śarīra of the Tathāgata's true form,
the 昭景寶瓶 (Zhāojǐng Bǎopíng) and the浮光德水 (Fúguāng Désuǐ).
It is like observing an interlocking chain, or seeing a dragon pearl.
Unless it is due to sacred virtue and divine power,
one cannot encounter such rarity.
Heavenly beings place it on their heads, and people near and far return their hearts to it.
I humbly heard that the 阿育王寺 (Āyùwáng Sì) urgently requires adornment.
Tens of millions in gold and sandalwood are bestowed, enriching the ten treasuries.
Treasures are arranged from the river treasury, and springs emerge from the water balance.
With Bhikkhus carrying earth, a grand edifice is being constructed.
With Arhats pulling ropes, a lofty pagoda will soon be erected.
Overwhelmed with joy and applause,
I respectfully present one million coins.
Although my sincerity is like scattering flowers, and my heart is inexhaustible,
my meager contribution is but a drop, insignificant compared to the empty space.
I lightly present this as something heard.
I humbly send this with awe and perspiration. Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
Scholar 顧疌 (Gù Jié) respectfully conveyed the imperial decree,
to bestow a gilt-bronze ascetic Buddha statue and Buddha footprints,
along with offering implements, to be offered for worship.
I humbly reflect that in six years under the Bodhi tree, you transcended the four Māras.
With the thousand-spoked wheel of your feet, your virtue perfected ten thousand good deeds.
Thus, you enable those who hear and see to awaken and comprehend, and to dispel defilements upon encountering you.
The heavenly grace is profound, extended to commend and cover me.
I respectfully adorn the temple
and purify my body and mind.
Gazing up at the light of compassion,
I humbly await your glorious descent.
Even with a thousand eloquent speakers and four kinds of wisdom, one cannot express one's heart.
How can a light brush and weak bamboo slip convey gratitude?
Unable to contain my humble feelings,
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks. Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
Master of Records 周昂 (Zhōu Áng) respectfully conveyed the imperial decree, bestowing grace and consideration.
Your minister immediately proceeded to 建元寺 (Jiànyuán Sì) to await the Dharma body.
The golden mountain arrived and stopped.
The royal messenger inquired with solicitude; the glorious favor accumulated repeatedly.
I am speechless in expressing my gratitude; I cannot contain my humble feelings.
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks.
Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
Scholar 王景曜 (Wáng Jǐngyào) arrived and respectfully conveyed the imperial decree, extending an inquiry.
He also allowed your minister to follow the Śarīra into the palace to prostrate.
I respectfully observe that the autumn colors are clear and bright, foreshadowing an auspicious omen.
Your minister's body and mind have been free from obstacles and afflictions.
Tomorrow, I will respectfully accompany the precious casket.
I humbly bow and arrive with reverence.
It is as if I have grown wings without relying on supernatural powers.
My body ascends to the pure land, rising high to the celestial gates.
Treading on lotus flowers, this is beyond comparison.
Ascending the jeweled ladder cannot weigh against this.
Such special guidance and grace truly transcend my initial expectations.
Considering this earthly bondage, my joy and gratitude are boundless.
Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
Master of Records 陳僧聰 (Chén Sēngcōng) respectfully conveyed the imperial decree,
bestowing thirteen thousand pounds of copper
for the construction of the dew-receiving plate on the pagoda of 善覺寺 (Shànjué Sì).
This is called the treasure of 杻陽 (Niǔyáng),
and indeed the jade of 昆吾 (Kūn Wú).
Neither dry nor wet can change it; its wonder is seen in the nine divisions.
Adapting to cold and heat, it completes its use in the six pitches.
Moreover, a divine dragon carries its offspring, illuminating this wondrous pagoda.
A golden bird holds its belt, adorning this lofty spire.
函谷 (Hángǔ) would be ashamed of its songs,
and 臨淄 (Línzī) embarrassed by its auspicious omens.
The solar mirror holding the light is likened to the sun wheel.
The sweet dew entering the plate is truly called celestial wine.
My forest of words is inherently lacking, and my mind's eloquence is further ashamed.
I merely bear this profound grace; it is ultimately difficult to express my gratitude.
Unable to fully engrave this favor in my heart,
I respectfully submit this memorial.
Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
Scholar 王景曜 (Wáng Jǐngyào) respectfully conveyed the imperial decree, extending an inquiry.
He also allowed me to enter 光嚴殿 (Guāngyán Diàn) tomorrow to worship the Dharma body.

I respectfully observe that your minister, though crude, has received imperial grace. Tomorrow, I will respectfully arrive at the opening, thereby repeatedly ascending to the Pure Land. The accumulation of wind and depth of water are insufficient comparisons.
My humble heart trembles with joy, but I have no words to express my gratitude.
Unable to contain my humble feelings,
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks.
Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
I humbly observed the imperial decree,

appointing Supervising Construction Scholar 王曇明 (Wáng Tánmíng), Material Officer General 沈徽 (Shěn Huī), and Palace Guardsman 吳景 (Wú Jǐng) and others to oversee the construction of the pagoda at 善覺寺 (Shànjué Sì).
Therefore, I have received sacred grace, bestowing divine power.
These officials are commanded to construct this lofty spire.
The precious pagoda rises like clouds, needing no "Joyful Garden."
The crystal stands distinct, not like the "Dragon Sea."
Even a great turtle carrying mud is not sufficient to describe its grandeur.
Even cranes pulling ropes are inferior when compared to this.
Gazing up at your compassionate beneficence, my joy and gratitude are boundless.
Reflecting on my long-cherished wish, I privately shed tears and choke up.
Unable to fully engrave this favor in my heart,
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks.
Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], says:
Today, the imperial carriage proceeded to 善覺寺 (Shànjué Sì).
By divine power, the golden spire was erected.
It stands majestically, reaching high into the pure heavens,
connecting with the Kùlóu (庫樓) constellation and ascending further.
It is already tranquil and permanently equal to the Pure Land.
It will serve as a Buddhist work, eternally benefiting celestial and human beings.
Your minister's sincerity in bearing this favor on my head is one hundred times greater than ordinary.
Unable to contain my humble feelings,
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks.
Respectfully submitted.
The compassionate precious temple that you are building,
with the divine power of all Buddhas, does not require much effort.
As soon as you desired to exert power, it was immediately erected.
Visible and invisible beings rejoice and admire it; I also rejoice with them.
I regret that I cannot worship and behold it together with you.
This is my only regret.
This concludes the imperial decree.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
The imperial messenger respectfully conveyed the imperial decree,
bestowing two hundred thousand coins for your minister's Dharma assembly tomorrow,
and ten pounds each of white sandalwood, frankincense, and agarwood.
The imperial edict on yellow paper first opens the treasury.
Auspicious qi next gathers at the cassia palace.
Goods are weightier than tortoiseshell coins, and their fragrance surpasses beautiful herbs.
Scattering gold beneath the veranda only reaches military officials.
Accumulating grain to fill one's home barely benefits one's relatives.
None of these compare to using this to aid good fields, thereby opening the five coverings.
Entering this Dharma system will forever escape the four streams.
Even borrowing words from 敬祖 (Jìngzǔ), I would still be ashamed, finding it difficult to describe.
Even borrowing the eloquence of 君卿 (Jūnqīng), I would still know it is not enough to express thanks.
Unable to fully bear this favor,
I respectfully submit this memorial for your perusal.
Respectfully submitted.
Your minister, [given name omitted], submits:
The imperial messenger 呂文強 (Lǚ Wénqiáng) respectfully conveyed the imperial decree,
bestowing upon your minister one cypress pagoda pillar and ten thousand pounds of copper,
for the construction of the 天中天寺 (Tiānzhōngtiān Sì).
The nine provinces contribute gold; a thousand-zhang tree stands tall.
It will eternally illuminate the Dharma wheel, and a precious pagoda will soon rise.
The Xia would be ashamed of its divine cauldron; the Jin would detest its wind indicator.
It will allow blessings to cover the world and merit to reach boundless extents.
Your minister, with my mediocrity and foolishness, has received this supreme goodness.
Joy pervades my heart; the light of grace touches my countenance.
I have no words to express my gratitude for this inscribed favor.
Unable to bear it on my head,
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks. Respectfully submitted.
I have heard that
the nine regions are divided, and the four classes of people have different customs.
The murky waves are easily stained; the enterprise of wisdom is difficult to establish.
Therefore, the tranquil mirror of the Dharma body, when illuminated, responds.
It cleanses ignorance from the sea of desire,
and ferries sentient beings on the precious ship.
Sometimes, with light compassion and guidance, it abandons trivialities and smiles at pulling people with sorrow.
With eloquent words, it proclaims, and with slanting light, it enters the crown of the head.
Since the auspicious light manifested at the deer park, the golden river has hidden its brilliance.
Therefore, sentient beings in the Age of Degenerate Dharma yearn to have a form.
Though the thousand sages have different traces, their one wisdom follows the same path.
This disciple, [name omitted],
has long been lost in the waves of delusion, continuously flowing in the foam of suffering.
I have not grown the tree of intention nor lit the lamp of the mind.
But with a single thought of goodness, I respectfully build a thousand Buddhas.
Although the supreme and unconditioned ultimate form is difficult to discern,
and the subtle wisdom that is neither empty nor existent, who can observe it?
Yet, the dark hair like sunlight, and the lotus eyes like the moon face,
can perhaps eternally symbolize my sincerity and reverence, and forever entrust my heart's longing.
Bǐqiū Mǒujiǎ respectfully states.
I humbly consider that the Sun of Wisdom has hidden its light, and the Wheel of Compassion has ceased to respond.
Karma is driven by afflictions, and craving is woven with emotions.
We merely pity those who clasp the jewel in their garment, holding a precious name, yet are not enlightened.
Vainly we sigh over gold leaves, confused by empty words, until the crying stops.
If not for manifesting such excellent karma and establishing such wondrous affinities,
how can one leave this hall of the mind and move this cave of the body?
Therefore, the Shuǐjīng Lóngtǎ forever mourns and regrets the relic of the beard.
The Míngjìng Shíkān alone lingers over the lingering image.
Mǒujiǎ has long made a vow to extensively create one eighteen-foot dry-lacquer Buddha statue for all beings in the Six Realms and Four Births.
Years and months have already flowed by, and conditions are easily changed.
I always fear that this temporarily existing body might suddenly vanish like painted water,
and the retribution of returning to nothingness will be like a whirlwind, like lightning.
Now, therefore, I establish a sincere heart to fulfill this original vow.
So that its form is seen like a gathering of moons, and its traces are manifested like golden mountains.
Upon seeing its form, goodness may arise; upon hearing its name, evil may be abandoned.
Extinguish the pain and vexation of the six senses.
Remove the burning and scorching of the five fires.
But the four treasures are often empty, and the seven wealths are often lacking.
I look up at the twin lotuses and sigh alone.
I see the swastika, yet have no means.
If one can slightly part with their wealth from the five households and slightly donate the four necessities,
to form this hidden compassion and together achieve the cause and effect,
then the merit of a simple cloth will not only be for past lives,
but the reward of scattering flowers will truly be verified in future affinities.
Speaking of goodness, I am without extravagance.
In my words, I have much shame.
Respectfully stated.
In this prefecture, Qílánhán and Zhītí are established in rows.
Although many decorations are set up and abundant offerings are prepared,
observing their outward appearance, they are certainly splendid and luxurious.
But in the realm of intention, there is indeed something not yet widely promoted.
What is it?
Generally, casting gold, carving jade, hollowing lacquer, painting tiles—
this is indeed why we look up to transmit the manifested body and far extend spiritual awareness,
to admire the first dawn of the dragon vase,
and to follow the lingering reverence for the Crane Forest.
Therefore, sacrificing to spirits is as if they are present.
When the way of revering spirits reaches its utmost,
as the sage is now far away,
the principle of cherishing the sage must be profound.
The various temples in this land only temporarily display images on the day of manifestation;
from then onwards, they are sealed in boxes and chests.
Even to the extent that leaf-garments come off the body, and the flame-aureole departs the crown.
Sometimes ten venerables or five sages are kept together in one cupboard.
Or great bodhisattvas and tathāgatas are all hidden in one cabinet.
It can truly be said that the intention contradicts the action; the appearance is right, but the feeling is wrong.
The arrogant mind is abundant, but the diligent mind is scarce.
In ancient pagodas, red caskets only transmit relics.
The white umbrella on the elephant's head does not refer to the entire body.
Moreover, by painting images to commemorate the past,
it still causes officials and commoners to recognize reverence.
Casting gold into models
eventually made the lord of Yuè remember.
Matched with Lóng'ā, it can still leap from its scabbard.
Compared to tigers and rhinoceros, they are still said to come out of the box.
How much more so the greatest perfect compassion, the unsurpassed gathering of goodness,
whose name, when heard, removes afflictions, and whose form, when seen, leads one into the path!
Yet one can treat with contempt this carved incense, and store away this wooden image,
sealing away the crystal hair-curl, sealing the golden palm.
This is unlike Rājagṛha, where it long ago entered the four heavens.
And it is different from Jetavana, where the doors were closed for three months.
The jeweled hall oversees emptiness, and the jade steps are empty and spacious.
The thick curtains are not opened.
This is not like Dǒng Zhòngshū’s subtle scholarship.
The red walls are long covered.
It is like Hòu Bīn avoiding his enemies.
Moreover, the vast halls hang like clouds, and lofty ridges perch like birds.
If placed on a jade throne, adorned with gold inlays,
it certainly would not let dust obscure its magnificent form, nor eclipse its moon-like face.
With dense lapis lazuli windows,
light winds would naturally find it hard to enter.
And fine dragon-beard nets
would be enough to prevent flying swallows from passing through.
Moreover, the principle of reverence would certainly be exalted.
And the heart of prostration would be even more profound.
