Buddhism's eastward transmission was not yet particularly prominent.
It began in Luòjīng and flourished south of the Jiāng.
The late Commander of Cavalry, Wáng Shào of Lángyá Commandery,
possessed profound understanding and exceptional insight, believing in the subtle depths of the dharma.
To the north of his ancestor Wénxiàn Gōng, Chéngzǔ's ancestral temple, he built the Zhǐyuán Jīngshè (Zhiyuan Hermitage).
It was initially hedged with fragrant zhǐ trees,
hence its name was established based on the circumstance.
Although the halls and chambers were orderly and solemn, a precious stupa had not yet been erected.
Wáng Huàn, Wáng Shào's great-grandson, who was Minister of Personnel and Administrator of Southern Xúzhōu,
deeply understood the characteristics of the dharma and thoroughly comprehended its ultimate principles.
His diligent sincerity was outwardly manifest, and his benevolence inwardly pervasive.
For eleven years, he did not eat after midday.
Although he assisted in court affairs, his work was akin to tending a sacred grove.
Recently, he composed official documents for Xiāngzhōu and established his banner in Lílún,
his position rising with his years, his rank deepening with the seasons.
Reflecting on the emperor's profound favor and imperial affection,
he was entrusted with the important responsibility of a frontier commander in the east, a deep guardian of the outer defenses.
He merely wished to exhaust his abilities and wisdom, knowing no limit to what he could do,
to bring harmony to the people below and proclaim the sacred grace above.
However, he felt his strength was weak and the path distant, ultimately ashamed of his meager achievements.
Moreover, righteous deeds are confined to this life, while retribution manifests in the next.
This was not how to repay the immense bounty in the unseen world,
or to express sincere devotion in the distant eons.
Since leaving his official post at Hénggāo and retiring his insignia at Pàizhǔ,
he vowed to build a magnificent five-story stupa at the old temple.
He donated one-tenth of his provincial salary.
In total, he collected 360,000 (coins).
On the third day of the sixth month of Yǒngmíng 6 (488 CE) of Qí,
a propitious day when the wood element was about to begin its cycle,
a felicitous day when the Lord on High traversed the heavens,
he erected a lofty monument reaching to the azure clouds and planted profound foundations in the dark earth.
He reverently prayed that the imperial residence would receive blessings and that good fortune would return.
May the eight gods guard the chambers and all deities protect the body.
May the precious throne be eternally stable, firm as Mount Xūmí.
May the imperial lifespan be long and enduring, in line with the permanent abode.
May all saints extend auspiciousness.
May the celestial harmony be drawn from the utmost purity.
May the feudal kings be grand and prosperous.
May their noble lineage spread throughout Liáng and Chǔ.
May the many officials exemplify the virtue of deference.
May the common people demonstrate virtues worthy of honor.
May all sentient beings be joyful and content, their natures unharmed.
May abundant harvests bless the year, with surplus grain lying in the fields.
May the barbarians be brought to submission, and the border cities lay down their night watches.
May every household practice the Ten Virtues, and every person embrace the Six Pāramitās.
May demonic hordes bow their heads and heretics bend their knees.
May the fire be extinguished by removing its fuel, and swords be broken, their points blunted.
May the suffering in the netherworld be relieved without discrimination.
May divine transformation ascend to the highest heaven.
May the three realms and five paths all share this vow.

By inscribing a spiritual trace.
Like the venerable image,

Resplendent precious trees,

I wish to wander in that land,

The visible and invisible are orderly,

Indeed, the two cosmic forces harmonize their virtues,

Below, they penetrate deep springs;

The Ten Stages appear indistinctly in the imperial grove,

As for the matters recorded in silk scrolls, those manifesting auspicious diagrams,

None are like the "three-legged crow" reappearing after a thousand years,

These were not recorded in Shùn's day,
nor rarely descended in Yáo's years.
How could it merely be the red crow changing color,
or the black millet attracting attention?
Precious jade came from distant Běiróng,
crossing Ruòshuǐ to offer its essence.
Its luster was rare and wondrous,
unseen for ages.
White gold was recently discovered in Dōngshān,
cleaving the secluded cliffs to reveal auspiciousness.
It flowed over precipices and peaks,
unrecorded in the annals of great spirits.
Even the unsurpassed treasures of plain rings and the precious jewels of silver lamps are inferior to it.
However, gold, stone, and shell are hard, not a substance that floats.
Unless virtue is tempered and subtly cultivated,
and emotion reaches its peak to turn the spirit,
how could their solid, sinking bodies transform to reveal floating forms?
In the X month of Yǒngmíng 7 (489 CE),
an auspicious stone mysteriously emerged from Tiānjīn,
drifting in the sea, flowing back with the tide, returning to this place.
It displayed its uniqueness in Zhèhé and presented its wonder in the imperial garden.
Its luster was like fine jade, its color comparable to pure gold.
The Emperor, looking up, felt the deep gate was easily opened,
and inquired about the boundless mysterious responses.
Although the analysis of affairs is silent, the mind makes it an inch away.
He cherished its constant nature,
and praised its enduring quality.
There was nothing better than carving a wondrous image from Candana wood,
or depicting the lingering image beneath the Jīshù tree.
So he commanded skilled artisans
to engrave and carve it.
The spiritual form and auspicious flowers glowed as if divinely made.
As for the remnants of carving,
the discarded fragments,
whether round or square, large or small, all sank upon touching water.
He halted his chariot, paused his procession, and personally tested it.
It was truly because the Dharma-body was embodied
that it did not sink into the abyss of submerged jade.
But once separated by dissection,
it required the water of floating gold.
How supreme! Such a wondrous auspicious sign!
How marvelous it is!
I dare to inscribe this precious gift for the eternal blessings of heaven and humanity.

It universally covers all who soar.
How can it be limited to the three realms?
How can it stop at the ten directions?
Soaking the feet of ten thousand ages,
Lending a hand to a hundred kings.
One thought answers this,
Ten thousand years without end.
As enduring as the sun,
As long as the sky.
This temple was established by Cài Gōng, who campaigned in the west.
Formerly, he was part of the border command, participating in the initial construction.
Now, returning to tread its ground,
He observes the old and feels emotion.
Thus, this inscription is made,
To transmit its fragrant traces.
In Yǐngzhōu, in the third year of Yǒnghuī, at a certain year-cycle, month, first day of the month, and day.
The mountain spirits wander freely,
The land is far for practicing meditation.
Orchid chambers are thatched with fragrant grass,
Mountain ridge-roofs are framed against the smoke.
Looking south to the wilderness of Wū,
Looking north to the sky over Huái.
Distant are the forests and swamps,
Vast are the river fields.
With an empty mind, one observes tranquility,
With wisdom, pure enlightenment.
Remembering this place,
Sadly, it belongs to distant years.
Roaming in benevolence, relegated to the far,
Delighting in rewards, leaning on the banner.
Initiating the creation of a divine garden,
Accompanying the construction with spiritual rafters.
Gazing at the forbidden grounds, expanding the garden, observing the Jīu, clearing the mountains.
Carving stones to harmonize sounds,
Dwelling in principle, contemplating the profound.
The feathered banners moved far away,
Sadly parting from the pines and springs.
Entrusted with duties in the Eastern Kingdom,
Transforming one's presence in the Western Lotus.
Mountains changed, becoming level,
Grass and leaves decayed and shifted.
Again relying on the distant Hàn,
Again following the suspended banner.
Formerly departing from the wondrous tent,
Now attending the Brahma feast.
Eight times the sea crane soared,
Nine times the mountain cicada chirped.
The jade pendant of glory long concealed,
Noble deeds merely passed down.
As the clouds of Zhòu拱 gather,
We dare to announce the auspicious affinity.
Your humble servants reflect:
The Rightly Awakened One possesses great compassion and great pity,
Rescuing all sentient beings, providing a ferry for the masses.
I take refuge in the Three Jewels, reviving the sacred teachings.
I desire, together with all people within the four seas, to jointly arouse Bodhicitta and cultivate wholesome karma.
May the present and future generations forever create good causes and together ascend to the wondrous fruit.
It is appropriate to invite thirty śramanas who are well-versed in the Dharma-laksana and capable of propagation,
Each accompanied by two attendants, and one unsalaried official.
One hundred twenty catties of frankincense.
Five horses to be dispatched along separate routes to deliver sarira.
To erect pagodas in the previously mentioned prefectures.
For those without a designated temple,
A site with mountains and water at a temple location shall be chosen.
The pagoda shall be erected according to the former mountain.
For those without an existing temple, a pagoda shall be built at a pure and quiet temple site within that prefecture.
The responsible officials shall create a model and send it to the relevant prefecture.
For prefectures with many monks, three hundred sixty people.
Next, two hundred forty people.
Next, one hundred twenty people.

If there are few monks, all available monks shall perform services for me, the Empress, the Crown Prince, the various princes, grandchildren, and all officials, both inside and outside the court, all common people, and all beings, visible and invisible.
Each shall perform rites for seven days and repent.
From the day the rites begin, strike the bell, regardless of whether it's the same prefecture or a different one.
Allow people to make donations.
The money limit is ten cash or less.
It must not exceed ten cash.
The donated money shall be used to construct the pagoda.
If the amount is insufficient, conscript able-bodied men and use treasury funds. Monks and nuns throughout the land
Shall universally hold vegetarian feasts for the sarira.
The deadline is the fifteenth day of the tenth month, at noon.
Simultaneously inter them in the stone caskets.
From the Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngguǎn) and Prefect (Cìshǐ) downwards to the County Commandant (Xiànwèi) upwards,
Cease military affairs and suspend regular duties for seven days.
Specially supervise the performance of rites and the striking of bells, etc.
Strive with utmost sincerity and reverence to fulfill my intention.
The responsible officials shall implement this.
First year of Rénshòu, sixth month, thirteenth day, declared by Nèishǐ Lìng, Yùzhāng Wáng, your servant Jiǎn.
When the Emperor was still a hidden dragon,
A Brahmin śramana came to his residence.
He produced a sarira and said,
"Your patron is of good heart,
Therefore, I leave this for your veneration."
After the śramana left,
He sought it but did not know its whereabouts.
Afterwards, the Emperor and the śramana Tánqiān
Each placed sarira in their palms and counted them.
Sometimes there were few, sometimes many,
And they could not be fixed.
Tánqiān said,
"I once heard a Brahmin say that the Dharma-body transcends quantity and is not measurable by worldly means."
Thereupon, he first made a seven-jeweled casket to place them in.
The divine nun Zhìxiān said,
"The Buddhist Dharma is about to perish,
All divine beings have now gone west.
My child, you shall be the compassionate father of all under heaven, reviving the Buddhist Dharma.
All divine beings will return."
Afterwards, the Zhōu dynasty indeed suppressed Buddhist Dharma.
The Suí court received the mandate and revived it.
The Emperor often spoke of the divine nun, saying,
"My rise is due to the Buddha."
Therefore, in all sarira pagodas throughout the realm,
Images of the divine nun were made.
The Emperor and Empress, at the Fǎjiè Nísì in the capital,
Constructed a continuous-base stupa to fulfill an old vow.
Sarira were enshrined beneath it.
In the fifteenth year of Kāihuáng, during the late autumn night, there was a divine light.
It ascended from the base, circling clockwise around the lùpán.
It blazed like the flames of a smelting furnace.
This occurred four times within ten days.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of the first year of Rénshòu, the Emperor,
In the Rénshòu Hall of Rénshòu Palace,
On the day of his birth,
Year after year, on this day, with deep sincerity, he forever remembered
To cultivate blessings and good deeds to repay the kindness of his parents.
Therefore, he welcomed many eminent śramanas to discuss the ultimate path, intending to select thirty high and serene locations in various prefectures throughout the land to erect sarira pagodas.
The Emperor then personally took the seven-jeweled casket,
Presented thirty sarira,
Brought them out from within, and placed them on the imperial table.
Together with the śramanas, he burned incense and bowed in reverence.
He vowed that his disciples would always uphold the Three Jewels with the Right Dharma,
To rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
Then he took thirty gold vases and thirty lapis lazuli vases.
The gold vases were placed within the lapis lazuli vases.
The sarira were placed inside.
Frankincense was used as mud,
To seal their lids and impress them.
All thirty prefectures were instructed to inter them in bronze and stone caskets at noon on the fifteenth day of the tenth month.
All pagodas were to be erected simultaneously.
All the śramana, with diligence and devotion,
carried the śarīra and proceeded.
Upon first entering the prefecture's border, they first ordered every household to sprinkle and sweep, covering all filth and evil.
Laypeople and monastics, men and women, the entire city came out to welcome them from afar.
The Zǒngguǎn, Cìshǐ, and all officials
lined the road, walking to lead the way.
The four assemblies of the faithful had dignified and solemn demeanor.
Together, they brought precious canopies, banners, streamers, flower daises, image palanquins, Buddha tents, Buddha carriages, incense mountains, incense bowls, and all kinds of music,
all coming to make offerings.
Each held incense and flowers, some burning, some scattering.
They encircled and chanted praises, with harmonious and elegant Sanskrit sounds.
Following the dharma of the Āhán Jīng for the śarīra entering Kuṣinagara,
people from near and far gathered like clouds and mist.
Even the blind, the lame, the old, and the sick all crawled to get there.
The śramana faced the four assemblies of the faithful and proclaimed,
“The Most Honored One, with the boundless and infinite great compassion of a Bodhisattva, pities sentient beings to the very marrow of their bones.
Therefore, the śarīra are distributed to share good causes with all under Heaven.”
They also cited sūtra passages and various expedient means,
admonishing and instructing.
Deeply moved and sorrowful, tears fell like rain.
The great assembly, with one heart, joined their palms and knelt on their right knees.
Then the śramana read aloud the repentance text, saying:
“I, the Bodhisattva-precept-holding Buddha disciple, Emperor [Mǒu],
respectfully report to all Buddhas of the ten directions and three times, all Dharmas, and all worthy and sagely Saṅgha.
This disciple, by the blessings of the Three Jewels, serves as sovereign and father to the common people.
I wish to attain Bodhi together with all citizens.
Now I desire to distribute the śarīra to various prefectures to erect stūpas.
I wish for all to universally cultivate good karma and ascend to the wondrous fruit.

For this disciple, and the Empress, the Crown Prince, the numerous princes and their descendants, internal and external officials, all living beings visible and invisible in all Dharma realms, and those in the three evil paths and eight difficulties,
I perform repentance and practice the Way.
I respectfully invite the eternally abiding Buddhas of the ten directions, the twelve divisions of sūtras, the profound Dharma treasury, all revered Bodhisattvas, and all worthy and sagely ones.
May you arise compassion and accept the invitation of this disciple and others.
Descend to this place of practice to bear witness to this disciple's open repentance for all sentient beings.”
Thereupon, they prostrated according to the Dharma and all received the Three Refuges.
The śramana then declared,
“I, the Bodhisattva-precept-holding Buddha disciple, Emperor [Mǒu],
universally and openly repent for all sentient beings of the ten evil karmas committed since beginningless time.
Committing them myself, teaching others to commit them, and rejoicing upon seeing them committed.
By these karmic causes, one falls into hell, hungry ghost, or animal realms.
If born as a human, one has a short life, many illnesses,
is lowly, poor, holds wrong views, and is flattering and devious.
Afflictions and delusions prevent self-awakening.
Now, illuminated by the compassionate light of the Tathāgata,
regarding those numerous sins,
I have finally awakened to them.
My heart is deeply ashamed and remorseful, my fear endless.
Before the Three Jewels, I openly repent.
Relying on the Buddha's wisdom sun, I wish for all to be eliminated.
From this body until the attainment of Buddhahood,
I vow not to commit such sins again.”
When the great assembly heard these words,
they were deeply saddened, deeply joyful, deeply ashamed, and deeply fearful.
Engraving it in their hearts and carving it in their bones,
those who offered wealth, clothing, and even cut off their hair as offerings were countless.
Daily, they jointly held great vegetarian feasts, performed repentance rituals, and received precepts.
They requested to cultivate good and cease evil from now on.
Life after life, world after world, may they always be great ministers and subjects of the Dà Suí dynasty.
Without distinction of age, ethnicity, or region, all made this vow.
Even butchers and cruel criminals personally contemplated goodness.
When the śarīra were about to be placed in the casket,
the great assembly encircled them, packing and blocking the way.
The śramana held high the precious vase, touring it among the four assemblies.
Everyone wiped their eyes, gazed intently, and together beheld the bright light.
Their wails of sorrow and longing sounded like thunder.
Heaven and earth trembled for it.
All places where they were installed were like this.
The true body, having responded, the numinous stūpa will exist forever.
All under Heaven look up to and take refuge, and their blessings increase endlessly.
On the morning the stūpa was erected, the Emperor
stood facing west, holding a ceremonial jade tablet, in the Dàxīng Hall courtyard of the Dàxīng Palace.
He invited the Buddha image and three hundred sixty-seven śramana.
With banners, canopies, incense, flowers, praises, and music,
they came from Dàxīngshàn Temple and resided in the palace hall.
The Emperor burned incense and prostrated.
He descended to the eastern corridor,
personally leading civil and military officials.
They observed a vegetarian diet and kept precepts.
At that time, from the inner palace, the Eastern Palace, and throughout the capital,
to the vast multitude of dwellings accessible by boat and carriage,
all relatives and people universally upheld the sacred Dharma.
When the monks first entered,
an imperial edict ordered attendants on the left and right to secretly count them.
From Xiǎnyáng Gate to ascending the steps, they counted three times.
There was always one extra person.
The Emperor saw one unusual monk with his kasaya covering his shoulders.
He said to his attendants,
“Startle him; place him there. When he leaves,
count again.” Indeed, the one with the kasaya covering his shoulders no longer appeared.
When the śarīra were about to depart,
the Emperor said,
“Now that the Buddha Dharma is being revived, there must be a karmic response.”
Afterward, reports from various places all confirmed what he said.
In Yōngzhōu, a stūpa was erected at Xiānyóu Temple.
The weather was cloudy and snowy.
On the day the śarīra were to be interred, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were placed in the casket,
the clouds gathered again.
In Qízhōu, a stūpa was erected at Fèngquán Temple.
When they were about to make the casket,
twenty lǐ northeast of the temple,
four sections of veined stone were suddenly discovered.
They were lustrous like jade,
and perfectly even in size.
They were then taken to make the inner casket.
Thereupon, on the south wall of the large casket, a distinct color shone brightly,
forming the shape of twin trees.
They were three chǐ three cùn high,
with stems like pure white snow,
and leaves like agate.
On the north and east walls were shapes of birds, beasts, dragons, and elephants.
All four walls had flower shapes, rotating left and right.
Later, the foundation stones gradually changed, all becoming like crystal.
The śramana Dàoyán made a drawing of these twin trees and placed it in Xǔzhōu.
The leaves all turned green.
The following year, at Dàbǎochāng Temple in Qízhōu,
a copy of the auspicious image from Shǎnzhōu was obtained and placed in the Buddha hall,
to be worshipped before the door.
The great image thrice emitted red light,
flowing out of the door.
Then, outside the door, the thousand Buddha images and Guānshìyīn Púsà also frequently emitted light.
Within half a month, celestial flowers fell twice.
In Jīngzhōu, a stūpa was erected at Dàxīngguó Temple.
When they were about to make the casket,
three families each offered old, well-ground beautiful stones.
They were not native to the area.
They were then used and fit perfectly.
In Qínzhōu, a stūpa was erected at Jìngniàn Temple.
Previously, a monk of the temple dreamt that immortals descended and gathered, measuring the ground with a red cord and marking it with iron pegs.
When the stūpa foundation was determined,
it was exactly in that spot.
Again, auspicious clouds came to cover the śarīra.
At that time, it was October and snow fell,
yet the plants and trees near the temple all blossomed.
When the śarīra were about to be placed in the casket,
divine light shone far and wide.
Within the empty space, there were also sounds of praise.
In Huázhōu, a stūpa was erected at Sījué Temple.
The weather was cloudy and snowy.
On the day the śarīra were to be interred, the sun shone brightly.
There was a five-colored aura of light,
several zhàng above the ground,
shaped like a chatra.
It covered the top of the stūpa precisely.
From several tens of lǐ away,
looking at it from afar,
it was pure red and extended upwards to the sky.
After the śarīra were interred, clouds and mist rose again.
Auspicious snow scattered like celestial flowers,
landing on people's clothes but not wetting them for a long time.
In Tóngzhōu, a stūpa was erected at Dàxīngguó Temple.
The śarīra lodged at a nearby relay station.
It rained that night. The next morning, when the palanquin proceeded,
clouds and sun welcomed it, clearing up.
It entered through the south gate,
while it continued to rain as before in the north of the city.
Upon reaching the temple,
it became cloudy and rainy again.
Just before being placed in the casket,
the sun came out.
Many colored lights surrounded the sun like a wheel.
Previously, the temple monk Huìzhēn
dreamt of a holy person with a round halo around his neck, illuminating heaven and earth, coming from the west, entering the gate, and standing there.
When the śarīra palanquin arrived,
it stopped without reason at that very spot.
Thus, the stūpa foundation was determined there.
On the night of the eighth day of the twelfth month,
there was a five-colored round light
rising from the foundation, illuminating the entire city,
bright as day.
It was seen for fifty lǐ around.
The following year, in April, white light rose from the west of the stūpa,
shining to the east of the stūpa,
and disappeared after a long while.
Púzhōu built a stupa at Qīyán Sì.
On the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month,
the śarīra were at Rénshòu Sì under the prefectural administration.
That night, the hall was as bright as day.
On the twenty-eighth day, the foundation was laid.
The next day, the earth shook greatly and the mountains roared loudly.
There were sounds of bells and drums on the rock face.
On the seventh day of the tenth month, the śarīra were taken to Qīyán.
The earth moved again.
On the eighth day, the palanquin ascended the mountain, followed by thousands of people.
A strong wind came from below and rose upwards.
Carried by the wind, it soon reached the Buddha hall.
That night, there was a light on the stupa.
It was several feet long,
appearing and disappearing over ten times.
Inside the vase, there were also five streams of light that radiated out.
They then converged back into the vase.
There were also two lights,
both as large as bowls,
emerging from the west wall.
They merged into one stream and flowed into the stupa foundation.
It extinguished after a meal's time.
Soon after, it reappeared
and flowed into the hall.
There was also a great light on the mountain peak,
illuminating two hundred lǐ.
Those who observed from afar all said the mountain was burning.
On the night of the ninth, two more lights circled the stupa; one stream illuminated the west valley,
and the other stream illuminated the south valley.
On the twelfth, there was again a light in the hall, shaped like an incense burner.
It flowed to the stupa's dew plate
and extinguished after some time.
That night, there was again light on the dew plate,
sometimes scattered, sometimes gathered,
all resembling lotus flowers.
It extinguished after a watch.
On the night of the thirteenth, there was again light on the stupa,
resembling three Buddha images.
All were one chǐ high.
They remained for a long time.
On the night of the fourteenth, there were three streams of light
emerging from the hall.
One went straight up to the sky.
One flowed to the northeast.
One was shaped like a multi-storied building and illuminated the prefectural city brightly.
From the new moon to the full moon,
the temple and the city
constantly smelled of exotic fragrance.
Peach, plum, apricot, and crabapple trees bloomed profusely.
People gathered them for offerings.
On the night the śarīra were enshrined, there was again light,
emerging again from the stupa.
It was round like a large mirror.
Most of the lights were purplish-red,
but their appearance varied for those who saw them.
Some said it was like a great lightning bolt,
others like a blazing fire.
Two or three out of ten saw nothing at all.
There was a woman carrying her newly deceased infant, begging for help.
By night, the child revived.
Many encountered the light and were cured of their illnesses.
All prefectures experienced such phenomena,
but Qīyán Sì had the most.
This was because it was built by Tàizǔ Wǔyuán Huángdì.
Bìngzhōu built a stupa at the old Wúliàngshòu Sì.
The śarīra were initially in the dào chǎng.
The multitude bowed in reverence.
Those severely ill were cured.
On the morning the stupa was built, clouds and mist darkened the day.
Only afterwards did the sun shine brightly.
Five-colored clouds surrounded it.
When the śarīra were about to be enshrined, they emitted light, some one chǐ, some five cùn.
Innumerable heavenly deities
each held incense, flowers, banners, streamers, and precious canopies, covering the entire prefectural city.
Dìngzhōu built a stupa at Héngyuè Sì.
There was an extraordinary old man
who came to pay homage and offered a bolt of cloth.
He carried several baskets of earth.
People asked his name but he did not answer.
He suddenly disappeared.
This place previously had no water.
In the third year of Kāihuáng, when the temple was first being built, Báilóng Yuān, eight lǐ to its west, suddenly flowed eastward.
When the work stopped, the water ceased.
When the new stupa was about to be built,
the water flowed greatly again.
Xiāngzhōu built a stupa at Dàcí Sì.
The weather was overcast and snowy.
When the śarīra were about to descend, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were enshrined, the clouds gathered again.
In the eighth month of the year after the stupa was built,
Guāngtiān Nísì obtained a painting of auspicious signs from Shǎnzhōu.
It was placed in the Buddha hall.
Divine light frequently emitted like lightning.
There was also a five-colored cloud canopy,
directly above the hall.
It was seen four times in one day.
There were also white clouds,
shaped like trees, with fine rain of golden flowers.
The two flowers were shaped like large butterflies,
their color like blue lapis lazuli.
They hovered without descending,
then soared into the void and departed.
In the next year, in the first month, the temple again rained heavenly flowers.
Zhèngzhōu built a stupa at Dìngjué Sì.
When the śarīra were about to arrive,
there was a light east of the temple,
like a large shooting star.
It entered before the Buddha hall and vanished.
When the palanquin reached this spot, it stopped without cause.
Afterwards, the stupa foundation was laid on the west bank.
On the east bank, the old śarīra stupa had two lights
that flowed westward into the foundation site.
The temple monks held a vegetarian feast for two thousand people.
However, over ten thousand people ate, yet it was not exhausted.
One jar of rice produced over eighty basins of leftover food.
It fed two hundred temple members
and was exhausted only after several days.
When the śarīra were about to be enshrined,
the banners hanging on all four sides turned inward simultaneously without wind.
Sōngzhōu built a stupa at Xiánjū Sì.
Over ten thousand people followed the śarīra.
A rabbit ran up the slope against the procession, passed under the palanquin, and departed.
The weather was overcast and snowy.
When the śarīra were about to descend, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were enshrined, the clouds gathered again.
Bózhōu built a stupa at Kāijì Sì.
There was no stone in the region.
When the śarīra arrived,
three ready-ground square stones were obtained from three different places.
One resembled a case but had no bottom.
They were combined and used.
No modification was needed.
When digging the stupa foundation to the bedrock,
there were two undulating wells flanking it.
The weather was overcast and snowy.
When the śarīra were about to descend, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were enshrined, the clouds gathered again.
Rǔzhōu built a stupa at Xīngshì Sì.
The weather was overcast and snowy.
When the śarīra were about to descend, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were enshrined, the clouds gathered again.
Tàizhōu built a stupa at Dàiyuè Sì.
When the śarīra arrived in the prefecture,
that night there was a drum sound inside the Yuè Miào.
As dawn approached,
the triple gates all opened by themselves.
Some saw thirty horsemen emerge from the temple.
These were the Mountain God's retinue.
As the śarīra traveled from the prefecture to the temple,
having gone several lǐ,
a cloud canopy emerged from the mountaintop,
five-colored and triple-layered.
White qi, like a rainbow,
came to cover the śarīra, scattering into a great mist that dampened people's clothes.
Its appearance was like hanging pearls.
Its taste was like sweet dew.
From dawn until noon,
the mist gathered and returned to the mountain,
dividing into three sections.
It came and went,
like an army on the move.
This was also the Mountain God coming to welcome them.
At this, there was a sound within the vase and light emitted,
over one zhàng high.
It extinguished after a meal's time.
People scrutinized it
and saw that the golden vase lid inside the lapis lazuli opened by itself.
At the mouth of the vase was an inch of light like a chopstick,
brightly pointing west.
Although it rapidly turned, it never deviated.
This continued for eight days.
When about to be enshrined,
the light then scattered out
and returned into the golden vase, and clouds and mist rose again.
There was a child who could recite the Fǎhuá Jīng
who came to pay homage to the śarīra.
He then burned his body in the wilderness as an offering.
In the second month of the next year, on the sixth day,
the drums of Tàishān rang throughout the night.
Listening to the north, east, and west, it was the same.
Qīngzhōu built a stupa at Shèngfú Sì.
The foundation was dug five chǐ deep,
encountering bedrock that naturally formed a large case.
It was consequently used.
As the śarīra were about to be placed,
there was light within the vase,
moving up and down.
Móuzhōu built a stupa at Jùshénshān Sì.
When the śarīra first arrived,
two large purple zhǐ suddenly appeared on the road.
The weather was overcast and snowy.
When the śarīra were about to descend, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were enshrined, the clouds gathered again.
Suízhōu built a stupa at Zhìmén Sì.
On the sixth day of the tenth month, when digging the foundation, a divine turtle was unearthed.
On the seventh day, sweet dew descended upon a poplar tree by a stone bridge.
Innumerable black bees came to encircle it.
On the eighth day, at dawn, there was a great fog.
When the relics were brought to the temple,
the sky immediately cleared.
Passing through Guānghuà Xiàn,
a tree with joined branches was suddenly seen inside the gate.
Passing under a poplar tree,
five streams of sweet dew flowed down,
sprinkling upon the carriage.
Afterwards, it became overcast.
When the relics were about to be lowered, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were placed in the casket, the clouds gathered again.
The divine turtle had a remarkably unique appearance and color.
There was an inscription on its belly that read:
"Wáng Xīngzhōu, the military advisor, offered this."
Every day, when the casket was opened to view its head,
it would retract and could not be seen.
When the imperial envoy and director of the Bureau of Authorship, Wáng Shào, was ordered to inspect it,
the turtle extended its neck and legs fully,
allowing people to turn it over at will.
This continued for several days.
Then an inscription was seen on its head which read:
"Great King Eight, Eight."
"Seventy million years."
The Emperor personally touched and observed it.
When taken into his bosom or sleeve, it naturally became docile.
When released into the palace pond or grass,
it would return directly to the Emperor's presence.
Each time it was released, it would do the same.
Xiāngzhōu built a stupa at Dàxīngguó Sì.
The weather was overcast and dark.
When the relics were about to be lowered, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were placed in the casket, the clouds gathered again.
Yángzhōu built a stupa at Xī Sì.
The prefecture had suffered a long drought.
When the relics entered the territory,
that night, a great rain fell abundantly.
Jiǎngzhōu built a stupa at Qīxiá Sì.
A neighbor had dreamt beforehand
that the Buddha came from the northwest,
with jeweled canopies, banners, and flowers illuminating everything.
All the monks of the temple, holding flowers and incense, went out to welcome him.
When the relics arrived, it was exactly as dreamt.
Wúzhōu built a stupa at Dàyǔ Sì.
The relics crossed the Jiāng River five times in total.
No winds or waves arose.
Upon arriving at the temple, they emitted blue, yellow, red, and white light.
Purple ganoderma over two feet tall was found,
with four stems sharing three caps.
The weather was overcast and dark.
When the relics were about to be lowered, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were placed in the casket, the clouds gathered again.
Sūzhōu built a stupa at Hǔqiū Shān Sì.
This place was the qín terrace of Wáng Xún, the Minister of Education of the Jìn dynasty.
A brick casket was unearthed,
containing a silver box with one relic.
When floated in a bowl of water, it rotated clockwise four times.
When the relics first departed the prefecture,
rain fell.
Before reaching the temple, the sun came out.
Then multicolored clouds
followed the carriage,
lingering without dispersing.
Upon reaching the stupa site,
music was heard in the air.
Afterwards, the sky became overcast again.
When the relics were about to be lowered, the clouds temporarily parted.
As soon as the relics were placed in the casket, the clouds gathered again.
Before this, a stone well was dug inside the temple.
The well roared for two days,
which was an omen of the relics' impending arrival.
Héngzhōu built a stupa at Héngyuè Sì.
Monks carried the relics by water from Jiānglíng for over two thousand lǐ.
They encountered headwind four times.
When they wished for it to stop, it stopped.
They asked for tailwinds four times,
and all their desires were met.
When the foundation was first dug on Róng Fēng,
a white cloud, over two zhàng wide,
very neat and straight, came to the foundation site, circled it clockwise three times, and then dispersed.
Afterwards, it became overcast and dark.
When the relics were about to be lowered, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were placed in the casket, the clouds gathered again.
Guìzhōu built a stupa at Yuánhuà Sì.
When the relics were still over ten lǐ from the city,
thousands of birds flew in formation alongside the carriage.
They dispersed upon entering the city.
When the relics were about to be placed in the stupa,
five-colored clouds came to cover them.
Pānzhōu built a stupa at Língjiù Shān Sì in Hóngyáng Xiāng, Chóngyáng Lǐ.
Three stone caskets, placed during the late Sòng dynasty, were unearthed.
Two of them each contained a bronze casket,
holding two small silver statues.
One contained a silver vase holding a gold vase.
It is suspected that there were originally relics,
but now it is empty.
Afterwards, within the pit, there was an auspicious sign of cloud-like energy, as of immortals.
In the time of Liú Yìlóng, the ruler of Sòng,
there was a holy monk from Tiānzhú, Qúnhàbámó.
On his way to Yángdū, he passed Língjiù Sì,
and told the monks:
"There will soon be an extraordinary auspicious sign here.
Moreover, when a king ascends and comes, there will be a corresponding establishment.
Ultimately, when a holy lord, a Bodhisattva, comes, he will greatly expand and propagate it."
That winter, indeed, a flock of swallows jointly carried an embroidered image and deposited it inside the hall.
When Xiāo Dàochéng, the ruler of Qí, was first Prefect of Shǐxīng,
he visited this temple and built a white stupa.
In the third year of Tiānjīa of the Chén dynasty, a stele was erected in the temple with this inscription.
Such a holy lord's expansion and propagation is verified today.
Jiāozhōu built a stupa at Chánzhòng Sì.
Yìzhōu built a stupa at Fǎjù Sì.
The weather was overcast and dark.
When the relics were about to be lowered, the sun shone brightly.
As soon as they were placed in the casket, the clouds gathered again.
Kuòzhōu built a stupa at Fǎjiǎng Sì.
When the relics first departed the capital and lodged in Língāo,
a monk dreamt of losing the relics.
That night, Kuòzhōu had a light,
several zhàng high,
coming from the east and entering the temple.
It circled the Buddha stupa clockwise,
illuminating both inside and outside the city walls with brilliant clarity.
Those watching from afar suspected it was burning firewood.
The light gradually moved west and vanished after a short while.
The stupa's foundation was set exactly where the light disappeared.
There was also an unusually rich and fragrant aroma.
Guāzhōu built a stupa at Chóngjiào Sì.
Guózhōu reported,
though the prefecture did not receive relics,
they also invited monks to practice the Way.
A strange bird came and gathered on the beam.
It seemed to listen to the sutras without being startled or moving.
After one day and one night, it descended and stopped on the sutra-reading platform.
Everyone praised and stroked it.
They also carried it during their practice of the Way.
The dharma master administered the precepts to it before the Buddha.
After a long while, it left.
Wáng Wēi, the judicial clerk of Suízhōu, was escorting ninety exiles.
They encountered the relics on the road.
All the prisoners were released.
They were given a distant meeting time and place, and not one failed to comply.
People of Suízhōu had set up three hundred fish traps in the Yǐn Shuǐ.
Upon seeing the relics,
they also released all the fish.
Other prefectures were like this;
such instances were probably many.
During this tenth month, the Emperor
repeatedly found relics under his teeth during meals.
The Empress also did the same.
One was floated in a silver bowl of water
and shown to the officials.
In a moment, two were suddenly seen clinging together, rotating clockwise.
The two noblemen, along with Jìn Wáng Zhāo and Yùzhāng Wáng Jiǎn, were granted clams.
They were ordered to inspect them carefully.
Each found one relic inside a clam.
Within less than two decades,
nineteen relics were found within the palace in total.
Many emitted brilliant light.
From then on, people, both distant and near, lay and monastic,
offered all the relics they possessed.
The Emperor said,
"How can they all be genuine?"
The various śramaṇas collectively tested them.
Indeed, there were thirteen 'jade grains'.
The genuine relics were struck with iron but remained undamaged.
Your ministers, Xióng and others, say:
Your ministers have heard that the Great Enlightenment is perfectly complete, its truth illuminating both emptiness and existence.
The Utmost Sage is quiescent and still, his essence free from birth and death.
Therefore, even if his form is scattered like dust motes, it is still preserved in golden caskets.
Though his body is dispersed like blown dust, it still gives rise to precious pagodas.
Since the request for the ashes by Shìtí and later,
and the construction of stupas by Yùwáng,
there have been no distributions of relics to advance this sacred undertaking.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty, having accumulated causes over countless kalpas, has long attained Bodhi.
Descending as a human king, you protect this world.
In former times, the Way declined in fortune, and benevolent temples were ruined.
The lamp of compassion extinguished its light, and the ocean of wisdom ceased its flow.
Now that the imperial dynasty has risen, the Dharma drum is truly reverberating.
Within the entire realm, all has become a pure land; all living beings are covered by the Brahma cloud.
Last summer, in the sixth month, an imperial edict was issued,
inviting monks to escort the relics.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month, pagodas were simultaneously erected in thirty prefectures.
At Qīyán Sì in Púzhōu, the site chosen for the pagoda construction,
there were sounds of bells and drums on this mountain.
The relics were inside the lecture hall.
That night, a great brilliant light emanated from the pagoda in front,
extending into the hall, illuminating the entire room.
When the relics were about to be placed in the bronze casket,
another light appeared, like an incense burner,
ascending through the air to the precious vase of the pagoda.
Then purple flames arose,
sometimes scattering, sometimes gathering,
all forming lotus flowers.
There was also a bright light
above the pagoda, shaped like a Buddha image, with a perfectly formed lotus pedestal.
It remained for a long time before gradually fading away.
Another light appeared,
encircling the precious vase of the pagoda.
The monks of Rénshòu Sì within Púzhōu city gazed from afar at the mountaintop.
The light was like a tower,
making the mountain peaks and valleys clearly visible.
It illuminated the southeastern corner of the prefectural city
for a long time without diminishing.
That Qīyán Sì was built by Tài Zǔ Wǔ Yuán Huángdì.
Also, at the site of the pagoda in Huàzhōu,
at that time, though there were clouds, fog, and heavy snow,
it suddenly cleared up.
Directly above the pagoda, there was a five-colored wheel,
and after the relics were placed, the clouds and fog returned.
The Emperor and Empress also obtained relics,
which radiated brilliance and scattered colors, sometimes appearing, sometimes disappearing.
If not for utmost virtue, sincere devotion, and alignment with spiritual sanctity,
how could such divine power and wondrous signs manifest these extraordinary wonders?
Your ministers are fortunate to live in this prosperous era,
having witnessed a time of great peace.
We live to encounter this good karma,
finally escaping the realm of worldly troubles.
We cannot but leap with joy.
We respectfully submit this memorial to offer our congratulations.
Let it be known.
Your Majesty reflects that the Righteous Enlightenment protects all beings.
It saves living beings from the sea of suffering,
and rescues the ignorant from the burning house.
Therefore, I sincerely dedicate myself, forming thoughts of reliance and refuge.
I wish for all subjects and common people within the realm, as well as those in the unseen and visible worlds,
to jointly uphold this sacred undertaking and together create good causes.
Hence, I distributed the relics and built divine pagodas.
And the Great Sage, out of compassion, frequently displayed auspicious lights.
Within the palace, relics descended miraculously, their origin unknown,
appearing naturally.
We joyfully placed them on our heads, having experienced something unprecedented.
This is truly the great fortune of all beings, extending this auspicious blessing.
How could it be due to my humble sincerity alone that such a response was evoked?
Reading the memorials from the princes and dukes, my awe and reverence deepen.
I, along with the princes, dukes, and all common people,
should redouble our efforts to promote and strengthen the Three Jewels.
Now there are still fifty true forms of the relics.
The relevant authorities should follow the previous method and distribute them throughout the country.
May all beings in the three evil paths and six realms be freed from their hindrances,
and may all sentient beings attain the wondrous fruit.
The responsible officials are to implement this.
The envoys from the three kingdoms of Gāolì, Bǎijì, and Xīnnluó were about to return.
Each requested one relic to build a pagoda and offer veneration in their respective countries.
The imperial edict granted permission for all.
An imperial edict ordered the construction of a pagoda at Dàxīngshàn Sì in the capital.
The relics were first placed in the Imperial Secretariat's main hall.
They departed on the morning of the second day of the twelfth month.
At that time, the sky was clear, the air was mild, and the wind was calm.
Precious carriages, banners, streamers, incense, flowers, music, and all sorts of offerings filled the streets.
Monks and laypeople, men and women, numbered countless millions.
Their attire and procession were orderly and dignified.
The Grand Pillar of the State and Sīkōng, Āndé Wáng Xióng, and those below him, all walked on foot to the temple.
A grand "unhindered assembly" (wúzhē dàhuì) was held, and penitential rites were performed.
There was a blue magpie that mingled among the crowd.
Some drew their sabers and threw them as offerings.
They landed among the people without harming anyone.
On the twenty-third day of the first month of Rénshòu Nǐán two,
relics were again distributed to fifty-one prefectures to establish sacred pagodas.
The governor-generals, prefects, and officials from county lieutenants upwards,
were ordered to suspend normal duties for seven days to invite monks to perform rites.
They were taught to beat the gong and donate ten coins.
All followed the previous practice.
The date was set for the eighth day of the fourth month, at noon.
Throughout the entire country and its dominion, the relics were simultaneously placed and sealed into stone caskets.
The auspicious signs that occurred were separately recorded as follows:
Héngzhōu, Quánzhōu, Xúnzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Hóngzhōu, Hángzhōu,
Liángzhōu, Dézhōu, Cāngzhōu, Guānzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Jìzhōu,
Yōuzhōu, Xúzhōu, Jǔzhōu, Qízhōu, Láizhōu, Chǔzhōu,
Jiāngzhōu, Tánzhōu, Máozhōu, Bèizhōu, Sòngzhōu, Zhàozhōu,
Jìzhōu, Yǎnzhōu, Shòuzhōu, Xìnzhōu, Jīngzhōu, Liángzhōu,
Lánzhōu, Lìzhōu, Lùzhōu, Lízhōu, Cízhōu, Wèizhōu,
Biànzhōu, Qǐzhōu, Xǔzhōu, Yùzhōu, Xiǎnzhōu, Cáozhōu,
Ānzhōu, Jìnzhōu, Huáizhōu, Shǎnzhōu, Luòzhōu, Dèngzhōu,
Qínzhōu, Wèizhōu, Míngzhōu, Zhèngzhōu.
Héngzhōu's memorial states:
When the relics arrived at the prefecture to establish the sacred pagoda,
they reached the prefecture on the fourth day of the third month.
Immediately, together with the prefectural officials,
we surveyed and inspected the proposed site.
Only Lóngzàng Sì within the jurisdiction was suitable for constructing the pagoda.
On the tenth day of that month, the ground was measured and the foundation dug.
By the sixteenth day, at wèishí (1-3 PM),
a wind came from the south.
The fragrance within the temple was exceptionally unique and incomparable.
Monks, laypeople, officials, and private citizens all experienced it.
There was also an old man named Jīn Zàn,
who had suffered from anosmia, unable to smell fragrance or foul odors,
for over twenty years.
At that time, being among the crowd, he also smelled the fragrance.
Consequently, his nose was cured.
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
approaching noon, as the relics were about to be placed,
the light was bright and clear, the sky vast and cloudless.
From the sky, precious fragments and celestial flowers rained down,
resembling thin flakes of gold and silver,
of mixed sizes, scattering profusely
like falling snow.
First, they descended onto the stone casket at the pagoda's foundation,
then spread throughout the temple and the city.
All had varied colors, glittering with golden crystals reflecting the sun.
At that moment, people used their clothes to catch them,
and also picked them up from the ground.
A great multitude of over one hundred thousand monks and laypeople
all saw and obtained them.
Also, at two locations, east and west of the pagoda column, unusual vapors suddenly appeared.
Their color was yellowish-white, initially fine, then coarser,
like smoke from a beacon fire, twisting and turning like a dragon, ascending directly.
It circled the pagoda top, soaring into the clear sky.
Its length was immeasurable.
It disappeared after a long while.
There were also four white cranes
that came from the northeast, circled above the pagoda, and departed to the southwest.
By the twentieth day, at yǐshí (9-11 AM),
the pagoda foundation was just completed.
Again, precious fragments and celestial flowers rained down,
and what was collected filled one dòu (a unit of measure).
Then the attendant military officer, Wáng Liàng, was dispatched
to present them first.
The Emperor opened the flowers and found three more relics within the precious fragments.
He was exceedingly joyful.
Yíngzhōu's memorial states:
When digging the ground to place the stone casket for the relics,
at a depth of about six feet,
a truly purple light suddenly appeared from the earth.
It disappeared shortly after.
The earth then had black markings,
interspersed to form seal script characters that read:
"Zhuanlún Shèngwáng Fótǎ" (Buddha Pagoda of the Wheel-Turning Holy King).
We respectfully report this for your knowledge.
Lízhōu's memorial states:
When digging the foundation for the relic pagoda,
a tile inscription was found underground which read:
"May joy last for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years, unending."
Guānzhōu's memorial states:
Above the relic pagoda, there was a five-colored cloud shaped like a carriage canopy.
It appeared at noon that day and lasted until evening.
Wèizhōu reported:
The relics sent [to us] emitted light multiple times.
Furthermore, there were many sick people, some suffering from blindness, others from ailments of the five viscera.
They made vows and prostrated themselves, and their illnesses were all cured.
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
when the relics were about to be placed down,
at noon, the sky suddenly showed a piece of five-colored cloud,
whose fragrance was extraordinary.
In an instant, golden flowers descended.
On the morning of the ninth day, silver flowers again descended,
covering the entire city and administrative center.
The larger flowers were like elm pods,
the smaller ones resembled sparks.
Everyone was able to collect them in containers and offer them respectfully.
On that day, there also appeared a black dog with floppy ears and a white chest.
In front of the reliquary pagoda, it extended its left leg and bent its right leg.
Seeing people walking the path (performing circumambulation), it would get up and walk the path.
Seeing people observe vegetarianism, it would also observe vegetarianism.
It would not eat if given food at an improper time.
It only desired to drink clean water.
On the morning of the next day, it arose to break its fast.
Only when given porridge did it begin to eat.
Previously, there were several fierce dogs inside the monastery.
Whenever they saw a wolf-dog,
they would all compete to bark and bite it.
But if they saw this dog enter the monastery,
they would all lower their heads and wag their tails.
At that time,
the onlookers, including men and women, totaling over 300,000 people,
all did not recognize this dog.
They did not know whence it came.
Qínzhōu reported:
When the relics were about to be placed down, the earth trembled slightly for seven days, and on the eighth day, it trembled greatly.
Yǎnzhōu reported:
By imperial decree, the relics were distributed for the construction of pagodas.
Since Pǔlè Sì in Xiáqiū Xiàn was the most pristine,
the relics were respectfully enshrined there.
On the twenty-fifth day of the third month,
we diligently began to construct a case and cover for them.
When it was first polished, its body was only green in color.
But when the work was completed, it transformed to resemble agate.
Five colors were intermingled, and the patterns shone brilliantly.
Furthermore, white jade grew within it.
It was translucent both inside and out, illuminating objects like water.
Its inner and outer surfaces were completely clear, reflecting people like a mirror.
Regarding the transport of the relics,
Cáozhōu reported:
On the twenty-ninth day of the third month,
a red light appeared from the relics on the inner city wall.
On the fifth day of the fourth month, at shēnshí (3-5 PM),
the relics appeared among twin trees,
and a lion also appeared.
On the fifth day of the fourth month, at hàishí (9-11 PM),
the relics emitted a golden light,
seven cùn long.
On the sixth day of the fourth month, at mǎoshí (5-7 AM),
a dragon flower tree appeared.
Below it, Buddha images emerged together.
On the sixth day of the fourth month, at mǎoshí (5-7 AM),
the outside of the lacquered reliquary board emitted light,
like the color of a golden flower.
On the sixth day of the fourth month, at shēnshí (3-5 PM),
on the northern board of the lacquered reliquary,
transformed Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, twin trees, and other forms appeared.
On the sixth day of the fourth month, at hàishí (9-11 PM),
yellow and white flower-like light,
four or five cùn long, emerged from within the reliquary shrine.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, at chénshí (7-9 AM),
cloud and mist, golden light, and other forms appeared behind the lacquered reliquary board.
At sìshí (9-11 AM), behind the lacquered reliquary board appeared śāla twin lotus flower shadows, Buddha images, a multitude of monks, and lion forms.
At wǔshí (11 AM - 1 PM), a five-colored cloud appeared above the pagoda.
After noon, on the inner board of the lacquered reliquary, śāla twin trees, a forest, multi-storied buildings, and other scenes appeared.
On the ninth day, on the inner board of the lacquered reliquary, patterns of piled stones and a laid foundation appeared.
After jiǎ (midnight to 3 AM), outside the lacquered reliquary board, a large śāla tree, monks holding incense burners, and other figures, as well as a golden Buddha image, appeared.
It resembled the appearance of the Crown Prince at his birth.
It was golden yellow in color.
Behind it were three monks,
wearing purple-yellow monastic robes,
holding incense burners in their hands, making offerings.
The fragrance was different from earthly scents.
It was smelled constantly every day.
Jìnzhōu reported:
The relics emitted light three times in front of the pagoda.
All were purple in color.
Everyone witnessed it.
Qǐzhōu reported:
The relics arrived in the prefecture on the fourth day of the third month.
On the fourteenth day, at chénshí (7-9 AM),
the color inside the glass bottle was white like the moon.
In an instant, it transformed into red.
By the second day of the fourth month, it transformed into purple light,
or sometimes appeared blue.
It flowed and revolved within the bottle,
coming and going,
circulating without cessation.
Monastics and laypeople gazed upon it,
all returning to and relying upon its true form and appearance.
After a long time, it dispersed.
On the seventh day, at wǔshí (11 AM - 1 PM),
the divine image reappeared.
Its transformation and brilliance were no different from before.
Xúzhōu reported:
On the twenty-eighth day of the second month, the relics stayed overnight at an驛 (inn) forty-five lǐ west of the prefecture.
That night, it was cloudy and rainy.
The relics emitted light,
forty-five lǐ towards the prefecture.
The monks of Jìngdào Sì looked towards the northern mountains to observe the light.
The image came from the direction of the inn, where the relics were.
The stone reliquary cover for the relics was polished and completed on the fifth day of the fourth month.
Subsequently, two immortals,
four monks,
one lay practitioner,
one qílín,
one lion,
and two fish appeared.
The rest were all in the form of mountains and waters.
Dèngzhōu reported:
On the sixth day of the fourth month, the stone reliquary of the relics transformed into jade and agate.
The stone had inscriptions.
The three characters Zhèng, Guó, and Dé appeared.
Furthermore, immortals, qílín, and fèng appeared.
Ānzhōu reported:
After submitting a memorial requesting to enshrine the relics in the monastery,
the Dharma master Jìngyè and officials of the prefecture measured the foundation.
At shēnshí (3-5 PM), a fragrant aroma suddenly
wafted, filling the air and arriving.
Its exquisite fragrance was something never before encountered in the world.
Monastics and laypeople were all astonished and followed it to its location.
The fragrance permeated everywhere and only dispersed completely by the fifth watch (3-5 AM).
Again, on the eighth day of the fourth month,
the day for walking the path (circumambulation), a grand vegetarian feast was offered.
At wǔshí (11 AM - 1 PM), when the relics were about to be placed down,
over ten thousand monastics and laypeople were present.
The Dharma master ascended the high seat,
holding the relics in his hands to show the assembly.
Everyone was filled with grief and could not control themselves.
Immediately, a red color
emerged from the mouth of the bottle in the master's hand,
and then twice emitted light,
one chǐ high.
As the relics were lowered into the stone reliquary, a white cloud suddenly appeared,
round like a cover.
It was directly above the reliquary, rotating clockwise several times.
After circling, it returned to its original point of emergence and disappeared.
Furthermore, there was a Buddha pavilion south of the pagoda.
At that time, it was locked, and a Bodhi assembly was established beneath it for the relics.
Two guards were assigned to watch over it.
Suddenly, sounds of many people walking were heard from above the pavilion.
When they checked, the pavilion door was still closed.
After a short while, the walking sounds were heard again, and they immediately ran to report.
The abbot came, and together they opened the pavilion door to investigate.
There were only Buddha images;
nothing else was seen.
Furthermore, on the day the relics were placed,
at shēnshí (3-5 PM), the Dharma master Jìngfàn and the dhūta monk Jìngtāo,
behind the reliquary pagoda,
by the waterside cliff,
administered Bodhisattva precepts to monastics and laypeople.
The crowd saw schools of fish swimming in formation,
their heads all facing south, as if wishing to take refuge.
There were over ten thousand of them.
Two Zen masters were invited to board a boat and enter the water to administer precepts to the fish.
Then, all the fish inside turned their heads towards the boat,
following and circling as if listening to the Dharma.
Zhàozhōu reported:
The relics arrived in the prefecture on the fourth day of the third month.
We, your servants, enshrined them and built a pagoda at Wénjì Sì within our jurisdiction.
On the second day, during the circumambulation and ritual,
the relics emitted a red light at the pagoda site.
From wèishí (1-3 PM) to shēnshí (3-5 PM), various forms were seen.
Sometimes like images,
sometimes like multi-storied buildings.
Sometimes white light was seen,
alternately large and small.
It circled the relics,
circulating the bottle.
Sometimes hidden, sometimes visible.
Sometimes slow, sometimes fast.
Officials, monastics, and laypeople all witnessed it.
They were astonished, joyful, wept, and the monastery was abuzz.
On the fourth day, it again emitted red light,
shining like gold.
It was over one chǐ long horizontally and vertically.
Purple and green colors alternated, appearing three times.
After a long time, it disappeared.
Also seen was a Buddha image over two chǐ tall,
seated on a lotus pedestal.
Furthermore, two Bodhisattvas attended on either side,
over one chǐ tall.
From mǎoshí (5-7 AM) to sìshí (9-11 AM), these various forms were seen.
Over twenty thousand people, monastics and laypeople from the four assemblies,
all gazed upon them.
Yùzhōu reported:
The śarīra bottle emitted white light.
In a short while, it turned into five colors, swirling within the bottle.
Its form was extraordinary.
Also, when carving the śarīra inscription,
the stone itself had no unusual qualities.
When carving reached the character '皇帝' (Huángdì),
from the top dot and vertical strokes to the horizontal strokes,
wherever it was carved, it appeared as if formed from engraved gold.
Lìzhōu reported:
On the 26th night of the third month, during the first watch, the śarīra emitted light,
illuminating the entire yá within like the moon.
Míngzhōu reported:
On the 8th day of the fourth month, when the śarīra was interred,
and the ground was dug to place the stone casket,
an image was found.
Wèizhōu reported:
On the 3rd day of the fourth month, after the fast concluded,
outside the golden bottle containing the śarīra,
its color was a brilliant, vivid red, extraordinarily beautiful.
Sometimes it moved along the bottom of the glass bottle,
or sometimes it floated along the sides of the bottle.
It emitted light, shining outwards as it moved up and down the bottle.
By the 8th day, it was still shining as brightly as before.
Míngzhōu reported:
On the 11th day of the third month, a sweet dew fell from heaven upon the śarīra.
It ceased on the 13th day.
There was a bhikṣu of virtuous conduct, Sēng Méng,
who had previously suffered from a waist and leg ailment that prevented him from traveling.
On that day, he heard that the śarīra was about to arrive.
The entire monastery rushed out.
Sēng Méng, being afflicted by his illness, could not personally receive it.
He ordered his disciple Fǎzàng to assist him out of his dwelling.
With a sincere heart and correct mindfulness, he was immediately able to stand and walk.
He went about ten *lǐ* outside the city to personally greet the śarīra.
As a result, his illness gradually healed, and he became able to walk.
Máozhōu reported:
The śarīra arrived at the prefecture on the 27th day of the second month.
On that day, it was placed according to the prescribed rites.
All men and women developed a bodhicitta heart,
vying to take refuge.
The mute could speak,
and the paralyzed could all walk.
The stone casket transformed, becoming like *liúlí*,
transparent both inside and out.
On the 12th day of the fourth month, gold and silver flowers rained down from heaven.
We report and respectfully present this.
Jìzhōu reported:
The śarīra emitted light.
Five colors illuminated the entire city administration.
At that time, there was a monk who had previously suffered from blindness
and was also able to see the śarīra.
Furthermore, there was a person who had suffered from paralyzed waist and legs for fifteen years.
Since the śarīra arrived at the prefectural seat,
this afflicted person prostrated and made a vow,
and immediately regained the ability to move.
Sòngzhōu reported:
On the 4th day of the third month, the śarīra arrived at the prefecture.
In the market courtyard of Sòngchéng County, which was under its jurisdiction, there was an old well.
Its water had always been salty and bitter, and its color was previously red,
entirely unfit for consumption.
A county resident, Hú Zǐgān, took water from it to mix with mud.
He was surprised that its color was white and tasted it, finding it very sweet.
On the 3rd day of the fourth month, the śarīra in the pagoda emitted red light.
On the 6th night, during the fifth watch, the monastery again emitted white light.
On the 7th day, at *chénshí* (7-9 AM), white flowers rained from the sky within the monastery.
Eyewitnesses described it as a dense, misty shower,
resembling fine snow.
It did not fall to the ground.
On the 8th day, at *wǔshí* (11 AM-1 PM), as the śarīra was about to be placed into the casket,
white cranes soared above the pagoda base in the sky.
Huáizhōu reported:
The śarīra was placed at Chángshòu Temple in the prefectural city.
On the 5th day of the fourth month, at *chénshí*,
a male pheasant flew to the side of the casket.
Its demeanor was calm and composed, its feathers fresh and vibrant.
It flew and rested without any sign of fear.
Yáng Mài, a resident of Hénèi County, specifically showed it
to over six thousand people, both secular and monastic.
All witnessed it.
The imperial envoy, bhikṣu Líng Càn, immediately administered the precepts to it.
The pheasant faced the master as if listening to the Dharma.
The master said,
"This pheasant is a wild bird.
According to inner Dharma principles, it should not be confined."
So, he ordered it to be sent to Tàihángshān north of the city and released.
Beside the śarīra pagoda, there was also a track.
It came from thirty paces southeast of the pagoda
directly to the pagoda, with no return trace visible.
Nor was there any entry point.
Sometimes it was four inches wide,
sometimes three inches wide.
It wound and coiled like the tracks of a dragon or snake.
Court ladies, monastics, and laypeople all witnessed it together.
On the 8th day, before noon, as the śarīra was about to be placed into the pagoda casket,
it emitted light from outside the bottle.
It revolved several times, its splendor shining brightly.
Sometimes it was high, sometimes low,
sometimes hidden, sometimes appearing.
Biànzhōu reported:
The śarīra arrived at the prefecture on the 2nd day of the third month.
It was temporarily placed at the prefectural lodging.
On the 6th night, the great virtuous monks Huìchè and others
suddenly smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
On the 8th day, various monks escorted the śarīra towards the pagoda.
Five people, including the great virtuous monk Sēng Càn,
again smelled the fragrance.
Forty-odd paces from the gate of Huìfú Temple,
a blue light then emitted, illuminating the open tent.
It disappeared after a long time.
This temple had śarīra
that was being offered and worshipped in the monks' quarters.
On that day, Zhāng Xiāngrén from Qǐzhōu
saw the śarīra within the temple in the monks' quarters again emitting blue light.
It exactly resembled the color and form of the newly arrived śarīra.
On the 10th day, he again saw red light illuminating the temple's Buddha hall.
It was five *chǐ* high. That night, at the fourth watch, he again saw mixed blue and red light in the temple.
There was also an old woman
who had suffered from a waist ailment for over twenty years,
using a staff and crawling on the ground to move.
Hearing that the śarīra had arrived at the temple,
she made an effort to come and prostrate.
In the presence of the multitude, she saw the śarīra's light,
and her waist was immediately cured, allowing her to walk without a staff.
Luòzhōu reported:
The śarīra arrived at the prefecture on the 16th day of the third month.
It was immediately placed inside Hánwáng Temple.
On the 23rd day, a fragrance suddenly descended,
unprecedented in the world.
On the 7th night of the fourth month, as the first watch was ending,
an east wind suddenly arose, extinguishing the lamp flames.
A divine light illuminated the southeast of the Buddha hall.
A fragrant wind also came.
Officials, monastics, and laypeople all witnessed and smelled it together.
Thus, their devotion greatly increased.
On the 8th day, as the śarīra was about to be interred,
the branches and leaves of the *tóng* tree beside the pagoda bent downwards.
Yōuzhōu reported:
On the 26th day of the third month, the śarīra was placed in Hóngyè Temple.
When the stone casket was first polished,

Purple flames rose, and the stone was mottled,

It was lustrous and shining, its light like *liúlí*.
By the 2nd day of the fourth month, fasting and circumambulation began.
By the 3rd day, at *hàishí* (9-11 PM),

Lamp light illuminated the courtyard, and the multitude of stars shone brightly at night.
A white light unfolded and contracted above the Buddha's palanquin.
On the 8th day, as the śarīra was placed into the casket,

Among them, there were many unusual depictions of birds, beasts, and forests.
It is truly difficult to describe them in detail.
Those with clear and distinct patterns

Xǔzhōu reported:
On the 3rd day of the third month, at the beginning of the night, ninety *lǐ* north of the prefectural city, in its northern border,

Two colors, purple and red, illuminated the city inside and out.
All the common people saw the divine light.
On the 7th day of the fourth month, in the prefectural main hall,

On the 8th day, at the pagoda of Bànháng Temple,

At *wǔshí*, as the śarīra was about to enter the stone casket,

On that day, about a hundred paces southwest of the pagoda,

a dry pond, not located on any of the four sides,

At that time, over twenty thousand monastics and laypeople who watched all drank from it.
Qí recorded these auspicious responses and presented them in a memorial to the throne.
In Jīngzhōu, the śarīra manifested clouds like a carriage canopy,

Many birds soared around the pagoda.
In Jìzhōu, there was originally one śarīra,

An unusual fragrance was smelled, and sounds emanated from the clouds,

Large flocks of birds flew below the pagoda.
In Chǔzhōu, on the day of circumambulation,

In Jǔzhōu, there was originally one śarīra,

When the foundation was dug, a bronze pagoda was suddenly found underground.

In Yíngzhōu, the śarīra emitted light three times.

In Hóngzhōu, a white-collared crow led the way for the relics.
When the relics arrived at Dézhōu,

Large birds circled the pagoda.
In Zhèngzhōu, the relics emitted light.
Banners hung inward.
When the relics arrived at Jiāngzhōu on the day of circumambulation,

In Cízhōu, the relics manifested a white cloud canopy, like a flying immortal.

A memorial from Yōngzhōu stated:
On the twelfth day of the fifth month of the second year of Rénshòu,

On the fifth night of the sixth month of the second year of Rénshòu,

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the second year of Rénshòu,

That night, it rained jeweled fragments and silver flowers.
The fragrance was exceedingly unusual and incomparable.
From the Shǎnzhōu relics,
from the shēn hour on the fifteenth day of the third month,

There were twenty-one phenomena in total:
four times light was emitted;
within the light, flower trees were seen;
twice there were five-colored clouds;
birds were found when excavating the ground;
the stone reliquary transformed;
eight shāluó trees;
water was seen beneath the trees;
one reclining Buddha;
three bodhisattvas;
one divine nun;
birds were seen inside the reliquary;
three golden flowers;
auspicious clouds formed a wheel;

Shèlì was in Shǎnzhōu city.
On the twenty-third night of the third month, at the second watch.
Dàtōng Sì, Shànfǎ Sì, and Chǎnyè Sì all saw a bright light.

Their form and color were distinct.
After a long time, they vanished.
Their color was initially red.
Soon after, it turned white.
Later, it scattered like mercury.
Everything within the entire room was illuminated.
Shèlì was in Dàxīngguó Sì.
On the second night of the fourth month, at the second watch.
Língshèng Sì saw a bright light.
It clearly illuminated the fruit trees in front of the courtyard and the vegetation on the north slope.
Wherever the light shone, their forms were visible.
A bird was dug up from the ground beneath the pagoda foundation.
Shèlì came towards Dàxīngguó Sì.
On the twenty-eighth of the third month, at the hour of mǎo.
Sīmǎ Zhāng Bèi and Dàdūdū Hóu Jìn jointly inspected the foundation construction, having dug five chi deep.
There was a commoner from Yùshān Xiāng, Ménxiāng Xiàn, Dù Huàyún.
Suddenly, a bird emerged from under his pickaxe.
It was bluish-yellow, as large as a quail.
It tamely walked within the pagoda, resting peacefully.
When held, it showed no fear.
Before it could be presented, the bird died.
Now, when performing meritorious deeds
within the shèlì pagoda, an extraordinary bird was obtained.
Since its emergence was unusual,
it was deemed a propitious omen.
Now, a separate drawing of the bird's form
is respectfully attached for imperial perusal.
Five-colored clouds seen again.
On the fifteenth of the third month, at the hour of shēn.
Shèlì arrived at the three-li gully south of Shǎnzhōu city.
Immediately, there were five-colored clouds.
They rose densely from the southeast.
Suddenly, they all formed a canopy.
Then, they changed to a purple-gauze color.
