At that time, both monastics and laity witnessed this.
On the twenty-eighth day, at the hour of wèi.
At Dàxīngguó Sì.
Again, there were five-colored clouds.
They came from two directions, northwest and southeast.
They merged above the shèlì pagoda.
Forming a single mass.
At that time, there were Wénlín Láng Wéi Fàn, Dàdūdū Yáng Mín, and officials and commoners.
All observed it together.
The clouds dispersed after a short while.
Sounds heard twice.
Shèlì was in the prefecture.
On the night of the twenty-third of the third month.
A sound emerged from the precious seat.
Like the sound of beating a drum for silence among humans.
It ceased at the third [watch].
Later, at Dàxīngguó Sì.
On the fifth of the fourth month, at the hour of yǒu.
Another sound emerged, louder than the previous one.
Both monastics and laity heard it.
Inside and outside the stone casket, on all four sides, were seen Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, divine nuns, sāluó trees, light, etc.
On the seventh of the fourth month, at the hour of sì.
Wishing to send an envoy to present the four types of auspicious signs, such as the emitting light.
Before departure.
Sīmǎ Zhāng Bèi, along with Xiáo Xiàn Lìng Zhèng Qiányì, Ménxiāng Xiàn Chéng Zhào Huáitǎn, Dàdūdū Hóu Jìn, and others who were like commoners, Hóu Qiān.
Went to inspect the stone casket within the shèlì pagoda foundation.
They collectively saw the stone patterns on the east face of the casket spontaneously arise.
Zhāng Bèi and the others were astonished.
Turning towards the north face, he reverently brushed it with his sleeve.
As he did so, he saw a pair of sāluó trees.
They faced each other east and west, with branches and leaves fully formed.
They were deep green in color.
In an instant, monastics and laity rushed to gather.
Again, on the outer west face.
Washing it with water.
They immediately saw that the leaves of the two trees had five colors.
Next, on the outer south face, there were again two trees.
Their branches were somewhat straight.
Their leaves were yellowish-white.
Next, on the outer east face, there were again two trees.
Their color was green, and their leaves were long.
Beneath the trees on all four sides, there were water patterns.
Between these two trees.
The envoy Wénlín Láng Wéi Fàn first saw a bird lying on its back.
When Sīmǎ Zhāng Bèi looked next,
the bird was already standing.
In front of the bird were three golden flowers.
The bird's shape, size, and feather color were no different from the one previously obtained by digging.
In a moment, the bird moved towards the southwest.
Stopping beneath the Buddha and resting inside the casket.
Near the southwest corner, there was also a Bodhisattva.
Seated on a flower platform, facing east.
There was a standing nun facing the Bodhisattva, with palms joined.
They were two cun apart.
Inside the west face, there were again two Bodhisattvas standing together.
One was golden, facing south.
One was silver, facing north.
They were about three cun apart.
On the western edge, there was a reclining Buddha.
Lying on its side, head facing north, face facing west.
These three Bodhisattvas within the stone casket all emitted red and purple light.
About one chi high.
From the hour of sì to wèi, their forms remained unchanged.
After being depicted in a drawing, their colors gradually faded.
The number of monastics and laity observing was not small.
This casket was originally bluish-grey, with a dark base.
At the time of witnessing the auspicious sign, it turned clear white.
Inside and out, it was translucent and bright on all four sides.
People were sent to sit on all sides, and they could see each other without any obstruction.
Inside and outside the casket, on all four sides.
In total, one Buddha, three Bodhisattvas, one nun, one bird, three branches of flowers, and eight trees were seen.
Now, a separate drawing is made.
Respectfully attached for imperial perusal.
When descending, clouds arose from the four directions, forming a wheel shape.
There were also spontaneously appearing banners and canopies.
And fragrant clouds above the pagoda, with light appearing twice.
On the eighth of the fourth month, at the hour of wǔ, shèlì was to be lowered.
At that time, both monastics and laity cried out in sorrow.
Suddenly, clouds arose simultaneously from the four directions.
Like smoke and mist.
Gradually ascending to the position of the sun.
Immediately, they encircled the sun, forming a halo.
Like a carriage wheel.
Inside, there was a separate mass of white clouds, round and obscuring the sun.
The sunlight gradually became faint, like a small cup.
Surrounding the outside of the wheel.
Successively, clouds formed the spokes.
The wheel and spokes were both red and purple.
When the shèlì had been lowered.
The clouds dispersed, and the sunlight returned to its bright and clear state.
Again, outside the northwest wall of the pagoda courtyard.
There were large, spontaneously appearing banners and canopies.
There were also those who saw banners and canopies encircling the shèlì.
At that time, it was thought that someone was holding banners as an offering.
When the shèlì had been lowered, the banners and canopies suddenly disappeared.
At that time, not a few monastics and laity witnessed this.
At the hour of xū, Sīmǎ Zhāng Bèi and others.
Saw green cloud-like vapor rising from within the pagoda.
The clouds were very fragrant.
Immediately, he called the envoy Wénlín Láng Wéi Fàn and Dàxīng Sì's Zhèntán Chàng to enter and observe.
Zhāng Bèi and Wéi Fàn and others all saw flowing light moving towards the northwest and southeast.
It disappeared in a moment.
What then is Dharma?
It is to rely on standards for practice.
To purify the spirit and wash away delusions, that is its aim.
What then is Righteousness (Yì)?
It is that which has profound principles, which a thousand sages do not alter in its form.
And ten thousand heresies cannot reverse its essence.
In secular law, there are the Five Constants (wǔcháng).
Benevolence, Righteousness, Propriety, Wisdom, and Trustworthiness.
A hundred kings do not change its canon.
And all worthies praise and support it, so it does not fall.
In the Dharma, there are the Two Truths (liǎngdì).
Namely, ultimate truth (zhēn) and conventional truth (sú).
From which all Buddhas are born.
And by which all beings attain transcendent awakening.
Therefore, while the secular preserves the Five Constants,
delusions and confusion persist endlessly.
The Way (dào) relies on the Two Truths,
and superior wisdom shines ever brighter.
Hence, conventional and ultimate truth are the steps and foundation for emerging into the Way.
And the Right Dharma is the path to entering emptiness.
Thus, the treatise says:
Without the conventional, there is no way to access the ultimate.
Without the ultimate, there is no way to abandon the conventional.
It also says:
All Buddhas, when teaching the Dharma, always rely on the Two Truths.
This is the general outline of the established doctrine.
As for the streams of Mahayana and Hinayana, full and partial teachings,
the canons of the Three Baskets and Eight Treasuries.
Illuminating the clarity and obscurity of the mind's dust.
Understanding the different paths of karmic retribution.
Passing through wisdom and understanding to reflect the mind like a mirror.
Comprehending worldly phenomena to illuminate with divine insight.
If described in this way, it is called Dharma and Righteousness (fǎyì).
As for practicing as taught.
And discerning the spiritual abode.
Then the Four Reliances (sìyī) are upright.
One first investigates consciousness in perverse emotions.
The Eightfold Noble Path (bāzhí) illuminates the Way.
Promoting the pure mind beyond illusory realms.
The Three Learnings (sānxué) open its profound treasury.
The One Consistency (yīguàn) unifies its true source.
Gradual cultivation and foundation building will naturally lead to its attainment.
But because the hidden pass is difficult to open,
and the master stone is easily obscured.
Unless aided by verbal methods,
there is no way to ascend.
Therefore, since ancient times, monastics and laity alike have sought the way.
To purify the spirit.
And temper the mind.
Some write treatises to guide understanding.
Others discuss and express their feelings.
Through words, the sagely mind is revealed.
By traces, the profound truth is propagated.
Formerly, the Liáng Dynasty already narrated its essence.
Now, the Táng Dynasty further expands its reach.
Each has its ambition.
Showing that such words have never ceased through the ages.
Ānchǔzǐ asked Xuánmíng Xiānshēng,
"I have heard that 'families that accumulate good deeds are sure to have an abundance of blessings,'
and 'families that accumulate bad deeds are sure to have an abundance of misfortune.'
It is also said,
'The Way of Heaven shows no favoritism; it constantly aids the good.'
These are the aphorisms of saints and enlightened ones,
grand beacons for ten thousand generations.
This means that one's actions are completed in oneself,
but blessings flow to future generations;
evil is manifest in one's deeds,
but guilt is incurred in the unseen world.
However, when saints perform good deeds,
there is no principle they do not exhaust; when principles are exhausted and good is accumulated,
it should remain unchanged throughout generations.
When one performs no good deeds, and evil is passed down,
it should also be dark for a hundred generations.
If good has a fixed gateway,
and evil has an appointed lineage,
then what benefit is there in cultivating practice for future generations?
Furthermore, there are those who discipline themselves and follow the Way,
whose words and actions cause no harm,
yet they suffer heavenly punishments, a hundred kinds of suffering, fully beset by troubles.
While others indulge their nature and passions, acting with wanton cruelty,
they live in prosperity and honor, and their descendants flourish abundantly.
Judging by this,
what, after all, is the reward for accumulating good deeds?
The five emotions and six desires are ever-present in the human heart.
To prune and adorn, to guard against and keep at bay external matters is the greatest suffering.
If humans and ghosts are indifferent to taking and leaving,
why not follow what is pleasant and force oneself to endure what is bitter?"
Please resolve my doubts to dispel my confusion."
The先生 replied,
"Excellent is your question, my son!
Sīmǎ Qiān had a saying:
'How does Heaven repay the good person?'
Xún Yuè also said,
'Those who embellish deceit and act treacherously
find contentment in their own lifetime,
while those who uphold the Way and follow principle
cannot escape the suffering of hunger and cold.'
These two gentlemen doubted it before and could not distinguish it.
My son, you are perplexed by it now;
is this not fitting?
Allow me to try to explain.
Humans are endowed with the nature of the Two Principles (Heaven and Earth) to be born,
and receive the qi of the Five Constants to be nurtured.
Nature has periods of long and short life;
thus, there is a distinction between Péng (Zu) and a short-lived person.
Qi has differences in refinement and coarseness;
thus, there is also a distinction between the wise and the foolish.
This is the natural and unchangeable principle.
Thus, Yáo and Shùn were great sages, yet Zhū and Jūn were raised.
Gǔsǒu was extremely foolish, yet gave birth to Yǒu Shùn.
Yán Huí was a great worthy, but died young and had no heirs.
Shāng Chén was extremely evil, yet his descendants prospered.
Yí and Shū were utterly benevolent, yet starved to death in a desolate mountain.
Dào Zhí acted with wanton cruelty, yet enjoyed wealth and happiness until his end.
Bǐ Gàn was loyal and upright, yet was killed without hesitation.
Zhāng Tāng, a cruel official, had seven generations of descendants who held high office.
All such examples are innumerable.
Verifying them among sages and worthies is thus,
and seeking them among ordinary people is also thus.
Therefore, we know that wisdom and foolishness, good and evil, long life and short life, prosperity and adversity
each have their allotted fate,
and are not brought about by accumulated deeds.
Considering the profound distance of Heaven and Earth,
and the vastness of yin and yang,
is humanity within them not merely like a grain of rice in a great granary,
or a hair on a horse's body?
Yet the minor deeds of a common man,
the petty affairs of human relations,
one good and one evil, all lead to unseen retribution.
To wish to change the natural distinction of long and short life, or to make a saint out of Zhū or Shùn,

Kǒng's (孔氏) discourse states:
Though the holy path is subtle,
even Yán (顏) nearly achieved it, but his understanding was not comprehensive.
Principle ultimately converges to one ultimate.
A certain Daoist (Dàoshì) of the New Discourse (Xīnlùn) holds that:
Profound insight is subtle and does not allow for stages.
Diligent study is boundless; why should one limit oneself?
Now, setting aside Shì's (釋氏) gradual awakening but adopting its ability to reach,
and setting aside Kǒng's (孔氏) "nearly achieved" but adopting its "one ultimate."
The "one ultimate" differs from "gradual awakening"; "ability to reach" is not "nearly achieved."
Thus, although the principles they abandon are combined and adopted,
they are nevertheless separated from Kǒng (孔) and Shì (釋).
I say the two discussions are words for saving beings,
and the Daoist's (Dàojiā) chanting is a saying of gaining insight.
I dare to mediate between them.
I humbly consider the New Discourse (Xīnlùn) to be correct.
This is a casual reply to your intent.
I hope for some realization.
Fǎ Xù (法勗) asked:
I respectfully peruse your clear discourse.
It clarifies that the ultimate principle (zōngjí) is subtle, yet one can awaken to it suddenly.
Although I rejoice in this new analysis, I have some doubts.
Those who are enlightened comprehend principle and transcend desires.
The ordinary, deluded, are ensnared by defilements.
Transcendence of desires is rooted in seeing principle.
Being ensnared by defilements stems from deviating from the ultimate.
How can this be explained?
The sūtra says:
New learners without Prajñā (般若) are like blind people
without a guide—this is holding onto principle.
Eliminating suffering becomes evident in this way.
If one's seeking does not gradually approach the great ultimate and aspire to it,
but remains entangled in dust and defilements, then one's efforts will be in vain for kalpas.
The desired fruit will be distant, and one will be full of hesitation.
I await your excellent instruction.
First reply:
The Dao (Dào) and the mundane (sú) are opposite; their principles are not related.
Therefore, one guides through expedients (quán).
Though expedients are provisional, their aim is not provisional.
Though wisdom is true, its function is not true (in the sense of ultimate reality itself).
The non-true does not harm the true.
The root is in helping beings.
The non-provisional does not fulfill the provisional.
When beings are helped, one returns to the root.
If so, kalpas of inaction are empty.
Diligent aspiration for the fruit is like the bright sun.
Xù (勗) asked again:
According to your discourse,
since Kǒng (孔) and Shì (釋) have the same Dao (Dào),
the expedients (jiǎ) for saving beings should also not differ.
However, in the realm of the spiritual path (shéndào),
even Yán (顏) was not taught by Kǒngzǐ (孔子).
And the subtlety of Ultimate Reality (shíxiàng)
is something even the ignorant must be taught by Shì (釋氏).
How then can the teachings of the two Sages be so contradictory?
Second reply:
The two teachings differ because they respond to beings according to their regions and the places they transform are different.
Broadly comparing them:
Their observation is on the people.
Huárén (華人) (Chinese people) are easily enlightened to principle but
are difficult to accept teachings.
Therefore, Kǒng (孔) closed the path of accumulated learning but opened the "one ultimate."
Yírén (夷人) (barbarians) are easy to accept teachings but
are difficult to be enlightened to principle. Therefore, Shì (釋) closed the path of sudden enlightenment but opened the "gradual awakening."
Although gradual awakening can reach, it obscures the reality of sudden enlightenment.
Although the "one ultimate" is understood, it leaves no hope for accumulated learning.
This is because Huárén (華人) (Chinese people) understand principle without gradual steps but falsely claim the Dao (Dào) has no learning.
Yírén (夷人) (barbarians) understand principle through learning but falsely claim the Dao (Dào) has gradual steps.
Hence, although the expedient (quán) and the real (shí) are the same, their functions differ.
Formerly, Xiàng Zǐqī (向子期) considered Confucianism and Daoism (Rú Dào) as one.
Yīng Jífǔ (應吉甫) said Kǒng (孔) and Lǎo (老) could be equated.
All wished to glimpse the ultimate.
How much more so for those who possess true reality!
Xù (勗) asked a third time:
Re-examining your reply,
you stated that because the Huá (華) and Yí (夷) have different natures (easy and difficult),
the two Sages presented differing teachings.
This emphasis on adapting to regional customs
can be called excellent.
However, the profound ultimate brightly illuminates and sets standards from above,
while the ignorant masses blindly follow from below.
Therefore, the standard-setter should carefully consider their governance,
and those who follow must affirm its ultimate principle.
Now, Kǒng (孔) abolished the path of sagely learning,
while Shì (釋) opened the path of gradual awakening.
Since the snares and traps (quántí) are already confused,
how can the common people return to the true?
Third reply:
Winter and summer have different natures,
yet they rely on spring and autumn as beginning and end.
Day and night have distinct functions,
yet they depend on dawn and dusk for their alternation.
How much more so for the most subtle principle? How can it directly connect with the coarsest people?
Therefore, those who adhere to gradual awakening
thereby secretly achieve sudden understanding.
Those who rely on rites and teachings
thereby covertly complete their path to becoming a sage.
Becoming a sage does not go beyond the Six Classics (liù jīng),
yet the Six Classics attain sudden understanding.
One does not see the Tripiṭaka (sān zàng),
yet through the Tripiṭaka, the snares and traps (quántí) are distinctly evident.
Why doubt their confusion?
Fish and rabbits are already caught; the common people are thus saved.
Sēng Wéi asked:
Chéng Xīn Lùn Fǎshī
holds that the ultimate principle (zōngjí) is subtle and profound, allowing no gradual ascent.
He suggests that scholars, upon reaching the extreme of existence,
will naturally find non-existence to be like a tally-slip matching its counterpart.
Why, then, is it necessary to speak of non-existence?
If one must rely on non-existence to exhaust existence,
how can this not be called gradual enlightenment (jiànwù)?
First reply:
Indeed, as long as defilements (léi) are not exhausted,
non-existence cannot be attained.
Only by exhausting the faults of defilements
can one begin to attain non-existence.
When defilements are exhausted, then there is non-existence,
truly like a tally-slip. To remove these defilements,
one must necessarily rely on supplementary teachings.
During the time of existence, one learns but does not awaken.
Awakening is beyond existence, reached by relying on learning.
However, gradual ascent (jiējí) is a teaching for the foolish;
true insight is a matter of sudden enlightenment (yīwù).
Wéi asked again:
The treatise says:
“Awakening is beyond existence, not attained gradually.”
This implies that scholars pursuing the ultimate principle should daily advance their understanding.
If their understanding does not advance daily, it is as good as not being spoken of.
If understanding advances daily, is that not gradual enlightenment?
Second reply:
Indeed, understanding (míng) is not attained gradually; faith (xìn) is aroused by teaching.
Why do I say this?
Because faith aroused by teaching has the merit of daily progress.
What is not illuminated gradually has no share in immediate insight.
However, when the aspiration for the Way and good intentions arise,
defilements diminish, and impurities are suppressed.
Suppression is similar to non-existence; goodness is different from evil.
What is undertaken here is not simultaneous, nor is the mind inherently free of defilements.
It is only through a single awakening (yīwù) that all hindrances (wànzhì) are simultaneously exhausted.
Wéi asked a third time:
The reply said:
“Through teaching, faith
has the merit of daily progress.
What is not illuminated gradually
has no share in immediate insight.”
Those who revere teaching and uphold the ultimate principle,
even if they do not permanently apply it,
at the time of upholding it,
how can they not temporarily merge with non-existence?
If we allow for this temporary merging,
it is still better than not merging at all. How is this not gradual?
Third reply:
Temporary (zàn) means provisional (jiǎ).
True (zhēn) means constant (cháng).
Provisional knowing (jiǎzhī) is impermanent.
Constant knowing (chángzhī) is not provisional.
How can the temporary nature of provisional knowing now infringe upon the truth of constant knowing?
The idea that temporary merging is better than no merging
is indeed as Lái (來) said, with a slight corroboration.
When Wū Chén (巫臣) admonished King Zhuāng (莊王),
things were remote from him,
hence principle (lǐ) preceded emotion (qíng).
When he later married Xià Jī (夏姬),
he was already involved with things,
hence emotion was above principle.
Emotion and principle thus alternate, and things and self incline mutually.
This also represents the unrestrained indulgence of ordinary knowledge (zhōngzhī).
If one takes the admonishment as an awakening,
how can one tolerate the delusion at the time of marriage?
Moreover, south is sacred,
and north is ignorant.
Turning one's back on the north and facing the south
is not called stopping at the north.
Facing the south and turning one's back on the north
is not a claim of having reached the south.
However, facing the south allows one to turn their back on the north.
This is not stopping at the north.
This is not stopping at the north.
Therefore, ignorance (yú) can be eliminated.
It allows one to reach the south.
Therefore, awakening (wù) can be attained.
Is the temporary merging of provisional knowing the same as or different from true knowing?
First reply:
It is different from true knowing.
Lín (驎) asked again:
In what way is it different?
Second reply:
Provisional knowing means defilements are suppressed.
Thus, principle is temporarily in use, and its function is temporarily within principle.
Its knowing is not constant.
True knowing means illumination is tranquil. Thus, principle is constantly in use, and its function is constantly within principle.
Hence, it is eternally true knowing.
Lín asked a third time:
Defilements do not remove themselves.
Therefore, one seeks principle to remove defilements.
Now, with provisional knowing, one merges, and principle is indeed in the mind.
If it is in the mind, and defilements do not go away,
how will they be removed?
Third reply:
Defilements arise due to the mind.
The mind's contact creates defilements.
If defilements are constantly touched, the mind darkens daily.
If teaching is applied, the mind suppresses defilements daily.
The suppression of defilements continues for a long time until defilements are extinguished.
However, the time of extinction is after the suppression of defilements.
Suppression of defilements and extinction of defilements appear similar but are actually different.
This must be carefully observed.
The nature of extinguishing defilements
is when self and other are forgotten, and existence and non-existence are viewed as one.
The state of suppressing defilements
is when others and self have different sentiments, and emptiness and reality have distinct views.
Distinguishing reality from emptiness, and others from self, leads to entanglement.
When there is one non-existence, and self and other are the same, one emerges into illumination.
Lín Wéi asked:
Three ages (sānshì) are longer than a hundred years.
Three thousand (sānqiān) is wider than Chìxiàn (赤縣).
Four divisions (sìbù) are more numerous than households.
Seven treasures (qībǎo) are more marvelous than stones and sand.
These also represent distinctions of size and greatness.
Therefore, transformations have far and near.
Can this not be considered so?
First reply:
Facts and principles (shìlǐ) are not the same, always forming four aspects.
There are naturally small and large, each finding its appropriate place.
There are also the wise and the foolish, acting contrary to proper methods.
This is what is called "the world is the same, but the times are different; things are right, but people are wrong."
For example, in governing a small state (jiēzhī zhī zhèng), there are also those who use a large knife (niúdāo pèixǐ) and listen to petitions.
Are all of them like Táng Yú (唐虞)?
To say that words (yán) completely exhaust the physical body in Wǔchéng (武城),
and that the long ages universally cover the whole world,
I have not heard of this.
Furthermore, while all are called wonderful awakening (miàojué), and their lands (guótǔ) are refined or coarse,
one cannot speak of superior or inferior sages based on the refined or coarse nature of their lands.
The responses of their manifested traces (jǐngjì) are not what is to be relied upon.
Wéi asked again:
The treatise says:
“Sometimes the Way is vast, but its affairs are narrow;
sometimes affairs are right, but people are wrong.”
Now, one cannot judge the crudeness or subtlety of the Way by the smallness or greatness of its affairs.
These words are truly profound.
But my doubt is not in this.
Suppose that Zhōu Kǒng (周孔) indeed did not exhaust the ultimate.
They responded to the world with it,
and thus considered themselves as the ultimate.
This is simply because the world was far from the sages and not enough to explain the ultimate.
When the subtle descends several levels to connect with the coarse masses,
the coarse cannot fathom it.
However, the subtlety of several levels is not called ultimate subtlety.
Extending this,
those who govern the world are subtle to the coarse.
However, compared to the truly subtle, they are still coarse.
By using the subtle to address the coarse,
there is nothing that is not exhausted.
By seeking the subtle with the coarse,
one cannot see its origin.
Nothing is not exhausted,
hence it is called exhaust all principles (qiónglǐ).
One cannot see its origin,
hence one looks up to it as ever higher.
How can we now equate what Yán Shì (顏氏) revered with the ultimate subtlety?
Second reply:
Now, we do not rely on what Yán (顏) upheld
to call it the ultimate.
We only say that Yán (顏) was "almost there."
Then Kǒng (孔) knew "the subtle."
Moreover, if we allow Yǔ Chāng (禹昌)'s words,
Kǒng (孔) was not speaking of the fundamental.
In terms of Yáo's (堯) emulation of Heaven, their essences were the same.
How can the ultimate essence be judged by the smallness or greatness of existence?
Wéi asked a third time:
Are all things that ordinary people cannot fathom,
and which are boldly proclaimed, to be considered sacred?
Third reply:
Indeed, if a bold proclamation concerns a worthy person, we still acknowledge their worthiness.
If it concerns a sage,
how can we, on the contrary, deny them to be a sage?
People use it daily without knowing, common folk are deluded and confused.
Only the Buddha fully comprehends the lofty true reality.
Now, to want to make the lofty reality known to the deluded and confused,
this has never been the case.
If it is truly unknown,
how can one not believe the bold proclamation?
Since we affirm Shì (釋) (Buddha)'s bold proclamation as right,
why do we deny Kǒng Chāng (孔昌)'s (Confucius and Laozi's) bold proclamation as wrong?
Zhú Fǎgāng [竺法綱] asked.
Reverently reading your profound discourse, I have explored the ultimate principle.
Your wonderful judgment of expediency and reality preserves the essence of Confucianism and Daoism.
The inherited teachings of Kǒng [孔] and Shì [釋] (Confucius and Buddha) are eloquently expressed with a balanced approach.
This new discourse is truly fitting.
It can be said to guide the source of the current and polish to emit brilliance.
You replied in detail to Xù Wéi’s [勗維] question.
Some say it is through expediency that one penetrates,
or that one learns but does not awaken.
This makes profound sentences mere embellishments,
unrelated to one’s heart and feelings.
This I find uneasy.
Why do I say so?
The Dao [道] and its forms are as separated as heaven, a perilous chasm of almost two thousand li.
If one’s learning does not gradually align with the ultimate principle, there will be no resemblance whatsoever.
Though one gallops with a starting point, one’s thoughts do not exceed one’s station.
How can one ascend the divine cliff, and from where can one transcend the peaks?
If one diligently pursues existence while passively embodying non-existence,
it is like wielding a brush beside Zhōng [鍾] and Zhāng [張], or matching the skill of Yì [羿] and Yǎng [養].
This is clearly not the case.
For even among things that are similar, if not greatly obstructive, one cannot perfect one by merely enjoying the other.
How much less so when existence and non-existence are utterly contrary, yet one claims they can mutually penetrate?
Furthermore, you say,
if defilements are not yet exhausted,
non-existence cannot be attained.
It is only when the defilements are fully exhausted
that non-existence can be attained.
I ask:
The profound Dao [大道] is like a sickness in the vitals, and the mysterious path [玄路] is like a broken axle.
Nothing is more prominent than the defilement of clinging to existence.
Existence cannot remove existence.
That which removes existence must be non-existence, which is not yet present.
[Defilements] must first be exhausted.
Only then can one attain non-existence.
If, as you say, non-existence is attained when defilements are exhausted,
then the defilements remove themselves, not truly needing non-existence to await them.
If they truly do not need non-existence to await them, then they cannot but be without non-existence.
Therefore, non-non-existence is noble.
It is like profound darkness dispelling itself, not needing fire or sun.
If it does not need fire or sun, then fire and sun cannot but be established.
This also clearly shows the supremacy of non-existence.
If one falls into a hierarchy and marvels at sudden enlightenment,
one will stumble here.
In your leisure, I hope you will kindly clarify this.
Shì Huìlín [釋慧琳] asked:
I have reread your insightful discussion three times.
Your distinction between the two schools and your deliberation on Confucianism and Daoism
indeed hold something profound in this discourse.
However, regarding the removal of gradual enlightenment in Buddhism and the abandonment of Kǒng [孔] (Confucius) as an approximation,
I am somewhat perplexed.
Buddhism speaks of gradual progress;
therefore, it is the self-manifesting that has gradual progress.
Kǒng’s [孔] lack of gradual progress is also because he speaks of the self-Dao [自道] without gradual progress.
How do we know this to be so?
“A person of middling capacities can be spoken to about what is above him.”
“Long practice can change one's nature.”
These are the teachings of the Kǒng [孔] clan.
“One joining with the Dao [道] field is not attained by stages of the ten bhūmis.”
This is the assertion of the Buddhist school.
How can such a clear distinction between gradual and abrupt enlightenment be argued by the two sages in their detailed discussions?
Is it not merely that the teachings are considered limited by culture, and principles constrained by reason?
I fear that the arguments for rejection and separation might be lengthier than the new discourse.
Xù Dàorén [勗道人] challenged, saying:
"The cessation of desires arises from embodying principle.
This means that one who 'daily diminishes' awakens to principle by oneself."
The discourse states:
"The Dao [道] and the mundane are fundamentally opposite and unrelated.
Therefore, expediency is used to connect them.
When the purpose is served, one reverts to the origin."
I ask:
Will the temporary adoption of expedient methods, which are habitual to the mind,
ultimately become a lasting concern?
Will the day of enlightenment and the empty principle of the sūtras completely contradict each other?
If it permanently turns away from empty talk and becomes an unspoken doctrine,
and if it supports each other from beginning to end, then one can arrive by following the teaching.
He did not reply to Wéi Lín [維驎].
The argument for 'temporary knowing' is truly splendid.
However, it contradicts the established argument.
The temporary leads to confusion and loss of principle.
It does not use fire drilling to cause perplexity.
If facing south can lead to Yuè [越],
and turning north can abandon Yān [燕],
then it is truly that Yān [燕] is north and Yuè [越] is south.
If contemplating emptiness can cleanse the mind,
and diminishing existence can remove defilements,
then there are also foolish people who become empty saints.
In that case, one should only diligently practice prajñā [般若] to forget daily, gaze at the road to Yǐng [郢] and advance swiftly.
What further worry is there about losing one's place?
I fear that the assertion of 'one awakening'
will again stumble upon the analogy of north and south.
Reading both challenges, I rejoice as if momentarily confronting them.
The rich rhetoric and broad discourse fill my eyes splendidly.
It can be said to be the utterance of a superior person.
Yet, my mind is not fully satisfied.
I will briefly extend my previous intention, though I have no means to reply in person.
I hold my brush with prolonged thoughts.
Xiè Língyùn [謝靈運] bows.
The challenge states:
"Among things that are similar, if not greatly obstructive,
one cannot perfect one by merely enjoying the other.
How much less so when existence and non-existence are utterly contrary, yet one claims they can mutually penetrate?"
This doubt arises from being constrained by habitual learning.
Indeed, one who specializes in writing
naturally may not be skilled in archery.
But one who is skilled in archery and then also enjoys writing,
why can't they excel in both?
If one clings to existence and does not move towards the ultimate principle,
that is naturally the fault of the one who clings.
What prevents one from attaining non-existence and eliminating stagnation?
To use the "non-inclusive existence"
to question the "inclusive non-existence"
is not only for Zhōng [鍾] and Hú [胡] to be ashamed of their archery against Gēng [更] and Lǐ [李], and Yì [羿] and Yǎng [養] to be ashamed of their calligraphy against Luó [羅] and Zhào [趙].
The stumbling upon analogies will then fully confirm the regret of clumsy calculations.
Now, let's follow its origin.
Indeed, relying on non-existence to subdue existence,
once it is subdued, existence is forgotten.
One cannot know at the time of subduing.
If one knows, one no longer discerns.
Therefore, the talk of "sitting and forgetting" and "daily diminishing" came recently from Lǎo [老] and Zhuāng [莊].
That phenomena arise from causes and then cease has old sayings in the sūtras.
In this way, how can defilements remove themselves without the aid of non-existence?
Moreover, just as light illuminates darkness, a new功 (merit/effect) lies in fire and sun.
But fire and sun do not claim credit for their功 (merit/effect) in profound darkness.
Prajñā [般若] does not speak of its benefit to the ignorant.
Extending from this,
why need more words?
Although Kǒng [孔] said to "speak of what is above,"
he also said that "saints have no hierarchy."
Shì Wéi [釋維] said "one joining,"
yet also said that "all beings have Buddha-nature."
If all beings have Buddha-nature, their path has a return.
What is doubted here is the gradual teaching.
If saints have no hierarchy, their principle is valuable.
What is doubted here is the approximation.
Are the two sages on different paths, or is it merely the circumstances that make it so?
The difficulty of "rejection and separation" then becomes an argument whose length in words is not merely an "angular bow"?
The challenge states:
"If it permanently turns away from empty talk and becomes an unspoken doctrine,
and if it supports each other from beginning to end, then one can arrive by following the teaching."
This can be called the rhetoric of Gōngsūn [公孫] and the domain of debaters.
Indeed, wisdom is the root of expediency,
and expediency is the use of wisdom.
Now, taking the sage's intent, wisdom is the words of the sūtras.
Thus, expediency relies on expediency as a guide.
Therefore, the three vehicles are all like snares and traps.
Since the intent is to return to the ultimate principle,
prajñā [般若] is like a fish or a rabbit (i.e., means to an end).
It is truly because people are mostly foolish,
so the teachings are circuitous.
If everyone could grasp the intent,
what would be the value of gathering enlightenment?
The argument of "temporary knowing" primarily means that those who have (existence) can give counsel for reaching the principle.
This is like mutual credit and debit.
It is not what is meant by awakening to the Dao [道].
How does it contradict the established argument?
"Yān [燕] is north and Yuè [越] is south" contains the idea of encountering an empty saint.
Since its principle is correct,
I have quite gained from it.
If the diligent one forgets daily, and the observer advances swiftly,
this is also truly as the Tathāgata said.
But diligence is not yet attainment, and observation is not yet arrival.
At this time, it can be called "moving towards the ultimate principle."
Once attained and arrived, it can be called "one awakening." Will there be no commonality?
Do reins come galloping and one calls it a different type of carriage?
The discourse states:
"Belief arising from teachings has the merit of daily progress,
but it is not what is understood by gradual enlightenment,
nor does it have the portion of direct insight."
I ask:
If belief arises from teachings but has no portion of direct insight,
then it is a blind belief in the sage.
If one blindly believes in the sage, and the principle does not concern the mind,
it is merely that one is free from the fault of not being a sage.
How then can there be the merit of daily progress?
The discourse states:
"The temporary is provisional.
The true is constant.
Provisional knowing is impermanent.
Constant knowing is without provisionality."
It also says:
"When provisional knowing subdues defilements,
principle temporarily serves as its function, and the function temporarily resides in principle.
Its knowing is not constant."
I ask:
If temporary knowing is provisional knowing,
then it is not unknowing.
It is merely that one's perception of principle is still shallow,
and one cannot yet apply it constantly.
Although it cannot be compared to the illumination of true knowing,
how can it be said to have no portion of direct insight?
If temporary knowing is not yet seeing principle,
how can it be said that "principle temporarily serves as its function"?
Moreover, how can one call "unknowing" "knowing"?
The discourse states:
"When teachings are used, the mind's defilements are daily subdued.
The longer the defilements are subdued, the more they are extinguished."
A question was posed:
If teachings are used but then become obscured by obstacles,
how are they obscured?
If one has not yet seen the principle at all, and wholeheartedly believes in darkness,
when one wholeheartedly believes, it is merely belief.
To say that this is being obscured by obstacles,
this is merely thinking that two things cannot operate in parallel.
If one is engaged, the other is neglected.
It is not that the principle is obscured by obstacles, where one (obstacle) can contend with the other (principle) and make it obscured.
In all such mental states, who is not like this?
An obscuration like this is fundamentally no different.
One relies, one is obscured, circulating without end.
Even if it continues for a long time, how can the obscuration be eliminated?
Hóng (弘) replied:
The discourse of sudden enlightenment often speaks of having a mind.
But there has yet to be a way to reconcile the different views,
thus it is difficult to express it in words.
Upon reviewing your discussion, much has been explained.
However, there are still some points not well understood.
Let me try to list them as above, asking if they are acceptable.
This doubt is not exhausted.
To allow both our intentions to be fully understood by the reader,
it would be delightful to have an unprompted reply and to discuss it face-to-face.
Holding the brush, my emotions swell.
It is truly inexpressible.
A question was posed:
If one believes based on teachings but lacks the capacity for inner illumination,
is this then believing in the Sàintrén (聖人) in darkness?
If one believes in the Sàintrén (聖人) in darkness, and the principle does not engage the mind,
it could be considered a fault of disrespecting the Sàintrén (聖人).
How could there be the benefit of daily progress?
The answer is:
Yán Zǐ (顏子) embodied two [virtues] but had not yet reached illumination, yet he inclined towards goodness.
All above this level are cases of believing in darkness.
But teachings have a principle that can be followed,
and I have the will to seek that principle.
Therefore, it is said to engage the mind.
Cì (賜) achieved two [virtues].
Huí (回) achieved ten.
How can it be merely avoiding fault?
There is truly the benefit of daily progress.
A question was posed:
To temporarily know is to perceive as provisional.
One who knows
is not unknowing.
It is merely that one’s understanding of the principle is superficial,
and one cannot apply it consistently.
Although it cannot be equated with the illumination of true knowledge,
how can it be said that there is no capacity for inner illumination?
If temporary knowing is not yet seeing the principle,
how can it be said that the principle is temporarily in use?
And by what is this knowing called knowing?
The answer is:
To know yet not know,
it is precisely because of provisional knowing that it is so named.

He abandoned the worldly pleasures of the three palaces.
He extended two seats to inquire about the Dao.
Xuānchéng Wáng (Prince Xuancheng) and other princes, marquises, and imperial relatives also all gave rise to deep faith.
And cultivated pure conduct.
They were perfumed by the fragrance of precepts for their well-being.
They donned dyed robes and took their places.
Cicada-crowns cast their shadows, and belts gracefully swayed.
Those who passed through the golden gate and ascended the jade steps were numerous, forming crowds.
Then, the imperial outriders warned, moving north, and the palanquin with spears and halberds turned east.
The gate resounded with pure chanting, and incense smoke wafted from the sides.
He wore the robe of pure dwelling.
He ascended the seat of Xūmí (Sumeru).
Eight kinds of wondrous sounds were uttered without hindrance.
The ten directions listened intently, and each received understanding according to their kind.
The profound meaning, though poured out, was inexhaustible.
The eloquent discourse, ever repeated, became ever new.
Even the senior monks with long years of study.
Who had often fallen into partiality.
And clung to specialized interpretations and multiple schools.
Yet had not fully understood the sūtra text.
They changed their narrow views to measure.
And looked up to the great venerable one to ask questions.
Thereupon, he wielded the sword of wisdom to sever the net of doubts.
He showed them the way out of confusion and guided them back to the right path.
All of them were suddenly enlightened, their doubts dissolved like ice, and they joyfully paid homage with their heads.
Like lotus flowers gradually unfolding.
Like the new moon steadily growing.
All the listeners, from the Crown Prince, princes, marquises, imperial relatives, and royal in-laws.

To the Shàngshū Lìng (Minister of the Department of State Affairs) Hé Jìngróng (Hé Jìngróng), the hundreds of officials and ministers, the foreign envoy Zhǔ Cuī Chángqiān (Zhǔ Cuī Chángqiān), the deputy envoy Yáng Xiūzhī (Yáng Xiūzhī), and miscellaneous envoys from foreign lands, a total of one thousand three hundred and sixty people.
All traveled over nine relay stations, a journey of ten thousand lǐ.
They galloped, yearning for the imperial transformation.
Upon hearing the heavenly Dharma, they leaped with joy and bowed their heads to perform the utmost reverence.
Their praises followed from their lower ranks.
Also, a thousand learned monks were specially invited to the Tóngtàisì (Tongtai Temple).
At night, they debated the doctrine.
All of them were famed like dragons and elephants, their wisdom illuminating rivers and seas.
Their transmission of learning was like pouring from a vase.
Their chanting was like swift rain.
The Śramaṇa Shì Fǎlóng (Shì Fǎlóng).
Approaching a hundred years of age.
His learning encompassed the three baskets (Tripitaka), and his understanding penetrated the eight dhyānas.
He expounded the Dharma and saved people, gaining renown north of the passes and frontiers.
He heard that Zhōngguó (China) was to lecture on the Móhē Bōrè Jīng (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra).
Therefore, he traveled from afar to attend.
At that time, the Saṅgharaja Huìlìng (Huìlìng) had not yet begun the lecture.
The monastics and laypeople in the capital also did not know that the Emperor was going to lecture.
On the day the lecture began.
There were also innumerable foreign monks.
All unknown to the public.
They gathered together at the Dharma seat.
Therefore, it is known that light shone everywhere, and earth spirits proclaimed it.
How could it be necessary to dispatch elephant-riding envoys?
It mysteriously matched the timing of signal drums.
Shì Fǎxiǎn (Shì Fǎxiǎn) from the Āyùwángsì (Aśoka Temple) in Kuàijī Màoxiàn (Maoxian, Kuaiji).
He cultivated ascetic practices and aspired to seek wisdom and understanding.
His contemplation was equal to Yùduō's (Utpala),
And his sincerity matched Bōlún's (Pulon).
Thereupon, at the lecture venue, he declared his vow.
He pricked his blood and sprinkled it on the ground to show his utmost sincerity.
In the past, people cut their bodies for offerings and dissected bones for writing scriptures.
They took refuge in the True Dharma, not begrudging their lives.
Comparing now with ancient times, it is truly not an empty saying.
The lecture lasted twenty-three days in total.
From the opening of the lecture until its conclusion.
Daily, widespread offerings were made, universally distributed throughout the capital.
Civil and military attendants were also given extra rewards.
The Emperor had governed the realm for over forty years.
He personally practiced frugality and lived a simple life.
He often used a small hall that barely sheltered him from wind and rain.
His dwelling place, the sitting mat, was barely enough for his knees.
Externally, he abolished the ritual of three hunts.
Internally, he screened out feasts with a thousand bells (dishes).
What the chief cook managed saved ten thousand gold pieces annually.
The expenses of the Yètíng (Imperial Harem) were reduced by hundreds of millions annually.
In addition, he extensively collected land taxes, like gathering treasures from a tumultuous sea.
The treasury swelled with interest, like the inexhaustible dragon gold.
Therefore, he was able to avoid burdening the people's labor and harming the nation.
Wealth and Dharma were both bestowed, flowing ceaselessly.
During this lecture.
Mysterious and miraculous events occurred in abundance, beyond comprehension.
First, the Buddha statues in the palace all emitted brilliant light.
Second, the great earth quaked, with all sorts of rising and sinking motions.
Third, it always rained at night and cleared up in the morning.
The pure air was beautiful, and no dust arose.
Fourth, when the wooden clapper sounded and the lecture hall was about to convene.
Shoulder-to-shoulder, wheels entangled, filling the four gates.
Yet, people and horses were harmonious and did not alarm each other.
Fifth, the Dharma seat provided could seat ten thousand people.
Yet, the countless multitude of beings felt no crowding.
Sixth, the four sections (of the assembly) far and wide all heard the wondrous discourse.
Those outside the verandas listened and greatly benefited.
Seventh, pure offerings were widely spread, and the kitchen did not prepare beforehand.
Wondrous food appeared in due time, with a hundred flavors overflowing.
Eighth, a fragrant, exotic aroma, diffused by the wind, filled the senses.
Ninth, melodious and elegant music spontaneously resounded.
Tenth, praises for goodness resonated throughout the empty space.
These are surely the former Buddhas bearing witness and the devas responding to the sensations.
It surpassed the leaping treasures of ancient spirits and excelled the rain of flowers of past auspicious signs.
At this time, people throughout the land cheered and clapped, and all sentient beings rejoiced.
They wished to participate in the field of blessing and vied to practice joyful giving.
The Emperor delineated their intentions and made great vows for them.
I secretly thought that holding even one phrase can generate abundant good deeds.
And even two words heard in passing can lead to superior rewards.
How much more so when the Great Vehicle is widely propagated and the True Dharma extensively proclaimed.
Leading to the simultaneous awakening of wisdom roots and the shared attainment of the wondrous fruit.
It should now be secretly placed in precious cases and transmitted in golden characters.
To shine for ten thousand kalpas.
And benefit the great thousand worlds.
How magnificent!
It is indeed impossible to praise its virtue adequately.
I, a humble minister, was present at the lecture.
My duty involves recording historical events.
Therefore, I respectfully recorded the events of the time to establish.
This preface.
The First Day: The Title of the Prajñā Sūtra was Expounded.
第一日 發般若經題 (Dì yī rì fā Bōrèjīng tí)
Fú Xī (庖羲) was truly divine.
The Eight Trigrams (Bā Xiàng) were thus arranged.
King Wén of Zhōu (Zhōu Wén) was supremely sagely.
The six cosmic divisions (Liù Xū) were thus extensively displayed.
These are merely partial doctrines that guide the common folk,
not the great teachings that penetrate all directions.
As for Emperor Míng of Hàn (Hàn Míng) who personally lectured on Confucianism from the palace,
and Emperor Jiǎnwén (Jiǎnwén) who discussed commentaries and again dispensed with specialized classics,
it was like Líng Ruò (靈若) observing the well brickwork,
or Yúnmèng (雲夢) being contained within the chest.
The Emperor embodies the ultimate Way and propagates its glorious deeds.
Truly wise and brilliant, he acts as the supreme ruler (yuánhòu).
The ten bhūmis (shí dì) are thus brought forth, responding to the human king (rén wáng).
The eight blessings (bā fú) are generated, rightly belonging to the world's master (shì zhǔ).
His profound vision is boundless, reaching back to the beginning of kalpas (chén jié).
His serene illumination penetrates beyond the universe (yǔ hé).
He humbles his non-action (wú wéi) to appear as if he has learning.
He cultivates both generosity (tán) and forbearance (rěn), and equally practices meditation (chán) and wisdom (huì).
He transcends cities and kingdoms with great renunciation,
just as in the time of the royal palace.
He measures treasures from the four heavens,
and on the day of the turning wheel (zhuǎnlún), he treats them lightly,
like a swan's feather.
He discards them like worn-out shoes.
Therefore, he governs kings with the Way,
his deeds surpassing historical records (fāng cè).
If he had not possessed the supreme virtue of innate wisdom,
and harbored divine insight in his breast,
penetratingly matching the three clarities (sān míng) and equaling the two wisdoms (èr zhì),
who could have achieved this?
The Golden-Character Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra (Jīnzì Mōhē Bōrě Bōluómì Jīng)
is indeed the most venerable of Dharma texts,
and the ultimate teaching for attaining Buddhahood (yuán shèng).
It opens its discourse by illuminating the essence through non-form,
and begins its journey in congruence with ultimate realization.
Its profound meanings are like gathering clouds, its deep texts pure and rich.
Few scholars of previous generations were able to comprehend it.
The Emperor (Huángshàng) cherishes the Mahāyāna, wandering through the Dharma treasury.
His understanding aligns with the Way, his mind embraces dhāraṇī (zǒngchí).
He personally utters royal words, more exquisite than imperial edicts (lúnfú).
He guides with distant snares of an enlightened mind,
marking the wondrous essence of empty understanding.
He then had it inscribed on emerald silk and carved into golden characters (jīn zhuàn).
All the precious ornaments are beyond price.
Auspicious mushrooms (zhī yīng) yield in skill, gold and jade (jīn bì) shine in harmony.
Although the glorious light illuminated the Hétú (Hétú),
compared to this, it is not an auspicious sign.
Even the green jade immortal tablets (xiān jiǎn)
are inferior to this.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ), in his leisure time from myriad affairs,
and during his free moments from attending court,
likened himself to the scented breeze, wishing to hear the extensive discourse.
He earnestly pleaded, and then was granted permission.
On the first day of the second month (jǐ wèi shuò) of the guǐ chǒu year, the fifth year of Zhōngdàtōng (Zhōngdàtōng),
on the 26th day (jiǎ shēn), the imperial carriage (yú jià) exited the Dàtōng Gate (Dàtōng Mén) and proceeded to the Tóngtài Temple (Tóngtài Sì) to commence the lecture.
A great assembly (wú zhē dàhuì) was held for both monastics and laypeople.
Ten thousand cavalry charged like dragons, a thousand chariots moved like thunder.
Heavenly music played nine times, and Brahma sounds (Fànyīn) converged from four directions.
Trembling and filling, dust and mist linked to the sky,
to reach the Bodhimaṇḍa (dàochǎng) and establish the field of blessings (fútián).
Then, the dragon robe (lóng gǔn) was set aside, and the Dharma robe (fǎ fú) was worn with veneration.
The palace was adorned with purple jade, the throne was high and wide,
unrivaled by the higher realms.
New learners could not ascend.
With a serene heavenly countenance, an imperial edict (zhàoyīn zhǐ) was issued.
He spoke with swift and extensive eloquence,
displaying fearless words.
Ineffable complexities were illuminated, and difficult problems unraveled themselves.
Whatever was asked was instantly clarified, like melting ice.
Obscure meanings were dismissed, and nets of doubt were all removed.
It was like a suspended mirror that hides nothing, or a goblet awaiting to be poured.
Moreover, long mats stretched across the steps, with thousands of officials (guānmiǎn) gathered.
The hall was filled to overflowing, monks piled up like mountains.
They sat shoulder-to-shoulder facing the side halls,
and linked seats around the high corridors.
There was no room for an awl to stand, no space for a thorn.
They received the pervasive nourishment of the Dharma rain,
rejoicing in the sweet dew and forgetting to return home.
Like a hundred rivers flowing to the great ocean,
like myriad stars looking up to the sun and moon.
From the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ), kings, and marquises,
down to the Grand Councilor (Shìzhōng) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Yuán Áng (Yuán Áng) and others,
six hundred ninety-eight people.
And the chief monk Huìlìng (Huìlìng) and other scholarly monks, one thousand people filling the seats.
During the day, they listened with one mind.
At night, they again composed essays based on the teachings.
The remaining monks, nuns, male devotees (yōupó sāi), female devotees (yōupó yí), male court officials, Taoist priests (dàoshì), female court officials, Taoist priestesses, white-robed lay scholars,
Persian envoys (Bōsī Guó Shǐ),
Khotan envoys (Yútián Guó Shǐ),
and naturalized people from the northern settlements (Běiguǎn Guīhuà Rén),
in the lecture hall and those provided with lodging,
totaled three hundred nineteen thousand six hundred forty-two people.
Also, the imperial guards (wǔwèi) from the two palaces who were on night duty,
holding their halberds and stationed in golden armor,
all received lecture provisions and special stipends from the treasury.
This amounted to tens of thousands more, not included in the regular audience.
A foreign monk named Shāhéyēshē (Shāhéyēshē),
nearing a hundred years old,
who had meditated in the Dántè Mountain (Dántè Shān),
heard that there would be a great lecture in China (Zhōngguó) and thus traveled from afar.
His spiritual intuition had connected in advance, traversing myriad miles in a mere咫尺 (zhǐchǐ).
As his language was not understood, it was conveyed through multiple interpretations.
His understanding of the Tripitaka (Sānzàng) was divinely illumined by the Emperor's wisdom (shèng qíng).
Also, the Persian envoy (Bōsī Guó Shǐ) Zhǔ Ānjūyuè (Zhǔ Ānjūyuè),
a barbarian from a distant land (huāng fú yuǎn yí), was invited to a nearby seat.
He prostrated himself, baring his head, joyfully receiving what he had never heard.
Many people from various backgrounds, upon hearing the Dharma, valued it greatly.
Immediately, four people shaved their heads at the same time.
Previously, there was the Dharma Master Bǎozhì (Bǎozhì Fǎshī),
whose supernatural powers (shéntōng) were unfathomable and spiritual traces (língjì) numerous.
There is a separate biography for him. In the first year of Tiānjiān (Tiānjiān), when the Emperor (shàng) first ascended the throne,
he was still focused on rites and music, not yet having time for the mission of Féyáng (Fényáng).
In the ninth month of that year, the Dharma Master
personally brought a whisk (chěnwěi shàn) and an iron staff (tiě xīzhàng) and presented them to the Emperor,
but spoke no words.
The Emperor had not yet grasped his intention.
Now, more than thirty years have passed.
A small rope was tied to the handle of the fan,
which was always used to secure a wedge (wǎng xiē).
The traces of this remain clearly visible.
By this time, the Emperor (yù) rang the staff and ascended the hall,
holding the fan and delivering the lecture.
Thus, it is known that the one who shakes the great trichiliocosm (dà qiān) and roars the Dharma
indeed has a hidden congruence.
At this time, it was early spring.
Every evening, rain poured down.
But when the Dharma drum (fǎ gǔ) sounded in the morning, it would immediately become clear and bright.
More than two weeks passed, filling three sevens (21 days).
The mild spring weather was harmonious, and the clouds and scenery were auspicious.
On the day of the lecture's conclusion, the four assemblies (sì zhòng) gathered like clouds.
As the repentance ceremony (chàn lǐ) was completed, the great images of the ten directions in the main hall suddenly emitted light.
It started from between the eyebrows (háojiān), spreading around the ten thousand characters (wànzì).
Auspicious signs (líng xiàng) blazed forth, golden figures shone brightly.
Shortly after, the Bodhisattva statues (púsà xiàng) on the left side, representing the ten directions, continued to emit light.
It originated from below their right ribs (yòu xié) and reached up to their shoulders.
The Sacred Emperor (Shèng Yù) personally prostrated in reverence, and the great assembly all witnessed it.
Therefore, it is known that this manifestation from the face confirms the meaning of the teachings.
As for the disciples of extensive learning (duō wén dìzǐ), internal sages who set an example,
the right-hand scribe (yòushǐ) recorded their words, truly embodying imperial principles (dì zé).
Thus, the Emperor (nǎi mìng) ordered his close officials to compile and record the events of the time.
All the inquiries were comprehensively documented.
Some questions were on interpretations that had long been obscure, and doubts about future understandings.
Some were on fundamental principles that had not yet been revealed, and requests for prior enlightenment.
Those who sought clarification were all expressing their inherent habitual tendencies.
Sometimes, on different days and at different times, the meanings unfolded in sequence.
Sometimes, though there were back-and-forth discussions,
it was ultimately one question of the imperial wisdom (shèng zhǐ).
All were answered appropriately,
like an echo responding to a sound.
Taking all beings as his mind is manifested in this.
Future scholars should understand this intent.
The Emperor (shàng) has propagated the Dharma for a long time.
All the scholarly monks, near and far, gathered together in the capital (Jīngshī).
However, the learning of monastic households (sēng jiā zhī xué) adheres to traditional teaching methods,
relying solely on verbal transmission and ear-listening.
Few are able to diligently research the sutra texts and seek ultimate meanings.
The Emperor (shàng) always provided comprehensive explanations for them.
His divine inspiration and comprehension of the meaning preceded his words.
When citing passages, he could recall dozens.
His precision, detail, clarity, and richness were beyond anyone's ability to follow.
The older monks, like candles extinguished,
lost their spirit and were tongue-tied, without exception.
The multitude looked up in admiration, their hearts filled with joy.
Such matters cannot be fully described by brush and ink.
Furthermore, the arguments put forth by various foreign monks
were not necessarily related to the established teachings.
They simply harbored doubts and came to seek resolution.
Some would recite verses (jì sòng) before asking questions.
Some, after finishing their questions, would praise and make vows.
Some would return to their seats after speaking,
unrecognized by the crowd.
Some would leave immediately after their questions,
their whereabouts unknown.
Their appearances and demeanor were unusual, making it difficult to discern whether they were ordinary or holy.
During this lecture,
the Crown Prince (Dōng Chǔ) initially requested only seven days.
The monks, looking up in veneration, were unwilling to stop.
They repeatedly requested an extension, and were granted another fourteen days.
However, the multitude seeking further instruction continued to murmur ceaselessly.
The Emperor (shàng), due to long-standing state affairs,
did not grant their further requests.
As he was about to conclude the session,
the Emperor (huángdì) distributed property everywhere.
Coins, silk, silver, tin staffs, and other items,
amounting to two hundred one kinds,
valued at nineteen million ninety-six thousand.
Huáng Tàizǐ奉嚫 (bù chén) jade scriptures.
格 seven precious sutra boxes, etc.
And further made offerings of scriptures.
Also bestowed money and silk upon monks,
amounting to three million four hundred and forty-three thousand.
The six palaces donated two million seven hundred thousand.
The emperor personally attended to the myriad people, humbling himself.
What the司服 (Sīfú) bureau was responsible for, what the饔人 (yōngrén) were in charge of,
if it were not the court's institutional regulations,
but merely the expenses for personal sustenance,
then the太官 (Tàiguān) would spend ten thousand [cash] on provisions for one day, and a thousand gold annually.
The emperor accepted none of this.
He provided for himself separately.
He wore coarse, washed clothes, and his utensils were like earthenware bowls.
He ate one vegetable meal a day and did not eat after noon.
In heat and cold, the robes that covered him were nothing but coarse cloth.
His personal residence, the便殿 (Biàndiàn), was no more than a square丈 (zhàng).
What was formerly a tent-throne was now a low bed.
There were no attendants nearby, nor any playthings in sight.
To his left and right were only scriptures and scrolls.
Before him, only incense burners and tin staffs were seen.
He sat from dawn until late in the day before resting.
At night he sought the Dharma treasures, and at daybreak he was still awake.
His benefit was only for others, his restraint only for himself.
These are truly the constant activities of his daily life, the true record within the palace.
Furthermore, palace maids were ordinarily allocated tens of millions annually.
All of this was stopped and cut, nothing was retained.
Although Emperor Wén (Hàn Wén Dì) of Hàn wore clothes that did not reach the ground,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ (Guāngwǔ Dì) consumed only dozens of bushels of grain,
compared to him, they are as nothing.
The temples and stupas he built, and all the vegetarian feasts,
did not rely on people coming from afar,
nor were they like the great feasts (dàpú) of ritual.
All of them were financed by the resources of mountains and marshes,
as pure wealth in accordance with the Dharma.
Expenditure was determined by income; no funds were sought from outside.
The labor for each task was limited to the agreed wage.
Thus, he was able to construct buildings equal to celestial palaces.
And provide meals akin to those in the 'fragrant accumulation' (Xiāngjī) heavens.
The grand ceremonies of the national dynasty were none other than the three元 (yuán) festivals.
The crowds for the three元 (yuán) festivals numbered only tens of thousands.
Preparation began a year in advance, and only then could they proceed.
Supervision was complex and considered a major undertaking.
As for this assembly, it originated from pure wealth.
People from far and near wished to be part of the occasion.
Joyfully they requested to participate, vying for blessings.
They did not await orders nor require levies.
Sweet-smelling millet arrived as scheduled.
Hundreds of thousands of people feasted, yet it was inexhaustible.
From this, we know it was due to the emperor's transforming power
and the culmination of the people's good roots.

As for the regular military and state expenditures and the constant reserves in the treasury, it is truly that with the world considered a public instrument, not a single autumn hair is infringed upon.
Initially, the emperor established thirteen kinds of 'inexhaustible treasuries' (wújìnzàng).
There were two categories: 'releasing life' (fàngshēng) and 'charitable giving' (bùshī).
The benefits of these treasuries were already immeasurable.
And every month, during the vegetarian feasts,
he again gave money and food to various temples.
He also separately ordered Zhāng Wénxiū (Zhāng Wénxiū) to arrive.
Daily he would go to the slaughterhouses, where lives were threatened by cauldrons and chopping blocks.
He immediately redeemed and saved countless lives.
This was his constant practice.
Wénxiū (Wénxiū) had previously been a transport official.
He had frequently distributed transport rice to the poor.
He was supposed to be executed.
The emperor, pitying his sincerity, mercifully forbade it.
Not only did he pardon his grave crime,
but he also bestowed upon him the title 'utmost arrival' (zhìdào).
Since it was neither a market transaction based on warmth,
nor like Jí Àn (Jí Àn)'s request for punishment,
the pardon for a humble person was far greater than in times past.
Wénxiū (Wénxiū), having received this great favor,
never once slacked off.
Sometimes he could not eat at noon,
yet his feet did not rest as he traveled throughout the capital.
His steps were as swift as flying.
Beating drums, raising banners, carrying burdens, and rushing about,
he released and saved all types of domestic animals and wild beasts, exhausting all four categories of living beings.
At that time, from court officials to commoners,
all rejoiced and participated.
Furthermore, there were eleven million one hundred and fourteen thousand coins.
The emperor categorized their intentions and listed ten items.
Some donated wealth to participate in the Dharma activities,
some donated wealth for offerings,
some donated wealth to practice compassion,
some donated wealth to request sutra recitation,
some donated wealth for festival provisions,
some donated wealth for releasing lives,
some donated wealth for general charity,
some offered their bodies to the great assembly,
some burned their fingers to make offerings to the Three Jewels,
some, upon hearing the Dharma lectures, sought to become monastics.
In the past, when the Tathāgata taught the Path, people attained enlightenment differently.
Thus, the 'Dharma Eye' (Fǎyǎn) saw that there were countless beings, and their root natures were not uniform.
The emperor, for all these people, simultaneously made great vows; the vow text is seen separately.
This humble minister, attending the lecture hall,
respectfully establishes this preface, generally presenting six categories of principles and answers to questions.
One fascicle, collectively recording thirteen.
On the first day, Dūjiǎng (Dūjiǎng) Fǎbiāo (Fǎbiāo) of Zhīyuán Sì (Zhīyuán Sì) chanted, saying:
Móhē Bōrě Bōluómì Jīng (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra).
The decree stated:
Mànqiàn (曼倩) said, "Discourse is easy."
Yet, when it comes to the ultimate truth, it is even more ineffable.
Though I exhausted both ends, I still felt ashamed of my four replies.
Indeed, wisdom does not move; the ultimate truth is unspoken.
It is profoundly unfathomable, transcending and uniquely distant.
It illuminates the entire realm of emptiness without moving its light.
It exhausts the limits of existence without exerting its power.
Dwelling without dwelling is how it dwells.
Attaining without attaining is how it attains.
A hundred distinct blessings universally enter into non-arising.
Ten thousand diverse good deeds all converge in equality.
Thus, it can guide the multitude of blind to journey together,
like six boats crossing the waters in unison.
It accomplishes the wondrous fruit of Bodhi,
and enters the profound gate of Nirvāṇa.
The three insights (三明) cannot fathom its mechanism,
and the seven skills of debate (七辯) cannot proclaim its reality.
The Great Sage, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn), did not deviate from his original vow,
but with the power of expedient means (fāngbiàn) guided all sentient beings.
He spoke of names and forms where there are no names and forms,
enabling seekers of the Dao to recognize the path, and those who ask for directions to know the way home.
Therefore, in Rájagr̥ha (Wángshèchéng), he roared the great lion's roar and expounded the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra (Móhē Bōrě Bōluómì Jīng).
This sūtra is also called the Great Chapter Sūtra (Dàpǐn Jīng).
Ancient traditions suggest there were five periods of Prajñāpāramitā (Bōrě).
However, upon exhaustive examination of sūtras and treatises, this claim is not found.
There is only the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Humane Kings (Rénwáng Bōrě),
whose title is listed at the end of the fascicle, containing its full text.
The first [period]: The Buddha expounded the Great Chapter Prajñāpāramitā (Dàpǐn Bōrě) in Rájagr̥ha.
The second: The Buddha expounded the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā (Jīngāng Bōrě) in the Jèt林vana (Jíhuán Lín) in Srāvastī (Shèwèi Guó).
The third: The Buddha expounded the Heavenly King Prajñāpāramitā (Tiānwáng Bōrě) in the Jèt林vana in Srāvastī.

All Buddhas have three bodies.
First, the Dharma-body (*Fǎshēn*).
This refers to what is realized by the perfect mind.
Second, the Reward-body (*Bàoshēn*).
This refers to what is induced by myriad good deeds.
Third, the Transformation-body (*Huàshēn*).
This refers to what appears according to circumstances.
Now, concerning Shìjiāmóuní Fó:
His Dharma-body was realized long ago, and His Reward-body was perfected long ago.
His present appearance is merely a Transformation-body.
It is said that in the past, at the place of the Shìjiā Fó, He made the Bodhi vow to share the same name.

Thus, it is known that for those who flourish in the Way, their teachings are profoundly cultivated;
for those who prosper in their endeavors, their writings are splendidly radiant.
I humbly reflect that
His Majesty the Huángdì,
with the swiftness of Qí, has ascended the throne, and his sagely reverence凝旒.
With the ten good deeds, he propagates benevolence,
transforming and softening the remotest regions.
With the four immeasurables, he regulates customs,
his influence rising higher than before Xūsuì.
Yet, he still exalts the profound norm and composes words,
adorning the constant source and expanding his insights.
His grace pours down, like dirty silk, retaining thoughts for the Gěiyuán.
Thus, in the leisure after creating all things, he personally extended his sagely directive.
At the end of rectifying names, he specially penned a splendid title.
We monks bear the grace of his beneficent patronage,
and treasure the favor of his enduring prosperity.
At first, we were solemnly summoned, and our hearts trembled with trepidation.
We humbly believed that
the Emperor's intention is difficult to grasp, and the profound ford is rarely traversed.
Vainly pondering with a side-pipe (limited vision),
we sighed that chaos had not yet opened.
Indeed, relying on the cries at the gate,
at times, it was as if Xiàngwǎng was attained.
Lántái Tàishǐ and Zǔ Shìjí Kāiguóhóu of Yìngshān Xiàn, Mǒu,
tirelessly offered his discerning wisdom, reviewing without impediment.
So, together we plucked the finest blossoms from the forest of forgiveness,
and gathered the swift feathers of Qíshān.
We sought out the extraordinary explanations from the eight storehouses,
and controlled the spiritual essence of the three points.
With these, one work was completed, compiled into ten volumes.
Comparing their profound insights, the achievements defy description.
However, as the ocean of teachings is vast and the gate of Dharma still broad,
although the essential and subtle meanings have been fully presented in previous compilations,
the comprehensive and abundant writings still require a separate record.
I humbly believe that one who ascends Jīngshān desires to offer something to Liánchéng,
and one who travels along the Chu coast wishes to present tribute in a wrapped 󱨈.
How much more so when the rare treasures of the Dragon Palace illuminate the field of emotion,
and the lingering fragrance of the Deer Park blossoms on the leaves of characters.
If one harbors sincere aspirations, who can forget to offer them?
Furthermore, with the established precedent of lending and borrowing and the clear rules in place,
when spread out in four directions and examined, the jade-like treasures are all gathered.
Comparing their distinctions, orchids and chrysanthemums separate themselves.
There is a guide that leads them here,
like the abundant confluence of the Eastern Ocean.
Each returns to its proper place,
like the gōng and zhǐ notes of the southern yue.
Connected by meaning, there are altogether ten chapters.
Each chapter is divided into upper and lower parts, forming twenty volumes.
It spans over 1,500 scrolls,
and lists over 360 articles.
The ten established chapters are each structured into four categories.
The first two establish the realms of truth and convention.
The next pair clarifies the causes of defilement and purity.
The middle four lay out the paths of cultivation and realization.
The last two present the models for drawing in and guiding.
In sequence, these form a narrative, each subordinating multiple items.
This ensures that the great meaning shines clearly and the ultimate words are not lost.
It vaguely displays the widely opened thousand gates,
and boasts the combined storage of a hundred passages.
It is like the dawn stars compiled into a volume,
whose pearls are truly incomparable and scattered.
It is like spring clusters woven into brocade, certainly not crafted yet beautifully arranged.
This is truly due to a deep understanding of the profound insight,
thus causing the subtle meanings to mysteriously converge.
That it is not disordered has its basis.
However, a single hair can indicate the phoenix's splendor,
thus the recorded content is not extensive.
A pair of flying birds is insufficient to exhaust the swan island,
thus its remaining beauty is hard to fully describe.
Since it is limited by the teachings of the Golden Mouth,
it truly incurs no criticism of "jade屑" (fragments).
In the process of selecting and deleting, even the slightest detail, in deliberating what to keep or discard,
fearing to cause error a thousand miles away,
every time we added careful review, repeating it thrice.
It was on the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the third year of Lóngshuò that the imperial pronouncement was first received.
Up to the fourth day of the fifth month of the first year of Líndé,
the two parts, front and back, are now fully completed in "sweat green" (inked bamboo slips).
The former is concise yet comprehensive,
the latter is broad yet without杂.
May it be able to uphold the grand綱 of the Dharma net,
and encompass the essential keys of the Dharma gate.
May it open the excellent path to cessation of mind,
and provide the spiritual garden for extensive hearing.
I humbly wish that the supreme taste of "tíhú" (ghee) may forever nourish the imperial heart,
and the bright pearl of "bōrě" (Prajñā) may eternally illuminate the imperial grasp.
May these writings not fall into oblivion,
and the true tradition be suspended with the sun and moon.
May this fortune be boundless,
and the imperial reign be as firm as the heavens and earth.
The above one chapter, Guǎn Duō Fǎ Jù.
From the time the six yáo began and the eight guà were arranged,
writing was initiated,
and canonical texts made manifest.
Phoenix seals, dragon diagrams, golden tablets, and jade characters;
a hundred schools with different paths, myriad volumes divided into sections.
Although their principles delved into profundity and their words exhausted all phenomena,
their records of emotions and encapsulations of nature did not go beyond the human realm.
Starting from the beginning and reaching the end, how could they encompass what is beyond the mundane?
There are also the sayings of Zàngshǐ and the discussions of Yuánlì,
precious scriptures that are extravagant and embellished texts that are bizarre.
They are like carving ice, achieving nothing,
or writing in the air, lacking substance.
Compared to the profound meanings that pierce through flowers and the abstruse words written on leaves,
the vastness and breadth of the two vehicles and the profundity and secrecy of the eight storehouses,
which compete in depth and shallowness to compare their superiority and inferiority—
this is like comparing the smallness of an ant mound to the towering heights of Sōng Huà,
or the insignificance of an ox's puddle to the vastness of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
Its manifest meanings and hidden rules,
its gate of liberation and garden of total retention,
past and future, both accord with true suchness.
Initial and final minds all return to right enlightenment.
It guides the deluded beings from the ocean of desire,
where emotional dust and mental defilements dissolve together.
It leads the prodigal son to the chamber of compassion,
where the jewel in the robe and the jewel in the topknot both arrive.
Its transformation overflows realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and its merits cover kalpas as many as specks of dust.
How great and ultimate it is!
It cannot be described by words.
Up to the time when it was jointly sought by Yǔ and circulated by Zhōu, when it reached Hàn through daily communication,
Cài Yīn traveled west, and Zhúlán journeyed east.
The words of the Golden Mouth and the doctrines of the Precious Platform
filled silks and piled up bamboo strips, spreading throughout the central domain.
However, the scrolls were numerous and complex, and the stream of teachings deep and expansive.
The true form and original source were ultimately difficult to fully examine.
