When our imperial Táng created this (new era), and the sagely sovereign ruled,
the profound teachings were proclaimed, and the monastic community sincerely united.
They transmitted brilliance and spread spiritual essence, illuminating and moistening the whole realm.
Sanskrit sounds and chanting filled the capital.
The prosperity of its propagation is beyond comparison and difficult to fully describe.
At that time, there was a great virtuous master from Xīmíng, Dàoshì Fǎshī, whose courtesy name was Xuányùn.
He was a leader of the Buddhist gate.
As a child, he showed extraordinary intellect, playing with sand,
and took tonsure in his youth.
His compassion was profound, receiving ants (showing kindness to all beings),
and he completed his ordination on the platform of fully receiving precepts.
His precept-virtues were perfectly clear,
like protecting pearls.
His understanding of the Vinaya was refined and clear,
like rejoicing upon seeing one's reflection in a mirror.
He loved and admired Mahāyāna, thoroughly understanding the true form.
Thus, with his brilliance and erudition, he was summoned to reside at Xīmíng.
There, in his leisure after studying the Five Parts (Agamas), he thoroughly read the Three Storehouses (Tripitaka).
He felt that throughout ancient and modern dynasties, many works had been created,
but even with elegant tastes and fine words, they were insufficient for extensive records.
Therefore, he culled the essence from the garden of literature,
and smelled the sandalwood of the great meaning.
He compiled and recorded them by category,
naming it Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
It comprises one hundred chapters,
compiled into ten fascicles.
Its meaning is rich, its text concise,
like unifying the extensive essentials of Yúshì.
Its traces proclaim the mirror of the Way,
aspiring to the vast clarity of Yòushàng.
With its words, its Way is made manifest.
It brings forth the ultimate profundity without omission,
and encompasses the subtle gates completely.
It was on
the tenth day of the third month of Líndé third year of Dà Táng, in the year of Shè tí, the month of Gūxǐ.
The compilation was completed.
May those who compile profound words search the scrolls and gain the pearl of meaning.
May those who follow the right path peruse the text and drink sweet dew.
Read it to know the subtle,
observe it to see the profound.
May it illuminate equally with the surrounding scenery,
and endure together with the revolving heavens.
I have read your recent communication.
I understand that you wish to hear about the principles of the Way (Dàoyì).
Indeed, the Buddhist teachings are profoundly deep, and their ultimate truths are subtle and pure.
The Way of the Single Mark (yī xiāng zhī dào) is distant and unfathomable.
The Gate of Non-Duality (bù èr zhī mén) is silent and without echo.
Unless one has a deep understanding of the Esoteric Doctrine (xuánzōng) and a precise comprehension of the Subtle Meanings (miàoyì),
how could one easily distinguish such matters?
As for propagating the orthodox teachings,
it lies in benefiting sentient beings.
As for the inner meaning for this disciple,
I truly cherish and delight in it.
However, to delve deeply and reach far,
there is much I have not yet fully understood.
As for the principle of benefiting others,
what is there to discuss?
All the monks have entered the Dharma gate,
and their journey in the Way is daily expanding.
As for the Dharma Master (fǎshī),
there is even less need for explanation.
You say you wish to receive instruction;
this is truly something I do not comprehend.
I hope you understand this point,
and I will not say more.
Tǒng bows.
Your Highness, with innate wisdom and superior knowledge,
delves into subtle meanings with divine insight,
possesses naturally excellent eloquence,
and delivers profound discourses that transcend the mundane.
Each time we converse, the entire gathering is captivated.
This truly causes the devas to praise your goodness,
and indeed makes Shì and Fàn rain down flowers.
Although this humble monk knew the right direction in youth,
in old age, I have accomplished nothing.
I am presumptuously added to the company of the enlightened,
yet I am ashamed of my lack of understanding and do not withdraw.
How can I not desire to partake in these profound principles?
Do I dare to entreat you?
It is truly to long to hear your profound discourse.
Now, I am humbly favored with a reply to my intention,
but it has not yet granted the wishes of the multitude.
Reflecting on my casual remarks, I am deeply apprehensive.
My thirst and longing are genuine; my hunger and emptiness are not feigned.
Reflecting on my thoughts and examining my desires, I again pray to hear.
I only hope that the sweet dew will be revealed,
so that I may forever dispel my vulgar parsimony.
I humbly pray that by your Four Great Vows (sì hóng běnshì),
you will graciously grant my triple request.
Respectfully and earnestly presented.
I have again read your recent communication.
I understand that you still wish me to elaborate on the meanings.
I cannot explain how this would be beneficial, as stated before.
I am even more ashamed to speak about the revealing of the sweet dew.
If it is merely to briefly outline the doctrinal principles,
there is no reason not to do so.
But I am ashamed to compare a fish eye to the night-shining pearl of the Dharma Master.
Tǒng bows.
Your minister Tǒng presents.
I have received an imperial edict from your left and right sides
conveying the imperial decree.
You have graciously bestowed a water-rhinoceros ruyi scepter.
This is indeed what is needed for the Way (Dào) and its principles (Yì).
The luster of white jade cannot compare to its preciousness.
The quality of coral is not as rare as this.
The carving, once completed, was first bestowed upon the common and humble.
It is like receiving the hairpin of Emperor Hàn (Hàn Dì);
it is like obtaining the seal of Zhào Yáo.
I respectfully receive your divine awe and will display it in the various lecture halls.
This will surely make the joyful Arhats (Luóhàn) lament having abandoned their alms bowls,
and the great scholars (shuòrú) like Wáng Shì abandon their arguments of "black foals."
A bear-adorned precious sword,
Zǐ Huán (Cáo Pī) would be ashamed of his great gift.
A yak-tail whisk,
Zhāng Chǎng would be ashamed of his old ceremonial object.
This extraordinary grace has specially descended; I am deeply grateful and overjoyed.
I am unable to contain my humble feelings.
I respectfully submit this memorial to be heard.
Respectfully presented.
The principles of the Two Truths (Èr Dì) are indeed profoundly subtle.
Unless one has an open mind,
one cannot comprehend their vastness and depth.
There is not just one method for clarifying the Way.
To summarize, it does not go beyond "object" (jìng) and "wisdom" (zhì).
Sometimes, meaning is clarified through the object;
sometimes, conduct is manifested through wisdom.
As for the Two Truths, they are about clarifying meaning based on the object.
If one is confused about this method, the Three Existences (sān yǒu) will not cease.
If one comprehends its essence, all defilements (wàn lèi) will be eradicated.
What are called the Two Truths?
One is the Ultimate Truth (zhēndì).
The second is called the Conventional Truth (súdì).
The Ultimate Truth is also called the First Noble Truth (dì yī yì dì).
The Conventional Truth is also called the Mundane Truth (shìdì).
Ultimate Truth and Conventional Truth are named based on their established essences.
First Noble Truth and Mundane Truth are named based on praise and censure.
If spoken in sequence,
one should say: one, Ultimate Truth;
two, Conventional Truth.
One and two combined,
the number would be three.
Not only does the number exceed two,
but also the names have a front and back.
This is inconvenient for the meaning.
Since the Ultimate is not due to the Conventional,
and the Conventional is also not born from the Ultimate,
it can only be said that there is one Ultimate and one Conventional.
"Ultimate" (zhēn) means "real" or "actual."
This means equality, with no other phenomena
that can cause confusion.
"Conventional" (sú) means "aggregation" or "collection."
These phenomena can arise,
creating delusive and artificial appearances.
"First Noble" (dì yī yì)
is a beautiful name specifically established within the realm of non-arising.
It means this phenomenon is supreme, most subtle, and none can surpass it.
"Mundane" (shì) means "separation" or "differentiation."
It refers to arising and ceasing, flowing and changing, without a fixed form.
The Nirvana Sūtra says:
"What transcendent beings know is called the First Noble Truth.
What mundane beings know is called the Mundane Truth."
This is a textual proof of the principle of praise and censure.
The naming of the Two Truths differs.
"Ultimate," "Conventional," "Mundane," etc., are spoken of with a single meaning.
The First Noble Truth is spoken of with two meanings.
It means that this principle's virtue is supreme (first), and its meaning is also supreme (first).
The mundane (shì) is delusive and artificial, so it has no meaning.
Therefore, only the name "Mundane" is established.
"Truth" (dì) means "to be firm and real."
The Ultimate Truth is firmly and truly ultimate.
The Conventional Truth is firmly and truly conventional.
The Ultimate Truth is free from existence and non-existence.
The Conventional Truth is both existence and non-existence.
"Both existence and non-existence" is a provisional name.
"Free from existence and non-existence" is the Middle Way (zhōngdào).
The Ultimate is the Middle Way.
Its essence is non-arising.
Since the Conventional is a provisional name,
its essence is arising phenomena.
Huìchāo of Nánjiàn Monastery asked:
"Delusive and artificial appearances are called conventional.
Being free from existence and non-existence is called ultimate.
I do not know whether the delusive and artificial is of the same essence as the ultimate, or if it is different."
The imperial decree (lìngzhǐ) replied:
"What mundane beings know has arising phenomena as its essence.
What transcendent beings know has non-arising as its essence.
Based on sentient beings,
it should be explained in this way.
If we speak of the Ultimate, then 'existence' (yǒu) is 'emptiness' (kōng).
The Conventional points to 'emptiness' as 'existence.'
According to this meaning, they cannot be different."
He also asked:
"Since the Ultimate and Conventional are said to be of one essence,
I do not know if the Ultimate Truth also has arising and activity,
or if arising and activity are independent and not related to the Ultimate Truth."
The imperial decree again replied:
"The ultimate principle is tranquil and has no arising or activity.
It is the deluded consciousness of ordinary people that subjectively perceives arising and activity."
He also asked:
"I do not know whether there is arising and activity which ordinary people perceive subjectively,
or no arising and activity which ordinary people perceive subjectively."
The imperial decree again replied:
"If there were arising and activity, it would not be called subjective perception.
Because there is no activity, yet activity is perceived, it is subjective perception."
He also asked:
"If phenomena have no arising or activity, then there should only be one truth."
The imperial decree again replied:
"This principle is eternally tranquil; this is one truth in itself.
The subjective perception of arising and activity is another truth.
According to this, there should be two, not one."
He also asked:
"Is there subjective perception, or is there no subjective perception?"
The imperial decree again replied:
"According to sentient beings, there is this subjective perception."
He also asked:
"If there is subjective perception based on sentient beings,
then according to the Dharma, there should be no perception of activity."
The imperial decree again replied:
"The Dharma is indeed without activity,
but it does not prevent those who are subjectively deluded from perceiving activity."
Dānyáng Yǐn Jìn'ānwáng Xiāo Gāng諮 asked:
"The explanation and meaning, based on human understanding, differentiate between existence and non-existence.
I am unsure whether the illusory and non-existence
are merely one entity, or if there is indeed a difference."
The Master replied:
"What ordinary people perceive is its arising and activity.
What sages perceive is its non-existence.
When discussed based on benevolence, they are indeed different entities.
If speaking of their identity, then they are not different.
It is fully as I have just explained, no need for further discussion."
He further asked:
"If the true is not different from the conventional,
and the conventional is not different from the true,
how can it be that what ordinary people perceive takes existent phenomena as its substance,
while what sages perceive takes non-existence as its substance?"
The Master replied:
"By means of the conventional, one knows the true;
by means of the true, one sees the conventional.
Discussing it from this perspective, it naturally becomes non-different.
When distinguishing views based on individuals, there is indeed a difference between existence and non-existence."
He further asked:
"Since the substance of conventional truth is said to be illusory,
how can this illusion be perceived within reality?"
The Master replied:
"The substance of reality itself is free from illusion.
Deluded individuals arbitrarily construct it,
deeming it to exist.
This does not harm the real substance, which is intrinsically profound and empty."
He further asked:
"What sages perceive is non-flowing.
What ordinary people perceive is flowing.
Since flowing and non-flowing are different,
I, the ignorant one, believe they cannot be one."
The Master replied:
"I am not saying that flowing and non-flowing are each one entity.
I am simply saying that ordinary people arbitrarily perceive this flow within the non-flowing.
From this perspective, they can be considered one."
He further asked:
"The substance of ultimate tranquility is intrinsically non-flowing.
Ordinary people perceive flow, but this flow does not depart from the true substance.
If so, then there is only one truth, and the two truths are not established."
The Master replied:
"The substances are always identical, and the principle cannot be different.
However, ordinary people perceive illusion, while sages behold ultimate tranquility.
Based on ordinary people and sages, the names of the two truths can be established."
Zhāotísì Huìyǎn諮 asked:
"Ordinary people perceive the conventional, taking existent phenomena as its substance.
Sages perceive the true, taking non-existence as its substance.
I am unsure whether existence and non-existence
are merely seen as different, or based on what meaning can they be distinguished as one?"
The Master replied:
"Ordinary people construct existence out of non-existence.
Sages discern non-existence from existence.
Existence and non-existence are identical; this refers to a single entity."
He further asked:
"I am unsure, if this can be spoken of as one,
what is the name of this one?"
The Master replied:
"Precisely because existence is not different from non-existence, and non-existence is not different from existence,
it is named 'one', and there is no other name."
He further asked:
"If non-existence is not different from existence,
and existence is not different from non-existence,
and only one is perceived,
how then can there be two?"
The Master replied:
"Ordinary people perceive existence, and sages perceive non-existence.
Since these two perceptions are distinct, they constitute two."
He further asked:
"Sages perceive non-existence, and non-existence can be called a truth.
But how can ordinary people's perception of existence be called a truth?"
The Master replied:
"What sages perceive as non-existence is a truth for sages.
What ordinary people firmly believe to be existence,
is therefore a truth for ordinary people."
Qīxuánsì Tánzōng諮 asked:
"Do sages perceive conventional truth, or do they not perceive conventional truth?"
The Master replied:
"Sages know that ordinary people perceive conventional truth.
As for sages, they no longer perceive this."
He further asked:
"Since sages do not perceive conventional truth,
how do they teach and transform sentient beings using conventional truth?"
The Master replied:
"Sages, being free from delusion, naturally do not perceive conventional truth.
This does not prevent sages from knowing what ordinary people perceive.
Therefore, they compassionately adapt to the inclinations of beings by speaking of the two truths."
He further asked:
"Sages know that ordinary people perceive conventional truth.
Is this ordinary person that same conventional truth or not?"
The Master replied:
"This ordinary person is precisely conventional truth.
Sages also do not perceive this ordinary person."
He further asked:
"Since sages do not perceive ordinary people,
how do they know that ordinary people perceive conventional truth?"
The Master replied:
"Although sages themselves are free from the notion of an ordinary person,
they are still capable of knowing that there are ordinary people
who consider themselves to exist.
Therefore, they compassionately respond to their inclinations by speaking of conventional truth."
Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng Wáng Guī諮 asked:
"I am unsure, since the true and the conventional are not the same,
how can there be the meaning of identity?"
The Master replied:
"What sages attain is their own perception of non-existence.
What ordinary people attain is their own perception of existence.
The perceptions themselves are different.
This does not prevent the conventional from being within the true."
He further asked:
"I am unsure, since there is no difference,
yet it is said to have two meanings.
Does the meaning depart from the substance,
or is the meaning identical to the substance?"
The Master replied:
"They do not depart from each other, hence it is called one substance.
The difference in perception between the ignorant and the sages naturally forms different meanings."
He further asked:
"Do ordinary people merely perceive the conventional, or can they also perceive the true?"
The Master replied:
"They can only perceive the conventional, and cannot perceive the true."
He further asked:
"Since the substances are identical, how can they not behold the true?"
The Master replied:
"If ordinary people perceived the true, they should not behold the conventional.
Since beholding the conventional is deluded, how can they perceive the true?"
Línggēnsì Sēngqiān諮 asked:
"If 'first' means 'having nothing superior',
this is a term of praise.
'The true being separate from the conventional' should also be a term of praise."
The Master replied:
"This very substance is true;
it cannot be called praise.
The 'first ultimate truth' (Dìyīyìdì) establishes an additional beautiful name,
which is why it is praise."
He further asked:
"Since 'no one is superior to me' can be called praise,
and 'my substance is true',
why is it not praise?"
The Master replied:
"'No one is superior to me' is why it can be called praise.
'My substance is true' is also 'my truth'.
Therefore, it is not praise."
He further asked:
"'I have no superior';
this can be called praise.
'I am not false'; why can this not be praise?"
The Master replied:
"'Not false' and 'true' are names for the substance itself.
It is like someone understanding the meaning of a text and calling it 'understanding the meaning'.
It merely accurately describes its actual substance;
how can it constitute praise?"
He further asked:
"If nothing can transcend this Dharma,
how can it immediately be praise?"
The Master replied:
"Since it is said to be 'untranscendable',
how can it not be praise?"
Luópínghóu Xiāo Zhènglì諮 asked:
"I am unsure whether conventional truth is existent phenomena or not."
The Master replied:
"The substance of conventional truth is precisely existent phenomena."
He further asked:
"Since the conventional is an arbitrary perception,
how can there be existence?"
The Master replied:
"It is because of arbitrary perception that there is existence,
hence there are existent phenomena."
He further asked:
"Arbitrary perception creates existence.
In reality, there are no phenomena.
If in reality there are no phenomena, what is spoken of as existence?"
The Master replied:
"This very existent phenomenon is called arbitrary perception.
And this very arbitrary perception is called existent phenomenon."
He further asked:
"If it is arbitrary perception, there should be no existence.
If there must be existence, why is it called arbitrary perception?"
The Master replied:
"Since it is called arbitrary perception,
in reality, there is no existence.
However, due to arbitrary perception, it is considered to exist,
resulting in this arbitrary existence."
Héngshān Hóu Xiāo Gōng 諮 inquired:
I am unclear, since the Ultimate Truth (Dìyī Yìdì) has defined categories,
why does the Conventional Truth (Shìdì) alone lack defined names?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
As the conventional is superficial and common, there is no meaning to discern.
He further inquired:
If there is no meaning to discern,
how can it be called a truth (dì)?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Ordinary people perceive it clearly,
hence the name "truth" is established.
He further inquired:
If ordinary perception can receive the name "truth,"
it should also be that ordinary perception can accept the character "meaning" (yì).
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Ordinary people perceive it clearly,
hence the name "truth" can be established.
But the superficial and common has no meaning;
how can one forcibly assign it the character "meaning"?
He further inquired:
Although the superficial and common has no true meaning,
it is not without the meaning of the superficial and common.
Since there is this superficial and common,
how can it not receive the name "meaning"?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
It is precisely because it is superficial and common that there is no meaning to discern.
If there were meaning to discern, what would it be called superficial and common?
Zhōngxīng Sì monk Huái 諮 inquired:
Lìngzhǐ explains, saying:
The ultimate does not depart from the conventional;
the conventional does not depart from the ultimate.
I am unclear, the ultimate is formless,
while the conventional has form.
Since form and formless are different,
how can they be of the same essence?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Form and formless are different in this respect.
However, what ordinary people perceive as existent,
is precisely what the sages perceive as non-existent.
Considering it this way,
one can achieve no distinction.
He further inquired:
Since it is one dharma,
how can it be seen as two?
If there are two perceptions, how can it be one dharma?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
The principle is indeed not two,
but depending on what is perceived by beings,
thus there can be two.
He further inquired:
If there are two perceptions,
how can they not contradict each other?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
If the dharma were truly two,
then contradiction would be possible.
The dharma is always not two;
people's perceptions are self-twofold.
Based on this,
how can there be contradiction?
He further inquired:
If people's perceptions are twofold,
one can speak of two people.
But since the principle is one,
how can there be two?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Although the principle is not twofold, it becomes twofold according to people.
Shǐxīng Wáng's fourth son, Xiāo Yìng 諮, inquired:
The Ultimate Truth (Dìyī Yìdì)—its meaning is ultimate (dìyī).
Is its virtue also ultimate or not?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Since its meaning is ultimate,
its virtue is also ultimate.
He further inquired:
Simply saying "ultimate"
already encompasses both virtue and meaning.
Why add the character "meaning" again, leading to redundancy?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Simply saying "ultimate" still leaves the meaning obscure.
When "ultimate" (dìyī) sees "meaning" (yì), it can be perfectly beautiful.
He further inquired:
If adding the character "meaning" makes it perfectly beautiful,
why not add the character "virtue" (dé) to make it perfectly beautiful?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
"Ultimate" (dìyī) is virtue;
why wait to add it again?
But by adding the character "meaning," both virtue and meaning become beautiful.
He further inquired:
Simply calling it "ultimate" is sufficient to see its beauty.
Singly adding the character "meaning" seems somewhat restrictive.
Lìngzhǐ replied:
"Ultimate" (dìyī) represents virtue.
Adding the character "meaning" again,
both beauties are presented.
How can there be any restriction?
Wú Píng Shìzǐ Xiāo Lì 諮 inquired:
The general meaning states:
The Ultimate Truth (Dìyī Yìdì) and the Conventional Truth (Shìdì) are named by praise and criticism.
The two truths, ultimate (zhēndì) and conventional (súdì), are named by establishing their essence.
Upon examining the principle of the ultimate truth, it is subtle and beyond words and thoughts.
I am unclear how it can be said to have a fixed essence.
Lìngzhǐ replied:
When speaking of its formlessness, there is no ultimate that is not ultimate.
We provisionally name and speak of its form to define its essence as ultimate.
He further inquired:
If the ultimate truth is essenceless,
yet we provisionally use words to discern its essence,
I am unclear, if the ultimate truth is formless,
why do we not provisionally use words to discern its form?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Provisionally using words to discern its essence already risks disparaging its virtue.
If we were to further provisionally use words to discern its form, it would defile the profound void.
He further inquired:
The ultimate truth is profound and void, transcending words.
Now that we speak of "ultimate truth,"
is this not provisionally using words to discern its form?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
This name is provisionally used;
the name itself is a form.
This does not harm the principle that it is formless and voidly quiescent.
He further inquired:
I am unclear, this provisional use of words to discern essence,
is it in accord with the principle or not in accord with the principle?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Speaking of names when there are no names is not entirely in accord with the principle.
He further inquired:
If provisionally using words to discern names,
the names are not in accord with the principle,
I am unclear, what does this provisional use aim to explain?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Although not in accord with the principle,
for the sake of guiding sentient beings, names and forms must be used in explanation.
Sòngxī Sì's Huìlìng 諮 inquired:
The ultimate truth takes non-arising as its essence;
the conventional truth takes arising phenomena as its essence.
Yet it is said that non-arising is arising,
and arising is non-arising.
Is this mutual inclusion within the essence,
or mutual inclusion within the meaning?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
It is mutual inclusion within the essence;
the meaning is not mutually inclusive.
He further inquired:
If the meaning is not mutually inclusive,
how can the essence be mutually inclusive?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Ordinary people see existence;
sages perceive non-existence.
Difference arises from perception;
as for the essence, it is always mutually inclusive.
He further inquired:
If the essence is not twofold, why does it need to be mutually inclusive?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
If the essence is not distinct and twofold, but causes perception to be twofold,
since perception is twofold and different, it is necessary to clarify the essence as mutually inclusive.
He further inquired:
If, as you explain,
it is indeed clarifying mutual inclusion from the perspective of people.
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Viewed by people as two,
this is why the two truths are named.
Clarifying mutual inclusion from the perspective of people's views is also a great hindrance.
Shǐxīng Wáng's fifth son, Xiāo Yè 諮, inquired:
The ultimate truth (zhēndì) is called ultimate (zhēn).
Is it truly ultimate or not?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
It is truly ultimate.
He further inquired:
When a Bodhisattva unites with the ultimate,
does he forget the conventional and forget the ultimate or not?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Forgets the conventional and forgets the ultimate,
hence it is called uniting with the ultimate.
He further inquired:
If forgetting the conventional and forgetting the ultimate is why it is called uniting with the ultimate,
how can forgetting the conventional and forgetting the ultimate be considered truly ultimate?
Lìngzhǐ replied:
If one clings to the conventional and clings to the ultimate, how can it be considered truly ultimate?
It is precisely by relinquishing both that it is called truly ultimate.
He further inquired:
If forgetting the conventional and forgetting the ultimate is truly ultimate,
then forgetting the ultimate and forgetting the conventional should also be truly conventional.
Lìngzhǐ replied:
Forgetting the conventional and forgetting the ultimate is how the ultimate is seen.
Forgetting the ultimate and forgetting the conventional makes it even more evident that it is not conventional.
He further inquired:
When a Bodhisattva unites with the ultimate,
having forgotten the conventional and forgotten the ultimate,
now calling it "truly ultimate" would become contrary to the principle.
Lìngzhǐ replied:
It is provisionally called "truly ultimate";
ultimately, one naturally forgets the ultimate.
The relinquishment of both is called "real,"
how can it be contrary to the principle?
Xīnghuáng Sì Fǎxuān 諮曰:
Yìzhǐ 云:
“俗諦是有是無故 以生法為體.
未審有法有體可得稱生.
無是無法.
云何得有生義?”
Lìngzhǐ 答曰:
“俗諦有無相待而立.
既是相待故並得稱生.”
又諮:
“若有無兩法並稱為生,
生義既一,
則有無無異.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“俱是凡夫所見故生義得同是有是無.
焉得不異?”
又諮:
“若有無果別,
應有生不生.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“既相待立名,
故同一生義.”
Chéngxiāng Hóu Xiāo Qí 諮曰:
“未審第一之名,
是形待以不?”
Lìngzhǐ 答曰:
“正是形待.”
又諮:
“第一無相有何形待?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“既云第一,
豈 得非待?”
又諮:
“第一是待.
既稱第一,
世諦待於第一,
何不名為第二?
若俗諦是待而不稱第二,
亦應真諦是待不名第一.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“若稱第一是待,
於義已足.
無假說俗,
第二方成相待.”
又諮:
“若世諦之名不稱第二,
則第一之稱無所形待.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“第一褒真.
既云相待,
世名是待,
直置可知.”
Guāngzhái Sì Fǎyún 諮曰:
“聖人所知之境,
此是真諦.
未審能知之智,
為是真諦,
為是俗諦?”
Lìngzhǐ 答曰:
“能知是智,
所知是境.
智來冥境得言即真.”
又諮:
“有智之人,
為是真諦,
為是俗諦?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“若呼有智之人即是俗諦.”
又諮:
“未審俗諦之人,
何得有真諦之智?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“聖人能忘於俗,
所以得有真智.”
又諮:
“此人既冥無生,
亦應不得稱人.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“冥於無生不得言人.
寄名相說常自有人.”
Línggēn Sì Huìlìng 諮曰:
“為於真諦中見有,
為俗諦中見有?”
Lìngzhǐ 答曰:
“於真諦中橫見有俗.”
又諮:
“俗諦之有為實為虛?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“是虛妄之有.”
又 諮:
“為當見妄,
為當見有?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“見於妄有.”
又諮:
“無名相中何得見有名相?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“於無名相見有名相,
所以妄有.”
又諮:
“於無名相妄見為有,
譬如火熱,
惑者言冷.
得就熱中有冷相不?
若於無相而有名相,
亦於火中應有此冷.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“火自常熱妄見有冷,
此自 惑不嘗異.”
Xiānggōng Sì Huìxìng 諮曰:
“凡夫之惑,
為當但於真有迷,
於俗亦迷?”
Lìngzhǐ 答曰:
“於真見有,
此是迷真.
既見有俗不成迷俗.”
又諮:
“若使解俗便成解真,
若不解真豈得解俗?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“真理虛寂惑心不解.
雖不解真何妨解俗?”
又諮:
“此心不解真,
於真可是惑.
此心既解俗,
於 俗應非惑.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“實而為語通自是惑.
辨俗森羅於俗中各解.”
Zhuāngyán Sì Sēngmín 諮曰:
“三十心中所得空解,
為是真解,
為是俗解?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“可名相似解.”
又諮:
“未審相似為真為俗?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“習觀無生不名俗解.
未見無生不名真解.”
又諮:
“若能照之智非真非俗,
亦應所照之境非真非俗.
若是非真非俗則有三諦.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“所照之境既即無生,
無生是真豈有三諦?”
又諮:
“若境即真境,
何不智即真智?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“未見無生故非真智.
何妨此智未真,
而習觀真境?
豈得以智未真而使境非真境?”
Xuānwǔ Sì Fǎchǒng 諮曰:
“真諦不生不滅,
俗諦有生有滅.
真俗兩義得言有異.
談其法體只得是一.
未審體從於義,
亦得有二不?”
Lìngzhǐ 答曰:
“體亦不得合從於義.”
又諮:
“未審就凡聖兩見得 言兩義,
亦就凡聖兩見得言兩體?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“理不相異,
所以云一.
就凡聖兩見,
得有二體之殊.”
又諮:
“若使凡者見有聖人見無,
便應凡夫但見世諦有,
聖人應見太虛無.”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“太虛亦非聖人所見.
太虛得名由於相待.
既由待生並凡所見.”
又諮:
“凡夫所見空有得言是一不?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“就凡為語有實異無.
約聖作談無不異有.”
Jiànyè Sì Sēngmǐn 諮曰:
“俗人解俗為當解俗參差而言解俗,
為當見俗虛假而言解俗?”
Lìngzhǐ 答曰:
“只是見俗參差而言解俗.”
又諮:
“俗諦不但參差,
亦是虛妄.
何故解參差而不解虛妄?”
Lìngzhǐ 答:
“若使凡夫解虛妄,
即是解真不解虛妄.
所以名為解俗.”
Guāngzhái Sì Jìngtuō 諮曰。
未審聖人見真。
為當漸見。
為當頓見。
令旨答曰。
漸見。
又諮。
無相虛懷。
一見此 現萬相並寂。
未審何故見真得有由漸。
令旨答 曰 。
自凡之聖。
解有淺深真自虛寂。
不妨見有由漸。
又諮。
未審一得無相並忘萬有。
為不悉忘。
令旨答。
一得無相萬有悉忘。
又諮。
一得無相忘萬有者。
亦可一得虛懷窮彼真境。
不應漸見。
令旨答。
Rúlái 會寂自是窮真。
淺行聖人恒自漸見。
又諮。
若見真有漸不可頓會。
亦應漸忘萬有不可頓忘。
令旨答。
解有優劣故有漸見。
忘懷無偏故萬有並寂。
法身虛寂。
遠離有無之境。
獨脫因果之外。
不可以智知。
不可以識識。
豈是稱謂所能論 辯。
將欲顯理不容默然。
故隨從言說。
致有 法身之稱。
Tiānzhú 雲達摩舍利。
此土謂之法身。
若以當體則是自性之目。
若以言說則是相待立名。
法者軌則為旨。
身者有體之義。
軌則之體故曰法身。
略就言說粗陳其體。
是常住身。
是金 剛身。
重加研覈其則不爾。
若定是金剛即為名相。
定是常住。
便成方所。
所謂常住。
本是寄名稱曰金剛 。
本是譬說。
及談實體。
則性同無生。
故雲佛身無為不墮 法 。
故 Nièpán Jīng 說。
Rúlái 之身非身。
是身無量無邊無有足迹。
無知無形畢竟清淨。
無知清淨而不可為無 垢 。
稱曰妙有而復非有。
離無離有所謂法身。
Zhāotí Sì Huìyǎn 諮曰。
未審法身無相不應有體。
何得用體以釋身義。
令旨答。
無名無相乃無體可論。
寄以名相不無妙體。
又諮。
若寄以名相不無妙體。
則寄以名相不成無相。
令旨答。
既雲寄以名相。
足明理實無相。
又諮。
若寄以名相而理實無相。
理既無相雲何有體。
令旨答。
寄言軌物何得無體。
又諮。
亦應寄言軌物。
非復無相。
令旨答。
軌物義邊理非無相。
所言無相本談妙體。
又諮。
真實本來無相。
正應以此軌物。
何得隱斯真實。
強生言相。
令旨答。
真實無相非近學所窺。
是故接諸 膚淺。
必須寄以言相。
Guāngzhái Sì Fǎyún 諮曰。
未審法身常住。
是萬行得不。
令旨答曰。
名相道中萬行所得。
又諮。
既為萬行所得。
豈 言無相。
若必無相豈為萬行所得。
令旨答。
無名無相。
何曾有得寄以名相假言有得。
又諮。
實有萬行實得佛果。
安可以無 相全無所得。
令旨答。
問者住心謂實有萬行。
今謂萬行自空。
豈有實果可得。
又諮。
現有眾生修習萬行。
未審何故全謂為無。
令旨答。
凡俗所見謂之為有。
理而檢之實無萬行。
又諮。
經說常住以為妙有。
如其假說何謂妙有。
令旨答。
寄以名相故說妙有。
理絕名相何妙何有。
Zhuāngyán Sì Sēngmín 諮曰。
未審法身絕相。
智不能知。
絕相絕知。
何得猶有身稱。
令旨答曰。
無名無相曾有何身。
假名相說故曰法身。
又諮。
亦應假名相說是智所照。
何得不可以智知。
不可以識識。
令旨答。
亦得寄 名慧眼所見。
又諮。
若慧眼能見。
則可以智知。
若智不能知。
則慧眼無見。
令旨答。
慧眼無見。
亦無法可見。
又諮。
若雲無見有何法身。
令旨答。
理絕聞見實無法身。
又諮。
若無法身則無正覺。
正覺既有。
法身豈無。
令旨答。
恒是寄言故有正覺。
正覺既在寄言。
法身何得定有。
Xuānwǔ Sì Fǎchǒng 諮曰。
未審法身之稱為正在妙本。
金姿丈六亦是法身。
令旨答曰。
通而為論本迹皆是。
別而為語止在常住。
又諮。
若止在常住不應有身。
若通取丈六。
丈六何謂法身。
令旨答。
常住既有妙體。
何得無身。
丈六亦能軌物。
故可通稱法身。
又諮。
若常住無累方稱法身。
丈六有累何謂法身。
令旨答。
眾生注仰妄見丈六。
丈六非有有何實累。
又諮。
若丈六非有指何為身。
令旨答。
隨物見有謂有應身。
又諮。
既曰應身何謂法身。
令旨答。
通相為辨故兼本迹。
覈求實義不在金姿。
Héi-lìng of Líng-gēn Temple consulted, saying:
"I am unsure whether 'dharmakāya' is so named because it is the ultimate wisdom,
or because it is free from phenomenal characteristics (相 xiàng)."
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"Without names and without characteristics, this is the dharmakāya of aggregated collection (集藏 jí-zàng).
Perfect and ultimate wisdom, this is the dharmakāya of true wisdom (實智 shí-zhì)."
Héi-lìng again consulted:
"If it is without names and without characteristics, then there is no body and no non-body.
Since there is a dharmakāya, how can it be said to be without characteristics?"
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"It is precisely because it is without characteristics that it is called dharmakāya."
Héi-lìng again consulted:
"If it is called dharmakāya because it is without characteristics,
then wisdom, names, and characteristics are no longer dharmakāya."
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"Since it is wisdom without characteristics, how can it not be dharmakāya?"
Héi-lìng again consulted:
"If there is a body, how is it called without characteristics?
If it is without characteristics, how can it have a body?"
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"In the absence of names and characteristics, 'dharmakāya' is provisionally spoken."
Héi-lìng again consulted:
"If 'dharmakāya' is provisionally spoken, it lies precisely in names and characteristics.
How can one directly point to 'without characteristics' and call it dharmakāya?"
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"Since names and characteristics are provisionally established in the 'without characteristics,'
how can one speak of dharmakāya as distinct from this 'without characteristics'?"
Jìng-ān of Líng-wèi Temple consulted, saying:
"I am unsure whether the dharmakāya responds [to beings] or not."
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"The dharmakāya has no response."
Jìng-ān again consulted:
"Originally, it was called dharmakāya because of its manifest responses and transformations.
If there are no manifest responses and transformations, how is it called dharmakāya?"
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"It is originally called dharmakāya because of its principle-body (軌則之體 guǐ-zé zhī tǐ).
The talk of manifest responses and transformations is not what we uphold now."
Jìng-ān again consulted:
"If there are no manifest responses and transformations, how can it be a principle to be followed?
Since it is a principle for beings, how can there be no manifest responses and transformations?"
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"Living beings look up to it and receive benefit.
Therefore, it is said to be a principle.
When the conditions for transformation are complete, what is there to respond and transform?"
Jìng-ān again consulted:
"If it can benefit living beings, then it becomes manifest response and transformation.
If there are no manifest responses and transformations, how can it benefit beings?"
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"When it can generate reverence and aspiration, the principle establishes itself.
Why bother for the perfected being to condescend and respond to worldly dust?"
Jìng-ān again consulted:
"Since it generates reverence and aspiration, how can there be no manifest responses and transformations?
If there are no manifest responses and transformations, what is the benefit of reverence and aspiration?"
Lìng-zhǐ replied:
"It is precisely because the World-Honored One's ultimate divine subtlety is exceptionally profound
that merely looking up to him naturally brings protection.
If one were to benefit only after a response,
how could he be called supremely divine?
To benefit without responding,
this constitutes the ultimate perfection.
If it must truly respond, how would it differ from a bodhisattva?"
Your servant Tǒng presents:
Court scribe Wàn-ān
reverently proclaimed the imperial decree:
"Since Your servant has now completed the lecture, I extend gracious solicitude and inquiry."
I respectfully reflect that the profound and recondite correct teachings encompass all scriptures.
They equalize the handle of the Dipper to ordain the four seasons,
and are like the sun illuminating all nations.
Your servant, without estimating my shallow mediocrity, lightly dared to proclaim them, yet cannot fathom the celestial patterns nor merely observe the jade treasury.
Shame and trepidation intertwine, giving me no peace in sleeping or waking.
Above, the imperial messenger descended; below, I received your benevolent presence.
Honored with such unique kindness, I know not how to express myself.
Unable to bear my humble sentiments,
I respectfully append this memorial to express my gratitude.
Respectfully submitted.
Your servant Tǒng presents:
Court scribe Zhōu Áng
reverently proclaimed the imperial decree:
"Deign to attend Your servant's current completion of the lecture."
I respectfully reflect that the ultimate truth is subtle and recondite, and its subtle words are profound and abstruse.
It is not something I am capable of deeply studying or looking up to.
Thus, though unworthy, I have been entrusted with this explanation.
I ought to yield my place,
but instead, I have received the grace of imperial instruction.
I am truly suited to studying,
yet instead, I have received the imperial edict to expound the sutras.
I secretly think that by wielding the strategy of the Eight Powers (八威 bā-wēi),
divine beings cannot interfere;
by consuming the essence of the Nine Elixirs (九丹 jiǔ-dān),
one can command the host of immortals.
Your servant, upholding the imperial might, instructs this company of students.
Proclaiming the sacred decree, I enlighten all scholars.
Forging and refining divergent masters, I have long molded the stagnant.
I am about to make Huì-shī (惠施) ashamed of his distinctions,
and Gōng-sūn (公孫) abandon his "hard and white."
Wáng-shēng (王生) exhausted his eloquence and spirit,
and Fǎ-kāi (法開) accepted defeat, forever hidden on the eastern peak.
The imperial messenger's gracious presence further illuminated the lecture hall.
I bear this unique kindness on high, not knowing how to express myself.
Unable to bear my humble sentiments,
I respectfully append this memorial to express my gratitude.
Respectfully submitted.
Your servant Tǒng presents:
Hòu-gé Yìng-chì (後閤應勅) Mù-fó-zǐ (木佛子)
reverently proclaimed the imperial decree:
"Deign to bestow the imperial commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one complete set of ten fascicles, totaling one hundred and one volumes."
For one in a cold land to see the sun is not enough to call it a wonder;
for one gathering herbs to meet an immortal, how can that be compared to this joy?
Your servant respectfully reflects:
What is elucidated by the six lines (六爻 liù-yáo)
is the utmost profundity exhausted in the signs of change;
what is compiled by the Four Books (四書 sì-shū)
commands life only within the mundane realm.
How could they encompass cause and effect,
or articulate this teaching of the jeweled city?
Encompassing both ultimate truth and conventional reality,
this text reveals the full moon (perfect wisdom).
It is about to spread the Dao throughout the great thousand worlds and equalize transformation across billions [of realms].
Clouds of consciousness will cover, and rain will permeate the body-fields.
How can we again discuss Emperor Táng's (唐帝 Táng-dì) tortoise-shell writings or King Zhōu's (周王 Zhōu-wáng) archives?
Why wait to engrave it on tablets and basins, or dismiss the teachings of Qiū (丘) and Sù (素)?
The marvelous scripture of sweet dew has been bestowed with unique grace first.
Reflecting on my own foolishness, I cannot sufficiently express my rejoicing and gratitude.
Unable to bear the utmost reverence,
I respectfully present this memorial of gratitude.
Your servant Tǒng presents:
Proclamation officer Wáng Huì-bǎo (王慧寶)
reverently proclaimed the imperial decree:
"Deign to bestow the imperial commentary on the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, two fascicles, sixteen volumes."
Sweet dew enters the crown,
wisdom water irrigates the heart.
It is like encountering light in darkness,
or like the hungry gaining satiety.
I respectfully reflect that the two realms, formless and desireless, are a shared abode;
neither words nor principles, the three vehicles gather like clouds.
The four analytical powers cannot reach its limit;
the eight kinds of speech cannot exhaust its meaning.
Responding to the heavenly mechanism, this sacred work is bestowed.
It is endless like true suchness,
and hangs eternally with the sun and moon.
I merely observe obtaining pearls from Mt. Bǎo-chōng (寶舂山) and the great sea.
How can Your servant truly be so capable as to constantly receive such guidance and covering?
Zhāng Shū's (張書) Valley Brush is not enough to express my heart.
Raising my sleeves, I speak at length, yet cannot express my joy in song and dance.
Unable to bear the utmost joy and gratitude,
I respectfully present this memorial of gratitude.
Respectfully submitted.
Wáng Bái (王白) respectfully addresses:
I understand that you recently went to Kāi-shàn (開善) to listen to the Nirvāṇa lecture.
You indulged in the mountain scenery, with your mind beyond the mundane world.
Green pines and white mists were delightful everywhere.
Strange peaks and grotesque rocks made you forget to return at the sight's limit.
Moreover, the Dharma water flowed in the morning, and heavenly flowers fell at night.
You went and forgot to return,
in accordance with ancient sayings.
I, Wáng, am tied to affairs and duties, so I could not go alone.
Looking up to your noble example, my heart is tied in knots.
Respectfully submitted.
Wáng Bái (王白) respectfully addresses:
The long silence in communication always causes me to worry.
The wind is severe and the cold intense; I wish you well and peaceful.
I respectfully understand that at the Pure Name Dharma assembly, you personally received the golden words.
The precious teachings of Deer Park and the principles of Vulture Peak were agreeable.
The subtle and secret treasury has thus become exalted,
and the adorned bodhimaṇḍa has since been widely propagated.
Not only does the lamp of the mind shine brightly at night,
but the flower-buds of intention also fly in the morning.
Moreover, I reflect that Hóng-míng (弘明) originally specialized in inner teachings.
Now, accompanying the chariot of the ten good deeds,
he opens the path of the eight righteous policies.
He causes the water of Prajñā (波若 bō-rě) to flow,
washing away the dust of consciousness.
By this, the spring blossoms will truly become autumn fruits.
I, Wáng, often recall the splendid assembly at Huá-lín (華林) where I also held a humble seat.
From dawn till night, I was bathed in the marvelous words.
After the session concluded and the day remained, I retired to ponder further.
We joined hands to ascend and gaze, also exchanging talk and laughter.
Looking up at the nine stories, peering down a hundred feet,
the golden pond stirred the moon, and jade trees embraced the wind.
At such a time, one could truly call it Dharma joy.
Now, the teachings of this volume are passed on to one corner.
Hearing that the rain of wisdom is profusely flowing, my joy fills me completely.
I merely draw from the suspended river, yet have no way to receive the teachings.
Empty and without possession, my spirit is not polished.
Due to ignorance and attachment, I lament being difficult to extricate.
Furthermore, since my arrival, meaningful words have been scarce.
Old memories are exhausted, and new insights are not yet imbibed.
I am ashamed of my oral recitation and also lack inner discernment.
I will forever bid farewell to pouring from a bottle and ultimately be ashamed of staining a scroll.
Moreover, the cloud of compassion has spread, and the ocean of wisdom is also deep.
I hope that the remaining drops and waves will occasionally sprinkle and brush me.
However, separation accumulates, and speaking of it fills my eyes.
I wish you would graciously accept my words.
My words do not fully convey my intent.
Respectfully submitted.
Guǎngxìn Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu Xiāo Yìng.
Trembling with fear, I confess my crimes deserving of death.
Upon receiving your letter and kind instruction,
your pure words and splendid prose are immensely beautiful.
Your consolation and sympathy are profound.
These past days, the severe cold and frost have been bitter.
I humbly wish that your daily life is harmonious and pleasant.
May the people be rich and prosperous, without any excessive burdens or harm.
Your humble servant is dim-witted and ignorant, shallow in learning and an ordinary person.
Yet I have been able to hold a scroll before your jade steps, personally receiving your teachings.
My ears feasted on sweet dew, my heart absorbed your pronouncements.
Your celestial thoughts are profound and deep, your sagely wisdom vast and intricate.
With your three insights and one clear perception,
you dispel the doubts of long-held confusions.
With your fourfold eloquence fully expounded,
you elucidate difficult concepts, bringing instant understanding.
How could it be that the Hàn Emperor dreamt of a Brahmin, and the sounds of Dharma were again propagated?
Though the Jìn Emperor focused his mind, subtle words only then appeared.
Every evening, I hasten to the jade banquet, every morning I ascend the vermilion steps.
I never fail to recall the delightful gatherings in the fragrant groves and the Dharma seat in the Xuanpǔ.
Your Royal Highness drags your slippers amidst the precious clouds,
perhaps leisurely inquiring about the Way.
You adjust your robes at Bówàng,
sometimes bending your head to smile.
At that time, I was mistakenly placed at the end of the mat, privileged to hear the pure discussions.
I personally heard your words and frequently enjoyed your presence.
As for the lectures now,
Your Royal Highness is separated by a boundary.
Yet you graciously bestow heavenly praise, even reaching your humble servant.
Who does not admire such benevolence?
How can one not cherish such virtue?
My heart inclines eastward,
always placing admiration first.
Your humble servant has long been obscured and admired you.
Though I hear profound doctrines, my foolish heart is difficult to enlighten.
I was just about to rush to Fénxiāng to seek clarification from a lower seat,
when suddenly your esteemed command arrived.
You sought my humble words.
As I read it, I was flustered, looking up and down in shame and embarrassment.
May this be a gracious jest, bringing a little relief to my humble sentiments.
It is like expecting a compassionate cloud and a sea of wisdom,
but instead having to look up to a humble pitcher for help.
I am ashamed of my accumulated unworthiness and return to my mediocre, humble state.
Your humble servant's delusive attachments have accumulated, and my worldly defilements are not yet dissipated.
Recently, my self-care has been amiss, and I have contracted an illness midway.
I could not partake in the complete understanding, missing the final parts of the teaching.
I only blame myself, but ultimately it concerns my karmic destiny.
I wonder how you have been calming your spirit these days.
Perusing Confucian histories, surely it does not harm your well-being?
Your humble servant often visits the western post, fully partaking of your virtuous deeds.
I humbly hear your instructions above Zhānghuá,
or listen to lawsuits beneath the sweet pear tree.
You never cease your prolific writing and literary work all day long.
Pure discussions and profound talks continue until late into the night.
Guests like the spring blossoms
ascend to the seat of honor and enter the hall.
Guests like the autumn fruits
are welcomed to the empty seat and enter the inner chamber.
Literary masters and repositories of righteousness gather here.
This is truly the greatest joy, experienced at this very moment.
Your humble servant once traveled to Liángyuàn and received your special favor.
Now I am isolated from your clear countenance, separated from your presence for a long time.
My heart is filled with longing; when I speak of it, tears well up.
I only hope that your esteemed words will occasionally reach me.
I humbly wish you to take good care, and I will seek your further instruction soon.
I deeply engrave and carry your kind instructions.
Yìng, crimes deserving of death, crimes deserving of death.
A Buddha is one who is awakened.
Awakened means knowing.
Between an ordinary person and a Buddha-land,
the establishment of knowing good and evil has never been different.
However, what is known in the Buddha-land is the correct path to obtain good.
What is known by an ordinary person is the erroneous path that loses good.
The knowledge of the correct path possessed by an ordinary person is not different from the knowledge of a Buddha.
It is precisely because what is considered good is not truly good that they lose the correct path.
Therefore, the knowledge of an ordinary person is not different from the knowledge of a Buddha.
It is due to the difference in the object of knowledge, while the knowledge itself is not different.
What an ordinary person knows is not that what is known is not good.
It lies in seeking good but ending up with not good.
If this heart of seeking good is accumulated,
one will eventually find the path of returning to good.
Or if the path is found, one will reach Buddhahood.
This is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.
It truly lies in their inherent knowledge nature, which is constantly transmitted.
All-encompassing wisdom and sentient beings in the five paths and six realms
share the capacity for receiving knowledge.
There is no difference in this capacity.
Question:
Is receiving knowledge not knowledge?
Answer:
No.
Question: What is its essence?
Answer:
Continuous and imperishable.
Being continuous and imperishable is why it can receive knowledge.
If the efforts of cultivation in this life gradually accumulate,
then the principles known in the future life will become more refined.
This refined knowledge
will continue to manifest until Buddhahood, without interruption.
If there is ignorance in this life, then what is known in the future life will become darker.
This darkened knowledge
will also manifest until the six realms.
The faculty of receiving knowledge receives knowledge according to conditions.
The quality of knowledge, whether good or bad, is not related to this faculty of receiving knowledge.
Question:
I have heard your explanation regarding knowledge and non-knowledge.
Receiving knowledge, receiving knowledge, is inherently continuous and imperishable.
Knowledge naturally arises from causes and conditions,
and is conceptually related to this faculty of receiving knowledge.
Answer:
There is this continuous and imperishable (principle) that arises from natural causes and effects.
With causes and effects,
how can there be no good and no evil?
The nature of all sentient beings
is to love life.
The paths to seeking life are diverse and not uniform.
Once they wander, their paths diverge.
In a single thought, various conditions arise interactively.
Within a single cause and a single effect, there are differences.
The nature that loves life is common to all myriad beings.
What is naturally endowed is not established by conditions.
Therefore, the love of life is not due to conditions,
and conditions are not happiness.
Though they all reside in a physical form, each life is a distinct entity.
Once a single thought arises, it summons various conditions.
Each condition follows the thought and arises.
Good and evil thoughts are indeed different.
Both rely on external assistance, and the process is the same.
For example, without water or soil, a grain sprout cannot grow.
Since the nature of causes and conditions and consciousness are fundamentally different,
the certainty of cause and effect is undeniable.
However, good and evil arising independently can still encounter obstacles.
Although they are said to arise independently,
once they arise, they become a cause.
Internal causes and external conditions truly stem from this.
When an ordinary person has a single thought,
their seven-foot body is no longer concerned with the object of that thought.
When an ordinary person has a single thought,
a sage has no thought that is not utterly exhausted.
A sage is inexhaustible.
The seven-foot body is inherently like emptiness.
With this seven-foot body that is like emptiness,
all myriad inexhaustible thoughts are encompassed.
Thus, they can be different from ordinary people.
When an ordinary person temporarily forgets their seven-foot body during a single thought,
then their eyes cease to see, and their feet cease to walk.
When they forget their eyes and feet,
how are they different from those without eyes and feet?
An ordinary person's temporary non-existence is a temporary non-existence; before it truly ceases, existence has already followed.
When thought and form are divergent, there is temporary forgetfulness.
When thought and mind reconcile, they reunite.
When thought is in one part of the seven-foot body, other parts
are like another person; thus, it is not different from not being oneself.
However, an ordinary person's temporary non-existence is very brief.
A sage's permanent non-existence is very distant.
The path of the ordinary and the sage is fundamentally the same.
To temporarily forget with a single thought makes one an ordinary person.
To forget all myriad thoughts makes one a great sage.
Speaking in this way, body and spirit are almost the same.
Some people doubt that cause and effect are perfectly aligned, without the slightest deviation.
The arrival of good and evil are all predetermined karma.
Yet the cultivation of the six perfections all requires effort.
If this exerted effort itself has a prior cause,
and the cause ripens and the effect forms, they spontaneously attract each other,
then the merit of exerted effort cannot be established.
The cultivation of the six perfections would almost be abolished.
Śākyamuni achieved his state through nine kalpas of courageous effort.
The cause of this courageous effort was determined in beginningless time.
It did not originally rely on the nine [kalpas],
so how can it be said to arise?
I believe that emotional perception and cause-and-effect are fundamentally two distinct things.
First there is emotional perception, then there is cause and effect.
Once emotional perception is stirred, cause and effect follow.
Without emotional perception, what would cause and effect rely on?
Because consciousness has two paths, their combination is fundamentally different.
Since their roots are different, their essences are not the same.
The separate arising of emotional perception is not an obstruction in principle.
The difference between the six perfections and nine kalpas is not to be doubted.
Among all classes of sentient beings, discernment and wisdom vary greatly.
Ranks differ, forming thousands upon thousands of layers.
Insects do not match birds.
Birds do not match dogs and horses.
This is clearly and obviously true and cannot be denied.
Furthermore, among human beings, the wise and the foolish have different natures.
They cannot understand or comprehend each other.
The difference between Yānběi and Yuènán is not enough to compare.
The foolish do not distinguish between beans and wheat.
The perverse do not know love and respect.
From this point upward, nature and understanding gradually expand.
Bān Gù’s nine ranks could not even encompass one ten-thousandth of it.
Why is there a distinction between the wise and the foolish?
It is due to knowing and not knowing.
What the foolish know is little.
What the wise know is much.
Yet all things intertwine.
All directions are vast.
Emotions and natures are obscure.
Principles and interests are profound and mysterious.
Following their path to seek their principles,
since there are differences in clarity and obscurity,
a distinction of high and low is formed.
From this, mutual disparities make the grades increasingly severe.
Exhausting their origins and reaching their ultimate core,
mutual esteem and admiration must eventually reach a limit.
Once that path is exhausted, nothing, however minute, is left unexplored.
This, too, cannot be denied.
Moreover, the five senses each have their own domain.
Ears and eyes each have their own functions.
When the mind operates, the body is forgotten.
When the eyes are used, the ears are neglected.
Why? Because spiritual emotions are shallow and weak, and mental thoughts are cluttered.
To achieve everything with one thought is impossible.
Since it cannot achieve everything, confusion and entanglement constantly assail.
Before one thought is completed, other issues arise concurrently.
When many issues arise concurrently, they are again subject to the same reason of not being able to encompass all at once as before.
This stems from shallow delusion.
Shallow delusion becomes illness.
The illness lies in attachment to existence.
Not shallow and not deluded arises from encompassing forgetfulness.
Through this encompassing forgetfulness, this encompassing illumination is attained.
From ordinary people to perfect enlightenment,
one first moves from delusion to non-delusion.
From not encompassing to being able to encompass.
This, too, cannot be denied.
Furthermore, insects have short lifespans, but the essence of sentience is not different.
Some are born in the morning and die in the evening.
Some do not know spring and autumn.
From this point onward, lengths of life vary.
Since there is a short, how can there not be a long?
Vain indulgence shortens life, good cultivation increases longevity.
If one is good and then even better, how can this not be so?
This, too, cannot be denied.
If life can be cut short, then longevity cannot be without an end.
If there is no end, then life cannot be exhausted.
The distinction between form and spirit is thus established.
However, if the form can be nourished, why should the spirit be unique?
The spirit is subtle, the form is coarse; the distinction is clear.
Nourishing the form can lead to imperishability.
How can nourishing the spirit have an end?
If nourishing the spirit has no end,
then there is no birth and no death.
Comparing beginning and end, how can such people not exist?
From ordinary people to sages, the meaning of sentience is the same.
But matters have their subtleties and coarseness.
Therefore, people have their ordinary and their sagely.
If sages can exist eternally, why should ordinary people perish?
The origin is the same, but the end is different; this principle is not universally applicable.
How could the great sages’ teachings be so deluded?
Your argument states:
Form is spirit.
Spirit is form.
It also states:
The human body is one.
Therefore, the spirit cannot be two.
If, according to your elegant argument, these two things cannot be separated,
then the seven orifices and the hundred parts would be nowhere without spirit.
Since the functions of the seven orifices are different,
and what the hundred parts operate is not one,
the spirit would also respond according to the matter.
Then its name should also change according to the matter.
Spirit is the name in contrast to form.
And forms within the form each have their functions.
Then spirits within the spirit
should also each have their names.
Now, when speaking of form, there are differences like the four limbs and hundred parts, and distinctions like bending, extending, listening, and receiving.
Each has its name.
Each has its function.
To say that spirit has only one name but its functions are divided among the hundred parts,
this is something I deeply do not understand.
If form and spirit are analogous,
not an iota can be different.
Why? Because the names for form are many,
but the names for spirit are few.
If, according to your argument,
a seven-foot spirit means spirit is nowhere without form,
and form is nowhere without spirit.
A knife is only sharp at its blade.
What is not the blade does not receive the name "sharp."
Thus, "blade" refers to a part of the whole body.
"Sharpness" is a characteristic of a specific part.
Since a knife and its sharpness are not the same,
how can form and spirit be arbitrarily equated?
Furthermore, a knife of yesteryear is now forged into a sword.
The sharpness of the sword is the sharpness of the knife,
but the form of the knife is not the form of the sword.
The function of sharpness remains unchanged,
but the form of the substance has shifted.
Just as in a previous life one was Jiǎ, and in a later life one is Bǐng,
the ways of Heaven and humanity may differ,
yet the spirit of past consciousness is still transmitted.
How is this different from a sword becoming a knife or a knife becoming a sword?
There is no difference.
Moreover, the substance of one knife is divided into two knife forms.
The form is already divided,
yet each has its sharpness.
Now, if we take the body of a single ox and cut it in two,
then the life of drinking and eating immediately ceases.
The function of bearing heavy loads is not divided.
How can you use the analogy of a knife and its sharpness to describe form and spirit?
Your argument states:
The knife and its sharpness are like form having spirit.
The knife is entirely one sharpness.
Form is entirely one spirit.
When spirit functions in the body, there are distinctions of ears, eyes, hands, and feet.
The function of the hand is not the function of the foot.
The function of the ear is not the function of the eye.
But the function of sharpness is applicable everywhere.
It can cut down dragons and snakes.
It can sever wild geese.
It is not limited to one specific place.
It can cut the melons of Dōnglíng.
It is limited to one specific place.
It can cut the bamboo of Nánshān.
If you say that the function of sharpness can also be divided,
then feet could grasp objects,
and eyes could hear sounds.
If you say that the back of the knife is also sharp, and both sides are also sharp,
it's just not yet forged and sharpened.
If sharpness is applied universally in all directions,
then the body of sharpness would have nowhere left to stand.
Square and straight forms cannot apply sharpness.
The function of sharpness lies precisely in one side, in the hair-thin edge.
How can spirit and form be entirely one if they are compared to this?
If the knife is entirely sharpness,
then the spirit's function should divide with the body.
If the principle of the knife and its sharpness were truly one,
then eyes could be placed under the shoulder blade,
and a nose could be placed on the back.
Is this possible?
No, it is not.
If you consider this analogy exhaustive,
then it is not exhaustive.
If you say it is fundamentally not exhaustive,
then it cannot be used as an analogy.
If form is spirit and spirit is form,
and the two rely on each other, then there should be no one-sided demise.
Then on the day the body dies, the form should also vanish.
But now, the knowing spirit perishes, and the unknowing form remains.
This means spirit is fundamentally not form, and form is fundamentally not spirit.
Again, they cannot be forcibly made into one.
If you say that the sum of the substances of the hundred parts is called form,
and the sum of the functions of the hundred parts is called spirit,
then since the hundred parts each have their divisions,
an eye is an eye-form,
an ear is an ear-form.
An eye-form is not an ear-form,
and an ear-form is not an eye-form.
Then the spirit also divides with the hundred parts.
Then the eye has an eye-spirit,
and the ear has an ear-spirit.
The ear-spirit is not the eye-spirit,
and the eye-spirit is not the ear-spirit.
But in a paralytic body, half of it has already withered.
The withered half is like wood and stone.
Like a frozen corpse, it remains imperishable for ages.
Then the spirit of this half
should also perish with this half.
If half the spirit perishes while half the body remains,
then the simultaneous perishing of form and spirit is even more alarming and startling.
For instance, the corpse of Èrfù remained uncorrupted for a hundred million years.
The body of Dānkāi still retains its substance at Luófú.
If spirit and form were one, these two gentlemen should not have had their spirits perish while their forms remained.
Your argument also states:
Those that are born suddenly die suddenly.
Those that are born gradually die gradually.
Please allow me to use your矛 to attack your盾.
"Die gradually" refers to the corpses of the deceased, which begin without consciousness and eventually decay.
If so, then form and spirit were originally one entity.
If the form is ill, the spirit also declares illness.
If the form perishes, the spirit also declares perishment.
The function of gradualness should be with the form.
If the form first perishes but has not yet decayed (gradualness), how can the spirit alone not be considered gradual from beginning to end?
The treatise also states:
"The living person's body transforms into the deceased's bones."
Considering the treatise,
if the living person's spirit and living person's body
have already transformed into bones,
then why wouldn't the living person's spirit also transform with the body?
If it transforms with the body, then it should be of the same substance as the body.
If the body is identical to the bones,
then the spirit of the dead cannot be different from the spirit of the living.
This would mean that what was previously called death is not yet death.
If the body is not the bones,
then the living spirit transforms into the dead spirit.
The transformation of the living spirit into the dead spirit
is precisely the three periods.
How can one say it is not extinguished?
If the spirit follows the body, and the body is already unconscious,
since the body is unconscious and the spirit originally has no substance,
unconsciousness itself means the spirit's demise.
If the spirit perishes but the body remains,
this is also illogical.
If, though the body is unconscious, the spirit still has consciousness,
and the body and spirit cannot be separate,
then the dead body mentioned earlier would, in turn, not be a withered tree.
The magistrate of Quántíng, Lìngdé,
had a certain Zhū Sānyì.
Not only was he acutely perceptive in external studies,
but he was also profoundly enlightened in internal faith.
He often contemplated the Mahāyāna in his heart and recited the Prajñā on his lips.
Suddenly, he adhered to a theory of naturalness,
and thus formed a clinging to inherent nature.
Perhaps this was an act of appearing to concur with wrong views,
or perhaps it was a genuine reversal of understanding.
Furthermore, it harms the true essence and excessively injures the ultimate Dao.
I shall therefore compose a counter-argument to dispel his attachment.
Although the wording may not be worth adopting, the reasoning may be worth observing.
If you share my views,
I hope you will thoroughly examine it together.
Master Yùzī
sighed mournfully, saying:
"Indeed, all phenomena and all natures are principles of naturalness.
Precisely because it is natural,
it cannot be altered or exchanged.
Therefore, even though a good person knows that goodness cannot be relied upon,
a good person ultimately cannot be evil even for a moment.
Conversely, an evil person, knowing that evil is not to be deterred,
also cannot be good even for an instant.
Moreover, one who embodies benevolence does not know oneself to be good,
and one who embodies foolishness does not perceive oneself to be evil.
All are naturally so."
The guest to his right, who was a high official,
suddenly changed his expression and said:
"How stubborn is the master's doctrine!
It deviates from the Great Dao and misrepresents the words of the Sages."
The master said:
"Who governs the Great Dao? What did the Sages say?"
The official said:
"The Great Dao has no master yet masters everything.
The Sages said nothing yet said everything."
The master said:
"Please explain what they said.
Did they speak of the causes of life and destiny?
Please explain what they governed. Did they govern the retribution of good and evil?"
The official said:
"How could it not be so?
Heaven and Earth, upholding the work of the Great Dao, sustain and nourish.
The Sages, aligning with the virtues of Heaven and Earth, established teachings.
They ordered benevolence, righteousness, and the five virtues to restrain the heart,
and expounded the Odes, Documents, and the six arts to instruct in one's profession.
These are the words of the Sages.
'A family that accumulates good deeds will surely have abundant blessings.
A family that accumulates evil deeds will surely have abundant calamities.'
Therefore, it is said:
'The Sage has no partiality; he is always with the good people.'
The six extremes are enumerated, and punishment is meted out.
The five blessings are presented, and good hearts are encouraged.
Three generations serve as generals, witnessing the power of their downfall.
Seven generations cultivate goodness, possessing the nature of prosperity.
Chén Shǎng was favored but not ennobled.
Bǐng Chāng was estranged but inherited the state.
These are the effects of the Dao.
How can the master say that everything is merely a principle of naturalness and cannot be altered?"
The master smiled and replied:
"Those whom the world calls 'rope-pullers,'
when the rope is exhausted, they do not know how to adapt.
Such are those like the official.
Allow me to respectfully present my humble views to you.
Indeed, the two cosmic forces are revealed, and the six children (elements) are applied.
The myriad people are nurtured, and the five materials are utilized.
This sentence indicates that all phenomena are entirely so,
and humans are the most spiritual of all living beings.
They receive the exquisite essence of nature,
are endowed with the qualities of beauty and ugliness, fullness and diminishment,
harbor emotions of sorrow, joy, happiness, and anger,
are destined for poverty and prosperity, longevity and shortness of life,
and are sealed with the natures of foolishness and wisdom, good and evil.
Indeed, sorrow, joy, happiness, and anger are concealed within the emotions,
and are stirred by external objects.
Poverty, prosperity, longevity, and shortness of life are hidden within destiny,
becoming clear only when events unfold.
Beauty, ugliness, fullness, and diminishment are manifested in the form,
appearing from birth.
Foolishness, wisdom, good, and evil are sealed within nature,
becoming evident through use.
These eight phrases
comprehensively exhaust human affairs.
All arise from the patterns of naturalness;
there is no one who creates them.
For if there were one who created them, there would inevitably be effort.
If there were one who put them in and took them out, there would inevitably be leakage.
If there were one who dealt with them, there would inevitably be errors.
These three are not the achievements of a creator.
Thus, Mòzǐ said:
'If the creator took three years to make one leaf,
how few leaves there would be in the world!'
Indeed, the Sages set up expedient means to accomplish their teachings,
borrowing apparent events to exhort and deter.
Seeing the strong and brave bully the weak and timid,
and fearing that punishments might not restrain them,
they then presented the deterrent of calamity for wickedness.
Grieved that cultivating goodness was not encouraged,
and knowing that nature and destiny cannot be easily changed,
they ordered blessings for goodness to encourage it.
Therefore, listening to their words, it seems as if there are no discrepancies,
but verifying their events, not one in ten thousand is proven true.
You believe that flourishing descendants
are caused by following the Dao,
and that lacking descendants to offer sacrifices
is brought about by past misdeeds.
You believe that living in ease and pleasure
is the clear reward for good people,
and that experiencing hardship and poverty
is the manifest punishment for evil people.
Sūn Shúáo, in his youth, did not bury a snake,
nor did he achieve the nobility of a Chancellor in his old age.
Bǐng Jí had no hidden virtues before,
yet ultimately attained the dignity of a Prime Minister.
If that were the case, then the Dao of Heaven would, by granting exalted glory and illustrious destiny,
reward the utmost foolishness of Gun and Sǒu.
And by granting Shāngjūn and Dānzhū,
it would recompense the supreme sageliness of Yáo and Shùn.
Tàibó had no fault of playing with soldiers for three generations,
yet adopted a successor from Zhòngyú.
The founder of Hàn had no record of accumulating good deeds for seven generations,
yet accomplished an enterprise that matched Heaven.
Jīzǐ was said to enjoy the five blessings,
yet suffered the pain of extinction himself.
Kǒngzǐ said that blessings accumulate for the good,
yet personally endured the sorrow of a homeless wanderer.
Yán Huí, past seventy,
met an untimely end.
Rǎn Bóniú, first among the four teachings,
drew sighs of lament.
Yet Shāngchén repeatedly ruled the King of Jīngnán,
and Mòdùn continuously resided in Sàiběi.
There were no smiling ghosts at Shǒushān,
and only resentful souls in the Mìluó River.
Kāngchéng changed his hometown because of his surname,
but could not avoid the calamity of a minor sage.
Wáng Bāo mourned the transformation of the Lǒng tree,
and consequently suffered undeserved disaster.
Two students resided in Wèi,
who is to blame for the pain of the boat?
Three benevolent ones were in Bó,
what was the guilt for the cruelty of being disemboweled?
As for those near the capital and in recent generations,
not recorded in books,
but witnessed before our very eyes,
there are those whose stomachs harbor the dangers of Mèngmén, and whose hearts store the poison of jackals and vipers.
Their thoughts are only bent on harming others,
and their conduct is always predicated on benefiting themselves first.
The sharp point of an awl is pushed,
and a valley's insatiability is questioned.
Yet they enjoy outward glory of a hundred carriages and inward wealth of a thousand measures.
They recline on rich brocades, sit amidst delicacies,
and live their lives in opulent leisure, jingling gold and wearing jade.
Conversely, there are those who cherish a hundred bi-discs as an embrace, and luminous pearls as their nature.
Their hearts cannot bear to kill a hibernating insect,
and their hands cannot bear to break a growing twig.
They possess extraordinary talents but are not employed,
accumulate noble aspirations but are ignored.
They are marginalized among the common populace,
and sink to the bottom of their villages.
They embrace hunger and cold until they die,
and are buried alongside deer.
Their sacrifices are lonely, their widowed children destitute,
their names unheard, swallowed up and extinguished like lightning.
How regrettable are such cases!
Are they but one person?
From this, one knows that the ferocity of Jié and Zhí
fears not the approaching calamity,
and the earnest conduct of Mǐn Zēng does not necessarily bring forth future blessings.
Therefore, Hégūanzǐ said:
'Indeed, destiny is natural.
The virtuous do not necessarily attain it,
nor do the unworthy necessarily lose it.'
This is what he meant."
The Grand Master said,
"If you, Sir, quote the words of the Hundred Schools,
then those who strive for fame, like Lièzǐ, must be incorruptible (lián).
The incorruptible are poor.
Those who strive for fame must be yielding (ràng).
The yielding are humble.
If this is so, then poverty and lowliness are conditions achieved by those who dedicate themselves to establishing a reputation.
Conversely, wealth and high status
are obtained by those who are greedy and competitive.
How then can fame be a natural course (zìrán zhī shù)?"
The Master said,
"This is but a one-sided view,
not comprehensive in its reasoning.
Indeed, wealth and high status inherently involve greed and competition,
but wealth and high status are not obtained solely by greed and competition.
Poverty and lowliness inherently involve incorruptibility and yielding,
but poverty and lowliness are not invited solely by incorruptibility and yielding.
There are those who are wealthy and esteemed without seeking it through greed,
and those who are poor and humble without being incorruptible or yielding.
Moreover, you seldom speak of fate (mìng).
The Way is broadened by humans.
Therefore, the principles of human nature and destiny (xìngmìng zhī lǐ)
were topics the ancient sages were reluctant to discuss.
Are the constant workings of Heaven's Way (tiāndào) truly concerned with good and evil retribution?
For example, a warm breeze rotates flowers, and a cold gale scatters snow.
Some are cast beneath excrement,
while others ascend above the jade steps.
The wind has no intention of favoritism,
yet flowers and snow have distinct paths of purity and defilement.
Heaven's Way has no intention of love or hate,
yet human nature and destiny (xìngmìng) have different paths of fulfillment and obstruction.
You have heard of Yú Gōng who waited for an enfeoffment, and it arrived;
Yán Mǔ who awaited a funeral, and it occurred.
If one sees a good person and immediately says their descendants will surely prosper,
or if one sees an evil person and immediately says their descendants will surely perish,
this is like spending one's whole life guarding a tree stump, hoping to catch another cunning hare.
Thereupon, the Grand Master composed himself and apologized, saying,
"My understanding is one-sided and obscured the comprehensive path;
I clung to what was narrow and near, forgetting what was distant and vast.
Now, receiving your profound words, I am suddenly enlightened.
It is like Shū Shǔ, a concealed corpse for ten thousand ages, suddenly comprehending,
or the Zhongshān drunkard, not yet a thousand mornings in stupor, abruptly awakening.
Please allow me to engrave these words on my sash for constant reflection."
Someone asked,
"Zhūzǐ relied on abstract discussions
to express the depths of his mind,
and his arguments regarding feelings and pointing to affairs are deeply interesting.
However, upon closer examination of ancient texts, there are points he has not fully addressed.
The emotions of sorrow, joy, happiness, and anger
encompass the nature of good and evil.
When the means of sustenance are insufficient,
then conflicts and struggles arise.
Those of equal talent and knowledge cannot control each other.
Heaven gave birth to benevolent sages (rénshèng) precisely to oversee and govern.
Music (yuè) was created by the sages,
and rites (lǐ) were instituted by the former kings.
Three thousand rituals (sānqiān zhī yí) were established to inspect conduct,
and the harmony of the five tones (wǔyīn zhī hé) was used to guide the heart.
Ranks were set up to encourage good,
and punishments were imposed to deter evil.
Not a single detail was overlooked, and retribution was as swift as an echo.
Was it not because of actions that jade and silks were presented?
Could drums and bells harmonize spontaneously?
The thousands of regulations we see are all products of human effort,
and the myriad distinctions are all created by human intelligence.
You, Sir, are a subject of Tāng and Wǔ,
a disciple of Zhōu and Kǒng.
