You move within the teachings and embrace orthodox doctrine.
Yet you say that good people do not rely on their goodness,
and evil people do not heed warnings against evil.
Goodness cannot invite blessings,
and calamity cannot repay evil.
How can such talk not contradict reason?
Even flying insects and crawling creatures know how to avoid and approach.
How much more so humans, the most intelligent beings, who are treated as merely natural objects?
Is this not like the poem of Gaohou, where the comparisons are inappropriate?
My understanding of this matter is incomplete, and I respectfully await your clear response."
The reply was:
"In the past, Lú'áo traveled north and encountered barren lands,
lamenting that his footprints had not yet extended far enough.
The River God (Hé Zōng) looked east into the boundless sea,
then sighed that the autumn waters were not plentiful enough.
You, Sir, are accustomed to what is near, which has become your nature,
and it is not easy to discuss what is distant and great with you.
Now, you attribute bending and stretching, bowing and rising, to the mind's deliberation;
carving and chiseling, cutting and shaping, to the body's and hands' actions.
You say that rites and music were made by sages,
and sages were born of Heaven and Earth.
Allow me, Sir, to take an example close to home—from your own body—and then it can be extended to all things.
When you hear with your ears, see with your eyes, step with your feet, and grasp with your hands, what do you think causes these actions?
If your body has an ailment, you do not even know if it is cold or hot.
Where do sorrow, joy, happiness, and anger arise and cease?
Where in your body is the consciousness that knows where consciousness is?
Where in your body is the wisdom that knows where wisdom resides?
If consciousness pervaded the entire body, then if the body were injured, consciousness would be fragmented.
If wisdom arose with affairs and vanished with affairs, then wisdom would cease to exist.
Indeed, consciousness does not know consciousness, and wisdom does not know wisdom.
From this, we infer the distant from the near
and extrapolate from one category to others.
Thus, we know that rites and music do not know their own origin or how they were instituted.
Sages do not know their own origin or how they were born.
Even the Two Forms (liǎngxiàng) do not know their own origin or how they were established.
Therefore, diverse forms and differing thoughts accumulate and abound.
Stillness and movement, union and dispersion, arise and perish of themselves.
Those who move and are still do not know their master.
Those who are born and perish do not understand their root.
Indeed, the principle of spontaneity (zìrán zhī lǐ) is evident.
What is called 'non-spontaneous' is actually the great spontaneity (dàzìrán).
What is said to involve 'action' is actually the great non-action (dàwúwéi).
You said,
'Heaven gave birth to sages to oversee and govern.'
Why then did Táng and Yú have successive sages, supplemented by five ministers?
Wén and Wǔ shone with renewed brilliance, augmented by ten capable ministers?
Could it be that Heaven's Way (tiāndào) is unable to ensure consistency from beginning to end,
or that later generations blame Heaven and Earth?
Great Shùn and great Yáo surely did not wish to produce unworthy sons.
Lóngfèng and Bǐgān surely did not delight in being executed.
Kǒngzǐ traveled extensively, enduring hardships, and finally said he would not shrink from holding a whip.
Yán Huí (Yán Chēng) dared to die, yet his loving father had to beg for a carriage.
Those three sages and three benevolent ones
could be said to have excelled in choosing what to take and what to leave.
Heaven can cause the Eastern Sea to suffer drought,
but this is not as effective as redressing the grievance of a filial wife.
Earth can cause a high city to revert to a moat,
but this is not as effective as saving the fallen Qǐliáng.
Therefore, honor and disgrace, life and death, are naturally determined.
If even sages and benevolent ones cannot escape this,
then if you deeply ponder these humble words, the principle will become evident."
Qǐngyí Gōngzǐ (請疑公子) addressed Tōngmǐn Xiānshēng (通敏先生) saying:
When the two primary forces (heaven and earth) first separated, all creatures came into being and depended on them.
When the seven luminaries (sun, moon, and five planets) were suspended,
the myriad people looked up to them.
However, what happens before birth and after death is something that the "symbols attached to existence" (繫象) have not clarified,
and what transpired from ancient times to the present has not been fully investigated by the wise and saintly.
Yet, the gentlemen who yearn for profundity (希玄君子) compete to explore and delve into these matters,
and famous individuals who admire reason (慕理名人) vie to probe and investigate.
What Yǔ Zī (㝢茲) stated vigorously expounds on spontaneity,
while what Jiǎ Shì (假氏) elucidated grandly sets forth retribution.
Although the "arrows and blades of spontaneity" (自然鋒鏑) initially gained victory,
the "spears and shields of retribution" (報應干戈) were defeated later.
However, my foolish mind is difficult to enlighten, and my dim understanding is easily misled.
With these two theories intermingling, I do not know which is correct.
Tōngmǐn Xiānshēng (通敏先生) then clapped his hands and replied:
I have considered the clear arguments of the two gentlemen,
and indeed each excels in a particular corner.
Spontaneity leans on Lǎozi (老子) and Zhuāngzi (莊子),
while retribution derives from Zhōu Gōng (周孔) and Kǒngzǐ (孔子).
It can be said that Chǔ (楚) has already lost, but Qí (齊) has not yet gained.
Now I will expand upon and present these matters for you.
Regarding the Sān Fén (三墳) and Wǔ Diǎn (五典),
the principles of good and evil are not yet clearly manifest.
Regarding the Bā Suǒ (八索) and Jiǔ Qiū (九丘),
the paths of the hidden and the manifest are still obstructed.
Moreover, how much less so for the arrogant official of Qīyuán (漆園傲吏) and the confused madman,
who alone claimed to be the patriarch of creation
and solely adhered to the nature of spontaneity?
This was merely a way of rectifying the customs of his time,
and not a profound strategy that truly accorded with reason.
Now, I ask:
What is the aim of the foundation of spontaneity?
Does it involve cause and effect, or does it not?
If one says that spontaneity still discusses cause and effect,
then the situation is like Móudùn (牟盾),
where two statements contradict each other, a cause for laughter among fools
and sorrow among the wise.
It has already collapsed and does not need much refutation.
If one says there is absolutely no retribution and entirely cuts off cause and effect,
then the way of sovereign and minister, father and son, cannot function.
What use are the words "benevolence, righteousness, filial piety, and compassion"?
One should then commit evil to invite blessings and do good to bring disaster.
It would also be like striking fire to get ice, or planting beans to grow wheat.
One has never seen a sound harmonize with an opposing echo, or a bent shape cast a straight shadow.
If one takes Fàngxūn (放勳), a supreme sage, giving birth to Dānzhū (丹朱),
and Chónghuá (重華), of ultimate virtue, being born to Gǔsǒu (瞽叟),
as examples of things happening spontaneously,
I secretly find this unacceptable for you.
The way of closest kinship
is called natural inclination.
Yet, each person's actions are entirely unrelated to it.
Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) cultivated virtue in their previous lives,
thus they were endowed with such spiritual intelligence.
Gǔsǒu (𩨬叟) accumulated evil in his former lives,
thus he was destined to be so stubborn and ignorant.
Moreover, they formed a deep connection again and became reflections of each other,
intending to manifest sainthood through an ordinary person and transform ignorance with wisdom.
If there had been no Gǔsǒu's (瞽叟) wickedness,
how could the beauty of harmony and accord (克諧) be known?
If not for the sainthood of Fàngxūn (放勳),
who would have transformed the evil of a dissolute wanderer?
Thus, Ānán (阿難) and Tiáodá (調達) were both brothers of the World-Honored One (世尊).
Luóhóu (羅睺) and Shànxīng (善星) were both descendants of the Tathāgata (如來).
Yet, Ānán (阿難) always attended and served him closely,
while Tiáodá (調達) constantly stirred up harm and rebellion.
Luóhóu (羅睺) protected the jewel without transgressing,
while Shànxīng (善星) broke the vessel beyond repair.
Observing this,
you can surely understand.
If one says that each has its own unchangeable nature,
this is entirely incorrect.
For example, when a hawk transforms into a dove, its original nature completely vanishes.
When an orange transforms into a trifoliate orange, its former taste disappears forever.
Once wealthy, now poor—
the principle of fixed nature is hard to maintain.
Once noble, now lowly—
where is the saying about assigned destiny?
Lǚ Wàng (呂望) was a cattle butcher,
yet he eventually became Grand Tutor.
Yī Yǐn (伊尹) was a pot-bearer,
yet he ultimately rose to be Prime Minister.
Dài Yuān (戴淵) was a scourge to his four neighbors,
yet later achieved great renown.
Zhōu Chǔ (周處) was the source of three harms,
yet in his later years was praised for his virtuous conduct.
Jīé Wáng (闍王) committed sins deserving of Avīci Hell,
yet suddenly changed his ways.
Yù Wáng (育王) committed immeasurable transgressions,
yet suddenly was able to revere goodness.
If based on the principle of inherent nature,
how could such meanings exist?
Good people would only do good,
and could not entertain evil for even a moment.
Evil people would constantly do evil,
and could not generate a single thought of goodness.
Thus, glory and decay, favor and disgrace, would all be governed by inevitability.
Ignorance and wisdom, honor and lowliness, would be eternally unchangeable.
Could it be so?
Absolutely not!
Furthermore, if one takes people who cultivate virtue instead experiencing sorrow and worry,
and those who do good instead suffering downfall,
as being the fate of spontaneity,
this is also incorrect.
If one performs good deeds hoping for reward, one is even further from goodness.
If one cultivates virtue to seek fame,
one is even further from virtue.
If one must possess the nature of a pure jade tablet
and harbor the heart of a precious gem,
originally having no intention of renown
and never delighting in wealth and status,
then a splendid reputation will surely emerge, and auspicious blessings will arrive.
Perhaps, not meeting a discerning listener, one might be like scattered wood.
Not encountering one who distinguishes jade, one might be like sunken mud.
Temporarily remaining hidden like a dragon brings no loss.
How could the virtue of a phoenix
be confined to this small world,
or disturbed by worldly affairs?
One can certainly persevere in poverty without needing to worry about gains or losses.
For example, Tàibó (太伯) nobly yielded and left a fragrance for a thousand generations.
Zhòngní (仲尼) faced hardship and passed down his name for ten thousand generations.
Yán Huí (顏回) died young—this was specifically his destiny.
His karma was not long.
Rǎn Bóniú (冉伯牛) suffered that illness—
this must have been due to his karmic disease not yet being severed.
The two sons being executed
further revealed the wickedness of Wèi Líng Gōng (衛靈公).
The three benevolent men being killed
clearly showed the transgressions of Yīn Zhòu (殷紂).
Starving on Shǒushān (首山)
did not exempt them from the charge of seeking fame.
Sinking in the Mìluó River (汨水)
still left the blame of harboring resentment.
Furthermore, determined karma
cannot be saved by divine power.
If retribution must be received,
how can it be averted by sagely wisdom?
These all arise from past causes, not created in the present.
If one says that those who make butchery their business live for a hundred years,
and those who harbor theft accumulate vast wealth,
and takes this as being due to their fixed nature,
this is also incomprehensible.
This is because a small good deed in a former life brought about this destiny and wealth.
The heavy calamities of this life have not yet invited their karmic retribution.
Because their sins are great and they deserve much suffering,
their punishment is delayed, and their evil is allowed to continue.
Once their misfortunes are full and their transgressions accumulated,
then their nests will be overturned and their eggs shattered,
to perpetually return to the crucible and Avīci Hell,
forever dwelling in the Avīci Hell.
Therefore, the scripture says:
"If evil is not accumulated, it cannot destroy one's body."
This is what it refers to.
There are also instances of karmic retribution being clearly observed and heard.
For example, Wáng Mǎng (王莽) usurped the throne and had his head displayed on the execution platform.
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) was cruel and brutal, and his corpse was exposed in the marketplace.
Jìn Hóu (晉侯) killed Zhào Shuò (趙朔),
and suffered the grief of being trapped in a latrine.
Qí Zhǔ (齊主) harmed Péng Shēng (彭生),
and experienced the pain of falling from a carriage.
The downfall of the Xià (夏) dynasty was due to the sins of Jié (桀).
The extinction of the Yīn (殷) dynasty was due to the faults of Zhòu (紂).
Thus, it is known that the meaning of cause and effect is intricate and difficult to determine.
The principle of karmic retribution is varied and uncertain.
These are what are called retribution in this life, retribution in the present, and retribution in future lives.
Qǐngyí Gōngzǐ (請疑公子) said:
If the theory of spontaneity is untenable in principle,
then the argument for retribution must be correct in expression.
Yet, your previous statement also said:
"What the two gentlemen narrated are both not in accordance with reason."
I wonder if this meaning can be explained to me.
Tōngmǐn Xiānshēng said:
"Since you have sincerely and repeatedly requested,
I too have reluctantly replied.
But reflecting on my own mediocrity and shallow understanding,
I have not yet fully expounded its profound essence.
Seeking the Dharma, it is fundamentally non-existent.
If non-existent, then there is no arising.
The principle itself is not non-existent.
If not non-existent, then there is no ceasing.
If there is no arising and no ceasing, where do all phenomena reside?
If neither existent nor non-existent, where are all things lodged?
Sweeping and pure,
the path of searching is thus cut off.
Serene and equal,
there is no way to choose or reject.
How can there be a principle of karmic retribution to seek, or thoughts of good and evil to obtain?
It is precisely because ordinary beings have not yet understood this ultimate truth
that they forcibly stir up disputes and strongly create distinctions.
It is like a thirsty person chasing a mirage,
when water is in the rivers and ponds;
or an eye-diseased person seeing flowers,
when the sky has never had trees.
Merely to draw them closer and relieve their heavy delusions,
I subtly show cause and effect and briefly manifest karmic conditions.
This causes fixed attachments to be removed and natural views to be quelled.
If one attains the correct principle and awakens to this true Dharma,
what further existence can there be?
And what non-existence can there be?"
Thereupon, the two or three gentlemen looked at each other, their hearts startled.
They gladly grasped the meaning,
stepped back from their seats, respectfully prostrated themselves, and said:
"Today, it can be said that we 'heard the Way in the morning and would gladly die in the evening' [Zhāo wén xī sǐ],
'came empty and returned full' [Xū wǎng shí guī].
All accumulated obstructions are overthrown,
like leaves falling in the autumn wind.
Numerous doubts are dispersed,
like ice melting in the spring sun.
We shall respectfully abandon our former confusion and together follow the later practice."
The three realms are divided into sections,
the four modes of birth possess their natures.
All roam together in the burning house,
and together sink in the sea of desire.
Therefore, the King of Dharma [Fǎwáng] took on the role of an island and bank,
and the enlightened ones responded to the call for vehicles.
They guide those lost in delusion
to return to this excellent land.
Since the precious clouds shone from the west and the river of Dharma flowed eastward,
sweet dew overflowed,
spreading its influence with the wind.
The Imperial House [Huángjiā] governs the heavens,
reveres the Way, and honors the Dharma,
liberating all beings from conditioned existence,
and guiding sentient beings to non-duality.
Therefore, they carved sandalwood and made paintings, constructed stone and sculpted gold,
spreading throughout myriad nations, equal to dust and sand in number.
Furthermore, they decreed that officials and those involved, both monastic and lay [zī sù],
with sincerity surpassing flesh and bone,
should gather all verses and stanzas from the Dragon Palace [Lónggōng].
All that was proclaimed by the Golden Mouth [Jīnkǒu] was compiled and transcribed.
Each had three parts,
totaling a certain number of scrolls.
With this merit, their minds are like empty space.
With impartial giving, no thought is left untouched.
Borrowing our vows, may we together ascend to the highest fruit.
On this date, so-and-so Hénán said this and that.
I have heard that
the nine rivers [Jiǔhé] traced their paths and stored up numinous mounds,
and the four corners of the land were measured, their writings stored in numerous jade tablets.
There were also the texts carved on stone by the Three Sovereigns [Sānhuáng] in Qīngqiū and Zǐfǔ,
and the numinous flying characters of the six *jiǎ* in green slips and yellow cords.
But how can they compare to the Tathāgata's [Rúlái] secret treasury?
It is like a bright pearl.
It is what all Buddhas take as their teacher, akin to a pure mirror.
The Four Noble Truths [Sìdì] Dharma of Deer Park [Lùyuàn],
and the Eight Aspects of Truth [Bājiàn] text of Níyuán:
even the immense strength of Xiāngshān cannot carry them.
In the year of Zhaoyáng,
when the dragon constellation [Lóngjí] was in Tiānjǐng,
in reverence for so-and-so,
we reverently created the entire Buddhist Canon [Yīqiè Jīngzàng].
It begins with the teaching of arising and ceasing [shēngmiè],
and concludes with the doctrine of Nirvāṇa [Níhuán].
The treatises are rare;
there are short verses and long prose passages,
green-headed and silver-cased, profound texts in jade boxes.
Língyáng took elixirs,
and Zhǐguān had immortal characters.
Guānyǐn observed the *qì*,
and received profound words.
Never has there been a Nāgārjuna [Lóngshù] with such sharp faculties
that he could not read through the titles,
nor a Śrāmaṇa [Sītuó] with such shallow practice
that he had not heard of them even when sitting in the same seat.
All the sounds of India [Tiānzhú]
and all the leaves of the palm [bèiduō]
were divided into eight portions for the kingdoms,
and the texts were moved to Kasmira [Jìbīn].
The stones were exhausted down to six *zhū*,
and the writings returned to the great sea.
We sincerely pray that the divine spirits of the past, riding on this power of the Way,

May the four directions be peacefully attached, and all blessings appear.
May enemies and kin in the six realms of existence together ascend to perfect enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Precepts disciple, Yáng Guǎng (楊廣), bows to the Buddha.
Reflecting on how the Tathāgata appeared in the world, his voice and teachings covered all beings.
With diligent and subtle effort, he compiled the Dharma Treasury.
Dìshì (帝釋) and the Cakravartin kings were entrusted with it.
Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas received and propagated the great teaching,
liberating countless beings up to the present day.
The Supreme One rescued the drowning, unifying a hundred kings.
On the day the four seas pacified Chén (陳),
there was no flaw in the Way or among the populace.
But among the ignorant people of the southeast, lingering embers incited trouble.
Therefore, the strategic plan was adopted to pacify the coastal regions again.
The campaign did not exhaust the army, and peace was achieved in due time.
Furthermore, there was deep concern that many sacred images and venerable sūtras had been reduced to ashes, their knotted cords and ink lines obliterated in ditches.
For this reason, orders were sent far and wide for the armies to collect them from all directions.
Before a full month had passed, the light boats had all arrived.
Then, the officials in charge of scholarship were ordered to record them by name,

Yìfǔ (義府) pondered deeply and verified their origins.
Through careful analysis and comparison, many were restored to their original categories.
They were adorned and repaired, making the old like new.
The four treasuries on the precious platform comprise nearly one hundred thousand scrolls.
Therefore, a grand vow was made to ensure their eternal circulation.
The vow text was also written and attached to the end of each scroll.
Repeated attendance at court audiences meant the work was only recently completed.
Now, I personally uphold and receive the main treasury on the precious platform.
As for the secondary treasuries and below,
they are for the Huìrì (慧日) Fǎyún (法雲) dào chǎng (道場),

Since the Brahma palaces vary in size,
and the number of monks also differs,
the sūtra collections are distributed according to their quantity, after careful consideration.
As the givers are earnest,
the recipients should also be diligent.
Preserve the original Dharma text for a long time and widely propagate the Dharma.
If anyone wishes to copy the text, they should come to the temple to do so.
Do not allow it to be scattered and lost, thereby losing the unconditioned.
The former Buddhas and latter Buddhas are surely of the same golden mouth.

On Mount Sūmí (須彌), all the sages together uphold them.

Scattered across Jambudvīpa (閻浮), it is likewise so.
Recalling those who transcribed and created them,

The diligence of their minds and hands, what immeasurable merit!

Self-practice and transforming others are fully contained in the sūtras and vinaya.
Considering my shallow understanding, I am truly ashamed before those who are thoroughly learned.
Cause and effect,

How can one not know that to perfect oneself

The profound teachings of the inner canon naturally concern the Sangha.
Why should I, a mere nobody, bear such a burden?
I am only glad to rely on past good roots, having been born and raised in the royal palace.

Merely clinging to the sūtras and vinaya without following the Buddha's precepts,

Opening the breast and offering ghee, the methods differ.

Different paths lead to the same destination; a hundred thoughts converge into one.
Inner and outer merge, their meaning united.

Clinging to Lalitavistara (黎耶) instantly leads to true awakening.
Lion's armor (師子嚴鎧) is, conversely, criticized by snails and clams (蠃貝).

If the taste of the sea is equalized, then ghee will be produced.
The emperor's (聖御) dark-blue jewels, the golden wheel flying in the sky, the clouds moving—
collecting all good into benevolent longevity,
unifying the One Vehicle in a grand assembly,
awakening sentient beings and saving all creatures.
The sūtras now propagated spread throughout the universe.
The latent power of all sages will surely operate in other realms,
so that all may ascend to Bodhi (菩提) and quickly attain eternal joy.
This is the disciple's expression
of following the great vow,
with infinite equality and tranquility.
This message is sent to be proclaimed.
May those with wisdom reflect and rejoice.
Shāméng Xuánzàng (沙門玄奘) says:
In the first year of Zhēngguān (貞觀),
I, Xuánzàng (奘), traveled to the Western Regions
to seek the Tathāgata's secret treasury
and trace Śākyamuni's (釋迦)遗旨.
I obtained a total of six hundred fifty-seven fascicles,
all brought back on white horses.
In the eighteenth year of Zhēngguān (貞觀),
I finally returned to the capital.
I immediately received an imperial edict
to unravel and translate them at Hóngfú Dào Chǎng (弘福道場).
Now, I have translated sūtras such as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
I humbly pray for your gracious favor to provide a preface for these sūtras.
I earnestly hope for an imperial decree before circulating them in Central China.
I have also compiled a work titled Xīyù Zhuàn (西域傳) in twelve volumes in total.
I respectfully send the court attendant, Lǐ Jìngyī (李敬一), to present it.
I am overwhelmed with trepidation.
I respectfully present this memorial to report.
I respectfully state.
I have fully read and understood the intent of your letter.
Dharma Master, your aspirations have long been lofty, your conduct beyond the mundane.
You sailed the precious boat to reach the other shore,
sought the wondrous Way, and opened the Dharma gate.
You extensively propagated the great teaching and cleansed away all sins.
Therefore, when the cloud of compassion was about to roll up,
you spread it to shade the four empty spaces.
When the sun of wisdom was about to dim,
you brightened it to illuminate the eight extremities.
Is it not the Dharma Master who spreads and brightens them?
My learning is shallow and my mind clumsy; I am still lost in worldly matters.
How much more so the profound and subtle teachings of Buddhism!
How could I fathom them?
Your request for a sūtra title is something I have not heard of before.
You also mentioned:
"The newly compiled Xīyù Jì (西域記) I will personally peruse."
By imperial edict, Xuánzàng (奘) is still earnestly requested to present his petition for the sūtra title and preface.
I have heard that
the Two Instruments (Heaven and Earth) have forms,
manifesting covering and carrying to contain all life.
The Four Seasons are formless,
secretly alternating cold and heat to transform all things.
Therefore, when one gazes at heaven and observes the earth,
even the ignorant and foolish can discern their beginnings.
Yet, discerning Yin and penetrating Yang,
even the wise and sagely rarely exhaust their principles.
However, Heaven and Earth encompass Yin and Yang, and are easy to know
because they have forms.
Yin and Yang dwell within Heaven and Earth, yet are difficult to fathom
because they are formless.
Thus, it is known that what is manifest in form is verifiable;
even the foolish are not confused.
What is hidden in form cannot be seen;
even the wise are bewildered.
How much more so for the Buddha-Dharma, which is profoundly abstruse,
traversing the unseen and controlling the tranquil!
It broadly saves all beings
and governs the ten directions.
Its majestic spiritual power is supreme,
and its divine might is without limit.
When great, it fills the universe;
when small, it encompasses a hair's breadth.
Without annihilation or birth,
it remains undiminished through a thousand kalpas.
Appearing and disappearing,
it sustains a hundred blessings for all time.
Its wondrous Way is profoundly subtle;
one follows it without knowing its limits.
The flow of its Dharma is pure and serene;
one drinks from it without discerning its source.
Therefore, how could the ignorant and foolish, the petty and vulgar,
embrace its essence and purpose without doubts?
However, the rise of the Great Teaching
originated in the Western Land.
It ascended to the Hàn court, illuminating a dream,
and shone upon the Eastern Region, spreading compassion.
In ancient times, when the form was divided and traces scattered,
its words spread without being uttered, yet brought transformation.
In that world of constant appearance and reality,
people looked up to its virtue and knew how to follow it.
When the luminous shadow returned to truth, and the ritual moved beyond this world,
the golden image veiled its radiance,
no longer reflecting the light of three thousand worlds.
The beautiful form opened its diagrams,
revealing the thirty-two marks in the void.
Then, subtle teachings were widely propagated,
saving all sentient beings from the three evil paths.
The bequeathed instructions were extensively proclaimed,
guiding all living beings to the ten stages.
However, the true teaching is difficult to uphold;
none can unify its ultimate purpose.
Partial doctrines are easy to follow;
thus, heterodoxy and orthodoxy become entangled.
Hence, the doctrines of emptiness and existence
are sometimes affirmed or denied by custom.
The Great and Small Vehicles
sometimes rise or fall with the times.
There is a Dharma Master Xuánzàng,
a leader of the Śramaṇas.
In his youth, he possessed pure intelligence,
early comprehending the essence of the three emptinesses.
As he grew, his spirit attuned deeply,
first embracing the practice of the four忍.
The pine wind and moon over water
were not enough to compare to his purity and brilliance.
Immortal dew and bright pearls
could not match his clarity and luster.
Therefore, his wisdom penetrated without impediment, and his spirit perceived the unformed.
He surpassed the six dusts and transcended them.
He was unique throughout a thousand ages.
Concentrating his mind on the inner realm,
he lamented the decline of the True Dharma.
Resting his thoughts in the profound gate,
he grieved over the errors in the profound texts.
He desired to categorize and analyze the principles, widely propagating previous insights,
to cut off falsehoods and renew truth, opening the way for future learners.
Therefore, he set his heart on the Pure Land and traveled to the Western Regions.
He journeyed through dangers, venturing alone with his staff.
Accumulated snow flew in the morning; he lost his way between paths.
Startling sand rose in the evening; he lost his bearings beyond the sky.
Across ten thousand li of mountains and rivers,
he pushed through mist and clouds, advancing his shadow.
Through a hundred cycles of cold and heat,
he trod through frost and rain, moving forward.
His sincerity was great, his toil light; his quest profound, his wish achieved.
He traveled throughout the Western lands for seventeen years,
exhaustively exploring various countries, seeking the True Teaching.
Amidst the twin Sāla trees and eight rivers, he tasted the Dharma and breathed the wind.
At Deer Park and Vulture Peak, he gazed upon wonders and revered the extraordinary.
He received the ultimate words from the ancient sages
and accepted the true teaching from the supreme worthies.
He delved into the profound gates of mystery, exhaustively researching the abstruse work.
The path of the One Vehicle and the Five Precepts
galloped in his heart's field.
The texts of the Eight Treasuries and Three Baskets
surged in his ocean of words.
From the countries he had visited,
he gathered the essential texts of the Three Baskets,
a total of six hundred and fifty-seven scrolls.
He translated and distributed them in Zhōngxià, proclaiming the glorious work.
He drew compassionate clouds from the western extremity
and poured the Dharma rain upon the eastern border.
The sacred teaching, once incomplete, was made whole again.
Living beings, once burdened by sin, regained their blessings.
He moistened the dry flames of the burning house,
together pulling them from the迷途.
He illuminated the murky waves of the water of love,
together reaching the other shore.
Thus, it is known that evil falls due to karma, and good rises due to conditions.
The cause of rising and falling rests solely with human beings.
For example, the cassia growing on a high ridge, only with clouds and dew can its blossoms flourish.
The lotus emerging from clear water, flying dust cannot defile its leaves.
It is not that the lotus is inherently pure or the cassia inherently chaste,
but rather that what they rely on is lofty, so minor things cannot hinder them;
what they depend on is pure, so turbid things cannot contaminate them.
Even plants and trees, without consciousness,
still rely on goodness to achieve goodness.
How much more so for humanity, possessed of awareness,
not to seek blessings through auspicious connections?
It is hoped that this sūtra will circulate, enduring endlessly like the sun and moon,
and this blessing will spread far and wide, eternally great like Heaven and Earth.
Shāmén Xuánzàng says:
I humbly heard that the six trigrams, in exploring profundities,
are confined to the realm of birth and death.

has not yet entered the realm of True Suchness.

with a jade-like disposition, has descended, and with a golden wheel, governs the heavens.

and encompassed the boundless Dharma-realm.

In the past, Xuánzàng, shaking his staff, briefly visited Jù Shān.
Though his journey was ten thousand li, he relied on imperial majesty as if it were咫尺.
Not traveling on a thousand-petaled lotus, he reached the twin Sāla trees in an instant.
He collected the Three Baskets,
exhausting what was stored in the dragon palace.
He researched the One Vehicle,
fathoming the bequeathed meaning of Vulture Peak.
All these, he brought on white horses and presented to the purple palace.
Soon, an imperial decree was issued, granting permission for translation.
Xuánzàng's understanding is inferior to Lóngshù's,
falsely enjoying the honor of transmitting the lamp.
His talent differs from Mǎmíng's;
he deeply shames the quickness of emptying the vase.
The sūtras and treatises he has translated

Then, bearing the imperial grace, he focused his mind

It is like the sun emitting a thousand rays,
its principles encompassing the gates of all wonders,
like a Dharma cloud moistening a hundred grasses.
The one sound expounded is rarely encountered in countless kalpas.
That this humble person could personally hear the Brahmic sound,
leaping with joy as if receiving a prophecy,
is an extreme honor.
I respectfully present this memorial to the court
to express my gratitude.
Respectfully submitted.
My talent is inferior to jade and chime;
my words are ashamed of being unscholarly.
As for the inner doctrines, I am particularly unskilled.
The preface I composed yesterday was deeply crude and clumsy.
I only feared defiling the ink on golden tablets
and marking tiles and pebbles among a forest of pearls.
Suddenly receiving your letter, I mistakenly accepted your praise.
Reflecting repeatedly, my shame only deepened.
My virtues are not worthy of praise; your thanks are given in vain.
Indeed, to make manifest and propagate the true teaching,
without wisdom, one cannot broaden its scope;
to extol and elucidate subtle words,
without sagacity, none can determine their purport.
For the Sāṃkhya-sūtra,
is the profound doctrine of all phenomena,
the standard and measure of all scriptures.
It encompasses the grand and far-reaching, the abstruse and profound.
It reaches the ultimate subtlety of emptiness and existence,
embodies the key principles of production and cessation.
Its words are rich, its Way expansive;
those who seek it cannot fathom its source.
Its writing is clear, its meaning obscure;
those who follow it cannot ascertain its bounds.
Therefore, it is known that where the holy compassion extends,
no karma is good but it is attained;
where the wondrous transformation spreads,
no evil condition but it is cut off.
It unfolds the threads of the Dharma-net,
propagates the true teaching of the six Pāramitās,
rescues all sentient beings from suffering,
and opens the secret doors of the Tripiṭaka.
Thus, its name flies far without wings,
its Way endures forever without roots.
The Way's name flows with blessings,
remaining constant through countless ages;
it responds to calls with manifested bodies,
imperishable through kalpas as dust.
Morning bells and evening chants
intertwine two sounds on Gṛdhrakūṭa;
the sun of wisdom and the flow of Dharma
turn the twin wheels in Mṛgadāva.
Jewel canopies, filling the sky,
meet and fly with soaring clouds;
cultivated spring forests
blend their colors with celestial flowers.
Humbly, I submit that His Majesty the Emperor,
with blessings endowed from the lofty heavens,
rules the eight directions with folded arms;
his virtue covers the black-haired people,
and all nations pay homage with respectful salutations.
His grace reaches even decaying bones,
as the stone chamber receives the palm-leaf scriptures;
his benevolence extends to insects,
as the golden casket circulates the Brahmanic verses.
This has enabled the Anavatapta Lake to connect with the eight rivers of China,
and Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to join the verdant peaks of Sōngshān and Huàshān.
I humbly believe that the Dharma-nature is tranquil and still,

yet it manifests to those who express sincere devotion.
How can one speak of lighting the torch of wisdom

or bringing down the rain of Dharma

Thus, a hundred different streams converge into the sea,

How could one compare the superiority or inferiority with Tāng and Wǔ,
or their sagely virtue with Yáo and Shùn?
Dharma Master Xuánzàng,
from an early age cherished intelligence and established a simple resolve.
His spirit was pure even in childhood,
his being rose above the frivolous world.
He fixed his mind in a quiet chamber, hid his traces in a secluded cliff,

Transcending the realm of the six dusts,
he walked alone in Kapilavastu.
Comprehending the purport of the Ekayāna,
he transformed beings according to their capacities.

He journeyed far across the Gaṅgā, ultimately reaching the land of full letters; he frequently climbed the snowy mountains, further obtaining half a pearl.

On the sixth day of the second month of the nineteenth year of Zhēngguān

He led the Dharma-stream of the great ocean,
washing away defilements inexhaustibly;

illuminating the darkness ever brightly.
If not for having cultivated profound auspicious connections over a long time,

It is said that the Dharma-nature abides eternally,
matching the brightness of the three luminaries;
our emperor's blessings are complete,
firm like the two cosmic forces.
I humbly observe the imperial prefaces to the various sūtras,
illuminating the past and surpassing the present;
their reasoning contains the sound of metal and stone,
their prose embraces the moistness of wind and cloud.
I, Zhì, presumptuously add a speck of dust to a mountain and a drop of dew to a stream

I, Zhì, have always been without talent or learning, and my nature is not intelligent.
I have rarely studied the various texts of the inner doctrine.

I am deeply ashamed to have troubled the master to come so far.

who was broadly versed in profound meanings.

In the year Guǐmǎo, he first conceived the idea.

Is this not grand!
Now,
observing birds and setting down writing,

spread vast waves through the Nine Streams.

the meaning of the text is largely the same.

all possessed remarkable talents and extensive knowledge, broad and profound.

The mind encompasses light and darkness,
revealing the main thoroughfare for entering the mechanism.
Thus, it is known that the companions of Mǎnyuàn (滿願)
take the small path to nurture life.
Those of Tiānrè (天熱)
rely on deviant paths to transform beings.
Striking and raising, examining thoroughly to suit the Way,
great parables lie in expedient strategies.
Not awaiting imposing appearances, but only preserving detachment.
If such words are complete, then they are understood by those who practice.
Or, those who do not understand will rashly instigate heresies.
If they see deviant and perverse actions, they become even more confused.
They do not reflect on their own vexations and delusions,
but solely fear others' improper conduct.
At that point, they blindly follow, causing ruin and destruction.
Ordinary people
die lamenting the cruelty.
Superior saints
grieve over the brutal and outrageous complacency.
Since ancient times, rulers and emperors,
reflecting on the rise and fall from historical mirrors,
unfurled vast nets that could swallow a boat,
and spread broad policies of tolerance and nurture.
They elucidated benevolent customs throughout the world,
thus achieving great peace.
They promoted established norms for public service and retirement,
enjoying these great benefits.
Others, however, were meticulous in their investigations and accusations, going against the maxim of "not overcooking small fish."
They gathered faults and errors,
issuing strict decrees that sought to extract every last drop of fat.
Later, when disaster struck and calamity spread,
no defenses could be opened; they wept, hiding in corners.
In an instant, they were utterly destroyed, becoming a laughingstock for all under heaven.
Therefore, I have compiled these political achievements, revealing the wise and enlightened.
Some defied edicts to make upright statements;
some initiated discussions to thoroughly examine righteous proposals.
Some praised and esteemed the noble and lofty;
some bore grief and eloquently composed elegies.
This path can be traced and is fully detailed in the following sections.
In the seventh year of Yìxī of the Jìn dynasty, on a certain day in the fifth month,
the Daoist Zhī Tán-dì passed away.
He was sixty-five years old.
Alas, how mournful!
The Dharma Master's lineage originated in the Western Regions;
he was born in Kāngjū.
He adopted the name of his country as his clan name.
Having devoted himself to the master's teachings,
he then took the Dharma surname Zhī.
He moved to Qiānqiū-lǐ, Dū-xiāng, Wūchéng-xiàn, Wúxīng-jùn.
Drawing on the pure essence of the Metal element,
and supported by the beautiful rhythms of Yang,
his lineage from a distant land gave birth to an extraordinary talent,
harmonizing with rivers and mountains, endowed with spiritual essence.
His understanding and sentiments were profound and pure; his demeanor was bright and solemn.
His Daoist attainments were manifest according to Heaven's timing;
his virtuous conduct was evident in his innate disposition.
His steadfast enlightenment was uniquely outstanding;
various distractions were insufficient to stir his heart.
His sincerity was deep and firm;
no amount of public opinion could sway his resolve.
Thus, transcending the mundane and excelling in his pursuits,
his wisdom emerged in his youth.
He delved into the subtle and indulged in the profound,
illuminating the Dao in his later years.
Therefore, he was able to stir the spiritual wind in the divine realm,
and spread wonderful transformations in the latter age.
He inherited the clarity of previous sages,
and Daoists and laypeople alike harbored respect for him.
He traveled extensively, proclaiming the great doctrine.
He subtly explored the recondite and profound, clarifying the subtle with elegant discourse.
Furthermore, he was skilled in composing literary works,
and his discerning appreciation flowed freely,
thus he had already harmonized with and surpassed the prevailing trends, leading his contemporaries.
In his middle years, the Master deeply felt that it was difficult to establish a secluded dwelling near the city,
and moreover, his nature, like mountains and waters, inherently loved nature.
The tranquility of the external world, its silence, embodied the heart of Heaven itself.
Therefore, he declined worldly connections and secluded himself in rocky ravines.
He then built his dwelling in Kūn-shān of Gùzhàng, Wúxīng-jùn.
He pursued the Dao and promoted transformation for over twenty years.
The profession he inhabited and promoted
could cleanse the mind and purify the soul.
The beauty of the trap and image [i.e. nature]
was sufficient to exhaust one's interests and prolong one's years.
Therefore, those who aspired to his principles and returned to benevolence gathered from all directions.
Those who admired his style and cherished his pursuits came from afar to seek his guidance.
At that time, many influential heroes of the age frequently invited him for vegetarian meals and lectures.
The Master responded to things with an open mind,
never allowing movements or stillness to bother him.
He expressed sincerity and expounded righteousness,
never distinguishing between Daoists and laypeople in his approach.
His virtue of holding to unity
was also praised by near and far.
He was about to sweep clean the mysterious path and uphold the declining customs,
to transcend the external and subtly pave the way, following the tracks of mysterious enlightenment.
Alas, he did not live long, fell ill, and passed away.
Those who knew him deeply feel the pain of his loss.
Deep emotions mourn the passing of a good man.
Indeed, to be honored without rank,
to live in glory and die in sorrow—this is what is meant.
Although the ultimate truth is mysteriously one, and existence and non-existence are determined at the very beginning of form,
and profound insight illuminates that the body is no different from decaying earth,
yet, those whose emotions still dwell in the realm of joy and sorrow,
and whose hearts have not yet obliterated the feelings of separation and reunion,
how can they not feel sorrow and joy over gain and loss?
How can they not feel sad when facing the long separation?
If the profound nothingness is difficult to comprehend,
then let us rely on writing to express our admiration.
Taking up a weak brush to express our feelings,
spreading his pure radiance limitlessly,
we compose this elegy, which says:
