Zuānyǎng zhī tú zì yuǎn ér lái.
Xū zhì shí guī biànyú zhéjì.
Dìhòu chú'èr zhī zūn.
Fānyīng dǐngzǎi zhī zhòng.
Mò bù yīdào zōngshī zhānyóu jiéjìng.
Ér hóngliàng suì'ào bù yǐ guìjiàn chuǎn qí gùmà.
Yízhěng yuānshēn bù yǐ hánshǔ pǐn qí huáibào.
Suǒyǐ kuòzòng xiàngmò chóngzhèn tuíliú zhě.
Fǎshī qí rén yǐ.
Qǐxùn zhī yuán yǒuxiàn.
Fùshǒu zhī gē huì zhōng.
Fēnghuǒ gàozhēng.
Yùtián míng yú wēishí.
Língshèng miè xiàn.
Lǚgōng yuè yú gàojiàn.
Chūnqiū liùshíjiǔ.
Wūhū āizāi.
Wàibǐng gěngshí nèizī tònghún.
Mùtí wǎngjì xíngshí fúyán.
Nǎi zuò lěi yuē.
The world is stagnant and vast.
The sea of suffering is long and distant.
Desire covers and conceals profoundly.
The net of love spreads widely.
The lamp of Dharma does not shine.
The sun of wisdom is obscured by haze.
Decayed dwellings are burned and collapse.
Blazing fires rise and float.
The two cosmic principles are destroyed.
Counting them, there are years.
The three kalpas are vast and distant.
Who can count the empty kalpas?
From darkness, how can one know?
Drowning in the currents, one cannot cross.
With successors becoming scarce,
it truly requires a destined age.
A brilliant sage is born.
The descent of his spirit is from his own karma.
He embodies auspicious signs and contains a vessel [of wisdom].
His extraordinary nature was evident in childhood.
His divine sagacity was clear in youth, his profound insight manifest early.
Like jade initially gleaming,
like pearls emerging from a spring.
He detested the defilement of dust.
He transcended and comprehended the profound and subtle.
He renounced the bonds of ignorance.
He purified and cut away emotional attachments.
In childhood, he established his principles.
In his youthful years, he followed a master.
He upheld rules with reverence.
His exemplary conduct was majestic and awe-inspiring.
He held himself with pure integrity.
His mind and actions were virtuous and prudent.
He learned to discern the secret sources.
He inquired to exhaust distant principles.
He illuminated what was previously hidden.
Past doubts were clarified by his reflection.
His craftsmanship was effortless, his achievements doubled.
His thoughts were lofty, his undertakings flourishing.
Arriving at middle age,
his profound wisdom was vast and extensive.
He expounded the Dharma of emptiness in cycles.
Clouds were cleared, and the sun shone brightly.
He rode the main path as if it were level.
Provisional teachings opened as if unobstructed.
All sentient beings, vast in number,
regarded him as their object of veneration.
His fame spread to the right of the Hé.
His brilliance was marked to the left of the Jiāng.
His reputation was proclaimed due to his virtue.
His renown was rich because of his Way.
He encouraged and sought out [learners].
He delighted in teaching and instructing.
His benevolence was like the earth.
His ambition was as high as the peaks.
He stopped meals to attend to the hungry.
He gave away his padded clothes to pity the cold.
His accumulations never ceased for a day.
His wealth was used to provide for the destitute.
He would rather be humble than arrogant towards beauty.
He did not value a pleasing countenance.
This profound and auspicious virtue permeated.
It was equally distributed to those in humble dwellings.
Where his teachings reached,
obscure understanding became clear.
Where his wisdom guided,
tasks were accomplished with sincerity.
He met the deluded with abundant goods.
He comforted the confused with genuine compassion.
Relying on his subtle guidance and seeking his essential teachings,
none failed to prosper.
The perilous road is ever distant.
The opening and guiding have a limit.
Birth and death alternate.
Moment by moment, it never ceases.
Passing years hold little time.
The western light suddenly presses on.
How can the changing clouds stop?
He is about to journey to the pure land.
Alas, how sorrowful!
His body was deeply afflicted by illness.
His perception reached the four diseases.
Acupuncture, moxibustion, physicians, and shamans
failed to alleviate his condition with their prescribed dosages.
He set his mind on the Dharma journey.
He directed his thoughts to the compassionate precepts.
He did not abandon his brave diligence.
He vowed to save all fallen beings.
Alas, how sorrowful!
What gathers must eventually part.
Temporary assemblages must yield.
We share sorrow in the white forest.
In the dead of night, silence reigns.
People speak of exhorting virtue.
We look up at the sky, as if he ascends.
He departs for that dark blue palace.
He leaves this dusty abode.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Subtle words are utterly lost forever.
The boat and raft are destroyed at the distant shore.
The magnificent splendor of the lofty dust is ravaged.
The carved beauty of the majestic hall is overgrown.
He abandoned his form as if casting it away.
To what realm did his spirit transfer?
His disciples look up to his guidance with longing.
Their tears of blood flow in vain, moved by his passing.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Dharma Master's name was Zhìchēng.
His family, of a certain commandery and surname, lived previously.
He drew from the clear springs of the Fén and the Huì rivers,
embodying the pure essence of the Hé River and the mountains.
He accumulated spiritual causes in previous lives,
attaining a nature of wisdom in Jambudvīpa.
He was upright and pure, having been endowed with these qualities from the beginning.
He obtained warmth, kindness, reverence, and frugality as his very essence.
However, his natural disposition was truly profound,
encompassing brilliance and concealing its radiance.
He blended gradually with the common people,
so no one could fathom his depth or shallowness.
It was as if a tiny flower of an inch had hidden its light in a deep ravine,
or a foot-long treasure remained unappraised for a city.
Those who observed him knew not his greatness or beauty.
Those who listened from afar could not hear his grand name.
Bound by military service, he rose from the common fields.
When he reached the age of thirty,
he began to peruse the various sūtras.
Retreating, he sighed, saying,
"A hundred years pass in a flash, and fame and achievement are considered important.
But fame does not last, and achievement is hard to secure.
Moreover, good fortune, misfortune, regret, and stinginess have been proven by the Confucian classics.
Transformations, risings, and falls have been acclaimed by past sages.
How can one know that beyond the towering heights and vast expanses,
there exists a boundless, all-encompassing great support for the hidden and the manifest?"
"There is a master;
I know where to return!"
Thereupon, he made a deep bow to the five precepts and knelt in reverence before the four noble truths.
All sharpness was blunted, and all entanglements were resolved.
In the Dàmíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
there was a Zen Master Yìn in the Yì region,
who practiced severe asceticism and had profound insight, rising to become an imperial preceptor.
The Venerable One, hearing of his reputation, presented himself and performed all due courtesies.
Master Yìn spoke of returning to Yōngshǔ.
So they went hand in hand in the same boat.
In the first year of the Tàishǐ era of the Sòng dynasty, he left home at Yùlěi.
His sincerity moved both humans and devas, and his faith pierced through metal and stone.
With an upright heart and Prajñā, he advanced steadily on the path.
Thereafter, with reverence, he followed his master, seeking out worthies to discern his aspirations.
He roamed through the nine divisions of the scriptures and traversed the three vehicles.
What Mólúo had expounded and translated,
and what the Dragon King had concealed,
though he received, recited, and chanted it,
he did not take it as his primary doctrine.
He often said, "Cultivating the mind is a trace.
If the traces are subtle, the mind is disciplined.
Propagating the Dharma is action.
If the actions are subtle, the Dharma exists.
For settling the superior and governing the people, nothing is more important than ritual.
For restraining evil and moving towards good, nothing is higher than the Vinaya.
That which can drive one from the burning house and cross the sea of suffering,
allowing one to see the three evil paths without treading them,
and endure myriad kalpas without decline,
is it not the Vinaya?"
So he cast aside the branches and leaves, concentrating his thoughts on the root.
He reined in his mind and purified his heart, taking this as his personal mission.
Thereupon, staff in hand, he journeyed a thousand *lǐ* to study.
Carrying scriptures and holding his alms bowl, he travelled a hundred *shè* without rest.
He looked west towards Mount Jīng and passed south through Lǐpǔ.
He travelled throughout Huáxià, collecting widely strange and remarkable teachings.
His body was like earth and wood, but his mind and understanding were like jade.
There was no height he did not aspire to,
no fortress he did not attack.
His sleep was so restless that his mat did not warm,
and when his thoughts reached their peak, he had no time to eat.
After entering the path for three years, he studied with his master in four lectures.
His teaching was excellent, his efforts doubled, and his practice flourished, his understanding of the scriptures becoming clear.
He often said, "The Dharma does not fall to the ground,
each person has their own merits.
Why should the learning of Xuānnǐ always be from one master?"
At that time, there were two Venerables, Jùyǐn,
senior high-ranking monks, whose reputations rang like phoenixes in Xīchǔ.
And the eminent Vinaya Master Duōbǎo Yǐng, who was widely learned and reviewed old knowledge, rising like a brush in Dōngdū. While the Dharma Master was in Jiānglíng,
he received guidance from Jùyǐn.
And when he returned to Jīngluò, he considered Yǐng Gōng his beneficial friend.
Both weighed the best and harvested the essence of words,
discarding chaff to dine on choice grain,
combining salt and plum to create a rich stew.
Their reasoning was refined and their meaning profound;
superficial scholars could not follow in their footsteps.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
he first lectured on the Shísònglǜ (Ten Recitations Vinaya) at Zhènzé.
He expounded on the particulars of practice, bringing the divine path within reach.
His eloquent discussions reached the clouds and the Milky Way,
and his profound insights penetrated the boundless.
The eighty thousand dignified practices were explained with tranquil clarity,
and the chapters and verses of the five divisions converged like waves.
From this, later generations understood the lineage, and previous masters revised their views.
His brilliant and excellent reputation became increasingly renowned.
The Dharma Master responded without choosing a direction, having abundant capacity.
He spoke lucidly all day, and the matter was contained within his words.
He established Qīyún at Jùqū,
and built Yánzuò at Jiànyè.
His commands did not require strictness, and his rooms were quiet.
His work did not need acceleration, yet buildings stood in rows.
Since the Fāngděng sūtras came to our land,
transforming "barbarian" into "Han,"
great talents and profound scholars gathered shoulder to shoulder.
Families of the Fǎhuá and Wéimó sūtras
appeared here and there.
The teachings of the Nièpán and Chéngshí sūtras
attracted disciples everywhere.
But the Vinaya Canon was most scarce at that time.
To shake the robe and hold the collar (lead the movement) truly belonged to him.
As for the vast and profound sources,
which perplexed the old masters,
and the steep, hidden, and complex passages,
which caused earlier practitioners to abandon their efforts,
he meticulously dissected them, breaking down every entanglement,
uncovering the profound and reaching the distant, with unique insight.
Thus, he was able to attract people from south of Hù to north of Wāngōng,
who, seeking his voice and responding to his call, came from thousands of *lǐ* away.
His disciples increased year by year, their understanding of the scriptures renewing daily.
He sat in the high hall, receiving the four assemblies,
turning the wheel of Dharma, and being attended by fellow practitioners.
For over twenty years, gentlemen said that this path was thus revived.
He refrained from congratulating or mourning, and avoided worldly customs.
He never passed through red gates or splendid mansions.
Qí Jìnglíng Wénxuān Wáng (Emperor Wénxuān of Qí), valuing lightweight chariots and having a mind empty of the eight *jiě* (liberations),
once invited the Dharma Master to lecture at his princely temple.
Though he consented to humble himself and come,
some suggested that he should observe guest-host protocol.
The Dharma Master smiled and replied,
"I have no time for that."
When he took his rightful place on the dais, the warmth and cold of debate began.
At that time, the Dharma assembly was vast, and prominent scholars were like a forest.
The host's reputation had spread, and many guests were formidable.
When he began his topic and presented his discourse, doubts and difficulties emerged like spear points.
The Dharma Master responded to changes like an echo, as if he had not even paused to listen.
Those confined by their arguments collapsed,
and those relying on their strength were disarmed.
All were compelled to shift and waver, losing their foundations and their branches.
The observers called it a grand gathering.
The Dharma Master's nature was originally unyielding, yet he could welcome others with joy.
Questions filled the hall, but he never showed displeasure.
He emptied himself and embraced broad learning, encouraging everyone to exhaust their talents.
Those who relied on him, whether close or distant, were taught as one.
When young, at home, he was a filial son and a loyal friend.
Having cast aside worldly attachments and the four *shè* (means of attracting beings), he forgot both love and aversion.
Letters from relatives were sealed and unopened.
Internal sorrow and grief were suppressed and not expressed.
He often said,
"The secular and the sacred are different. How can one, like Yǒutuó (Upāli), who personally received the teachings, learn his words and ignore his instructions?"
His afflictions were extinguished and immediately dismissed.
As for the Dharma Master's lectures on the Shísònglǜ,
from Wúxīng to Jiànyè, he lectured over forty times.
He compiled eight chapters of interpretive notes,
using concise language to illustrate the precepts.
Scholars transmitted and narrated them,
considering them to be unsurpassed in ancient and modern times.
He was seventy-two years old in spring and autumn.
In the third year of Qí Yǒngyuán,
his spirit departed at Ānlè Monastery in Jiànkāng County.
Monks and nuns flocked to attend, as if they had lost a brother or sister.
Truly, it was faith unspoken, a feeling unsummoned.
As for his reverence and simplicity, joy and anger did not show on his face.
He understood people well and was good at guiding them, selecting and nurturing without omission.
At that time, when faced with wealth, he was honest in taking and righteous in giving.
He was clear-minded and magnanimous, unwavering in the face of change.
Vast and dignified,
the Bó and Jié seas, the Hé River, and Mount Huá could not contain his measure.
Truly, he was a model of pure conduct,
and a standard for a tranquil mind.
His disciples, such as so-and-so, mourn the collapse of the central beam,
and grieve that his virtuous voice is forever silenced.
We wish to make this sincere record as proof,
hoping that his fragrance will endure without shame.
The Dharma Master's monastic name was Sēngjǐng.
His original surname was Ōuyáng.
He was a native of Xiāngxiāng, Héngyáng.
He possessed the good karma from beginningless time,
and attained profound enlightenment in this life.
From a young age, his inner harmony pervaded his being naturally.
He loved reciting sūtras and excelled at maintaining discipline.
His conduct was principled, and his speech and actions were without fault.
He became an orphan at ten.
He served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His mother sought a spouse for him.
However, he had no interest in a good family.
He declined, but could not refuse the command.
As a young man, he was constrained by worldly duties.
At that time, military horses grazed in the fields,
and urgent dispatches arrived daily.
He personally donned armor and helmets, traversing mountains and rivers,
for nearly ten years.
Although he faced difficulties externally,
internally he cultivated compassion.
Therefore, even before leaving the secular world,
he already possessed the practice of calming the mind.
Later, while traveling through Péngzhōu, he saw Lúyuè and was pleased by it.
From then on, he had the aspiration to end his life there.
He returned to Xiāngchuān.
Gradually, he abandoned worldly things that were not to his taste, becoming so absorbed in the Dao that he forgot to eat.
He consumed only vegetables once a day.
Later, he was able to leave his fortified home and separated from his wife.
Suddenly, he dreamt that the deity of Lúshān bowed to him respectfully, saying:
"Lúshān is a lofty peak, rising to the heavens.
It is known as Sāngōng.
With its thousand-zhang sheer cliffs, it wishes to invite a true person to reside there.
If the true person does not comply,
then this mountain will be eternally abandoned."
He also dreamt of being invited to go to Xiānglú Fēng and Shímén Dǐng.
He saw silver pavilions, golden towers, cinnabar springs, and jade-green trees, rugged and sculpted, rare and unique in the world.
Thereupon, at cockcrow signaling dawn,
he set off lightly on his morning journey.
At that time, many monks in Jiānglíng practiced diligently.
Some told the Dharma Master:
"The Dharma activities in Jīngzhōu are flourishing greatly."
He therefore traveled eastward.
From Xiàshǒu, he floated westward.
He met the Daoist Sēngjìng, who profoundly understood Chan meditation.
He then said:
"This is truly my teacher."
So he shaved his head and followed him.
Residing in the Zhúlín Chánfáng, he began to abstain from solid food.
Silently he contemplated the Dao.
Sometimes he would stay awake until dawn.
The imperial inspector heard of his reputation and was pleased, wishing to invite him.
Someone said:
"This gentleman can be visited,
but cannot be forced to come."
Thereupon, he repeatedly visited the thatched hut,
and then sincerely requested to receive the precepts.
People from the Jiāng and Hàn regions also turned towards him like clouds.
Previously, the Shénshān Temple had been remarkably efficacious,
and those who offended it suffered calamities,
numbering more than ten.
The Dharma Master built his dwelling beside it.
The deity then appeared and paid obeisance to him,
making two divine youths serve him morning and evening.
A sorceress saw them and questioned him.
The Dharma Master did not answer.
The Lúshān deity again came to earnestly invite him.
In the seventh month of the tenth year of Yǒngmíng,
he took his staff and ascended the peak.
What he saw during his journey was exactly as in his dream.
He immediately used stone as a foundation,
building against the cliff, sitting upright and contemplating.
Tigers and leopards formed his companions.
Virtuous predecessors such as Tánlóng and Huìyuǎn
also settled here.
However, since human traces were rare,
they could not bear the solitude.
Moreover, the mountain's misty atmosphere
caused headaches and fevers, and before long, all of them descended.
Only the Dharma Master went alone and never returned.
He cut off provisions of grain
and did not avoid the harshness of frost and dew.
At times, grasping vines, he traversed dangerous paths,
moving as if flying.
There were also groups of demons who disliked the Dharma Master's presence,
and could cause thunder and wind to change as a test.
When the Dharma Master showed his confirmed divine power, the hordes of demons ceased.
After a long time, he again explored dangerous and secluded places, building a stone bridge and a stone chamber.
This was a spiritual mountain's secret place where a hundred deities roamed.
When the Dharma Master expounded the precepts and offered incense,
all the deities bowed their heads and prostrated at his feet.
In ancient times, the divine man Wú Měng was able to enter and explore this place.
Since then, only the Dharma Master has again reached it.
From Xīhuáng's time until now, there have been only two such individuals.
Initially, two years after the Dharma Master entered the mountain,
the flavor of Chan began to manifest. Whenever he concentrated his mind and entered tranquility,
he would distinctly see Maitreya Tathāgata.
He often said:
"This is a karmic affinity cultivated in past lives."
In the spring of the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
he suddenly told his disciples:
"My lifespan should be ninety years,
but the remaining years are of no benefit to the world, and my body is a burden to people.
I wish to rescue and assist all sentient beings,
and cannot remain here much longer."
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month,
he marked the western end of the highest ridge as the place for his remains.
No one knew this.
Seven days later, he fell ill.
Seven days after falling ill, he passed away.
He was fifty-eight years old.
At the moment of death, he clasped his palms and said:
"May I be born immediately in the three lower realms to save all beings from suffering."
He also said:
"I offer my body to birds.
Be sure not to bury it."
Originally, the Dharma Master had summoned several people from the lower monastery,
for a summer retreat and to teach.
Someone said to the Dharma Master:
"Now we wish to go down the mountain to seek a doctor."
They also urged him to eat and drink.
The Dharma Master said:
"I am burdened by this body.
When I have no body, what burden will I have?
Do not speak further."
Sixteen days after his passing,
his appearance was as if alive.
Two fingers were curled and clasped.
When stretched, they would return to their original state.
Venerable bhikṣus all said:
"Indeed, many enlightened persons follow the number seven.
Did not the Dharma Master's illness and death follow this pattern?"
The two fingers not stretching
also had good reason.
Initially, Xiānglú Fēng was so isolated and steep that even birds could not reach it.
Since the Dharma Master began his work,
a pair of black birds often came to nest.
When the Dharma Master passed away,
the birds also left forever.
The Dharma Master's deep roots in past lives, his long-standing pure karma,
made compassion, joy, and equanimity a natural part of his character.
Subtle, profound, and mysterious powers arose from his mind.
He entered the mountain forests and did not leave,
transcending worldly honors with detachment.
As for rare delicacies that strengthen bones,
and the arts of alchemy that prolong life,
these were all like discarded sandals to him.
Only with a straightforward mind and firm resolve did he focus on the priceless Dharma vessel,
cherishing the illusory city and aspiring to the other shore.
His profound depth was unfathomable,
hence he could not be fully described.
Bǐqiúní Shì Jìngxiù.
Her original surname was Liáng (梁) clan.
She was a native of Wūshì, Āndìng.
Her ancestors originated from Shàohào, reaching Bó Yì who assisted Yǔ in controlling the floods.
He was granted the surname Yíng (嬴).
During the reign of King Xiào of Zhōu,
his sixteenth-generation descendant Fēizǐ was enfeoffed in Qín.
His great-grandson Qín Zhòng became a marquis and earl for King Xuān.
When King Píng moved eastward, he enfeoffed Qín Zhòng's youngest son in Liáng.
This was Liáng Bó.
During the reign of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
Liáng Lín served as the Grand Administrator of Tàiyuán.
He moved his residence to Běidì.
Thus, Wūshì became a county of the people.
From that time onwards, their prosperity flourished for generations.
Their virtuous reputations intertwined, and their official caps shone brilliantly, one after another.
In the first year of Yuánjiā of Hàn,
Liáng Jǐng served as the Shàngshū Lìng.
He had studied the Hán Shī in his youth and was a renowned scholar of his time.
During the Wèi dynasty, Liáng Shuǎng served as the Zǒuchángshǐ of Sītú and Mìshū Jiān.
He was extensively learned in various books and excelled at discussing profound principles.
In the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
Liáng Chǎn served as the Inspector of Liáng and Yǒng two prefectures.
He was the Bhikkhuni's great-grandfather.
Chǎn's grandson, Huī, served as the Pàoqí Cānjūnshì and Yúyáng Tàishǒu for Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo of Jìn.
He encountered the disruption of Yǒngjiā, falling into the fake Zhào regime.
He served as Mìshū Jiān and Zhēngnán Chángshǐ.
Later, he was able to return to Jìn.
He served as Sànqí Shìláng.
His son, Chóu, styled Dàodù.
His son, Càn, who was Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ, served the Sòng dynasty.
He was Cānjūnshì of the Zhēnglǔ mansion and was enfeoffed as the Dū Tínghóu of Lóngchuān County.
The Bhikkhuni was the fourth daughter of this Dū Tínghóu.
She possessed profound wisdom from past kalpas.
She embodied subtle understanding in her youth.
Her nature was harmonious and graceful,
not like ordinary children.
At a young age, her divine spirit was keen and clear,
surpassing that of ordinary children.
She practiced benevolence, revered the Dao, and cleansed her mind in the Dharma gate.
By the age of ten, her compassion became even stronger.
She renounced cosmetic adornments,
and abandoned embroidered and brocade playthings.
She recited sutras, practiced the Way, and observed a long fast, eating only vegetables.
At the age of twelve, she sought to leave home.
Her family members strongly forbade and suppressed her, none of them permitting it.
Thereupon, she prayed with a sincere heart, concentrating her mind on a single thought.
Consequently, she repeatedly received auspicious signs and frequent omens.
Her fourth uncle, Chāo, was the only one who became aware first.
He persuaded those within and without the family.
Thus, her noble aspiration was fulfilled.
Her innate intelligence was sharp, and from a young age, she stood out from the crowd.
By the age of seven, she naturally observed vegetarianism.
When monks were invited to her home to perform rituals,
she heard them read the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which prohibited eating meat.
From then on, she became a long-term vegetarian and did not consume meat.
When her parents realized this,
if she received fish or meat, she would immediately discard it.
Once, there was a foreign monk, Pǔliàn,
who came from the capital.
He frequently visited the Liáng household.
She immediately took the Five Precepts.
She diligently and reverently upheld them, never violating them.
Day and night, she constantly dedicated herself to prostration, reading, and recitation.
She had no other occupations.
When her hands were capable of writing, she often transcribed sutras herself.
All her possessions were used solely for meritorious deeds.
She did not pursue worldly pleasures.
She desired to enter the Buddhist path at a young age.
However, her parents obstructed her, causing years to pass.
It was not until she was twenty-nine that she achieved her aspiration.
She shaved her head in Qīngyuán and became a disciple of the temple abbot.
She served her master with utmost devotion and filial piety.
She anticipated his intentions and followed his instructions.
She exhausted her body and strength, yet still feared she might fall short.
She personally practiced the three karmas, diligent day and night without slackening.
In all monastic tasks and duties, she always took the lead.
She was diligent and hardworking, attending to every matter.
There was a well-digger, Master Mǎ,
who saw her at Qīngyuán.
He immediately prophesied, saying,
"This nun will be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven."
Also, once while sitting in meditation inside the Buddha hall,
three people gathered together suddenly heard a sound in the air,
like the roar of an ox.
Two nuns were frightened, bewildered, and trembled.
She, however, remained calm and composed.
She slowly rose from her seat,
returned to her room, and holding a candle, checked the source of the sound.
When she reached the Kūlán,
the two nuns heard someone speaking in the hall, saying,
"Make way, Master Mǒu Jiǎ is returning."
Later, she was again sitting in her meditation room.
Several companions were there.
One nun was snoring in her sleep.
This nun, in her dream, saw a person
whose head touched the roof,
saying,
"Do not be alarmed, it is Master Mǒu Jiǎ."
Thereupon, this nun dared not sit again.
Also, at one time, while meditating,
a companion nun had a small errand and wished to get down from her seat for a moment.
She saw a person clapping their hands to stop her, saying,
"Do not disturb Master Mǒu Jiǎ."
Thereupon, holding her breath, she slowly exited, marveling at what had never happened before.
Such incidents of this kind were very numerous.
Since they were not recorded immediately,
many were lost and forgotten.
They cannot be fully described.
She was naturally observant of the precepts and monastic rules.
In every movement and posture, she wished to follow them.
Thus, she invited the Vinaya Master Huī to lecture.
She thought to herself,
"I only have one thousand [coins]."
She worried in her heart that the matter could not be accomplished.
That night, she dreamed of crows, magpies, mynahs, and sparrows, each riding a carriage.
The carriages were all equipped with canopies.
The size of the carriages corresponded to the birds' shapes.
They all sang in unison,
"We are going to assist Master Mǒu Jiǎ with her lecture."
Upon waking, she was overjoyed.
She knew the matter would succeed.
When it came to the lecture,
she obtained seventy patrons to offer provisions.
The fruits and food were all exquisite.
Later, she again invited Vinaya Master Yǐng to explain the monastic rules.
He began the lecture, saying,
"The pure vase water naturally smells fragrant like the fragrance of a water garden."
She was deeply pleased by this.
Afterwards, she attained samadhi during meditation.
She did not rise until midnight.
Having no other companions,
she then thought to herself,
"Am I not committing a transgression?"
She immediately consulted the Vinaya Master.
The Vinaya Master replied,
"You have not committed any transgression."
She still hesitated in her mind, fearing some oversight.
Furthermore, she saw that many nuns in other temples
did not follow the Dharma.
Thereupon, she sighed with lament, saying,
"Alas, the great teachings are not far away,
but their spiritual lineage is gradually declining.
If one does not acknowledge faults and blame oneself,
how can one guide others?"
She immediately confessed her sins and practiced mānatva.
Thereupon, both sections of the Sangha in the capital sighed with admiration, saying,
"Such a person,
whose observance of the Vinaya is clear and whose conduct accords with the Dharma,
still contemplates her shortcomings!
How much more so for us, who commit many transgressions in our every action and do not feel ashamed?"
They then unanimously undertook a universal confession, leaving no one out.
Also, in Nányuán, she received the precepts from Vinaya Master Yǐng.
On the day she received the precepts,
the pure vase water again smelled fragrant as before.
The nuns of Qīngyuán and other temples
all received the precepts anew.
The Vinaya Master then also went to the temples in succession,
expounding the chapters on the precepts and propagating the great teachings.
Thus, the monastic regulations spread far and wide and continue to this day.
Vinaya Master Yǐng also instructed her to address the nuns of all temples,
that those with high beds or secular clothing should change everything.
She complied with the order and enforced it, and everyone obeyed.
The revival of the Vinaya collection began anew from this point.
Later, she again received the precepts from the Tripiṭaka Dharma Master.
The pure water and its fragrance were again as before,
no different from Qīngyuán.
Her disciples were numerous and held different views.
Her master had already passed away, and she no longer had anyone to attend to.
Therefore, she thought of establishing a separate dwelling place,
where she could outwardly adhere to sacred principles and inwardly cultivate deep tranquil meditation.
In the eighth month of the seventh year of Dàmíng of Sòng,
the late Huáng Xiūyí and Princess Nánchāng,
who deeply revered the Three Jewels and admired her virtuous conduct,
first established a pure dwelling.
She wore plain cloth and felt no warmth, and ate coarse food, forgetting hunger.
She personally handled mud and tiles, diligently working day and night.
In the third year of Tàishǐ of Sòng,
Emperor Míng bestowed upon it the name Chánlín.
This was probably because her nature loved tranquility, and there were indeed spiritual omens.
Moreover, in making reliquary niches and creating statues, nothing was left undone.
She also transcribed and collected various sutras, ensuring they were complete.
While painting and dyeing,
the two brothers, the Sāgāra Dragon King, spontaneously appeared.
Their manifestation lasted a full day without fading.
Acquaintances who came and went all personally witnessed them.
She attracted and accommodated over ten people to live together.
She instructed and encouraged them all to practice meditation and recitation.
Whenever holy monks were invited,
there would always be unusual signs on the offerings of fruits and food.
Also, at one time,
she devoutly invited the assembly of holy ones and offered provisions for seven days.
After completing the prostrations and repentance, she concentrated her mind and contemplated.
She then saw two foreign monks raising their hands and conversing.
One said, "Qūluó,"
and the other said, "Bīqūluó."
Their kāṣāya robes were the color of ripe mulberries.
She then took mud to create the color of the robes,
as she had seen.
Thereupon, nuns from near and far all imitated her, changing their clothes to variegated colors.
Thus, she was freed from the transgressions of the five great evils.
The monastic and lay communities have their divisions.
After this, she again invited five hundred Arhats from Ānóudá Chí.
Day after day, a grand assembly of both ordinary and sagely beings was held without restriction.
After nearly two fortnights of abundant offerings,
she again invited five hundred Arhats from the kingdom of Jìbīn.
This brought the total to one thousand.
And she invited ordinary monks following the previous custom.
Just one day later,
she saw a foreign Daoist monk
whom none of the monks recognized.
So, they tried to question him.
He said,
"I came from the kingdom of Jìbīn."
They asked again,
"How long have you been here?"
He replied,
"I have only been here for one year."
The monks felt this was unusual,
so they assigned someone to guard the gate and observe his movements.
After eating, he departed through the Sònglín gate.
The observer followed him
and saw him leave through the Sònglín gate.
After walking a dozen steps, he suddenly vanished.
She also once invited a holy monk.
A bathing vessel was filled with fragrant water and various items.
Then, she prostrated herself.
Inside and out, there was silence.
Suddenly, the sound of a dipper stirring in the vessel was heard,
as if someone was using water.
She thought perhaps someone had come out,
so they went to look together.
They only saw the water dipper moving by itself.
Thus, they knew it was supernatural.
Another time, she suddenly saw the entire house filled with light in the middle of the night.
She thought it was already dawn.
She got up and opened the door, seeing it was still dark outside, so she closed the door and returned to bed.
She slept again for a long time before it finally became light.
She also experienced a severe illness that was extremely critical.
Suddenly, she saw a great light pervading the world, mountains, rivers, and trees, vast and unobstructed.
Joyfully, she laughed to herself.
Those nearby asked in surprise.
She fully recounted what she had seen.
Immediately, she was able to get up, walk, prostrate herself, read, and recite as usual, without any difference.
Another time, she again fell ill,
also in a very critical state.
Suddenly, she raised both hands,
as if holding something.
Those nearby did not understand
and asked,
"What are you holding?"
She replied,
"I see a precious pagoda emerging from the ground.
I want to receive it.
There are banners, flowers, and musical instruments, everything is present."
Upon this, her illness vanished completely,
and she had no further ailments.
She also fell ill again,
and for several days, it was quite
critical, constantly fluctuating.
She faced east, clasped her hands towards the sky.
At one point, she urgently asked for incense and fire.
After a while, she clasped her hands
and then said,
"I see Maitreya Buddha, and Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and other sages.
I also see countless disciples filling the void."
A moment later, she saw Maitreya descending to be reborn in Kìtóumò Chéng.
She said, "There are people carrying banners, flowers, musical instruments, and three platforms to welcome me.
The banners, flowers, and musical instruments on these
are unlike anything in the human world.
One platform stopped halfway in the sky.
One platform was already halfway there.
One platform was not yet seen,
but only heard to exist.
At that time, two platforms had already been made.
Because of this omen, another platform was made."
She also said,
"There are two trees with precious flowers nearby.
When people came near the bed,
she said, 'Do not damage my flowers.'"
After this, her illness subsided.
Before and after, whenever she encountered illness, there were always auspicious signs.
Either a cool breeze came,
or a wondrous medicine was obtained,
or a strange fragrance was smelled,
and the illness would immediately heal.
The way her illnesses were cured
was always like this, gradually and completely disappearing.
The number of such instances is too great to record fully.
Also, in the third year of Tiānjiàn (504 CE),
she was ill for an entire summer.
One day, while sleeping, she saw Kōngkōngzàng Púsà.
She immediately circled and chanted praises.
The sound of the chanting echoed outside, and she awoke from her sleep.
Her ailment was immediately cured.
Another time, lying down in broad daylight,
she opened her eyes and saw a Buddha enter the room, with banners and canopies filling the house.
She told those nearby to burn incense, but then she herself no longer saw it.
Above, on the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the fifth year of Tiānjiàn (506 CE), she suffered from illness.
Her heart was distressed, and she could not drink.
The monk in charge of Péngchéng Sì
had a dream on the night of the nineteenth day of the sixth month.
He saw a place,
which he believed to be Tuṣita Heaven.
The dwellings were magnificent, unlike anything in the human world.
He said, "This is the dwelling place of (the deceased)."
He then saw (the deceased) there.
So, the monk spoke to (the deceased).
"Since you have been reborn in a good place, you should welcome and guide me.
I am your minor patron,
do not abandon me."
(The deceased) immediately replied,
"Master, you are a man and widely propagate the sutras and teachings.
You should naturally reside in a superior place.
I am a woman, how can I be of benefit?"
The monk again said,
"It is not like that.
Although I am a man, I cannot be diligent.
My adherence to precepts is inferior to yours."
At that time, her condition had already worsened.
She was too weak and did not wish to see the monk in charge, as they were not close.
As her illness progressed, she drank less and less congee.
Treatment was useless, and she gradually became critical.
By the twelfth day of the seventh month,
at that time, the sky rained cool.
Her chest oppression seemed to slightly recede.
She said,
"I dreamt that I was welcomed to the west end of the Buddha hall.
Everyone held banner poles, like chariots on the ground.
The banners were no different from the military drums and flags in the human world."
On the twentieth day, she stopped
taking congee or drinks.
On the twenty-second day, she asked to invite familiar monks for an assembly.
Her intention seemed to be a farewell.
On the twenty-fifth day, she said,
"I see Buddhas of the ten directions filling the sky."
On the twenty-seventh day, after noon, she fell into a deep sleep.
After the time it takes to cook two meals, she moved again and said,
"I ascended to Tuṣita Heaven and saw Maitreya and all the Bodhisattvas, all golden in color.
I myself held a pure, clear crystal vase
about three feet high.
I offered it to Maitreya.
He then emitted light that shone upon my body.
When I arrived in Tuṣita Heaven,
I did not see food, yet I was naturally full.
Therefore, I no longer needed human food.
I only heard that human food all smelled foul,
which is why I refused to eat it.
From that heaven, I obtained a Pólìhuā (Pārichattraka flower) and intended to bring it back
to give to the monk in charge.
Someone asked, 'Why do you want to take the flower away?'
I replied,
'I want to give it to the monk in charge.'
That person said,
'The monk in charge has human karmic retribution.
How can he eat heavenly food?
You are not allowed to take it.'
Then, wishing to see the monk in charge in his solitary abode,
I went to welcome him to meet me and told him,
'You should prepare good vegetarian food to offer to the Daoist monks meditating in the mountains.
Only by cultivating the three karmas
can one be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.'
The monk did not meditate,
which is why I told him to prepare food to offer to the mountain
Daoist monks, hoping to create a karmic connection with the meditators."
From the eighth month, her physical condition also worsened.
She no longer spoke of other matters,
only saying,
"There are thirty-two youths,
one named Gōngdé Tiān,
the second named Shànnǚ Tiān.
They are led by Jiāpíluó.
They constantly stay by my side
and serve me."
Or she would say,
"Someone has sent food and drink.
Let it be distributed among the assembly."
She also said,
"In the sky, music is played day and night, disturbing my ears."
From the imperial gate:
The Buddhist Dharma has become corrupted, and the śramaṇas are mixed.
They are insufficient to uphold the great teaching,
but instead become a den for fugitives.
Furthermore, various evil intentions frequently arise, and wicked deeds are repeatedly heard of.
They ruin the Way and disturb the populace, causing resentment between humans and gods.
Let warrants be issued to the temples' elders and chiefs to thoroughly purge them.
Those who violate this hereafter shall be severely punished.
The responsible parties should draft detailed regulations
and implement them quickly.
To the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
Recently received the memorial from you and others.
I understand that you wish to swiftly appoint a Grand Director of Monks (Shāmén Dūzǒng).
I have diligently searched and selected the virtuous and sagacious, reflecting upon it day and night.
As for the one to succeed the Buddha's charge, I know not to whom to entrust it.
Some possess lofty virtue and venerable age,
their principles unencumbered.
Others have profound capacity and farsighted insight,
holding aloof from worldly affairs.
Now, I consider Sa-mén Sēngxiǎn (僧顯), the eminent master and abbot of Sīyuǎn Temple.
His benevolence and elegance are admirable, his character as clear as the wind and bright as a mirror.
He is deeply perceptive, subtly enlightened, and possesses a clear and bright Dao heart.
He is indeed fit for this responsibility,
to harmonize the wondrous assembly.
I have already verbally instructed this recently.
He may be appointed Grand Director of Monks (Shāmén Dūzǒng).
Furthermore, the position of Vice-Regent (Fùyí Èrshì) is one that both monastics and laypeople commonly share.
Previously, due to Huī Tǒng (輝統) single-handedly managing affairs, this position was abolished.
Now, to assist the virtuous and commend the good, such a person is indeed needed.
Sa-mén Sēngyì (僧義), the eminent master of Huángjiù Temple,
is respectful in conduct, serene in spirit, warm, intelligent, cautious, and upright.
His spiritual work is distinguished, and his Dao virtue is excellent, making him suitable for this supportive role.
He may be appointed Grand Superintendent (Dū Wéinà) to glorify the wise disciples.
To the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
Profound awareness and clear detachment transcend worldly concerns.
Profound models and lofty profundities are entrusted to the realm beyond words.
However, without words, how can the teachings (jiào) be expounded?
Without the world (shì), how can the truth (zhēn) be manifested?
Therefore, the three baskets (sānzàng) spreading their influence must rely on the disciplinary canons (jièdiǎn).
The six perfections (liùdù) manifesting transformation are certainly based on subtle ripples.
Since the eastward transmission of the elephant teachings (xiàngjiào) more than a thousand years have passed.
During the Qín and Hàn dynasties, worldly splendor and prohibitions grew increasingly strict.
Thus, wise individuals of previous generations established precedents as appropriate,
emphasizing or de-emphasizing aspects according to the times, to benefit the profound mysteries.
In the time of the previous dynasty, a monastic code (sēngjìn) was established.
Minor details that were unclear should be rectified and established.
Recently, I saw the Director of Monks (Shāmén Tǒng) Sēngxiǎn (僧顯) and others memorialize, saying:
"We wish to revise and settle the regulations."
I shall, with my limited understanding, jointly examine the supreme canons with them.
Since matters arose hastily, they have not yet been thoroughly investigated.
For now, a temporary law may be instituted to roughly address worldly concerns.
The Imperial Antechamber (Diàn) must present a memorial together to further refine its core.
To the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
To promote and assist spiritual endeavors, there is nothing like honoring the profound.
To cultivate divine wisdom and imbue one's aspirations, who surpasses the heroic sages?
Thus, Zhōu Dàn (周旦) composed his "Proclamation of Fellowmen" (Péng zhī Gào).
Shìjiā (釋迦) proclaimed the text of the "Good and Knowing."
Therefore, those in high positions value accepting the worthy,
and those with superior virtue esteem befriending the benevolent.
Though I am ignorant and dull, how can I not earnestly hope for this?
In the time of the previous dynasty,
in managing the realm,
there was no time for internal models.
Consequently, the imperial court lacked lofty and profound figures,
and the inner chambers (zǐtà) were short of transcendent customs.
Regarding the principle of admiring goodness and the resources for the field of blessings,
it was truly insufficient.
I intend to have eminent masters of excellent virtue visit me from time to time,
so that they may receive instruction in the Dao (dào) in audience and adorn the imperial court upon their return.
It is hereby decreed that those in the Imperial Antechamber (Diànzhōng) are permitted three entrances per month.
The number of individuals and their Dharma names will be separately submitted in a dispatch.
To the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
To rely on the profound and return to the wondrous truly requires the true Dharma wind.
To partake of wisdom and practice compassion truly culminates in the fruit of enlightenment.
Thus, the three summer retreats (sānyán) regulate the constant norms of the Dao.
The nine summer schools (jiǔxià) warmly expound the excellent principles of the Dharma.
It is decreed that all prefectures (zhōuzhōu) shall establish a pure assembly for this summer retreat.
Large prefectures (dàzhōu) shall have three hundred people,
middle prefectures (zhōngzhōu) two hundred people,
and small prefectures (xiǎozhōu) one hundred people.
They shall be permitted to hold lectures and discussions in various places.
All provisions shall be supplied by the monastic granary (sēngqí sù).
If the grain is scarce or the disciples are few, and unable to meet these numbers,
the Bureau of Monastic Affairs (Zhāoxuán) may quantify the reduction and report it back.
Each shall respect and commend the worthy masters,
and truly promote those with insightful virtue.
Do not allow for corruption and indolence, hindering future generations.
To the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
Sa-mén Chěng (逞), the Director of Daoists (Dàoréntǒng) of Xúzhōu,
possessed broad understanding and refined character.
His spiritual work was clear and extensive, his grasp of principle profound and pure.
His pure reputation and distinguished renown
early manifested in Xú and Pèi.
His heroic spirit and profound attainment
flowed throughout Qiáo and Sòng.
He recently lectured on the Dharma in Běijīng, benefiting both monastics and laypeople.
He received offerings at the imperial banquet, beautifully spreading his teachings in the capital.
Such benevolence and wisdom are what I greatly admire.
As the cause and condition have ended, he has passed into another world.
Upon recently learning of his demise, my heart is filled with sorrow.
Now, the road through Yǎn, Pú, Qīng, and Sì is not far.
My grief for his virtue further increases.
It is hereby decreed to issue three hundred bolts of silk to Xúzhōu for memorializing his merit.
Additionally, a vegetarian feast for five thousand people shall be arranged.
To the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
To respond to the tradition and aspire to the former sages,
and to follow the path of the Dao (dào) tradition,
entrusts the comprehensive overview of profound principles and transcendent strategies.
Now that he has relinquished his worldly name,
it is appropriate to provide him with special offerings.
Based on the meaning of the "eight liberations" (bājiě),
eight hundred bolts of silk shall be bestowed annually,
in accordance with the four classes of disciples,
and disbursed according to the four seasons.
Furthermore, the foundation of cultivating good deeds truly relies on sustenance.
The cause of providing food is praised in the inner canons.
It shall be provided according to the monthly stipend of high-ranking court officials.
The reason for drawing distant analogies to profound principles
is not solely to encourage the worldly mind,
but also to inspire the aspiration for the Dao (dào).
To the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
Hùijì (慧紀), the eminent master of Xúzhōu,
possessed profound wisdom and steadfast detachment, with pure and empty Dao (dào) insight.
His heroic and unadorned conduct transcended the mundane world.
His comprehensive and extensive accomplishments were rarely matched.
He illuminated the Dharma in Pēngfāng, and his reputation flourished in Huáyì.
His discussions in the Sòng region caused his virtue to be revered far and wide.
Thereupon, in times past, he proclaimed the truth at Lùyuàn,
serving as a master for the capital's monastics, garnering admiration from the assembly of worthies.
Suddenly, the demon of death abruptly destroyed this virtuous vessel.
Upon hearing this, I am filled with sorrow and profound grief.
It is hereby decreed that Xúzhōu shall bestow three hundred bolts of silk,
and arrange a five-hundred-person vegetarian feast,
to promote further blessings.
The reason people fail to attain the Dao (dào)
is due to their minds and spirits being clouded and deluded.
The reason minds and spirits are clouded and deluded
is due to external things disturbing them.
The major disturbances are three:
first, power, profit, glory, and fame;
second, enchanting beauty and charming grace;
third, rich flavors and fatty delicacies.
Although glory and fame are used daily in the mind,
they ultimately do not cause constant hindrance.
Enchanting beauty and charming grace are already deeply entangling.
Rich flavors and fatty delicacies cause the most severe hindrance.
All myriad affairs,
are merely branches and leaves of these three.
The sages know that if these three things are not severed, there is no way to attain the Dao (dào).
Therefore, they had to establish laws to make it simple and easy to follow.
If one were to directly state that these three things are the root of delusion,
and all should be strictly prohibited,
yet these three things are what human nature is most deluded by,
and difficult for thoughts to dispel.
Even if there is a prohibition,
it is difficult to immediately follow.
It is like crossing a river in a boat:
would one not wish to go straight to the other bank?
But since the river current is swift,
there is no way to cross directly.
One must go with the current, turning obliquely for a long time to reach it.
It is not that one does not wish for speed, but that the matter is difficult.
The prohibition of these three things should have a starting point.
Why? Because food, for humans, cannot be completely ceased suddenly.
Among the emotional nature, nothing is more burdensome than these three.
Therefore, pushing back late-night eating to before noon.
After noon, one is pure and free of affairs.
Because of this freedom from affairs, thoughts can be simplified.
Initially, it may not be focused,
but over time, it becomes habitual.
Thereupon, one is bound by the eight branches [of the path],
and restrained by prohibitions and precepts.
The desire for charming beauty has no way to advance.
The various hindrances of glory and fame are gradually dispelled as appropriate.
Thus, it is said that ancient Buddhas did not eat after noon.
This is truly a trap and snare for dispelling hindrances,
a shortcut to reaching the Dao (dào).
Yet some universally believe it is merely about not eating.
This is to be confused about the direction,
not knowing the path.
The performance of Buddhist rituals must have its principles.
Currently, when people summon and invite many monks, they only hold one assembly.
This is probably because when the Buddha was alive, he often accepted people's invitations.
This is why it is imitated.
However, when the Buddha was alive in the past,
the Buddha and the assembly of monks,
within the Saṅghārāma, did not originally prepare their own food.
At the appointed time, they would go out with their alms bowls to bring blessings to sentient beings.
Today, among the assembly of monks, not only are few able to observe the midday meal,
but there are some who are plump and indulge in rich, delicious food, with abundant and luxurious kitchens.
Now, when they are additionally summoned and invited,
they come later, only out of necessity.
With mouths accustomed to rich food,
they are offered only vegetarian provisions.
Stretching their necks and furrowing their brows, they are certainly unable to relish it.
Since it is not received with joy, it cannot generate blessings.
This is unlike the past, when they could not provide for themselves.
These are not those who rely on the four assemblies of disciples with no place for body or mouth.
Is seeking blessings in this way not rather the opposite?
Strictly speaking, its meaning is not so.
Why? Those who have renounced home originally relied on alms begging.
The precepts and monastic rules are clear on this.
No one is permitted to set up their own kitchen or keep lay servants.
Now that they acquire enough within the monastery, the practice of alms begging has ceased.
Some, if they carry their bowls to a door,
are then called "monk-disciples who engage in vile and lowly deeds."
Since this is scorned and shamed by all,
no one resumes alms begging.
Among later generations, those who seek the truth are few.
Thus, they say that the practice of begging for food cannot be resumed.
How could the esteemed son of King Śuddhodana, a Cakravartin,
carrying his alms bowl and going forth to bestow blessings upon donors,
be inferior to the common Śramaṇa of a thousand years later, who personally instructs servants to manage his own sustenance?
Today's invitation of monks to an assembly,
since it can somewhat resemble the practice,
If it is argued that alms begging is no longer practiced,
and also that invitations are no longer extended,
then the practice of alms begging will be abandoned forever.
If this practice is abandoned, then monks are not of the Buddha's lineage.
If the Buddha's lineage is cut off, then the Three Jewels will fall to the ground.
Those who hold assemblies today
should reflect on the past,
when for forty-nine years the Buddha led Bhikkhus into the city to beg for food.
Their deportment and conduct were always in harmony with their minds.
If one seeks the Way in this manner, where will the Way lead?
If one cultivates the mind in this way,
then holding assemblies is acceptable.
Your Majesty asks: "I have heard that some devote themselves to the nine elixirs,
soaring like cranes to the realm of Xúan Zhōu.
Others, after six years of arduous effort, shed the burden of煩惱 (fánnǎo).
Some focus their minds on the arts of spirits and ghosts,
clarifying methods of尸解 (shījiě).
Others expound the essentials of dependent origination,
perceiving the path of Nirvāṇa.
Thus, Tài Yī expounded his dharma, culminating in light ascension.
The Tathāgata demonstrated the principle, revolving around寂滅 (jìmìe).
Since Zǔ Lóng ceased his tracks and Liú Zhuāng was moved by a dream,
from then on, people converted and it spread widely.
There are even those who abandon relatives, forsake burdens, leave their country, and forget their homes.
Monasteries fill the mountains and forests.
Saṅghārāmas are found throughout the prefectures and commanderies.
If gold could be transmuted,
Huái Nán would not have met his execution.
If divine power were self-existent,
how could Yāng Jué have become a giant whale? If riding dragons is not real,
then Jīng Shān would have no longing for clinging to the beard.
If controlling elephants is illusory,
then Chán Luò would not have awakened to the strangeness of luminous pearls at night.
I am truly perplexed by the agreement of these rights and wrongs.
Furthermore, there are crowds of black-robed individuals,
half of the common populace.
The number of yellow-robed adherents
exceeds the registered households.
Thus, national provisions are insufficient for this.
Royal expenses are thereby diminished.
I wish to select the correct path and eliminate the heterodox arts.
Firstly, it would benefit the nation and household.
Secondly, it would not confuse the populace.
Moreover, this widespread competition has been going on for a long time.
To suddenly eliminate it mid-course would be truly difficult.
As for the rise and fall of the two traditions, the length and shortness of the two paths,
one can point out their superiorities and inferiorities
without hesitating in one's words."
The minister replies:
“Your servant has heard that the Way of Heaven and destiny are not spoken of by the Sages.
This is because the principle transcends verbal expression, making it difficult to describe.

each follow what is natural to them,
and delight in what they delight in.
How can a person in rough clothes and with sores be entangled in their midst?
I was born in the wilderness,
and am naturally fearful and hard to approach.
My heart trembles at the sight of Yúntái and Zhūwū,
and my hopes are cut off from high canopies and green sashes.
Instead, drenched in mist and dew, I yearn for leisure and ease.
I always think of washing in clear streams and resting on peppercorn hills.
This longing, waking and sleeping, has been with me for a long time.
Just as worms eagerly devour soil, and people desire heaven's will,
it was not until my hair turned gray that I found a dwelling in a mountain cave.
My residence is on Jīnhuá Shān in Dōngyáng Jùn.
Dōngyáng is indeed the western part of Kuàijī.
Here grow slender bamboos;
the mountains and rivers are beautiful, and the marshes are lush and dense.
If its peaks rise one upon another, they touch the heavens and connect with the clouds.
If dense forests are spread out, they are green in spring and evergreen in winter.
If winding streams flow deep, they are ten *ren* to the bottom.
A cloud assembling over an inch will surely scatter rain for a thousand *lǐ*.
Truly, it is a magnificent, airy, and bright place,
a sacred and secluded dwelling.
Thus, Dìhóng traveled here to cast his tripod,
and the Rain Master stayed here, riding the smoke.
Therefore, the ravines bear the name of Chìsōng,
and the mountains are endowed with the title of Jìnyún.
In recent times, Jiāng Zhìzhōng, who struggled through the mire, and Wáng Zhēngshì,
who soared above the dust,
like a coiled dragon and perched phoenix,
all gathered in this place.
This is truly because the clear streams and white rocks attract recluses.
Jīnhuá Shān was anciently called Mǎ'ān Shān.
It harbors spirits and conceals sages, listed in immortal records.
Zuǒ Yuánfàng said of this mountain:
"It can escape floods and the five weapons;
it can conjoin divine elixirs and nine transmutations."
At the head of Jīnhuá is Zǐyán Shān.
Its color is purplish-red, hence its name.
It meanders down slopes and declines towards deep pools.
Its peaks soar high, obscuring the sun and moon.
Ascending from the foot of the mountain, it becomes gradually higher and steeper.
The path is winding and perilous; one ascends in single file.
By the side of the path is a deep ravine, roaring and echoing.
Looking down, one sees the treetops;
the scorched plains and rocky settlements are not only dangerously suspended.
When halfway up the mountain, there is a broad marsh and a great river.
Marshes and dry lands rise and fall.
My dwelling is truly located here.
My residence is surrounded on three sides by mountains.
Around it is an elephant-like outer wall.
In front of the city wall is a desolate plain.
My gaze extends to the east.
To the west, it is flanked by two ravines where springs flow all four seasons.
Clear ripples gently sprinkle, each drop making a sound.
White waves leap and foam, surging into a melody.
Canals draw water, and intersecting ditches are intricately arranged.
Cascading streams pour from the eaves of the house,
and rushing torrents circulate around the steps, supplying water without the need for ropes and buckets.
Washing is done without pitchers and basins.
Trees of maple, *qí*, *yǐ*, and *lì*,
and woods of *zǐ*, cypress, cassia, and camphor,
display different forms and colors, thousands of species and ten thousands of kinds.
They bear red fruits and enclose green berries.
They grow white stems and draw out purple stalks.
They are dense and bushy, their branches entwining.
The wind pipes a song, and hanging branches spread leaves over eaves and windows.
My chambers are by the valley and ravine.
Flower stamens cluster until spring fades away.
When duckweed grows and springs flow, there is *dūliáng* exuding fragrance,
and *zhìxiāng* sending forth perfume.
*Chánglè* bears frost,
and *yínán* receives dew.
Lotus flowers, red and splendid, reflect in the water.
Acorus, with azure leaves, sways with the wind.
Leaning on the balcony and gazing endlessly, one dispels worries and forgets illnesses.
In the hills and valleys, various medicinal herbs grow in thickets.
Earth's marrow raises its stems, and mountain sinews draw out their joints.
Golden salt is heavier than white jade,
and five pulses are more precious than bright pearls.
They can nourish one's nature, dispel ailments, restore youth, and maintain complexion.
No need for Cuī Wén's yellow powder,
nor for Fù Jú's purple pills.
Fluttering birds, born of wind and rain,
with green wings, red feathers, plain plumage, and emerald crests,
rustle their wings and sing melodious sounds.
They are tame and accustomed to the garden pond, feeding with chickens and ducks.
As for the *chāo*, it heralds the day, its sound like bells and drums.
The calling *zhīxiàn* announces the dawn, its sound like lutes and zithers.
Black gibbons sing clearly through the thin mist,
and flying *tiáo* chant eternally, riding the smoke.
Their clamorous, resonant sounds please the heart and delight the ears.
Truly, these surpass pipes and flutes, outshine *shēng* and *huáng*.
To the east of my dwelling rises the Zhāotí Sì.
It backs against the cliff and faces the ravine; its layered eaves capture the light.
Its profound chambers overlook the void, vast and tranquil.
It receives auspiciousness and generates purity, looking left and right.
It is a dwelling for the benevolent and wise.
Thus, eminent virtues and famous monks gather here like clouds, shaking their staffs.
They cultivate the mind with the seven *jué* and condemn the five *chén*.
The fragrant smoke of precepts is dense, bathing in the water of meditation.
When incense burners burn at night and the dharma drum is heard at dawn,
I slip on my sandals and gather my robes,
personally performing prostrations.
I inquire about the Way from sagacious people and drink in the harmony of supreme teachings.
Each time I hear that "this shore is turbulent, that shore is eternally peaceful,"
I feel delighted, as if ascending a spring terrace and transcending the universe.
Only goodness is joy.
How can these be mere words?
To the southeast of the temple is a Daoist temple pavilion.
From the cliffside of the pavilion, one looks down at clouds and rain.
Orchid towers and fragrant pavilions are dimly hidden among the bamboo groves.
Flying pavilions are numerous and intricate amidst the misty clouds.
There are ascetics who stop eating for a day,
and guests who seek immortals year after year.
They eat star marrow and inhale flowing *xiá*,
then will ride dragons and cranes in cloud clothes and rainbow garments.
Below the temple is a stone well.
It stands erect in the middle of the ravine.
Its carvings and cuttings closely resemble human artistry.
Leaping streams converge and cascade, surging and roaring.
Like lightning strikes and thunderous roars, it startles the eyes and shocks the soul.
In front of both the temple and the Daoist temple, tall bamboos are planted.
Dense and rustling, they cover the hills and climb the mounds.
Beyond the bamboos are fertile fields.
Their boundaries connect, and mountain spring water enriches them.
Lush, moist, and fertile,
they cannot be compared to Zhèng Bái's canals in Zhāng.
They yield abundant red millet, and ducks and geese are well-fed.
Spring turtles are as delicious as fine amber, and green chickens;
winter mushrooms are as prized as frosty quails.
Muslin is taken from the hills,
and coarse clothes come from the inner garden.
Wild rice and rushes press close by the ponds,
and *jiānguǎi* grasses fill the plains and lowlands.
Resources for sustenance and daily use are all abundant, filling cliffs and peaks.
At the beginning and end of the year, during agricultural breaks,
when turbid wine is newly brewed and clear wine is newly
ripe, village elders
come with their wine pots.
They spread mats beneath the trees, arrange wine vessels, and set out cups.
When the wine flows and ears are warm, they dance repeatedly with joyous shouts.
They loudly discuss granaries and eloquently talk about crops.
They laugh, sing, and raise cups to toast each other.
Life is for enjoyment!
How can this joy be criticized?
If one can wear what one spins and eat what one cultivates,
working at sunrise and resting at sunset,
and considers eating late as having meat and idleness as precious,
seeking nothing from the world and offending nothing,
unable to distinguish honor from disgrace, unaware of praise or slander,
then one can wander freely between heaven and earth,
with a heart free from alarm and apprehension.
How can such a person be compared in superiority or inferiority to Jī Shēng, who bit a sword, or Yáng Zǐ, who fell from a阁?
Shì Zhēn-Guān of Quán-Tíng Guāng-Xiǎn-Sì.
Sent a letter to the Commander-in-Chief, Dàn-Yuè.
I humbly hear that
the Siyi Bodhisattvas
rectify the Dharma when it is on the verge of decline,
and the high personages of the Ten Bhūmis
uphold the profound scriptures when they are on the verge of extinction.
They are able to ensure that the traces of Mt. Gū-Shān do not lack the custom of quiet meditation,
and that the remaining sprouts of the Jī-Shù may fully practice the way of circumambulation.
I humbly observe that His Imperial Majesty has now issued a strict decree, stating that all monks and nuns
whose names are not registered
shall be made to abandon their Dharma vows and become common people,
leaving their monasteries to return to their native villages.
Since there is no one under heaven who is not a subject of the king,
it is right to respectfully comply with the utmost diligence and reverence.
However, my foolish heart secretly has some doubts.
Since the inception of the Buddhist Dharma over a thousand years ago,
it has been circulating in this land for several hundred years.
How prosperous are the numerous monks!
Though courts and cities frequently change and customs often shift,
the lamp of wisdom ever shines bright, and the fragrance of precepts is always potent.
The blessings thus created are beyond words.
The spiritual omens manifested are heard in historical records.
For instance, the monk Fú-Tú shone brightly in Yè,
and the Dharma Master Gāo-Zuò left a fragrant legacy in Gǒng-Luò.
Some in the Kūn-Míng pond recognized the remaining ash from the Kalpa fire,
and in Cháng-Shā Monastery, they felt the residual shade of a broken body. Dào-Kāi entered the land, and the immortal's star appeared.
Fǎ-Chéng passed away, and the auspicious sign of a dark-blue horse arose.
There were those with blue eyes and red beards, yellow pupils and white feet,
with connected eyebrows heralded by fame, and large ears known by name.
All without exception, their minds were as clear as still water, and their peaks of wisdom stood like mountains.
Their profound moral prestige
resembled the noble conduct of Jiā-Yè,
and their solemn demeanor
was similar to the pure practice of È-Pí.
In recent years, deceit has grown, and integrity has daily waned.
Yet the great foundation of the true Dharma should not yet be extinguished.
Suddenly, their original aspirations are violated, and their former resolve is taken away.
None fail to look up at the high halls with sorrow or bid farewell to their old rooms with sadness.
When will they hope to return to their cherished Dharma seats?
There is no day for them to return to their beloved Chan gates.
It is not a divergent path,
yet there is the sorrow of parting ways.
Though it is not the Hé-Liáng,
the pain of a verbal farewell is concluded.
If failing to register one's name is considered a grave offense,
then protracting this blame and suffering is also worthy of pity.
A person who has left worldly life must cultivate the Way.
They are permitted the rites of those beyond the world,
not constrained by the regulations within the realm.
Some who have not registered their names or are unrelated to official records
all wander afar, gathering knowledge,
finding peace and benefit wherever they go, residing in temples and asking for food in their midst.
Some are under the trees of an ascetic,
or in the caves of a monastery.
How can such people be expected to register?
If one's meritorious deeds are incomplete and many precepts are violated,
then one should indeed retire from the Way; this is certainly true.
But holding to and violating precepts are hard to discern, and saints and ordinary people are mixed.
It is like the fruit of the āmrā tree, ripe and unripe are hard to distinguish,
and the medicine of Snow Mountain, true and false are hard to tell apart.
Suddenly, on the peak of Kūn, jade and stone are burned together,
and in the great marsh, dragons and snakes perish alike.
What a pity!
Alas, how lamentable!
Moreover, they cut off love for their parents, put on black robes, and cut their hair.
They have no servants and are forever estranged from wives and children.
Some are in their old age or suffering from illness,
single and poor.
All rely on their disciples to care for them.
If they are scattered overnight [like rain],
they will suddenly die in ditches.
Thus, some throw themselves into the abyss [Jùn],
and some hang themselves with long ropes and perish.
Though the pain of Mì-Luó is great, this is still lighter in comparison.
The sorrow of the barren valley is not as heavy as this.
Furthermore, extraordinary talents and profound scholars are all entrusted to the younger generation.
Listening to lectures and chanting scriptures all depend on the late bloomers.
Therefore, Sū-Tuó attained precepts while still a young child, and Shēn-Zǐ gained fame not as an elder.
If such individuals are all made to abandon their robes,
I fear that this Dharma gate will have no successor.
The Dharma wheel will cease,
and the monasteries will be empty.
If the eight battle formations are not rested and the four borders are filled with ramparts,
the vanguard is relied upon, and the rear is entrusted.
I, your humble servant, believe that these people will almost certainly become useless.
If they truly possess the ability to pull up stakes and throw stones,
or the strength to pull iron and bend hooks,
then they should all join the army and have long been involved in the vanguard.
If, however, they still wear their black robes and remain in the temples,
it means they are accustomed to valor and light-hearted, yet deeply devoted to the Way.
If they are not as frail and refined as Wèi-Jiè,
they are then as frivolous and cowardly as Mèng-Chǎng.
Since they are not skilled in archery and horsemanship, fighting in formation is futile.
Even if they wear armor, they will still think of their monastic robes.
Holding shields and spears, they will still doubt their staff.
They will surely turn pale and be startled at the distant sound of war drums.
Their souls will flee and spirits be intimidated at the sight of distant military banners.
I fear this will only hinder the prestige of the Commander,
and be of no benefit to the bravery of the two generals.
If it is said that they do not pay royal taxes or contribute to the national treasury,
and therefore they are all made to pay their levies,
but these floating individuals are like duckweed scattered and tumbleweeds flying.
These unconstrained people are generally poor and will remain so.
In their villages, they have no land or houses,
and in the capital, they lack patrons.
When they put on shoes, both heels are exposed;
when they gather their robes, both elbows show.
Compared to Dǒng-Shēng's hundred patches, they still seem lightly adorned.
Seeing Yán-Zǐ's single bamboo basket, one might even suspect them of being well-fed.
Seeking rotten soil as medicine,
how could they recognize purple pills? Wearing clothes made of discarded rags,
how could they encounter yellow silk? As for the rites of wealth and goods,
they have no means to embrace the jade disc.
Truly, they should be exempted.
If they remain in the Way,
they can still sustain themselves by alms.
But if they are returned to civilian life, they will have nowhere to send their provisions.
I humbly reflect that the Imperial Dynasty's reign is just, sacred, revered, and enlightened.
Following in the footsteps of Xuān-Xī and standing shoulder to shoulder with Yán-Hào.
The custom of holding a mirror (for self-reflection) is far-reaching,
and the transformation through 'letting robes hang' is profound.
Moreover, it supports the Three Jewels as pillars and propagates the Ten Virtues.
In the past, Hàn-Míng was spiritually moved, dreaming of a golden man.
Jìn-Wǔ was only able to gather a jade statue for his restoration.
Comparing the present with the past, they are put to shame.
Perhaps the emperor is a deep protector of scriptures, like the immortal Yù-Dà-Wáng.
The precious pagodas thus completed resemble the king Wú-Yōu.
Bringing the obscure to light,
like Cháo-Fù's purity and tranquility.
Recruiting fishermen and hunters,
like Xu-Yán-Shēng's nobility.
I, your humble servant, believe that those monks and nuns who are now to be defrocked,
if they have already abandoned monastic robes and do not follow the path of cultivation,
or if they always reside in shops and markets, or constantly in fields and gardens,
should all be subject to civilian laws and employed as directed.
However, if they are devoted to Chan meditation and understanding, living purely on vegetables and in tranquility,
or if they have merits in chanting and their Buddhist voices are noteworthy,
or if they repair stupas and temples, or build Buddhist scriptures,
with salvation at heart and study as their duty,
and even those who are emaciated and old,
or poor and sick,
who are fortunately of no use to the registered households,
they should all be allowed to remain in the temples and be recorded in the monastic registry.
We certainly hope that the precious treasure of the ten cities may emerge from Jīng-Shān,
and within a hundred steps, fragrant herbs may be found.
Thus, the temples will be rid of worldly monks,
and the assembly will have no guests who drink wine.
Praying diligently six times a day,
always with the nation's welfare at heart,
cultivating the three karmas diligently,
must be centered on the sovereign.
Will not the seen and unseen rejoice, and humans and spirits be happy?
Mystical powers will protect, and good karma will assist.
Then the two cosmic forces will harmonize, and the six qi will be regulated.
Warhorses will rest their saddles, and military banners will be furled.
The remote borders will surrender,
without needing the army from Dān-Shuǐ.
Jade and silk will come to court, recalling the assembly at Jī-Shān.
How joyful this will be!
Truly, how delightful!
If, perchance, the borders face unforeseen circumstances or military provisions are lacking,
a small expenditure can be planned; I humbly await your levy.
I respectfully reflect that you, Commander-in-Chief Dàn-Yuè,
externally delve into classics and records,
and internally fathom profound scriptures and treatises.
Your talent is high in the strategist's tent, and your responsibility is as weighty as salt and plums.
I earnestly hope you will condescend to consider this humble opinion and focus your attention on the true Dharma.
Please examine this small suggestion and graciously review it.
If there is even a single point worth adopting, I deeply hope
you will kindly and thoroughly consider it,
and not allow orchids and wormwood to be hoed together, or fragrant and foul odors to mix.
May the immortal's realm once again turn the wheel of Dharma,
and may lecture seats be spread again in the elder's garden.
Then the virtue of support
will be as high as Hēng-Dài,
and the merit of protection
as vast as the deep ocean.
This humble thought causes me immense trepidation.
I secretly heard
that leaving home and entering the monastic life is expansive and tranquil, like empty space.
Being in the secular world, confined by its cage, is comparable to being in a prison.
Not only do the sūtras have clear pronouncements on this,
but it is also universally observed in the mundane world.
I briefly heard that the Fǎshī has overturned his boat
and intends to revert to secular attire.
This is a momentary brilliance,
not a profound, long-term plan.
How do I know this?
Moving from suffering into joy,
one does not yet know the joy within joy.
Moving from joy into suffering,
one then truly knows the suffering within suffering.
Your disciple believes that although the Fǎshī and I have no old ties,
our acquaintance has not been shallow.
Good medicine is never sweet,
and loyal advice is certainly unpleasant to the ear.
Seeing his deviation, I cannot bear not to speak.
Moreover, how could one abandon the immense achievements accumulated over thirty years overnight? How regrettable!
I respectfully consider your lofty aspirations,
but I do not understand your profound intentions.
Could it be a strategy from behind the curtain,
seeking to gather Zhāng Liáng (張良)?
Or is it like the reclining dragon, seeking Zhūgě (諸葛) from afar?
Can Huáng Shí's (黃石) art of war be encountered again?
