The "three visits to the thatched cottage" will not be met a second time.
The five ranks of feudal titles are rarely encountered.
Between the inner chamber and the outer gate, it is difficult to turn red (noble) and easy to turn white (commoner).
The sound of a reed pipe and a phoenix flute is not something one can always hear.
Dancing girls and singing courtesans, to revisit them would be a futile effort.
Those who seek them are as numerous as ox hair.
Those who obtain them are as few as ox horns.
Beyond this, what else can one observe?
If the Fǎshī were to retreat now,
it is unlikely there would be anything satisfactory.
You would lose all ten great benefits of the present moment.
What are they?
Buddhist Dharma does not disdain small streams;
those who enter it are honored, and those who take refuge are esteemed.
Above, they do not bow to the Son of Heaven;
below, they do not yield to feudal lords.
They alone enjoy the world, doing nothing and being at ease.
This is the first benefit.
The body is free from the toil of labor;
the mouth partakes of the fragrant food of the gods;
the mind is free from the concerns of wives and concubines;
the body is adorned with simple monastic robes.
In the morning, there is no worry of treading borders;
in the evening, no hardship of traveling a thousand *lǐ*.
Looking up and down, enjoying leisure, how can this not be joyful?
This is the second benefit.
The body has no heavy responsibilities, and one's residence is surely in a prosperous city.
White walls and vermilion gates naturally inspire reverence.
Playing the *qín* at night and the *sè* during the day is self-entertainment.
Writing in the morning and composing poetry in the evening, discussing feelings and stamping one's feet.
This is the third benefit.
Even if thorns grow on the royal road and bridges transform into long ditches,
how can alley officials or gatekeepers dare to summon you?
Not an inch of silk is paid to the imperial treasury, nor a *dǒu* of rice
delivered to the public granaries or the warehouse superintendent.
Why should one seek such benefits? This is the fourth benefit.
Outside the gate, though there be clamor, I sleep peacefully.
In the alley, though there be talk, I show no alarm.
My household is free from disputes, big or small.
My gate is free from strong or weak retainers.
Coming and going is as I please, freely passing to and fro.
This is the fifth benefit.
An unaccomplished monk
is still superior to a secular person.
Even if one harbors thoughts of killing,
the hand is free from the transgression of taking life.
Secretly harboring affection for winning, it is utterly clear.
Such worldly charm, with ten thousand times more vexations and defilements, is superior to a layperson.
Once one enters the river of love, one sinks forever, unable to escape.
This is the sixth benefit.
Hearing the sound of the bell, one offers reverence.
Seeking the fragrant aroma, one's mind is aroused.
In the morning, beholding the venerable image; in the evening, perusing the precious scrolls.
Moments of good karma are born from this.
Tiny drops of water gradually fill a great vessel.
One does not yet know karmic causes and effects,
but good and evil are clear.
From this perspective,
its benefits are innumerable.
Even a wise layperson
still has the concerns of dusty affairs.
Even if they are greeted with a snap of the fingers from afar and people bow their heads near and far,
the form departs, but the mind remains; the body moves, but the intention stays.
Those who have attachments can achieve this;
the poor and suffering will never have the opportunity.
It is right before one's eyes, visible without words.
This is the seventh benefit.
Under trees in the mountains, it is inherently difficult to expect this.
Pillowing on stones and rinsing one's mouth in streams is truly rare.
Such things are inconceivable.
Such people are hard to meet;
single-minded people are rarely encountered.
The Fǎshī has not yet finished learning,
and has been cultivating excellent causes for wisdom.
To retreat now is utterly illogical.
This is the eighth benefit.
Opening embroidered sūtra cases,
one sees past causes.
Unrolling lapis lazuli scrolls,
one verifies future effects.
Knowing causes and knowing karma, one commits no transgression.
Knowing blessings and knowing retribution, how can one commit sins?
Above, without a boat or oars,
one sees the sorrow of drowning.
Below, losing a buoyancy bag,
one faces the danger of sinking.
This is the ninth benefit.
You broadly save all beings, becoming a teacher of gods and humans.
Those who move on land, water, and air all revere you.
Speaking, it is always *ācārya* (阿闍梨) and *upādhyāya* (和上).
Writing, one always offers reverence and *namas* (和南).
Near and far, people sigh in praise; the noble and the humble look up in awe.
If the Fǎshī were to retreat now,
the consequences would be immediately verifiable.
As soon as the *kāṣāya* (袈裟) is removed,
people will address you as "you" and "I."
As soon as you unveil your shoulder, your name can be called directly.
As for equal acquaintances, that goes without saying.
Even inferiors may not show deference.
A mere change of address and the seating arrangement would be vastly different from before.
A little freedom, and they would address you as a mere gentleman.
If you do not bend your knees and lower your eyebrows, you will have no way to communicate.
Bowing and greeting, you will not be accustomed to the proper etiquette.
With such singular focus, how can one associate?
This is the tenth benefit.
Briefly stating these ten matters, you would vainly lose this opportunity.
How can the profound path within be fully expressed?
I respectfully surmise, benevolent one,
that your mind resides in a demonic realm, bewildered by demons.
Your intentions are attached to an evil path, allowing evil to change your nature.
Even if eyebrows are like slender willow branches, what is there to care about?
Even if cheeks are like red peaches, how can they last long?
Sharing a quilt and dividing a pillow,
there is still the sorrow of Chángxìn (長信).
Forgetting time in sitting and sleeping,
one cannot avoid the resentment of Qiū Hú (秋胡).
Even the goddess of the Luò (洛) River was not able to bewitch Dōng'ā (東阿).
What do the transient beauties of the world have to do with you, sir?
Indeed, the heart is the face.
If one speaks of intimacy, then it is sharing breath and heart.
But once infatuation passes, one grows weary of even sleeping together.
The Fǎshī has not yet mastered self-reflection; how can he comprehend selling flowers?
Not having attained the power of knowing others' minds, how can you know their intentions?
Alas, the cassia tree is consumed by a great fire!
What a pity that a bright pearl is buried in mud!
Your disciple's blunt counsel today
will surely be ridiculed by the Fǎshī.
How many common people are there in the world, what criticisms and what limits?
Moreover, one person's retreat from the path does not ensure security.
Considering this, it is truly hard to understand.
It is like scattered瓦礫 (wǎlì) on the road, which no one is surprised by.
But a tiny piece of gold makes ten thousand men stop in their tracks.
To speak plainly, the Fǎshī's accomplishments in entering the path are complete,
but the ways of the secular world have not yet been cultivated.
How is this different from exchanging pure gold for red copper, or silver for lead and tin?
It is lamentable and regrettable; it is still worth pondering what is tolerable and what is unbearable.
Only then will you know its true value. I wish you would abandon secular affairs and cease worldly anxieties,
aligning with right mindfulness and fulfilling both aspiration and conduct.
Give it a little more careful thought, and you will reflect more.
Regret it beforehand, and there will be no need for later sorrow.
If your disciple's calculations are for the distant future, it is ten years;
in the medium term, you will certainly know anguish.
In the near term, within three to five years, you will vainly lament, "What can be done?"
Ten thousand regrets and ten thousand sorrows, how can you know they will reach so far?
Mistaking yourself and regretting yourself, you will forever abandon this life.
Then you will know that a broken string can be mended, but a departed affection is hard to retain.
Perhaps flowers growing in fire can be called rare.
A deluded person who knows how to return is not far from the path.
Fortunately, quickly discard and hasten to ascend the right path.
The Fǎshī is not ignorant,
yet is deluded by foolishness.
Similar to Ānán (阿難), you are being vexed by a demon.
You must rely on the power of the Three Jewels to subdue these evil hordes.
Erect the banner of *Prajñā* (般若), and the celestial demons will naturally submit.
If these words resonate, then immediately abandon your humble abode.
If they do not meet your lofty aspirations, then mercifully overlook this profound strangeness.
Sēng Tánjī respectfully writes.
The Emperor, the great Dàn Yuè,
possesses virtue that grasps the universe and a mind as clear as the white sun.
He illuminates the path of impartiality
and reveals and conceals transformations unpredictably.
He can awe the common people and extend compassion to monastics.
He controls the profound principles and points out the way out.
He desires to make the pure and aspiring, who practice asceticism, manifest their traces in an enlightened age.
He wishes to prevent monks of meager virtue from returning to lay life in shame.
Thus, a clear edict was issued, requiring them to undergo a test of their skills.
It was promulgated to all zhōus, inquiring about their studies and practices.
I humbly consider that there are many paths to entering the Way, surely not just one standard.
Based on observations, there are five reasons why people may be deemed "insufficient."
What are they?
Perhaps there are monks and nuns who have lived in temples since birth, living frugally and self-sufficiently.
Their aspirations are earnest, and they do not violate any prohibitions.
They burn incense, circumambulate stūpas, and prostrate diligently.
They put their palms together, bow their heads, and forget sleep for meals.
However, by nature they are dull-witted and have no affinity for reading and recitation.
They study with great hardship but cannot comprehend a single character.
Now, evaluating the reported intention, it seems that only those who can recite texts and are intelligent are considered fit.
To reconsider the test for monks, it should not lead to their expulsion.
Actual practice is what truly matters.
The true intention tends to seek only the "intelligent and decisive."
However, to be practical but not intelligent
is the root of practice.
To be intelligent but not practical
is merely an aspect of wisdom.
If practice is considered to have merit,
then one does not demand perfection in a single person.
If practice is considered not to make a monk,
then one demands complete knowledge.
The wisdom of the Great Awakening is inconceivable.
All the dharmas it enacts are revered by devas and humans.
How much more so for ordinary people to presume to alter them?
The multitude of saints themselves spoke of various spiritual transformations.
Even they could not add or subtract from this great Dharma.
Great persons, upon appearing in the world, understand origins and discern opportunities.
With ingenious and varied methods, they gradually transform people.
The capacities and practices of sentient beings are all different.
This caused the saints to preach sūtras with mutual variations, not uniform.
Yet, internally and externally, they are interconnected, with no discord or strangeness.
Moreover, like Kǒngzǐ who led three thousand disciples, of whom seventy-two were accomplished.
Only a few entered his inner chambers.
How could the rest be expelled?
Now, each zhōu, jùn, and xiàn has students.
How many possess the virtue of Yán Yuān?
Can we, because they are not equal to Yán Yuān, abolish the jùns and not establish them?
Can we, because there are virtue-less and obstinate monks, collectively return them to lay life?
Those who are not equal to Yán Yuān are still superior to common villagers.
Those who are virtue-less and obstinate monks are still superior to external path practitioners.
Submitting to these two paths,
this is "insufficient" reason number one.
Perhaps there are those who specialize in dwelling beneath trees, carrying staffs and alms bowls.
They eat as they encounter it, living by right livelihood.
They immediately abandon fame and have no desire for gain.
Through rational contemplation, they eliminate defilements, yet they may lack textual recitation.
Judging their entry into the Way, their inner practice is abundant.
But examining their textual understanding, their external merit is lacking.
Why must all those gathered in the capital be virtuous monks?
And all those isolated in forests and wilderness be considered not practitioners?
Thus, fruits have ripeness and unripeness.
One cannot judge by color or appearance.
People have rises and falls.
One cannot judge by form or name.
I dare to reconsider this.
This is "insufficient" reason number two.
Perhaps there are those who sponsor sūtras and create images, exerting effort for many years.
They repair gāláms, toiling for many seasons.
They sacrifice themselves to benefit others, not allowing hardship to trouble their minds.
They bestow joy upon others, not allowing hunger and poverty to change their resolve.
But they lack intellectual ability; daily recitation does not exceed one phrase.
Morning and evening they dwell uneasily, reading less than a few pages a day.
According to their dedication, their good deeds are not in vain.
Judging their aspiration, they are true children of the Buddha.
Now, to unjustly expel them from monastic life
is to wrongly condemn practitioners, their straightforward nature suddenly deemed wrong.
This is "insufficient" reason number three.
The Buddha said that monks are fields of blessing; it is difficult to harm or suppress them.
Even if their years are few and their form is ordinary,
their Dharma robes are revered.
How can one bestow in the morning and take away in the evening, adding injury?
Love and hate are impermanent.
How can one demand their successes or failures from a single individual,
and establish an inconstant standard among the twelve profound canons?
I fear this does not accord with the saintly mind and greatly deviates from the grand principle.
It harms compassion above and diminishes proper transformation below.
I only fear that later generations will transmit and suffer the slander of falsely accusing monks.
This is "insufficient" reason number four.
Now, in the great Zhōu dynasty, the number of monks and nuns is not large.
Yet the monasteries stand tall, numbering more than ten thousand.
They should attract and gather the two monastic assemblies to fill them.
Stirring the bells and sounding the Dharma for the nation.
To exhaustively seek out their strengths and weaknesses with expediency,
to meticulously search for faults and transgressions, and then expel them back to lay life,
thus leaving the pillars empty.
If distant and nearby foreign countries hear of this,
they might suspect that soldiers are being sought among the monastic communities,
or land is being taken from beneath stūpas and temples.
This is truly strange.
But obstinate monks, if they are employed, are not enough to raise an army.
Giving temple land to the people cannot enrich the nation.
Defilements are not suddenly removed; nature manifests gradually.
All sentient beings possess various defilements.
If one were to suddenly dismiss and demand complete cultivation, this would destroy the Buddhadharma.
It would not only harm oneself, but Māra would surely gain an advantage.
What does this mean?
To only cultivate pure goodness and diligently offer供養 (gòngyǎng),
and to dismiss all who are purely evil, returning them to lay life.
This view profoundly destroys the Three Jewels.
If one regards the coarse and fine equally, Māra will have difficulty gaining an advantage.
Why? If one returns a purely good person to lay life, they become coarse.
Yet, even coarse people can give rise to good qualities.
In the principles of the sūtras, one should not question the coarse or fine nature of practice.
Only by not returning to lay life will one ultimately become a Buddha's child.
Reflecting on advancing and retreating, I have considered this three times.
This is "insufficient" reason number five.
This humble monk, in his remaining years, with his lowly body, dwells in Guān Yòu.
Admiring the transformation and receiving grace, I am able to preserve my monastic practice.
Therefore, sighing and leaning on my staff, I send forth this sincere plea.
The transgression of my mistakes, I humbly increase my trepidation and deference.
Respectfully submitted.
I humbly consider that
the clear Wèi River and the turbid Jīng River
together blend into the source of the tide.
The long pines and short arrows
all possess a quality of strength and constancy.
Fortunately, we are endowed with the five constant virtues of the spirit,
and it is proper to encompass the Three Teachings.
Therefore, the Confucian child from Quèlǐ
expounded the Classic of Rites by the Zhū and Jì Rivers.
Kāshyapa from Kǔxiàn
transferred the wondrous Way to Liúshā.
Although they encompassed the two realms, Heaven and Earth,
they were confined to this one lifetime.
How can this compare to establishing the true Dharma in the Lùyuàn
and sweeping away delusive thoughts on Jùshān?
When the half and full teachings are presented, the provisional and the real become manifest.
Truly, teachings have shallowness and depth, but people have no inner or outer distinctions.
The Chan Master's virtuous reputation spreads far and wide; his conduct is exalted beyond the ordinary.
Receiving the four kinds of sustenance,
he attained recitation by tending sheep.
Carrying a satchel for a thousand *lǐ*,
he encompassed the Dragon Palace.
Thus, he could inwardly penetrate the Nine Divisions
and gather the secret treasures of the Snow Mountains.
Outwardly, he encompassed the Seven Summaries
and possessed the ancient classics of Bìshuǐ.
Zhī Dùn's inscription on Tiāntái,
and Zhú Zhēn's record of Luófú.
Tán Fù composed verses on the Seven Ridges and chanted about the Three Rivers.
Bǎo Shī brilliantly refuted Zhuāng Shēng,
and Qú Gōng compiled his treatises.
It was like swallowing the clouds and mists of Yúnmèng or pointing to things in one's palm.
Moreover, he perfectly upheld the pure precepts as if protecting a luminous pearl.
He skillfully maintained the monastic rules as if facing a clear mirror.
He inherited Ráluóyún's secret practices
and planted the field of blessings of Bīntóu.
By gently drawing from the water of meditation, he ascended to discernment and contemplation.
Under the high shade of the Chan tree, he would surpass joy and equanimity.
Therefore, he did not find Xiāoxiāng distant, and arrived in Xīlù.
He planted his staff at Lóngquán, which then became a monastic residence.
Turning his carriage at Mǎgǔ, he immediately founded a *saṅghārāma*.
Carving a niche in the ridge required no gathering of sand.
Building a stupa relied on the mountain; constructing a garden required no
scattering of gold to buy land. Scholars gathered like clouds.
Sleeves rustled like Huáyīn's; Dharma companions thronged.
Their numbers rivaled Jìxià.
In the Chan chambers, morning began with the fragrance of *dùruò*.
The *caitya* opened in the evening, briefly entering Táoyuán.
The Buddhist chanting on Xiāngshān
echoed with Ruǎn Xiào's whistling.
The wondrous sounds of the Rìdiàn
harmonized with Sūn Qín's zither.
The constant pines of Zǐgài still waved with superior eloquence.
The divine well of Hóngyá polished his exalted mind.
Thus, his talent was sufficient to "buy a mountain," and his virtue surpassed that of riding in the same carriage.
His sublime conduct was like a high peak, with walls of a thousand *rèn*, sheer and impassable.
As a disciple, my karmic winds stir my thoughts, and my body sinks in the sea of desire.
Since Zhǔgōng fell, nearly two *jì* have passed.
By day, I am weary from "sitting and galloping"; by night, I am startled by sorrowful dreams.
I have been unable to forget the distinction between self and other, to turn my chariot towards the One Vehicle, to cast away the clutter of my breast, and to brightly open the three insights.
While I lament the "rat on the vine," I am even more pained by the "bird in a cage."
In my youth, when I was devoted to study, my family received bestowed books.
I thoroughly delved into the Five Rites and was satiated with the Three Metaphysical Classics.
I largely ceased to wear out leather bindings and wrote what remained of my insights.
At my weak冠 (twenty years old), I collected from a hundred schools.
When I entered officialdom, I lingered in literary pursuits.
Although I could not "gather from Lóngmén and ascend Kuàijī,"
nor "compose a rhapsody on a wren and sing of a parrot,"
if one were to seek even a single detail,
I would still somewhat resemble the ancients.
However, I deeply understand that gatherings are like bubbles and attachments cause grief.
I constantly wish to shed the worldly understanding and greedily savor the true reality.
One day, in Yúnchéng, I inquired at Wěiguǎn.
Bending my knee, my heart rejoiced at the shared encounter, like meeting someone who ties one's socks.
Before I finished offering the shoes, I opened my heart and immediately sighed.
In a flutter of longing,
I brushed off the worldly net, cast aside the threads of entanglement.
Washing my cap-strings in the blue waves, I embraced the jug on the shady side of the Hàn River.
Eating the nine-turn elixir, I dispelled my hidden sorrows.
Gradually awakening to the three emptinesses, I shall ascend to the endurance of suffering.
Though a celestial bridge is seen as jade, it does not prevent one from seeking a teacher.
Breaking a peach from a deep ravine does not hinder seeking instruction.
I hope that the overwhelming vital energy will occasionally respond to Záo Chǐ,
and profound discussions at Yànmén will sometimes answer honored guests.
May winter be warm as spring; I wish to cherish your pure conduct.
Though your chamber is near, the person is far, which truly pains my innermost thoughts.
My remaining words are fragmented and simple; I regret they are not like gold or jade.
Indeed, the One True Reality is always profoundly still;
the subtle and wondrous thus share the same profundity.
The ten thousand sages take advantage of opportunities,
and their differing traces are due to accordance or opposition.
Therefore, there was the enlightened Way in Xīguān and the discourse on benevolence in Dōngyě.
Carving and uncarved wood change their craftsmanship; existence and non-existence differ in their perspectives.
Now, if we summarize these two gates and trace these two teachings,
will they not converge into the Three Turnings and enter the Five Vehicles?
Using the shallow to reach the deep, and relying on the provisional to manifest the real.
This is like four streams dividing into different names at first,
but the eight rivers controlled by the sea ultimately have no distinct taste.
The *dàn yuē* (patron) from youth displayed extraordinary talent and harbored excellent aspirations from an early age.
His brilliant words excelled the world, and his elegant demeanor partook of the profound.
His wisdom delved into the Five Sciences, and his learning encompassed the Three Teachings.
It truly is beneficial to forget;
he treads the unfettered path of Yán Shēng.
Diminishing oneself for the Way,
he emulates the profound traces of the Lǐ clan.
Although the Six Classics are comprehensive and vast, and the Hundred Schools are numerous and rich,
sages and worthies have different standards, and Confucianism and Mohism diverge.
Some subjects are broad with rich prose,
while others have lofty words and profound meanings.
Yet none are not received as a bottle receives, or spoken like a river pours.
The bright mirror is tireless; the great bell awaits being struck.
Zǐjiàn drew from it with wondrous writings;
Chángqīng was ashamed of his own lofty interests.
Thus, even when Qín and Chǔ were divided,
and the ruins of Zhōu gave way to the changed customs of Liáng,
the "white eyebrows" and "green eyes"
did not surpass the value of turtle-shell and jade.
Perched phoenixes and reclining dragons
did not differ in their "fish-and-water" relationship.
Moreover, his insight purified the "suffering-emptiness" and his will rejected worldly dust.
Though his body was in the grand halls, his vessel was in the rivers and lakes.
Therefore, he sighed over entanglements and spoke of worldly nets.
His words were like Yīng Lù's, his tone harmonized with Zhāng Yán.
He lamented the swift passing of the "vermilion fire"
and pitied the rapid flow of the "clear waves."
He should indeed wash his feet to follow the Way and wash his ears to renounce fame.
The "nine-turn elixir" fills the emptiness; the "four gates" ward off illness.
After that, he seeks the Eightfold Path to savor the One True Reality,
unties the Ten Fetters, and dispels the Three Sufferings.
How can such virtue not be supreme?
My mirror of discernment is hard to purify, and the dust of my mind is easy to block.
I am ashamed that my meditation is not like "Huá Water," and my precepts are not like "grass ties."
My talent is only enough to "withdraw the candle," my learning falls short of "transmitting the lamp."
Inwardly, I feel shame concerning my lacking virtue;
outwardly, I do not mingle freely with the world.
Therefore, I linger in a small hill, dwelling physically among reeds and willows.
I sit solitarily among towering peaks, my will entrusted to bamboos and pines.
I observe the four seasons through wind and frost,
and await the three ten-day periods by gazing at the moon.
Thus, at night I hear mountain birds, which still replace the "Nine Songs."
By day, I watch swimming fish, briefly recalling the "two masters."
My humble door and worn robes are in their original state and not ailing; the grand gate with paired carriages is to me like clouds.
What I lament is that "mice are easy to invade the tree," and "monkeys are hard to quiet."
My thoughts are weary of "Jìutóu," my mind tired of "Jīzú."
As for the forest shedding autumn leaves,
I have never had the clarity of a Pratyekabuddha.
The valley echoes with spring orioles,
but I still feel the lament of meager knowledge.
Suddenly, I received your inquiry, a glimpse of your glorious reputation.
Your profound spirit is like an orchid, your clear voice like jade.
Truly, it fills my eyes with joy,
but in reality, I press my chest with much shame.
Although my knowledge is inferior to "Tiānchí," I have not yet discerned the discourse of "Běimíng."
Yet my situation is like a "muddy well," and I am ashamed to hear talk of "Dōnghǎi."
What I hope is that such a person will cherish me.
Huángshí is not far; let us make a date for tomorrow morning.
A white colt can be tethered, for a lasting morning.
I respectfully admire your pure sentiments; I will write to you when I have time.
My words are not refined; how can I express this reply?
On the twenty-third day of the eighth month, Míng Hé Nán.
The secular world is impermanent.
Upon hearing that Dharma Master Yán has passed away,
my grief is profound and cannot be stopped.
The sorrow and pain of longing are truly unbearable.
The Dharma Master, at a young age, renounced the secular world and soared above the dust.
His aspirations were vast and grand; his understanding and wisdom were refined and enlightened.
His spiritual platform and divine dwelling could be revered but not peered into.
His sea of wisdom and source of Dharma could be traversed but not fathomed.
Like a bright mirror, it reflected repeatedly without weariness.
Like a great bell, it responded to all who came to strike it.
When he encountered the decline of the Way, and the Xuan thread was broken,
he settled his will in secluded cliffs, firm and unyielding.
High positions and generous emoluments could not sway his thoughts.
Stern authority and strict laws were insufficient to intimidate his heart.
In walking meditation and serene sitting, he saw no difference between ease and hardship.
His precepts and monastic rules were consistent from beginning to end.
When the Sagely Emperor began his reign, the likeness Dharma revived.
He was prominently declared the foremost among the black-robed monks.
He humbled himself from the highest imperial position
to uphold the righteousness between teacher and disciple.
The Three Jewels were widely protected by him,
and the Two Truths were proclaimed through him.
Truly, he was sufficient to follow the footsteps of Chéng Shí and surpass Ān Yuǎn.
Yet, the pillar of Dharma suddenly toppled, and the boat of benevolence quickly sank.
It is not merely that grief entangles the four assemblies,
but also that sorrow pains this single person.
My teacher, carrying his staff and holding his alms-bowl, early received his instructions.
Entering his hall and his inner chamber, I understood the entirety in detail.
My feelings of "being in the three" [years of mourning]
naturally lead to a hundred constant laments.
He is gone! What can be done?
Impermanence! What can be done?
Due to illness and hindrance, I cannot offer my condolences in person.
Thus, my grief is deep and knotted.
I respectfully send this plain letter,
full of sorrow and unorganized.
Your disciple, Xuē Dàohéng, bows.
In the third year of the Dàyè reign of Emperor Yáng of Suí, new laws, statutes, and ordinances were promulgated, stating:
"All monks, Daoist priests, and others who have petitions or requests,
must first offer respects before presenting their cases."
Although this order existed, the monks ultimately did not follow it.
At that time, the śramaṇa Shì Yàncóng could not bear this situation,
so he wrote the Fútián Lùn to resist it.
The intention was satire.
Those who speak are blameless,
and those who hear should take it as a warning for themselves.
Later, when the Emperor held court,
none of the śramaṇas offered respects.
In the fifth year of Dàyè, at the southern suburbs of Xījīng, a grand cultural display was arranged.
Both traditions came for an imperial audience.
The monks still did not bow.
An imperial edict was issued, saying:
"The regulations have been in effect for a long time.
Why do the monks not offer respects?"
At that time, Master Míngshàn replied:
"Your Majesty, in widely protecting the Three Jewels, should follow the words of the Buddha.
The sūtras do not command bowing to lay people,
therefore, we dare not violate the teachings."
Another edict was issued, saying:
"If you do not bow and show respect,
then why did you offer respects during the time of Emperor Wǔ of Sòng?"
He replied:
"Emperor Wǔ of Sòng was a tyrannical ruler with biased policies; those who did not show respect were often executed.
Your Majesty is different from him; there is no need to bow down."
The edict said: "Just bow."
The monks stood firm.
In this manner, several times they were ordered to bow.
The monks said:
"If Your Majesty insists that monks bow,
we should remove our monastic robes and wear lay clothes.
This bowing would not be too late."
The Emperor was placid
and soon stopped.
The next day, when a grand vegetarian feast and Buddhist ritual were held, nothing was mentioned about it.
Later, he told his officials:
"I thought there were no capable people among the monks.
Yesterday, at the southern suburbs, there were indeed capable people in the responses."
Thereafter, until the end, none bowed.
As for the Huángjīn (Daoist) priests and priestesses,
when they first heard the order to bow, they immediately formed a line,
and bowed repeatedly without stopping.
The Emperor did not deign to question them.
An essay.
In the past, during the Eastern Jìn dynasty, Grand Commandant Huán Xuán 桓玄 debated an order for Śramaṇas 沙門 to revere the sovereign.
Lúshān’s 廬山 Fǎshī Yuǎn 法師遠, with his eminent reputation and profound virtue,
was grieved that the banner of wisdom was about to fall,
and pained that the jewel of precepts was about to sink.
So he composed the “Lùn Shāmén Bù Jìng Wángzhě 論沙門不敬王者” (Essay on Śramaṇas Not Revering Sovereigns).
The ceremony of reverence was consequently set aside at that time.
However, since the words were intricately woven and subtle, and the allusions profound and obscure,
later scholars, in perusing it, found its meaning difficult to grasp.
Taking advantage of a leisurely day, I shall now re-expound upon it,
renaming it “Fútián Lùn 福田論” (Essay on Fields of Merit), stating:
Suddenly, a distinguished guest arrived from afar,
remotely attributing to the Huán 桓 clan a re-statement of the former proposal.
The host, maintaining his proper thoughts for a long time,
raised his voice and responded, saying:
“It seems the guest has not yet heard the essentials of the fields of merit.
I shall now discuss them for you.
What are these 'fields of merit' you speak of? They are the Three Jewels.
Those whose achievements are perfected in subtle wisdom and whose enlightenment is complete are the Buddhas.
The profound principles, tranquil and subtle, and the true teachings, pure and sincere, are the Dharma.
Those who observe the precepts, preserve truth, and whose deportment transcends the mundane are the Saṅgha.
All are guides for the four kinds of birth and vessels for the six realms.
They are exalted above humans and devas, heavier than gold and stone.
To liken them to precious jewels is an insufficient comparison.
The Buddha, as the master of the Dharma, establishes the doctrine.
The Dharma, as the Buddha’s teacher, is the foundation.
The Saṅgha, as disciples, venerates this Buddhist Dharma.
It can be said that the revered and the humble share the same position, and the root and the branch share the same gate.
Though there are three kinds in speech,
in essence, they are one.
They preside over fifty lifetimes [kalpas],
and propagate eighty-thousand scriptures.
Their spoken guidance points only to this utmost extremity.
They quiet sound and extinguish shadow, exhausting the era of the twin Sāla trees.
They carve sandalwood and inscribe leaves, preserving the path of a single transformation.
Sages and worthies arise successively, and schools of learning are passed down.
They gather in harmony to abide and uphold this entrusted mission.
The golden man shone in the Hàn 漢 palace.
The simulated Dharma spread to the Luòpǔ 洛浦.
Both uphold the former enlightened ones and follow the ancient statutes.
They aspire to the transcendent and embark on their spiritual journey,
abandoning the mundane to establish virtue.
Official honors cannot sway their aspirations.
Relatives cannot entangle their emotions.
Their clothes are cut from faded colors.
Their hair is shorn, destroying their appearance.
They do not wear crowns to maintain their dignity.
How can they bind belts for adornment?
Even the emperors in the heavens constantly offer reverence.
The kings on earth naturally always pay respect.
With both sūtras and vinayas, this Dharma remains unchanged.
Whether ancient or modern, its way is unimpeded.
Estimating the importance of emperors and kings,
and the relative greatness of gods,
the eight directions admire their virtue, and the four seas return to their benevolence.
It has not been heard that monks and nuns prostrate themselves before them.
If you hold a different view, please present your elegant opinion.”
The guest said:
“The Zhōuyì 周易 says:
‘The great virtue of heaven and earth is life.’
‘The great treasure of the sage is his position.’
Lǎozǐ 老子 says:
‘Within the domain, there are four great things,
and the king is one of them.’
I humbly submit that there is nothing that is not the king’s land,
on which he establishes his nation.
There is nothing that is not the king’s subject,
bound to him as their lord.
He emulates heaven and earth, covering and carrying the myriad people, like spring and summer, fostering the growth of all things.
He illuminates them with the light of the sun and moon,
and moistens them with the qi 氣 of clouds and rain.
The six directions universally honor him as the ocean.
The common people all look up to him as the constellations.
Barbarians change their ways, and horses and cattle turn back.
Even serpents bear favors from Suí Hóu 隋侯.
Fish still feel gratitude towards the Hàn 漢 emperor.
How can there be those exempted from the household registry,
who assume the Dharma gate, forgetting the wide benevolence of liberation,
and abandoning the grand creation of offerings?
They boast of their own greatness, while humility and reverence are utterly discarded.
How are they different from beasts?
If they can truly command spiritual powers and achieve sagehood,
and their path pervades the world, then the principle is beyond words.
But now, they merely shave their heads, yet still increase the three poisons.
They vainly change their robes, yet are still stained by the six dusts.
They do not cultivate patience in precepts, nor do they attain concentration and wisdom.
They violate clear teachings and are no different from common folk.
How can they rely on the effort of chanting scriptures to resist paying respect to the ‘myriad chariots’?
And on the distinction of their appearance to neglect reverence for the single ruler?
In the past, bhikṣus saluted householders by touching their feet.
Bodhisattvas bowed their heads to arrogant assemblies.
If these texts are again made manifest, where is their meaning?
If one considers the expedient path difficult to follow, yet the Buddha-nature worthy of respect,
how much more so when the ruler’s presence is nothing but a divine descent?
Bóyáng 伯陽 established a model for ten thousand generations.
Zhòngní 仲尼 laid down rules for a hundred kings.
As for audiences and bows, they must follow court regulations.
Only Śramaṇas dare to be arrogant and disrespectful.
If this can be endured, what cannot be tolerated?
This corrupt custom is difficult to change, and evil trends easily persist.
If not for an enlightened emperor, who can rectify it?
Suddenly, extraordinary changes arise,
inviting accusations of faithlessness.
My sincere words are well-founded; I hope you will examine them carefully.”
The host said:
“What I establish is internal.
What you challenge is external.
The internal is connected to Dharmic principles.
The external is limited to human affairs.
They are so utterly distant; how can they be compared?
This shows you have studied but not grasped, heard but not fully understood.
I shall now clarify what confuses you.
Let me briefly enumerate the essentials, totaling seven points.
No virtue unrequited is the first.
No goodness uncontained is the second.
Unimpeded skillful means is the third.
Tranquil extinction without glory is the fourth.
Dignity not to be transgressed is the fifth.
Robes not to be confused is the sixth.
Causality not to be forgotten is the seventh.
The first four points respond to your challenge.
The latter three points are drawn out to form a standard.
I have heard that Heaven does not speak, yet the four seasons run their course.
The king does not speak, yet the myriad states are governed.
What power does the emperor possess that the people cannot name?
He accomplishes without dwelling on it, acts without relying on it.
This is the ultimate goodness of the former kings,
the utmost virtue of the great man.
All beings equally partake, and all subjects are equally bound.
Fortunately, they are different from grass and trees, and somewhat distinct from insects and birds.
Bearing the round (sky) and treading the square (earth), they embrace beneficence in their every move.
Eating grain and drinking water, they are filled and hold gratitude.
Since you have been gracious enough to permit renunciation and kindly allowed entry into the path,
cutting off coarse karma from the past,
and praying for wondrous fruit in the future,
having received profound kindness, they naturally wish to repay it amply.
They rely on the benefit of myriad good deeds.
How can it be in the reverence of a single person?
To pursue repayment through good deeds is truly profound.
To demand reverence through bodily bows yields shallow benefit.
Indeed, if monks lose their proper dignity, worldly people will diminish their remaining blessings.
The Buddha has clearly stated that monks do not bow to laypeople.
If it is known to be trustworthy, the principle should naturally be upheld.
If it is deemed difficult to rely on, the practice should be abolished.
How can one worship them seeking their blessings, yet humble them and demand their reverence?
If they were to follow the rituals, they would become like laypeople.
Yet, though you ask for blessings, you see no benefit.
This means they are preserved yet seem abandoned, monks yet resemble commoners.
They are neither white nor black; they cannot be named.
I have seen that only the suburban sacrifices and general offerings persist.
Revering blessings as supreme, monks still disdain this.
If they are disrespectful, how can one make monks bow to laypeople?
Heaven and earth can be overturned, but this ritual is rarely transgressed.
This is further expounded as the first point: ‘No virtue unrequited.’
As the Dharma gradually declines, people also become more degenerate.
There are few saints, as you truly say.
Though they dwell in the mundane stream, they still wear the armor of patience.
Even if they lack in precepts, they still discuss the canon of wisdom.
They are as noble as stūpas, as revered as the Buddha.
Returning to them generates goodness.
Destroying them accumulates sin.
With a resolute initial resolve,
they renounce the difficult attachment to love.
Leading ordinary beings, they ultimately aspire
to attain distant enlightenment.
Thus, on the day they shave their heads, heavenly Māras are intimidated from afar.
On the day they don their robes, Śakra Deva is joyful from afar.
A courtesan briefly donned them, and her outflows were fulfilled.
A drunkard temporarily cut his hair, and a karmic connection was immediately formed.
Dragon children relied on them to cease their fright.
Elephant kings saw them and stopped their fear.
Their spiritual power lies here, and their dignified robes are the cause.
Many who have not yet received the full ordination still proclaim the Buddha’s intent.
Even the young should not be slighted, for they illuminate the Saṅgha’s power.
After Pōlí 波離 was converted, the Śākya clan submitted their hearts.
Nítuó 尼陀 also returned, and the concealed king yielded his will.
Indeed, whether old or young, those who can be teachers are the Dharma.
Without distinction of humble or noble, what is preserved is the Way.
Then, between the wise and the foolish, in moments of silence and speech,
the ripe and unripe appear similar, and discerning them is not easy.
Discernment by the flesh eye might miss the jewel.
But with equal faith, one might encounter the true.
As soon as four people gather, a Saṅgha is formed.
Since the Saṅgha widely embraces, the Buddha is also universally present.
Seeing the distinctiveness of boiling water (as a metaphor for purification), one then sends offerings to the Saṅgha.
Seeing the marvel of brocade (as a metaphor for rarity), one then presents robes to the assembly.
The Saṅgha’s majestic virtue is not immense?
It is sufficient to be called the supreme field of merit and the essence of the sacred teaching.
This is the second point: ‘No goodness uncontained.’
If one speaks of Vimalakīrti’s accomplishments, he had long ascended to the cloud-dwelling stage.
His pretense of illness originally transcended the worldly realm.
He had long practiced spiritual powers, and all marveled at his eloquence.
New students respectfully saluted, sincerely thanking him for the Dharma gift.
This matter was an expedient measure, not a constant rule.
There are many examples where times temporarily change their conventions.
For instance, Kōngzàng 空藏 was disrespectful, yet the Tathāgata did not blame him.
Śrāmaṇeras with great vows, their Upādhyāyas yielded priority.
A superficial glance would find all these astonishing.
But a closer examination of the scriptures reveals them all to be common paths.
The Bodhisattva Tidakṣa alone distinguished himself with lofty deeds.
to warn those arrogant individuals,
this prostration of humble heart is established.
It is solely performed with a straight path, employing utmost sincerity.
Since it is not for the benefit of the Three Worlds, how can it be a constant rule?
To create a dharma based on circumstances is truly rare.
If it were to widely spread teachings, it would be difficult to establish it as a formal monastic rule.
The Great Sage manifested the clarity of two wisdoms,
and established the regulations of the five sections.
He abolished distinctions of rank and age, preserving the rules of the precepts and the length of monastic residence.
From beginning to end, the general teaching benefited both the sharp and the dull, who equally revered it.
The old and young had their order, without confusion between former and latter.
It was not that a single practice or separate undertaking was made universal for all seven assemblies.
This is a natural principle,
clearly visible.
In ancient times, when a wife died, one would sing and beat a basin.
When a body was buried, it was wrapped in silk and covered with earth.
These are also the customs of common folk.
How can they generally encompass the regulations of enlightened kings?
Moreover, the Buddhist scriptures are profound and subtle, the words of the sages recondite.
To be fixated on one aspect is truly contrary to the four dialectical skills.
This is what is called the third unimpeded expedient.
Furthermore, Zhōu (周)'s keeper of the archives was long burdened by royal service.
Lǔ (魯)'s minister of justice had already become the nation's prime minister, yet their traditions reverted to Daoist morality, initially called "nameless."
Their teachings were found in the Shī (詩) and Shū (書) classics, ultimately concluding that they "do not act."
They followed the example of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜), and observed the rules of Wén (文) and Wǔ (武).
Who else but these would bow respectfully?
The customs of Cháo Fǔ (巢父) and Xǔ Yóu (許由), looking back to antiquity, still excel.
The integrity of Bó Yí (伯夷) and Shú Qí (叔齊), when compared to today, still stands out.
It is like soaring high, reaching for the ten powers, and transcending the four streams.
They detest the suffering of conditioned existence,
and rejoice in the extinction that has no companions.
They are not bound by thoughts of the imperial court,
nor do they let their emotions flow towards royal affairs.
Such natural liberation is indeed different from the company of Confucian scholars.
This is what is called the fourth tranquil and unadorned extinction.
As for worshipping ghosts and spirits, revering mountains and rivers in due order,
these are grand state rituals and beautiful tales in historical records.
Spirits are respected by kings,
yet monks may not perform rituals for them.
Monks are revered by spirits,
so how can kings in turn receive their reverence?
Such disparities between high and low would contradict the true Dharma.
With robes turned upside down, how can one compare?
Spirits are commanded to protect; now they come to the monks.
The culmination of prayers and requests opens up.
The power of incantations ultimately has no reason to bow.
This is what is called the fifth that rituals cannot transgress.
Originally, the rise of emperors and kings
must have been the embodiment of true individuals.
Though their supreme virtue is hidden in a pure mind,
their outward form still displays secular characteristics.
Therefore, when the Way is manifested in monastic robes, feelings of diligence should be intense.
When karma is hidden within the Xuan (玄) gate, physical reverence should cease.
Seeking out old facts, there is ample prior evidence.
Kings such as Bìnbó (頻婆) and Jìngfàn (淨飯)
in the past had all attained Buddhahood.
They diligently practiced faith and obedience, relying on the Dharma in every matter.
Even when they saw ordinary monks, they still thought of them as venerating the Buddha.
Not kneeling to one's parents is not considered filial piety,
and this is permitted as not being the sin of unfilial conduct.
Not bowing to the sovereign is not considered disrespect,
so how can it be a fault of disrespect?
The objects of the law are different; the objects of the law are already distinct.
The substance is not mixed, and the regulations follow from this.
This is what is called the sixth that robes cannot be confused.
Carefully examining the wondrous Tārā (多羅) scripture, the true words of Shìjiā (釋迦),
it says:
Dwelling in the Kṣatriya (剎利) caste and being honored,
protected by Prajñā (般若),
with the four faiths unbroken and the ten good deeds unimpaired,
serving the Buddha and revering the Sangha, accumulating merits and virtues.
Only then will the essence of the sun and the image of the moon descend,
and the red light and white aura be felt.
Once the golden wheel turns, jewels will again be suspended.
Responding to heaven and aligning with the people, governing the world and holding the mirror,
one begins to establish the art of the Five Constants,
and ultimately propagates the Way of the Eightfold Path.
It is also fitting to examine past lives and recall previous causes,
to revere the Buddha's teachings and honor the Sangha jewels,
to increase the fragrance of precepts and enhance wisdom power.
Naturally, the celestial foundation will rise higher,
comparable to the vastness of Brahmā (梵)'s palace.
The sagely lifespan will be eternally firm,
as long as the kalpa-stone.
Thus, when thunder and lightning reach their peak, and dragons and tigers are majestic,
blessings will surely be reliant on both, for anger is incurred if violated.
When words are spoken and orders issued, they spread like wind bending grass.
Since the monastic prostration is suppressed, who would dare to rebel?
But I fear there will be harm to unseen merits and no aid
to one's awe-inspiring work. How can one be sincere and devote one's life like this?
This is what is called the seventh that causes cannot be forgotten.
Above, I have briefly presented my intention and roughly dispelled your doubts.
If you wish to be widely learned, you should consult the great scriptures.
The guest said:
The principles and examples my host cited just now are numerous.
Although I am dull and ignorant, I have somewhat understood them.
The text comprehensively covers the seen and unseen, and the arguments encompass both internal and external.
However, regarding the sacrificial rituals, I still have some confusion.
The Zhōu Yì (周易) says:
"One yin and one yang is called the Dào (道); the immeasurability of yin and yang is called Shen (神)."
I humbly believe that the obscure path of Shen (神) is separated from the human realm.
To perform sacrificial rites, one must rely on ritual officials.
The Bèngcháng (奉常) was originally established specifically
to preside over the Tàizhù (太祝).
Even if one knows about ghost matters, one ultimately belongs to the ranks of officials.
The true Buddha has already hidden, and the holy Sangha has also passed away.
We rely on the unseen path, entirely ascending to mysterious spirits.
Ordinary people of this latter age
briefly dedicate merit
and jointly aspire to leisure and freedom.
They learn from each other to shave their heads
and manage Dharma assemblies.
That is why they are given their Dharma robes.
They guard pagodas and monasteries,
which is why they are exempted from secular duties.
However, as soon as they touch the king's law,
they fall into the common populace.
Since they are treated like those who manage sacrifices, how can they be called "treasures"?
To bow to the Son of Heaven is certainly a constant ritual.
To stubbornly cling to obstinacy is definitely not comprehensive knowledge.
The old system of the Sòng (宋) dynasty, its custom is not far off.
It should simply be adopted; what further words are needed?
The host said:
You know one thing but not the other.
Please listen to my excellent words and dispel your strange ideas.
I have heard that Guǐ (鬼) means "return,"
the place one enters after death.
Shen (神) means "spirit,"
that which the form relies upon.
Guǐ (鬼) is inferior to humans and confined to evil paths.
Shen (神) is superior to forms and encompasses all sentient beings.
When the mind has spiritual wisdom, it is called Shen (神).
When it is hidden and difficult to know, it is called "immeasurable."
Analyzing its substance and function, it can be active or static.
Categorizing its nature and desires, it has yin and yang.
The essence of the Zhōu Yì (周易) is precisely this.
Different paths are manifested in the one vital energy,
and sincere words are lacking in the six consciousnesses.
The gradual nature of teaching can thus be known.
Guǐ (鬼)'s retribution is communicated subtly, coming and going secretly.
They are given the title Shen (神) specifically for this.
Let me try to explain:
Receiving the legacy of parents,
endowed with the portions of Qian (乾) and Kun (坤),
one can exist through vital energy,
and establish one's form.
As for one's own Shen (神) path,
it must be the karma of my mind.
It has never been generated by Qian (乾) and Kun (坤),
nor obtained from parents. Consciousness contains the embryo,
and the storehouse pervades empty space.
Intention carries karmic seeds, overflowing the world.
Going and then being reborn,
like a continuous flame.
Coming and then departing again,
like constantly turning water waves.
Its roots cannot be seen at the beginning;
how can its end be perceived when investigated?
When turbid, it becomes ordinary;
when clear, it becomes holy.
The Shen (神) path is subtle and recondite; its principles are indeed difficult to comprehend.
The highest of Shen (神) is called the Great Awakening.
It is beyond thought and discussion; how can names and forms exhaust it?
The true body fundamentally has no change or decay.
The born blind naturally cannot see it.
They rely on imagination to pursue old traces,
and wholeheartedly delight in the remaining Dharma.
If one wishes to bear the responsibility of transmission,
and open the gate to profound wonders,
one must rely on these monastic disciples, who receive this entrustment from the Buddha.
Borrowing the cloud of compassion as inner image,
and relying on imperial might as external strength,
the mysterious wind reaches far and wide to this extent.
The teaching pervades the three worlds, and the community is divided into four sections.
Two follow the Dao (道), and two adhere to secular customs.
Those who follow the Dao (道) have venerable robes and deportment.
Those who adhere to secular customs engage in ceremonial offerings.
The venerable image refers to Bhikṣus (比丘) and Bhikṣuṇīs (比丘尼).
The ceremonial offerings refer to Upāsakas (優婆塞) and Upāsikās (優婆夷).
Those whose image is venerable are not yet involved in the divine ranks.
Those whose duty is ceremonial offering are subject to imperial decrees.
The people of ceremonial offerings are originally the same as those who manage sacrifices.
I am not in that position; why do you misinterpret?
Your frank words reveal my deeper meaning.
The principle is already clear;
do not be confused again.
At the beginning of Sòng (宋),
this suppression was temporarily implemented.
That also deviated from the truth;
it is not worth discussing.
The customs of the frontier regions are not beautiful to behold.
Suddenly to force conformity with them
is utterly strange.
The guest said:
How profound this discussion is!
Having been taught the good path, I beg to take my leave.
When the August Táng dynasty commenced its rule, all religions flourished concurrently.
However, concerning Buddhist Dharma, it was especially exalted and heavily relied upon.
The old imperial residence in the capital was converted into Xīngshèng-sì.
Besides this, monasteries such as Huìchāng-shèngyè-sì, Cíbēi-zhèngguǒ-jíxiān-sì, and others
were constructed one after another.
As for Daoist temples, they were not widely known among the populace.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé [621 CE], there was a Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐlìng) named Fù Yì.
Previously, during the Yellow Turban Rebellion, he deeply resented monks.
Upon seeing the state accord special reverence [to Buddhism],
his heart became even more troubled.
He then submitted eleven articles advocating the abolition of Buddhist Dharma, stating:
"Buddhist scriptures are wild and absurd, speaking of hidden demonic matters.
They harm the state and ruin families; no benefit to the world has been heard.
I request that the barbarian Buddhist邪教 (xiéjiào) be returned to Tiānzhú.
All śramaṇas should be sent back to their hometowns.
Then, the family and state will prosper, and the teachings of Lǐ and Kǒng will prevail."
Emperor Gāozǔ tolerated his minor arguments,
and the court ministers allowed his reckless speech.
Consequently, an imperial edict was issued, asking the monks:
"Discarding parents' hair and beard,
abandoning the official attire of sovereign and minister—
in which discipline lies the benefit?
Beyond which sentiment lies the advantage?
Regarding these two matters of harm and benefit, please provide a subtle explanation."
There was a śramaṇa from Jìfǎ-sì in Xiāngyáng, Shì Fǎlín.
Indignant at Fù Yì's words, he listened for an opportunity.
Upon learning of this question, he immediately responded, saying:
"Lín has heard that the ultimate Dao transcends words; how can the Nine Schools debate it?
The Dharmakāya has no form; it is not what the Ten Wings can explain.
But the four realms are vast, adrift in the sea of desires.
The three realms are teeming, falling headlong into the mountain of evil.
The ignorant burn themselves in delusion,
and ordinary people drown without escape.
This is why the Perfected Ones descend,
and the Great Sages arise in the world.
Thus, they open the gate of liberation
and show the path of peace and safety.
Thereupon, royal descendants in Tiānzhú renounced affection and love to leave home,
and noble dignitaries in Dōngxià abandoned glory and splendor to enter the Dao.
They vow to escape the two kinds of birth and death,
and aspire to seek the one wondrous Nirvāṇa.
They promote goodness to repay the four great kindnesses,
and establish virtue to aid the three realms of existence.
This is their benefit.
They destroy their form to achieve their aspiration,
hence they abandon hair and beautiful appearance.
They transform their customs to align with their Dao,
hence they discard the splendid attire of sovereign and minister.
Although their form is deficient in serving parents, they harbor filial piety within.
Though their rites deviate from serving their lord, their heart holds gratitude.
Their benevolence covers both enemies and kin, achieving great accord.
Their blessings reach both the hidden and the manifest; how can they be restricted by minor transgressions?
The wise ones,
by relying on the Buddha's words, gain benefit.
The common people,
by undermining the sacred teachings, incur harm.
By punishing evil, the corrupt will reform themselves.
By promoting good, the enlightened will inspire transformation.
This is the general idea.
The teaching of Shìjiā by the Ménxià prioritizes purity.
It emphasizes staying far from defilements and severing greed and desires.
Therefore, it promotes the excellent karma and cultivates good roots,
guiding the ignorant and providing a ferry bridge for all beings.
For this reason, scriptures are expounded to regulate disciples.
They train their bodies and minds, abandoning all attachments.
Clothing and food are provided by the four communities.
Since the Perfected One passed away and the Dharma-image began to circulate,
in later generations, there has been increasing decline and abuse.
There are indeed vulgar and lowly individuals
who seek to exalt themselves,
and lazy and idle people
who merely wish to evade corvée labor.
They rashly shave their heads and claim to be renunciants.
Their appetites are insatiable, and their pursuits ceaseless.
They enter and exit villages, moving about markets.
They drive livestock and accumulate wealth.
They make a living by farming and weaving, and profit by trading.
Their affairs are like those of ordinary households, their traces like commoners.
When they advance, they violate the rules of the precepts;
when they retreat, they lack the instruction of etiquette.
Some even personally commit robbery and themselves break into houses.
They fabricate falsehoods and associate with powerful villains.
They repeatedly fall into the net of the law, trapping themselves in severe punishment.
They defile the true suchness and destroy the wondrous Dharma.
They are like weeds that taint good seedlings,
and like mud that mixes with clear water.
Furthermore, the land of a gañhāra (qíluó) is originally called a pure abode.
The place for settling the mind should naturally be serene and quiet.
In recent times, many temples have been built,
not seeking quiet and spacious environments,
but only pursuing noisy and bustling locations.
Their construction is uneven, and their roofs are disordered.
They attract hidden individuals and harbor wicked people.
Some are close to brothels and near butchers' and vintners' shops.
Dust fills their rooms, and the smell of mutton and fish fills the roads.
This only fosters a mind of disrespect
and diminishes the meaning of reverence.
Moreover, Lǎo Zǐ's teachings primarily value emptiness and tranquility.
He nurtures his will in non-action and abandons worldly emotions.
Preserving one's true nature and guarding unity is called the Xuanmen (Xuánmén).
Being busy with worldly affairs greatly deviates from this principle.
I, having received the mandate to govern the realm, am keen on promoting religious teachings.
I deeply ponder the benefits and am intent on protecting and upholding them.
I wish to distinguish between jade and stone, to discern between fragrance and foulness.
May the wondrous Dao endure forever, and the field of blessings be eternally firm.
To rectify the source and clarify the stream, it is appropriate to conduct a purge.
All monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and Daoist priestesses
who are diligent in practice, adhere to the precepts,
shall all be allowed to reside in major monasteries and Daoist temples.
The government will provide them with clothing and food, ensuring no shortage.
Those who cannot diligently advance in their practice, or whose precepts are deficient,
and are unfit for offerings, shall all be defrocked.
Each shall return to their hometown.
The relevant authorities shall clearly stipulate regulations and act in accordance with the religious teachings.
All matters that violate the regulations must be stopped and cut off."
In the eleventh year of Zhēngguān, the emperor made a tour to Luòyì.
The Huángjīn had previously debated with monks.
This was heard by the Throne.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, which stated:
"Lǎojūn's teachings are based on purity and emptiness.
Shìjiā's principles depend on cause and effect.
If one seeks their teachings,
the paths of guidance are different.
If one seeks their essence,
the winds of broad benefit are equally effective.
However, the rise of the Great Dao began in primeval times,
its source from the beginning of namelessness.
Its affairs are beyond the visible,
it moves beyond the two primary forces (Yīn and Yáng),
it encompasses and nurtures myriad things.
Therefore, it can govern the state, bring about order, restore simplicity, and return to pristine purity.
As for the rise of Buddhism,
it originated in the Western Regions.
It reached the Later Hàn dynasty,
only then spreading to the Central Land.
The principles of its divine transformations are manifold,
and the karmic retributions are not uniform.
In recent times, faith in it has grown deeply.
People hope for blessings in this life,
and families fear calamities in the next.
Because of this, those attached to worldly customs laugh aloud when they hear the profound teachings,
while those fond of novelty contend to return when they see the ultimate truth.
At first, waves surged in the villages,
finally, it spread like wildfire in the imperial court.
Thus, the rites of a foreign custom
became prominent, preceding all wonders,
while the teachings of Zhūhuá
were relegated to behind the One Vehicle.
This deviation and forgetfulness of return has lasted for generations.
Now the imperial destiny prospers,
relying on the blessings of supreme virtue.
The empire is greatly pacified,
also due to the merits of non-action.
It is proper to clarify and expound this profound transformation.
From now on, in matters of fasts, offerings, conduct, and standing,
as for the appellations, male and female Daoists may precede monks and nuns.
May the custom of returning to the origin be vigorously promoted throughout the nine regions,
and the custom of honoring ancestors be passed down for myriad generations."
At that time, the monks in the capital each submitted fervent remonstrances.
The relevant officials did not accept them.
Shāmén Zhìshí, a talented and intelligent man of a later generation, bright in both internal and external knowledge,
led several elder monks to accompany the imperial retinue and present a memorial.
They reached Guānkǒu.
Their memorial roughly stated:
"We, monks, etc., say:
Our years are advanced like the setting sun,
just now encountering an era of great peace.
Our appearance is frail like willow,
just now meeting a wise and enlightened sovereign.
We humbly hear that a father has remonstrating sons, and a ruler has remonstrating ministers.
Although we are ordained,
we are still among the ranks of subjects and sons.
If there is a transgression, we dare not conceal it.
How dare we not present it!
We respectfully observe the imperial edict.
The state's lineage originates from the Pillar-Bearer.
The custom of honoring ancestors is manifested in previous edicts.
It has been announced throughout the realm without being called 'virtuous'
that Daoists should be above monks and nuns.
We uphold and follow this, how dare we resist the edict!
However, Lǎojūn's teachings for governing the state and managing the family,
and the robes and articles he wore, were not altered.
He did not establish temples or lead disciples.
He resided beneath the pillar to preserve his true nature,
hidden at Lóngdé to cultivate his character.
The wise see him and call him wise;
the foolish see him and call him foolish.
Only the Sīkòu of Lǔ could recognize him.
Today's Daoists do not follow his teachings.
The caps and robes they wear are all remnants of the Huángjīn.
They are fundamentally not descendants of Lǎojūn.
They practice the defiled arts of the Sān Zhāng
and abandon the subtle gate of the Five Thousand.
Instead, they resemble Zhāng Líng, haphazardly practicing spells and incantations.
From the Hàn and Wèi dynasties onwards,
they have always used ghost-dao to influence common customs.
They falsely claim to be descendants of Lǎojūn,
but are actually sprouts of heterodox ways.
If their status is above that of monks,
we sincerely fear that the genuine and false will merge, harming the nation's transformation.
If we do not make this presentation, how can we express the sentiments of subjects and sons?
We have respectfully compiled records from Daoist scriptures and various histories of Hàn and Wèi concerning the precedence of Buddhism over Daoism,
as presented separately.
We humbly pray for Your Heavenly Compassion to graciously listen and examine."
An imperial decree stated: "The principle of ruler-parent's righteousness is weighty among the three instructions.
The way of love and reverence is paramount among all actions.
Although the two schools of Buddhism and Daoism transcend ordinary realms in their principles,
the practice of respect and filial piety accords with Confucian teachings.
Thus, in places of supreme reverence,
the rite of kneeling and bowing is not performed.
This custom has continued for a long time, up to the present day.
The Sòng dynasty briefly changed this practice,
but soon reverted to the old custom.
We uphold the heavenly principle to promote filial piety,
and draw upon earthly righteousness to propagate propriety.
We encourage this through moral teachings, spreading it to both the genuine and the common.
And the foundation of Làixiāng has been firmly established as a heavenly structure.
The transformation of Liánhé has been entrusted to the kings for their regulation, which is presumably the reason for this.
Now we wish to order male and female Daoists, monks and nuns to bow to the emperor, empress, and crown prince, their parents.
However, we fear this might violate their long-held feelings.
This should be referred to the relevant officials for detailed discussion and reporting."
The 15th day of the fourth month of the second year of Lóngshuò.
Guānglù Dàfū, Yòuxiàng, Tàizǐ Bīnkè, Shàng Zhùguó, Kāiguó Gōng of Gāoyáng Jùn, Minister Xǔ Jìngzōng proclaimed.
Monks Wēixiù and others said:
"We respectfully receive the clear imperial edict ordering monks to bow and kneel before the ruler and parents.
It is right to follow this, and there is no reason to resist the imperial command.
However, both Confucianism and Buddhism have put forth texts of righteous remonstrance,
and in expanding their teachings, both have offered humble advice.
We, monks, bear the heavy grace of the state,
which has opened up rites beyond worldly concerns.
We reside peacefully throughout the land,
able to propagate the mind of transcending the mundane.
Therefore, since ancient times, emperors have uniformly followed this practice,
respecting their rites of transforming customs,
and preserving their actions of resisting conventional rituals.
This has allowed the scriptures and teachings to expand, gradually increasing generation after generation.
The patriarchs have been distant, but have appeared from time to time.
From Hàn to Suí, practitioners faced many obstacles.
The winds of spiritual mountains were still obscure,
and the transformations of immortal gardens were still sparse.
It was not until the imperial dynasty vigorously arose, extending its borders overseas,
that the Five Indias and the Five Sacred Mountains were equally pacified.
Shénzhōu and Dàxià shared culture.
The imperial mission greatly prospered,
and the paths of light chariots connected continuously.
All admired these holy traces and established their legacies, thus,
Buddhist monastics came and went ceaselessly.
If now we are to return to bowing to ruler and parents, this would contradict all scriptures.
It would immediately give rise to criticism shocking to common customs,
or evoke expectations of denigration.
In the past, when Jìn Chéng was young,
Yǔ Bīng forged an edict.
Huán Chǔ fabricated deceit.
Wáng Mì spoke out in protest.
And in the late period of Sòng Wǔ, when he was about to impose tyrannical rule,
he ordered monks to bow to the sovereign, but soon ceased it.
This was indeed because the matter was not a state-governing custom,
and the principle exceeded ordinary heavenly rites.
Although it was called rumor, it ultimately led to public discussion.
Moreover, Xià Bó commanded bowing and incurred the wrath of heaven.
Wèi Táo carried out executions and brought down the blame of pestilence.
These instances have long been recorded and widely heard.
We, monks, bearing this, are alarmed and distraught, feeling homeless.
We fear that once an imperial decree is issued, it will be universally enforced in all nations.
This will inevitably make the world look with disdain,
thus propagating the reputation of disrespect.
In distant future generations, there might even be tales of imitation and wrongdoing.
We humbly pray that Your Majesty, who has revived the Three Jewels and compassionately embraced all living beings,
personally accepts the injunctions of transmission
and strives to fulfill the trust of the disciples.
We, monks, inwardly adhere to the orthodox teachings, firmly abstaining from kneeling and bowing.
Outwardly, we obey the clear imperial edict, ordering adherence to Confucian rites of reverence.
Looking up and down, we are profoundly ashamed and fearful.
If we do not make this petition, it would go against the analogy of subjects and sons.
Or, if we obscure Buddhist teachings, we would fall into the crime of deceiving the ruler.
We have respectfully listed the scriptural texts that prohibit bowing to secular authority,
daring to present them to you.
We humbly pray that Your Heavenly Compassion will graciously cast an eye upon them.
Then the court discussions will be harmonious, ultimately following the path of the Jìn ministers.
Neglecting common talks, it will all return to the measure of the Qí Empress.
We defile your majesty and are filled with deep trepidation.
Respectfully submitted."
Submitted on the 21st day of the fourth month of the second year of Lóngshuò.
At that time, over two hundred monks from the capital
went to Pénglái Gōng to submit a memorial and request.
The Left and Right Chancellors said:
"The imperial edict orders detailed discussion on whether to bow or not, which is not yet settled.
You may wait until later." The monks then withdrew.
Thereupon, a great assembly was held at Xīmíng,
where they deliberated together and presented a joint memorial.
It was heard from various officials that...
Sēng Dào Xuān 僧道宣 and others respectfully state:
Since the moving of the carriages from Jīnhé 金河 and the spreading of the teachings from Yùmén 玉門,
through successive sagacious and wise reigns and the flourishing of good ministers,
none have failed to bow their heads, seek the Dharma, and turn towards its clear guidance.
Thus, monasteries stand facing each other, and benevolent temples are spread out like chess pieces.
Heavenly and human beings look up to the path of the field of blessings;
the seen and unseen harbor the rites of the righteous path.
Sincere believers gather like a forest,
and noble guests assemble like clouds.
This enables the teaching to be divided into three methods,
providing a model for ten thousand generations;
the positions of the four assemblies are established,
spreading the pure example of the five vehicles.
Recently, however, due to the vastness of the sea of Dharma, it has become difficult to distinguish categories.
Offenses have increasingly become manifest,
soiling the imperial gaze.
An extraordinary edict was issued,
commanding obeisance to one's sovereign and parents,
displaying a compassionate heart,
and clearly making an exception to the court discussion.
We monks, bearing this clear mandate, are deeply moved and shed tears.
This is truly because our conduct has fallen short in these times,
leading to the emperor's concern and distress.
Moreover, since the Dharma teachings spread eastward, they have often encountered ups and downs.
Three times they have been suppressed, and five times compelled to prostrate.
These were never eras of enlightened peace,
but rather ruled by tyrannical monarchs.
Thus, their decrees were not strategies for governing the nation,
and their deviation from the norm drew censure from good historians.
It is difficult to reverse these matters and return to the old ways.
We humbly contemplate that the Great King (Dàwáng 大王) presides over Jīngdiàn 京甸, controlling the instruments of government.
Both clergy and laity have found relief, and myriad affairs are at peace.
Now, the Dharma gate is closed, and its teachings cannot be transmitted.
At this juncture for eliminating obstacles and overcoming difficulties,
at this time for rescuing the drowning and supporting the imperiled,
we monks find it hard to reach the imperial gate with our pleas.
We merely crane our necks towards the nine heavens in vain;
the heavenly steps are rarely ascended,
and we remain anxious with myriad worries.
Therefore, we presume to present our humble petition,
disclosing it in the hope
that your generous compassion will be extended, and further grace will be bestowed.
This would be to uphold the entrusted teachings,
where pure wind spreads to the nine continents;
the True and Semblance Eras would revive,
and auspicious blessings would illuminate the four seas.
Overwhelmed by our extreme distress,
we present this petition in full.
We are deeply ashamed and mortified by our intrusion.
Respectfully submitted.
The twenty-fifth day of the fourth month.
Sēng Dào Xuān 僧道宣 and others respectfully state:
Since the eastward transmission of the Three Jewels, more than six hundred years have passed.
The four assemblies have established the causes of refuge and precepts,
and the five assemblies have opened up the duties of the field of blessings.
A hundred kings have upheld the transformation of the supreme path,
and for ten thousand generations, the wind of the only sage has been fanned.
Thus, the entire world knows where to return, and all beings turn towards it.
However, since the sun of wisdom has set for over a thousand years,
right conduct is hard to attain, and strict rules are easy to transgress.
Consequently, weeds and tares have defiled the green fields,
and the young have harbored the signs of old age.
These are extensively listed in previous scriptures and heard by all.
Moreover, with the sage hidden, ordinary monastics serve as vessels.
Who else but them can manifest the Dharma in later generations?
Therefore, images of gold, stone, and clay represent the true form;
the Dharma robe and shaven head symbolize the complete monastic.
Based on this, belief and destruction lead to two distinct karmic retributions.
Deviating from this cultivation, all are not the righteous path.
Furthermore, the true and false nature of monastics, their ripeness and unripeness, are difficult to discern.
The depth of their conduct and virtue confounds both fools and the wise alike.
Hence, the scriptures speak of universal offerings,
boundless as the ocean;
the Vinaya establishes distinct rules,
like a shore with boundaries.
Since the lineage has been established, the recognized teachings are followed.
This allows for the establishment of proper deportment for those who leave secular life,
and the attainment of perfect virtue leading to truth.
Thus, devas and nāgas pay reverence, and both the unseen and seen turn their hearts.
Protection and propagation are cherished, and meritorious service flows ceaselessly.
Recently, however, as times have been defiled and people have fallen into decline,
some have secretly adopted monastic attire with deceit,
and others, presumptuously, have relied on emptiness.
Their conduct is not moved by worldly dust,
but their path is obscured by laws and regulations.
Upon hearing this, the emperor issued the command for obeisance to one's sovereign and parents,
turning his heavenly gaze and issuing an imperial edict from court.
We monks, examining ourselves, are filled with shame and fear, as if scorched by fire.
We look at each other, helpless, not knowing where to turn.
We humbly reflect that the Buddha's teachings universally encompass the four assemblies.
Even the unseen and seen dare to harbor whispered discussions.
When people bear this entrusted legacy,
how much more so when they embody this righteousness and goodness, with the establishment of the Dharma as their purpose,
setting an example for the imperial court and enlightening both the clergy and laity.
Now the Three Jewels are in decline, and their salvation depends on circumstances.
We therefore presume to present our counsel,
hoping for salvation and relief.
If we are rescued and allowed to continue our old way of life,
then the entrusted teachings will find their home, and protection and propagation will remain.
