We are deeply apprehensive about presuming to submit this brief statement.
Respectfully submitted.
The twenty-seventh day of the fourth month.
Liè Zǐ 列子 says:
During the time of King Mù of Zhōu (Zhōu Mù Wáng 周穆王), a transformation-person came from the far west.
He reversed mountains and rivers, and moved cities and towns.
His myriad transformations were inexhaustible.
King Mù respected him as a spirit and revered him as a sage.
This marks the beginning of Buddhist influence.
Zhū Shìxíng's 朱仕行 record of Sēng Dào'ān's 僧道安 scriptures says:
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng (Qín Shǐhuáng 秦始皇), eighteen Śramaṇas from the Western Regions came to convert Shǐhuáng.
He did not comply and imprisoned them.
That night, a six-zhang (zhàng 丈) tall Vajra-being
broke open the prison and released them.
Shǐhuáng bowed his head in apology.
The Hàn Shū 漢書 says:
During Emperor Wǔ's Yuánshòu (Yuánshòu 元狩) reign,
the Western Regions were opened, and a golden man was obtained.
He was over a zhàng 丈 tall.
He was displayed in the Gānquán Gōng (Gānquán Gōng 甘泉宮).
The Emperor considered him a great deity,
burning incense and worshipping him.
Later, Zhāng Qiān (Zhāng Qiān 張騫) was sent to Dàxià (Dàxià 大夏) to search for information.
He reported about the country of Shēndú (Shēndú 身毒),
which is Tiānzhú (Tiānzhú 天竺) (India).
They called him Fútú (Fútú 浮圖),
which is Fótuó (Fótuó 佛陀) (Buddha).
This is when the name and form of the Buddha were first known.
Chéng Dì's (Chéng Dì 成帝) Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě (Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě 都水使者) Liú Xiàng (Liú Xiàng 劉向) said:
When Xiàng 曏 examined the imperial library,
he frequently saw Buddhist scriptures.
This indicates that it was already present during the Zhōu (Zhōu 周) and Qín (Qín 秦) dynasties,
and Shǐhuáng's burning did not completely eradicate it.
During Emperor Āi's (Āi Dì 哀帝) Yuánshòu (Yuánshòu 元壽) reign,
Jǐng Xiàn (Jǐng Xiàn 景憲) was sent to the country of Dàyuèzhī (Dàyuèzhī 大月氏).
He returned having recited Fútú (Fútú 浮圖) scriptures.
At that time, fasting and precepts began to spread somewhat in Hàn (Hàn 漢) territory.
According to this, the Dharma had been heard of before,
then it was secretly hidden midway and later revived.
During Emperor Míng's (Míng Dì 明帝) Yǒngpíng (Yǒngpíng 永平) reign in the Later Hàn (Hòu Hàn 後漢),
the emperor dreamt of a golden man flying before his palace.
He then sent Qín Jǐng (Qín Jǐng 秦景) and others to the Western Regions to seek the Buddha Dharma.
Consequently, the Three Jewels were transmitted eastward to Luòyáng (Luòyáng 雒陽).
A painted statue of Shìjiā (Shìjiā 釋迦) was erected;
this is the Buddha Jewel.
The Sìshí'èr Zhāng Jīng (Sìshí'èr Zhāng Jīng 四十二章經) was translated;
this is the Dharma Jewel.
Jiā (Jiā 迦) and Zhú (Zhú 竺) came to present themselves;
this is the Saṅgha Jewel.
A monastery was established west of the city gate of Luò (Luò 雒),
converting people and spreading the teachings from near to far.
This was successively maintained until the end of the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty.
During the Wèi (Wèi 魏) dynasty, five rulers over forty-five years,
reverence deepened gradually, and no destruction or prostration was heard of.
During the Wú (Wú 吳) dynasty south of the Yangtze, four rulers over fifty-nine years,
Sūn Quán (Sūn Quán 孫權) initiated the spread of the Buddha Dharma.
An auspicious omen was felt, and a monastery named Jiànchū (Jiànchū 建初) was established.
Later, Sūn Hào (Sūn Hào 孫皓), with his tyrannical rule, intended to suppress it.
His ministers advised against it, and he desisted.
He summoned monks and received the five precepts.
In Shǔ, there were two rulers for forty-three years.
During that time, among military, state, and political strategies, Buddhism was not heard of, whether in belief or destruction.
The Sīmǎ clan of Jìn established their government in the east and west.
There were twelve rulers
for one hundred and fifty-six years.
The four emperors of the Central Court highly esteemed it to the extreme, and no dissenting views were heard.
Only in the sixth year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of the Eastern Jìn,
after Chancellor Wáng Dǎo and Grand Commandant Yú Liàng passed away, Yú Bīng assisted in governance.
The emperor was a young child.
He issued an imperial edict for monks to bow.
At that time, Minister of Personnel Hé Chōng and Minister Xiè Guǎng, etc.,
argued against bowing.
There were three back-and-forth discussions.
The matter was then dropped.
Sixty-two years later,
in the Yuánchū era of Emperor Ān,
Grand Commandant Huán Xuán, with the awe-inspiring power to shake the ruler, issued a decree for them to bow.
Minister of Personnel Huán Qiān, Central Secretariat Wáng Mì, etc., remonstrated, saying:
"Though the inner intention of a Śramaṇa is profound in reverence,
they do not express it through physical prostration as a ritual.
Their traces fill the land, yet their aspirations transcend the mundane world.
Therefore, no foreign ruler fails to show them respect, for the Way resides in them, making them noble.
They are not made light or heavy by persons. Looking back, the great Dharma has flowed eastward for a considerable time.
Although customs have shifted and governments changed,
its propagation has remained constant.
Is this not because its unique transformative power
has daily utility in nurturing and gradually influencing?
And its pure and simple style
causes no harm to flourishing peace?"
Huán Xuán then sent a letter to Dharma Master Yuǎn of Lúshān,
citing Lǎozi's idea of equating kings and marquises with the "three greats."
Yuǎn replied with the proper etiquette for those outside the mundane,
not subject to the rites of the Central Kingdom.
He then wrote "On Monks Not Bowing to Kings" in five chapters.
The matter consequently ceased.
When Emperor Ān returned to power,
he again highly esteemed and honored Buddhism until Emperor Gōng.
There were eight rulers of the Sòng Liú clan for five *jì*.
Although Emperor Xiàowǔ, in the sixth year of Dàmíng, temporarily ordered bowing to the ruler,
it soon reverted to the former policy.
The Qí, Liáng, and Chén dynasties lasted for more than one hundred and ten years.
Reverence reached its peak, and faith and esteem deepened.
The Wèi clan in the Central Plains had more than ten rulers for one hundred and fifty-five years.
The Buddhist Dharma greatly flourished.
This is fully seen in Wèi Shōu's excellent history.
Only in the seventh year of Zhēnjūn of Emperor Tàiwǔ, listening to slander, he suppressed the Dharma.
After five years, he died from a plague.
Buddhism was then revived and continued until Emperor Jìng.
Since the Jìn lost control of the Central Plains,
and emperors were proclaimed south of the Yangtze,
the country was divided into sixteen states, and these pseudo-governments maintained their faith in the Dharma without diminishing it.
Only Hèlián Fúfú, who occupied Xiàzhōu,
was cruel and insatiable, delighting in killing.
He wore Buddha images on his back and ordered monks to bow to them.
Later, he was struck by lightning and died.
He was then swallowed by the Northern Dài.
His wife and children were tortured and executed, as fully recorded in Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's "Qí Shū."
The Gāo Qí in Yè had six emperors for twenty-eight years.
Their faith and esteem surpassed previous times, and there were no two opinions in the state.
The Yǔwén Zhōu clan had five emperors for twenty-five years.
Initially, Emperor Wǔ highly esteemed the Buddhist Dharma.
Later, he adopted Zhāng Bīn's suggestion
and then embraced Daoism, intending to eliminate Buddhism.
There was Dharma Master Ān,
who wrote "On Two Teachings" to oppose him.
The treatise stated:
"The teachings of the Nine Schools
teach only about one's person,
and are called 'external teachings.'
The teachings of the Three Vehicles
teach the calming of mental delusions,
and are called 'internal teachings.'
Lǎozi is not a teaching master;
his teachings are subsumed under the humility of the Yì.
The emperor heard this, and finding the reasons for preservation and abolition contradictory,
he abolished both.
In less than five years, he died, and his government shifted.
The Suí clan inherited the mandate, with two emperors for thirty-seven years.
Emperor Wén highly esteemed and revived Buddhism.
Stupas were erected throughout the land,
in over one hundred *zhōu*.
All manifested auspicious signs,
as fully recorded in illustrated biographies.
Emperor Yáng, succeeding to the throne, reformed the previous dynasty.
Although he ordered monks to show reverence, they ultimately did not yield.
Since the great transformation spread eastward over six hundred years,
there were three suppressions and five orders to bow.
These actions were neither in line with the classical principles of statecraft
nor were they policies of enlightened rule.
The cruelty of mutilation befell chaotic dynasties,
and the rituals of suppression were propagated in times of decline.
Therefore, affairs and principles deviated from the norm, yet often reverted to the old ways.
This is truly because the Three Jewels are the foundation of refuge and precepts,
and the Five Assemblies occupy the position of fields of blessing.
Although belief and destruction alternate, and calamities and misfortunes shift,
this is due to human ups and downs.
Based on the Way, there has never been rise or fall.
Thus, over a thousand great Sages appeared in the great eon of the Bhadrakalpa,
lived for sixty thousand years,
and upheld the Right Dharma of the Buddha's gate.
Moreover, sixteen venerable ones spread transformation in the three continents,
and nine hundred million Arhats protected and supported the four assemblies.
Based on this, the count of ages has not yet ended.
How can emotional judgment make it conform to Confucian classics?
Furthermore, the *gǔ* hexagram of the *Yì* does not serve kings and marquises,
and the *rùxíng* of the *Lǐ* does not serve the Son of Heaven.
Among the four positions in secular society,
there are still those who do not yield.
How much more so for those who abandon the secular to follow the Way,
yet are expected to conform to the rites of subjects and servants?
Moreover, the August Heaven Lord on High, the spiritual deities of mountains and rivers, and the rulers of men
all offer sacrifices and bow down.
Now, monks receive the Buddha's precepts and possess the Buddha's deportment.
The devas, nāgas, and eight divisions worship their Way and admire their appearance,
all prostrating before monks.
Therefore, they receive hidden blessings and manifest auspicious signs in abundance.
Having heard this from ancient traditions,
how can it be equated with Lǎozi, who equates kings and marquises with the "three greats"?
Thus, the very essence of a Śramaṇa's existence
is not to regard wealth and beauty, nor to be entangled by honor and emolument.
They view worldly customs as floating clouds
and perceive life and form as a mirage.
This is why they are called "those who have left home."
Therefore, those who leave home do not observe family rites.
Those who leave the secular world do not adhere to secular customs.
Their Way is clear,
an enduring canon unchanged for a hundred generations.
Its scope is extremely vast, so I will briefly state it.
Now, I list Buddhist sūtras and treatises that clarify that Śramaṇas do not bow to laypeople.
The lower volume of the *Fànwǎng Jīng* says:
"The Dharma for those who leave home is not to bow to kings, parents, or six relatives.
Nor do they respectfully serve ghosts and spirits."
The sixth volume of the *Nièpán Jīng* says:
"Those who leave home do not bow to laypeople."
The *Sìfēn Lǜ* says:
"The Buddha ordered all Bhikkhus to bow to each other according to seniority.
They should not bow to any laypersons."
The fifty-third volume of the *Fó Běnháng Jīng* says:
"After King Shútóudán and all his relatives and officials
bowed to the Buddha in turn,
the Buddha said:
'O King, you may now bow to Upāli and the other Bhikkhus.'
The King heard the Buddha's teaching, immediately rose from his seat,
and prostrated to the five hundred newly ordained Bhikkhus,
bowing in sequence."
The *Sàzhēnīgàn Jīng* says:
"If one slanders the Dharma of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Mahāyāna Dharma,
criticizing or obstructing it,
one commits a root sin. Moreover, if one slanders, saying there is no good or evil karma or retribution, and has no fear of future generations,
and oneself acts and teaches others to firmly persist in this,
this is called a fundamental grave sin.
Great King,
if one commits this sin and does not repent,
one will burn away one's roots of good and suffer incessant pain.
Because the King performs this unwholesome grave karma,
Brahmacārī Arhats, sages, and holy people will leave the country.
The devas will weep, and good ghosts and spirits will not protect the country.
Ministers and chief ministers will contend and harm each other.
Thieves will rise from all four directions, and the Heavenly King will not descend.
Dragon Kings will hide, and water and drought will be unbalanced.
Countless deaths will occur.
People at that time will not know this fault,
but will resent the devas and complain to the ghosts and spirits.
Therefore, a king who practices the Dharma should act to save this suffering,
and not commit this fault.
More details are as stated in the sūtras."
There are also many other treatises that are not recorded here.
Sēng Dàoxuān and others respectfully addressed the court chancellors and various officials.
We humbly observe the imperial edict ordering monks to show respect to their sovereign and parents.
The principles involved are profound and not to be fathomed by superficial understanding.
Indeed, the conduct of those who have left home (to become monastics) follows the regulations of the enlightened saints.
The distinction between the sacred and the secular has been a consistent practice among all emperors.
When Gàn Mù was in Wèi,
he held himself aloof and yet visited Wén Hóu.
Zǐ Líng resided in Hàn,
and offered a long bow when he sought Guāng Wǔ.
They, though adhering to minor paths, still cherished the principle of lofty detachment.
How could these śramaṇas not uphold the virtue of serene independence?
However, the Three Jewels are held in high regard,
used to establish the rituals of reverence.
The five assemblies express their sincerity,
thereby initiating the path of the field of merit.
Now, if we are made to conform to Confucian rites,
then the Buddha is not one who transcends the mundane world.
If we bow down to sovereign and parents,
then the monastic is not a figure worthy of respect.
This would mean the universal abandonment of the Three Jewels,
and the precepts would vanish from human society.
Confucianism and Daoism would be esteemed as teachers, and the Confucian classics honored above Buddhist scriptures.
In ancient times, during the Jìn and Sòng dynasties, there were established precedents.
The Eight High Officials deliberated thoroughly, providing ample guidance.
We monks bear the heavy trust of the nation, having left home to pursue the path.
We uphold the Dharma and practice the Way, aspiring to follow the sacred principles.
If suddenly ordered to bow, it would burden the profound scriptures.
We are at a loss, restless and not knowing where to turn for refuge.
We respectfully list internal scriptures and historical precedents,
presenting them in detail as before,
for the consideration of the court assembly, humbly requesting their careful examination.
Respectfully submitted.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month,
more than a thousand people, including civil and military officials, those of the ninth rank and above, and provincial and county officials, gathered.
They all sat in the central hall of the capital to deliberate on the matter.
At that time, Sà Mén Dàoxuān of Xīmíng Sì in the capital,
Sà Mén Wēixiù of Dàzhuāngyán Sì,
Sà Mén Línghuì of Dàcí'ēn Sì,
and Sà Mén Huìyǐn of Hóngfú Sì, along with over three hundred other monks,
brought scriptures and previous memorials,
presenting historical precedents to argue their case.
At that time, Sīlǐ Tàicháng Bó Lǒngxī Jùnwáng Bó Chā addressed the śramaṇas, saying,
"The imperial edict orders secular officials to deliberate.
Masters, you may withdraw."
At that time, the discussions among the officials were varied and could not reach a unified conclusion.
Lǒngxī Wáng said,
"The Buddha-Dharma has been transmitted through imperial dynasties for a long time.
An imperial edict has been issued ordering bowing to sovereign and parents, and permission for court deliberation has also been granted.
Currently, the arguments of the assembly cannot be universally followed.
Since the Sīlǐ (Minister of Rites) is in charge of this duty,
he may propose a suggestion first.
Those who agree should sign their names.
Those who disagree should abstain."
At that time, Sīlǐ Dàfū Kǒng Zhì,
holding the brush, drafted a statement as follows.
After ordering the principal clerk to read it aloud,
people then signed according to their ranks.
More than half of them signed.
Zuǒ Sùjī Cuī Yúqìng said,
"The imperial edict orders individual officials to present their views separately.
It is not appropriate to follow this immediately.
The Sīlǐ may dismiss the assembly; each can submit a separate memorial to the Terrace (court)."
At that time, the submitted arguments were varied, some supporting, some opposing, and some mixed.
Now, we shall carefully categorize them according to the responsible department.
First, arguments against bowing will be listed.
Next, arguments for combining (Buddhist and Confucian) bowing will be presented.
Finally, arguments for performing the bow will be described.
All good and bad opinions are recorded as follows.
It is humbly considered that all those holding office,
though observing the Way of respecting superiors,
when acting as teachers, still possess the principle of not being subjects (of the sovereign).
How much more so is the Buddha's teaching, which transcends the mundane world?
Shaving the head is akin to disfiguring the body.
Carrying a staff is different from wearing hairpins and formal attire.
Leaving home is not a realm for caring for parents.
Detaching from the dust (of the world) is certainly not a place for seeking fame.
Its merit is profound in saving sentient beings, and its Way is supremely lofty.
Why must we break their profound gate and drag them into the Confucian track?
Wearing monastic robes and performing Confucian bows,
living in the secular world and conforming to secular rites?
Preserving their teaching yet destroying their Way?
Seeking their blessings yet bending their bodies?
After repeated scrutiny, this is deemed contrary to universal principle.
Moreover, though the Daoist teaching preserves hair and skin,
leaving home and transcending the mundane world ultimately leads to the same goal.
Furthermore, it sets a distant standard for the heavenly structure and greatly establishes the imperial foundation.
Its principles rely on solemnity, formally conforming to loftiness.
They all follow old customs without violating established norms.
If alterations must be made, it may not be in accordance with ancient practices.
Though respecting sovereign and parents weighs heavily on the divine heart,
the Dharma is difficult to diminish, and thus (the matter) remains in the sagely thoughts.
Since we have received the edict to inquire about humble opinions,
we dare to express our utmost sincerity.
We fear not pleasing (Your Majesty),
and thus are deeply fearful and trembling.
In shaping the forms of the two energies (Yin and Yang),
the venerable father is called the greatest尊 (of respect).
In utilizing the five materials,
the great sovereign is marked as noble as heaven.
As for the rites of kneeling and bowing,
those transformed (by secular education) all follow them.
As for the ways of diligent service and providing for parents,
all living beings commonly observe them.
Indeed, in the case of sovereign and parents, their principle transcends all words.
However, the two schools of Daoism and Buddhism leave the dust (of the world) and abandon worldly customs.
Their single principle of emptiness and non-being departs from existence to meet emptiness.
Auspicious signs appeared in Vimalakīrti's (維摩) house,
expounding verses of compassion.
Vital energy floated over Hángǔ Pass,
opening chapters of Daoist virtue.
Living among trees and geese,
they cultivate life in contemplation.
Ceasing the forms of color and sound,
they take nirvana as their mind.
Those who adhere to rites and observe decorum
cannot fully grasp their profundity.
Those who cherish loyalty and practice filial piety
have not savored their vastness.
The principle exists before the Great Ultimate.

From recent antiquity until the present era,

When sorrow enshrouded the twin Sāla trees, and lamentations arose from the three calls,

Confucian scholars were constrained to control the Dharma.
Therefore, it is proper to assist in perfecting the old teachings.
How should new rites be imposed?
It is indeed fitting to yield the solemnity of the imperial screen
and uphold the principles beyond the mundane world.
To entrust the weighty respect for parents
and permit roaming within the circle (of the Way).
In our foolish judgment, adhering to old customs is appropriate.
Your subject has heard that the three calamities transform fire and the six degrees accumulate to an even greater extent.
The two characters form the sūtra, and a hundred achievements are distant.
Therefore, the white hair-mark manifests
to expound the One Vehicle through ten thousand kalpas.
The purple qi floats as a shadow,
blending the myriad distinctions into one unity.
There was a Confucian ferry that again embarked on a different course,

Therefore, it is known that by following names to demand reality and aligning tracks to rectify forms,

By purifying the mind, diligently practicing, cultivating the future, and repenting the past,

Buddhism serves as an inner defense,

Confucianism serves as an outer restraint,
but cannot encompass the spiritual platform.
There is also the Xuánzōng, with its simple principles, that shakes and moves all things.
The soaring Péng and the escaping yì'àn both shorten the Chūn and expand the Jūn.
Without action, without affairs, what is gained, what is lost?
Thus, the two teachings of Daoism and Buddhism are both the Three Jewels.
Buddhism takes the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha as its principle.
Daoism takes the Dao, the Canon, and the Master as its meaning.
How can it merely be that they provide a refuge for life and a means to cultivate nature?
Indeed, they also serve as the foundation for governance, enhancing influence and deepening transformation.
However, the Bhikṣus are not enlightened, and the Xiānshēngs are often eccentric.
They rely on their transcendence from the mundane and act freely.
They take arrogance as boastfulness.
Living in the lowliness of commoners,
they directly present their bodies to the Emperor.
Forgetting the grace of nurturing,
they do not bow down to the Sāndà.
This is indeed what the ruler and father ought to reform,

Therefore, the imperial edict was issued to correct these abuses.
Although those who practice filial piety and loyalty speak forthrightly to change the course,
they also examine antiquity, cherish the Dao, and consider various opinions.
Those who harbor echoes do not let the valley's sound disappear.
Those who touch dust do not let the mountain block the fine.
It is essential to have the praises of the common people
to offer the words of the woodcutters.
Why? Because the Grand Scribe journeyed west over a thousand years ago,
and the Dharma flowed eastward for about six hundred years.
Although it has undergone changes in city and court, the matter has not been diminished or increased.
Only Yǔ Bīng demanded the prostration of the Śramaṇas,
and Huán Xuán debated the rites of the Bhikṣus.
Fortunately, Hé Chōng submitted a memorial, and Huìyuǎn presented a letter.
The matter ultimately did not proceed, and the Dao did not fall.
Therefore, the great Yìjīng was compiled by three Sages,
and the Gu hexagram did not serve kings or marquises.
The great Lǐjì pervaded the two cosmic forces, and Confucian scholars did not serve the Son of Heaven as subjects.
There were also Yán Líng who sat haughtily before Guāngwǔ,
and Yàfū who made a long bow to Hàn Wén.
How could armor be said to offend the unicorn?
Thus, people are not entangled by the snare.
How could the old take precedence over the master's Dao?
How could the Dharma companions come after military glory?
Above are the Nine Heavens' True Emperors and the Ten Stages' Bodhisattvas.
Below are the Nánshān Sìhào and the Huáinán Bāgōng.
Some pay their respects with the wind,
while others roam by riding the qi.
They are unified by one principle, impossible to subdue.
Could there not be such people among ten households of loyalty and trustworthiness?
With the establishment of the five punishments, those who are bound by the three wooden instruments do not prostrate.
How can it be that those who possess the five virtues and are in the three types of mourning should prostrate?
As for those whose crimes are not blamed,
their sincere reverence for virtue is enough to be tolerated and nurtured.
Thus, among all sentient beings,
and all living creatures,
none fails to dedicate their lives to loyalty.
But they do not serve kings as subjects.
None fails to exhaust their efforts to honor filial piety.
But they do not respect their parents.
Although the three chapters are simplified and the three-foot laws are lightened,
if one falls under this category,
even if their offenses are as great as three thousand,
they are not subjected to severe punishment,
nor are they placed under heavy blame.
Is this not because the Daoist and Buddhist systems differ from those of Yáo and Kǒng?
To harm and destroy is precisely contrary to ritual and teaching.
The lotus flower is not the color of tying sashes.
The palm leaves differ from the purpose of carving jade tablets.
People take binding their belts as a standard ritual,
while Daoists wear their caps without belts.
People take binding their hair as an elegant adornment,
while Buddhists shave it off and do not adorn it.
Leaving one's country is not disloyalty.
Leaving one's family is not unfilial.
They leave the dust of the world and cut off love for their ruler and parents.
They conquer desires and abandon affection for their wives and children.
The principle distinguishes them among types of beings,
and they cannot be measured by ordinary standards.
Nothing is more important than parents in life,
yet sons do not thank them.
Nothing gives more generously than Heaven and Earth,
yet beings do not repay them.
The grace of ruler and parent transcends names and images.
How can bowing and prostrating even repay one ten-thousandth of it?
As for those who leave home, do they completely fail to repay their ruler and father?
One thought is certainly to wish for the well-being of the human king as the primary aspiration.
The Four Noble Truths greatly benefit parents.
They are meant to eliminate kalpas of defilement and eternally escape birth and death.
How can this be compared to merely bending the knee for ultimate loyalty
or providing material support for pure filial piety?
If they must be included in the mundane realm,
and placed in Confucian marketplaces,
lowering their demeanor and diminishing their rites,
then nothing is more unfilial than ending the lineage.
Why not compel them to marry?
Nothing is greater disloyalty than not being a subject.
Why not order them to call themselves subjects and concubines?
If the monastic robe becomes court attire,
and they call themselves "poor Daoists" while hurrying to bow,
then both their deportment and rites will be lost, and their titles will also be mismatched.
I deeply fear that the benefit of a single kneeling
will not increase the dignity of the Emperor,
and the effort of a single bow will conspicuously reveal the fall of the three vestments.
So, how can that which is impossible be done?
A king without a father serves the Sānlǎo.
A king without brothers serves the Wǔgēng.
Even the dignity of a ruler has someone to respect.
The respect shown to the Dharma robes is not respect for the person.
If their number is diminished, their Dao is debased.
If the number can be debased, then the Dao is said to be deficient.
How can it be like this: to preserve respect within oneself
and preserve the Dao in things?
If respect is preserved, one is at ease.
If the Dao exists, things are respected.
To respect things is to honor the Dao,
and to honor the Dao is also to respect oneself.
Moreover, the form is like the body,
and the Dao is like the shadow.
Just as the body is like a sound,
the Dao is also like an echo.
When the body moves, the shadow follows.
When the sound rises, the echo responds.
When the Dao is exalted, the form is honored.
When the body declines, the Dao ceases.
How can the Dao residing in the body be made to yield to a body outside the Dao?
How can one expect people outside the world to retain reverence within the body?
Furthermore, they adhere to unity and reside in the Dao, not separated from the dust of the world.
If they can be bowed to, this means the Dao is mundane and can be mundanely mundane, and also partake of the Dao.
Then unity would have two, and the Dao would not be practiced exclusively.
How can one distinguish the ordinary domains of Dao and the mundane and preserve the utmost sincerity of singularity?
According to the Saṃghikā Vinaya,
the monastic robe is revered like a Buddha pagoda.
The monastic robe is called the field-of-merit garment.
Its name "wearing away"
comes from its ability to wear away afflictions.
Its name "armor" for patience
comes from its ability to subdue demonic armies.
It is also likened to the lotus flower unsoiled by mud,
and it is the banner-sign of all Buddhas.
Thus, the meaning of the monastic robe is profound.
If one were to harm this Buddha pagoda and destroy that banner-sign,
it would diminish patience and further devalue the field of merit.
This would cause great uncertainty and ultimately lead to confusion about what to accept or reject.
To remove one's robe and bow is to transgress the mundane, not to follow the decorum of a scholar.
To tidy one's robes and hurry forth means the black robe differs from the rites of court homage.
Therefore, meditation quietly resides in the realm of Śrāvastī,
and walking keeps away from the place of high gates.
The principle cuts off court requests, and affairs deviate from glorious audiences.
Is it not to say, "I respect their Dao,"
that they are invited to come?
If they are invited and then debased, what is the purpose?
Lúshān is where virtue and the Dao reside,
not subject to selective choosing.
Gāntáng is where judgments were heard and rested,
evoking the thought of "do not cut it down."
Mountains and trees are without consciousness,
yet they preserve things through virtue.
Dharma and Dao are abundant,
so how can one honor the Dao and abandon people?
The saying goes:
"If people can broaden the Dao, then the Dao also needs people to be practiced."
Although the position of a king is minor,
it is above all feudal lords.
How can the rites of those who practice the Dao be debased?
If it is said that both are deceitful,
then they can be unified and suppressed.
The way to suppress them is to cut them down.
This would mean much is taken away,
not merely being debased.
If it is said that both are greatly beneficial,
then they should be exalted.
The way to exalt them is to honor them.
How can one honor their Dao and yet make them show deference?
Even if gold and jade are taken as true images,
reverence is not increased by gold and jade.
Even if straw dogs are used to honor idols,
they are not made lighter by straw dogs.
Reverence ultimately relies on the Dao, and importance is not determined by external things.
Just as things cannot alter the Dao,
so too the Dao always follows things.
Śramaṇas wear their robes crosswise,
valuing the Dharma robes.
Is it not that everyone respects their Dharma robes, and not merely depends on the person?
The principle of not prostrating is elevated by the scriptures and monastic rules.
The Dharma is entrusted to kings; its affairs rely on their protection and upholding.
The Law is constant.
Constant practice is not easily changed.
One corner may be reformed, but a thousand gates might be damaged.
To remove barriers is to protect the Law.
To obstruct is to risk the Law's collapse.
Rather than let it collapse, why not protect it?
Why must one compromise oneself for the sake of monks?
Or be constrained by monastic robes?
So that those who seek refuge from all nations reside amidst mere trifles?
The saying goes: "Benefit others by what benefits them."
Then the method of benefiting can also be based on their profound understanding to create benefit.
When the sunlight shines high, the imperial destiny is honored.
The sea connects to the celestial river, and branches link to the precious structure.
Relying on the supreme Dao,
it expounds boundless undertakings.
Other clans and families still respectfully revere the past.
With divine foundations and spiritual traditions, how could the Dao reject the present?
This is the first reason why it is absolutely impermissible.
The Moon Kingdom (Yuezhī) and the Eastern Country (Dōngguó) await this auspicious reign.
The still waters and profound waves, the Dharma clouds moisten with splendor.
Great celebration of liberation,
manifesting the blessings of permanence.
Even former kings and emperors still followed it.
With a sagely sovereign and worthy ministers, why should this change occur?
Although I, your foolish subject, have a thousand thoughts, not one is worthwhile.
If such a creation yields no benefit for the future,
it will incur even a minute fault across kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Gangā River (Hénghéshā jié).
Even if all under heaven were to shatter their heads and all beings grind their bones to powder,
how could this atone for the responsibility of concealment,
and absolve the crime of disloyalty?
This is the second reason why it is absolutely impermissible.
This is why your subject diligently pursues this matter with earnest sincerity.
Scratching my head and pressing my heart, pouring out my liver and draining my gall,
I humbly pray that the sagely court will revive the supreme teaching,
and the Evergreen Nāgavana (Nàiyuàn) will forever turn the Dharma wheel.
With one heart, joyfully record these individuals.
May a hundred blessings brightly shine on the imperial registry.
Then, even if I die, I will live, and it will be acceptable day and night.
I humbly consider that the imperial edict is subtle and delicate, making the meaning difficult to either accept or reject.
If the imperial will is uniform, then one can be led by it.
If the sagely thoughts seek broadly,
then who would not exhaust their deliberations?
As for me, being mediocre and ignorant, how can I presume to speak?
To consider both teachings as nonexistent,
then they are exalted in the sagely reign.
If they are sagely and exalted, then they are not nonexistent.
To consider both teachings as existent,
then they are edited and revised in a clear era.
If they are revised in an era, I fear they are not existent.
This is why I hesitate at the crossroads, with two ends conflicting.
The Dao should preserve its traces, but the principle has not yet satisfied my heart.
How can one peer into heaven through a tube, or measure the sea from a frog's perspective?
The principle transcends the realm of mere approximation,
and the matter surpasses the scope of knowledge.
Naturally, I could lay down my brush and ink, quiet my voice and silence my presence.
Yet I wish to dwell like a bird in a cage, or secretly blow a pipe in a reed organ,
to startle the deaf and make them conform to customs,
and to equally guide the blind and the aged.
Though I have much to express in my heart,
it will ultimately not reach their ears and eyes.
It is simply that the eight winds blow afar,
and all sounds offer their notes.
The two luminaries rise and shine,
and a thousand forms do not hide their shadows.
Here, I seek the light, hoping to turn the tide.
My heart, like a sunflower, turns toward the sun, offering a drop from the dew.
Thus, I brazenly endure summer heat and tread on thin ice in spring.
My trepidation is already extreme,
and my fear and awe are intertwined.
Respectfully submitted.
I humbly consider that in the order of the imperial court, solemn respect comes first.
And among the favors of birth and nurture, filial support is paramount.
The two teachings, Buddhism (Shì) and Daoism (Lǎo), now completely invert this.
They confront emperors with ritual,
and receive respect from parents.
Yet they have been tolerated from ancient times until the present day.
Tracing its profound origin, there must be a reason for this.
It is perhaps because shaved heads differ from caps and crowns,
and kaṣāyas (jiāshā) have no connection to official robes.
Having left home, they naturally have no familial respect.
Having abandoned secular life, how can they be bound by court rituals?
As for the profound teaching's purity and emptiness, and the Daoist (Dàofēng) style's far-reaching breadth,
they value their practices highly and do not bend to kings and marquises.
Emperors have subjects they do not consider as such—
this is what is meant.
Since the state preserves their Dao, it does not compel their bodies to bend.
I hope that the previous chapters will be followed, without deviating from the old customs.
Respectfully submitted.
Deliberation on prostration:
It is clear that Buddhist monastics (shāmén) should prostrate.
In ancient times, when the enlightened emperor (Huángjué) governed the world, he still initiated the distinction between belief and destruction.
How could it be that in the degenerate age of the Dharma image (xiàngmò), the discussion of broad principles did not flow?
Recently, because the ocean of Dharma (Fǎhǎi) is vast and diverse, and categories are difficult to distinguish, there has been defilement of the profound principles (xuányóu).
This has been somewhat heard by the court.
This has led to those who cling to texts,
abandoning the Dao to follow people.
Comparatively speaking,
it cannot be called a great proponent of universal methods.
This is why I examine old facts and, accordingly, admonish them.
May the virtuous gentlemen who revere Buddha
perhaps examine this in detail.
I humbly consider that the purple qi (zǐqì) rises to manifest truth,
and the profound feminine (xuánpìn) wind spreads westward.
The white rainbow (báihóng) sinks and transforms,
and the essence of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) flows eastward.
Reins of feathers soar through the clouds,
casting shadows on the imperial capital (Wángjīng) and condensing myriad wonders.
The ferry of compassion illuminates silence,
opening the Golden Garden (Jīnyuán) and melting into the ultimate Dao.
Its principles encompass both emptiness and existence (kōngyǒu),
its truths penetrate the subtle and the ethereal (xīyí).
It removes and aids earthly defilements, cleansing and washing away karmic accumulation.
The divine Dao supplements the teaching; here there is evidence.
Straightforward conduct has already been followed,
and abuses should rightly be rectified. Originally, the respect for the Three Powers (sān zhī jìng) and the Six Ranks (liù wèi),
establishes the image of high and low.
The foundation of a hundred virtues and the Four Beginnings (sì shǐ),
signifies discourse on boundless gratitude.
When the root is established, then the Dao is born.
When respect is expressed, then rites are harmonious.
This is truly the beginning of kingly transformation,
and the constant principle of heaven and earth.
The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher,
and the Emperor takes Heaven as his model.
Among the Four Greats (sì dà) in the realm, the King is one.
Since the kingly Dao (wángdào) is in balance,
the heavenly law (tiānfǎ) is naturally consistent.
The body is a vessel for the Dharma, and the Dharma is the root of the Dao.
Daoists (huángguān) admire the Dao, and Buddhist monks (zīshang) venerate the Buddha.
To show respect to one's sovereign and father is to subtly conform to the profound waves. Moreover, if the disciplinary records (jièlù) are merely lofty,
one still shows solemnity in prostration.

How much more so when the difference in status is vast, and one completely abandons reverence by bending the knee? It must be that they live alone in mountains and forests, forgetting both self and others,
blending kin and strangers, treating favor and disgrace equally.
Benefiting me is not considered right,
harming oneself is not called wrong.
One should naturally be as if emotionless,
clear and eternally serene.
How could one need to bow one's head before Kāśyapa (Jiāwéi),
and respectfully prostrate before a Heavenly Venerable (Tiānzūn)?
Their mortal forms are no different from secular people,
and showing respect does not violate the truth. Moreover, Bóyáng's (Bóyáng) teachings (xùxùn) are on harmonizing light,
and never lightly expounding teachings through ordinary rites.
This subtly accords with the virtue of humility and reverence,
and far corresponds to the rule of illuminating one's neighbors. Furthermore, among the Three Extremes (sān jí), the teacher is at the bottom.
If even the bottom shows respect,
why doubt the fundamental? If kaṣāyas (jiāshā) differ from dragon-embroidered robes (lóngfǔ),
and gauze caps (hú jīn) are distinct from pheasant-feather caps (bì biàn),
then if the attire is that of a warrior (róng),
why must the prostration be elaborate (huá)?
Each should follow their own root, without violating constant norms.

As for those whose virtuous conduct is steadfast and reclusive, whose pure rules shake the secular world, whose spiritual transformation resonates, whose precepts and conduct are diligent and earnest,
whose literary brilliance shines like a phoenix (tóngluán) or a crane of the clear sky (xiāohè),
who are heralded by brocade banners (jǐn jīng) as auspicious beasts (zhēngshòu) and whose jade talismans (qióngfú) command spirits—
those who are outstanding in virtue and advanced in age,
they may be exempt from the rite of prostration.
All others, initial learners and later aspirants, whose reputation is obscure,
should all be ordered to show respect to their sovereign and father.
Please immediately compile this into a permanent constitution. If this is done, then the advancement of virtue and cultivation of practice,
and the path of transcendence from the dust will be increasingly lofty.
The dedication to asceticism and dwelling on the altar,
and the heart's resolve to enter the Dao will be further encouraged.
The profound traditions will spread afar, and national principles will be harmonized.
This can perhaps be clearly shown to the scenery,
then quiet and unified, the deviations will be from our own making. Why cling to the old?
Indeed, to reflect on the principle of impermanence,
one must rely on extraordinary illumination.
Heaven's profound scrutiny embodies wisdom and discerns the subtle.
It explores the hidden traditions beyond phenomena,
and reaches the profound essence within the cycle.
Although it may temporarily startle ordinary hearing,
it will ultimately establish the Great Dao.
Respectfully submitted.
I humbly consider that Daoist (Dàojiào) teachings are ethereal and empty, and the Buddhist (Shì Mén) gate is secret and silent.
As for illuminating benevolence, aiding beings, and upholding righteousness as the core,
the principles of Confucian (Rúfēng) discourse are not different. As for those of advanced virtue and old age,
whose precepts and disciplines are flawless,
who dwell in forests and secluded valleys,
valuing their practices highly—
such individuals may be accorded high respect.
As for those who are young and ignorant, whose cultivation lacks merit,
who betray truth and mingle with the mundane, whose hearts and actions are often contrary—
it is difficult to justify their exemption from prostration. Rather, whether at home or in the nation, serving parents and serving the sovereign,
how can the ritual of not prostrating be taught? I humbly request that prostration be mandated and established as a constitution for later generations.
Respectfully submitted.
I secretly consider that
the two paths, Buddhism and Daoism, are identical in their emptiness and stillness.
Even if one cannot refine one's mind beyond the mundane world and cast off the shadows of human society,
one should still keep one's conduct separate from common customs and one's affairs distinct from the times.
However, those who leave home today often mingle with the dust of the world.
Outwardly, they exalt themselves by being unyielding,
but inwardly, they are preoccupied with private solicitations.
They merely have the name of entering the Dao,
but ultimately lack the reality of departing from worldly ways.
When it comes to the domains of ruler and parent, where rites encompass both minister and child,
and where filial piety and reverence are esteemed, the righteousness runs deep for family and state.
Without a system of regulations, how can order be maintained?
I humbly request that for Buddhist monks and nuns, Daoist priests and priestesses,
those whose Dao is deemed necessary for the times and whose affairs are due to Dharma assemblies,
even when appearing before the ruler, be allowed to follow the old customs without change.
Beyond this, all others should perform prostrations and bows.
If they return to visit their parents, the path of a child should be clearly expressed.
When in their monasteries or temples, they may follow the Buddhist scriptures.
This would hopefully make them ashamed of being lowly and submissive,
gradually eliminating superficial competition,
and allow them to respect themselves through morality and the Dao,
progressively promoting the teachings and Dharma.
I boldly present this foolish suggestion,
and am filled with shame and trepidation.
Respectfully submitted.
A discussion by the Bureau of Rites regarding the prostrations of Buddhist monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and priestesses before the ruler and parents.
One thousand five hundred thirty-nine people debated and requested non-prostration.
The above is the discussion by Grand Master of Ceremonies Línghú Défēn and others.
They stated: "We humbly believe that all officials in their positions uphold the way of serving their superiors.
When one acts as a teacher, there is still the principle of not being a subject.
Moreover, the Buddha's promulgation of the Dharma transcends ordinary rules.
Shaving the head is akin to harming one's body;
shaking the staff is different from wearing a hairpin.
Leaving home is not a matter of filial support,
and departing from the dust of the world is not a place for seeking fame.
Their merits in saving sentient beings are profound, and their Dao is supremely lofty.
Why must we break open their mystic gates and pull them into the tracks of Confucianism?
To wear the Dharma robes and perform worldly prostrations?
To walk the path of Confucius and perform Buddhist rites?
To preserve their teachings but destroy their Dao?
To seek their blessings but bend their bodies?
A thorough investigation of the essential principles suggests this might not be appropriate.
Furthermore, although the Daoist tradition preserves one's hair and skin,
leaving home and transcending the mundane world ultimately leads to the same goal.
In addition, they establish a distant heavenly structure and greatly initiate an imperial foundation.
Their righteousness relies on solemnity and their style conforms to loftiness.
These two teachings have been continuously passed down for a long time.
Upon the arrival of our Táng Dynasty, their noble influence spread even wider.
Although the imperial grandeur extends far and wide, it truly depends on divine assistance.
And the sacred wheel constantly turns, aided by unseen help.
If we were to suddenly change the old ways now, it would be of no benefit to the future,
and would create a tiny speck of suffering over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Then, if all under heaven were to sacrifice their bodies and be pulverized,
how could we atone for the hidden responsibilities
and cleanse the sin of disloyalty?
Rather than making a mistake in initiating changes,
it is better to err in preserving what is established.
Confucius said,
'Benefit people by what benefits them.'
Lǎozǐ said,
'The Sage has no constant mind;
he takes the minds of the hundred surnames as his mind.'
The benefits brought by these two teachings are immense,
and the hearts of the common people are widely faithful.
To alter what benefits them is not the way of benefiting;
to go against their original minds is not the meaning of having no mind.
We request that the old practices be followed, and non-prostration be allowed."
We humbly believe that Your Majesty's
virtue surpasses that of the most ancient emperors, and your achievements illuminate even the most humble inquiries.
While respect for ruler and parent may originate from your divine heart,
the difficulty of undermining the Dao and Dharma should still occupy your sagely thoughts.
Since we have received the imperial edict seeking humble opinions,
we dare to express our utmost sincerity.
We fear not reaching a balanced conclusion
and are filled with deep trepidation.
One thousand three hundred fifty-four people debated and requested prostration.
The above is the discussion by concurrently acting Senior Censor, Grand Master of the Imperial Sacrifices, Yán Lìběn and others.
They stated: "Your servant has heard that 'the rigid yield, and the soft survive' –
this is the subtle essence of the mysterious wind.
And 'responding to forms, tolerating humiliation' –
this is the subtle teaching of the Buddhist path.
Thus, it can open the source of goodness for the lowly
and promote the meaning of 'not despising.'
Therefore, the voice-hearers (Śrāvakas) lower their ritual to householders,
and the Grand Astrologer (Lǎozǐ) pledged his allegiance to King Zhōu.
These are the models for black-robed monks
and the clear mirrors for yellow-capped Daoists.
Since then, their foundational principles have been lost,
and successive generations have been submerged in their true essence.
Customs cling to their mistaken paths.
When one person acts,
all things observe.
They regulate heaven and earth and drive emperors and kings.
They turn the golden wheel in the pure land
and construct the jade capital in the mystic realm.
Consequently, those seeking the true Dao (Daoist priests) follow the ancient tradition of 'storehouse-keeper,'
and the shaved-head monks (Buddhists) propagate the splendid canon of 'prostrating the feet.'
Furthermore, the great sun shines in the heavens,
displaying its unparalleled brilliance.
The great emperor is honored and rules the universe,
reaching the utmost noble position among the three powers (heaven, earth, humanity).
Although the regulations of the two teachings sever them from worldly appearances,
their affairs only involve leaving home;
they cannot escape the state.
They all received their forms from the mirror of Yu the Great
and all look up to the transforming influence of Yao.
How can they resist ritual before the imperial residence and uniquely exalt their true path?
To lightly esteem elders and arrogantly treat superiors is perverse in human conduct.

Deeply troubled by worldly matters.

Respectfully recorded.
Buddhist scriptures state that monastics (shāmén) who have left home should not bow to their parents.

The Fànwǎng Jīng (Fànwǎng Jīng) states:

The Shùn Zhèng Lǐ Lùn (Shùn Zhèng Lǐ Lùn) states:

The mysterious teaching has spread eastward for over six hundred years.

Their inner reverence for ruler and parents would not dare to be negligent.

And cultivating reverence in the heart has a long tradition.

They looked up, hoping for the divine Yǔ,
to dredge this Dharma stream.
Shì Yàncóng said:

I delighted in this matter in my youth and have searched extensively as an adult,

Reverence (敬) communicates sincerity of heart;

Those with compassionate minds and virtuous qualities,

Moreover, the profound and excellent compassionate concentration cannot be invaded by weapons or poisons.

In later ages, many students of the gate follow their own minds.

Observing their admonishing texts and grasping the depth of their earnestness,

Therefore, when the superior person hears this, tears flow endlessly.

Furthermore, life and death alternate, not just morning and evening.

What benefit is there for the spirit?
Therefore, the perfect ones lament and are often saddened by the deluded beings.
Great Bodhisattvas speak out, sighing over the resentful souls in affliction.

The essence of Śākya's teachings is compassion.
The most important aspect of compassion is valuing the preservation of life.

If one eats the father of a sentient being,
that sentient being will also repay by eating one's father.
If one eats the mother of a sentient being,
that sentient being will also repay by eating one's mother.
If one eats the child of a sentient being,
that sentient being will also repay by eating one's child.
Such is the cycle of enmity and retribution, mutually devouring.
Through kalpas and long nights, there is no end.
As the sūtras say:

The ghost also, for five hundred lifetimes, severed her life-root.
All these are stated in the sūtras.

I have already roughly explained how the karmic hindrances of fish and meat invite bitter fruits.

The lifespan in Jambudvīpa is said to be 120 years,

Change and decay are swift, with no distinction between old and young.
The sūtras say,
"In a single thought, there are sixty kṣaṇas."

It is extremely difficult to escape hell.

Although one may observe a long fast and eat only vegetables,

that too is impossible.
Why is this?
Because even if you do not commit various sins in this life,
if the karmic retribution of a later life is strong and there are no present skillful means,
the suffering of the three evil paths and the like cannot be prevented.

All bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs must believe the Buddha's words.
You should exert yourselves.

Vegetables, fish, and meat are all but one delusion.

All those who cannot abandon fish and meat say,
