Such statements are all erroneous views.
Now, let me roughly explain again.
It is not so.
If a person has eaten vegetables for a long time, their *róngwèi* (nutritive and protective *qì*) circulates smoothly.
Such people are often prone to heat.
When *róngwèi* circulates smoothly, they can eat and drink.
Because they eat and drink, their *qì* and strength are full.
Thus, vegetables are not cooling and can be nourishing.
All ascetic practitioners also eat vegetables,
and most of them are prone to heat, yet are strong.
Their minds are clear and refreshed, with less dullness and fatigue.
Fish, by nature, are generally cold.
Blood and腥 (fishy smell) by their nature increase a hundred ailments.
Therefore, it is reasonable that the minds of those who eat fish and meat are dull and turbid.
All four limbs naturally feel heavy, not to mention
the future retribution of suffering in the three evil paths.
Immediately, the four great elements (body) are in disharmony.
Is this not delusion?
Everyone's mind has its own attachments.
Those who enjoy fish and meat consider them warming and nourishing.
This is an erroneous view and should not be believed.
There is another kind of person
who, upon eating vegetables and feeling cold, breaks their vegetarianism.
This is because the practitioner has not grasped the true meaning of vegetarianism.
Vegetables and fish/meat are like water and fire.
One has just begun to gain strength from eating vegetables,
and then eats fish and meat again.
The fishy smell of fish and meat can negate the power of vegetables.
Therefore, the deluded say,
"Vegetables are cold by nature."
Those who frequently break their vegetarianism
neither gain the power of vegetables
nor the perverse benefits of fish and meat.
They are often weak and cold, with little capability.
All bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should also know one more thing:
eating fish and meat is the realm of Māra; it is practicing Māra's deeds.
An irresolute mind often encounters obstacles.
Internal and external Māras work together to disturb one.
Therefore, practitioners should remember:
fish, meat, and alcohol are Māra's potions.
Hence, it goes without saying
that those who eat fish and meat and indulge in alcohol
are abandoned by good deities, and have no righteous *qì* within.
Such people are often afflicted and distressed.
There is another kind of person
who, though able to eat vegetables,
relies on this with arrogance and much anger.
They are prone to greed.
Such people also fall into Māra's realm and experience much distress.
Furthermore, there is another kind of person
whose external conduct appears mature, but whose inner mind is crude and evil.
When they see someone superior to themselves, they constantly harbor resentment and jealousy.
All their unwholesome actions are concealed.
Such people also tread the path of Māra.
Even though they eat vegetables, they experience much distress.
If one's mental strength is resolute and righteous, and one eats vegetables sparingly,
such people
are largely supported by wholesome power.
They are often capable.
If there is anyone who is not upright, they should reflect and awaken.
Do not expect resolute people with an irresolute mind.
All great virtuous bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who have already achieved their practice,
from today onward, should skillfully guide others,
so that those who have not yet achieved it may all achieve it from now on.
If you have already practiced, may your will and strength be firm.
If you have never practiced, may you all reform.
Let us together sow the seeds of Bodhi today.
Do not be surprised.
Disciple Xiāo Yǎn.
What was reported earlier:
368 temple officials, 25 venerable monastics, 574 Dharma-studying monastics, 39 Dharma masters.
The total number of bhikṣus listed above is 1,006.
369 temple officials, 68 Dharma-studying bhikṣuṇīs, 5 Dharma masters.
The total number of bhikṣuṇīs listed above is 442.
The total number of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs listed above is 1,448.
All, on the 22nd day of the fifth month, at the fifth watch (3-5 AM),
were called out to the gate of Fèngzhuāng.
On the morning of the 23rd day,
Fǎyún of Guāngzhái Temple
ascended the high seat facing east in front of the Huálín Hall to serve as the Dharma teacher.
Huìmíng of Wǎguān Temple
ascended the high seat facing west to serve as the *dūjiǎng* (chief expounder).
They recited one-fourth of the "Four Marks" chapter from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
explaining the meaning that meat-eaters sever the seeds of great compassion.
Fǎyún elucidated.
The imperial carriage personally attended.
Mats were spread on the ground north of the high seats.
The two assemblies of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs sat in order.
After the discourse,
Dàochéng of Qíshé Temple
again ascended the high seat facing west,
and recited this text on severing meat.
Next, he recited the transmitted sayings.
After reciting, he again bowed and repented.
A general midday meal was served, and then they departed.
On the 23rd day,
it happened that some bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs later
still said,
"There is no prohibition against meat in the Vinaya, nor a method for repenting meat consumption."
On the 29th day of that month,
an imperial edict again invited 141 Dharma-studying bhikṣus and 57 Dharma-studying bhikṣuṇīs
to the Huálín Huáguāng Hall, where Fǎchāo of Zhuāngyán Temple,
Sēngbiàn of Fèngchéng Temple,
and Bǎodù of Guāngzhái Temple, three Vinaya masters,
ascended the high seats. Seats were laid on the ground for the imperial retinue.
The other bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs also did likewise.
The imperial edict asked the three Vinaya masters, Fǎchāo and others, saying,
"The ancients said,
'To stop boiling, nothing is better than removing the firewood. To end faults, nothing is better than silence.'
For a disciple to remain silent is indeed very easy.
But I wish to perfect others and ensure the continuation of the Buddha's lineage, to jointly propagate the Dharma teachings with all bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Moreover, in this matter, I cannot remain silent.
Therefore, I have now gathered everyone before the great assembly
to seek the intent of the Vinaya.
I hear various
bhikṣus say,
'There is no Dharma for prohibiting meat in the Vinaya,'
and 'There is no Dharma for repenting meat consumption.'
How have the Vinaya masters guided people up to now
to cause them to have such doubts?"
Fǎchāo respectfully replied,
"The Vinaya teachings are one,
but people interpret the underlying meaning of the text differently.
According to Fǎchāo's understanding,
although the Vinaya permits the consumption of three kinds of pure meat,
its true intent is to permanently prohibit it.
How do we know this?
First, it clarifies the prohibition of ten kinds of impure meat.
Next, it allows the eating of three kinds of pure meat.
It has not yet allowed the eating of nine kinds of pure meat.
Such gradual prohibition
indicates the intent for permanent prohibition.
Fǎchāo has always taught
in this manner."
The Emperor then asked Vinaya Master Sēngbiàn,
"How do you guide people?"
Sēngbiàn respectfully replied,
"Sēngbiàn's understanding of the general meaning has always
not differed from Fǎchāo's.
However, teachings have shallow and deep levels,
and they guide beings in stages.
If one discusses eating three kinds of pure meat,
it is rationally a fault.
But since the teaching has not yet reached its ultimate,
it therefore permits such.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng asked Fǎshī Bǎodù again.
How do you provide guidance?
Bǎodù replied:
What this ignorant and limited one understands is merely the gradual teaching.
Therefore, the Vinaya texts permit eating three kinds of pure meat.
If the Nirvāṇa Sūtra fully clarifies the correct principle,
it does not permit eating meat.
If one is of sharp faculties,
from the teaching regarding the three kinds of pure meat,
one immediately understands to not eat any.
If one is of dull faculties,
one must await the later teaching.
The Emperor also asked Fǎshī Fǎchāo.
The previous answer was an interpretation beyond the text.
If we base it on the Vinaya text, how would you decide?
Fǎchāo replied:
My daily understanding is just as I previously stated.
The Emperor asked Fǎshī Sēngbiàn.
Do your views align with Fǎshī Fǎchāo's?
Sēngbiàn replied:
They align with Fǎchāo's understanding.
The Emperor asked Fǎshī Fǎchāo.
Have you always interpreted the Vinaya in this way?
Do all Vinaya masters eat meat or not?
Fǎchāo replied:
I do not know how others are.
Fǎchāo himself has never eaten meat.
The Emperor asked Fǎshī Sēngbiàn.
Do you eat meat?
Sēngbiàn replied:
I never used to eat meat.
In middle age, due to illness, I occasionally relented.
The Emperor asked Fǎshī Bǎodù.
And what about you?
Bǎodù replied:
I originally resided in Dìnglín and later moved to Guāngzhái.
In neither place was meat brought in.
If I were elsewhere, for illness, I could not avoid relenting either.
The Emperor asked, "When you expound the Vinaya, do you eat meat?" Bǎodù replied:
When expounding, there are always disciples present.
In the midst of disciples, I dare not.
The Emperor asked, " 'Dare not' has two meanings.
Is it 'dare not eat' or 'dare not not eat'?"
The Emperor then asked Fǎshī Sēngbiàn.
When you expound the Vinaya on a daily basis, do you allow your disciples to eat meat
or not allow them?
If you do not allow eating meat, then those who eat meat should be expelled.
If you allow it, how do you explain it?
Sēngbiàn replied:
If we speak according to the teaching, it does not entirely say "not allowed."
If we discuss its intention, it has not always broadly permitted it.
The Emperor asked, "I am now asking directly.
According to the teaching, is it allowed or not allowed?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "According to the teaching, it is not forbidden."
The Emperor asked, "Is 'not forbidden' the same as 'allowed' or 'not allowed'?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "Following the principle, it permits them to eat three kinds of pure meat."
The Emperor asked, "One may not have seen the killing,
one may not have heard the killing.
How can one be free from doubt?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "If there are causes and conditions for seeing, there is no need to doubt.
If there are causes and conditions for hearing, there is also no need to doubt.
Only when one encounters it can one doubt."
The Emperor asked, "Buying fish and meat with money,
is this doubt or not doubt?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "If according to the ultimate truth within the truth, it is certainly doubt."
The Emperor said, "You must not see it from the ultimate truth within the truth."
Sēngbiàn replied, "If we discuss it from the ultimate truth,
the assembly of monks should not purchase fish and meat.
Is the current question, in this matter, doubt or not?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "If according to the teaching, it is not doubt. For whom do the people in the market kill?"
The Emperor replied, "They kill for the buyers."
Sēngbiàn said, "But the buyers do not have this thought."
The Emperor asked, "Since the meat buyer is not confused,
how can he not know that it is killed for the buyer, and yet not have this thought?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "At that time, they have the thought of 'already dead meat'."
The Emperor asked, "Is 'dead' referring to self-dead,
or is 'dead' referring to killed?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "This point is a statement within the ultimate truth.
When discussing it according to the teaching, one can only say this."
The Emperor asked, "Since the Fǎshī expounds and guides people,
and is a bulwark of the Dharma for people,
how can you say 'one can only say this'?
Just answer: what intention should people have when buying?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "The intention of buying that which is self-dead."
The Emperor asked, "If it is self-dead, then there should be such things everywhere in monasteries too.
Why must one go to a butcher's house to buy?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "From the perspective of the ultimate truth, it is indeed doubt."
The Emperor asked, "If from the perspective of the ultimate truth, it is indeed doubt,
how can one avoid doubting meat-eating?"
Sēngbiàn had no further reply.
The Emperor asked again,
"Should this meat be regarded as having the taste of meat,
or the taste of vegetables?"
Sēngbiàn replied:
"It is still regarded as having the taste of meat."
The Emperor asked, "Is it out of compassion that one eats meat,
or without compassion that one eats meat?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "This is not compassion."
The Emperor asked, "If it is not compassion,
how can it not be killing?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "From the perspective of the ultimate truth, it should always not be allowed.
In terms of actual events, it is like this."
The Emperor asked, "Does the Vinaya teaching intend for people to attain liberation?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "It enables people to attain liberation."
The Emperor asked, "Does eating meat lead to liberation?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "No."
The Emperor asked, "If so, why does it allow eating meat?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "It is spoken for practitioners of shallow practice,
to lead them to deeper practice."
The Emperor asked, "Is it spoken for those who have received the full precepts,
or for those who have not received them?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "It is spoken for those who have received the full precepts."
The Emperor asked, "Since it is spoken for those who have received the full precepts,
not for novices,
how can it be that allowing eating meat is leading them to deeper practice?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "This is the initial teaching, not the ultimate teaching."
The Emperor asked, "What do you mean?
The initial teaching teaches people who have received the full precepts?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "Sēngbiàn's understanding goes only this far."
The Emperor asked again,
"When did the Vinaya teaching originate?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "It originated after the eighth year, up until Nirvāṇa."
The Emperor asked, "If so, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra prohibits meat.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra prohibits meat.
The Aṅgulimāla Sūtra also prohibits meat.
The Mahāmegha Sūtra and the Bāoxiàng Sūtra all prohibit meat in their Vinaya sections.
If it goes up until Nirvāṇa, how can there be no prohibition on meat-eating?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "The Vinaya continues the initial teaching.
That is why it is so."
The Emperor asked, "Since the Vinaya says it continues the initial teaching up until Nirvāṇa,
then by Nirvāṇa, it should have stated the prohibition of meat."
Sēngbiàn replied, "If on the side of the prohibitive teaching,
this is a continuation of the initial teaching, applicable through the five periods.
It does not mean everything is the same."
Sēngbiàn's explanation goes only this far.
The Emperor asked, "Since the Fǎshī is a great Vinaya master,
guiding the assembly,
today the assembly expects your judgment, Fǎshī.
You cannot say 'only this far.'
'Only this far' cannot stand,
and 'not only this far' also cannot stand.
I just ask, is this Upāli's Vinaya?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "It is."
The Emperor asked, "When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa,
since Upāli was personally present,
how can the Vinaya text not prohibit eating meat?"
Sēngbiàn replied, "This is a continuation of the earlier, proximate teaching."
The Emperor asked, "If you say it approaches the teaching,
the proximate teaching also does not clearly prohibit eating meat.
Furthermore, before Nirvāṇa, Kāśyapa already practiced not eating meat.
If the Dharma is different from this,
then it is not Upāli's Vinaya.
It is the Vinaya of a different school.
How can you use this to expound and convert the monastic assembly?"
Sēngbiàn did not reply again.
The Emperor asked Fǎshī Bǎodù,
"Since your teachings and practices are the same as his,
how do you explain these words?"
Bǎodù replied:
"Matters within the Vinaya were expounded by Upāli,
and matters within the Sūtras were all expounded by Ānán."
The Emperor asked, "If so, then matters within the Vinaya should not all be found in the Sūtras."
Bǎodù replied, "If matters in the Sūtras draw upon the Vinaya,
and matters in the Vinaya draw upon the Sūtras."
The Emperor asked, "When the Buddha expounded the Sūtras, he made certain regulations,
which were then compiled into the Vinaya.
How can it then 'draw upon the Vinaya'?
If Sūtras all draw upon the Vinaya,
then the expounding of Sūtras should be after the Vinaya."
Bǎodù replied, "I merely mean that there are places in the Sūtras that clarify precepts.
I ignorantly believe they should be related."
The Emperor asked, "If we speak of relatedness,
when have the meanings of the Three Baskets not been related?
There are Vinaya and Abhidharma within the Sūtras.
There are Sūtras and Abhidharma within the Vinaya.
There are Sūtras and Vinaya within the Abhidharma.
I am not saying there is no such meaning.
But I ask, Fǎshī, the Vinaya you are currently expounding,
is it Upāli's Vinaya,
and does it not contradict the Sūtras?"
Bǎodù replied, "What I am currently expounding is Upāli's Vinaya.
It does not contradict the Sūtras."
The Emperor asked, "If it is Upāli's Vinaya and does not contradict the Sūtras,
then the meaning of prohibiting meat should not differ from the Nirvāṇa Sūtra."
Bǎodù replied, "The Nirvāṇa Sūtra explicitly prohibits meat. Although the Vinaya text does not clearly state it,
Upāli's intention has never been to permit meat."
The Emperor asked, "Since the Vinaya is a complete teaching,
and Upāli did not permit meat,
how can there be no text to that effect in the Vinaya?
Fǎshī, this explanation is very contradictory.
It is only suitable for explaining to novices (Śrāmaṇeras) and probationer nuns (Śikṣamāṇās) in the monastery.
You must not use this to answer disciples."
Bǎodù replied, "This ignorant one's understanding indeed reaches its limit here."
Zhì again asked.
The various Vinaya masters below the seat,
how do they understand it?
Dào'ēn of Lóngguāng Sì respectfully replied,
"The Vinaya texts do not prohibit it.
The Pàrīnirvāṇa Sūtra explicitly prohibits it."
He asked, "Whose Vinaya (rules) is the Dharma master expounding?"
He replied, "It is the Buddha's Vinaya."
He asked, "The citations are indeed vast and profound.
I just don't know if this Vinaya is Upāli's Vinaya."
He replied, "Upāli respectfully recounted the Buddha's Vinaya."
He asked, "Did Upāli collect all of what the Buddha said?"
He replied, "He collected what was said during the first four periods,
but not during the Pàrīnirvāṇa period."
He asked, "If that is the case, how could Kāśyapa have said to Ānanda,
'From where did the Buddha preach the Dharma
until the Pàrīnirvāṇa period, collecting the Sūtra Piṭaka?'
And how could he have said to Upāli, 'From where did the Buddha preach the Dharma
until the Pàrīnirvāṇa period, collecting the Vinaya Piṭaka?'
How can it be said that only the first four periods are taken and not the Pàrīnirvāṇa period?"
He replied, "During the Pàrīnirvāṇa period, no more precepts were established."
He asked, "The Pàrīnirvāṇa Sūtra says,
'He who eats meat severs the seed of great compassion.
From this day forth, I command all my disciples
never again to eat any kind of meat.
All meat is prohibited, including that of animals that died naturally.'
This kind of prohibition,
is it a precept or not a precept?"
Dào'ēn did not reply again.
Zhì again asked,
"The various Vinaya masters personally expound the Vinaya,
and the various great Dharma masters all expound the Mahā Pàrīnirvāṇa Sūtra.
How is it that sometimes they 'unleash the 'su' (vegetarian diet)?'
What is the meaning of 'su'?
If one does not 'unleash' 'su',
then 'unleashing' it is not 'su'.
If 'su' can be made 'not su',
since precepts are pure,
can purity also be made impure?"
"These Vinaya masters personally violate this teaching.
What is said in external writings,
'climbing over a short wall to steal and copy writings,'
precisely means this." Fǎchǒng of Xuānwǔ Sì respectfully replied,
"Closing the door to defilement is called 'su' (purity/vegetarianism); opening the door to defilement is called 'not su'."
He asked, "If that is the case, how can the monastic community open the door to defilement?"
He replied, "They actually should not open it.
But the desire and attachment are deep,
which is why it is so."
He asked, "How does one repent?"
He replied, "Sincere and utmost devotion is repentance.
He who can repent is a great hero (mahāsattva)."
He asked, "Do the learners repent immediately?
For instance, when disciples invited various Dharma masters, numbering up to a thousand,
and the guiding master led them to repent,
did the Dharma masters repent at that time?"
He replied, "How could they not repent?"
He asked, "If they repented, would they eat meat again after leaving the monastery?"
He replied, "Certainly not.
But among them, there are many ignorant ones,
who perhaps cannot avoid eating again."
He asked, "Eating again after leaving the monastery,
how does it compare in severity to the initial act?"
He replied, "It is the same."
He asked, "Why is it the same?
The first time, one simply ate.
Afterwards, one has already vowed before the Buddhas and then eats again.
How can it be the same?"
He replied, "The first person has no shame (hrī) and no fear of wrongdoing (ottappa);
the later person has shame.
Thus, there is an aspect in which the later person is superior to the first."
He asked, "If that is the case, one could first claim shame and painfully beat the person in front,
saying, 'I am ashamed of you, so I beat you.'
'I am ashamed of you, so I eat you.'"
He replied, "It is like a person with great wrong views who has no shame.
Since they know shame,
they are therefore understood to be different from those who are shameless."
He asked, "To first claim shame and yet still eat,
this is to knowingly and intentionally commit a transgression,
not to be called shame.
If one did not know at first,
it might be a mistake.
To later feel shame is truly shame.
Is it not to knowingly and intentionally commit a transgression?
Its sin is greater than not knowing.
Furthermore, shame means not repeating the transgression.
If one directly transgresses again,
it is also a violation of the initial intention.
Arguing this, the sin is therefore even greater."
He replied, "The sūtras contain clear text.
Jīvaka said, 'You have shame,
therefore your sin can be extinguished.'
Shame is a pure (white) Dharma."
He asked, "Dharma master, you have the words of the sūtra but not its meaning. This means:
If after committing a sin, one later knows shame,
this is a pure Dharma.
It does not say that one initially feels shame and then intentionally commits a sin,
considering that a pure Dharma."
He replied, "The sūtra also says, 'Shame is the supreme garment.'
If that is the case, then there is also the meaning of 'not the supreme garment.'"
He asked, "The meaning is also thus.
If one is actively committing a sin,
even if one claims shame, it will ultimately be of no benefit.
If after committing a sin, one can generate shame,
that is truly the supreme garment."
Fǎchǒng did not reply again.
After Fǎchǒng finished his replies,
the three Vinaya masters all stepped down.
He then ordered Jǐngyóu of Shǐxīng Sì
to ascend the high seat
and read the sūtra texts concerning the prohibition of meat, as explained in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra and the Aṅgulimāla Sūtra.
They are now recorded as follows.
Mahāpārinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter 7, On the Four Marks, Part One. At that time, Kāyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Shìzūn,
a person who eats meat should not be given meat [as alms].
Why?
I see that those who do not eat meat acquire great merit.”
The Buddha praised Kāyè,
“Excellent, excellent!
You are now truly able to understand my intention well.
A Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva should be like this.
Good man,
from today onwards, I do not permit Śrāvaká disciples to eat meat.
When receiving alms from Dánmóyè,
one should regard this food as if it were one’s own child’s flesh.”
Kāyè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Shìzūn,
why does the Rúlái not permit eating meat?”
“Good man,
those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion.”
Kāyè again said,
“Why did the Rúlái previously permit Bhikkhu to eat three kinds of pure meat?”
“Kāyè,
these three kinds of pure meat were progressively restricted according to circumstances.”
Kāyè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Shìzūn,
for what reason are the ten kinds of impure [meats], and even the nine kinds of pure [meats], again not permitted?”
The Buddha told Kāyè,
“This too was gradually restricted according to circumstances.
You should know that this is precisely the meaning of presently prohibiting meat.”
Kāyè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How is it that the Rúlái praises fish and meat as delicacies?”
“Good man,
I do not speak of fish and meat as delicacies either.
I speak of sugarcane, polished rice, rock candy, all grains, wheat, black rock candy, milk, cheese, butter, and oil as delicacies.
Although I spoke of being allowed to possess various clothes,
what should be possessed must be of a faded color.
How much less should one be attached to the taste of fish and meat!”
Kāyè again said,
“If the Rúlái prohibits eating meat,
then those five kinds of flavors—milk, cheese, buttermilk, raw butter, cooked butter, sesame oil, and so on—
and various clothes, Kāoqiéyé clothes, conch shells, leather, gold and silver utensils,
and such things, should also not be accepted.”
“Good man,
you should not follow the views of those Níqiàn.
All the precepts laid down by the Rúlái have different intentions.
Therefore, eating three kinds of pure meat was permitted.
Due to a different consideration, ten kinds of meat were prohibited.
Due to a different consideration, all [meats], including those that died naturally, are completely prohibited.
Kāyè,
from today onwards, I decree to all disciples
that they shall not eat any meat again.
Kāyè,
for those who eat meat,
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
all sentient beings, hearing the scent of their meat, will generate terror.
For example, if someone has been near a lion,
others who see them and smell the lion’s odor also generate terror.
Good man,
just as a person who eats garlic has a foul and repulsive odor,
others who see them and smell the odor abandon them and leave.
Even those who see them from afar do not wish to look,
much less approach them.
Those who eat meat are also like this.
All sentient beings, hearing the scent of their meat,
are all terrified and generate the thought of fearing death.
Living beings that move on land, water, or in the air all abandon them and flee,
all saying, ‘This person is our enemy.’
Therefore, Bodhisattvas do not habitually eat meat.
To save sentient beings, they manifest eating meat,
but although they appear to eat it, in reality, they do not.
Good man,
such Bodhisattvas do not even eat pure food,
how much less would they eat meat!
Good man,
countless centuries after my Nirvāṇa,
the four kinds of Sages will all attain Nirvāṇa again.
After the destruction of the Right Dharma, during the Age of Semblance Dharma, there will be Bhikkhu
who appear to uphold the Vinaya, read and recite few scriptures,
are greedy for food and drink to nourish their bodies.
The clothes they wear are coarse, ugly, and repulsive.
Their appearance is haggard, without dignity.
They raise cattle and sheep, carry firewood and grass.
Their heads, beards, hair, and nails are all long and sharp.
Although they wear kasaya, they are like hunters.
They scrutinize slowly, like cats stalking mice.
They constantly proclaim, ‘I have attained Arhatship.’
They suffer from many illnesses and sleep in filth.
Outwardly, they appear virtuous and good, but inwardly, they harbor greed and jealousy.
They are like Brāhmaṇas who observe the vow of silence, and so on.
They are truly not Śrāmaṇas but appear as Śrāmaṇas.
Their wrong views are rampant, and they slander the Right Dharma.
Such people
destroy the precepts, right conduct, and deportment established by the Rúlái, speak of the fruit of liberation as departing from impurity,
and destroy the profound and secret teachings.
Each, following their own will, speaks in opposition to the sūtras and vinayas,
and says,
‘The Rúlái has permitted us all to eat meat.’
They generate this theory themselves,
saying it is spoken by the Buddha.
They dispute with each other, each claiming to be a Śrāmaṇa Śīzǐ.
Good man,

They use precious canopies and leather sandals, associate with kings, ministers, and elders.
They practice divination of stars and constellations.
They diligently practice medicine.
They keep male and female slaves.
They possess gold, silver, lapis lazuli, conch shells, agates, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, jade, cowrie shells, and various fruits.
They learn various crafts.
Painting, pottery, writing, teaching.
Planting roots and plants.
Worm magic and incantations.
Compounding various medicines.
Performing music and dance.
Using incense and flowers to adorn their bodies.
Playing dice and Wéiqí.
Learning various skills. If there is a Bhikkhu who can renounce such evil deeds,
that person shall be called my true disciple.”
At that time, Kāyè again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Shìzūn,
Bhikkhu, Bhikkhunī, Upāsaka, and Upāsikā live by depending on others.
If, when begging for food, they receive food mixed with meat,
how can they eat it in a way that accords with the pure Dharma?”
The Buddha said,
“Kāyè,
they should wash it with water to separate it from the meat,
and then eat it.
If their eating utensils are stained by meat, but as long as there is no taste, it is permitted to use them without fault.
If they see that the food
contains a lot of meat, then they should not accept it.
All visible meat should not be eaten.
One who eats it commits a fault.
I now proclaim this prohibition against meat.
If expounded broadly, it would be endless.
The time of Nirvāṇa is approaching,
therefore, it is briefly stated.
This is called the Laṅgqié Āpóduōluó Bǎojīng, Volume 4, which is able to answer questions.”
At that time, Dàhuì Púsà asked in verses, saying,
“Those Bodhisattvas
who seek the Buddha path,
as for wine, meat, and onions,
how should their food be?
May the Supreme Honored One
mercifully expound
on what fools covet,
which is foul, nameless,
and savored by tigers and wolves.
How can it be eaten?
Those who eat it generate various faults;
not eating it is meritorious and good.
May you please explain to me
the faults and merits of eating and not eating.”
After Bodhisattva Dàhuì finished asking in verse,
he again said to the Buddha,
“May the World-Honored One
please explain to us the merits and demerits of eating and not eating meat.
I and the bodhisattvas
in the present and future shall preach the Dharma to various sentient beings who yearn for meat,
so that those beings may turn towards compassion,
and having attained compassion, clearly and quickly achieve ultimate unsurpassed Bodhi in their respective stages.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having ceased in their own stages,
shall also attain unsurpassed Bodhi.
Those who follow evil, heretical doctrines,
all the externalists,
who hold to deluded views of permanence and impermanence,
still have prohibitions against eating meat.
How much more should the Tathāgata, the protector of the world,
who has achieved the True Dharma, not eat meat?
The Buddha said to Dàhuì,
“Excellent, excellent!
Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well.
I shall explain it to you.”
Dàhuì replied to the Buddha,
“Yes, I shall receive your teaching.”
The Buddha said to Dàhuì,
“There are immeasurable reasons why one should not eat meat.
However, I shall now briefly explain them to you.
All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have by various karmic conditions continuously been one’s six kinds of relatives.
Therefore, because of this thought of kinship, one should not eat meat.
The flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, cows, horses, humans, and other animals,
which butchers sell indiscriminately, should not be eaten.
Because it grows from impure substances, one should not eat meat.
When sentient beings smell it, they all become terrified,
like Cāṇḍālas and Ḍombas.
Dogs see it and are disgusted, barking in fear in groups, so one should not eat meat.
Furthermore, it prevents practitioners from cultivating compassion, so one should not eat meat.
It is desired by the ignorant, is foul and impure,
and brings no good reputation, so one should not eat meat.
It prevents various incantations from succeeding, so one should not eat meat.
Those who kill generate consciousness upon seeing the form,
and become deeply attached to its taste, so one should not eat meat.
Those who eat meat are abandoned by all devas, so one should not eat meat.
It causes bad breath, so one should not eat meat.
It causes many bad dreams, so one should not eat meat.
Tigers and wolves in empty forests smell it and come, so one should not eat meat.
It causes one to have no moderation in eating, so one should not eat meat.
It prevents practitioners from generating revulsion and detachment, so one should not eat meat.
I constantly say,
‘Whatever food one consumes,
one should think of it as the flesh of one’s child,
or as medicine.’
Therefore, one should not eat meat.
To permit eating meat
is impossible.
Furthermore, Dàhuì,
in the past there was a king
named Sīzǐ Sūtuósuō.
He ate various meats and eventually ate human flesh.
His ministers and people could not endure it and immediately plotted rebellion and cut off his salary.
Because eating meat has such faults, one should not eat meat.
Furthermore, Dàhuì,
all those who kill do so for profit, slaughtering and trading living beings.
Those ignorant sentient beings who eat meat
use money as a net to catch various meats.
Those who kill,
whether with money or with fishing nets,
take those beings of the sky, water, and land,
killing them in various ways, slaughtering and trading for profit.
Dàhuì,
there is no fish or meat that comes without being taught, sought, or desired.
For this reason, one should not eat meat.
Dàhuì,
sometimes I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat,
or restricted ten kinds.
Now, in this Sūtra, I completely prohibit all kinds at all times,
removing all expedient means.
Dàhuì,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha
does not even eat anything,
how much less fish and meat?
Nor does he teach others to do so,
because great compassion precedes all actions.
He regards all sentient beings as his only child.
Therefore, he does not permit eating the flesh of one’s child.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,

First I spoke of ‘seen, heard, or suspected,’

Due to deluded thoughts and lack of awareness,

Like the fault of craving,

Wine, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic

Sentient beings in future ages,

will say, ‘This is pure and blameless,’
‘The Buddha permitted us to eat it.’
Think of eating as taking medicine,

Contentment gives rise to revulsion.
Practitioners should practice mendicancy.
For those who abide in compassion,

Tigers, wolves, and all other fierce beasts

If one eats blood and flesh,

Therefore, practitioners

Eating meat shows no compassion or wisdom,
forever turning away from proper liberation,
and violating the holy signs.
Therefore, one should not eat it.
Being born into Brahman families,
and places of practice,
and into wise, wealthy families,
this is due to not eating meat.
Aṅgulimāla Sūtra, Volume 1:
Elder Kāśyapa
abandoned various delicious foods,
abandoned meat-flavored food,

Aṅgulimāla Sūtra, Volume 2.”

I seek their grace and repent.
Having repented,

I shall constantly practice the gentle and harmonious mind, the enduring mind, the non-negligent mind, the tranquil mind, the truly righteous mind, the unmixed mind, the non-avaricious mind, the superior mind, the great mind, the compassionate and peaceful mind, the mind of virtuous joy, the mind that liberates all, the mind that protects sentient beings, the mind without self-possession, the Tathāgata-mind.
I shall cultivate such vast, superior, and wondrous minds.
I shall diligently seek extensive learning and cultivate the *dhyāna* of detachment.
I shall uphold precepts purely and remember to repay kindness.
I shall always be joyful and never abandon sentient beings.
Life is fickle, fate is perverse.
The net of consciousness and emotions are discordant.
Clouds of karma cast shadows.
The sun of wisdom hides its brilliance.
The path is winding and long.
The night is endless with no return.
To ascend Mount *Lǔ* is to see little.
To cross the sea is difficult to reach the other shore.
Confusing ordinary stones for jade,
distinguishing pebbles as precious gems.
Lost, one fails to comprehend.
Without the proper way, what can one rely on?
Body, speech, and mind are the origins of the three calamities.
Therefore, the *sūtra* says:
"When there is a body, suffering arises.
When there is no body, suffering ceases."
Since we know their affliction and suffering, we should suppress and eradicate them.
The essential method for eradicating suffering is none other than repentance.
The method of repentance is,

first, to purify one's mind, quiet one's thoughts, straighten one's posture, compose one's appearance, be respectful in one's bearing, and solemn in one's demeanor, inwardly harboring shame and regret, outwardly expressing it.
The *Shū* says:
"There is no ritual without reverence."
"Arrogance must not be prolonged."
It also says:
"To be able to correct one's faults is to be without fault."
The *sūtra* says:
"Regard all sentient beings with the thought of kinship."
Each must examine their own faults,
and then repent.
From beginningless time until this life,
due to our bodily and mental actions, we have created all kinds of bitter karma.
And because of ignorance, we have often violated the supreme teachings.
Thus, we have become arrogant and lazy, disrespectful in our conduct.
Sleeping and sitting, we are unrestrained; acting, we are frivolous and haughty.
Sometimes entering or exiting monastic quarters, ascending halls and temples,
performing prostrations or circumambulations without humble and respectful posture.
Or before parents, teachers, superiors, equals, inferiors, good friends, and acquaintances,
we dress improperly and act in ways that deviate from the Dharma.
We observe things without propriety, acting contrary to proper conduct.
Or we steal the property of the Three Jewels, or the belongings of relatives, or anything owned by others,
plundering and forcibly taking,
deceiving, augmenting, or diminishing, infringing upon others' rightful shares.
Or we indulge in lewdness and licentiousness,
at inappropriate times and places,
without distinction, like animals,
not even sparing relatives.
Or we commit the five heinous crimes, burning and dousing with water and fire,
plundering, trapping, and burying, inflicting poison upon the innocent.
Or we brand and mutilate, cut off feet and ears, torture and flog, hack and shoot,
injure, destroy, cut, sever, harm, and tear apart,
slaughter, butcher, roast, burn, boil, broil, decay, and scald.
All such sins,
whether for lust,
or for material gain,
or for avarice,
or for ignorant self-grasping,
without shame towards the wise, without blushing before the enlightened.
Now, contemplating these faults, they follow like a shadow to the form.
With fear, shame, compassion, and sorrow, we repent. After repenting with pain,
those who have harmed us,
from now on, let them be true good friends.
Life after life, let us face each other and instruct with the Dharma.
May the Buddhas of the ten directions especially extend their protection.
We repent the karmic obstructions of the body, vowing never to commit them again.
Next, we repent the karma of speech.
This is the gate of affliction and suffering,
the beginning of calamities and burdens.
The *Shū* says:
"A single word can build a nation."
"A single word can destroy a nation."
It also says:
"Words and actions are the pivots of a noble person."
"Once the pivot is moved, it determines honor or disgrace."
The *sūtra* says:
"Do not engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, false speech, or frivolous talk."
"Do not flatter, use flowery words, incite, or cause confusion."
Therefore, we know that the calamity of speech incurs truly heavy retribution.
As extensively shown in the *Zì'ài Jīng*, detailing these karmic phenomena.
And as the *sūtra* says:
"Even if life is at stake, do not utter false words."
How much less should one incite right and wrong through jest or frivolity?
Always repent the karma of speech with an upright mind.
Next, repent the karma of mind.
The mind is the root of body and speech,
the gate of sin and merit.
The *Shū* says:
"Control the seven emotions and practice the nine thoughts."
"Think without evil, and act always correctly."
The seven emotions are joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, dislike, and desire.

The nine thoughts are: seeing, think of clarity; listening, think of keenness; countenance, think of warmth; demeanor, think of respect; speech, think of loyalty; conduct, think of reverence; doubt, think of questioning; anger, think of difficulty; seeing gain, think of righteousness.
These are all for cleansing the mind, removing evil, and pursuing righteousness.
The *sūtra* says:
"Do not indulge in greed, anger, ignorance, or wrong views."
Thus, we know that the myriad evils flow like rivers, and events originate from the mind.
How do we know this?
If a thought arises in an instant,
then the mouth utters evil words.
Speech is manifested by intention,
leading to heavy sins.
Now, if one wishes to seal one's speech and rectify one's body,
it is not as effective as first curbing one's mind and then breaking one's intention.
Therefore, the *sūtra* says:
"When concentrated in one place, nothing is left unresolved."
Once the mind accords with the Way,
bodily faults cease without being suppressed.
Once intention accords with reason,
verbal errors disappear without being prevented.
However, the karma of body and speech is coarse and easily suppressed.
The karma created by the mind is subtle and difficult to completely eliminate.
Its manifestations are extensively described in various *sūtras*.
Joy arises from birth and perishes, suffering exists as long as the body is whole.
Karma is created by intention,
and actions rely on words as a trap.
Gain and loss are entirely dependent,
honor and disgrace are intertwined.
Even the swift *yànjì* cannot overtake,
nor can the mighty *Zhōu Kǎi* engrave in vain.
The root of delusion is like a wind's beginning,
the realm of craving is like a hoisted banner.
If one does not strive for singleness of purpose,
how can one reach the four *dhyānas*?
The sūtras say:
Crimes have no fixed form.
They are created according to causes and conditions.
Since they are born from causes and conditions,
they also perish according to causes and conditions.
Having already repented of one's grave evils,
then the three karmas are all clear.
If one also wishes to adorn one's form,
one must purify the six sense organs.
Thus, one knows that the mind drives and employs all consciousnesses,
just as a ruler comprehensively directs all his ministers.
Therefore, the *Shū Yún* says:
A ruler of men should be as vigilant as one who reins six horses with a rotten rope.
This means that he fears and respects the control of things, lest he fail.
Testing this matter, it is clearly understood.
But when confronted with the myriad external situations that stimulate both inner and outer (senses),
they interact and connect with the mind and consciousness.
Thus, the sūtras say:
If the mind-king is righteous, then the six ministers will not be perverse.
One must each feel shame and restrain the sense organs and consciousnesses.
As stated in the "Chapter on Mind and Intention" of the *Fǎjù Jīng*:
Once there was a Dàorén
who practiced the Way by a river.
He constantly thought of the six dusts, never finding peace.
A tortoise emerged from the river.
A water dog was about to devour the tortoise.
The tortoise withdrew its head, tail, and four legs, hiding them within its shell.
The dog could not get an advantage and left; the tortoise then came out
and managed to enter the water.
The Dàorén was enlightened by this.
He thought, "I am not as good as the tortoise.
I indulge my six passions,
unaware of the approach of death.
Revolving through the five paths is all due to the mind-root."
Therefore, it is necessary to fully clarify the karmic offenses of the six sense organs.
Since beginningless time,
my eye-root, due to causes and conditions, has pursued various forms.
Seeing beautiful things,
I could not cultivate learning.
Seeing unwholesome karma,
I readily followed and performed it.
Having obtained these two eyes, their purity is very little.
I only see forms of shamelessness and disgrace,
and do not see forms of the sage's spiritual powers, skillful means, and functions.
Although I have two eyes, I am no different from the blind.
This is the first great shame.
Since beginningless time,
my ear-root, due to causes and conditions, has pursued external sounds.
Hearing talk of righteousness, goodness, faithfulness, loyalty, encouragement, and beauty,
I could not cultivate learning.
Instead, I generated resentment and vexation.
Hearing evil things,
I gladly acted upon them.
Because of these causes, I only hear all unwholesome sounds,
and do not hear the sound of the pure, righteous Dharma.
The Buddhas of the ten directions constantly preach the wonderful Dharma,
but I do not hear it, being no different from one born deaf.
This is the second great shame.
Since beginningless time,
my nose-root, due to causes and conditions, if it smelled the wonderful fragrance of righteous teachings, precepts, and virtues,
would initially not be pleased to smell it,
but instead generate obstruction.
If it smelled the fragrance of evil desires and seductive charms,
I would deeply indulge in it.
Because of this karma,
I fell into the great hells,
and was born in remote lands.
I do not smell the five-part fragrance of the sages,
nor do I smell the fragrance of the three vehicles, four comprehensive means, etc.
This causes me to wander in saṃsāra, always separated from goodness.
This is the third great shame.
Since beginningless time,
my tongue-root, due to causes and conditions, has created an exceptionally large number of offenses.
Greedily attached to rich flavors and impure speech,
due to these karmic conditions, I constantly sink into saṃsāra.
This is the fourth great shame.
Since beginningless time,
my body-root, due to causes and conditions, has created many offenses.
Valuing myself and belittling others, increasing ignorance and attachment.
Because of this karma,
I receive a lowly retribution,
and have no way to connect with the excellent causes related to the Buddha.
This is the fifth great shame.
Since beginningless time, my mind-root, due to causes and conditions, has created all kinds of evils.
Regarding the sūtras of enlightened beings, which extract from suffering and offer the essential path,
my mind does not aspire to practice them, but instead generates resistance and rejection.
Instead, I learn heretical doctrines,
and scheme for sinful seeds, leading to a lack of true faith.
Seeking fame and profit, I increase my ego-view,
and my perversity is especially grave.
Only at the time of death will I regret the wasted time.
This is the sixth great shame.
The beauty of the capital,
the songs that wind around the rafters,
fat horses and light furs,
fragrant delicacies and sweet wine—
in the darkness, they proliferate,
as the foolish and arrogant compete for desires.
The appearance is loose, the soul floats, the body delights in touch, the mind delights in thought.
The spiritual *Cài* constrains the roots,
the sentimental *Kuí* guards the feet.
Even insects and plants might be cautious;
why aren't humans diligent?
Looking back through distant eons,
entangled by the three karmas, deluded by the six sense organs,
defiled by attachment, moistening karma, submerged until now,
birth, old age, sickness, and death are truly great sufferings.
Therefore, the sūtras say:
One body dies and again receives another body.
The countless cycles of birth and death –
if all the grass and trees under heaven were cut down to make counting sticks,
they could not count my past bodies.
Therefore, the enlightened rise above and ascend beyond the bound realms,
while foolish beings, greedy for life, constantly sink into the prison of birth and death.
Thus, one must recognize faults to be able to bid a long farewell.
As the *Bāotāi Jīng* says:
Sentient beings conceive in the womb,
dimly, vaguely, like floating dust.
In the womb for ten months,
forty-two transformations, with subtle suffering, poison, and pain that is hard to endure.
The foul place is restrictive, worse than a prison.
Hunger, thirst, cold, and heat are worse than a hungry ghost.
If the mother is full, it is pressing and blocked; if the mother is hungry, it is faint and choked.
Eating cold food is like ice; eating hot food is like fire.
Drinking too much is like drifting on a great ocean.
Moving quickly is like falling into a perilous valley.
Sitting for a long time is like being pressed by earth.
Standing for a long time is like hanging in an outhouse.
Fumes from below, pressure from above, there is no moment without suffering.
When about to be born, the difficulty doubles,
like a naked body rushing onto blades, with cries that shake and tear.
Although experiencing this suffering, many are not complete.
Whether one day, a hundred days, one month, or ten months,
they may be aborted in the womb,
or the mother and child may die at birth.
One should contemplate that this birth is truly a great suffering.
Next, contemplate the suffering of old age.
The sūtras say:
When old and the roots have matured, the form changes and color fades.
Sitting and rising are extremely painful; the remaining life is short.
The *Nièpán Jīng* says:
Just as a lamp wick relies solely on oil,
when the oil runs out, the light and wick will not last long.
Humans are also like this.
They rely solely on the oil of youth.
When the oil of youth runs out, how can the wick of old age and decrepitude last long?
It is also like a broken axle, no longer useful.
Like a flower touched by frost, people do not wish to look at it.
Again, the sūtras say:
This day has passed,
and life diminishes accordingly,
like a fish in shallow water.
What joy is there in this?
One should contemplate that this old age is again a great suffering.
Next, contemplate the suffering of sickness.
All arise from wind, cold, heat, and irregular eating and drinking.
When the four seasons change, water and earth become unbalanced.
Furthermore, this composite body, this fragile form,
hopes to be free from the imbalance of the four great elements and without a single affliction.
How can this be?
When suffering afflicts the body, the mind is vexed and clogged with sorrow.
Seeking to live brings no relief; seeking to die brings no cessation.
Pain and suffering in a hundred ways, deep worries intertwine.
When excrement and urine are foul,
wife and children change their expressions.
When the body cannot be controlled,
bystanders change their color.
What's more, when one is alone and sick,
who is willing to support?
Therefore, the sūtras say:
A loving father and filial son, when they reach sickness and death, cannot save each other.
This is the ultimate truth.
It is truly a great suffering.
Further contemplate the suffering of death.
The sūtras say:
Death is the end.
Breath ceases, spirit departs, the body is desolate.
Humans and things are one system; nothing is born without an end.
Again, the sūtras say:
The destination is far, without companions,
without any destruction, those who see are sorrowful and poisonous, etc.
The sūtras also say:
Born alone, dying alone, one must bear it oneself.
Dim and obscure, the time of meeting is uncertain.
Therefore, the sages regard the body as an affliction.
How could they, through death, again receive life?
Coming and going in the five paths exhausts my spirit.
I vow to sever the source of greed and cut off the root of birth.
Therefore, the suffering of death truly arises from this body.
The Tathāgata's renunciation of home expressed this meaning.
Luxuriant blossoms are prone to fade.
Thick plantains bear no fruit.
Hair like stars, skin like a globefish.
Cherishing the light, wasting the day.
The two physicians secretly speak.
The ten shamans' arts are in vain.
Life is gone.
Tall pines rustle mournfully.
Becoming form, then transforming spirit.
Following karma, the substance perishes.
Gnawing the navel brings reproach.
Alas, how confusing!
The body is the root of suffering.
It is what one creates and accumulates oneself.
Amidst life and death, one further increases evil karma.
Unable to repent and reform, or follow the Buddha's words.
Therefore, one especially needs to deeply reproach oneself.
The Sūtra says:
"When seeing others' faults, the mouth must not speak.
If one's own body has evil, one should reveal it."
The Book says:
"Hearing of others' faults is like hearing the names of one's parents.
The ear may hear, but the mouth must not speak."
It also says:
"A jūn​zǐ reveals his faults."
The Sūtra says:
"Praise others' goodness, do not speak of your own beauty."
The Book says:
"A jūn​zǐ extols others' beauty, and does not boast of his own goodness."
The Sūtra says:
"Forgiving oneself can be used as a parable:
Do not kill, do not strike."
The Book says:
"What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others."
Now, by comparing the Sūtras and Books,
the core of the inner and outer teachings is equally the same.
It is precisely that the meaning is different, the names are different.
If the principles were contrary and the meanings divergent,
then such a shared outcome would not be possible.
The reason for calling them "inner" and "outer" is not based on physical division,
but simply refers to the manifestation of the mind.
The Sūtra says:
"The Buddha teaches the Dharma to sentient beings to dispel darkness and delusion,
just as a skilled physician prescribes medicine according to the ailment."
The Book says:
"The Way of Heaven shows no favoritism; it only supports the benevolent."
If a monastic observes emptiness and impermanence,
厭lì life and death, and practices transcending the world,
this is considered "inner"; deviating from this is "outer."
If a lay person takes refuge in the Sān​bǎo,
upholds precepts, cultivates goodness, and practices rites and righteousness,
this is considered "inner";
deviating from this is "outer."
Now, both monastics and laypeople,
all know that the praise of "inner beauty" comes from the mind,
and the name of "outer evil" lies in actions. How can one not abandon outer evil and diligently cultivate inner good?
If one wishes to practice, one must first reproach oneself.
One should know that seeking advancement is a temporary name,
while retreating and examining is a true method.
One who wishes to travel a thousand lǐ
must pack provisions and guard their feet to achieve it.
One who wishes to ascend to the other shore
must gather wisdom as provisions and complete precepts as feet to climb.
The reason why one can achieve results
is truly due to retreating, examining, awakening, observing, testing, and weighing the light and heavy.
Thus, one can cut off ignorance and sever old age and death.
When foolish darkness is extinguished, the light of wisdom shines forth.
When the four phases shift, the virtue of precepts becomes manifest.
Therefore, it is known that integrity and humility are the omens of advancement,
while craving advancement is the sprout of regression.
Indeed, those who seek and gain through illusion will deeply cherish love and thus suffer the pain of falling and collapsing. This
is the path of external teachings.
Those who retreat and gain through reality will have no defilement or attachment in their minds.
Thus, they attain the constant joy of Nièpán.
This is the path of Buddhism.
Now, one should only retreat and examine one's shortcomings to reproach oneself.
If one is determined to seek advancement, one will surely harm oneself and others.
Examining mistakes through introspection benefits both self and others.
One should know that self-reproach in thought and word
is the path of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Examining one's bodily actions
is the trace of liberation.
Therefore, as mentioned above, if one skillfully reproaches oneself,
then there is no goodness that will not gather.
Looking to those who advance in virtue,
none dare to tarry.
Consulting my small wisdom,
it is merely 太康.
Is there no universal technique
to overcome this thorny wilderness?
Even with the 重lí,
it also illuminates the light of a firefly.
Following emotions, internally burdened.
Facing affairs, externally harmed.
With one lift of the layered net,
one vainly thinks of soaring high.
The feeling of self-reproach is still obscure,
the true meaning is not yet clear.
Therefore, I examine the mind through actions,
and test what has been cultivated.
Knowing my shortcomings, I feel even more trepidation.
What is this examination and testing?
Examine this body of mine:
From dawn to noon,
from noon to dusk,
from dusk to night,
from night to dawn,
and even in every moment, every quarter of an hour, every thought, every instant.
How many thoughts, how many actions, how much good, how much evil?
How many thoughts wish to destroy afflictions?
How many thoughts wish to subdue demonic enemies? How many thoughts contemplate the Sān​bǎo and the Four Noble Truths?
How many thoughts contemplate suffering, emptiness, and impermanence? How many thoughts contemplate repaying the kindness and compassion of parents?
How many thoughts wish to endure suffering on behalf of sentient beings? How many thoughts aspire to the Bodhisattva path?
How many thoughts wish to practice generosity and uphold precepts?

How many thoughts wish to practice patience and diligence? How many thoughts wish to practice meditative absorption and manifest wisdom? How many thoughts wish to practice compassion and aid the five destinies?
How many thoughts wish to encourage and practice what is difficult to practice?
How many thoughts wish to transcend and seek what is difficult to discern?
How many thoughts wish to endure suffering to establish the Buddha-Dharma?
How many thoughts wish to become a Buddha and liberate all beings?
Having examined the mind above,
next, examine the mouth according to the time divisions above.
Since dawn,
how many profound sentences have been uttered?
How many scrolls of scriptures have been opened and read?
How much text has been recited rationally?
How many times have the Buddha's merits been praised?
How many times have Bodhisattva practices been extolled?
How many times have praises and rejoicings been made?
How many times have dedications and vows been made?
Next, examine the body according to the time divisions above.
How many times has the body been bent in prostration to the Buddha, how many bows?
How many times has the body been bent in prostration to the Dharma and Saṅgha?
How many times have laborious tasks been performed, such as sweeping stūpas and cleaning the ground?
How many times has incense been burned, flowers scattered, and lamps lit?
How many times has dust been brushed away and offerings arranged properly?
How many times have banners been hung, stūpas marked, and hands clasped in offering?
How many tens or hundreds of circumambulations around the Buddha have been made respectfully?
Through such examination,
what accords with reason is very little, what deviates from the Way is extremely much.
Pure and good karma is barely worth mentioning.
Heavy obstacles of affliction fill the eyes densely.
How can liberation be attained when hindrances accumulate even more?
As examined above, self-salvation is fruitless.
How can there be leisure to discuss the good and evil of others?
Therefore, one must instruct and reproach oneself in the three karmas,
knowing how much good and evil one has done.
Amidst the tumultuous winds and vast obscurity,
the worldly customs cling and bind.
Competing in appearance, with internal guilt.
Who feels shame for the flaws of their heart?
Reflecting again on emotional reversals,
thrice examining the superficiality of oneself.
The noble are in peril from excess,
the poor are intimidated by the arrogant and extravagant.
Wandering in the Six Defilements, tangled in the Seven Evils.
Not planning at the beginning,
a runaway horse is hard to net.
The superior had already examined their conduct.
There were many instances of neglect and idleness.
It is due to these Four Greats that slackness and indolence are brought about.
Therefore, he admonished them to awaken.
Indeed, the Three Realms are vast and the Six Paths are numerous.
None do not rely on the Four Greats, which mutually support each other to form a body.
When gathered, it is a body; when scattered, it returns to emptiness.
However, wind and fire are different in nature, and earth and water differ in quality.
Each seeks to be suitable according to its share.
The ways to seek suitability are not one.
Therefore, they easily contradict and move.
Thus, if one great is out of tune, all Four Greats fall ill.
Now increasing, now decreasing, ailments and diseases continuously arise.
Wind is light, but earth is heavy.
Water is cold, but fire is hot.
They mutually afflict and distress.
There is no time to attain peace.
The sūtra compares them to four snakes.
Truly, they are to be feared.
Moreover, these Four Greats are without shame, without disgrace, without grace, and without righteousness.
I now fear their discomfort.
Therefore, I provide for their necessities.
However, those Four Greats have never felt shame or gratitude.
How do I know this?
For example, when mournful winds and frost cause things to wither, and severe winter brings snow,
one immediately needs cotton padding, fur coats, warm bedding, and heated rooms.
If it is the stifling heat of late summer, scorching and blazing,
one again needs light fine silk, spacious rooms, fans, and ivory mats.
When spring and autumn change seasons and the climate is cool and refreshing,
one again needs light and soft clothing and adornments.
Furthermore, when eating, one needs rich and rare delicacies to be abundant.
When drinking, fruits, warm drinks, and cold water are provided as needed.
Enduring suffering to seek pleasure.
All these are what the Four Greats require.
And I have never refused to provide for them.
Yet these Four Greats seek without shame.
They do not care whether there is enough or not.
If there is, they are never satisfied with replenishment.
If there is not, they coerce and compel one to obtain it.
Like hunger needing food, it cannot be lacking even for a moment.
Should there be any disharmony, internal anxiety and external conflict increase the fire element.
They do not know my hardships.
They do not pity my emptiness.
They only desire to seek greedily without rest.
This is called being without shame.
What is being without disgrace?
Your needs are endless.
I provide for you extensively.
You accept it readily, without any hint of shame.
While I exert my wisdom and exhaust my plans to provide for you,
you never show any concern for me.
In a short period, you do not need clothes and food.
What is being without grace?
Now that you have received such provisions from me,
you have never performed good deeds for me.
Having obtained my clothes and food, feeling full, warm, and joyful,
you instead contemplate and commit all sorts of evil.
A little meditation, chanting, and bowing, and immediately laziness arises.
What is being without righteousness?
This body of Four Greats
cannot be hoped for.
It cannot be trusted.
I now provide for you in various ways,
but you, in turn, perversely give rise to various attachments.
You compel me to commit killing, stealing, and illicit sexual acts.
Since I am foolish and unable to restrain or reform,
I follow along, giving rise to various diseases.
Or I suffer royal law, imprisonment, and whipping.
All brought upon by you.
While I endure suffering,
you also gain no benefit.
Yet you still do not realize,
and continue to seek and demand.
From today onwards,
I will no longer follow you to wander in the great sea of old age, sickness, birth, and death.
You should follow me on the path,
performing various good deeds.
Only then can I provide you with clothes and food according to your share,
merely enough to sustain the body and remove hunger and thirst.
You should diligently urge yourself,
so that I may soon attain the Five-Part Dharma Body,
constantly transforming and traveling freely without hindrance.
Swift is a hundred years.
Entangled are the Six Roots.
Appearing and disappearing in confusion and doubt.
Dwelling and moving in attachment.
Toiling, I seek.
Bustling, you provide.
Virtue daily diminishes.
Only misfortune accumulates.
Greedy people corrupt their kind.
Insatiable desires bring ruin.
Bright enlightenment is not hoped for.
Why weep for the dark void?
The superior had already examined their conduct.
He knew that they were far from the reality of the Way.
By severely blaming and reproaching oneself, there is a path to progress.
Although previously the faults of both monastic and lay people were discussed generally and indistinctly,
nevertheless, the sins of lay people are heavy, and the sins of monastic people are light.
But among monastic people,
the differences in conduct and stages of practice are hard to distinguish as ripe or unripe.
However, when viewed from the paths,
one can still roughly see their traces.
Those who are monastic now have not yet reached the holy realm,
yet those who look up to them constantly apply the standards of saints to blame ordinary people.
This is truly because the Great Teaching is superior and profound,
those who revere it bear heavy blame.
The Dharma-Vinaya is subtle and profound,
those who believe in it have deep expectations.
How do we know this?
If one wishes to see an elegant form and a wondrous body,
one should behold a person of dignified and beautiful appearance.
If one wishes to observe the style of benevolence, righteousness, and abundant virtue,
one should seek conduct that is polite and righteous.
Why do we often see many mouths competing
to criticize and discard all outer paths?
It is precisely because they are not worthy of comment,
and so criticism ceases.

What is hell?
The sūtras widely explain.
Beneath this continent are the eight great hells.
The lowest is Ābí [Avīci],

Their nature is cruel and savage, without any compassion or forbearance.

Someone asked the hell-guards,

Moreover, the sūtra says:

Moreover, body, speech, and mind are the beginning of karma generation.

Present retribution, born retribution, future retribution—

Therefore, the treatise says:

However, the previous nine types of karma encompass both good and evil.

Therefore, practitioners must first contemplate and break through this.
From this human body, there can be a way out.

The two strong bonds, the two obstructive dharmas, the two kinds of defilement, the two hailstorms, the two carbuncles, the two burning dharmas, the two kinds of illness.

All is suffering.
Therefore, the sūtra (jīng) says:
All three realms are suffering; what is there to enjoy? Yet sentient beings are always deluded, saying:
The world is permanent and joyful.
The cause of joy beyond the world is impermanent and suffering.
How profoundly deluded, instantly falling into this inversion!
A mere prick of the body immediately feels the sensation of suffering.
How can it be called joy?
I will briefly cite a few points to prove that it is only suffering.
If one considers food and drink as joy,
then one should eat much, and the body would be harmonious and the mind pleased.
Why does a slight deviation from proper measure turn into illness?
If one considers clothing as joy,
then one should wear one set in spring and summer, with endless love.
Why different clothes for cold and hot seasons?
Clearly, one does not enjoy it, thus it is the root of suffering.
If one considers a dwelling as joy,
why does one not stay in one place permanently?
Since one constantly moves,
it is clear one is avoiding suffering.
If one considers wife, children, and relatives as joy,
then one should always sing and laugh together.
Why, in an instant, does impermanence bring wailing and
choking? It should be known that relatives are truly the root of suffering.
If one considers beautiful forms as joy,
then one should always please the mind and eyes, forever comforting the body.
Why, in a moment, do facial features change, hair turns white, face turns dark, grieving the youthful beauty and radiance?
Therefore, it is known that this form itself is suffering,
it does not come from outside.
If one says that pleasant sounds are joy,
then one should find constant enjoyment in the intricate melodies of strings and flutes, listening without weariness.
Why is it that after a short while, one feels drowsy and tired, and the ears no longer enjoy listening?
One should know that this is suffering.
If one says that heavy drinking is joy,
then it should be that one's desires are satisfied, worries are dispelled, and there are no troubles for a long time.
Why then does the mind become confused, the heart悶 (mèn) and the bones and joints ache terribly?
Or, because of this, one is whipped, shackled, and bound,
losing one's life, dying young, ruining one's family, and destroying one's country,
suffering immeasurable pain.
If one says that companionship is joy,
then one should roam freely all day, never knowing weariness.
Why is it that every time one climbs a height, one gets tired after a short while?
Afterwards, even if mutually invited, one no longer feels like going.
If one says that lustful indulgence is joy,
then one's blood and vital energy should be strong, eyes bright, and spirit invigorated.
One should remain young and not age, strong and not change.
Why is it that indulging one's passions and desires always leads to fatigue and exhaustion,
draining the brain and marrow, causing dizziness and blurry vision,
heart palpitations and shortness of breath, weakening of muscles and bones,
dry mouth and chapped lips, and trembling of the four limbs?
This extraction from the five viscera leads to a shortened lifespan.
One should know that lustful indulgence is truly the root of suffering.
If one says that glory and position are joy,
then they should remain unchanged from beginning to end, without shame or disgrace.
Why is it that between promotion and demotion, joy and sorrow arrive instantly?
The above points are presented in broad terms.
However, these six senses (liù chén) and five emotions (wǔ qíng), where the mind roams,
are nothing but suffering.
Therefore, the Great Saint (Dàshèng) awakened and perceived the Three Realms (Sānjiè) as a prison, knowing suffering.
Not deluded, he achieved liberation from life and death.
The mind, resentful, stirs and churns.
