How long will the vast night last?
When will one finally awaken from this long, drawn-out state?
The Buddha (Fó), the World-Honored One (Shìzūn), said:
The Three Realms (Sānjiè) and the human world are all accumulations of suffering.
It is not just one suffering,
but also impermanent, without self, and impure.
Ultimately, it returns to emptiness.
Beyond the mundane world,
there is permanence, joy, self, and purity, complete with the eight freedoms (bā zìzài).
Yet sentient beings (zhòngshēng) remain perpetually deluded, mistaking it for joy.
How lamentable!
Furthermore, regarding the one suffering (yī kǔ), there are eight aspects.
What are these eight sufferings (bā kǔ)?

They are: the suffering of birth (shēng kǔ), the suffering of old age (lǎo kǔ), the suffering of sickness (bìng kǔ), the suffering of death (sǐ kǔ), the suffering of separation from loved ones (ài biélí kǔ), the suffering of meeting with those one hates (yuān zēng huì kǔ), the suffering of not getting what one seeks (qiú bùdé kǔ), and the suffering of the five aggregates of attachment (wǔ shèng yīn kǔ).
Within each suffering, there are yet other sufferings.
Therefore, all practitioners (xíngrén) spur themselves on to cultivate the Way,
regulating body, speech, and mind, diligently and unceasingly.
Ignorant ordinary people (qún xiǎo) call this suffering.
But the Great Saint (Dàshèng), with perfect insight, penetrates and understands the three kinds of knowledge (sāndá),
knowing that these small sufferings are the very cause of great joy.
Although there is toil and fatigue, what is sought is great.
This is not called suffering.
Therefore, various practices are cited to demonstrate their use for those with a mind for it.
If one sacrifices one's life to show compassion for sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) golden body, with pervasive light, and whose every action—walking, standing, sitting, lying down—shakes the great chiliocosm (dà qiān).
If one bows to parents, teachers, and sages,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) high and bright ushnisha (dǐng xiàng).
If one does not deceive sentient beings (zhòngshēng) and praises their virtues,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) urna hair (méijiān háo xiàng).
If one practices loving-kindness (cí'ài) and benevolence to save sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) dark blue, conch-shaped hair (gàn qīng luófà xiàng).
If one offers lamps and light to others,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) topknot emitting sunlight (dǐng chū rìguāng xiàng).
If one looks upon sentient beings (zhòngshēng) with a compassionate heart,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) pure eyes with fluttering lashes (jìng mù shàng xià xùn xiàng).
If one abstains from rich flavors and converts people with the Ten Good Deeds (shí shàn),
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) forty uniform and close-set teeth (sìshí chǐ qí mì xiàng).
If one speaks kindly words with a firm will,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) four white and pure canine teeth (sì yá báijìng xiàng).
If one abstains from the four vices of speech,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) broad, square jaw and long, wide tongue (fāng jiá chē guǎng cháng shé xiàng).
If one practices generosity with impartiality,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) seven limbs full and rounded (qī chù hé mǎn xiàng) when he achieves Buddhahood.
If one endures hardship with resolute practice,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) lion-like chest (shīzǐ yì xiàng).
If one practices righteous and pure medicine to save people,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) upright and proper body (shēn fāngzhèng xiàng).
If one acts with loving-kindness and does not strike sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) long, slender arms and fingers (xiū bì zhǐ cháng xiàng).
If one watches the ground when walking and does not tread on insects,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) feet not touching the ground (xíng bù dào dì xiàng).
If one supports and assists suffering sentient beings (zhòngshēng) with one's hands,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) hands with inward and outward grasping (shǒu nèi wài wò xiàng).
If one practices the Four All-Embracing Virtues (sì shè) to embrace sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) webbed hands and feet (shǒuzú wǎng xiàng).
If one offers to good people with a pure heart,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) marks of wheels with a thousand spokes on hands and feet (shǒuzú lún qiān fú lǐ xiàng).
If one gives clothes to hide faults and cover up evils,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) retractable male organ (mǎ yīn cáng xiàng).
If one preaches the Dharma (Fǎ) to eliminate suffering and death, one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) deer-like shanks (lù chuǎn cháng xiàng).
If one adorns well and does not dislocate the limbs of sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) interlocked bones (gōu suǒ gǔ xiàng).
If one is gentle and compliant, circumambulating stupas (tǎ) and following others,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) hair curling to the right (yòu xuán máo xiàng).
If one levels roads and removes thorns,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) one hair per pore (yī kǒng yī máo xiàng).
If one does not wear luxurious clothes and bathes others,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) fine and soft skin (pífū xì ruǎn xiàng).
If one sweeps stupas (tǎ) and removes filth,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) body not collecting dust (shēn bù shòu chén xiàng).
If one cultivates myriad practices and always wishes for perfection,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) svastika mark on the chest (xiōng wànzì xiàng).
If one forsakes country, city, wife, and children,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) Pure Land (Jìngtǔ) with a retinue of sages (xiánshèng).
If one practices self-restraint in eating and offers delicious food to others,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) supreme flavor (shàngwèi xiàng).
If one constantly recites and does not speak ill of others,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) dharani-like fragrant mouth (zǒngchí kǒu xiāngqì xiàng).
If one preaches the Dharma (Fǎ) to guide sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) face free from hunger and thirst, with full and luminous eloquence (miàn wú jīkě mǎn kǒu guāng biàncái xiàng).
If one upholds the precepts without fault,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) perfectly complete Dharma-body (Fǎshēn yuánmǎn xiàng).
If one practices dhuta (tóutuó) asceticism in the mountains,
one will attain the Buddha's (Fó) state where all defilements are eradicated (chén lěi dōu jìn xiàng).
If one abandons luxurious halls for meditation in quiet groves,
sentient beings (zhòngshēng) consider it suffering and cannot do it.
But a Bodhisattva (Púsà), with strong will and great aspirations,
does not consider it suffering.
Thus, one attains natural palaces and seven-jeweled residences, quickly achieving Buddhahood (chéng Fó).
Sentient beings (zhòngshēng) are still adrift in the sea of transmigration (shēngsǐ hǎi zhōng).
Is this not caused by perverted delusions?
Therefore, one should diligently and vigorously cultivate this practice,
and then one will exit the Three Realms (Sānjiè).
Adjusting robes, one measures the sea of afflictions;
raising steps, one dispels the dust and impurities.
The three kinds of sensation (sān shòu) cease like rain,
the eight sufferings (bā kǔ) are like floating clouds.
One offers one's heart, looking up to perfect ultimate reality;
one fully commits one's being, entrusting it to the squared mound (earth).
In the morning, one roams with pure companions;
in the evening, one gathers with the assembly of Vulture Peak (Língshān).
Lamps of merit illuminate afar,
fragrant temples offer auspicious incense.
Bowing one's head, one looks upon human customs,
truly, tranquility is king.
Indeed, cause and effect (yīn guǒ) lead to reciprocal responses (gǎnyìng), influences generate each other,
a necessary principle without error or deviation.
However, the actions (yèxíng) of sentient beings (zhòngshēng) are not pure; good and evil are used alternately.
Due to this impurity, the retribution (bào) is both refined and coarse.
Some are noble, some lowly, some beautiful, some ugly.
Their circumstances are not uniform.
Not understanding the original actions leads to doubt.
What is this?
For example, those who diligently uphold the precepts
should attain longevity, prosperous descendants, and honored relatives.
Yet, one sees their lives cut short, and their families decline and perish.
Those who kill and harm should suffer short lives and their dependents destroyed.
Yet, they live long, their clans are strong, and their supporters numerous.
Honest and incorruptible conduct should attract wealth.
Yet, one sees poverty, while greedy and thieving people, who should face destitution, are seen to be prosperous.
This is because their merits are now lightly received in this life.
As stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (*Jīngāng Bōrě*):
"Because of upholding the sūtra (jīng), one is scorned by others.
This person's past evil karma (zuìyè) should have led to falling into evil paths.
Because of being scorned now, the past karma (zuìyè) is extinguished."
The reason for these doubts
is due to ignorance (wúmíng) and delusion, leading to false views and perversion.
One cannot understand the karmic forms of the three times (sānshì yèxiàng).
Now, a few points are briefly presented.
The world is deluded by things; these are used for admonition.
May those who are discerning recognize them to remove doubt.
Wise people (zhìrén) consider birth to be suffering.
Therefore, they cannot bear foolish people (yúfū) who cling to life and consider birth as joy.
This is the first delusion.
Wise people (zhìrén) know that if there is no birth, there is no death.
Hence, they speak of the joy of Nirvāṇa's (Nièpán) tranquility and extinction.
But foolish people (yúfū) fear death and do not know the way to avoid death.
This is the second delusion.
Wise people (zhìrén) consider living at home to be suffering.
They liken it to a prison.
The scriptures say: "Cut off attachment to arrogance and extravagance."
But foolish people (yúfū) cling to it, considering it glory and joy.
This is the third delusion.
Wise people (zhìrén) know the burdens of wife and children.
Therefore, they compare them to cangues and shackles.
The scriptures say:
"Cut off attachment to what is loved."
But foolish people (yúfū) consider affection and love to be happiness.
This is the fourth delusion.
Wise people (zhìrén) know that family relations are the root of bondage.
They abandon them as if they were enemies.
But foolish people (yúfū) cling to them, considering them superior enjoyment.
This is the fifth delusion.
Wise people (zhìrén) know that honor and profit are the means of self-destruction.
The scriptures say:
"Cut off attachment to quick advancement."
But foolish people (yúfū) do not consider slander and harm, only seeking nobility.
This is the sixth delusion.
Wise people consider forms, sounds, smells, and tastes to be the root of suffering.
The *Shū* says:
"Cutting off passion lies in overcoming desires."
Yet foolish commoners become mired and intoxicated by them.
What has been listed before should leave no room for doubt.
Therefore, wise people should diligently exert themselves.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are inseparable from one's body.
Do not give rise to doubts and let life pass in vain.
Now, I will present more to illustrate the nature of doubt.
Seeing someone who practices *bùshī* (giving) die early from illness, one develops a suspicious mind and becomes stingy.
Seeing someone who observes the precepts and does not eat after noon,
one suspects they will fall ill and should rather nourish themselves.
Seeing someone who practices *rěnrǔ* (patience), restraining their mind and body,
one worries they will suffer and advises them to relax their intentions.
Seeing someone who recites sūtras,
troubled by illness due to their daily efforts to comprehend principles, one advises them to rest.
Seeing someone who eats only vegetables,
become thin and weak from illness, one advises them to eat rich and delicious foods.
Seeing someone practicing *zuòchán* (seated meditation),
become ill, one advises them to lie down.
Hearing advice and guidance, one merely follows one's innate disposition,
becoming lazy and self-indulgent, conforming to popular customs.
They have never considered that one might hear the *Dharma* in the morning and die in the evening, as if saving one's head from burning.
How can one be so lazy and return to common ways?
To swear by death itself,
only then can one be said to have resolve.
The path of life is not a single principle.
The threads of knowledge are indeed abundant.
Vainly startled by the wealth of Dōnglíng,
idly lamenting the poverty of Běiguō.
Guó Shēng indeed committed wrongs,
while the Yán clan truly embodied benevolence.
Meeting misfortune reveals past *yè* (karma);
practicing goodness will converge in this body.
Diligent worry leads to eternal peace and tranquility;
ease and comfort ultimately lead to bitterness and hardship.
A good reputation is considered weighty;
but how can it compare to planting good causes?
Having already come to know the evils of lay men and women,
and also witnessing the flaws and shortcomings of monastic *sēng* and *ní*,
and hearing about the gate of doubt and perversion,
one withdraws to reflect, truly feeling shame and remorse.
The *Jīng* says:
"One who possesses shame and remorse fully can eliminate the obscuring darkness."
Therefore, it also says:
"Shame and remorse are like iron hooks,
capable of preventing people from wrongdoing."
If there is no shame or remorse,
one is no different from beasts.
The *Nièpán* says:
"There are two white *Dharma*s that can save all sentient beings:
one is shame (*cán*), and the other is remorse (*kuì*)."
*Cán* means not committing evil oneself;
*kuì* means not teaching others to commit evil.
*Cán* means feeling internal shame;
*kuì* means revealing it to others.
Because of shame and remorse,
one is able to respect parents and teachers.
Bearing shame and remorse,
sins are extinguished.
The manifestation is thus.
Each must feel shame and remorse and comply with the pure white *Dharma*.
The matters are countless,
but ten points are briefly listed as an outline.
First, shame and remorse towards all Buddhas.
The *Rúlái* (Tathāgata) in the past wished for us to be freed from suffering and attain peace.
Therefore, they gave rise to the *bódítí* mind and practiced the *bódítí* path,
enduring suffering and humiliation to now achieve the *fǎshēn* (Dharma-body).
They constantly expounded the *zhèngfǎ* (Right Dharma) for us.
Yet I cannot practice according to what was taught.
Second, shame and remorse towards parents.
My lamentable parents labored greatly to give birth to me.
They raised and instructed me, always filled with worry and apprehension.
Having become a child, I do not follow their admonitions and instructions.
Instead, I learn violence and arrogance, despising the noble and the humble.
By deviating from being a dutiful child, I have lost my good name.
This is deeply shameful.
Third, shame and remorse towards one's children.
Though they are truly able to pay respects morning and evening,
and provide care without fault,
yet they ultimately suffer in poverty with nothing to give them.
This causes the children to have no means of establishing themselves.
Moreover, lacking guidance and instruction, the children become ignorant and foolish.
This is truly shameful.
Fourth, shame and remorse towards teachers and monastics.
My parents, though they gave birth and instructed me,
could not enable me to escape the sea of birth and death.
Now these teachers and monastics teach me to leave home and receive the higher precepts,
to conceive the embryo of an *Luóhàn* and attain the fruit of an *Luóhàn*.
Yet I violate them.
This is deeply shameful.
Fifth, shame and remorse towards disciples.
Though they are able to diligently cultivate morning and evening according to the teachings,
I instead stubbornly obstruct them, contradicting the sacred words.
This causes their *dàoyè* (spiritual endeavors) to achieve not an inch or a foot of merit,
and their life passes in vain, with no *fǎ* (Dharma) to uphold.
Considering this burden, I am also deeply ashamed.
Sixth, shame and remorse towards emperors.
They constantly guide the world with the Ten Virtues.
Thus, the country is peaceful, and the five grains are abundant.
Therefore, the common people settle their homes and resume their livelihoods.
Those who have left home enjoy peace and comfort, free to meditate and recite sūtras.
But now I am lazy.
This is deeply shameful.
Seventh, shame and remorse towards *tányuè* (donors).
The primary aim of leaving home is liberation.
The physical body relies first on clothing and food.
Therefore, laypeople generate blessings for the *Dào* (Path),
supplying necessities, thus promoting the *zhèngyè* (Right Dharma).
Yet I sometimes fail to show complete respect.
This is also deeply shameful.
Eighth, shame and remorse towards good friends.
Spiritual companions guide one, showing the causes and conditions for seeing the Buddha.
They enable one to fully practice pure conduct, as the great *Jīng* clearly demonstrates.
Yet I hear their admonishments and take them as enemies,
turning away from the Three Refuges and bowing to gods and popular customs.
Deluded and attached, I defy proper instruction.
This is deeply shameful.
Ninth, shame and remorse towards those I have taught.
Due to my lack of virtue, I have not planted causes for a long time,
preventing them from awakening and crossing over to salvation.
Thus, those who listen merely waste their effort.
Even if they hear various good teachings, they do not attain pure inner peace, causing self-reproach.
This is deeply shameful.
Tenth, shame and remorse towards *tiānlóng shénguǐ* (devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts) who protect the *Dharma*, and the unseen deities.
I originally made a vow to save all beings.
Therefore, all *tiānlóng* protected me without causing trouble.
But I am deficient, my will is not constant.
I only know that I have betrayed their grace and merely increase my shame and remorse.
The divine balm's bestowal is weighty,
the dark wine's grace is not yet profound.
The bright pearl is above the *Suí* River,
the moist jade is in the Lán fields.
Endowed with the utmost of heaven's nature,
relying on respect for the *Dào* is exalted.
Feathers and fur are united by power,
wheels and tracks connect with each other.
Repaying kindness moves me with previous elegance,
responding to words cherishes remaining grace.
Following the path, there are often many errors;
reflecting, how can I be without worry?
The meaning of shame and remorse is fundamentally about falling short.
If one can fully adhere to the correct practices,
then there is no need for shame and remorse.
The *Shū* says:
"If, upon introspection, one finds no fault,
what is there to worry about? What is there to fear?"
It also says:
"If the heart is without blemish,
why worry about having no home?"
Now, since the profound principles are difficult to master, and every tendency goes astray,
countless transgressions are committed in a single thought.
Since transgressions are countless, shame and remorse should also be countless.
The main points have already been briefly stated.
The countless branches and offshoots cannot be fully enumerated.
This chapter is established again
to allow those who seek the meaning in the text to know that no principle is left uncovered.
Indeed, sentient beings, due to their self-view, cannot attribute beauty to others
and take evil upon themselves.
Thus, they cannot cultivate the myriad good deeds.
Seeing others' superior conduct, they wish to surpass them.
How can such extreme lack of shame go unnoticed?
Now, I will list positions to make it clear,
hoping that one may restrain one's actions.
If one sees a sincere person practicing shame and remorse,
one who cannot do it oneself wishes that person would not do it.
Seeing people practicing *bùshī* and *chíjiè* (holding precepts) open the gate of liberation,
one wishes they would stop early.
Seeing people practicing *rěnrǔ* and *jīngjìn* (diligence), one who cannot do it oneself
wishes they would soon retreat and vanish.
Seeing those with extensive learning and practicing *dìng* (meditation),
one who cannot do it oneself does not wish them to do it.
Seeing those practicing *cí bēi xǐ shě* (compassion, pity, joy, equanimity),
one who cannot praise or encourage them wishes them not to practice.
Seeing those who eat only vegetables,
since one does not do it oneself, one encourages them to retreat and fail.
Seeing people who practice subduing the mind and should be ashamed of the *Dharma*,
one instead encourages them not to practice, deviating from the Eightfold Noble Path.
Seeing people studying and reciting sūtras,
since one lacks this practice oneself, one does not want them to do it.
Seeing those circumambulating and prostrating,
since one is lazy oneself, one envies them and causes them not to practice.
Seeing someone chanting *fànyīn* (Sanskrit chants),
since one cannot match them, one wishes they would not do it.
Seeing those practicing *jīngxíng* (walking meditation) and *tóutuó* (ascetic practices),
one who cannot do it oneself instead slanders and destroys them.
Now, in this latter age,
preaching the *Dharma* and enlightening people is considered the highest.
Righteousness demands generating faith, eradicating transgressions, praying for blessings, and propagating the Dharma.
But now, ascending the fearless seat,
one opens the floodgates to broad laughter and jesting,
adorns one's words with self-beautifying rhetoric,
speaks grandiosely, provokes discord, slanders, and retaliates.
Their demeanor is arrogant and obstinate, utterly devoid of humility.
They never reflect and repent, thinking, "My understanding is not yet profound,"
but rather interrogate seekers as if they err in their scriptural study.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
“If one preaches the Dharma for gain, fame, or out of a heart that loves factions,
this is called ‘not preaching the Dharma correctly.’ ”
If it benefits others,
increases their faith,
extinguishes their afflictions,
gives rise to pure karma,
and enables them to know shame and remorse, opening the eightfold noble path,
this is called “good preaching.”
Just as in a past life,
there was the Bhikṣu Kǔ'àn,
who preached that there are sentient beings, a self, a person, and a lifespan,
which contravened the Buddha's words.
Upon death, he entered the Avīci Hell,
lying on his back, on his stomach, and on his left and right sides,
each for nine hundred trillion years.
After that, he further experienced various other hells.
Beyond that, his followers suffered unspeakable pain.
Therefore, it is known that not relying on the Buddha’s teachings and slandering the Correct Dharma,
the sin is truly grave.
It should be known that being a Dharma Master is indeed difficult.
If good, it leads to immeasurable blessings.
If evil, it incurs equally grave sins.
Hence, a Dharma Master should feel extreme shame and remorse.
However, living in the world,
the urgency of sustaining life lies in clothing and food.
Because of this clothing and food, there is profound toil and disturbance.
The required silk, wadding, and leather,
without exception, involve harming lives, mutilating beings, donning others' skin and flesh,
to nourish one's own physical body.
Even when eating a single grain of food,
without effort, it cannot enter the mouth.
Reflecting on past efforts, considering my stomach,
what goes in above comes out below, a constant, ceaseless flow.
And yet, amidst this,
one selects the finest and fattest,
ingests the soft and smooth,
craves delicious flavors,
without shame or disgrace.
In an instant, it transforms and becomes putrid, unbearable to approach.
Walking or sitting, it is no different from being in a latrine.
How can a wise person
be greedy for food?
If one is greedy, one should feel great shame and remorse.
What distinction is there then between oneself and beasts?
In winter, the fox arranges its thick fur;
in spring, the silkworm spins its light thread.
The body, however, becomes an obstacle;
the mind, in turn, deceives itself.
The hand is bound by the daily tasks,
while in youth,
one drives chariots to pursue knights-errant,
pours wine to dally with enchanting beauties.
One only considers the present good,
how can one know the sorrow after death?
Startled and filled with shame,
one forever bids farewell to emotional attachments.
Indeed, one who can resolve doubts,
and internally generate the merits of shame, remorse, encouragement, and praise,
is a good friend (śubhāmītra).
Now, desiring to cultivate myriad practices,
without a good friend, there is no way to advance on the path.
The Sūtra says:
“Just as a sandalwood leaf in an Īlā forest,
its leaf smells foul.
But an Īlā's foul-smelling leaf in a sandalwood forest,
its leaf becomes fragrant.”
The Book says:
“Living with good people
is like entering a room of orchids and fragrant herbs;
after a long time, one also becomes fragrant.
Living with bad people
is like being in a fish market;
one becomes smelly along with them.”
It also says:
“Close to ink, one inevitably turns black;
close to cinnabar, one inevitably turns red.”
Therefore, it is known that a good friend can accomplish Buddha-deeds,
is a great cause and condition, is the complete practice of pure conduct.
A good friend can now lead me to ascend to the Pure Land.
An evil friend can now trap me and plunge me into hell.
Therefore, the kindness of a good friend is impossible to repay.
The principles of good and evil are clearly manifest.
But if one simply follows one's inclinations to suit the path, the progress will be slow.
If a good friend encourages and praises, the courageous heart will be swift.
The Sūtras have passages on encouragement and discipline.
Books have discussions on encouraging learning.
It should be known that essential practices are truly accomplished through encouragement.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
“A Bodhisattva personally practices generosity,
and also encourages others to practice generosity.
They personally uphold precepts, endure humiliation, cultivate diligence, practice one-pointedness of mind, and wisdom,
and also encourage others to do these things.”
Thus, delightful and beautiful things are admired with joy and longing—
this is the constant human emotion.
Now, if one only has a heart of desire and longing,
but does not perform the deeds of desire and longing,
its fruits will not be seen.
It is like someone without food thinking of flavors;
it will ultimately not alleviate their hunger or thirst.
Therefore, a few essential, widely practiced matters are briefly introduced
to serve as a warning.
Some now have wealth and riches, a warm household, sufficient provisions, not needing to toil or seek, as things naturally come.
Others are poor and suffering, hungry and wretched, their bodies weary.
They long for wealth all day,
but wealth never arrives, even for a moment.
Because of this suffering, they are encouraged to practice generosity and diligently cultivate blessings.
If some have robes and garments, splendid and fully equipped,
while others lack even a full foot of cloth, filthy, foul, and mixed.
Therefore, they are encouraged to give away clothes and dwellings.
If one sees sweet delicacies and rare treats covering tables and multiple platters,
while others barely have wild herbs and are distressed by poor vegetables.
Therefore, they are encouraged to give away food and drink.
If one sees honor and prominent positions,
riding in fine carriages, wearing light clothing, enjoying oneself freely and comfortably,
while others are humble and lowly, not esteemed by anyone,
sitting and lying in mud, ditches, and filth.
This suffering is detestable.
They are encouraged to cultivate blessings, eradicate arrogance, and practice humility and reverence.
How can others always be noble while I always remain base?
If one sees a dignified appearance and speech that brings great benefit,
while another has a short, ugly face and speaks violently.
This suffering can be abandoned.
They are encouraged to practice patience.
If one sees strong willpower, few illnesses, capable of strenuous activity, and unobstructed in practicing the Dao,
while another is often sick and uneasy, their actions achieving nothing.
Seeing this suffering, they are encouraged to give medicine
to help them progress.
Therefore, the Fǎjù Jīng says:
“Practicing the Dao at four times, one can overcome all suffering.”
First, when young and powerful.
Second, when possessing wealth.
Third, when encountering the Three Jewels, a field of blessings.
Fourth, when considering that all things must inevitably separate and disperse.
Constantly practicing these four,
one will certainly attain the path.
One should diligently urge oneself,
not waiting for others' encouragement.
A rattan heart transformed by an orchid room,
Īlā grass changed by a sandalwood cliff.
Vermilion and azure inevitably fade,
how can silk and stones always remain white?
A crooked shaft can be straightened by a rope,
twisted wood can be carved and embellished.
One basketful of earth can become a mountain,
but one might grow weary halfway through a hundred li journey.
The illustrious Hàn had its kings and ministers,
but the great Chǔ truly had no security.
Strive hard, virtue is not alone.
True words are not spoken in vain.
Formerly, others were encouraged and praised.
I now redouble my efforts.
Whenever discussing the essentials of effort and encouragement,
one must rely on circumstances and causes for practice.
If the mind and will are scattered,
then progress will have no anchor.
However, relying on circumstances and causes for practice,
precepts are its beginning.
It can be said to be the primary gateway to entering sainthood,
the correct path to leaving the mundane.
If one deviates from this teaching,
one will forever dwell in the three lower realms, severed from humans and heavens.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Just as the great earth gives birth to all things,
so too are precepts.
They can give rise to the human and heavenly flowers and fruits for living beings."
Hence, the Sūtra says:
"If there were no these precepts,
all good merits and virtues would not arise."
This is because suffering in the three lower realms is entangled with karmic obstructions,
while the excellent fruits of humans and heavens are worthy vessels for the Way.
To experience excellent fruits, they cannot arise without precepts.
Therefore, the Sages first expounded this teaching.
The two categories of precept methods are the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
The fundamental principle for the seven assemblies' elementary learning is the Three Refuges.
The Great Vehicle's ultimate teaching must uphold the Three Pure Precepts as its foundation.
All are fully revealed in the Sūtras and Vinayas,
their models prominent, regulating conduct and actions,
clearer than a mirror.
Now, I will briefly mention their general meaning,
to illuminate the common customs.
The reason why the origin of generating precepts must rely on the Three Jewels is
that the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha Jewels are revered by heavenly beings and humans.
Taking refuge and generating faith will certainly lead one out of conditioned existence.
If one takes refuge in evil gods, it will instead increase suffering.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Take refuge in the Buddha, a pure layfollower,
do not take refuge in various heavenly gods."
Therefore, one must first determine right and wrong to know what is adverse and what is compliant.
The Sūtra says:
"Faith is the source of the Way, the mother of merits and virtues.
Wisdom is the cause of liberation and emergence from conditioned existence."
These are truly sincere words.
If there is no this faith,
the mind and will will be floating and hollow, and taking refuge and precepts will not be obtained.
Therefore, establishing faith is paramount when setting out.
What are the Three Refuges?
They are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
These three are worthy of reverence, hence they are called Jewels.
What is the Buddha?
Self-awakened and awakening others, the Great Wisdom without a teacher, the Five-fold Dharma-body.
What is the Dharma?
That which can be a norm and rectify, the truth of cessation, Nirvāṇa, purity without characteristics.
What is the Saṅgha?
That which can harmonize and unite the assembly, the merits of those beyond learning, the state of cessation for oneself and others.
What is Refuge?
That which can be relied upon and turned towards.
What are Jewels?
That which can bring benefit and joy, the support for a correct mind.
Near, one attains humans and heavens; far, one ascends to beyond learning.
This is the distinction of the Three Jewels.
If discussing the ultimate teaching,
the principle is simply one unified whole.
Its illumination is all-pervasive.
Its pervasive illumination is equal awakening,
called the Buddha Jewel. Its essence is nothing but Dharma,
called the Dharma Jewel.
Its supreme virtue is always harmonious,
called the Saṅgha Jewel.
This is the Three Jewels of same nature, one in essence but three in meaning.
When living beings comprehend and realize, believing and knowing their Buddha-nature,
they depart from this cycle of birth and death, giving rise to benefit and joy.
Therefore, everything takes refuge in it.
First, the Three Refuges for turning away from error. Second, the Three Refuges for the Five Precepts.
Third, the Three Refuges for the Eight Precepts. Fourth, the Ten Precepts.

The Sūtra says:
There are eight difficult conditions difficult to overcome.
First, the difficulty of hell.
Second, the difficulty of hungry ghosts.
Third, the difficulty of animals.
Fourth, the difficulty of borderlands.
Fifth, the difficulty of long-life heavens.
Sixth, although born as a human, the difficulty of being blind, deaf, mute, and unable to hear and receive.
Seventh, although born as a human with complete six faculties,
one has worldly intelligence and eloquent wisdom, but believes in evil and holds perverted views,
disbelieving the Three Jewels and wantonly insulting them.
After the death of this body, one immediately falls into the three lower realms,
sinking according to karma, only emerging after a long time.
Even when in the human realm, one is still born into a family with incorrect faith.
Eighth, the difficulty of not seeing the True Dharma during the periods between Buddhas.
One is born in vain for a lifetime, increasing evil views,

Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"To be born in vain and die in vain is most pitiable."
Practitioners of the Dharma should first revere this meaning.
The great matter of birth and death cannot be taken lightly.
I will now briefly list a few reasons for self-congratulation, keeping them in mind.
The Buddha said:
"Hell is difficult to avoid."
Yet now we are able to avoid this suffering together.
This is the first self-congratulation.
The Buddha said:
"Hungry ghosts are difficult to escape."
Yet now we are able to be far from this suffering together.
This is the second self-congratulation.
The Buddha said:
"Animals are difficult to abandon."
Yet now we are able to not plant this cause together.
This is the third self-congratulation.
The Buddha said:
"Born in borderlands, one knows not benevolence and righteousness."
Now we are in the central land, cultivating propriety and wisdom.
This is the fourth self-congratulation.
The Buddha said:
"Born in long-life heavens, one knows not how to plant blessings.
When blessings are exhausted and life ends, one still falls into evil paths."
Yet now we do not amuse ourselves with worldly pleasures but turn to offerings.
This is the fifth self-congratulation.
The Buddha said:
"A human body is difficult to obtain.
Once lost, it does not return."
There is the analogy of the blind turtle and the floating log.
Now we have obtained a human body.
This is the sixth self-congratulation.
The Buddha said:
"Complete six roots are difficult to obtain."
Now we have no defects.
This is the seventh self-congratulation.
The Buddha said:
"The body of a brave man is difficult to obtain."
I have already obtained it.
The Buddha said:
"For women, one must know that Buddha-nature is indeed the brave man."
I already know this.
The Buddha said:
"Evil eloquence is difficult to abandon."
I now take refuge in the True Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"Before the Buddha and after the Buddha are great difficulties."
Now we together resolutely make a vow.
Having seen the form-body and heard the True Dharma,

The Buddha said:
"To see the Buddha is difficult."
I now prostrate before the images spoken of by the Buddha.

The Buddha said:
"To hear the Dharma is difficult."
I have now fully heard it.
The Buddha said:
"To leave home is difficult."
I shall now follow the assembly.
The Buddha said:
"To leave home with single-minded faith is even more difficult."
I now have a single mind, daring not to have two views.

The Sūtra says:
"The Sahā world is a land of five defilements,

Therefore, many who give rise to the Mahāyāna vow
Come to this land
To take saving suffering as their provisions,
And removing afflictions as their essential practice.
Cultivating good in this land for one day

The reason for this
Is precisely that in a place of extreme suffering, the mind is not inclined towards good,
Yet one is able, amidst intense suffering,
To resolutely give rise to the intention to endure suffering and accept humiliation.
How can this not be extraordinary?
As it is said, "a lotus flower blooming in fire,"
This is truly rare.
Other pure lands are lands without opportunities for cultivating merit,
Which is why they are inferior to this land.
Why?
In pure lands, the seven treasures are abundant,
So there is no need for giving alms to help the poor.
In pure lands, the monastic discipline is perfectly pure,
So there is no need for upholding precepts to help those who violate prohibitions.
In pure lands, there is no humiliation and no need for patience.
In defiled lands, nothing is not humiliation.
To be able to be patient in humiliation
Surpasses other lands.
In pure lands, diligence is like saving one's head from fire,
So there is no need for strenuous effort to help the lazy.
People in pure lands
Enter the stream of Dharma,

So there is no need for tranquil meditation to help a distracted mind.
In pure lands, wisdom is bright and full,
So there is no need for eloquent speech and skillful explanations to help the foolish.
Furthermore, people in pure lands

But the power of great vows is inferior to that in defiled lands.
The four ways of embracing and the four immeasurables are similarly useless.
Because pure lands are joyful,
The heart to save from suffering is weak.
Because defiled lands are full of suffering,
The heart to advance in goodness is strong.

Regarding dedication (Huíxiàng),
It means non-attachment.
Originally, all sentient beings cultivate myriad practices,
Sacrificing body, life, and wealth.
The reason they do not attain liberation from transmigration
Is entirely due to their attachment to karmic rewards, unable to relinquish them.
If one can avoid clinging to one's mind,
Cultivating and embracing deliverance,
Whatever small merits one has, dedicating them to all sentient beings towards the Buddha path,
Then one will no longer be attached to karmic rewards.
And thus, one will be thoroughly liberated from transmigration.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
“Practicing as taught,
Dedication is of great benefit.”
Therefore, all good deeds performed
Should be dedicated,
And sentient beings should also be exhorted not to be attached to karmic rewards.
Why?
This very physical form is the root of karmic rewards.
Though we nourish, adorn, and embellish it all day long,
It will inevitably die; cherishing it is in vain.
Only the utterly ignorant would crave and love this body.
Those with a little wisdom,
How could they not be repulsed by it at all times?
Therefore, the wise pat their chests and speak from their hearts,
Not allowing attachment to perpetuate transmigration.

To all Buddhas and holy ones, I declare:
From this life backward to beginningless time,

From early childhood, I harbored a heart greedy for desires.
I knew not compassion and could not discern karmic retribution.
I believed that furry beasts and scaled creatures were rightly for the kitchen.
There was no sense of connection, nor was there any room for compassion.
Chopping in the morning, roasting in the evening, month after month, year after year.
Filling my belly and stomach, nothing else could satisfy.
In the past, when I was young and naive, my spirit was undeveloped.
In my playful wanderings, I wantonly committed atrocities.
Creeping creatures, flying creatures, and swimming creatures — none escaped being brought to the chopping board.
If I happened to encounter them, I would cruelly capture and kill them.
Recalling them now, the variety of species was truly abundant.

I loved books and records,

Dividing peaches and cut sleeves were also quite frequent.

My aspirations have known both sadness and joy, a nature commonly endowed.
Shifting anger and excessive righteousness sometimes occurred.
Stern looks and harsh words were unavoidable daily.
Moreover, my words and actions were jesting, never carefully examined.
Transgressions arose as soon as they were touched, falling into oblivion without record.
All day long, I was troubled and did not cease until dusk.
The dull and confused karmic fruits to come will be generated from this.
The previous thought barely vanished, and the next thought arose again.
A foot of waves ceaselessly, an inch of time rushes by.

Now, before the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times, and before the present Saṅgha and great assembly,

The evil deeds committed in the past were created by the mind.

If one does not base it on the ultimate truth to empty and extinguish existence,

Now, by arousing this shame and repentance, I grind away the past defilements.
When defilements are removed, emptiness becomes inherent nature.
Since its nature is empty, the sins have no place to cling.
Spreading hair and prostrating, seen and unseen beings bear witness.
This thought, once formed, will continue ceaselessly.
Polishing daily, shining yearly, without end from life to life,

Moreover, the evil inflicted upon me

If I do not extinguish this strong causal link, future evils will be met again.
Now I shall cut it off completely and forever cease future conditions.
The Way is everywhere.
If there is a cause, there is a response.
May this sincerity of today be conveyed to all.
